paragraphs: Let \(G\) be a grid diagram and \(\mathcal R=\mathbb F_2[[U_1,\ldots,U_n]]\). The ordinary minus complex \(\mathbf A^-(G,s)\) is the part of \(C^-(G)\) with Alexander filtrations \(A_i\le s_i\). Section 2.2 gives the intermediate complex the filtrations \(\mathfrak F_i(x)=-A_i(x)\), \(\mathfrak F_i(U_{i,1})=-1\), and \(\mathfrak F_i(V_{i,j})=1\) for \(j\ge2\), with other variables of filtration zero. On the printed part \(\mathfrak F_i\le s_i\), the asserted \(\mathcal R\)-linear resolution map sends a monomial without \(Y\)-factors to \[\widetilde P\!\left(\prod_{(i,j)\in J}V_{i,j}^{n_{i,j}}x\right)=\prod_i U_{i,1}^{A_i(x)-s_i-\sum_{j=2}^{p_i}n_{i,j}}\prod_{(i,j)\in J}U_{i,j}^{n_{i,j}}x,\qquad J=\{(i,j):1\le i\le\ell,\ 2\le j\le p_i\}.\] The claim includes that this formula lands in the ordinary minus complex over \(\mathcal R\).

For a general hyperbox of chain complexes with size vector \(\mathbf d\), Section 2.1 imposes the local-map relations (1) only for displacements \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^n\). It then asserts, before compression, that the sum of all local maps defines a differential on the uncompressed total space \[C_* = \bigoplus_{\varepsilon\in E(\mathbf d)}C^\varepsilon_{*+\|\varepsilon\|};\] in particular this sum is required to square to zero.

Let \(\vec L\subset S^3\) be an oriented link with integral framing \(\Lambda\), let \(G\) be a sparse grid diagram for the link with at least one free marking, and fix a Spin\(^c\) structure \(\mathfrak u\) on \(S^3_\Lambda(L)\) and a formal complex structure \(\mathfrak c\) on \(G\). The proof of Theorem 1.2 asserts that the completed minus surgery complex \(\mathcal C^-(G,\Lambda,\mathfrak u,\mathfrak c)\), an infinite direct product of modules over a power-series ring computing completed minus Heegaard Floer homology over \(\mathbb F_2[[U]]\), can be replaced by a quasi-isomorphic complex of finite total dimension over \(\mathbb F_2\) using the cited vertical and horizontal truncations. This assertion is made for the completed complex itself, without a restriction to one grading or a finite quotient.

Let \(K_v/\mathbb Q_p\) be finite, let \(Y/K_v\) be smooth and geometrically connected, and fix \(y_0\in Y(K_v)\). Let \((\mathcal E,\nabla,F^\bullet)\) be an algebraic vector bundle of rank \(m\) with flat connection and an exhaustive separated decreasing filtration whose graded pieces are vector bundles. On a sufficiently small admissible neighborhood \(U\) with \(H^0_{\mathrm{dR}}(U/K_v)=K_v\), suppose \(\mathcal E\) has a full horizontal basis. Definition 3.1 (Article PDF pages 15–16) defines the period map \(\Phi:U\to\mathcal G_{y_0}^{\mathrm{an}}\) by pulling \(F^\bullet\mathcal E\) back along the horizontal transport \(T^\nabla:\mathcal O_U\otimes_{K_v}\mathcal E_{y_0}\to\mathcal E|_U\), which is the identity at \(y_0\).

After shrinking and choosing a frame with \(F^i\mathcal E\) spanned by the first \(m_i=\operatorname{rank}F^i\mathcal E\) basis vectors, write \(\nabla=d+\omega\). In local parameters \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_m(K_v[[t_1,\ldots,t_n]])\) be the unique solution of \[dT=-\omega T,\qquad T(0)=I_m.\] Equation (5.1) and the construction on PDF pages 40–41 define \(\widehat\Phi\) by the flag whose \(i\)-th subspace is spanned by the first \(m_i\) columns of \(T\).

The asserted identification is that \(\widehat\Phi\) is the Taylor expansion of the pullback period map \(\Phi\). Lemma 5.5 therefore identifies the scheme-theoretic image of this column-defined \(\widehat\Phi\) with the Zariski closure of \(\Phi(U)\). After any chosen embedding \(\iota:K_v\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), Lemma 5.6 makes the analogous identification for the complex period map and \(\widehat\Phi_{\mathbb C}\). The direction of transport and the use of columns of \(T\) are part of the claim being checked.

Let \(K\) be the number field of Section 6, let \(v\mid p\) be a self-conjugate place, and let \((A,V)\) be a symplectic pair of continuous \(G_K\)-representations as in Definitions 4.3–4.4: \(A\) is a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_p\)-algebra, \(V\) is a locally free \(A\)-module of rank \(2d>0\), and \(V\) has a perfect alternating \(A\)-bilinear pairing into a free rank-one \(A\)-module, compatible with the \(G_K\)-actions. Suppose that \(V\) is de Rham at the places above \(p\), has Hodge–Tate weights in \(\{0,1\}\) at \(v\), and is unramified and pure of weight one outside a finite set. No split or reduced hypothesis on \(A\) is stated.

Put \(\Sigma=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_p\text{-alg}}(A,\mathbb Q_p)\). For \(\psi\in\Sigma\), write \(G_\psi\) for its stabilizer, \(G_{w_\psi}=G_v\cap G_\psi\), and \(V_\psi=V\otimes_{A,\psi}\mathbb Q_p\). Proposition 6.7 asserts that at least one of the following holds: (a) some \(\psi\) satisfies \([G_v:G_{w_\psi}]\ge4\) and \(V_\psi\) is GSp-irreducible as a symplectic \(G_\psi\)-representation; (b) some such \(\psi\) admits a nonzero isotropic \(G_\psi\)-subrepresentation \(W\subseteq V_\psi\) with \[\dim_{L_{w_\psi}}F^1D_{\mathrm{dR},w_\psi}(W)\ge\tfrac12\dim_{\mathbb Q_p}W;\] or (c) \[\#\{\psi\in\Sigma:[G_v:G_{w_\psi}]<4\}\ge\frac{\dim_{\mathbb Q_p}A}{d+1}.\] Here \(L_{w_\psi}\) is the local field corresponding to \(G_{w_\psi}\).

Let \(N\ge3\) and let \(u\) be an \(x_N\)-monotone global obstacle solution in the sense of Definition 2.8: \(u\ge0\), \(\Delta u=\chi_{\{u>0\}}\), the coincidence set \(\mathcal C=\{u=0\}\) has nonempty interior and lies in \(\{x_N\ge0\}\) with \(0\in\partial\mathcal C\), \(\partial_Nu\le0\), and its quadratic blow-down is \(p(x')=\tfrac12x'{}^TQx'\) with \(Q\) positive definite and \(\operatorname{tr}Q=1\). For \(0<\delta<1\), choose \(\widehat r>1\) so that the far part of \(\mathcal C\) lies in \(T_\delta=\{(y',t):t\ge0,\ |y'|^2<t^{1+\delta}\}\). Writing \(a=(N-1)(1+\delta)/2\), equations (3.5)–(3.6) assert, for \(|x|>\widehat r\), \[\int_{\widehat r}^{2|x|}t^{a+2-N}\,dt\le C(1+|x|)^{a+3-N},\qquad \int_{\widehat r}^{2|x|}t^{a+1-N}\,dt\le C(1+|x|)^{a+2-N},\] where \(C\) may depend on the fixed parameters but not on \(x\).

The displayed estimates do not separate zero or negative values of the integrated exponent. In the \(N\ge4\) part of Proposition 4.1, the paper invokes them with \(\delta=1/3\) to obtain \(V_{\mathcal C}(x)\ge-C(1+|x|)\) for the generalized Newtonian potential \(V_{\mathcal C}\) defined in Section 3.

Fix \(N\ge3\) and a quadratic form \(p(x')=\tfrac12x'{}^TQx'\) on \(\mathbb R^{N-1}\), where \(Q\) is symmetric positive definite and has trace one, as in Definition 2.8(iv). Lemma 6.1 asserts that there is a unique ellipsoid \(E'=\{y':\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}y_i^2/a_i^2\le1\}\), with \(a_i>0\) in the chosen diagonal coordinates, for which \(P=\{(y',y_N):y_N\ge0,\ y'\in\sqrt{y_N}\,E'\}\) is the coincidence set of a global nonnegative solution \(u_P\) of \(\Delta u_P=\chi_{\{u_P>0\}}\) satisfying \(u_P(rx)/r^2\to p(x')\) in \(C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) for every \(0<\alpha<1\). No volume or semiaxis normalization of \(E'\) is imposed.

The lemma also states that, for each \(\gamma>0\), the scaled paraboloid \(\gamma P\) corresponds to \(u_{\gamma P}(x)=\gamma^2u_P(x/\gamma)\), with the same quadratic blow-down and the expansion \(u_{\gamma P}=p+V_{\gamma P}\). Its proof begins by asserting uniqueness of an ellipsoid whose Newtonian potential on its interior is a constant minus \(p\).

Lemma 2.3 is stated for a global nonnegative solution \(u\) of the obstacle equation \(\Delta u=\chi_{\{u>0\}}\). It asserts that the quadratic blow-down has one of two forms: a half-space solution or a quadratic form whose Hessian has trace one. The stated domain does not exclude the identically zero solution.

Let \(k\ge1\) be an integer and let \(N\) be the quotient of \(S^3\times S^3\) by the free left \((1,k)\)-Hopf circle action. Lemma 6.3 considers the displayed smooth positive-Ricci deformation \(g_t\), \(0\le t\le1/2\), beginning at the product metric, with quotient metrics \(h_t\). In the left-invariant frame \(U_i,V_i\), the orthonormal frame is \[T_t=f_t^{-1}(U_1+kV_1),\quad X_2=U_2,\quad X_3=U_3,\quad W_1=a_t^{-1}(-kU_1+V_1),\quad W_2=(a_tb_t)^{-1}V_2,\quad W_3=(a_tb_t)^{-1}V_3,\] where \(a_t,b_t,f_t>0\) are the path functions constructed in the lemma and are constant near the endpoints.

Part (ii) asserts that \(\pi_{(1,k)}:(S^3\times S^3,g_t)\to(N,h_t)\) remains a Riemannian principal circle bundle with totally geodesic fibres and the constant connection \[\eta_t=\eta_0=\frac{U_1^*+kV_1^*}{1+k^2}.\] This fixed connection is claimed to be both Yang–Mills and in Coulomb gauge for every \(t\). In particular, with \(\omega_t=d\eta_t\), equations (74)–(75) assert \(\operatorname{div}_{h_t}\omega_t=0\) and hence \(\operatorname{Ric}_{g_t}(T_t,H)=0\) for every horizontal \(H\), including \(H=W_1\). Section 6.6 then claims that the family obtained using harmonic curvature representatives agrees with this earlier family on \(0\le t\le1/2\).

Let \(g(r)\) be the smooth family of metrics on the six-dimensional cross section \(S^3\times S^3\) used in Section 7.5, assume that its volume form is independent of \(r\), and let \(h(r)>0\). For the neck metric \(G=dr^2+h(r)^2g(r)\), equation (128) asserts the tangential identity \[\operatorname{Ric}^{G}_{ij}=\operatorname{Ric}^{g}_{ij}+h^2\!\left(-\frac{h^{\prime\prime}}h-5\left(\frac{h^{\prime}}h\right)^2\right)g_{ij}-\frac{7h^{\prime}}{2h}g^{\prime}_{ij}+\frac12g^{ab}g^{\prime}_{ai}g^{\prime}_{bj},\] where primes denote differentiation in \(r\) and repeated indices are summed. The printed formula contains no \(g^{\prime\prime}_{ij}\) term.

This identity is used for \(g(r)=\widetilde g_{t(r)}\), where \(\widetilde g_t\) is the constant-volume family of Lemma 7.2 with \(\operatorname{Ric}_{\widetilde g_t}>6\), to obtain the lower bound (135) from bounds on \(g^{\prime}\) and \(\nabla g^{\prime}\). Thus the local assertion under review is the stated Ricci formula under the constant-volume hypothesis, together with that use of it.

In the proof of Lemma 7.2, let \(\widehat g_r\), \(1/3\le r\le2/3\), be the smooth positive-Ricci, \((1,k)\)-circle-invariant family from Theorem 6.1, reparametrized from the standard product metric to its pullback by the specified end diffeomorphism. Equations (118)–(119) set \[\widetilde g_r=a_r\varphi_r^*\widehat g_r,\qquad a_r=\widetilde a\,\operatorname{Vol}(\widehat g_r)^{-1/6},\] with \(\widetilde a>0\) small enough that \(\operatorname{Ric}_{a_r\widehat g_r}>6\), and assert that \(\operatorname{Vol}(a_r\widehat g_r)\) is constant in \(r\). Here the cross section has dimension six and \(a_r\) multiplies the metric itself.

The product-model assertion in Section 2.2.1 and Propositions 3.1(4) and 5.1(4) states that the weighted circle action \(e^{i\theta}\cdot(u,v)=(e^{ia\theta}u,e^{ib\theta}v)\) on \(S^3\times\mathbb R^4\) is free when the integer weights \(a,b\) are coprime and \(a\ne0\). This freeness claim includes the zero section \(S^3\times\{0\}\).

Let \((M,p)\) be the manifold constructed in Section 2.2, with the construction scales \(r_j\to\infty\) and integer indices \(k_j\). The final paragraph of that section asserts that every pointed tangent at infinity obtained as a subsequential limit of \((M,s_j^{-2}g,p)\), for \(s_j\to\infty\), is a metric cone, although its basepoint need not be the cone vertex. The assertion covers the choices with unbounded \(k_j\) allowed by the construction.

At the specific scales \(s_j=r_j\), the same section states that a subsequence with \(k_j\to\infty\) has equivariant covering limit \((\mathbb R^4,0,\mathbb Z)\), with \(\mathbb Z\) acting by a unit translation, and quotient limit \(\mathbb R^3\times S^1\), as in equation (22). Example 2.3 permits such index sequences for the construction with \(\Gamma=\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\).

Equation (173) and the four-generator assertion are stated for the full group \(\operatorname{Diff}(S^3\times S^3)\): the induced action on \(H_3(S^3\times S^3;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2\) is claimed to have image in \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\), and the four displayed determinant-one maps are claimed to generate every component. No orientation-preserving restriction is included in that statement.

For a transcendental real number \(\xi\) and a positive integer \(n\), the abstract calls \(\omega_n^*(\xi)\) the infimum of the exponents \(\omega\) for which infinitely many algebraic numbers \(\alpha\) of degree at most \(n\) satisfy \(|\xi-\alpha|\le H(\alpha)^{-\omega-1}\), where \(H(\alpha)\) is the naive height. In contrast, the definition accompanying (1.2) takes the supremum of the positive real exponents satisfying \(0<|\xi-\alpha|\le H(\alpha)^{-\omega-1}\). The assertion examined here is the extremum in the abstract, in this stated approximation problem.

For a permutation group \(G\le S_n\), let \(N_n(G,H)\) count the monic integer polynomials \(x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n\) with \(\max_i|a_i|\le H\) whose Galois group is isomorphic to \(G\) as a permutation group. Let \(F_n(G,X)\) count degree-\(n\) number fields with that group and absolute discriminant at most \(X\), and let \(a(G)>0\) satisfy \(F_n(G,X)=O(X^{a(G)})\). Write \(k=\operatorname{ind}(G)=\min_{g\ne1}(n-\#\{\text{orbits of }g\})\), \(u=1/[n(n-1)]\) for primitive \(G\) and \(u=0\) otherwise, and let \(c=q(k,n-k)\) be the number of partitions of \(k\) into at most \(n-k\) parts.

Theorem 2 is stated for every permutation group \(G\le S_n\) and asserts \[N_n(G,H)=O\!\left(\min\left\{H^{n+1-k}+H^{\,n-\frac{(n-1)(1-1/k)}{a(G)+1-1/k-u}}(\log H)^c,\ H^{(2n-2)(a(G)-u)+1}(\log H)^{n-1}\right\}\right).\] This includes intransitive groups, without an irreducibility restriction on the polynomials. In Section 6 the algebra \(K_f=\mathbb Q[x]/(f)\) is allowed to be étale, yet its number is bounded using the number-field exponent \(a(G)\) in (23).

Let \(G\le S_n\) be a regular permutation group of order \(n\). With \(N_n(G,H)\) denoting the number of monic degree-\(n\) integer polynomials of coefficient height at most \(H\) and permutation Galois group \(G\), Corollary 6 asserts \[N_n(G,H)=O\!\left(H^{3n/11+1.164}\right).\] The corollary states no lower-degree restriction. Its proof substitutes the field-counting exponent \(a(G)=3/8+\varepsilon\), for arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(\operatorname{ind}(G)=(p-1)n/p\), where \(p\) is the smallest prime divisor of \(n\), into Theorem 2.

Let \(G\le S_k\), with \(k\le9\), and let \(M_{11}\) be the Mathieu group in its natural action on eleven letters. The direct product \(G\times M_{11}\) acts on disjoint sets of \(k\) and eleven letters. Corollary 8 asserts that the number of monic degree-\(k+11\) integer polynomials of coefficient height at most \(H\) and this permutation Galois group satisfies \[N_{k+11}(G\times M_{11},H)=O(H^{8.686}).\] The stated group range includes \(G=S_k\), and the degree range includes \(k=9\).

Section 5 counts irreducible monic integer polynomials of degree \(n\) and coefficient height at most \(H\) whose Galois group is primitive and different from \(S_n\). For \(K_f=\mathbb Q[x]/(f)\), write \(C\) for the product of its ramified primes and \(D=|\operatorname{Disc}(K_f)|\). The proof permits the explicit choice \(\delta=1/(2n)\). In Case II, where \(C\le H^{1+\delta}\) and \(D\le H^{2+2\delta}\), it asserts \[H^{1+(2+2\delta)(a-u)}(\log H)^{n-1}=O(H^{n-1}),\qquad u=\frac1{n(n-1)},\] using \(a=(n+2)/4\) for \(n\ge6\) and \(a=1\) for \(n=4,5\).

In Section 6, the monic-polynomial version of Case I permits every \(0<\delta<1/(n-1)\) and claims the bound \(O(c^{\omega(D)}H^n/D)\) for the relevant congruence conditions whenever \(C<H^{1+\delta}\). It invokes Proposition 26, whereas the stated monic estimate, Corollary 33, requires \(0<\delta<1/(2n-1)\). These are the numerical parameter choices whose use is at issue.

In Theorem 7, a permutation group on \(n=n_1+\cdots+n_k\) letters is written as a subdirect product of transitive groups \(G_i\) acting on its orbits. Suppose its factor counts satisfy \(N_{n_i}(G_i,T)=O(T^{\alpha_i}(\log T)^{\beta_i})\), with the factors ordered so that \(\alpha_1\le\cdots\le\alpha_k\). Here height is \(H(f)=\max_i|a_i|\) for a monic integer polynomial. In the proof, the number \(M_{n_1}(G_1,H_1)\) of the first-factor polynomials of exact height \(H_1\) is bounded by \[M_{n_1}(G_1,H_1)=O\!\left(H_1^{\alpha_1-1}(\log H_1)^{\beta_1}\right).\] This individual-shell estimate is inferred from the cumulative bound on \(N_{n_1}(G_1,T)\), without a separate shell-counting or regularity hypothesis.

For a primitive permutation group \(G\le S_n\) different from \(A_n\) and \(S_n\), Corollary 3(a) asserts \(N_n(G,H)=O(H^{n-3})\) for \(n\ge28\) and \(N_n(G,H)=O(H^{n-7/2})\) for \(n\ge53\). In the first estimate its proof uses \(\operatorname{ind}(G)\ge5\); for elemental groups in the second it uses \(\operatorname{ind}(G)\ge13\). With \(u=1/[n(n-1)]\) and arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon>0\), the claimed power savings from the second term of Theorem 2 are \[s(n,k,\varepsilon)=\frac{(n-1)(1-1/k)}{(n+2)/4-u+\varepsilon},\] using \(k=5\) at the threshold \(n=28\), and \(k=13\) at \(n=53\), respectively.

Separately, the optimization of Theorem 2 writes \(k=\operatorname{ind}(G)\), \(c=q(k,n-k)\), and chooses any valid field-counting exponent \(a=a(G)\). In the regime \(a>(n-k+2/n)/(2n-2)\), the logarithmic exponent is declared to satisfy \[b=(c-1)-(c-n)\frac{1-1/k}{a+1-1/k-u}<c.\] The finding examines these displayed arithmetic comparisons, including their threshold values.

In the exceptional finite groups of Lie type considered in Section 9.2, Theorem 9.3 requires, for a block \(b\) with defect group \(P\), a proper subgroup \(M<G\) that contains \(N_G(P)\) and is stable under every element of \(\operatorname{Aut}(G)_b\), the stabilizer of the block. This is the printed subgroup hypothesis before the additional character-theoretic conditions (i)–(v).

For the quasi-isolated 2-blocks of Theorem 10.17 with noncyclic outer stabilizer and noncentral defect, Theorem 11.3 chooses \(M=N_G(L)\), where \(L\) is the associated split Levi subgroup, and asserts that Lemma 6.6 verifies this hypothesis. Thus the application asserts stability under the full block stabilizer \(\operatorname{Aut}(G)_b\); the asserted stabilizer is not restricted to automorphisms preserving the chosen defect group. The finding concerns this subgroup requirement and its application, rather than a reformulation of all character conditions.

In the \(d=1_\varepsilon\) branch of the proof of Lemma 12.6, take the Levi subgroup \(L_{(d)}\), its normalizer quotient \(W_{(d)}\cong S_3\), and a character \(\psi\) in the stated transversal of \(\mathcal E_2(L_{(d)},s)^{W_2}\). The proof selects a height-zero constituent \(\psi_0\) on \(L_0=[L_{(d)},L_{(d)}]\cong\mathrm{SL}_3(q)\times\mathrm{SL}_3(q)\) with the specified stabilizer property. The order-three subgroup of \(W_{(d)}\) centralizes \(L_0\), while involutions interchange its two simple factors.

The asserted local extension step is that this \(\psi_0\) extends to a representation of \(L_0\rtimes W_{(d)}\) whose kernel contains all of \(W_{(d)}\). It is then multiplied by \(\Gamma(\nu)\), where \(\nu\) is the central character below \(\psi\), to construct the claimed extension on \(L_0V_{(d)}\). No triviality hypothesis on \(\psi_0\) on the two simple factors is imposed in this step.

Let \(\mathbf G\) be a connected reductive group with Frobenius endomorphism \(F\), put \(G=\mathbf G^F\), and suppose the group \(Z_F\) of \(F\)-coinvariants of \(Z(\mathbf G)/Z(\mathbf G)^\circ\) is cyclic. For every semisimple \(s\in(\mathbf G^*)^F\), put \(A(s)=C_{\mathbf G^*}(s)/C_{\mathbf G^*}(s)^\circ\), with the finite-group actions used in Section 1. Theorem 1.4(a) asserts a bijection between the \(Z_F\)-orbits in \(\mathcal E(G,s)\) and the corresponding \(A(s)\)-orbits of unipotent characters of the connected centralizer, and asserts that corresponding orbits have equal cardinality.

For a regular embedding \(\mathbf G\hookrightarrow\widetilde{\mathbf G}\), choose \(\widetilde\chi\) above \(\chi\), with Jordan correspondents \(\widetilde\psi\) and \(\psi\). If \(r\) is the size of the associated unipotent-character orbit and \(a=|A(s)|\), the proof uses \[\chi(1)=\widetilde\chi(1)/r,\qquad \psi(1)=a\widetilde\psi(1)/r.\] These are the orbit-size and Clifford-degree assertions tested by the finding.

Let \(H\) be a finite group and \(A\trianglelefteq H\) an abelian normal subgroup. An element \(h\) acts quadratically on \(A\) when \([h,[h,A]]=1\), equivalently \((h-1)^2=0\) on \(A\). Proposition 4.2 asserts that \(A\) is the unique maximal abelian normal subgroup of \(H\) if and only if no nonidentity coset in \(H/A\) acts quadratically on \(A\).

Under the additional assumption that \(H/A\) is a 2-group, Lemma 4.4 asserts that \(H\) is Cabanes unless there exists an actual involution \(h\in H\setminus A\) such that \((hth^{-1}t^{-1})^2=1\) for every \(t\in A\). The lemma asks for an element of order two in \(H\), not merely a coset of order two in the quotient.

In Section 10.3, let \(\mathbf G\) be the simply connected group of type \(E_6\) over the algebraic closure of its defining field, with the Chevalley torus convention of Section 10.2. Use the displayed affine Dynkin labeling and \(\alpha_0=-\widetilde\alpha\), the negative highest root. For the semisimple parameter with centralizer type \(A_2^3.3\), the three \(A_2\) root subgroups \(G_1,G_2,G_3\cong\mathrm{SL}_3\) have respective bases \(\{\alpha_1,\alpha_3\}\), \(\{\alpha_5,\alpha_6\}\), and \(\{\alpha_0,\alpha_2\}\). The text asserts that there exists an \(F\)-stable central subgroup \(Z\) of order three such that \[G_i\cap G_j=Z\quad\text{for every }i\ne j.\] This is a claim about each pairwise intersection of the algebraic root subgroups, prior to taking rational points.

Let \(H_0\trianglelefteq H\) be a normal subgroup of a finite group, let \(U\le H_0\) satisfy \(Z(U)\cong C_3\) and \(Z(U)\le Z(H)\), and let \(Z\le Z(H)\). For \(\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}(H)\), write \(\operatorname{Res}^H_U\chi=\sum_{\phi\in\operatorname{Irr}(U)}a_\phi\phi\). Lemma 12.9(a) asserts, for every constituent with \(a_\phi\ne0\), \[\bigl(\operatorname{Res}^{U}_{Z(U)}\phi\bigr)\phi(1)=\bigl(\operatorname{Res}^{H}_{Z(U)}\chi\bigr)\chi(1).\] Part (b) uses the analogous multiplication by degrees in the central restriction condition for the extension to \(UZ\). Neither multiplicity-free restriction nor equality of the degrees \(\phi(1)\) and \(\chi(1)\) is assumed.

Let \(G=\mathbf G^F\) be a finite reductive group in defining characteristic \(p\), let \(\ell\ne p\) be prime, and let \(s\) be a semisimple element of \(\ell'\)-order in its dual finite group \(G^*\). Write \(C_{G^*}(s)_\ell\) for the elements of \(\ell\)-power order in the centralizer of \(s\). The first display of Section 1.6 defines \[\mathcal E_\ell(G,s)=\bigcup_{t\in C_{G^*}(s)_\ell}\mathcal E(G,t),\] and states that this is a union of \(\ell\)-blocks. The displayed summands contain \(t\) alone and omit the fixed parameter \(s\); this is the definition examined by the finding.

Let \(N\) be a closed, connected, oriented Riemannian \(n\)-manifold, \(n\ge2\), which is not a rational homology sphere. In Proposition 5.1, \(N\) is the target of a sequence \(f_j:B_2^n\to N\) of nonconstant \(K\)-quasiregular maps with a fixed doubling constant \(D>1\), \(A(f_j)=\int_{B_1^n}f_j^*\operatorname{vol}_N\to\infty\), and a Sobolev–Poincaré limit for the normalized pullbacks. For arbitrary classes \(c_i\in H^{k_i}_{\mathrm{dR}}(N)\) with \(k_i>0\) and \(k_1+k_2=n\), let \(h(c_i)\) be their harmonic representatives and \(I=\int_Nc_1\wedge c_2\). The proof asserts the existence of \(\tau\in\Omega^{n-1}(N)\) satisfying \[\operatorname{vol}(N)h(c_1)\wedge h(c_2)=I\bigl(\operatorname{vol}_N+d\tau\bigr).\] No nonzero-pairing assumption \(I\ne0\) is made for these classes.

A connected oriented Riemannian four-manifold \(X\) is quasiregularly elliptic if it admits a nonconstant continuous map \(f:\mathbb R^4\to X\) in \(W^{1,4}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) satisfying \(\|Df\|^4\le KJ_f\) almost everywhere for some \(K\ge1\). Corollary 1.2 asserts that a given closed simply connected smooth Riemannian four-manifold is quasiregularly elliptic if and only if it is homeomorphic to one of \[\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\quad\text{or}\quad\#_j\mathbb{CP}^2\#_i\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^{2},\qquad k,j,i\in\{0,1,2,3\},\] with the zero-summand case interpreted as \(S^4\). Thus the sufficiency assertion applies to the given smooth structure on \(X\), whereas the preceding construction uses the listed models with their standard compatible PL and smooth structures.

Fix a nonidentity rotation \(Q\in\mathrm{SO}(n)\), a geodesic \(Q_t\) from the identity to \(Q\), and the standard covering \(\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n\). Example 7.3 declares the balls \(B_j=B(2^je_1,j)=B(a_j,r_j)\), for every integer \(j\ge1\), mutually disjoint. It defines \(h_Q\) to be the identity off their union, the translated rotation \(a_j+Q(x-a_j)\) on \(B(a_j,r_j/2)\), and the radial interpolation \(a_j+Q_{2-2|x-a_j|/r_j}(x-a_j)\) on the intervening annulus, and sets \(f=\pi\circ h_Q\).

For \(f_{a,r}:B_2^n\to\mathbb T^n\) defined by \(f_{a,r}(x)=f(rx+a)\), the example claims that the negative zooms \(f_{-je_1,j}\) yield the normalized pullback limit \(L_\pi\), whereas the positive zooms \(f_{a_j,r_j/2}\) yield \(Q^*L_\pi\ne L_\pi\). Here \(L_\pi\) is the constant normalized cohomological pullback of the standard covering in Example 7.2. The claimed radius of the positive zoom is \(r_j/2\) on the full domain \(B_2^n\).

Lemma 6.1 (Article PDF page 22) assumes that \(F(D^2u,Du,u,x)=0\) is a fully nonlinear elliptic equation on \(B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^n\), with \(F\) continuous in all variables, and that viscosity solutions \(u_k\) converge uniformly to \(u\). No uniform-ellipticity bound or monotonicity condition in the zero-order argument \(u\) is imposed by this lemma. Its proof takes \(x_0\in B_1\), \(0<r<\operatorname{dist}(x_0,\partial B_1)\), and a smooth function \(Q\ge u\) on \(B_r(x_0)\) with \(Q(x_0)=u(x_0)\).

For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), set \(Q_\varepsilon(x)=Q(x)+\varepsilon|x-x_0|^2-\varepsilon^4\), and take \(k=k(\varepsilon)\) large enough that \(u_k-Q_\varepsilon\) has a positive maximum \(m_\varepsilon\) at an interior point \(x_\varepsilon\in B_{\varepsilon/2}(x_0)\). The specific inference under examination is \[F\!\left(D^2Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),DQ_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),x_\varepsilon\right)\ge0.\] It uses \(Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)\) as the zero-order input despite the strictly positive contact-value difference \(u_k(x_\varepsilon)-Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)=m_\varepsilon\). The finding targets this step, rather than the general stability conclusion of the lemma.

Let \(E/F\) be the quadratic number-field extension in Section 11, \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n\times\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}\), and \(G'=\operatorname{Res}_{E/F}\mathrm{GL}_n\times\operatorname{Res}_{E/F}\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}\). Let \(a,b\) be the matching global \(Z\)-regular semisimple points of Proposition 11.4. Choose \(S\) as in that proof so that, for every finite place \(v\notin S\), \(a\in K_v\), \(b\in K_v'\), and the test functions are the unit spherical functions. For the unitary relative orbital integral using the standard Hermitian pair \((w_n,w_{n+1})\), Lemma 11.5 asserts, for every \(z=(z_1I_n,z_2I_{n+1})\in Z_{G'}(F_v)\), \[\operatorname{Orb}(\mathbf1_{K_v'},bz)\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z\in Z_{G'}(\mathcal O_v).\] The \(Z\)-regularity invoked in its proof requires the two invariants \(c_1^{w_n,w_{n+1}}(b)\) and \(c_{2n+1}^{w_n,w_{n+1}}(b)\) to be nonzero; it does not require them to be units.

In the unramified extension \(E/F\) of nonarchimedean local fields in Section 10.2, let \(G(F)=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\times\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}(F)\), \(G'(F)=\mathrm{GL}_n(E)\times\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}(E)\), and let \(K'\) be its standard hyperspecial compact subgroup. Let \(f'\in\mathcal H_{K'}(G'(F))\), and let \((x,y)\) be any pair in the full rational orbit \(G'(F)*(w_n,w_{n+1})\) for the action on Hermitian forms. Lemma 10.6 asserts, for every representation \(\pi\) in its normalized-relative-character setup, \[J^{x,y,\natural}_{\operatorname{BC}(\pi)}(f')=I^\natural_\pi(\operatorname{BC}(f')).\] Here the spherical base-change map is characterized by equality of its Satake eigenvalue at \(\pi\) with that of \(f'\) at \(\operatorname{BC}(\pi)\); the proof reduces to unramified \(\pi\).

The proof normalizes the spherical Whittaker vector so that the relevant normalized functionals have value one for every pair in that rational orbit. The cited Lemma 8.6, with odd residue characteristic, unramified extension and the stated unramified additive character, gives this value on the integral orbit \(X_j(\mathcal O_F)=\mathrm{GL}_j(\mathcal O_E)*w_j\). The original quantifier in Lemma 10.6 remains the full \(G'(F)\)-orbit.

Let \(E/F\) be the unramified quadratic extension of nonarchimedean local fields of characteristic zero used in Sections 2.4–3.3. Let \(V_n\) be the split Hermitian space, \(\Lambda_n\subset V_n\) its fixed self-dual lattice, and \(\tau\) the Hermitian adjoint. For \(x\in\mathrm{GL}_n(E)\) and \(T=xx^\tau\) in the indicated Hermitian space, put \(L=x^\tau\Lambda_n\), so that \(L^\vee=x^{-1}\Lambda_n\). The paragraph after (3.8) asserts \[T\text{ is integral}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subseteq\Lambda_n\subseteq L^\vee.\] Here integrality means preservation of \(\Lambda_n\); the intermediate lattice in the printed equivalence is the fixed \(\Lambda_n\), not an unspecified self-dual lattice.

For the nice formal schemes in the local trace construction, Theorem–Definition 3.4.13 defines the generic-fiber map by diagram (3.7), whose two left corners are \(E_C=(\widetilde{R^n\nu_*\widehat{\mathcal O}_X^+})_C\), whose upward left arrow is multiplication by \((1-\zeta_p)^n\), and whose bottom arrow is \((\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}\). Remark 3.4.15 identifies the resulting map with the inverse of Scholze's comparison. Theorem 3.5.2 requires the trace with generic fiber from Definition 3.4.14 and smooth-locus restriction from Definition 3.3.5, asserting that these two prescriptions agree on their overlap.

For the character spaces in the polystable tower construction, the paragraph after (4.6) and Lemma 4.2.15 assert that multiplication gives an \(\mathcal O_C\)-module isomorphism \[V_\chi\otimes_{\mathcal O_C}V_{\chi'}\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{\chi+\chi'}\] for every pair of characters, including rational characters at every finite tower level \(m\).

Theorem 1.3, pp. 4–5 (TeX lines 478–487), and Theorem 13.2, p. 84 (lines 5005–5032), prescribe the first component of the data as \[|\widehat\chi|(-1,v,\omega)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f_i(v,\omega)\] for arbitrary real \(\lambda_i,\lambda'_i\), not all zero, and assert injectivity of the pair of displayed initial-data components. The proof on pp. 84–85 chooses \(f_i\ge0\), supported on disjoint discs, with \(f_i\ge m_i a^{1/2}>0\) on a smaller ball. The \(C^0\) version on p. 87 replaces this lower bound by \(m_i g(v)^{1/2}a^{1/2}>0\) for every \(v>0\).

Write \(v=\underline u\), \(r=|u|\), and \(\mu=\mu^*\in(0,1)\). The introductory double-null gauge is \[g=-2\Omega^2(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)+h_{AB}(d\theta^A-d^A dv)(d\theta^B-d^B dv),\] with \(e_3=\Omega^{-1}\partial_u\), \(e_4=\Omega^{-1}(\partial_v+d^A\partial_A)\), and \(g(e_3,e_4)=-2\).

For the constructed MOTS graph \(u=-R(\omega,v)\), Proposition 12.4 and (12.5) assert spacelikeness under the stated additional smallness condition on \(v\partial_v f\). After obtaining \(R_v\ge(1-\mu)R/(2v)>0\), the proof identifies the induced metric components as \(g'_{AB}=h_{AB}\), \(g'_{Av}=2R_A\), and \(g'_{vv}=4R_v\).

Write \(v=\underline u\), \(r=|u|\), \(\mu=\mu^*\in(0,1)\), and \(k=\mu/(1-\mu)\). The prescribed spherical data at \(v=0\) have \(h=r^2\gamma_{\mathbb S^2}\), \(\Omega_0^2=r^k\), and \(\Omega^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\chi=2(1-\mu)/r\).

The second estimate in Proposition 4.3 asserts \[\sum_{i\le4}\|r^i\nabla^i(\Omega\operatorname{tr}\chi)\|_{L^2(S_{u,v})}\lesssim \frac{va\,\mathcal O^2}{r}.\] The asserted sum includes the derivative-zero term \(i=0\), without subtracting the spherical background expansion.

Write \(v=\underline u\), \(r=|u|\), and \(\mu=\mu^*\in(0,1)\). The introductory double-null gauge is \[g=-2\Omega^2(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)+h_{AB}(d\theta^A-d^A dv)(d\theta^B-d^B dv),\] with \(e_3=\Omega^{-1}\partial_u\), \(e_4=\Omega^{-1}(\partial_v+d^A\partial_A)\), and \(g(e_3,e_4)=-2\).

For the Einstein–massless-scalar system \(\operatorname{Ric}_{\alpha\beta}=\partial_\alpha\phi\,\partial_\beta\phi\) and \(\Box_g\phi=0\), the first line of (2.13) asserts a \(\nabla_3\alpha\) equation whose matter contribution is \[\left[\tfrac14(D_3\operatorname{Ric}_{44}-D_4\operatorname{Ric}_{43})+\tfrac16e_4\operatorname{Scal}\right]h_{AB}.\] Here \(\alpha_{AB}=W(e_A,e_4,e_B,e_4)\) is the trace-free extreme Weyl tensor.

For the unit group \(\Gamma\) in the CM construction and a free finite-index subgroup \(\Gamma'\), Proposition 2.27 asserts that the homological transfer \(H_{d-1}(\Gamma,\mathbb Z)\to H_{d-1}(\Gamma',\mathbb Z)\) is onto. It therefore chooses an integral preimage of a fundamental-cycle generator and requires evaluation after cohomological restriction to be \([\Gamma:\Gamma']\) times evaluation before restriction.

In Appendix A.2, an injective \(\Gamma\)-equivariant sheaf \(\mathcal I\) on \(X\) is asserted to descend to a flabby sheaf \(\widetilde{\mathcal I}\) on \(E\Gamma\times_\Gamma X\). The proof of (A.2.1) identifies its sections over an arbitrary open set with invariant sections of \(\mathcal I\) over the projection of that set to \(X\).

In Section 2.5, let \(A/R\) be the CM abelian scheme with bases and torsion-section data of Notation 1.18 and Section 2.4, and let \(\Gamma\) be the stated finite-index subgroup of CM units. Fix integral ideals \(\mathfrak f\) and \(\mathfrak c\ne\mathcal O_L\) with \((\mathfrak f,\mathfrak c)=1\), \(N\mathfrak c\in R^\times\), and \(D=A[\mathfrak c]\). Let \(x\in A[\mathfrak f](R)\cap U_D(R)\) be fixed by \(\Gamma\), and let \(f\in R[D]^{0,\Gamma}\). Write \([\mathfrak f]:A\to B=A(\mathfrak f^{-1})\). The construction does not assume \(N\mathfrak f\) invertible in \(R\), so this isogeny and its dual need not be étale.

For the admissible nonnegative multiindices \(\alpha,\beta\) of the Eisenstein–Kronecker construction, Proposition 2.31 asserts, after applying the natural map to \(R[1/N\mathfrak f]\), \[\operatorname{TSym}^{\alpha+\mathbf1}([\mathfrak f]^*)\bigl({}_{[\mathfrak f]}\operatorname{EK}^{\beta,\alpha}_{\Gamma,B}(f,x)\bigr)=\operatorname{TSym}^{\beta}([\mathfrak f]_\#)\bigl(\operatorname{EK}^{\beta,\alpha}_{\Gamma,A}(f,x)\bigr),\] in \(\operatorname{TSym}^{\alpha+\mathbf1}(\omega_{A/R})\otimes_R\operatorname{TSym}^{\beta}(\omega_{B^\vee/R})\otimes_RR[1/N\mathfrak f]\). The printed comparison has no isogeny-degree factor, including in its zero-moment specialization.

Use the complex uniformization \(A(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C^\Sigma/\Lambda\), a torsion-free unit subgroup \(\Gamma\), and the \(\Gamma\)-invariant residue function \(f:\mathfrak c^{-1}\Lambda/\Lambda\to\mathbb C\) with \(\sum_tf(t)=0\) of Sections 3.4–3.5. Definitions 3.15 and 3.18 form the explicit currents \(\varphi^{(n)}=\sum_{b=0}^n\sum_{j=0}^{2d}\varphi^{(b,j)}_{b+j+1}\) using the factor \((-1)^j\) in (3.4.1). Theorem 3.20 asserts that they are \(\Gamma\)-equivariant and satisfy \(\nabla^{\prime\prime}\varphi^{(n)}=\delta_f\operatorname{vol}\), with the connection and character signs fixed in the construction.

The specific algebraic identity used to identify their Fourier coefficients on page 41 is the truncated divided-power expansion \[(a+u)^{-j-1}=\sum_{b=0}^{n}\frac{(j+b)!}{j!}\,a^{-j-b-1}u^{[b]},\qquad u^{[b]}=u^b/b!,\] modulo terms of degree greater than \(n\), where \(j\ge0\), \(u=\widetilde l\) is the formal symmetric variable, and \(a=\pi\|l/\sqrt r\|_H^2>0\) for a nonzero dual-lattice mode \(l\) and \(r\in\mathbb R_{>0}^d\). The printed expansion has no alternating factor depending on \(b\).

Let \(\varphi:A'=A_{(n)}\to A\) be the étale isogeny in Section 5.5, let \(D'=\varphi^{-1}D\), and let \(f'=\varphi^*f\) on all of \(D'\), as defined in (5.5.1). At \(\mathfrak s=\mathfrak t=0\), Theorem 5.23 asserts \[\vartheta_A(f,x)=\sum_{a\in\ker\varphi}\varphi_\#\vartheta_{A'}(f',x'+a).\] Thus every summand uses the full pulled-back residue function, rather than a function supported on one selected kernel translate.

For the nontrivial tame modulus \(\mathfrak f\) in Theorem 5.27, Step 1 identifies the kernel of \[\operatorname{Gal}(L(p^\infty\mathfrak f)/L)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L(\mathfrak f)/L)\] with the local unit group \((\mathcal O_L\otimes\mathbb Z_p)^\times\) modulo the closure of all global units \(\mathcal O_L^\times\). The asserted kernel description uses all units rather than only units congruent to one modulo \(\mathfrak f\).

For the algebraic torus modules \(M\) allowed in Section 1.1 and a base ring \(R\) contained in a number field, Proposition 1.5 asserts \[M^\Gamma=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\operatorname{HChar}_L(\Gamma)}M(\mu).\] Here \(M(\mu)\) is the weight space and \(\operatorname{HChar}_L(\Gamma)\) selects weights trivial on \(\Gamma\). The module class is not restricted to \(R\)-torsion-free modules.

Let \(\Lambda\subset\mathbb C^\Sigma\), \(|\Sigma|=d\), be the lattice in Definition 3.11, let \(H(z,w)=\sum_{i=1}^dh_i z_i\overline{w_i}\) with \(h_i>0\), and put \(\langle z,w\rangle=\operatorname{Im}H(z,w)\). For \(\mu\in\mathbb N^d\) and shifts \(z,w\in\mathbb C^\Sigma\), consider the uncompleted Eisenstein–Kronecker series \(K^\mu(H,z,w,s,\Lambda)\) defined there, initially for \(\operatorname{Re}s>d+|\mu|/2\). Proposition 3.13 asserts meromorphic continuation with possible simple poles only at \(s=0,d\), and residues \[-\delta_{\mu,z}e^{2\pi i\langle-z,w\rangle}\quad\text{at }s=0,\qquad \frac{\delta_{\mu,w}}{\operatorname{vol}_H(\Lambda)}\quad\text{at }s=d,\] using the indicator notation of the proposition and its Mellin proof. In particular, its \(\mu=0,z=w=0\) case assigns residues \(-1\) and \(1/\operatorname{vol}_H(\Lambda)\). These are asserted for \(K^\mu\) itself, while the Mellin expression in the proof is for \(\pi^{-s}\Gamma(s)K^\mu\).

Definition 3.24 forms the Eisenstein sum over \(\Gamma\backslash(\Lambda+\Gamma t')\) for an arbitrary torsion point \(t'\), without requiring its coset to be fixed by \(\Gamma\). Lemma 3.25 asserts that replacing \(\Gamma\) by a finite-index subgroup \(\Gamma'\) multiplies this sum by \([\Gamma:\Gamma']\).

For the critical Hecke characters and periods in Corollary 4.15, the asserted algebraicity statement is \(L_{\mathfrak f}(\chi,0)/c^+_\tau\in\overline{\mathbb Q}^{\times}\). Membership is in the multiplicative group, and therefore includes nonvanishing for every character in the stated critical range; no separate nonvanishing hypothesis is imposed.

For a chord-arc Jordan curve \(\Gamma\), let \(s=\ell(\Gamma)/2\) and let \(\gamma(z,w)\) be the shorter connecting arc. The final comparison in Lemma 9.1 replaces \(\{(z,w):x,y\in\gamma(z,w)\}\) by a product of two length-\(s\) arcs and asserts \[\int_{z\in\sigma(x,y,s)}\int_{w\in\sigma(y,x,s)}|x-w|^{-4}|dz|\,|dw|\simeq\int_{w\in\sigma(y,x,s)}|x-w|^{-3}|dw|\simeq |x-y|^{-2}.\] The asserted constants are uniform as the two points approach each other.

For the hyperbolic minimal-surface setting of Lemma 18.2, at \(z=(x,t)\) the proof claims that the Euclidean center of the boundary sphere of the normal hyperplane is within \(O(t\sup_w\max_j|\kappa_j(w)|)\) of \(x\). It then uses the normal-antipodal construction to claim \(\rho(Q)=O(K_r(z))\), where \(K_r\) bounds principal curvatures on a fixed hyperbolic ball and \(\rho(Q)\) is the stated Euclidean reflection-distortion quantity.

For the regular height truncations \(S_t\) of the minimal surface considered in Lemma 20.1, let \(\kappa_g\) denote the geodesic curvature of the truncation boundary and \(\delta\) the hyperbolic convex-hull thickness. The lemma asserts \(\kappa_g=1+O(\delta^2)\) and \[\int_{\partial S_t}(\kappa_g-1)\,dL_\rho=O\!\left(\int_{\partial S_t}\delta^2\,dL_\rho\right).\] The proof then uses a trace-to-area estimate to make this boundary integral tend to zero.

For every pair of disjoint Euclidean balls of the same radius \(r>0\), separated by a gap \(\varepsilon>0\), Lemma 16.1 asserts that the associated hyperbolic half-spaces have distance \(\rho\simeq\sqrt{\varepsilon/r}\). The two-sided comparison is stated without an upper restriction on the ratio \(\varepsilon/r\).

For a smooth closed curve \(\Gamma\), with \(\ell(x,y)\) the shorter arclength between two points, Section 23 defines \[E^{j,p}(\Gamma)=\int_\Gamma\!\int_\Gamma\bigl(|x-y|^{-j}-\ell(x,y)^{-j}\bigr)^p\,|dx|\,|dy|\] and asserts that this integral is finite whenever \(jp\le2p+1\), including the equality case.

Let \(G=\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb R)\), \(\Gamma=\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\), and \(X=G/\Gamma\). A point \(g\Gamma\) represents the lattice \(\Lambda=g\mathbb Z^3\). The manuscript defines \[u(r)=I+rE_{23},\qquad
 a(t)=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{t/2},e^{-t/2}),\qquad
 a_0(\ell)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{\ell/3},e^{-\ell/6},e^{-\ell/6}).\] Its compact set is \[X_\varpi=\{g\Gamma:\|gv\|\geq\varpi
 \text{ for all }0\ne v\in\mathbb Z^3\text{ and all }0\ne v\in\wedge^2\mathbb Z^3\}.\] The exterior-square condition is essential: checking only lattice vectors would not test the theorem. For an oriented unimodular Euclidean three-dimensional lattice, the Hodge map identifies \(\wedge^2\Lambda\) isometrically with the dual lattice \(\Lambda^*=g^{-T}\mathbb Z^3\).

Use the parameters \(\beta,C_1,\varepsilon_1,s'\) of Section 11 and the interval notation \([L]=[-L/2,L/2]\). Let \(\ell\) be an integer with \(0\le\ell\le s'\). Lemma 11.4 considers the portions in \(\mathfrak C=[1.2\beta e^{-s'}]^2\) of two hyperbolas \[C:\ X=-\frac{Y}{w_1Y+k},\qquad C':\ X=-\frac{Y}{w_1'Y+k'},\] where \[e^{s'-10C_1\varepsilon_1s'}\le |w_1|,|w_1'|\le\beta e^{s'},\qquad e^\ell\le|k|\le e^{\ell+1}.\] For every \(0<A<e^{2s'-C_1\varepsilon_1s'}\), part (1) asserts that containment of \(C'\) in the \(Ae^{-3s'}\)-neighborhood of \(C\) implies \[|w_1-w_1'|\le Ae^{-s'+2\ell},\qquad |k-k'|\le Ae^{-2s'+2\ell},\] and asserts the converse as well. The proposed recovery scales do not include an additional loss from the observation-window factor \(\beta\).

Let \(X=\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb R)/\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\), with the diagonal flow \(a(\ell)\), thick part \(X_\varpi\), Lie-algebra balls, and canonical weight basis \(\mathsf u,\mathsf u^*,\mathsf a,\mathsf a_0,\mathsf v_1,\mathsf v_2,\mathsf w_1,\mathsf w_2\) fixed earlier in the paper. Lemma 4.2 is stated for every \(\beta>0\), every \(\ell\ge1\), and every \(x\in X\) such that \(a(-\ell)x\in X_{\beta^{1/4}}\). Suppose \(r_i\in[-\beta/2,\beta/2]\), \(\|(r_1,r_2,r_3)\|\ge\beta/4\), and \(v\in B_{\mathfrak g}(\beta)\) satisfy \[\exp(r_1e^\ell\mathsf u+r_2e^{\ell/2}\mathsf v_1+r_3e^{\ell/2}\mathsf w_1)x=\exp(v)x.\] Writing \(v=u\mathsf u+u^*\mathsf u^*+a\mathsf a+a_0\mathsf a_0+\sum_{j=1}^2(v_j\mathsf v_j+w_j\mathsf w_j)\), the lemma concludes \[|u^*|<\beta e^{-\ell}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|(v_2,w_2)\|\ge\beta e^{-\ell/2}.\] The asserted range includes \(\ell=1\).

Judgment: Minor, for the classical pointwise reading. Lemma 3.3, PDF page 17, equation (3.9), asserts for \(\omega\in C^1_0(\mathbb R)\) and its bounded harmonic extension to the upper half-plane that \[\partial_yu(x+i0)=H[-\omega'].\] The TeX label is `lem:normal_derivative_harmonic_extension`. The proof ends by passing through the Hilbert transform from \(C^1\) convergence of the boundary approximations. Such convergence does not imply finite pointwise convergence of the Hilbert transforms of their continuous derivatives.

For the spacetime constructed in the small-perturbation regime of Section 16 around its fixed subextremal Kerr background, let \(\theta_{(i)}^A\), \(i=1,2\), be the original angular charts and \(\theta_{(i),\mathcal{CH}^+}^A\) the new transported angular coordinates. Write \(v\) for the incoming null coordinate and \(v_{\mathcal{CH}^+}\) for its compactification. The angular Jacobians are \[J_i{}^A_B=\frac{\partial\theta_{(i),\mathcal{CH}^+}^A}{\partial\theta_{(i)}^B},\qquad J_{i,K}{}^A_B=\frac{\partial\theta_{(i),\mathcal{CH}^+,K}^A}{\partial\theta_{(i)}^B}.\] Proposition 16.11 asserts \(|J_i-J_{i,K}|\lesssim\varepsilon\) on the stated interior angular charts \(V_i'\), asserts that the new coordinates give a diffeomorphism in the interior, and asserts that \(J_i\) extends continuously to the Cauchy horizon in the original compactified coordinate structure \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^+},\theta_{(i)}^1,\theta_{(i)}^2)\).

Corollary 16.13 then asserts that every \(S\)-tangent tensor field continuously extendible in those original compactified coordinates is also continuously extendible in \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^+},\theta_{(i),\mathcal{CH}^+}^1,\theta_{(i),\mathcal{CH}^+}^2)\). Theorem 16.14 invokes this transfer and the angular Jacobian to conclude continuity of the metric in the new coordinates on \(W_\infty\times V_i\). The finding concerns these actual-coordinate assertions, including the claimed continuity in the old coordinate structure.

The domain includes the time variable; it is not a two-dimensional spatial slice.

Let \(\mathsf A(n,k)\) count permutations of \(n\) letters with \(k\) descents. The large-\(n\) check in the supplied function verify_bound_m1b_mult1a is intended to establish \[\mathsf A(n,4)<\frac{\mathsf A(n,1)^3}{200n}\qquad(20\le n\le199).\] Its implemented logarithmic right side is \(\log(n\mathsf A(n,1)^3/200)-0.1\), which the code treats as the buffered right side for that claim.

With \(\mathsf A(n,k)\) the Eulerian numbers, Lemma B.15 asserts, for \(n\ge11\), \[2\mathsf A(n,1)+\sqrt{\frac{48\mathsf A(n,3)\mathsf A(n,1)}{11}}+1+\frac{48\mathsf A(n,3)}{11\mathsf A(n,1)}+\sqrt{\frac{96\mathsf A(n,5)}{11\mathsf A(n,1)}}+1<\mathsf A(n,2).\] The supplied function verify_bound_m1a_final purports to check this full sum for \(20\le n\le199\); its comparison includes the computed terms bda, bdb, bdc and bdd but omits the separately computed bde term.

Let \(X\) be a smooth geometrically connected projective curve of genus \(g\) in characteristic zero, and let \(G\) be split reductive, with the Borel and twisted unipotent group used in Section 5.1.7. Definition 5.1.7.1 calls a dominant coweight-valued divisor \(D\) sufficiently large when \[\langle\alpha,\deg D\rangle>g-1\qquad\text{for every positive root }\alpha.\] Lemma 5.1.7.2 asserts that under this bound the torsor stack \(\operatorname{Bun}_N^{\Omega(-D)}\) is an affine scheme.

Lemma 2.7 (Article PDF page 8) assumes that \(R\) is an integral domain and \((\mathfrak a_i)_{i\ge0}\) is a graded sequence of ideals with \(\mathfrak a_0=R\), \(\mathfrak a_i\mathfrak a_j\subseteq\mathfrak a_{i+j}\), and \(\mathfrak a_{i+1}\subseteq\mathfrak a_i\). Suppose that the associated graded ring \[\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak a}R=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\mathfrak a_i/\mathfrak a_{i+1}\] is an integral domain. No separatedness condition \(\bigcap_{i\ge0}\mathfrak a_i=0\) is imposed.

The lemma asserts that there is a discrete valuation \(v\) of \(\operatorname{Frac}(R)\), finite on every nonzero element, whose valuation ideals are precisely \[\mathfrak a_i=\{f\in R:v(f)\ge i\}\quad(i\ge0).\] The proposed construction in its proof is \(v(f)=\sup\{i\ge0:f\in\mathfrak a_i\}\) for every \(0\ne f\in R\). Finiteness of this supremum is part of the asserted implication.

A perfectoid field here is a non-discretely valued, complete, real-valued field of residue characteristic \(p>0\), with surjective Frobenius on \(\mathcal O_K/(p)\). Its tilt is denoted \((K^\flat,v^\flat)\). The enlarged class \(\mathcal C\) consists of henselian valued fields of residue characteristic \(p\), with a distinguished nonzero nonunit \(\varpi\), semiperfect \(\mathcal O_v/(p)\), and algebraically maximal \(\mathcal O_v[\varpi^{-1}]\); its valuations may have higher rank.

Theorem 5.1.7, on article PDF page 34, considers two perfect henselian valued fields \((E,u)\) and \((E^{\prime},u^{\prime})\) extending the valued field \((\mathbb F_p(t),v_t)\), where \(v_t\) is the \(t\)-adic valuation. Both \(\mathcal O_u[t^{-1}]\) and \(\mathcal O_{u^{\prime}}[t^{-1}]\) must be algebraically maximal. Its two elementary-equivalence hypotheses are \(\mathcal O_u/(t)\equiv\mathcal O_{u^{\prime}}/(t)\) in \(L_{\mathrm{rings}}\), and \((\Gamma_u,u(t))\equiv(\Gamma_{u^{\prime}},u^{\prime}(t))\) as ordered abelian groups with a distinguished constant naming the value of \(t\). Under these hypotheses, it concludes \((E,u)\equiv(E^{\prime},u^{\prime})\) in \(L_{\mathrm{val}}\).

Corollary 5.3.5, on article PDF page 37, asserts that for a perfectoid field \((K,v)\), the \(L_{\mathrm{val}}\)-theory of its tilt \((K^\flat,v^\flat)\) is decidable relative to the \(L_{\mathrm{val}}\)-theory of \((K,v)\). Its proof chooses \(t\in\mathcal O_{K^\flat}\) with \(\mathcal O_{K^\flat}/(t)\cong\mathcal O_K/(p)\). It forms a theory \(T\) in \(L_{\mathrm{val}}(t)\) of perfect henselian characteristic-\(p\) valued fields \((F,u,t)\) for which \(\mathcal O_F[t^{-1}]\) is algebraically maximal, together with the quotient-ring axioms \[\mathcal O_F/(t)\equiv\mathcal O_{K^\flat}/(t)\quad\text{in }L_{\mathrm{rings}}.\] The asserted application of Theorem 5.1.7 is that, for every \(L_{\mathrm{val}}\)-sentence \(\varphi\), \[T\models\varphi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(K^\flat,v^\flat)\models\varphi,\] so that enumerating proofs from \(T\), using the stated oracle, decides \(\varphi\) or its negation.

In the proof of Fact 2.4.7, page 18, implication \((iii)\Leftrightarrow(iv)\), the manuscript writes \[\operatorname{disc}(m_a)=m_a'(a)^2=\delta_{K'/K}(a)^2.
 \tag{4.1}\] The same formula appears at source line 715. Page 17 defines a signed discriminant: \[D(f)=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2.\] This convention is respected here; the issue is not its sign.

In the standing homogeneous-space setting, let \(\Gamma<G\) be a cocompact irreducible lattice and consider the left-translation action of an abelian unipotent subgroup \(A\) on \(G/\Gamma\). Corollary 1.7 (Article PDF page 7) takes \[G=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)\times\mathrm{SL}(2,k_1)\times\cdots\times\mathrm{SL}(2,k_n),\qquad n\ge1,\quad k_j\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\},\] and \(A\cong\mathbb R^m\) consisting of upper triangular unipotents, with \(m\le1+n\). It asserts that there exists \(\ell\in\mathbb N\) for which this action is transversally \(C^{\infty,\ell,\infty}\) locally rigid. These hypotheses do not require a nonzero projection of \(A\) to a second factor.

The checked inference is the application of Theorem 9.2 in Section 11.4 (PDF page 86): the corollary's hypotheses are taken to provide the splitting furnished by that theorem. Theorem 9.2 retains the generating set \(E\) from Section 3.1(11) (PDF pages 22 and 64); in the product case, \(E\) contains \(u=E_{12}\) in the first factor and a nonzero nilpotent vector \(v\) in another factor, and the relevant friendly pair consists of nonzero vectors. Thus the stated application requires those generators to exist for the action under consideration, including the allowed case \(m=1\).

Let \(F\) be any field, \(H\) a finite group, \(B\) a finite \(H\)-module, and \(V\) a faithful finite-dimensional \(H\)-representation over \(F\), viewed as an affine space. For every codimension-one point \(x\in V^{(1)}\), let \(H_x\) be its stabilizer and choose \(f_x\in F(V)^\times\) with \(\operatorname{div}(f_x)=x\). Lemma 4.1 asserts that \((B\otimes_{\mathbb Z}F(V)^\times)^H\) is generated by \((B\otimes_{\mathbb Z}F^\times)^H\) and all elements \[N_{H/H_x}(b\otimes f_x),\qquad x\in V^{(1)},\quad b\in B^{H_x}.\] In particular, the asserted generating elements are required to belong to the invariant group for these allowed choices of \(f_x\); the lemma does not assume \(F\) algebraically closed or require the chosen \(f_x\) itself to be \(H_x\)-invariant.

Let \(p\) be prime, let \(\widetilde V,\widetilde W\) be finite-rank free \(\mathbb Z/p^2\mathbb Z\)-modules, and let \(V,W\) be their reductions modulo \(p\). In the alternative proof of Lemma 5.3, \(E\) is the inverse image of the block subgroup \(\mathrm{GL}(V)\subset\mathrm{GL}(V\oplus W)\) under reduction \(\mathrm{GL}(\widetilde V\oplus\widetilde W)\to\mathrm{GL}(V\oplus W)\). The proof asserts that every element of \(E\) restricts to an automorphism of \(\widetilde V\), and hence literal restriction defines a homomorphism \(\pi:E\to\mathrm{GL}(\widetilde V)\) compatible with the extension diagram. The assertion requires preservation of the lifted summand itself, not merely preservation after reduction modulo \(p\).

For a finite Galois extension \(L/K\) with group \(H\) and an \(H\)-module \(A\) regarded as a Galois module through that quotient, the source uses the Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre sequence \(H^i(H,H^j(L,A))\Rightarrow H^{i+j}(K,A)\). It calls the displayed segment \[H^1(L,A)^H\xrightarrow{\mathrm{tg}}H^2(H,A)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{inf}}H^2(L,A)\tag{2.3}\] a short exact sequence. The printed inflation target is \(H^2(L,A)\), and the description asserts endpoint exactness as well as exactness at the middle term.

In the later upper-unitriangular calculation, let \(Z=\{I+xE_{13}:x\in\mathbb F_p\}\), and let the diagonal torus \(T\) act by conjugation. Write \(\tau_{ij}(\operatorname{diag}(t_1,t_2,t_3))=t_i/t_j\). With the cohomology action \((t\cdot\chi)(z)=\chi(t^{-1}zt)\) and the equivariant connecting map \(H^1(Z,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Z,\mathbb Z)\), page 19 identifies \(H^2(Z,\mathbb Z)\) with the character module \(\mathbb F_p(\tau_{13})\). This is the second printed convention assertion examined in the finding.

In the finite-field argument for Proposition 14, let \(p\) be the odd prime of the paper's setting and \(\sigma\in\mathbb F_p\), \(\sigma\ne1\). Equation (71) (Article PDF page 20) sets \[\Phi(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&-\sigma t^2-4(1-\sigma)\\1&-t\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det\Phi(t)=(1-\sigma)(4-t^2).\] For \(s,t\) with nonzero determinants, the nonconcentration verification treats \[\Phi(s)^{-1}\Phi(t)\,\frac{\det\Phi(s)}{\det\Phi(t)}\] as an element of \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\).

After taking \(s=\sigma t+4(1-\sigma)/t\), with \(t\ne0\) and the displayed denominators nonzero, Equation (72) gives the normalized matrix \[g_t=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma(1+\sigma)t+4(1-\sigma)/t&-\sigma^2t^2+4(1-\sigma)^2\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] The same argument asserts that every proper subgroup \(H<\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\) has trivial second derived subgroup \(H''=[[H,H],[H,H]]=\{I\}\). Equations (73)–(76) use that universal subgroup assertion to reduce exclusion of proper subgroups to nontriviality of a double commutator of the \(g_t\). These are the normalization, matrix identity, and subgroup implication being checked.

Let \(p\) be odd, let \(1\le d,e<p\), and let \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) be the coefficients over \(\mathbb F_p\) in Lemma 12. Assume they are not all zero and that both values \(\alpha_3\pm2\sqrt{\alpha_1\alpha_2}\) differ from both \(2\) and \(-2\), with the square roots interpreted in the algebraic closure. The lemma asserts irreducibility of the torus curve \[\alpha_1y^e+\alpha_2y^{-e}+\alpha_3=x^d+x^{-d},\qquad x,y\ne0,\] and its proof supplies the asserted absolute-irreducibility argument via the fiber product of the two maps to \(\mathbb P^1\). The stated coefficient conditions do not exclude \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0\).

Let \(U_t\subset\mathbb F_p^\times\) be the group of \(t\)-th roots of unity, where \(t\mid p-1\) and \(t\le p^{3/4}\). Corollary 21 asserts the uniform estimate \[|\sigma(U_t)\cap U_t|\ll t^{3/4}\] for every nonidentity \(\sigma\in\operatorname{PGL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). The printed statement excludes only the identity and does not carry over the disjoint-divisor assumption of Proposition 20.

Let \(A/F\) be a positive-dimensional abelian variety over a number field, let \(\chi:G_F\to\{\pm1\}\) be any continuous quadratic character, including the trivial character, and put \(N^\chi=A^\chi[2^\infty]\). Use the usual Kummer local conditions, with an allowed unpacking tuple whose exceptional places include the archimedean places, the primes above \(2\), and the bad-reduction primes. In Definition 4.3 (Article PDF pages 22–23), \(\mathrm{Sel}^{2^k}N^\chi\subset H^1(F,N^\chi[2^k])\) is the preimage of the infinite Selmer group, and its image under multiplication by \(2^{k-1}\) lies in \(H^1(F,N^\chi[2])\).

Let \(\delta:N^\chi[2]^{G_F}\to H^1(F,N^\chi[2])\) be the connecting homomorphism for \(0\to N^\chi[2]\to N^\chi[4]\xrightarrow{2}N^\chi[2]\to0\). The paper defines \[r_{2^k}(N^\chi)=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\left(2^{k-1}\mathrm{Sel}^{2^k}N^\chi\big/\delta(N^\chi[2]^{G_F})\right).\] The final sentence of Example 4.4 asserts, for every \(k\ge1\), that this equals the usual rank from Section 1.1 (PDF page 2): the largest \(r\) for which \[(\mathbb Z/2^k\mathbb Z)^r\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Sel}_{2^k}(A^\chi/F)\big/\operatorname{im}(A^\chi(F)_{\mathrm{tors}}).\] The latter denominator is the full rational-torsion Kummer image. Example 4.4 does not impose the later generating-ramification hypothesis that would force every invariant torsion point to be killed by \(2\).

On pages 59–60, Proposition 10.5 asserts a universal \(C>0\). For real coefficients \(a_i\), an integer \(m\ge1\), a rational prime \(\ell\), and finite \[B=\sum_{i\ge0}|a_i|\ell^{mi},\] small values of \(f(z)=\sum_i a_i z^i\) on \(1,\ell,\ldots,\ell^{m-1}\) are claimed to imply \[|a_i|\le \ell^{(-i+C)m}(B\ell^{-m^2/2}+\epsilon)\quad(i\ge0).
 \tag{R1}\] With both signs of those nodes, the gain is claimed to be \(\ell^{-m^2}\) instead. The exact statements appear in `distribution.tex` lines 105 and 107.

For integers \(n\ge j\ge0\), Case 2.13 defines \(P(j\mid n)\) as the probability that a uniformly chosen alternating \(n\times n\) matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\) has kernel dimension \(j\). It sets this probability to zero when \(j\not\equiv n\pmod2\), and otherwise asserts \[P(j\mid n)=2^{-j(j-1)/2}\prod_{k=1}^{j}\frac{1-2^{-n-j+k}}{1-2^{-k}}\prod_{k=1}^{(n-j)/2}(1-2^{-2k+1}).\] Empty products are interpreted as one. This is the printed finite-dimensional distribution, not merely a limiting formula as \(n\to\infty\).

Let \(\ell\) be a rational prime, \(F\) a number field, and \(A/F\) an abelian variety. Let \(X(H)\) be the set of cyclic extensions \(K/F\) of degree \(\ell\) whose absolute discriminant is at most \(H\). Theorem 1.1 asserts that there are constants \(c,C>0\), depending only on \(A/F\) and \(\ell\), such that for every real \(m>0\) and every \(H>C\) satisfying \(m<c\log\log\log H\), \[\sum_{K\in X(H)}\exp\bigl(m\operatorname{rank}(A/K)\bigr)\le e^{Cm^2}\#X(H).\] The moment parameter is allowed to approach zero; it is not restricted to positive integers or to \(m\ge1\).

Let \(a,b\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(b(a^2-4b)\ne0\), and set \[A:y^2=x(x^2+ax+b),\qquad A_0:y^2=x(x^2-2ax+a^2-4b),\] \[K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{a^2-4b}),\qquad K_0=\mathbb Q(\sqrt b).\] Example 1.2 calls a squarefree integer \(d\) favored for \(A\) if, among its odd prime divisors at which \(A\) has good reduction, the number splitting in \(K_0/\mathbb Q\) is at most the number splitting in \(K/\mathbb Q\). The next sentence asserts that the natural density of favored \(d\) among squarefree integers is \(1/2\). That sentence uses only the preceding nonsingularity condition; the later assumption that \(K\) and \(K_0\) are distinct nontrivial quadratic extensions is not included there.

Proposition 3.4.10, page 37, equation (3.4.4), asserts \[\pi_{2n+2}(X\wedge X)\longrightarrow
 \pi_{2n+1}(X)\longrightarrow
 \pi_{2n+2}(\Sigma X)\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{R1}\] The following paragraph identifies the first arrow with a bilinear Whitehead product and, at \(n=0\), the commutator map. It explicitly uses this sequence to obtain the zero-connectivity surjection. The same text is in `main_revision.tex`, lines 1702–1709.

Throughout the paper, \(K\) is an algebraically closed complete extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\), \(X/K\) is a smooth projective connected curve, and \(G\) is a connected reductive group unless a narrower scope is specified. Write \(\Omega=\widetilde\Omega_X=\omega_X(-1)\). For \(G=\operatorname{GL}_n\), the Hitchin base is \[\mathcal A=\prod_{i=1}^n H^0(X,\Omega^{\otimes i})\otimes\mathbf G_a,\] and the spectral cover \(\pi:Z_b\to X\) is defined by the monic characteristic polynomial. The regular centralizer has Lie algebra \(\pi_*\mathcal O_{Z_b}\). In the discussion of relative cohomology, distinguish the projection \(q:X\times\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\) from \(\pi':Z\to\mathcal A\).

Lemma 8.2.7, p. 39, with proof in `main.tex`, lines 2398–2414, asserts that a double coset has a representative \[A'\in \operatorname{GL}_r(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle)
       \cap T^{-m}M_r(R\langle T\rangle).\] The proof claims that \(\operatorname{GL}_r(R[T^{\pm1}])\) is dense in \(\operatorname{GL}_r(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle)\), and uses this to obtain \[\operatorname{GL}_r(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle)
 =\operatorname{GL}_r(R[T^{\pm1}])U(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle),
 \qquad U(S)=1+\mathfrak m_KM_r(S^+).\] The claimed density, at source line 2404, is false.

Let \(K\) be an algebraically closed complete extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\), and let \(X/K\) be a smooth projective connected curve. In the case \(G=\operatorname{GL}_n\), write \(\Omega=\widetilde\Omega_X=\omega_X(-1)\) and \[\mathcal A=\prod_{i=1}^n H^0(X,\Omega^{\otimes i})\otimes\mathbf G_a.\] For \(b\in\mathcal A\), the spectral cover \(\pi_b:Z_b\to X\) is defined by the monic characteristic polynomial, and the regular centralizer has fibrewise Lie algebra \(\operatorname{Lie}J_b=(\pi_b)_*\mathcal O_{Z_b}\). Denote the projection by \(q:X\times\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\) and the spectral-family structure map by \(\pi^{\prime}:Z\to\mathcal A\).

The spectral cohomology sheaf is \(\Lambda=R^1\pi^{\prime}_{v*}\mathbb Z_p\), using the distinct structure-map notation of Theorem 7.0.1 on article PDF page 30. The Lie algebra sheaf \(\operatorname{Lie}J\) is on \(X\times\mathcal A\), so its relative first \(v\)-cohomology is taken along \(q\). With these names for the two maps, Theorem 1.4.1 on article PDF page 4 asserts a canonical isomorphism of \(v\)-sheaves over the full Hitchin base \(\mathcal A\): \[\psi:R^1q_{v*}\operatorname{Lie}J\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z_p}\mathbf G_a.\] The introductory display uses the letter \(f\) for both structural-map roles; \(q\) and \(\pi^{\prime}\) distinguish those roles here.

Section 5.5, p. 22, source line 1411, states without a genus restriction that there is an open dense \(\mathcal A^\circ\subseteq\mathcal A\) over which the spectral family is smooth proper with geometrically connected fibres.

In Lemma 8.4, Step 3, let \(P=Q_\lambda^{\rm fine}=Q\oplus_R^{\rm fine}R_\lambda\subset Q^{\rm gp}\) be the fine monoid pushout used in the local model. From torsion-freeness of \(Q^{\rm gp}\), and hence of \(P^{\rm sat}\), the proof concludes that the saturation morphism \[\operatorname{Spec}k[P^{\rm sat}]\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}k[P]\] is one-to-one on geometric points.

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\), take \(\eta,\delta_0>0\) as in Lemma 3.3, and let \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), \(\delta^{1-\varepsilon}\le\rho\le1\). Let \((\mathbb T,Y)_\delta\) be the essentially distinct tube/shading family covered by one \(\rho\)-tube \(\widetilde T\), satisfying Definition 2.1(a)–(b) with parameter \(\eta\) and \(\sum_{T\in\mathbb T}|Y(T)|\ge\delta^\eta\rho^{n-1}\). In particular, its every-scale covering condition supplies, at each scale between \(\delta\) and one, a cover with at most \(\delta^{-\eta}\) cover tubes essentially parallel to a common tube of that scale.

The unit rescaling in Definition 3.2 applies a rigid change of coordinates followed by \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto c(x_1/\rho,\ldots,x_{n-1}/\rho,x_n)\), where \(c=c(n)\asymp1\). It defines each \(\widehat Y(\widehat T)\) as the union of all \((\delta/\rho)\)-grid cubes meeting the affine image of the corresponding shading. After the refinement in the proof, equation (3.5) asserts \[\left|\bigcup_{T\in\mathbb T}Y(T)\right|\asymp\rho^{n-1}\left|\bigcup_{\widehat T\in\widehat{\mathbb T}}\widehat Y(\widehat T)\right|.\] Thus in dimension three the factor is \(\rho^2\), and the assertion compares volume with the rounded cubical enlargement, not only with the affine image.

For each \(\varepsilon>0\), Proposition 7.1 chooses \(\delta_0\) before the function \(f\) and asserts, for direction-separated \(\delta\)-tubes with \(0<\delta<\delta_0\), \[\left\|\sum_{T\in\mathbb T}\chi_{\pi_f(T)}\right\|_{L^{3/2}(\mathbb R^2)}\le\delta^{-1-\varepsilon},\qquad\pi_f(x,y,z)=(x+f(z)y,z).\] The stated function assumptions are \(1\le|f'|\le2\) and \(|f''|\le1/100\), without a bound on \(f(0)\) or \(\|f\|_\infty\).

Let \(E\) be a Borel subset of a product probability space with measure at least \(1-c\), as in Lemma 8.3. The lemma forms \(E'\) from whole product grid cells whose relative \(E\)-density is at least \(c\), and asserts that this threshold construction discards mass less than \(c\), thereby retaining at least \(1-c\) of the product-grid mass.

Over the nondiscrete algebraically closed nonarchimedean Banach fields used in the proof of Proposition 5.19, fix \(0<r_1<1<r_2\), a monic polynomial \(f(X)=X^n+a_{n-1}X^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0\), and \(r_1^n<|a_0|<r_2^n\). The displayed criterion asserts that all roots lie in the open annulus \(r_1<|z|<r_2\) if and only if \[|a_i|<\max\{r_2^{n-i},|a_0|r_1^{-i}\}\qquad(1\le i<n).\]

A \(q\)-cluster includes the exterior cell; a single bubble therefore has \(q=2\). Individual cells need not be connected. In \(\mathbb R^n\) only the exterior cell has infinite volume. Total perimeter counts each interface once. Reflection symmetry means invariance of each labelled cell, not just invariance of the union of interfaces.

Definitions 2.26 and 2.28, printed p. 100 (PDF 30), require stationarity and \[\delta_X^1 V=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 Q(X)=\delta_X^2 A-\langle\lambda,\delta_X^2V\rangle\geq0
 \qquad (X\in C_c^\infty).\] Perturbations are not restricted to reflection-symmetric fields or to preserving each connected component’s volume.

Remark 9.14, printed p. 161 (PDF 91), proposes taking a stable \(q\)-cluster whose \(q-1\) finite cells lie in one open hemisphere and reflecting it about the equator. It states that the resulting \(q\)-cluster is stable and has disconnected cells, as an example showing why connectedness of the total boundary is needed in Theorem 1.9.

Theorem 1.16, printed p. 211/PDF 23, asserts, for an open \(U\subset\Omega\) and \(\delta>0\), \[
 \nu_\star(V_\delta)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \nu_\star(\overline U)=0 ,
 \qquad
 U_\delta=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,U)\le\delta\},\
 V_\delta=U_\delta\setminus U .\] The overline on \(U\) in the conclusion was confirmed in the page image; text extraction suppresses it. The preceding prose allows general regular subdomains and does not require \(\overline U\subset\Omega\) or a positive distance to the exterior boundary.

For a nonnegative Landau initial datum \(f_0\in L^{\infty,k}(\mathbb R^3)\), with \(k\) in the range of Theorem 2.1 and \(\sqrt{f_0}\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)\), Appendix B allows arbitrary tails and vacuum regions. Given smooth \(0\le\eta\le1\), equal to one on \(B_1\) and supported in \(B_2\), it defines the approximate solution by \[f^\varepsilon(0,v)=(f_0(v)+\varepsilon)\eta(\varepsilon v)+(1-\eta(\varepsilon v))e^{-|v|^2}.\] The text asserts that these solutions converge to the solution with datum \(f_0\) in \(L^{\infty,k}\) for every exponent \(k\), and that \(\sqrt{f^\varepsilon}\to\sqrt f\) in \(L^\infty([0,T];H^1(\mathbb R^3))\). This convergence is used to pass monotonicity of Fisher information to the original solution.

The related six-dimensional regularization in the proof of Theorem 1.1 uses a cutoff on \(\mathbb R^6\) and the formula \[F_\varepsilon(v,w)=(F(v,w)+\varepsilon)\eta(\varepsilon v,\varepsilon w)+(1-\eta(\varepsilon v,\varepsilon w))e^{-|v|^2}.\] It is claimed to be strictly positive, Maxwellian at large \((v,w)\), and suitable for passing the six-dimensional inequality (3.5) to the original lifted function \(F\). The displayed tail depends on \(v\) alone.

In the proof of Proposition 7.40, let \(X\) be a finite pointed \(\Sigma_n\)-set, let \(V\) be a finite \(\mathbb F_p\)-module object as specified there, and let \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m\in\mathbb Z\). The asserted equivariant binomial expansion is \[\mathbb F_p[X]\otimes_{\Sigma_n}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\Sigma^{-\ell_i}V\right)^{\otimes n}\simeq\bigoplus_{n_1+\cdots+n_m=n}\Sigma^{-\sum_i\ell_i n_i}\left(\mathbb F_p[X]\otimes_{\Sigma_{n_1}\times\cdots\times\Sigma_{n_m}}V^{\otimes n}\right).\] The right-hand expression retains the untwisted permutation action on \(V^{\otimes n}\) after moving the total suspension outside the subgroup coinvariants. Equation (7.7) asserts the corresponding identity for the right-left extended functors \(F_X\), for arbitrary integer shifts.

Putting \(P_n=\Sigma|\Pi_n|^\diamond\), the subsequent general-\(V\) display asserts \[F_{P_n}\left(\bigoplus_i\Sigma^{-\ell_i}V\right)\simeq\bigoplus_{\substack{n_1+\cdots+n_m=n,\ d\mid\gcd(n_1,\ldots,n_m)\\ w\in B(n_1/d,\ldots,n_m/d)}}F_{P_d}\left(\Sigma^{1+\sum_i(1-\ell_i)n_i/d}V\right),\] with the Lyndon-word indexing set \(B\) of the source. The finding concerns these derivation steps for arbitrary \(V\); the proposition itself is stated for sums of shifts of the one-dimensional \(\mathbb F_p\).

For a continuous finite-dimensional real representation \(\rho\) of the reductive group in Section 3.2, let \(R(V)\) be its weights on the chosen maximal split Cartan subspace, \(\Sigma\) the restricted roots, and \(H_\alpha\) the corresponding coroot elements. The text defines evenness by \(\lambda(H_\alpha)\in2\mathbb Z\) for every \(\lambda\in R(V)\) and \(\alpha\in\Sigma\), equivalently \(R(V)\subset2P\). It defines \(\lambda\le\mu\) by \(\lambda(H_\alpha)\le\mu(H_\alpha)\) for all positive roots, asserts that every irreducible representation has a greatest weight for this order, and asserts that evenness may be tested solely on that highest weight for simple roots.

Proposition 3.6 states that, for every connected semisimple Lie group \(S\) and irreducible real representation \(\pi:S\to\mathrm{GL}(V)\), an \(S\)-invariant acute closed convex cone \(c\) exists if and only if \(\pi\) is proximal and even, where proximal means that its highest-weight space is one-dimensional. In that case it further asserts \[\operatorname{int}c\ \cup\ -\operatorname{int}c=\{v\in V\setminus\{0\}:\operatorname{Stab}_S(v)\text{ contains a maximal compact subgroup of }S\},\] with the analogous conclusion from containment of a maximal compact Lie subalgebra in the stabilizer algebra.

Under the general real semisimple Lie-group setup of Section 2.2, the text asserts that every long restricted root \(\alpha\) has a one-dimensional real root space: \[\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathfrak g_\alpha=1.\] The assertion is made before the separate multiplicity-one restriction used later in Theorem 3.4.

For every tuple \(v=(v_i)\) in the root spaces specified in Lemma 10.21(2), the lemma asserts a constant \(C\), independent of the tuple, such that \[\left\|\log(\exp v_1\cdots\exp v_N)-\sum_i v_i\right\|\le C\max_i\|v_i\|^2.\] The quantifier is global in the root parameters; the statement imposes no smallness restriction.

In Lemma A.2 (Article PDF pages 55–57), let \(A=\mathbb Q_p\langle t_1,\ldots,t_l\rangle_\rho\) be a Tate algebra with radii \(\rho_i\) in the value group, and let \(B=(B^0\xrightarrow{d^0}B^1\xrightarrow{d^1}B^0)\) be a two-periodic complex of \(A\)-modules, with \(d^1d^0=d^0d^1=0\) and finitely generated cohomology. In the proof's reduction to \(H^0(B)=0\), choose a finite free resolution \[0\longrightarrow F_k\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_2\longrightarrow F_1\longrightarrow H^1(B)\longrightarrow0\] as in (A.9).

The proof lifts \(F_1\) to \(\ker d^1\subseteq B^1\), and then lifts the next differential to \(B^0\). It asserts that these lifts extend inductively to a chain map from the bounded resolution \(\widetilde F\), with \(F_i\) in degree \(-i\), into the unrolled two-periodic complex \(\widetilde B\), as in (A.11). Periodization is then asserted to give a quasi-isomorphism \[\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}\widetilde F[2m]\longrightarrow\widetilde B\] as in (A.12). The checked assertion is this extension of the chosen lifts and its periodization; no further vanishing of the odd-degree cohomology of \(\widetilde B\) is assumed.

In the rational basis used in Lemma 5.1, fix the lattice denominator \(N\). The set of classes \(\beta\) satisfying \(\omega_i(\beta)\in N^{-1}\mathbb Z\) and \(\omega_i(\beta)>0\) for every coordinate \(i\), with zero adjoined, is asserted to be a finitely generated additive monoid. The inequalities in (5.2) are strict in every coordinate.

In Section 5.3 (Article PDF pages 33–38; printed pages 897–902), \(M_{\ell,r}\) is the paper's extra-twisted connected-sum manifold with cylindrical region \(X\times[-r,r]\), \(\ell\) sufficiently large, \(r\ge\ell\), and gluing angle \(\vartheta\notin\pi\mathbb Z\). Let \(D_{M_{\pm},\ell,r}\) be the induced modified first-order Dirac operators on its halves. The tangential boundary operator \(A\) anticommutes with Clifford multiplication \(\gamma\); \(F^\pm(A)\) are its positive/negative spectral subspaces, with \(\ker A\) excluded. Proposition 5.4 asserts that constants \(c_0,r_0>0\), independent of \(\ell\), exclude every nonzero eigenspinor with \[|\mu|<\frac{c_0}{\ell+r},\qquad r\ge r_0,\qquad\psi_\pm|_{\partial M_{\pm,\ell,r}}\in F^{\mp}(A).\] These are strict APS boundary conditions.

To prove Proposition 5.5, the paper assumes a normalized eigenspinor \(\psi\) of the closed-manifold operator, orthogonal to its parallel kernel spinor, with \(|\lambda|<c/(\ell+r)\). It constructs smooth cutoff spinors \(\psi_\pm\) vanishing at the boundary of each half. Equations (54)–(55) imply, after choosing one half, \[\|\psi_-\|_{L^2}\ge\frac12,\qquad\frac{\|D_{M_-,\ell,r}\psi_-\|_{L^2}}{\|\psi_-\|_{L^2}}\le\frac{Cc}{r}+O(e^{-r/C}).\] The first paragraph of PDF page 38 then infers that, for sufficiently small \(c\), the first-order operator on that half has an eigenvalue below the excluded absolute-value threshold even with full Dirichlet boundary conditions. This implication from a norm quotient to a Dirichlet eigenvalue, and its use of the strict APS exclusion, is the checked step.

Theorem 4.2 (Article PDF pages 20–21) considers the parameterized transfer operators \(\mathcal L_s\phi=\sum_j w_{j,s}(\phi\circ v_j)\), \(s\in[a,b]\), from (28). For some \(r>0\), each operator has a spectral gap in the paper's Hardy space \(H_r^{d,p}\), preserves positive functions on \([-1,1]^d\), and \(-\partial_s\mathcal L_s\) is positive. The theorem assumes constants \(D^-,D^+>0\), independent of \(s,x,\psi\), such that for every bounded \(\psi>0\) and every \(x\in[-1,1]^d\), \[-D^-\sup\psi\le\partial_s(\mathcal L_s\psi)(x)\le-D^+\inf\psi<0.\] Suprema and infima are over the real cube. This reproduces the original bounded-positive quantifier; the report's domain interpretation of it is discussed in the proof below.

Let \(\mathcal P_K\) be the stated polynomial projection, \(s_0\in[a,b]\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(\phi\in H_r^{d,p}\), with constants \(0<\phi^-\le\phi(x)\le\phi^+\) on the cube. Assume that real numbers \(\varepsilon^-<\varepsilon^+\) satisfy \[\varepsilon^-<(\mathcal P_K\mathcal L_{s_0}\phi-\lambda\phi)(x)<\varepsilon^+\quad\text{for every }x\in[-1,1]^d,\] and set \(\mathrm{err}=\|\mathcal L_{s_0}\phi-\mathcal P_K\mathcal L_{s_0}\phi\|_{H_0^{d,p}}\). The asserted enclosure for the unique parameter \(s_*\in[a,b]\) satisfying \(\rho(\mathcal L_{s_*})=\lambda\) is \[s_0+\frac{\varepsilon^--\mathrm{err}}{D^-\phi^+}<s_*<s_0+\frac{\varepsilon^++\mathrm{err}}{D^+\phi^-}.\] The theorem imposes no sign condition on either residual bound.

In the proof of Proposition 2.3, the analytic-function space \(B_0=B_1=\mathcal H^{2,2}_{R_A}\) is asserted to be dense in \(B_2=C^\alpha([-1,1]^2)\) with its full Hölder norm \[\|f\|_{C^\alpha}=\|f\|_\infty+\sup_{x\ne y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{\|x-y\|^\alpha},\qquad0<\alpha<1.\] This norm-density is used to invoke Baladi–Tsujii Lemma A.1; the space is not explicitly defined as the little-Hölder closure.

Fix \(\rho>0\) and let \(\Omega_\rho=\{z\in\mathbb C^2:|\operatorname{Im}z_1|,|\operatorname{Im}z_2|<\rho\}\). Section 10.1 defines \(\operatorname{Diff}^\omega_\rho(\mathbb T^2,\lambda)\) to consist of Lebesgue-measure-preserving real-analytic diffeomorphisms homotopic to the identity, whose lift \(F(x)=x+(f_1(x),f_2(x))\) and inverse lift have periodic displacement functions extending holomorphically and boundedly to \(\Omega_\rho\). With \(\|h\|_\rho=\sup_{\Omega_\rho}|h|\), it uses \[\widetilde d_\rho(F,G)=\max_{i=1,2}\inf_{n\in\mathbb Z}\|f_i-g_i+n\|_\rho,\qquad d_\rho(F,G)=\max\{\widetilde d_\rho(F,G),\widetilde d_\rho(F^{-1},G^{-1})\},\] and asserts that this complete metric space is Polish.

Using that ambient space, Theorem 27 asserts that \[\{(S,T):S,T\text{ are ergodic and Kakutani equivalent}\}\subset\operatorname{Diff}^\omega_\rho(\mathbb T^2,\lambda)^2\] is complete analytic, and hence non-Borel, in the fixed-strip topology. Definitions 16–17 formulate analytic and complete-analytic sets in Polish ambient spaces. The topology examined in this finding is the stated supremum metric on bounded holomorphic functions on the open strip.

For finite words \(C,D\), let \(L(C,D)\) be the largest matching size and \(\overline f(C,D)=1-2L(C,D)/(|C|+|D|)\). In the cited cases of Lemma 14, the proof infers from \(\overline f(C,D)>\alpha\) the matching-size bound \[2|K|<\alpha(|C|+|D|)\] for a match \(K\). This is the local implication under examination, rather than the whole conclusion of Lemma 14.

Definition 17 requires that every analytic subset \(A\) of an arbitrary Polish source space \(X\) admit a continuous reduction to the target: a continuous map \(f\) with \(x\in A\) if and only if \(f(x)\) is in the target. Fact 20 asserts that the set of ill-founded trees is complete analytic under this wording. No restriction to zero-dimensional source spaces appears in the recorded definition.

Let \(X_j\), \(1\le j\le\ell\), be separable reflexive Banach spaces, let \(A:X_1\times\cdots\times X_\ell\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and multilinear, and let \(X_j'\subset X_j\) be dense subspaces with stronger norms dominating \(\|\cdot\|_{X_j}\), whose stronger-norm closed unit balls \(B_{X_j'}\) are closed in \(X_j\). Fix \(m\), and let \(q\) be a seminorm on \(X_m'\) whose convergence on \(B_{X_m'}\) is controlled by convergence in \(X_m\). Proposition A.2 asserts that the condition \[q(x_m)=0\Longrightarrow A(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell)=0\quad\text{for all }x_j\in X_j'\] is equivalent to: for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that, whenever \(x_m\in B_{X_m'}\) and \(q(x_m)\le\delta\), \[\sup_{x_j\in B_{X_j},\ j\ne m}|A(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell)|\le\varepsilon.\] The latter supremum is over the other ambient Banach unit balls.
