Proposition A.1 gives the corresponding uniform conclusion for a fixed commuting measure-preserving system, sub-\(\sigma\)-algebras \(\mathcal Y_j\), and sequences \(a_j\) whose averages \(N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N\prod_jT_j^{a_j(n)}f_j\) converge in \(L^2\) on \(f_j\in L^\infty(\mathcal Y_j)\). If vanishing of one stated Host–Kra seminorm \(\lVert\!\lVert\!\lVert f_m\rVert\!\rVert\!\rVert_s\) forces a zero average, it asserts a \(\delta(\varepsilon)>0\), independent of all the 1-bounded input functions, such that seminorm at most \(\delta\) makes the limiting \(L^2\)-norm at most \(\varepsilon\).

The irrational-equidistribution branch of Corollary 2.7 claims that sequences \(a_1,\ldots,a_\ell:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z\) good for irrational equidistribution satisfy the convergence assertion (9) for every nilmanifold \(X=G/\Gamma\) with Haar measure \(m_X\), every commuting family of nilrotations \(T_jx=b_jx\), and every \(f_j\in L^\infty(m_X)\): \[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}T_j^{a_j(n)}f_j\quad\text{exists in }L^2(m_X).\] No rational-convergence hypothesis is included in that branch.

In particular, for \(\ell=1\), its sequence hypothesis is \(N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^Ne^{2\pi i a(n)t}\to0\) for every irrational \(t\), and the conclusion still ranges over all nilrotations, including rational circle rotations. The finding examines the existence of this limit, rather than the weaker rational-Kronecker-factor approximation (8).

In the proof of Lemma 3.3, the dual functions \(\mathcal D_s f\) are asserted to generate a dense family for the factor \(\mathcal Z_s\). The index \(s\) is the one used in the definition and identity (32); the construction does not use \(\mathcal D_{s+1}\).

Proposition 4.3 defines each maximizing set \(E_k\) by equality of its coordinate modulus with the maximum of finitely many coordinate moduli, and pastes the corresponding eigenfunctions over these sets. It asserts that the resulting function is an admissible non-ergodic eigenfunction, whose pointwise modulus must be zero or one. The set definition allows ties and does not assign a unique maximizing index.

Let \(s\ge1\) and let \((a_h)_{h\in\mathbb N^s}\) be any sequence of nonnegative real numbers. With \([H]=\{1,\ldots,H\}\) and normalized finite averages, Lemma 5.2 asserts for every \(H\in\mathbb N\) that \[\mathbb E_{h,h'\in[H]^s}a_{h-h'}\le\mathbb E_{h\in[H]^s}a_h.\] Its proof asserts the identity \[\mathbb E_{h,h'\in[H]^s}a_{h-h'}=\mathbb E_{h\in[H]^s}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{s}\left(1-\frac{h_i}{H}\right)\right)a_h.\] The displayed sequence domain is the positive box, although the difference indices in the left-hand side can have zero or negative coordinates.

The final sentence of Corollary 2.14 asserts positive lower density for the specified set of shifted primes. In the convention established by its preceding paragraph, this is relative density within \(\mathbb P-1\), not ordinary natural density among all positive integers. The statement retains that relative-density interpretation.

Let \(f:B\to N\) be a smooth submersion between manifolds without boundary, \(\dim N=n\), \(L\subset B\) connected and open with compact closure, and \(K=f(\overline L)\). Proposition 8.5 considers \(n\)-dimensional submanifolds \(S_a\subset\overline L\) with disjoint images, compact closures with finite boundary stratifications, shared codimension-one boundaries unless their images lie in \(\partial K\), and injective restrictions with continuous inverses on cells together with their shared boundaries. It asserts \[f\!\left(\bigcup_{a\in A}\overline{S_a}\right)=K\] without explicitly requiring the index set \(A\) to be finite.

Let \(n\ge2\), \(R>0\), and \(C_r=B_r^n(0)\times(-r,r)\). Theorem 6 assumes that \(M\) is a properly immersed, two-sided stable minimal hypersurface in \(C_{2R}\), with no singular set, \(\sup_{M\cap C_{2R}}|x_{n+1}|<R/2\), and \[E_6(R)^2=R^{-n}\int_{M\cap C_R}\bigl(1-(\nu_M\cdot e_{n+1})^2\bigr)\,d\mathcal H^n\le k(n),\] where \(k(n)>0\) is the dimensional smallness threshold. It asserts a finite smooth graphical decomposition over \(B_{R/2}^n\) and, in particular, \(\sup_{M\cap C_{R/2}}|A_M|\le c(n)E_6(R)\).

Theorem 7 assumes instead proper embedding in \(C_{2R}\setminus\Sigma\), where \(\Sigma\) is relatively closed and has locally finite \(\mathcal H^{n-2}\)-measure or, more generally, zero 2-capacity. With the same height bound, it defines \(E_7(R)^2=R^{-n}\int_{M\cap C_R}(1-\nu_M\cdot e_{n+1})^2\,d\mathcal H^n\), assumes \(E_7(R)^2\le k(n)\), and asserts the same form of estimate \(\sup_{M\cap C_{R/2}}|A_M|\le c(n)E_7(R)\). Both printed bounds are stated for arbitrary \(R\), with \(c(n)\) depending only on dimension and \(|A_M|\) the ordinary second fundamental form.

Let \(n\ge2\), \(R>0\), and \(M\) be a properly embedded, two-sided stable minimal hypersurface in \(C_{2R}\setminus\Sigma\), with \(\Sigma\) relatively closed and of locally finite \(\mathcal H^{n-2}\)-measure, or more generally of zero 2-capacity. Assume \(\sup_{M\cap C_{2R}}|x_{n+1}|<R/2\), and choose its unit normal \(\nu\). Theorem 7 defines \[E_7(R)^2=R^{-n}\int_{M\cap C_R}(1-\nu\cdot e_{n+1})^2\,d\mathcal H^n.\] It asserts that \(E_7(R)^2\le k(n)\) gives a smooth ordered graphical decomposition across \(\Sigma\) in \(C_{R/2}\) and \[\sup_{M\cap C_{R/2}}|A_M|\le c(n)E_7(R).\] The square outside the normal deficit is part of the stated excess, and the finding examines this asserted linear dependence on \(E_7\), including at unit scale.

Let \(k'/k\) be a finite Galois extension of degree \(d\), with \(d\) invertible in the coefficient ring \(\Lambda\), and let \(\sigma:X_{k'}\to X\) be the base-change projection in Theorem 6.13. For the admissible constructible sheaf or complex \(\mathcal F\), the proof asserts an isomorphism of étale sheaves or derived objects \[\sigma_*\sigma^*\mathcal F=\mathcal F^{\oplus d}.\] The assertion is global on \(X\), rather than a statement only about geometric stalk dimensions.

For the generalized wreath product \(H^{(\Gamma)}\rtimes(\Gamma\times\Gamma)\), with the left-right action \((\alpha_{(g,h)}b)_k=b_{g^{-1}kh}\), and an arbitrary normalized cocycle \(\omega_0\in Z^2(H,\mathbb T)\), page 3 declares \[\Omega((a,(g,h)),(b,(g',h')))=\prod_{k\in\Gamma}\omega_0(a_k,b_k)\] to be a normalized two-cocycle on the full semidirect product. The second base coordinate in this displayed formula is not transformed by the action of \((g,h)\).

The paper works over a complete algebraically closed extension \(K/\mathbb Q_p\), with \(X\) smooth and proper. A choice of lift to \(B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+/\xi^2\) and a continuous group splitting \(\mathrm{Exp}\) of the scalar logarithm enters the correspondence. The logarithmic differential bundle is Tate-twisted, and a Higgs field is integrable: \(\theta\wedge\theta=0\). Thus its symmetric-algebra action has commutative image \[B_\theta=\operatorname{im}\bigl(T_X\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_X}(E)\bigr),
 \qquad T_X=\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_X}^{\bullet}\widetilde\Omega_X^\vee.\] This image is coherent and torsion free as an \(\mathcal O_X\)-module. Those conditions matter when applying Theorem 3.22; they must not be discarded for arbitrary coherent quotients.

At the beginning of §3.3, p. 293 (PDF 33), the paper sets \[
 \alpha=\frac{1}{p-1}\quad(p\geq3),\qquad \alpha=2\quad(p=2)\] and correctly defines the power-series exponential on the open set \(p^\alpha\mathfrak m_K\).

In the proof of Lemma 5.7, p. 309 (PDF 49), the same \(\alpha\) is explicitly imported to define the closed Tate algebra \[
 \mathcal T_U=\mathcal O_U\langle p^{-\alpha}\partial_1,\ldots,p^{-\alpha}\partial_d\rangle.\] The proof then defines a continuous cocycle by \(\gamma_i\mapsto\exp(\partial_i)\). On p. 310 (PDF 50), it asserts that \[
 \varphi:R\langle p^{-\alpha}\partial\rangle
 \longrightarrow R\langle p^{-\alpha}T\rangle,\qquad
 \partial\longmapsto\log(1+T)\] is an isomorphism with inverse \(T\mapsto\exp(\partial)-1\). The next step asserts that \(\log(1+T)/T\) is a unit. These assertions supply the claimed equivariant isomorphism of the two Koszul complexes and complete Lemma 5.7 and Theorem 5.5. The original images confirm both the angle brackets and the explicit reference to §3.3; this is not an extraction ambiguity.

In Section 5.2.1, write \(W=\bigcup_i(A_i\cap C_i)\), where the \(C_i\) are disjoint \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^0_2\) sets and \(C_i=\bigcup_n C_{i,n}\) with each \(C_{i,n}\) closed. Define \(W_{i,n}(X)=\{x:\exists k,\ x\upharpoonright k\in X\}\cup(A_i\cap C_{i,n})\), \(\Phi_{i,n}(X)\) as the positions from which I wins this game, \(\Phi=\bigcup_{i,n}\Phi_{i,n}\), and \(P=\Phi^\infty\).

For \(p\notin P\), Case II of Lemma 72 assumes that I wins \(\{x:\exists k,\ x\upharpoonright k\in P\}\cup C_{i,n}\), and defines \[q\in Q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\exists r\preccurlyeq q,\ r\in P)\ \text{or}\ q\in T(C_{i,n}).\] It asserts that \(Q\) is an I-quasi-strategy, which must leave all II moves unrestricted, and hence that an I-winning strategy in the game restricted to \(Q\) would win the unrestricted game.

A Stein compact subset has a basis of Stein open neighborhoods. \(\mathcal O(K)\) and \(\mathcal M(K)\) are rings of germs on neighborhoods of \(K\); they are not rings of functions merely on the underlying point set. In §1.1 the paper permits general second-countable complex spaces, without an implicit connectedness or pure-dimension assumption. Normality is local and does not force distinct connected components to have the same dimension.

Proposition 4.2 is on pp. 23–24. Its proof starts with the normalization \(
u:\widetilde S	o S\), the points \(\widetilde s_i\) above \(s\), and finite surjections \(p_i:T_i	o\widetilde S\) which kill \(
u^*\alpha\) over disjoint neighborhoods \(\Omega_i\) of \(\widetilde s_i\). The first sentence on p. 24 asserts that the fiber product over \(S\) of the maps \(
u\circ p_i\) solves the original problem. The same construction is explicit in the released `compactStein.tex`, line 1299 (one-based). The essential inference is \[p_i^*
u^*\alpha=0\ \hbox{over }p_i^{-1}(\Omega_i\setminus
u^{-1}Z)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 p^*\alpha=0\ \hbox{near }p^{-1}(s)\setminus p^{-1}Z\] for \(p:\prod_S T_i	o S\). It need not hold.

Let \(K\) be a connected Stein compact subset of a normal Stein space \(S\) of dimension \(n\). Theorem 0.4 and the abstract assert \(\operatorname{cd}\mathcal M(K)=n\), where \(\mathcal M(K)\) is the field of meromorphic germs along \(K\). The introductory statement does not require \(S\) to have pure dimension \(n\); the general conventions permit disconnected complex spaces with components of different dimensions.

For the strata \[V_S^\star=\ker M_S\setminus\bigcup_{S_1\supsetneq S}\ker M_{S_1},\] Proposition 5.8 retains the outer sum over all original strata and imposes \(k_r=0\) on each inner sum. It then sets \(\mu=[\{0,\ldots,r-1\}]\), \(\widetilde S=S\cup\{\mu\}\), and replaces the constrained sum on \(V_S^\star\) by the sum on \(V_{\widetilde S}^\star\). Thus the reindexing treats adding the vanishing relation to the stratum label as equivalent to restricting the original exact-vanishing stratum.

Write \(\Omega_1(n)=\sum_{p^a\Vert n,\,p\equiv1\,({\rm mod}\,4)}a\), and let \(b(n)\) be the indicator of integers representable as a sum of two squares. After (8.2), the proof applies \[\sum_{n\le x}h(n)\ll\frac{x}{\log x}\prod_{p\le x}\left(1+\frac{h(p)}p\right)\] to \(h(n)=b(n)2^{\Omega_1(n)}\), invoking the version that requires \(h\) multiplicative and \(0\le h(n)\le d(n)\) for every \(n\). The source definition of \(\Omega_1\) counts prime factors with multiplicity.

On \(\mathbb R^2\), let \[P_t(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{t}{(t^2+|x|^2)^{3/2}},\qquad Q_tf=t\nabla(P_t*f).\] Let \(\rho\in\mathrm{BMO}(\mathbb R^2)\), let \(F\) be a bounded, compactly supported scalar function on \(\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\), and let \(m\) be a measurable scalar function on \((0,\infty)\) with \(|m(t)|\le1\). Write \(F^t(x)=F(x,t)\), \(\check F(x,t)=Q_tF^t(x)\), and define the nontangential maximal function \[N\check F(x)=\sup_{t>0,\,|z-x|<t}|\check F(z,t)|.\] Arbitrary dependence of \(F\) on \(t\) is allowed.

Proposition 2.3 and (17) (Article PDF pages 7–8; printed pages 639–640) assert that a universal constant \(C\), independent of \(\rho,F,m\), satisfies \[\left\|\int_0^\infty (Q_t\rho)\cdot(Q_tF^t)\,m(t)\,\frac{dt}{t}\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le C\|\rho\|_{\mathrm{BMO}(\mathbb R^2)}\,\|N\check F\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}.\]

With unstable-minus-stable convention fixed by (11.4) and the perturbation \(+\mu\Delta(\phi)\) fixed by (11.6), define \(c_{\rm in}^d(\Delta)=\left.\partial_\mu C_{\rm in}(\mu\Delta)\right|_{\mu=0}\). For \(\xi=\xi_3^+\) and the inner breather \(\phi_b\), put \[I(\Delta)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\int_0^{2\pi}\xi(z+s,\tau)\Delta(\phi_b(z+s,\tau))\,d\tau\,ds.\] Proposition 11.4 prints \(c_{\rm in}^d=+I/(2\pi i\mu_3)\), while Lemma 11.5 further identifies the derivative with the unnormalized integral \(I\).

Theorems 1.5 and 6.7 assert the existence of an absolute \(n_0\) such that, for every \(n\ge n_0\), every group \(G\), and all \(A,B\subseteq G\) with \(|A|=|B|=n\), the multiplication subsquare \(A\times B\) has a transversal unless one of the following configurations occurs for some subgroup \(H\le G\) and \(g_1,g_2\in G\). First, \(H\) fails the Hall–Paige condition and \(A=g_1H\), \(B=Hg_2\). Second, for some \(k\ge1\), \(H\cong(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^k\) and \[g_1A=H\setminus\{a_1,a_2\},\qquad g_2B=H\setminus\{b_1,b_2\},\] where \(a_1\ne a_2\), \(b_1\ne b_2\), and \(a_1+a_2+b_1+b_2=0\) in \(H\). Both normalizations in this second printed exception are left multiplications, even when the ambient group \(G\) is nonabelian.

Let \(G\) be a sufficiently large finite group of order \(n\). Its division digraph has an edge \(a\to b\) only for \(a\ne b\), with colour \(a^{-1}b\). Theorem 6.9 assumes \(V,C\subseteq G\), distinct \(x,y\notin V\), and \(|V|+1=|C|\ge n-\sqrt n\). It excludes \(e\) from \(C\) only when \(G\) is an elementary abelian 2-group. Under \(\sum C=y-x\) in \(G^{\mathrm{ab}}\), it asserts a directed rainbow Hamilton path from \(x\) to \(y\) on \(\{x,y\}\cup V\) with colours from \(C\).

The related Theorem 4.7 samples \((R^1)^{-1}\) and \(R^2\) as disjoint \(p\)-random subsets, and \(R^3\) independently, with \(p\ge n^{-1/10^{102}}\). With high probability it asserts a perfect matching in the multiplication hypergraph \(H_G[X,Y,Z]\) for every equal-size triple satisfying \[|(R_A^1\cup R_B^2\cup R_C^3)\mathbin\triangle(X\cup Y\cup Z)|\le\frac{p^{10^{18}}n}{(\log n)^{10^{18}}},\qquad\sum X+\sum Y+\sum Z=0\text{ in }G^{\mathrm{ab}},\] with \(e\notin Z\) required only for elementary abelian 2-groups. In the non-elementary case, its proof asserts property (P) for \(R^1\times R^2\): at least \(p^2n/1000\) pairs of the form \((u,u^{-1})\), even though \((R^1)^{-1}\cap R^2=\varnothing\). This matching step is passed to the orthomorphism and path constructions in Theorem 4.9 and Lemma 6.22.

Let \(H_G\) be the tripartite multiplication hypergraph of a group \(G\) of order \(n\), with vertex parts \(A,B,C\). For \(p\ge n^{-1/650}\), let \(A',B',C'\) be \(p\)-random subsets of the respective parts; the three subsets need not be independent. Put \(R=A'\cup B'\cup C'\). Lemma 3.9 asserts that, with high probability, simultaneously for every \(0\le q\le5p\) and every \(X\subseteq V(H_G)\setminus R\) satisfying \[|X\cap A|,\ |X\cap B|,\ |X\cap C|=(1\pm n^{-1/4})qn,\] the induced hypergraph on \(R\cup X\) has a matching leaving at most \(n^{1-10^{-4}}\) vertices of \(R\cup X\) uncovered.

Lemma 3.4 is stated for every sufficiently large \(n\) and every \((\gamma,\delta,n)\)-regular linear tripartite hypergraph, with part sizes and vertex degrees in the ranges prescribed by the regularity definition: approximately \(n\) vertices per part and degree \(\delta n\), within relative error \(\gamma\). Linearity means that a pair of vertices lies in at most one hyperedge. It asserts a matching leaving at most \[n^{1-1/500}+3\gamma n\] vertices uncovered. The statement gives no lower bound on \(\delta\) and no explicit requirement that \(\delta n\) grow with \(n\), so its displayed uniform scope includes bounded-degree regular examples.

Let \(G\) have order \(n\), let \(p\ge n^{-1/10^{100}}\), and let \(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\subseteq G\) be disjoint symmetric \(p\)-random subsets. Put \(Q=(Q_1)_A\cup(Q_2)_B\cup(Q_3)_C\) in the multiplication hypergraph \(H_G\), and \(t=p^{10^{10}}n/(\log n)^{10^{10}}\). Lemma 5.34 asserts that, with high probability, for every pair \(S,U\subseteq V(H_G)\) with \(|S|,|U|\le t\) and no identity vertex in \(S\), there is a matching \(M\) in \(H_G[Q]\setminus U\) with \(|M|\le2t\) and \(S\subseteq V(M)\). No assumption \(S\subseteq Q\) or \(S\cap U=\varnothing\) accompanies this universal saturation claim.

Let \(G\) be a countable group with a free factor system \(\mathcal F=\{[G_1],\ldots,[G_k]\}\), so that \(G=G_1*\cdots*G_k*F_N\), with finitely many peripheral factors and a free group \(F_N\) of finite rank. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a class of groups that contains \(\mathbb Z\) and is closed under isomorphisms, subgroups, extensions, and passage to finite-index supergroups. A group \(B\) satisfies the Tits alternative relative to \(\mathcal C\) if every subgroup \(H\le B\) either belongs to \(\mathcal C\) or contains a subgroup isomorphic to the rank-two free group \(F_2\). This quantifier includes infinitely generated subgroups.

Assume that every peripheral group \(G_i\) satisfies this relative Tits alternative. Theorem 6.3 asserts that \(\operatorname{Out}(G,\mathcal F^{(t)})\) also satisfies it. Here \(\operatorname{Out}(G,\mathcal F^{(t)})\) consists of outer automorphisms acting by conjugation on each peripheral factor. Thus the asserted conclusion is that every \(H\le\operatorname{Out}(G,\mathcal F^{(t)})\) lies in \(\mathcal C\) or contains \(F_2\). No finite-generation assumption is imposed on the peripheral groups themselves.

The more general Theorem 6.2 takes subgroups \(A_i\le\operatorname{Out}(G_i)\) and assumes that both \(G_i\) and \(A_i\) satisfy the relative alternative for every \(i\). It asserts the alternative for the subgroup \(\operatorname{Out}(G,\mathcal F^{\mathcal A})\) preserving each peripheral conjugacy class and inducing an element of \(A_i\) on each \(G_i\). Taking every \(A_i=\{1\}\) gives Theorem 6.3. These relative statements use the listed closure properties of \(\mathcal C\), without an additional assumption of closure under central quotients.

Consider Step 2a in the \(n=5\) proof of Theorem 1.5, which is stated for \(n\ge5\). Let \(\mathcal C\) be the reference catenoid and let \(H=\Delta_{\mathcal C}+|\mathrm{II}|^2\) have the positive eigenvalue \(\mu^2\), with eigenfunction \(\varphi_\mu\). Set \(\widetilde\varphi_\mu=\chi\varphi_\mu\), where \(\chi=1\) on \(\mathcal C\cap\{|X|<R/3\}\) and is supported in \(\mathcal C\cap\{|X|<R/2\}\). The initial functions \(\psi_0,\psi_1\in C_c^\infty(\mathcal C)\) are supported in this latter region and satisfy (1.19), \[\sum_{j=0}^{M}\left(\|\langle\rho\rangle^{1+j}\partial_\Sigma^{1+j}(\psi_0\circ F)\|_{L^2(dV_{\mathcal C})}+\|\langle\rho\rangle^{1+j}\partial_\Sigma^j(\psi_1\circ F)\|_{L^2(dV_{\mathcal C})}\right)\le1,\] for the fixed large regularity index \(M\). Here \(F\) is the source parametrization, \(dV_{\mathcal C}=\sqrt{|g_{\mathcal C}|}\,d\omega\,d\rho\), and \(\partial_\Sigma\) denotes \(\partial_\rho\) or \(\langle\rho\rangle^{-1}\partial_\omega\).

For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the printed one-parameter family varies the physical displacement and velocity by \[\Phi|_{t=0}=\Phi_0[\varepsilon(\psi_0+b\widetilde\varphi_\mu)],\qquad \partial_t\Phi|_{t=0}=\Phi_1[\varepsilon(\psi_1-\mu b\widetilde\varphi_\mu)],\] where \(\Phi_0[\eta]=F+(\eta\circ F)N\circ F\) and \(\Phi_1[\eta]=(1,0)+(\eta\circ F)N\circ F\), with the specified normal field \(N\). The negative sign in the physical-velocity correction is part of (5.24).

Using the fixed continuous extension of the initial data to \([-1,0]\) and the modulation/orthogonality construction, define \[a_+(t)=\boldsymbol\Omega(\vec\psi,Z_-)-e^{\mu t}\widetilde S(e^{-\mu t}F_+),\qquad q(t)=\dot a_+(t)=\mu a_+(t)-e^{\mu t}S(e^{-\mu t}F_+),\] and \(\mathcal Z(\psi_0,\psi_1,b)=q(0)\). The smoothing operators \(S,\widetilde S\), forcing \(F_+\), phase-space variable \(\vec\psi\), and mode \(Z_-\) are those fixed in Section 3.7. Assume the codimension-one condition \(\mathcal Z(\psi_0,\psi_1,0)=0\).

Step 2a claims that for every \(q_0\) with \(|q_0|\le\lambda_0=C_{\mathrm{trap}}\delta_{\wp}\varepsilon\), there is a \(b\) in a neighborhood of zero for which \(q(0)=q_0\). Its stated transversality input is \[\boldsymbol\Omega\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}\widetilde\varphi_\mu\\-\mu\widetilde\varphi_\mu\end{pmatrix},Z_-\right)\simeq1,\qquad |\partial_b\mathcal Z(\psi_0,\psi_1,0)|\gtrsim1,\] with the symplectic convention \(\boldsymbol\Omega(U,V)=\int(U_1V_2-U_2V_1)\,d\rho\,d\omega\). These are the printed leading-pairing and derivative assertions used to obtain the entire trapping interval.

In the \(n=5\) bootstrap of Section 5, put \(D=\partial_r+2/r\), and let \(X^k\) denote a product of the exterior commutators \(\widetilde rL,\Omega,T\). For \(0\le p\le2\), \(0\le j\le2\), and \(k+3j\le M-2\), (5.12) assumes \[\|\chi_{\ge R}r^pDX^kT^j\phi\|_{L^2(\Sigma_\tau)}\le2C\varepsilon\tau^{-1-j+p/2}.\] Proposition 5.2, under (5.1)–(5.12) and the orthogonality conditions (3.39), (3.51), asserts that sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\) and sufficiently large bootstrap constants improve the right-hand side to \(C\varepsilon\tau^{-1-j+p/2}\), as in (5.23).

The specific step examined is the closing proof's assertion that Lemmas 8.10–8.11 have already supplied this norm estimate. Their hierarchy uses \(\widetilde\psi=\widetilde r^2\psi\), its commuted versions \(\widetilde\psi_k\), and the energy \[E_k^p[\psi](\sigma)=\int_{\Sigma_\sigma}\chi_{\ge\widetilde R}\widetilde r^p(L\widetilde\psi_k)^2\,d\theta\,dr.\] The claimed implication concerns the transfer of this energy weight to the displayed \(r^pD\)-norm with the paper's \(L^2(\Sigma_\tau)\) convention; it is not a claim that the free-wave example satisfies every hypothesis of Proposition 5.2.

In the \(n=5\) part of the catenoid stability proof, let \(\Sigma_\tau\) be a leaf of the prescribed spacelike foliation of the modulated catenoid, with exterior coordinates \((\rho,\omega)\), \(\omega\in\mathbb S^4\). The convention in Section 2.1.5 uses the induced geometric volume \(dV_{\Sigma_\tau}\) unless another measure is specified. In the associated Euclidean coordinate \(y=\rho\omega\in\mathbb R^5\), write \(dy=\rho^4\,d\rho\,d\omega\). The passage immediately before (8.39) asserts that this Euclidean measure is comparable to \(dV_{\Sigma_\tau}\) for large \(\rho\): there are positive comparison constants independent of the exterior radius such that \[c\,dy\le dV_{\Sigma_\tau}\le C\,dy.\]

The same passage specifies that \(\partial_\Sigma\) denotes the coordinate derivatives \(\partial_\rho\) and \(\rho^{-1}\partial_\omega\). With these derivative and induced-measure conventions, Lemma 8.14 asserts that every \(\psi\in H^3(\Sigma_\tau)\) satisfies \[\|\psi\|_{L^\infty(\Sigma_\tau)}\le C\|\partial_\Sigma^2\psi\|_{L^2(dV_{\Sigma_\tau})}^{1/2}\|\partial_\Sigma^3\psi\|_{L^2(dV_{\Sigma_\tau})}^{1/2},\] where the comparison constant is independent of \(\psi\) and of the radial location of its support. These measure-comparison and interpolation assertions are used in the final pointwise bootstrap estimates.

Write \(\omega=(a,b,c)\in\Omega=[-1,1]^3\), with \(p_\omega=(a,b)\) and \(\ell_\omega=\{(a+t,b+ct):t\in\mathbb R\}\). A scale \(u\times v\times w\) is admissible when \(v\geq uw\). Equation (14), printed p. 1064, defines \[
d_{u\times v\times w}(\omega_0\to\omega_1)
=\max\left\{\frac{|a_1-a_0|}{u},
\frac{|b_1-b_0-c_0(a_1-a_0)|}{v},
\frac{|c_1-c_0|}{w}\right\}.\] An omitted coordinate, written \(\square\) in the paper, is equivalent to an infinite denominator. The paper explicitly treats coinciding point or line projections as multisets.

On printed p. 1047 (PDF p. 3), equation (3) defines \[
d_{\rm old}(\ell_0,\ell_1)
=|\operatorname{dist}(0,\ell_0)-\operatorname{dist}(0,\ell_1)|
+|\theta(\ell_0)-\theta(\ell_1)|.\] The distance to the origin is unsigned. Equation (17) on printed p. 1065 (PDF p. 21) asserts comparison of this line distance with \(d_{\square\times1\times1}\). The second line of (18) further asserts \[
d_{1\times w\times w}(\omega_0\to\omega_1)
\leq (2/w)d_{\rm old}(\ell_{\omega_0},\ell_{\omega_1})+2.\] The issue is the mathematical comparison, not just the word metric.

Write \(\omega=(a,b,c)\in\Omega=[-1,1]^3\), with \(p_\omega=(a,b)\) and \(\ell_\omega=\{(a+t,b+ct):t\in\mathbb R\}\). A scale \(u\times v\times w\) is admissible when \(v\geq uw\). Equation (14), printed p. 1064, defines \[
d_{u\times v\times w}(\omega_0\to\omega_1)
=\max\left\{\frac{|a_1-a_0|}{u},
\frac{|b_1-b_0-c_0(a_1-a_0)|}{v},
\frac{|c_1-c_0|}{w}\right\}.\] An omitted coordinate, written \(\square\) in the paper, is equivalent to an infinite denominator. The paper explicitly treats coinciding point or line projections as multisets.

Section 3.3, printed p. 1066 (PDF p. 22), defines \[\mathcal C_{u\times v\times w}
=(2^{-10}u\mathbb Z)\times(2^{-10}v\mathbb Z)\times(2^{-10}w\mathbb Z)\] and the rectangle family \(\mathcal R_{u\times v\times w}\) centered on this fixed lattice. For \(R=R_{u_0\times u_0w_0\times w_0}(\omega_0)\), Section 3.4 defines \[\psi_R(a,b,c)=
\left(\frac{a-a_0}{u_0},
\frac{b-b_0-c_0(a-a_0)}{u_0w_0},
\frac{c-c_0}{w_0}\right).\] Lemma 3.3 on printed p. 1068 (PDF p. 24) correctly states a phase-space isometry, then claims that \(\psi_R^{-1}\) bijects the fixed rectangle families. Its last proof paragraph explicitly claims the corresponding bijection of \(\mathcal C\) lattices. The shear term prevents that last assertion.

In the bifoliated-plane setting of Section 5, let \(G\) act on \(P\) preserving its transverse foliations \(\mathcal F^+\) and \(\mathcal F^-\), with the stated nontrivial, non-affine Anosov-like action. For \(a,b\in P\), write \(a\mathrel{\mathrm{TL}}b\) when both \(\mathcal F^+(a)\cap\mathcal F^-(b)\ne\varnothing\) and \(\mathcal F^+(b)\cap\mathcal F^-(a)\ne\varnothing\). This is the inclusive total-linking definition, which allows points on the same leaf.

Let \((z_n)\subset P\) be pairwise totally linked and converge to \(z\in P\cup\partial P\). Let \(w\in P\) be a non-corner positive fixed point of \(g\in G\), in the terminology of the paper, with \(w\mathrel{\mathrm{TL}}z_n\) for every \(n\). Define condition \((*)\) by the full quantifiers \[\exists i_0\ \forall i\ge i_0\ \exists K_i\ \forall k>K_i:\quad\left[\ \forall j\le i,\ \neg(g^{-k}z_i\mathrel{\mathrm{TL}}z_j)\quad\text{and}\quad\exists N_{i,k}\ \forall n>N_{i,k},\ g^{-k}z_i\mathrel{\mathrm{TL}}z_n\ \right].\] In particular, the tail threshold may depend on \(i\) and \(k\).

Corollary 5.8 asserts \[(*)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z\in\mathcal F^-(w),\] with ideal endpoints excluded from \(\mathcal F^-(w)\) by the source convention. Its hypotheses do not require \(z_n\notin\mathcal F^-(w)\), do not require \(z\ne w\), and do not require distinct terms. The subsequent extension argument invokes this criterion, and Remark 5.22 asserts that the same proof remains valid on later enlarged domains of the conjugacy map \(H\).

The proof of Theorem 7.1 constructs a closed auxiliary manifold \(N'\) by removing a periodic-orbit neighborhood from each of two closed flow manifolds and gluing the torus boundaries. It asserts that the resulting Anosov flow \(\phi_{N'}\) has an attracting set and no repelling set, and uses that asymmetry to exclude every direction-reversing self-orbit equivalence.

Example 1 asserts an Anosov-like action on the plane with horizontal and vertical foliations, generated by \[\tau_1(x,y)=(x+1,y),\quad\tau_2(x,y)=(x,y+1),\quad D_\lambda(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-1}y).\] Under its stated axiom (A1), every nonidentity group element preserving a leaf must have a fixed point on that leaf, with the prescribed transverse hyperbolic behavior.

Let \(G\) act on a bifoliated plane \((P,\mathcal F^+,\mathcal F^-)\), preserving both foliations. Definition 8.1 imposes topological hyperbolicity (A1), together with conditions (2) and (3). Condition (2) says that, for every sequence of pairwise distinct \(g_n\in G\) and every \(x\in P\) with \(g_nx\to y\), every foliated box \(V\) about \(y\), and every pair of compact sets \(K^\pm\subset\mathcal F^\pm(x)\), eventually exactly one of \(g_nK^+\) and \(g_nK^-\) is contained in \(V\). The compact sets are not required to contain a nondegenerate leaf segment.

Condition (3) requires, for every \(x\), sequences \(g_n^+\) and \(g_n^-\) with \(g_n^\pm x\to y^\pm\), such that for all neighborhoods \(V^\pm\) of \(y^\pm\) and all compact sets \(K^\pm\subset\mathcal F^\pm(x)\), eventually \(g_n^+K^+\subset V^+\) and \(g_n^-K^-\subset V^-\). The issue concerns these literal quantifiers in the proposed dynamical characterization; the printed condition (3) does not itself require the two sequences to consist of pairwise distinct elements.

Section 9.1 considers the family of pairs \((g,\Sigma)\in\mathcal M^{k,\alpha}(M)\) satisfying \(\|g\|_{C^{k,\alpha}}\le\Lambda\), \(\mathcal H_g^7(\Sigma)\le\Lambda\), and \(\operatorname{index}(\Sigma,g)\le I\). For every \(\delta>0\), it asserts compactness after removing the pairs within \(\delta\), in the specified metric-plus-varifold distance, of a bounded pair with hypersurface multiplicity \(m\ge2\). The displayed metric restriction is an upper bound, without a uniform lower positive-definiteness bound.

For a connected one-sided hypersurface \(\Sigma\subset M\) in the geometric class of Section 2, the paragraph before (1) asserts that there is a unique ambient double cover \(\widehat M\to M\) whose inverse image of \(\Sigma\) is connected and two-sided. The uniqueness concerns the ambient cover, rather than only the intrinsic orientation cover of the hypersurface.

In Appendix D let \(U\subset M\) be an arbitrary precompact open set with \(\partial U\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)=\varnothing\), and put \(\mathcal U=U\cap\Sigma\). For the specified Dirichlet operator and its lowest eigenspace \(E_1\), Lemma D.3(i) asserts \(\dim E_1=1\) and a positive first eigenfunction. No connectedness assumption on \(\mathcal U\) is included.

In the paper's setting, let \(M\) be a closed eight-dimensional manifold, \(k\ge4\) an integer, \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and \(g\) a \(C^{k,\alpha}\) Riemannian metric. Let \((\Sigma,
u)\) be a two-sided locally stable minimal hypersurface in the stated hypersurface class, with global unit normal \(
u\). Let \(G<\operatorname{Diff}(M)\) be finite and act freely on \(M\), with \(\gamma^*g=g\) and \(\gamma(\Sigma)=\Sigma\) for every \(\gamma\in G\). Its Jacobi operator is \[L_{\Sigma,g}=\Delta_{\Sigma,g}+|A_{\Sigma,g}|^2+\operatorname{Ric}_g(
u,
u).\]

The action on normal scalar functions is the action of Definition 8.1, \[(\gamma\cdot u)(x)=u(\gamma^{-1}x)\,\langle\gamma_*
u(\gamma^{-1}x),
u(x)angle_g.\] Thus a \(G\)-invariant solution means \(\gamma\cdot u=u\) for every \(\gamma\in G\), retaining the possible sign from reversal of the normal. Let \(C^{k,\alpha}(M)^G\) be the ambient invariant-function space used in the lemma, and write \(
u(f)=df(
u)|_\Sigma\).

A function \(u\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Sigma)\) has slower growth, in Definition 2.5, if \[\operatorname{AR}_p(u)\ge\gamma_2^+(C_p\Sigma)\qquad\text{for every }p\in\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma).\] Here \(C_p\Sigma\) is the tangent cone, \(\gamma_2^+\) is its specified second plus-branch indicial exponent, and the asymptotic rate is \[\operatorname{AR}_p(u)=\sup\left\{a:\lim_{s\downarrow0}\int_{A_g(p;s,2s)\cap\Sigma}u^2\rho^{-7-2a}\,d\Sigma=0\right\},\qquad\rho(x)=\operatorname{dist}_g(x,\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)).\] If the singular set is empty, the slower-growth condition is vacuous, as explicitly stated in the definition.

Lemma D.6 asserts that \[\mathcal F_G^{k,\alpha}=\{f\in C^{k,\alpha}(M)^G:L_{\Sigma,g}u=\nu(f)\text{ has no slower-growth }G\text{-invariant solution }u\}\] contains an open dense subset of \(C^{k,\alpha}(M)^G\), in its \(C^{k,\alpha}\) topology. The lemma does not assume \(\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\).

Let \(e:T^2\times[-r,0]\to T^2\times[-r,r]\) be a collar with bottom height \(-r\) and \(\partial_\rho e^2(y,-r)=1\). Proposition 7.2 treats \[e_t(y,\rho)=\left(e^1(y,t(\rho+r)-r),-r+\frac{e^2(y,t(\rho+r)-r)+r}{t}\right),\qquad t>0,\] as the proposed homotopy in the same collar space. In particular the image is asserted to remain in \(T^2\times[-r,r]\) throughout the homotopy.

For every smooth closed surface \(\Gamma\subset N_r(\Sigma)\), equation (6.1) asserts \[\bigl|\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma)-\|p_\#\Gamma\|\bigr|\le\Lambda r^2,\] where \(p\) is the tube projection and \(\Lambda\) depends only on the ambient manifold. The assertion contains no bound on the area or slope of \(\Gamma\).

With the parameter space \(X\), embedding space \(\operatorname{Emb}(\Sigma,M)\), and isometric torus orbit \(\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\) of Section 6, Lemma 6.4 asserts: for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\varepsilon'>0\) such that any continuous \(f:X\to\operatorname{Emb}(\Sigma,M)\) satisfying \(\mathbf F(f(x),\mathcal T(\Sigma,M))<\varepsilon'\) for every \(x\in X\) admits a continuous \(g:X\to\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\) with \(\mathbf F(f(x),g(x))<\varepsilon\) for every \(x\). Moreover, for every \(x\in\partial X\), \(g(x)\) must equal the non-parametrized oriented torus induced by \(f(x)\). No hypothesis in this lemma requires the boundary tori \(f(\partial X)\) already to lie in \(\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\).

The domain \(\operatorname{Emb}_0(T^2,N_r(C_q))\) is defined by belonging to the global embedding component in \(M\) and having essential image in the tube. The target \(\mathcal T_{\min}(q)\) fixes the orientation determined by \(q\). Proposition 7.2 includes \(k=0\) and asserts surjectivity onto every path component of that domain, without separately restricting the domain to the positive local homology class.

With \(\operatorname{isom}(M)\) explicitly the identity component of the isometry group, define \[\overline{\mathcal T}_{\min}=\operatorname{isom}(M)/\operatorname{isom}^+(M,T).\] For the stated lens-space range \(q\ne1\), \(p>2\), Proposition 2.3(3) asserts that this quotient has two points, and the following paragraph describes the connected \(\mathcal T_{\min}\cong\operatorname{isom}(M)\) as a \(T^2\)-bundle over it.

Under Proposition 5.10's arrangement hypotheses, if no smaller member of \(\mathcal B\) contains \(\sigma_W\), the asserted algebraic boundary identity is \[L^{\mathcal B}\cap E_W^{\mathcal B}=(L_{\sigma_W}^{\mathcal B_W}\times P^{\mathcal B_{/W}})\cup(P^{\mathcal B_W}\times L_{\sigma_{/W}}^{\mathcal B_{/W}}).\] Here \(L^{\mathcal B}\) is the union of the Zariski closures of the facets of the blown-up polytope. The allowed center may be larger than the Zariski span of the face it meets.

For the rational flag \(F:0\subset V_d\subset\cdots\subset V_1\subset V\) and parabolic endomorphism space \(\mathcal P_F\) of Appendix A.4, (A.25) asserts that the Gram assignment \([M]\mapsto[M^{\mathsf T}M]\) is a morphism \(\mathbb P(\mathcal P_F)\to\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V))\). It sends \(\mathbb P(\mathcal P_0\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathcal P_i)\) to \(\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V/V_{i+1}))\). Equation (A.26) then asserts that the corresponding iterated blow-ups induce a morphism \(B_F\mathbb P(\mathcal P_F)\to B_F\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V))\), where the target centers are the nested projective spaces \(\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V/V_1)),\ldots,\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V/V_d))\).

Writing \(\mathcal P_F^\circ\) for the open subset in which each specified row component is nonzero, (A.31) further claims that the map from \((A_P\times\mathcal H)\backslash(\overline A_P\times\mathcal P_F^\circ)\) takes values in \(B_F\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V))\setminus\widetilde{\operatorname{Det}}\). On the locus where all torus parameters are nonzero, this is the asserted morphism \(\mathbb G_m\backslash\mathcal P_F^\circ\to\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V))\setminus\operatorname{Det}\), \([M]\mapsto[M^{\mathsf T}M]\). The domain requires nonzero row components, not invertibility; the source explicitly notes that it is larger than the complement of the determinant locus.

For a rational flag \(0\subset V_d\subset\cdots\subset V_1\subset V\), let \(E_P\) denote the closed exceptional locus associated with its parabolic \(P\), and let \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Det}}\) be the strict transform of the determinant hypersurface in the iterated blow-up of the projective space of quadratic forms. Theorem A.2 identifies \[E_P\setminus(E_P\cap\widetilde{\operatorname{Det}})\cong\prod_{k=0}^d\left(\mathbb P\!\left(\mathcal Q(V/V_{k+1})/\mathcal Q(V/V_k)\right)\setminus\operatorname{Det}|_{V_k/V_{k+1}}\right),\] with \(V_0=V\) and \(V_{d+1}=0\). Here the determinant condition is imposed after restricting the form to the indicated successive quotient.

Equation (A.28) makes the corresponding identification for every subflag \(F'\le F\): it starts with the closed exceptional locus, described as a product of iterated blow-ups, removes only \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Det}}\), and obtains a product of unblown projective determinant complements. Theorem A.2 also asserts \(f(e(P))=f(X^{\mathrm{BS}})\cap E_P(\mathbb R)\) for the embedding of the Borel–Serre bordification, thus using the closed exceptional locus to identify the image of the open boundary stratum \(e(P)\). These are the product and stratum assertions under examination.

Footnote 3 asserts that minimizing the maximal coordinate arrangement by the face-intersection rule of Definition 5.13 gives the core arrangement: \[(\mathcal B^{G,\max})^{\min}=\mathcal B^{G,\mathrm{core}}.\] The statement concerns the actual arrangements of coordinate centers associated with the graph, not only a comparison morphism between their blow-ups.

For a nonzero vector \(v\in V\), let \(f_v:\mathcal Q(V)\to\mathbb Q\) be the scalar linear functional \(f_v(Q)=Q(v,v)\). The first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 9.4 asserts the ambient vector-space identity \[\ker f_v=\mathcal Q(V/\mathbb Qv).\] This assertion ranges over all quadratic forms, without restricting them to a positive semidefinite cone.

Let \(\pi_f(x,y,z)=(x+f(z)y,z)\), where \(f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R\) is twice differentiable with \(1\le|f'(z)|\le2\) and \(|f''(z)|\le1/100\) throughout the interval. Proposition 7.1 asserts that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there are \(\eta,\delta_0>0\) such that, for \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), every family \(\mathbb T\) of \(\delta\)-tubes satisfying the Tube Wolff axioms with error \(\delta^{-\eta}\), and every \(\delta^\eta\)-dense shading \(Y\), satisfy \[\left|\bigcup_{T\in\mathbb T}\pi_f(Y(T))\right|\ge\delta^\varepsilon.\] The Tube Wolff condition requires that each \(\rho\)-tube contain at most \(\delta^{-\eta}|T_\rho|\,\#\mathbb T\) tubes of the family; the underlying tube definition permits arbitrary directions.

Under the same assumptions, Lemma 7.12 asserts the existence of \(\rho\in(\delta^{1-\varepsilon^2},1)\) and a \(\delta^{4\eta}\)-dense shading \(Y'\subset Y\) such that, for \(A=\bigcup_T\pi_f(Y'(T))\), \(|A|\ge(\delta/\rho)^\varepsilon|N_\rho(A)|\). Its proof represents tube directions by lines \((a+ct,b+dt,t)\) after a refinement and rotation, although the statement does not impose transversality to the last coordinate. The cited cinematic-family step also treats \(\{a+bf(t)+dtf(t):a,b,d\in[-1,1]\}\) as cinematic under the displayed derivative bounds alone; no condition \(f(0)=0\) is included.

In the proof of Theorem 1.4, put \(\varepsilon=(3-\alpha)/4\) and \(\eta_1=(3-\varepsilon)\eta/6\). The covering and two-sided measure estimates yield \[(r/\rho)^{3-\varepsilon}\rho^{\alpha+\eta_1}\lesssim r^{\alpha-\eta_1},\qquad\delta\le\rho\le\delta^\eta r,\quad r\ge\delta.\] With this parameter choice the proof claims a contradiction as \(\delta\downarrow0\), for the dimension range \(\alpha<3\) that includes values arbitrarily close to three.

Let \(n\ge1\), and let \(\Omega^+,\Omega^-\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be disjoint open sets whose union satisfies the capacity density condition of Definition 2.2. Thus the complement has capacity bounded below at every boundary center and every radius below the diameter; for \(n=1\) this means \(\operatorname{Cap}_L(B(z,r)\setminus(\Omega^+\cup\Omega^-))\ge cr\). For the rescaled spherical sections \(V^\pm(x,r)=\{r^{-1}(x-y):y\in S(x,r)\cap\Omega^\pm\}\), let \(\alpha^\pm(x,r)\) be the characteristic constants determined by their first Dirichlet eigenvalues through \(\lambda=\alpha(n-1+\alpha)\), and put \[\mathcal A(x)^2=\int_0^1\min\{1,\alpha^+(x,r)+\alpha^-(x,r)-2\}\,\frac{dr}{r}.\]

Theorem B asserts that, outside an \(\mathcal H^n\)-null set, \(\mathcal A(x)<\infty\) if and only if \(x\) is a true tangent point of the pair. This means \(x\in\partial\Omega^+\cap\partial\Omega^-\) and there is a unit vector \(u\) such that, for every \(a\in(0,1)\), some \(r>0\) satisfies \((\partial\Omega^+\cup\partial\Omega^-)\cap X_a(x,u)\cap B(x,r)=\varnothing\), where \(X_a(x,u)=\{y:|(y-x)\cdot u|>a|y-x|\}\); one component of the truncated double cone lies in \(\Omega^+\) and the other in \(\Omega^-\). The theorem includes the planar case \(n=1\).

Let \(\Omega^+,\Omega^-\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be disjoint Borel sets, \(B_0=B(x_0,r_0)\), and \(\mu\) a Radon measure supported on \(E\subset B_0\), with \(\mu(B(x,r))\le C_0r^n\) and \(\mu(B_0)\ge c_0r_0^n\), where \(0<c_0<1\), as in Lemma 5.1. Write \(\varepsilon_n\) for the spherical discrepancy coefficient of Definition 2.4 and, with \(\psi(y)=e^{-|y|^2}\), set \[\mathfrak a^i(x,r)=\left|c_\psi-r^{-(n+1)}\int_{\Omega^i}\psi((x-y)/r)\,dy\right|,\quad c_\psi=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\psi,\quad \mathfrak a^2=(\mathfrak a^+)^2+(\mathfrak a^-)^2.\]

Lemma 9.1 asserts that for every \(\lambda\in(0,1/2)\) one can choose \(\epsilon=\epsilon(\lambda)>0\) and then \(\delta=\delta(\epsilon,\lambda)>0\) so that \[\int_0^{10r_0}(\varepsilon_n(x,r)^2+\mathfrak a(x,r)^2)\,\frac{dr}{r}<\delta\quad(x\in E)\] implies \(\mathfrak a^\pm(x,r)<\lambda\) for every \(x\in N_{2\epsilon r_0}(L_{B_0})\cap B_0\) and every \(r\in[10\epsilon r_0,r_0]\), where \(L_{B_0}\) minimizes \(\beta_{\infty,E}(B_0)\). Remark 9.2 and (9.3) prescribe the useful regime \(\epsilon\ll\lambda\), in particular \(10\epsilon<\lambda\); the centers in this assertion need not lie on \(L_{B_0}\).

Theorem A* and Lemma 11.1 seek a single Lipschitz graph \(\Gamma\) with \(\mu(\Gamma)\ge0.99\mu(B_0)\). Claim 13.1 replaces \(\mu\) by \(\mu|_{B_1}\) and the reference ball by \(\widetilde B_1/100\), although the selected \(B_1\) is guaranteed only \(\mu(B_1)\ge c(c_0)\mu(B_0)\). The proof treats a final \(99\%\) conclusion for the restricted measure as sufficient for the original \(99\%\) target.

In the measurability argument of Remark 2.6(ii), \(\Omega^+\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) is Borel. For a sphere \(S(z,r)\), its upper hemisphere \(S_H^+(z,r)\), and the height coordinate \(h=y_{n+1}-z_{n+1}\), the argument identifies the unweighted latitude integral \[\int_0^r\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\left(\{y\in S(z,r)\setminus\Omega^+:y_{n+1}-z_{n+1}=h\}\right)\,dh\] with \(\mathcal H^n(S_H^+(z,r)\setminus\Omega^+)\). This identity is the asserted coarea step used after the measurable-fiber construction; its integrand contains no factor correcting for the tangential Jacobian of height on the sphere.

Let \(\Omega^+,\Omega^-\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be disjoint Borel sets. For a nonnegative smooth function \(\phi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\) with \(\int_0^\infty\phi(t)t^n\sqrt{\log(e+t)}\,dt<\infty\), put \(\psi(y)=\phi(|y|)\), \(c_\psi=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\psi\), and \[\mathfrak a_\psi^i(x,r)=\left|c_\psi-r^{-(n+1)}\int_{\Omega^i}\psi((x-y)/r)\,dy\right|,\qquad i\in\{+,-\}.\] Lemma 3.3 asserts that there is a constant \(C_{1,\psi}\) such that for every \(x\), every \(R>0\), and every \(M\ge1\), \[\int_0^R\mathfrak a_\psi^i(x,r)^2\,\frac{dr}{r}\le C_{1,\psi}\int_0^{MR}\varepsilon_n(x,r)^2\,\frac{dr}{r}+C_n\int_M^\infty\phi(t)t^n\sqrt{\log^+(t/M)}\,dt.\] The coefficient \(C_n\) of the linear tail depends only on dimension; the hypotheses do not normalize the amplitude of \(\phi\).

For any two disjoint open subsets \(V^+,V^-\subset S^n\), let \(\lambda(V^\pm)\) be their first Dirichlet eigenvalues for the spherical Laplacian and let the corresponding nonnegative characteristic constants satisfy \(\lambda(V^\pm)=\alpha_{V^\pm}(n-1+\alpha_{V^\pm})\). The assertion following (1.5) states \[\alpha_{V^+}+\alpha_{V^-}\ge2,\] with equality if and only if \(V^+\) and \(V^-\) are complementary hemispheres. The rigidity conclusion is equality of the open sets themselves; the statement does not identify domains only up to modification by sets of Sobolev capacity zero.

Let \(\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be a Lipschitz graph through the origin with slope at most \(\tau\) relative to \(\mathbb R^n\times\{0\}\). Let \(B\subset B(0,r_0)\) be a ball of radius at most \(r_0/10\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(B,\Gamma)\ge100\tau r_0\), and let \(F\subset B\) and \(G\subset\Gamma\) be compact. Proposition 15.1 asserts, for every \(s>1\), \[\operatorname{Cap}_s(F)\frac{\mathcal H^n(G)^2}{r_0^n}\le C(\tau)\int_G\int_0^\infty\operatorname{Cap}_{s-1}(F\cap S(z,r))\,dr\,d\mathcal H^n(z).\]

Under these hypotheses, Lemma 15.2 asserts, for distinct \(x,y\in F\) and every \(\delta>0\), \[\mathcal H^n\{z\in G:\big||x-z|-|y-z|\big|\le\delta\}\lesssim_\tau\frac{\delta r_0^n}{|x-y|}.\] Both statements allow arbitrary compact \(G\subset\Gamma\); neither requires \(G\subset B(0,r_0)\). This unrestricted set of slicing centers is the scope being examined.

In Theorem 11.22 let \(X=\operatorname{Spc}(\mathrm{Exc}_d(\mathrm{Sp}^c,\mathrm{Sp})^c)\), and let \(V=V_{\le h+n}\) be the finite truncated subspace. The proof sets \[W=V\setminus\bigl(\overline{\{P_d([l],p,h)\}}\cap V\bigr)\] and asserts that finiteness and relative openness in \(V\) make \(W\) open in \(X\). It then chooses a compact object \(z\) with \(\operatorname{supp}(z)=X\setminus W\).

For a nontrivial cyclic \(p\)-group \(C\), the proof of Theorem 12.27 uses the ring map attributed to Theorem 10.33 as though its target were the ordinary Tate construction \((H\mathbb F_p)^{tC}\), and invokes its nonvanishing from ordinary Tate cohomology. The cited theorem actually supplies the construction indexed by the family \(\mathcal P(C)\) of all proper subgroups. The proof does not restrict \(C\) to order \(p\).

Let \(\mathrm{Sp}^c\) be the category of compact spectra and let \(J\) be a small collection of cone diagrams in \(\mathrm{Sp}^c\), as in Remark 2.37. Let \(\operatorname{Fun}_J(\mathrm{Sp}^c,\mathrm{Sp})\) be the full subcategory of functors carrying every diagram of \(J\) to a limit diagram, and let \(L_J\) be the left adjoint to its inclusion in \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathrm{Sp}^c,\mathrm{Sp})\). Assume that \(J\) is closed under postcomposition with \(x\otimes(-)\) for every compact spectrum \(x\). Proposition 2.38 asserts that \(L_J\) is a smashing localization compatible with Day convolution; in particular, the local category is presentably symmetric monoidal with Day product and unit \(L_Jh_{\mathbb S}\).

The proof claims that the inclusion of local functors preserves filtered colimits, and hence all colimits, because filtered colimits of spectra are left exact. The admissible diagrams in Remark 2.37 are not restricted to finite limit shapes. This unrestricted-limit implication, rather than an added finite-diagram variant, is the assertion being checked.

Remark 2.28 characterizes compact functors as precisely the retracts of finite colimits of the corepresentables \(h_X=\Sigma^\infty\operatorname{Map}(X,-)\). The displayed generating operations include finite colimits and retracts, without adjoining desuspensions of the corepresentables.

The first presentation in Corollary 8.13 presents the unital ring \(A(d)\) as \[\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/I,\qquad I=(x_ix_j-\sum_l\mu(i,j,l)x_l),\] using only the multiplication relations (8.11). No separate unit relation \(x_1=1\) is included, although \(x_1\) represents the unit in the claimed presentation.

Definition 10.27 defines the \(p\)-height of \(M\) as the infimum of \(h\in\mathbb N\cup\{-1,\infty\}\) for which \(M\otimes C_{p,h+1}=0\), with \(C_{p,0}=\mathrm{Sp}^c_{(p)}\). Example 10.28 asserts that every spectrum which is not \(p\)-local has infinite \(p\)-height, while Remark 10.29 identifies the convention with the corresponding finite-localization condition. The definition is applied to arbitrary spectra, not only \(p\)-local ones.

In the proof of Lemma 2.1 put \(P=\operatorname{Pic}(X)\otimes\mathbb C\), \(V=\Lambda\otimes\mathbb C\), and \(w=(W,-)|_P\). For projective \(X\) with \(\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Pic}(X)\ge2\), \(W^2<0\), and \(\delta^2=2-2n\ne0\), \(n\ge2\), the proof asserts that \[S=\{g\in O(V):\ker((g\delta,-)|_P)\ne\ker w\}\] is Zariski open. The set includes transformations at which the restricted functional \((g\delta,-)|_P\) vanishes.

A star body has a continuous positive radial function \(\rho_K\) on \(S^{n-1}\); its intersection body satisfies \(\rho_{IK}(\theta)=|K\cap\theta^\perp|_{n-1}\). Theorem 1.1 concerns all such bodies in \(\mathbb R^n\), \(n\geq3\), satisfying \(I^2K=cK\) for a positive scalar \(c\), and characterizes them as origin-centered ellipsoids. The fixed-point corollary forces a Euclidean ball. Convexity is not an initial hypothesis of the main theorem.

On printed page 551, PDF page 43, Section 9.1(4), equation (9.5) is \[h_K^{\,1-p}S_K=c\,d\theta,\qquad p\geq-n,\quad K=-K ,
 \] where \(h_K\) is the support function and \(S_K\) the surface area measure. The immediately following unnumbered display gives \[F_p(K)=\frac1p\int_{S^{n-1}}h_K^p\,d\theta+\frac1c|K|
 \] and asserts that equation (9.5) is its Euler–Lagrange equation under support-function perturbations. For \(p=0\), the parenthetical replacement is the log integral, again with the positive volume term. Both plus signs were checked on the acquired original page.

Remark 5.8 asserts that every positive-dimensional complete intersection in a smooth projective toric variety is geometrically connected. In the setup before Corollary 4.6, the defining equations are sections of general line bundles \(\mathcal O(D_i)\), without an ampleness assumption on these bundles. Theorem 5.6 uses one-dimensionality of both top-degree groups in \(\alpha^{2d}\) under this scope.

In the proof of Proposition 3.29, \(M\) denotes the full motive of a rigid analytic space in the category used to study good reduction over \(L\). The notation \(\mathbb T^1\) is the rigid generic fiber of the formal multiplicative group \(\operatorname{Spf}\mathcal O_L\langle u^{\pm1}\rangle\), and \(\mathbb T^k=(\mathbb T^1)^k\). For the formal charts occurring in the induction, the proof asserts \[M(X_{i\eta}\times\mathbb T^k)\cong M(X_{i\eta})(k)[k]\] and, in the Mayer–Vietoris step, \[M((\operatorname{Spf}A)_\eta\times\mathbb T^1)=M((\operatorname{Spf}A)_\eta)(1)[1].\] These are equalities for the full product motives; neither factor \(\mathbb T^1\) is defined here as a reduced motive or as the cofiber of its unit section.

After reducing to a fixed scheme \((X_i)^\sigma\) whose underlying support is the single point over \(s_i\), the proof of Theorem 1.6 asserts the scheme-level identity \[(X_i)^\sigma\simeq(X_i)^\sigma\times_{S_i}\{s_i\}.\] The premise recorded at this step is set-theoretic support at that point; annihilation of the structure sheaf by the base uniformizer has not been imposed.

In the one-dimensional situation of Section 3.3, the group quotient is a smooth curve and the morphism factors as \(f:X\xrightarrow{q}X/G\xrightarrow{g}S\). Identifying the Milnor number \(\mu_f\) with the local discriminant \(\operatorname{disc}(f)\) at \(f(x)\), the text asserts \[\operatorname{disc}(q)+\operatorname{disc}(g)=\operatorname{disc}(f),\qquad \operatorname{disc}(q)=a_{G,X}(1),\] and hence \(\mu_f-a_{G,X}(1)=\operatorname{disc}(g)\). The displayed composition formula gives the term for \(g\) no ramification-index factor and does not define it as a pulled-back weighted exponent. The final observation is that the equality under discussion extends to \(\sigma=1\) if \(g\) is étale at \(q(x)\).

For a prime \(p\), let \[V_p=\{(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb F_p^3\setminus\{0\}:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=3x_1x_2x_3\}.\] Join vertices by the three individual Vieta involutions, such as \(R_1(x)=(3x_2x_3-x_1,x_2,x_3)\). Theorem 1.4 asserts that the number of vertices in every connected component of this graph is divisible by \(p\), without excluding any prime. Coordinate permutations and a quotient by sign changes are not part of this graph definition.

Fix an even integer \(k\ge2\). The density \(\mathcal M_k(y)\), for \(y>0\), is defined in Theorem 1. Its weights in Theorem 3 are \[A_p=p^4-2p^2-p+1,\qquad
 Q(d)=\mu^2(d)\prod_{p\mid d}\frac{p^2}{A_p}.\] The constants \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) have the paper’s normalization. In particular \(\alpha>0\), \(Q(1)=1\), \(Q(d)\ge0\), and \[
 Q(d)\ll d^{-2},\] because \(\prod_p p^4/A_p\) converges: every factor is positive and \(1+O(p^{-2})\). None of the arguments below changes the normalization of the standard Bessel function \(J_\nu\).

Theorem3 states the exact Bessel series M_k(y)=alpha*sqrt(y)*sum_{d,s>=1}Q(d)J_{k-1}(4*pi*s*sqrt(y)/d)/s, followed by the leading coefficient alpha*(-1)^(k/2-1)*sqrt(2/pi) multiplying y^(1/4) F(sqrt(y)).

Fixed even integer k>=2; y>0 and y tends to infinity. A_p=p^4-2p^2-p+1; Q(d)=mu(d)^2 product_{p|d} p^2/A_p. alpha has the same positive normalization in both displays; J_nu is the standard Bessel function. Q(d)>=0,Q(1)=1,Q(d)=O(d^-2), since every local factor is positive and product_p p^4/A_p converges.

Fix an even integer \(k\ge2\). The density \(\mathcal M_k(y)\), for \(y>0\), is defined in Theorem 1. Its weights in Theorem 3 are \[A_p=p^4-2p^2-p+1,\qquad
 Q(d)=\mu^2(d)\prod_{p\mid d}\frac{p^2}{A_p}.\] The constants \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) have the paper’s normalization. In particular \(\alpha>0\), \(Q(1)=1\), \(Q(d)\ge0\), and \[
 Q(d)\ll d^{-2},\] because \(\prod_p p^4/A_p\) converges: every factor is positive and \(1+O(p^{-2})\). None of the arguments below changes the normalization of the standard Bessel function \(J_\nu\).
Assuming RH, sum_{d<=T}Q(d)=L-Delta/T+R(T) with R(T)<<_epsilon T^(-2+epsilon). Its proof shifts a Perron contour to Re(s)=-2+epsilon and counts only poles0,-1.
The displayed error contains X^(1/2) T^(3/16) and Y(PX)^(1/2)/T, but T=Y^(5/6) P^(5/12) X^(-1/12) is said to make them equal and recover Proposition3.1.

Let \(k\) be an uncountable algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let \(X\) be an irreducible variety over \(k\), and let \(G\subseteq\operatorname{Bir}(X)\) be a connected commutative affine algebraic subgroup. For a regular model of its faithful action, each \(G\)-invariant rational map \(f:X\dashrightarrow G\) defines the rational replica \(r_f(x)=f(x)\cdot x\); write \(\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G)\) for the resulting subgroup of \(\operatorname{Bir}(X)\). For a rational action this construction is transferred through a regular model by birational conjugacy.

Proposition 6.7 (Article PDF pages 28–29, with the field convention on page 4) asserts \[C_{\operatorname{Bir}(X)}\bigl(\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G)\bigr)=\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G).\] Thus every birational self-map commuting with all rational replicas is asserted to be a rational replica. The proposition does not require \(G\ne\{1\}\).

Let \(k\) be an uncountable algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let \(n\ge2\), as in Corollary 1.4 (Article PDF pages 3–4). The first step of its proof on PDF page 23 requires a homogeneous polynomial \[F\in k[x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}],\qquad\deg F=2n,\] that is irreducible over \(k\) and whose projective zero locus \(V(F)\subset\mathbb P_k^{n-1}\) is smooth.

The construction therefore asserts existence of such an \(F\) for every allowed \(n\ge2\), including \(n=2\). It then sets \(f=F(1,x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})\) and uses irreducibility to conclude that \(f\) is not a square in \(k(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})\). The checked assertion is this polynomial-selection step within the corollary's proof.

In Appendix C, let \(S\) be a closed oriented genus-two surface, let \(t:S\to S\) be the orientation-preserving diffeomorphism representing the chosen based mapping class, and let \(M_t\) be its mapping torus. Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero and \(\rho:\pi_1(S)\to\operatorname{Sp}_{2r}(K)\) a symplectic local system. Suppose an intertwiner \(B\in\operatorname{Sp}_{2r}(K)\) satisfies \[\rho(t_*\gamma)=B\rho(\gamma)B^{-1}\qquad(\gamma\in\pi_1(S)),\] so that \(\rho\) extends to \(M_t\), and assume \(H^0(S,\rho)=0\). Let \(V=H^1(S,\rho)\), with its induced symmetric quadratic form, and let \(T:V\to V\) be the monodromy map.

Put \(h=\dim\ker(T-I)\), the even fixed-space dimension in Lemma C.2.1, and let \(V_{(1)}\) denote the generalized \(1\)-eigenspace of \(T\). Define \[\det^{\prime}(1-T)=\det\big((1-T)|_{V_{(1)}^\perp}\big).\] The printed definition of \(\delta\) is the determinant of the quadratic form restricted to the ordinary fixed space \(V^{T=1}=\ker(T-I)\). Equation (C.2) asserts the equality of nonzero square classes \[(-1)^{h/2}\operatorname{RT}(M_t,\rho)=\det^{\prime}(1-T)\,\delta\quad\text{in }K^\times/(K^\times)^2.\] The fixed space used in \(\delta\) is the ordinary fixed space, while the space removed in \(\det^{\prime}\) is the generalized eigenspace; the hypotheses do not assume semisimplicity at eigenvalue \(1\).

Fix an integer \(r\ge2\). Let \(H_k^i\) be the dilaton-shifted modes of the self-dual \(\mathcal W^{-r+1}(\mathfrak{gl}_r)\) representation defined in (5.2)–(5.8) (Article PDF pages 48–50): \(\widehat J_\ell=\hbar\partial_{t_\ell}\) for \(\ell>0\), \(\widehat J_\ell=-\ell t_{-\ell}\) for \(\ell\le0\), and \[H_k^i=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\widehat J_{r-1}}{(r-1)\hbar}\right)W_k^i\exp\!\left(\frac{\widehat J_{r-1}}{(r-1)\hbar}\right).\] In particular \(H_k^1=\hbar\partial_{t_{rk}}\) for \(k\ge1\).

Proposition 5.6 (PDF page 52) takes any normalized formal series of the stable genus-expansion form \[Z(\hbar;\mathbf t)=\exp\!\left(\sum_{\substack{g\ge0,\,n\ge1\\2g-2+n>0}}\frac{\hbar^{g-1}}{n!}\sum_{a_1,\ldots,a_n>0}\Phi_{g,n}[a_1,\ldots,a_n]t_{a_1}\cdots t_{a_n}\right),\] where the scalar coefficients are symmetric in their positive integer indices. Suppose there are constants \(\nu_k\) for every \(k\ge1\), and a constant \(\mu\), such that \[H_k^1Z=\nu_k Z\quad(k\ge1),\qquad H_{-r+2}^rZ=\mu Z.\] It concludes \(Z=Z^{\Theta^r}\), the descendant potential of the Theta cohomological field theory from Definition 5.3. No KP, KdV, or cohomological-field-theory origin is required of the input \(Z\), and the endpoint \(r=2\) is included.

For the section \(S=S^c_{h'}[v](y_{t_0})\), the point \(p\) in Lemma 3.4, and its John normalization \(L\), the display before (3.20) asserts \[\frac{\operatorname{dist}(Lp,\partial LS)}{\operatorname{diam}(LS)}=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(p,\partial S)}{\operatorname{diam}(S)}\le\frac{t_2}{t_1}\le\frac1M.\] The asserted equality uses Euclidean distance to the whole boundary and Euclidean diameter, not ratios restricted to a single line.

The QNLS equation is \[i u_t+g(u)u_{xx}=N(u,u_x),\] with a real metric, smooth coefficients, and \(N\) at most quadratic in \(u_x\). The normalized metric has \(g(0)=1\); the cubic convention concerns the nonlinear perturbation of that constant. DQNLS additionally allows derivative dependence in the metric. The local thresholds are strictly \(s>1\) and \(s>2\), respectively (Theorem 2, p. 5). The endpoints are explicitly open, and generic optimality is Conjecture 3, not a proved ill-posedness theorem. Rough uniqueness is formulated for uniform limits of regular solutions, not arbitrary distributional solutions.

For long-time results the cubic symbol \(c(\xi_1,\xi_2,\xi_3)\) is phase compatible and conservative: \[c(\xi,\xi,\xi),\quad \partial_{\xi_j}c(\xi,\xi,\xi)\in\mathbb R.\] Defocusing additionally requires the positive lower bound in Definition 1.4; for QNLS it is \(c(\xi,\xi,\xi)\gtrsim\langle\xi\rangle^2\). This is stronger than mere reality or positivity at one frequency. Scattering on p. 3 is explicitly the weak sense of global spacetime estimates, not convergence to a linear solution.

Theorem 9, p. 40 (printed p. 260), equation (6.5), asserts, for \(\mu\approx\lambda\), \[
 \|\partial_x(v_\lambda\overline{v_\mu^{x_0}})\|_{L^2_{t,x}}
 \lesssim d_\lambda d_\mu\lambda^{-1/2}(1+\lambda|x_0|).\] Here the functions solve the independent paradifferential equations (4.2), p. 24, and \[d_\lambda^2=\|v_\lambda(0)\|_2^2+
       \sup_{x_0}\|v_\lambda f_\lambda^{x_0}\|_{L^1_{t,x}}\] by (6.1). Theorem 9 imposes the small-solution assumptions on the background \(u\), not a relation \(v_\lambda=P_\lambda u\). Page 40 explicitly allows independent \(v_\lambda\); p. 41 even allows normalization \(d_\lambda=1\).

Theorem C applies to every group quasi-isometric to a well-behaved hierarchically hyperbolic group containing Morse elements, and asserts that the non-Morse proportion in balls of radius \(R\) is \(O(R^{-1/2})\). Theorem 7.4 assumes a finitely generated group with a WPD loxodromic isometry that is weakly contracting through the indicated hyperbolic space, and asserts superpolynomial genericity of loxodromic elements. Neither statement excludes virtually cyclic groups.

For integers \(m,r,a\ge1\) with \(\gcd(r,a)=1\), the source considers the cyclic quotient \(T\)-singularity \(\frac1{mr^2}(1,mra-1)\). It asserts that the base of its miniversal \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein deformation is \(\mathbb C^{m-1}\), with parameters \(C_0,\ldots,C_{m-2}\), represented by \[\{xy=z^{rm}+C_{m-2}z^{r(m-2)}+\cdots+C_1z^r+C_0\}\subset\mathbb C^3/\mu_r^{1,-1,a}.\] Equation (4.1.3) has no \(z^{r(m-1)}\) parameter; the cyclic action has weights \((1,-1,a)\).

Proposition 4.2.7 uses this model in comparing a \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein smoothing of the toric surface \(V_Q\), for a \(T\)-polygon \(Q\), with the almost toric manifold \(A(Q_{\mathrm{nodal}})\). Its hypotheses require a proper flat holomorphic map \(\pi:\mathcal X\to D_\varepsilon\) from a complex manifold, submersive off zero, with central fiber \(V_Q\) and smooth nonzero fibers. It asserts, for small \(t\ne0\), a diffeomorphism \(\Phi_t:X_t\to A(Q_{\mathrm{nodal}})\) carrying the complex structure to one taming the indicated symplectic form. The local-model and total-space assertions are used in a discussion that includes the non-Gorenstein indices \(r>1\).

For the polygon \(Q\) in the proof of Theorem E, choose the least \(s>0\) such that \(sQ\) is a lattice polygon. The proof asserts that \(sQ\) meets the hypotheses of Theorem 5.3.1: it is dual Fano, is a lattice \(T\)-polygon, and has coprime affine edge lengths. In triangular cases it then obtains \(k=1\) in that theorem's construction.

Let \(Q\) be the triangle with a Delzant vertex adjacent to a \(T\)-vertex, written in Section 6.3 with vertices \((0,0),(0,mra-1),(mr^2,0)\), where \(m,r,a\) are positive integers and \(\gcd(r,a)=1\). In weighted projective space \(\mathbb P(1,mra-1,r,a)\), equation (6.3.1) sets \[S_t=\left\{xy=\frac{w^{mr}}{1+t}+\frac{t\,z^{ma}}{1+t}\right\},\qquad t\in\mathbb P^1.\] Proposition 6.3.3 asserts that these fibers form a \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein pencil, with \(S_0\cong\mathbb P(1,mra-1,mr^2)\) and \(S_\infty\cong\mathbb P(1,mra-1,ma^2)\).

It further asserts that for every \(t\ne0,\infty\), the fiber has the quotient singularity \(\frac1{mra-1}(r,a)\) at \([0:1:0:0]\) and is otherwise nonsingular. This parameter range includes \(t=-1\), where the displayed denominator vanishes; the assertion does not restrict to a small neighborhood of either endpoint or omit that parameter.

Lemma 6.5.1 asserts that Theorem 2.1.3 supplies all possible data for rational unicuspidal plane curves with one Puiseux pair. The statement includes no index condition restricting these curves to the odd-Fibonacci family classified by that theorem.

Theorem 1.1 asserts that a finitely generated contracting self-similar group \(G\), whose limit space \(\mathcal J_G\) has Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension \(\alpha<2\), is Liouville for every symmetric measure with a finite \(\beta\)-moment for some \(\beta>\alpha\). Theorem 1.3 asserts \(\operatorname{Cr}_{\rm Liouv}(G)\le p_c(G,\mathfrak B)\le\operatorname{ARdim}\mathcal J_G\). The general biset definition requires a free right action and finitely many right orbits, while faithfulness of the associated tree action is not imposed globally.

Let \(d\) be an Ahlfors-regular metric on \(\mathcal J_G\) with Hausdorff dimension \(\alpha\), and let \(\beta>\alpha\), \(p>p_c\). Proposition 5.6 asserts constants \(C\) and \(0<\lambda<1\) such that, uniformly in \(g\) and the left-infinite tail, \[\sum_{v\in X^n}d(\ldots x_2x_1g(v),\ldots x_2x_1v)^\beta\le C\lambda^n l(g)^p.\] Its metric hypothesis is Ahlfors regularity alone; the quasi-conformal hypothesis of Proposition 3.8 is not included.

In the Suzuki case of Proposition 7.10, let \(q=2^n\) with odd \(n\ge3\), and set \[r=\sqrt{2q},\qquad h=r/2,\qquad s=q/2-1,\qquad N=sh,\qquad m=(q-1)h=2N+h.\] Let \(J_d\) be the scalar antidiagonal permutation matrix of size \(d\), and let \(\xi=e^{2\pi i/(q-1)}\). In the selected basis the dihedral representatives are \[X=\operatorname{diag}(\xi I_h,\xi^2I_h,\ldots,\xi^{q-2}I_h,I_h),\qquad Y=J_{2N}\oplus(-I_h).\]

The printed calculation asserts the centralizer identity \[C_{\mathrm U(m)}(\langle X,Y\rangle)=\{\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_s,a_s,\ldots,a_1,b):a_1,\ldots,a_s,b\in\mathrm U(h)\}.\] Here centralizing means commuting with both specified matrices in this very basis. The same construction defines \[A=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}I_N&J_N\\ I_N&-J_N\end{pmatrix}\oplus I_h,\qquad C=A^{-1}(I_N\oplus J_N\oplus I_1)A.\] These are the asserted block formulas used in the centralizer and degree argument; the statement under review is their validity for every allowed Suzuki parameter.

For a finite \(G\)-graph with adjacent edges \(e=\{u,v\}\), \(e'=\{v,w\}\) and stabilizers \(G_{e'}\subseteq G_e\), Lemma 3.9 asserts that removing \(G\cdot e'\) and attaching an orbit of edges from \(u\) to \(w\) preserves the \(G\)-homotopy type. The statement does not assume that \(e\) and \(e'\) lie in different edge orbits.

For the general target Lie group \(\mathcal G\) and representation-space setup of Lemma 5.9, the first assertion says that the maps on \(\mathcal M\) induced by \(ww'\) and \(w i_v(g)w'\) are homotopic. It does not assume \(\rho_0(g)\) lies in the identity path component of \(\mathcal G\). The connected double-centralizer condition is stated only for the later quotient assertion.

In Section 1.1, curves are unoriented free homotopy classes, and \(s(X,\gamma,L)\) counts their mapping-class orbit up to length \(L\). In Section 2.6, \(\mathcal{MRG}_{h,b}\) has distinctly labeled boundary components. Cutting a nonseparating curve in genus \(g\) gives type \((g-1,2)\). Write \[Z=\mathcal{MRG}_{g-1,2}(1,1),\qquad \tau:Z\longrightarrow Z\] for the involution exchanging its boundary labels. An orientation of the curve distinguishes its sides. The full stabilizer \(\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\) contains orientation-reversing-on-the-curve mapping classes, whereas \(\operatorname{Stab}_0(\gamma)\) preserves that orientation.

For every nonnegative \(h\in C_c(Z)\), the measure in (5.1), weighted using the labeled ribbon-spine target, is asserted to be invariant under the full unoriented stabilizer \(\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\). It is then pushed locally to \(\mathcal T_g/\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\), without requiring \(h\) to be invariant under the boundary-label exchange \(\tau\).

Let \(f\) be an \(e^\varepsilon\)-bi-Lipschitz map in the hyperbolic setting of Lemma 4.8, and consider three pairwise disjoint, mutually nonseparating geodesics with center \(u\) and inradius \(r\). If \(u'\) is the center of the geodesically straightened image triple, the lemma asserts \(d(f(u),u')\le D(r,\varepsilon)\), with no separate dependence on or bound for the target inradius.

Let \(Y\) be a compact hyperbolic surface with geodesic boundary, and let \(e\) be any edge of its metric ribbon-graph spine \(S(Y)\), with dual orthogeodesic arc \(a\). The weight \(|e|_Y\) is the length of either closest-point projection of \(e\) onto \(\partial Y\), while \(\ell_Y(a)\) is the hyperbolic length of the shortest orthogeodesic in the dual arc class. Lemma 2.5 asserts \[|e|_Y\sim\log(1/\ell_Y(a))\] both as \(\ell_Y(a)\to0\) and as \(|e|_Y\to\infty\). Immediately before the lemma, \(f\sim g\) is defined to mean that \(f/g\to1\), not merely that the two quantities are comparable up to constants.

For the finite-rank Coxeter system in Theorem 2.1, the projection proof assigns an embedded path the complexity tuple \((n_1,\ldots,n_{\ell(g)})\), where \(n_j\) counts vertices of height \(j\). It asserts that its prescribed valley replacement strictly decreases this tuple and hence terminates, including when the valley is the identity, whose height is zero and is absent from the tuple.

For the isometry \(g\) and basepoint \(o\) on p. 652, the orbit polygon \[\gamma=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}[g^ko,g^{k+1}o]\] is asserted to be a \((\lambda,0)\)-quasi-axis with \(\lambda=d(go,o)/\tau(g)\). The convention explicitly requires the length of every continuous subpath to be at most \(\lambda\) times the distance between its endpoints, with no additive error.

For every nonidentity \(a\in F_n\), Theorem 3.10 forms \[G=F_n*_{\langle a\rangle}(\langle a\rangle\times\mathbb Z)\] and asserts that \(G\) is existentially \(C^*\)-residually-\(F_n\). The stated quantifier permits proper powers; it does not require \(\langle a\rangle\) to be a maximal cyclic centralizer.

In Theorem 3.5, a valid image-radius bound \(f\) satisfies \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}f(n)^{1/n}=1\). For a fixed integer radius \(R\) and the rapid-decay polynomial \(P\), the proof uses this to select an integer \(m\) such that \[P(f(2mR))^{1/(2m)}<1+\varepsilon/3.\] The premise is a liminf over all positive integers, whereas the selected values lie in the progression \(2mR\).

Corollary 3.8 asserts that if \(G*\mathbb Z\) is existentially \(C^*\)-residually-\(G\), in the sense defined in the paper, then the reduced group algebra \(C_r^*(G)\) is selfless and, consequently, has strict comparison. The hypothesis contains no nontriviality or infinitude requirement on \(G\). In the proof, the \(*\)-homomorphism \(C_r^*(G*\mathbb Z)\to C_r^*(G)^{\mathcal U}\) furnished by Proposition 3.7 is treated as injective using \(C^*\)-simplicity of \(G*\mathbb Z\); the statement itself is not restricted to the infinite groups for which that justification is given.

For the Torelli map \(\operatorname{Tor}:\mathcal M_6^{\mathrm{ct}}\to\mathcal A_6\), Theorem 5 asserts that \(\operatorname{Tor}^*\Delta_6\in R^5(\mathcal M_6^{\mathrm{ct}})\) generates the one-dimensional kernel of the \(\lambda_6\)-pairing \[R^4(\mathcal M_6^{\mathrm{ct}})\times R^5(\mathcal M_6^{\mathrm{ct}})\longrightarrow\mathbb Q.\] Thus it asserts that this particular assembled class is nonzero, and deduces \([\mathcal A_1\times\mathcal A_5]\notin R^5(\mathcal A_6)\). The proof on PDF page 58 invokes the complete Pixton relations and a computation with admcycles.

The supplied notebook forms \(v=M.\mathrm{kernel}().\mathrm{basis}()[0]\) and records rank one for the matrix with rows \(\Delta_6\) and \(v\). The bounded verification question is whether the retained evidence supplies nonvanishing of the assembled class in the certified tautological-ring quotient, rather than only its membership in \(\mathbb Qv\). The paper separately claims nonvanishing; the notebook describes the recorded test as proportionality, so this statement does not assume that the authors relied only on that rank test.

On p. 668 the locus \(\mathrm{NL}_g^r\) is defined by the exact-rank condition \(\operatorname{NS}(X)\cong\mathbb Z^r\), after which its global Zariski closure is taken. Theorem 13 applies the cited classification to this rank-two locus and includes the type-(ii) family for every divisor \(n\mid g\), \(n\ne g\). These are the printed exact-rank and closure conventions, rather than the rank-greater-than-one locus classified in the cited source.

Theorem 5 identifies the genus-six class as \[\operatorname{Tor}^*\Delta_6=\operatorname{Tor}^*[\mathcal A_1\times\mathcal A_5]-\frac{2370}{691}\lambda_5\in R^5(\mathcal M_6^{\mathrm{ct}}),\] and the concluding genus-six calculation again subtracts \((2370/691)\lambda_5\) from the sum of the excess-locus contributions. The paper's general normalization is \(c_g=g/(6|B_{2g}|)\), where \(B_{2g}\) is the Bernoulli number. The local assertion checked here is that the displayed coefficient of \(\lambda_5\) is its genus-six specialization; this is separate from the nonvanishing claim for the resulting class.

With \(\lambda_i\) the Hodge classes on the compactified moduli space of one-pointed genus-\(g\) curves, the source defines \(\Lambda(z)=\sum_{i=0}^g z^i\lambda_{g-i}\). It then asserts the formal generating-series identity \[1+\sum_{g\ge1}t^{2g}\int_{\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,1}}\frac{\Lambda(-1)\Lambda(0)\Lambda(z)}{1-\psi_1}=\left(\frac{\sin(t/2)}{t/2}\right)^{-z},\] attributing it to Propositions 3 and 4 of reference [12]. The displayed summands use \(\Lambda(-1)\) with that convention and contain no additional genus sign \((-1)^g\).

At the end of Section 4.5.6, work over the local Artin base \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) of the deformation \(\mathcal C\). When the compact-type curve \(D_v\) is reducible, let \(T\) be its irreducible component meeting the genus-zero component \(P\) at the node \(q\). Remove all nodes of \(T\) to obtain the smooth affine curve \(T^-\); its induced deformation \(\mathcal T^-\) is trivial. The printed construction deletes the components \(E\) and \(P\) from \(\mathcal C\) to obtain \(\mathcal Z\), then glues \(\mathcal Z\) to the entire trivial deformation of \(T\) along \(\mathcal T^-\), producing \(\pi:\mathcal X\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) and the section \(\mathcal Q\) at \(q\).

This family is then used in the identity \(\pi_*\mathcal O_{\mathcal X}(\mathcal Q)=\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\) from (39), whose hypotheses require a flat proper family with the stated pointed compact-type special fiber. The asserted applicability concerns the literal gluing even when \(T\) also meets other components at internal nodes and \(\mathcal Z\) retains pieces outside \(D_v\).

The higher-genus outlook asserts, for every \(g\ge8\), that \(IH^{2g-2}(\mathcal A_g^{\mathrm{Sat}},\mathbb Q)\) is not generated by the \(\lambda\)-classes. It gives no parity restriction on \(g\), and presents this as evidence for nonvanishing of \(\Delta_g\).

For the type-(ii) Noether–Lefschetz components of Theorem 13, indexed by a positive divisor \(n\mid g\) with \(n\ne g\), Section 7 calls \(g(n+1)/2\) their codimension in \(\mathcal A_g\). It then states that the expected codimension of each such component is the larger number \(\binom g2=g(g-1)/2\). Thus the printed claim is a codimension formula and a strict comparison, including the allowed endpoint \(n=1\).

For an orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism \(f(\theta)=\theta+b(\theta)\), write \(p=f^{-1}\) and \(\mathcal Bh=f'(h\circ f)\). Under the paper's fixed Hilbert-transform convention, the first identity on p. 40 asserts \[(\mathcal B^{-1}\mathcal H\mathcal B-\mathcal H)h=+\partial_\theta\int_{\mathbb T}\log\left|\frac{e^{ip(\theta)}-e^{ip(\eta)}}{e^{i\theta}-e^{i\eta}}\right|h(\eta)\,d\eta.\] The coefficient \(+1\) in this identity is propagated to the principal order-\(\varepsilon^2\) block in (4.31).

Lemma 3.3 constructs \(r_0=g+\varepsilon B_0\) without first harmonics and then \(r_\varepsilon=r_0+\varepsilon r_1\), using \(D_0=(\partial_\theta-\mathcal H)/2\) and \(D_0r_1=-\varepsilon A_{1,\rm printed}\). The displayed coefficient is \(A_{1,\rm printed}=\omega_0\partial_\varphi g-\tfrac34\partial_\theta(g^2)\). Equations (3.49)–(3.53) assert that the resulting approximate solution has residual \(O(\varepsilon^5)\), with no \(-\omega_0\dot\Theta\partial_\theta g\) term in that coefficient.

In the Nash–Moser scheme, let \(s_0>3\), \(\tau>1\), \(0<\mu<1\), and choose \(a_2,a_1,\mu_2,\delta,\mu_1,b_1\) as in (6.4). In particular, \(a_2>1+\tau\), \(a_1>3s_0+12\tau+15+3a_2/2\), \(\delta<(1-\mu)/(a_1+2)\), and \(\mu_1>12\tau+3+6/\delta\). Put \(N_0=\varepsilon^{-\delta}\), \(N_n=N_0^{(3/2)^n}\), \(\lambda=\varepsilon^{2+\delta}\), \(A_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{3-\mu}/\lambda\), \(L=2s_0+2\tau+3\), and \(R_*=2s_0+2\tau+4+3\mu_2/2\). The induction controls the increments \(u_k=\rho_k-\rho_{k-1}\) by \(\|u_k\|_L^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le C_*A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{-a_2}\), and permits \(\|\rho_n\|_{b_1}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le C_*A_\varepsilon N_{n-1}^{\mu_1}\).

The page-56 argument uses half-weight interpolation to obtain \(\|u_k\|_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\lesssim A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{(\mu_1-a_2)/2}\), then sums these bounds to assert the uniform inverse-input condition \(\|\rho_n\|_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le1\) for small fixed \(\varepsilon\). A later estimate (6.31) also replaces the \(s+4\tau+5\) state norm of the inverse bound (6.6) by a norm of order \(s+2\tau\). These are the interpolation, summation, and derivative-loss implications being checked; the constructed comparison sequence is not asserted to solve the nonlinear residual equation.

Consider \(T_0=\epsilon_1\Omega(\xi_0)\partial_\varphi+\partial_\theta[(c_{-1}(\xi_0,\rho)+\epsilon_2f_0(\xi_0,\rho))\,\cdot]\) on the periodic function spaces of Appendix A.4. Here \(0<\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\le\epsilon\) are small, \(\Omega,c_{-1}\) are independent of \((\varphi,\theta)\), \(\|\Omega\|^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}+\|c_{-1}\|^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le C_0\), and \(|\Omega|\ge C_0^{-1}\). Assumption (A.11) gives the absolute tame bound \(\|f_0\|_s^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le C_0(1+\|\rho\|_{s+\sigma_0}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)})\) for \(s_0\le s\le S\) when the low state norm is bounded, with \(\sigma_0\ge0\).

For \(\mu_2\ge4\tau+3\) and \(s_h=3\mu_2/2+2s_0+2\tau+1\), Proposition A.9 assumes \(\epsilon_1^{-1}\lambda+N_0^{\mu_2}\epsilon_2\lambda^{-1}\le\epsilon_0\) and \(\|\rho\|_{s_h+\sigma_0}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le1\). Its normal form has full speed \(c_{-1}+\epsilon_2c\), so \(c\) denotes the normalized correction. Part (4) asserts, for two states satisfying those bounds, \[\|\Delta_{12}c\|^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\lesssim\|\Delta_{12}c_0\|^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}+\epsilon_2\|\Delta_{12}\rho\|_{2s_0+2\tau+3}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)},\] uniformly in the small parameters. The proof initializes \(c_0=0\); the general proposition imposes no spatial-zero-mean condition on \(\rho\) and (A.10)–(A.11) are absolute bounds, not additional state-difference hypotheses.
