Let \(s_1,s_{*,1}\) be positive definite real \(d\times d\) matrices and let \(k_1\) be any real \(d\times d\) matrix. Define \[E_1=\begin{pmatrix}s_1+k_1^{\mathsf T}s_{*,1}^{-1}k_1&-k_1^{\mathsf T}s_{*,1}^{-1}\\-s_{*,1}^{-1}k_1&s_{*,1}^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad E_{*,1}=\begin{pmatrix}s_{*,1}+k_1s_1^{-1}k_1^{\mathsf T}&k_1s_1^{-1}\\s_1^{-1}k_1^{\mathsf T}&s_1^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\] and suppose \(E_{*,1}\preceq E_1\). With spectral norm \(|\cdot|\), set \(\widetilde\Theta_1=|s_{*,1}^{-1/2}s_1s_{*,1}^{-1/2}|\). Lemma 2.6 asserts \[|s_{*,1}^{-1/2}(k_1+k_1^{\mathsf T})s_{*,1}^{-1/2}|^2\le(\widetilde\Theta_1-1)\min\{2,\widetilde\Theta_1-1\}\] and \[\widetilde\Theta_1-1\le|E_{*,1}^{-1/2}E_1E_{*,1}^{-1/2}-I_{2d}|\le6(\widetilde\Theta_1-1).\] In particular, these bounds are claimed without requiring \(k_1\) to be skew-symmetric.

Let \(\omega_1,\omega_2\) be Poisson point clouds on \(\mathbb R^d\), of intensities \(\rho_1,\rho_2\ge0\), and let \(0<\lambda\le1\le\Lambda<\infty\). Equation (1.28) defines \[\mathbf a(x)=\left(1+(\Lambda-1)(\mathbf1_{B_1}*\omega_1)(x)+(\lambda-1)(\mathbf1_{B_1}*\omega_2)(x)\right)I_d.\] The text asserts that, irrespective of the intensities, this field is uniformly elliptic with lower and upper constants \(\lambda\) and \(\Lambda\). Proposition 1.1 further asserts that sufficiently small \(\max\{\rho_1,\rho_2\}\) gives (P1), (P2), and (P3), with coarse ellipticity contrast close to one for any \(\gamma\in(0,1)\).

Appendix D.1 uses the same additive formula with balls of radius \(1/3\). In both formulas, convolution of the indicator with the point measure counts overlapping inclusions with multiplicity. No truncation to an occupancy indicator or exclusion of overlapping balls appears in the definition whose positivity and ellipticity are being asserted.

Let \(h>0\) and let \(g\) be a real \(d\times d\) matrix-valued Gaussian field, each entry being a standard-mollifier convolution of a fractional Gaussian field with Hurst parameter \(-\sigma\in(-d/2,0)\). Proposition 1.3 sets \(\mathbf a=\exp(hg)\) and asserts that it satisfies (P1)–(P3), including coarse ellipticity with \(\Lambda_0=\lambda_0^{-1}=\exp(Ch^2\sigma^{-2})\), for \(C=C(d)\). The entry hypotheses impose neither symmetry nor independence; Appendix D.3 explicitly claims that the symmetric part of the exponential is nevertheless positive.

The related Proposition D.3 assumes instead that \(g\) is \(\mathbb Z^d\)-stationary, has dependence range at most \(L\ge1\), and satisfies \(\|g\|_{L^\infty(\square_0)}\le\mathcal O_{\Gamma_2}(h)\). For \(\mathbf a=\exp(g)\), it asserts (P2\(\dagger\)) for every \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), with \(E_0=C\exp(18h^2)I_{2d}\) and a minimal scale \(\mathcal S\) satisfying \[\mathbb P[\mathcal S>Lt]\le\exp(Ch^2\gamma^{-2}-ch^{-2}\log^2t).\] Its proof also uses the pointwise bound \(|A|\le(1+|\mathbf a|^2)|\mathbf a^{-1}|\) for the associated double-variable matrix \(A\). These uniform bounds are part of the issue even if one separately restricts the exponential to have positive symmetric part.

Let \(1<\sigma\le2\), \(m\in\mathbb N\), and let \(X_1,\ldots,X_m\) be independent centered real random variables satisfying \(X_k=\mathcal O_{\Gamma_\sigma}(1)\), where \(\Gamma_\sigma(t)=e^{t^\sigma}\). Thus \(\mathbb P(|X_k|>t)\le e^{-t^\sigma}\) for every \(t\ge1\). Lemma C.2 asserts the uniform tail estimate \[\mathbb P\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^mX_k>t\right)\le\max\left\{\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{40m}\right),\frac{128}{(\sigma-1)^3}\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^\sigma}{2\sigma}\right)\right\},\qquad t\ge1.\] The second term has no dependence on \(m\). This is the asserted sum bound, in particular in the range \(1<\sigma<2\); the individual tail assumptions alone are the hypotheses.

Set \(\overline A_j=A(\square_j)\) for the monotone coarse matrices and \(\Xi_j=\det(\overline A_j)^{1/d}\), as in (2.107). Lemma 3.4 asserts that, for \(\delta_1,\sigma\in(0,1/2]\), positive integers \(h,N\) with \(N\ge h\lceil2\delta_1^{-1}|\log\sigma|\rceil\), and every \(m_1\ge0\), either some \(m\in[m_1+h,m_1+N]\) satisfies \(\overline A_{m-h}\preceq(1+\delta_1)\overline A_m\), or \(\Xi_{m_1+N}\le\sigma\Xi_{m_1}\). The matrix inference used in its proof assigns a factor \((1+\delta_1)^{-1}\) to each determinant-root ratio when the first alternative fails. The finding checks that inference; it does not assert that every abstract matrix witness is realizable by a coefficient field.

The subsequent application (3.9) chooses \(\delta_1=\delta\sigma^2/2\), \(h=2n\), but \(N/h=\lceil2\delta^{-1}|\log\sigma|\rceil\), and asserts that Lemma 3.4 applies with that budget. A separate claimed implication concerns Proposition 3.3: its hypothesis (3.5) is \[\max\!\left\{\Pi3^{-(1-\beta)\ell/4},\ K_\Psi^8\Pi3^{-(\nu-\gamma)(1-\beta)\ell/2},\ \frac{K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}^{16d}\Pi^4}{(1-\gamma)^4}3^{-\ell},\ \frac{3^{-(1-\gamma)\ell}}{1-\gamma}\right\}\le\delta\sigma^2,\] together with \(m\ge100\ell\) and the matrix conditions (3.6). The proof's purported restatement (3.11) multiplies the first term by \(K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}^{3\gamma}/(1-\gamma)\), and then uses this stronger condition in Lemma 3.5. The issue is whether the stated hypotheses supply that strengthened premise.
The finite-range construction on pp. 142–143 requires smooth nonnegative cutoffs satisfying \[1_{B_{3^n}\setminus B_{3^{n-1}}}\le\eta_n,\qquad\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\eta_n=1\] on punctured space.

The subsequent definition by a heat convolution with \(\eta_n\) is identified in (D.22) with the compactly supported product kernel \(k_\alpha\eta_n\), and is used to assert finite dependence range for the resulting Gaussian fields.

In the weakly mixing system \((X,\mu,T)\) of Example 4.2, with the distinguished generic point \(a\) from the surrounding setup, take \(\sigma=\delta_a\otimes\mu^{\otimes k}\). For positive-measure open sets \(U_1,\ldots,U_k\), set \(U_0=U_{k+1}=X\) and let \(T_\Delta\) act diagonally on \(X^{k+1}\). The example asserts \[\{n:\sigma((U_0\times\cdots\times U_k)\cap T_\Delta^{-n}(U_1\times\cdots\times U_{k+1}))>0\}\supset\bigcap_{i=0}^k\{n:\mu(U_i\cap T^{-n}U_{i+1})>0\}.\] It concludes that the left-hand set has density one along every Følner sequence. The right-hand side consists only of measure-intersection conditions and does not require \(T^na\in U_1\), despite the Dirac zeroth coordinate.

Let \((X,\mu,T)\) be ergodic, \(k\ge2\), and \((\Phi_N)\) a Følner sequence in \(\mathbb N\). Let \(\tau\) be a probability measure on \(X^{k+1}\), invariant under \(\operatorname{Id}\times T\times T^2\times\cdots\times T^k\), whose marginals satisfy \(\tau_i\le i\mu\) for \(1\le i\le k-1\). Theorem 6.6 asserts, for arbitrary \(f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1}\in L^\infty(\mu)\) and every bounded \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb C\), \[\limsup_{N\to\infty}\left\|\frac1{|\Phi_N|}\sum_{n\in\Phi_N}b(n)(1\otimes T^nf_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T^nf_{k-1}\otimes1)\right\|_{L^2(\tau)}\le C_k\|b\|_\infty\min_{1\le i\le k-1}\|f_i\|_{U^k(X,\mu,T)}.\] Here \(C_k\) depends only on \(k\). No unit-ball restriction on the functions or compensating product of their supremum norms is part of the statement.

For an arbitrary measure-preserving system \((X,\mu,T)\), Lemma 6.7(iii) asserts: for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every choice of positive integers \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\), there is a constant \(C\), independent of the system, such that for all functions \(f_i\in L^\infty(\mu)\) with \(\|f_i\|_\infty\le1\), and every Følner sequence \((\Phi_N)\), \[\lim_{N\to\infty}\left\|\frac1{|\Phi_N|}\sum_{n\in\Phi_N}T^{c_1n}f_1\cdots T^{c_kn}f_k\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}\le C\min_{1\le i\le k}\|f_i\|_{U^k(X,\mu,T)}.\] The coefficients are not assumed pairwise distinct, the system is not assumed ergodic, and the claimed range includes \(k=1\).

For a cubic number field \(K\), let \(\rho_K\) be its two-dimensional standard Artin representation and set \(D_K=|\operatorname{Disc}(K)|\), so that \(L(s,\rho_K)=\zeta_K(s)/\zeta_{\mathbb Q}(s)\). Theorem 4.1 asserts that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), every \(t\in\mathbb R\), and every cubic field \(K\), \[|L(\tfrac12+it,\rho_K)|\ll_\varepsilon(1+|t|)^{O(1)}D_K^{1/4-1/128+\varepsilon}.\] The field quantifier includes cyclic and non-Galois cubic fields and imposes no primality condition on \(D_K\).

For the non-Galois \(S_3\) case, the asserted proof input is the application of the cited Blomer–Khan Theorem 1 to the associated \(\mathrm{GL}_2\) automorphic form \(\pi_K\), which the article specifies to have level \(D_K\), unitary central character, and weight \(0\) or \(1\). This is the level-aspect invocation used to obtain the displayed saving \(\delta=1/128\) for all such cubic fields.

Let \(V(R)\) be the space of binary cubic forms over \(R\), with the twisted \(\mathrm{GL}_2\)-action \((g\cdot f)(x,y)=(\det g)^{-1}f((x,y)g)\). Let \(n\ge1\) be any integer and let \(\phi:V(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb C\) be invariant under \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)\). For either discriminant sign define the stabilizer-weighted Shintani series \[\xi^\pm(\phi,s)=\sum_{[f]\in\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)\backslash V(\mathbb Z)^\pm}\frac{\phi(f)}{|\operatorname{Stab}(f)|\,|\Delta(f)|^s}.\]

For a prime power \(p^\beta\), equation (35) defines \[\mathcal C_{p^\beta}(\phi_{p^\beta})=p^{-4\beta}\sum_{f\in V(\mathbb Z/p^\beta\mathbb Z)}\phi_{p^\beta}(f)c_p(f\bmod p).\] The weight \(c_p\) is the splitting-type weight of Table 1, pulled back from \(V(\mathbb F_p)\) for every \(\beta\ge1\); in particular \(c_p(0)=p^{2/3}\). For tensor functions \(\phi=\prod_{p^\beta\parallel n}\phi_{p^\beta}\), set \(\mathcal C_n(\phi)=\prod_{p^\beta\parallel n}\mathcal C_{p^\beta}(\phi_{p^\beta})\), and extend to arbitrary invariant \(\phi\) by multilinearity.

Proposition 5.2 asserts that \(\xi^\pm(\phi,s)\) is holomorphic away from \(s=1,5/6\), has at most simple poles there, and satisfies \[\operatorname*{Res}_{s=5/6}\xi^\pm(\phi,s)=\gamma^\pm\mathcal C_n(\phi),\qquad \gamma^+=\zeta(1/3)\frac{2\pi^2}{9\Gamma(2/3)^3},\quad \gamma^-=\zeta(1/3)\frac{2\sqrt3\pi^2}{9\Gamma(2/3)^3}.\] The residue formula is asserted for general moduli \(n\), including higher prime powers, with no restriction that \(\phi_{p^\beta}\) itself factor through reduction modulo \(p\).

Let \(\Sigma=(\Sigma_v)\) be a finite collection of cubic local specifications: each \(\Sigma_v\) is a nonempty set of étale cubic \(\mathbb Q_v\)-algebras, and \(\Sigma_p\) contains all such algebras for all sufficiently large primes. Section 6.2 fixes \(\Sigma_\infty\) to one of \(\{\mathbb R^3\}\) or \(\{\mathbb R\times\mathbb C\}\). For a tuple of binary cubic forms \((f_p)_p\in\prod_pV(\mathbb Z_p)\), with corresponding cubic rings \(R_{f_p}\), define \[\chi_\Sigma((f_p)_p)=\prod_p\mathbf1_{\{R_{f_p}\otimes\mathbb Q_p\in\Sigma_p\}}.\] This definition is on all forms and orders; it does not require \(R_{f_p}\) to be maximal at the specified primes.

The paragraph before Corollary 6.7 asserts that \(\chi_\Sigma\) factors through the reduction map \[\prod_pV(\mathbb Z_p)\longrightarrow V(\mathbb Z/r_\Sigma\mathbb Z)\] to a \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z/r_\Sigma\mathbb Z)\)-invariant function. The prescribed modulus has one factor \(p\) for every specified prime \(p\ne2,3\), and uses the factors \(16\) and \(27\) for specifications at \(2\) and \(3\), respectively.

The source calls \(\Sigma\) an \(S_3\)-collection if at one prime \(p\), \(\Sigma_p\) consists of the unramified cubic field extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\), and at another prime \(p^{\prime}\), \(\Sigma_{p^{\prime}}\) consists of \(\mathbb Q_{p^{\prime}}\) times its unramified quadratic extension. It then asserts that \(\chi_\Sigma\) is automatically an \(S_3\)-function in the congruence sense defined before Theorem 6.6: one local factor is supported on reduction type \((3)\), and another on type \((12)\). Both the finite-congruence factorization and this support assertion apply to the all-order indicator just defined.

Fix the finite \(S_3\)-collection \(\Sigma\) and a smooth compactly supported function \(\Psi:\mathbb R_{>0}\to\mathbb C\) with \(\int_0^\infty\Psi=1\), as in Sections 8–9. For an irreducible integral binary cubic form \(f\), let \(R_f\) be its order in \(K_f=R_f\otimes\mathbb Q\), and let \(\operatorname{ind}(f)=[\mathcal O_{K_f}:R_f]\). Write \(\mathcal U_b(\Sigma)\) for the \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)\)-orbits satisfying the local specifications and \(\operatorname{ind}(f)=b\). Let \(D(s,f)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n(f)n^{-s}\) be the series defined from the reduction splitting types, \(E(s,f)=D(s,f)/L(s,\rho_{K_f})\), and let \(e_k(f)\) be the correction coefficients of Definition 4.7 and Proposition 4.8, \[\frac{E(1/2-s,f)}{E(1/2+s,f)}=\operatorname{rad}(\operatorname{ind}(f))^{2s-1}\sum_{k\ge1}e_k(f)k^{1/2-s}.\] The weight \(V^\pm\) is the fixed approximate-functional-equation weight of Proposition 4.3, with sign determined by \(\Sigma_\infty\).

For every sufficiently small \(\kappa_1>0\), Proposition 9.11 takes positive integers \(m_1,q_1,k,n\) and \(X\ge1\), assumes that \(m_1\) is powerful, \(q_1\) is squarefree, and \((m_1,q_1)=1\). Here powerful means that every prime divisor occurs to exponent at least two, with \(1\) permitted. Write \(n=n_1\ell_1\), with \((\ell_1,q_1)=1\) and every prime divisor of \(n_1\) dividing \(q_1\), and put \(\ell=\operatorname{rad}(\ell_1)\). The asserted estimate is \[\left|\sum_{f\in\mathcal U_{m_1q_1}(\Sigma)}e_k(f)\lambda_n(f)V^\pm\!\left(\frac{nkm_1^2}{\operatorname{rad}(m_1)^2|\Delta(f)|^{1/2}}\right)\Psi\!\left(\frac{|\Delta(f)|}{X}\right)\right|\ll_{\varepsilon,\Sigma,\Psi}X^\varepsilon H(n,m_1,q_1;X),\] where \[H(n,m_1,q_1;X)=\frac{X}{q_1^2m_1^{5/3}\ell}+\frac{X^{5/6+\kappa_1/3}}{q_1^{5/3}\ell^{1/3}}+\ell q_1^2m_1^{12}X^{9\kappa_1}+\frac{X^{1-\kappa_1}}{q_1^2m_1^{5/3}}.\]

The surrounding application fixes small \(\kappa_\downarrow,\kappa_\uparrow,\eta>0\), uses \(X^{1/8-\kappa_\downarrow}\le q\le X^{1/8+\kappa_\uparrow}\), and writes \(mq=m_1q_1\) with \(m\le X^\eta\); the section allows implicit constants to depend on these fixed choices. The proposition does not restrict \(\ell_1\) to be squarefree. Its proof specifically invokes the uniform prime-power coefficient assertions \[\mathcal A_{\ell_1}(\lambda_{\ell_1})\ll\ell^{-1},\qquad \mathcal C_{\ell_1}(\lambda_{\ell_1})\ll\ell^{-1/3},\qquad\ell=\operatorname{rad}(\ell_1),\] as the first- and second-main-term inputs.

Fix the finite \(S_3\)-collection \(\Sigma\) and let \(V(\mathbb Z_p)^{\max}\) be the locus of maximal cubic rings. Normalize additive Haar measure by \(\operatorname{vol}(V(\mathbb Z_p))=1\). For a tensor congruence function \(\phi=\prod_p\phi_p\), Section 6.2 defines \[\mathcal A^{\max}(\phi)=\prod_p\int_{V(\mathbb Z_p)^{\max}}\phi_p(f)\,df,\] with the unspecified local factors equal to \(1\). Section 8.2 then defines \[t_\Sigma(n)=\mathcal A^{\max}(\lambda_n\chi_\Sigma),\qquad T_\Sigma(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}t_\Sigma(n)n^{-s}.\] These coefficients use the unnormalized mass of the maximal locus in the probability measure on all forms.

The proof of Proposition 8.4 asserts, for every integer \(n\ge1\), \[t_\Sigma(n)=\prod_{p^j\parallel n}\ \sum_{\sigma\ \mathrm{compatible\ with}\ \Sigma_p}\frac{\lambda_{p^j}(\sigma)}{\#\mathcal O_\sigma},\] where \(\mathcal O_\sigma\subset V(\mathbb F_p)\) is the finite \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\)-orbit of splitting type \(\sigma\). It asserts that \(t_\Sigma\) is multiplicative and uses the Euler product \[T_\Sigma(s)=\prod_p\left(\sum_{j\ge0}t_\Sigma(p^j)p^{-js}\right).\] Thus the displayed local weights are reciprocal orbit cardinalities, and the local series use the same globally defined coefficients \(t_\Sigma(p^j)\).

Proposition 8.4 asserts meromorphic continuation of \(T_\Sigma\) to \(\operatorname{Re}s>1/3\) with a simple pole at \(s=1/2\) of positive residue. The proof gives the residue formula \[\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1/2}T_\Sigma(s)=\frac12\prod_p\left[(1-p^{-1})\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{t_\Sigma(p^j)}{p^{j/2}}\right].\] The statement under review includes the coefficient normalization, finite-orbit formula and Euler-product formulas used for this analytic conclusion.

Let \(\mathcal V^\pm=\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)\backslash V(\mathbb Z)^\pm\) be the orbit set of integral binary cubic forms of the indicated nonzero discriminant sign. For a positive squarefree \(q\), let \(\mathcal W_q^\pm\subset\mathcal V^\pm\) be the classes whose cubic rings are nonmaximal at every prime dividing \(q\). For squarefree \(m\), let \(\omega_m(f)\) and \(\omega_m^{(1)}(f)\) be, respectively, the number of all roots and of simple roots of \(f\) in \(\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)\). Proposition 6.1 asserts that for every compactly supported function \(\Psi:\mathbb R_{>0}\to\mathbb C\), \[\sum_{f\in\mathcal W_q^\pm}\Psi(|\Delta(f)|)=\sum_{k\ell\mid q}\mu(\ell)\sum_{f\in\mathcal V^\pm}\omega_{k\ell}(f)\Psi\!\left(\frac{q^4|\Delta(f)|}{k^2}\right).\]

Theorem 6.5 takes \(n\ge1\) and an invariant tensor function \(\phi=\prod_{p^\beta\parallel n}\phi_{p^\beta}:V(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb C\). Write \((q,n)=de\), where \(d\) is the product of the common primes at which \(\phi\) is simple in Definition 6.4. At those primes the relevant factor is defined modulo \(p\), and simplicity means \(\phi_p(1^3)=\phi_p(0)\). Assume additionally that \(\phi_p(0)=0\) for every \(p\mid d\), and write \(n=dm\), \((d,m)=1\), \(\phi=\phi_d\phi_m\). It asserts \[\sum_{f\in\mathcal W_q^\pm}\phi(f)\Psi(|\Delta(f)|)=\phi_d(1^21)\sum_{k\ell\mid q/(de)}\mu(\ell)\sum_{g\in\mathcal W_e^\pm}\omega_d^{(1)}(g)\omega_{k\ell}(g)\phi_m(g)\Psi\!\left(\frac{q^4|\Delta(g)|}{e^4d^2k^2}\right).\]

Both assertions sum once over each \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)\)-orbit, without the factor \(|\operatorname{Stab}(f)|^{-1}\). They precede the later \(S_3\)-support restriction and include cubic rings with nontrivial automorphism groups. The root counts appearing on the right are the root counts of a representative form as defined above.

Let \(n\ge1\), let \(q\) be positive and squarefree, and put \(d=(q,n)\), \(m=n/d\). Let \(\phi=\prod_{p^\beta\parallel n}\phi_{p^\beta}:V(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb C\) be \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)\)-invariant. Assume it is an \(S_3\)-function: one local factor is supported on reduction splitting type \((3)\), and a factor at another prime is supported on type \((12)\). Assume it is simple at \(d\) in Definition 6.4, so \((d,m)=1\) and \(\phi_p(1^3)=\phi_p(0)\) for every \(p\mid d\), and require \(\phi_p(0)=0\) at all such primes. There is no size or unit-norm restriction on the complex local factors.

For every smooth compactly supported \(\Psi:\mathbb R_{>0}\to\mathbb C\), every \(X\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), Theorem 6.6 asserts \[\begin{aligned}\sum_{f\in\mathcal W_q^\pm}\frac{\phi(f)}{|\operatorname{Stab}(f)|}\Psi\!\left(\frac{|\Delta(f)|}{X}\right)={}&\alpha^\pm\mathcal A_n^{(q)}(\phi)\widetilde\Psi(1)X+\gamma^\pm\mathcal C_n^{(q)}(\phi)\widetilde\Psi(5/6)X^{5/6}+\mathcal E,\\|\mathcal E|\le{}&C_\varepsilon d^{1+\varepsilon}q^{1+\varepsilon}m^{4+\varepsilon}E_m(\widehat{\phi_m})E_\infty(\widetilde\Psi;\varepsilon).\end{aligned}\] Here \(\mathcal W_q^\pm\) is the orbit set nonmaximal at all primes dividing \(q\); \(\alpha^\pm,\gamma^\pm\) are the fixed sign constants of Section 5.1; and \(\mathcal A_n^{(q)},\mathcal C_n^{(q)}\) are the product Haar integrals defined in Section 6.2, with the nonmaximal integration locus at \(p\mid q\), and with the extra factor \(c_p\) for \(\mathcal C_n^{(q)}\).

The transforms and norms in the displayed error are the source ones: \(\widehat{\phi_m}\) is the normalized finite Fourier transform, \(\widetilde\Psi(s)=\int_0^\infty\Psi(x)x^{s-1}\,dx\), and \[E_\infty(\widetilde\Psi;\varepsilon)=\int_{\mathbb R}|\widetilde\Psi(-\varepsilon+it)|(1+|t|)^{2+4\varepsilon}\,dt.\] For tensor functions, \(E_m(\psi)=\prod_{p\parallel m}E_p(\psi_p)\prod_{p^\beta\parallel m,\,\beta\ge2}\|\psi_{p^\beta}\|_\infty\), where for \(p\ne3\), \[E_p(\psi)=|\psi(111)|+|\psi(12)|+|\psi(3)|+|\psi(1^21)|+p^{-2}|\psi(1^3)|+p^{-4}|\psi(0)|,\] and \(E_3(\psi)=\|\psi\|_\infty\). The constant in the asserted error depends on \(\varepsilon\), with the displayed factor depending only on \(\phi_m\); no factor involving \(|\phi_d(1^21)|\) appears in that error bound.

abla\omega=0,\qquad
u=
abla^\perp\Delta_D^{-1}\omega,\qquad

abla^\perp=(\partial_2,-\partial_1).\] The Dirichlet condition is imposed on the stream function; it gives impermeability of the boundary, not a zero boundary value for vorticity. Theorem 1.2 quantifies over every \(\omega_0\in W^{1,\infty}(H)\cap L^1(H)\) with \(\left\lVert\omega_0ightVert_\infty=1\), as well as the corresponding whole-plane class (p. 3). It asserts the upper logarithmic growth rate \(2/\pi\). Theorem 1.1 supplies an example attaining that rate.

At the bottom of p. 5, immediately after the whole-plane differential inequality, the source invokes odd reflection in \(x_2\) to assert the same bound on \(H\), with the \(L^1\) mass doubled. Odd reflection does preserve the velocity representation and bounded-vorticity weak evolution. It does not, for the entire class in Theorem 1.2, preserve the finite Sobolev gradient used in the preceding argument.

In dimension three, Theorem 1.6 considers a non-cutoff Boltzmann kernel \(B(r,\cos\theta)=\alpha(r/2)b(\cos\theta)\), with \(\alpha(r)=r^\gamma\), \(b(\cos\theta)\asymp|\sin\theta|^{-2-2s}\), \(s\in(0,1)\), and \(\gamma\in(-3,0]\). Assuming the Fisher-monotonicity hypothesis of Theorem 1.2, it asserts that for a sufficiently large exponent \(q\), every admissible initial density \(f_0\in L_q^\infty(\mathbb R^3)\) has a global classical solution of the homogeneous Boltzmann equation. Here \(\|f_0\|_{L_q^\infty}=\|\langle v\rangle^qf_0\|_\infty\); the theorem does not add \(\gamma+2s>-2\).

The particular continuation implication in Section 10 is that bounded Fisher information, hence an \(L^3\) bound, together with propagation of arbitrarily high finite \(L^1\) moments supplies a uniform bound on \(\int\langle v\rangle^{k_1}f^{p_1}\,dv\), where \(k_1=1-3(\gamma+2s)/(2s)\) and \(p_1>3/(3+\gamma+2s)\), as required by Theorem 2.1. The interpolation there is between weighted \(L^1\) and \(L^3\). This norm implication over the theorem's full independent parameter range is the assertion examined; no finite-time blow-up solution is claimed.

For the repulsive power-law potential \(\psi(r)=\psi_0r^{1-q}/(q-1)\), the angular collision kernel \(b_{\mathrm{col}}\) is defined by the scattering integrals in Appendix A, with \(\gamma=(q-2d+1)/(q-1)\) and \(2s=(d-1)/(q-1)\). The numerical comparison seeks a nonnegative subordination weight \(\omega\) and \(b_\omega(c)=\int_0^\infty h_t(c)\omega(t)\,dt\) such that, for every \(c\in[-1,1]\), \[c_1(b_\omega(c)+b_\omega(-c))\le b_{\mathrm{col}}(c)+b_{\mathrm{col}}(-c)\le C_2(b_\omega(c)+b_\omega(-c)).\] The ratio \(c_1/C_2\), combined with the bound for \(\Lambda_{b_\omega}\), is used to support \(|\gamma|\le2\sqrt{\Lambda_{b_{\mathrm{col}}}}\).

The introduction describes the difficult comparison as empirical. Appendix A reports close agreement for the remaining three-dimensional range \(q\in(2,7/3]\), equivalently \(s\in[3/4,1)\), using its weight (A.1), and further two-dimensional tests approaching \(q=3/2\) from above, with an adjusted weight for \(q\in(3/2,2]\). The reported computations support the claimed physical parameter range, but finite sampling, quadrature, and spectral reconstruction are the evidence being checked; the statement does not turn them into a certified uniform continuum comparison.

For the finite poset \(S\) of isotropy subgroups ordered by inclusion, the definition before Proposition 3.3 assigns to every nonminimal \(G\in S\) a unique maximal strictly smaller member \(G^-\). The argument uses this predecessor to index orbit families and the later spectral-sequence first page. The subgroups are cyclic, but no chain or unique-predecessor condition on their occurrence in \(S\) is stated.

Definition 5.5 uses the ordinary cohomological grading \[d^{\rm raw}_{j,n}(X)=\min\{i:\text{an admissible class lies in }H^i_{S^1}(X,s(B))\}-2j,\] where admissibility specifies a leading term \(S^jU^k\) times the fixed-sphere-bundle Thom generator modulo the stated ideal. There is no subtraction of the fixed-point level. For \(E=E_{\mathbb R}\oplus E_{\mathbb C}\), with trivial circle action on \(E_{\mathbb R}\) and scalar action on \(E_{\mathbb C}\), Lemma 5.15 asserts \[d_{j,n}(\Sigma^E X)=\dim_{\mathbb R}E_{\mathbb C}+d_{j,n}(X).\]

Let \(Y\) be a closed oriented three-manifold with an \(S^1\)-action inducing the specified \(\mathbb Z_p\)-action, and let \(X\) be a smooth compact four-manifold with boundary \(Y\). Assume the boundary Dehn twist \(\Phi\) is smoothly isotopic to the identity relative to \(\partial X\). Lemma 3.1 constructs a collar diffeomorphism \(\tau(y,s)=(e^{if(s)/p}y,s)\), extended by the identity, with \(\tau^p=\Phi\), and an isotopy \(H_t\) from \(\Phi\) to the identity satisfying \(H_t\tau=\tau H_t\) strictly. The isotopy concatenates a shifted collar twist with an isotopy supported in the smaller interior copy of \(X\).

Lemma 3.3 asserts that these data extend the boundary action to a smooth homotopy coherent \(\mathbb Z_p\)-action on \(X\). It assigns \(\tau^i\) to one-simplices and \(H_t\tau^{i+j-p}\) to the carrying two-simplices, then uses strict commutation to compare paths over three-simplices. The final step asserts that contractibility of \(\operatorname{Homeo}^+([0,1])\) supplies compatible fillings over all higher simplices. Proposition 3.5 also asserts trivial homotopy monodromy. The issue concerns that higher-coherence step for this collar construction, not a claimed theorem for arbitrary topological groups.

Section 2 explicitly allows the dimension to be a real variable in \((1,\infty)\) (PDF p. 6, printed p. 250). It studies \[
 u''+\frac{n-1}{r}u'+f(u)=0,\qquad u(0)=\alpha>0,\quad u'(0)=0.\] The definition on PDF p. 12, equation (2.20), is \[
 P_2(r)=r^n\left((u')^2+\frac{n-2}{n}uf(u)\right)
             +(n-2)r^{n-1}uu'.\] Under (C1)–(C3) and (C7), Proposition 2.5(iii) on PDF p. 13 claims \(P_2(r)>0\) and \(-[P(r)/r^n]'>0\), for all \(r>0\) for a ground/bound state, and up to the largest zero for a nodal solution. The proof on PDF p. 14 uses \[nP_2(c_i)=(n-2)c_i^n u(c_i)f(u(c_i))>0\] at a nonzero critical point. This strict sign needs \(n>2\).

Fix \(\delta\in(0,1/4)\), let \(n\) be sufficiently large, and put \(a=1/\sqrt2\), \(T=\delta^{-1}n^{1/3}\), \(b=2^{-7/6}(3\pi)^{2/3}\). Lemma 3.21(3) requires a twice-differentiable \(h:[-T,T]\to\mathbb R\) satisfying, among its conditions, \[\sup_{|t|\le T}|h''(t)+a|\le\delta,\qquad\sup_{|t|\le T}|h(t)+at^2+bn^{2/3}|\le\frac{\delta n^{2/3}}2.\] These are simultaneous requirements with the same constant \(a\).

For the KPZ line ensemble \(H^S=(H^S_1,H^S_2,\ldots)\) normalized as in the cited Definition 1.2, Corollary 25.1 asserts convergence in distribution, as \(S\to\infty\), in the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets of \(\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\times\mathbb R\), to \(2^{-1/2}S^{(q)}\) with \(q=2^{-1/6}\). With the parabolic Airy convention of (2.3), \[S_j^{(q)}(t)=q^{-1}S_j(q^2t)=2^{-1/3}A_j(2^{-1/3}t)-t^2/2.\]

The proof instead identifies each subsequential limit with \(S^{(q)}\). In particular, at \(t=0\), its one-point formula (25.1) is \(\mathbb P(H_1^\infty(0)\le a)=F_{\mathrm{TW}}(2^{1/3}a)\), the distribution of \(S_1^{(q)}(0)\). The extra factor \(2^{-1/2}\) in the corollary's stated limiting law is the normalization under examination; this comparison at zero does not rely on the separate centering signs in (25.1)–(25.2).

Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) be any bounded Lipschitz domain, let \(1<q<\infty\) and \(0<\theta<\pi/2\), and let \[\lambda\in\Sigma_\theta=\{z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}:|\arg z|<\pi-\theta\}.\] For every solenoidal forcing \(F\in L^q_\sigma(\Omega;\mathbb C^2)\), Theorem 9.5 asserts that the Dirichlet Stokes resolvent problem \[-\Delta u+\nabla p+\lambda u=F,\qquad\operatorname{div}u=0\quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\] has a unique solution \[(u,p)\in W^{1,q}_0(\Omega;\mathbb C^2)\times L^q(\Omega;\mathbb C),\qquad\int_\Omega p=0.\]

The same theorem asserts the uniform velocity estimate \[|\lambda|\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|F\|_{L^q(\Omega)},\] where \(C\) depends only on \(q,\theta,\Omega\). The stated membership in \(W^{1,q}_0\times L^q\) is asserted for the entire interval \(1<q<\infty\), with no additional boundary smoothness or restriction to exponents near \(2\).

For an arbitrary Lipschitz graph \(\psi\), put \(D_R=B(0,R)\cap\mathbb H_\psi\) and \(I_R=B(0,R)\cap\partial\mathbb H_\psi\). Equation (2.13) and Remark 2.3 assert the fixed-ball trace inequality \[\|\eta-\beta\|_{L^{q'}(I_R)}\le CR^{1-1/q'}\|\nabla\eta\|_{L^{q'}(D_{2R})},\qquad\beta=|D_{2R}|^{-1}\int_{D_{2R}}\eta.\] The arbitrary-slope extension retains the fixed ball and this single average; it does not replace the intersection by a connected graph box.

Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge2\), be a bounded Lipschitz domain with connected boundary. Theorem A.1 asserts that there is \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon(d,\Omega)\in(0,1)\) such that, for every \(q\in(2-\varepsilon,2+\varepsilon)\) and every \(f\in W^{1,q}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\), there is a unique \(v\in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\) and normalized pressure \(\pi\in L^q(\Omega)\), \(\int_\Omega\pi=0\), satisfying \[-\Delta v+\nabla\pi=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}v=0\quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad v=f\quad\text{nontangentially on }\partial\Omega.\]

It also asserts nontangential limits for \(
abla v\) and \(\pi\), and \(\|(
abla v)^*\|_{L^q(\partial\Omega)}+\|\pi^*\|_{L^q(\partial\Omega)}\le C\|
abla_{\mathrm{tan}}f\|_{L^q(\partial\Omega)}\), extending the estimate to all \(1<q<\infty\) when \(\Omega\) is \(C^1\). The boundary-data quantifier contains no zero-flux condition \(\int_{\partial\Omega}f\cdot n\,d\sigma=0\).

For \(f(u,x,y)=|x-y|^{-1}e^{V(u)}\), Proposition 4.3 defines \[W(z)=\min_{1\le n\le T}a^{-n}\mathbb E_z[f(Z_n)^{p_0}],\qquad p_0>0,\quad0<a<1,\quad T<\infty.\] Theorem 4.10 uses \(d(z,z')=\sqrt{d^\beta(z,z')(1+W(z)+W(z'))}\), with \(d^\beta=1\wedge\beta^{-1}d_V\), and asserts \[d(\delta_{u,0,e_1},\delta_{u,x,y})\le Ce^{V(u)}\log|x-y|^{-1}.\] The estimate is used uniformly as the two spatial points approach one another.

Under Assumption 1.1, the forcing set \(F\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}\) is finite and symmetric, spans \(\mathbb Z^2\) over the integers, and contains modes of different lengths. With independent modes \(k_0,k_1\) and the single-mode shear maps \(f_{k,T}\) constructed in Lemma B.6, Step 4 claims that four successive segments with mode/time parameters \((k_0,T),(k_1,T),(k_0,-T),(k_1,-T)\), for sufficiently large \(T>0\), wind the normalized tangent direction around \(S^1\). Consequently they are asserted to reach every prescribed oriented direction from \((0,0,v_0)\).

For Lemma B.8, put \(K=\max_{k\in F}|k|\), \(R_k=\{y\in\mathbb T^2:|\sin(k\cdot y)|\ge1/(100K)\}\), and \(R=\bigcup_{k_2,k_3\ \mathrm{independent}}(R_{k_2}\cap R_{k_3})\). In Step 3, if \(|y_0|\ge1/(100K)\) and \(y_0\) belongs to none of the \(R_k\), the integer-span assumption is asserted to yield independent lexicographically positive modes \(k_2,k_3\in F\) with \(\cos(k_2\cdot y_0)<-1/2\). This is used in the recipe for moving \((0,0,y_0)\) to \(\{(0,0)\}\times R\). The two local recipes, rather than general controllability or the main mixing theorem, are the claims examined.

Let \(D\) be a symmetrized six-vertex configuration on a graph embedded in a disk, with internal vertices of degree four and labeled boundary vertices of degree one. Definition 3.16 constructs \(\operatorname{trip}_2\)-strands by starting at each boundary vertex and continuing across the opposite edge at every internal vertex until reaching the boundary. Proposition 3.21 asserts that \(D\) is well oriented if and only if (P1) no such strands self-intersect or double-cross, and (P2) the three connecting segments of any three pairwise crossing strands form an oriented triangle. Here well oriented means that there are no isolated components and every move-equivalent configuration has a simple underlying graph and cyclically oriented three-cycles, as in Definition 3.19.

Corollary 3.33 likewise asserts that an hourglass plabic graph is fully reduced if and only if it is monotonic. Full reducedness excludes isolated components and any move-equivalent graph with a four-cycle containing an hourglass. Monotonicity requires that \(\operatorname{trip}_2\)-strands neither revisit vertices nor double-cross, and that the common vertices of each \(\operatorname{trip}_1\)-strand and \(\operatorname{trip}_2\)-strand are consecutive along both. The written strand predicates start from boundary vertices and do not separately quantify over closed straight trajectories.

For the webs admitted by Algorithm 7.1, Step (4) requires a benzene relation that creates a forbidden four-cycle. The proof of Theorem 7.2 asserts that if this benzene move is the only change in the current iteration, the immediately following iteration performs the square reduction in Step (2).

Let \(K\) be a locally profinite group acting on a small \(v\)-sheaf \(F\), with quotient \(G=F/\underline K\) also a small \(v\)-sheaf. Using connected components of the underlying topological space with quotient topology, Lemma 3.2 asserts \[|G|=|F|/K,\qquad\pi_0(G)=\pi_0(F)/K.\] Its assumptions impose neither compactness of \(K\), properness of the action, quasiseparatedness nor local spatiality.

Let \(f:G\to H\) be an ad-isomorphism of the reductive groups over \(\mathbb Q_p\) in §6, and let \(b_H=f(b)\), \(\mu_H=f\circ\mu\) be the induced local shtuka data. Put \(G^\circ=G(\mathbb Q_p)/\operatorname{im}G^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbb Q_p)\), and define \(H^\circ\) analogously. Proposition 6.6(1) identifies \(\mathrm{Sht}_{(H,b_H,\mu_H,\infty)}\) with \(\mathrm{Sht}_{(G,b,\mu,\infty)}\times^{G(\mathbb Q_p)}H(\mathbb Q_p)\). Part (2) asserts that \(\pi_0(\mathrm{Sht}_{(G,b,\mu,\infty)}\times\mathrm{Spd}\,\mathbb C_p)\) is a \(G^\circ\)-torsor if and only if \(\pi_0(\mathrm{Sht}_{(H,b_H,\mu_H,\infty)}\times\mathrm{Spd}\,\mathbb C_p)\) is an \(H^\circ\)-torsor. The disputed step is the converse implication for this induced action, rather than the identification of diamonds in part (1).

For \(a\in F^\times\), the orbital integral is \[I(a,\phi)=\int_{J(F)}\phi(a,A)\psi((\operatorname{tr}A-N_J(A))/a)\,dA.\] The proof of Theorem 4.4(1) chooses \(B=a_0+\varpi^m\mathcal O_F\) and a small compact open \(K\) on which the phase is trivial, multiplies \(1_{B\times K}\) by the stated volume, and asserts \(I(a,\phi)=1_B(a)\).

Theorem 5.9(1) gives the analogous volume-multiplication instruction for the two test functions in the double integral over \(J\times Y'\), again asserting exactly \(1_B(a)\) when the phase is trivial. In both constructions \(a\) remains a parameter, not an integration variable.

For \(0<\alpha<1/2\), define \(\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(r)=r^{-(k+\alpha)/2}\) when \(r\ge\varepsilon\), and \(\varepsilon^{-\alpha}r^{-(k-\alpha)/2}\) when \(0<r<\varepsilon\). Lemma 4.7 asserts \[U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(0)=\int_{\mathbb R^k}\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(|x|)^2\,dx=\frac{2\operatorname{vol}(B_1)}\alpha\varepsilon^{-\alpha}.\] Corollary 4.8 then uses the stated coefficient \(C_\alpha''=2\operatorname{vol}(B_1)/\alpha\) as a uniform initial-interaction-energy bound for probability measures.

Lemma 6.6, PDF p. 27 / printed p. 1063, claims that \(U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(r)\) is non-increasing in \(r\) for every \(\alpha,\varepsilon>0\). Its proof invokes radial monotonicity of \(\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\), which need not hold when \(\alpha>k\).

Theorem 1.1 identifies \(\mathbb C[\mathring R_\beta]\) with the cluster algebra of the constructed seed. This statement is distinct from the general criterion in Proposition 3.14 and from the particular cohomological conclusion in Theorem 6.8. A seed on an affine variety, as defined on PDF p. 18, requires its initial torus to be an open dense subset. It does not already require every mutated variable to be regular on that variety.

Proposition 3.14 [1, PDF pp. 21–22; printed pp. 1099–1100] states that if \(X\) is affine, factorial and irreducible, \(\Sigma\) is an integral sink-recurrent seed on \(X\), and \(\mathbb C[X]\subset U(\Sigma)\), then \(\mathbb C[X]=A(\Sigma)\). The proof first treats the cluster tori as embedded in \(X\), and then invokes a codimension-two complement. The stated containment does not supply those embeddings.

The working group in [1, PDF p. 2] is complex, simple and simply connected, with a fixed pinning and opposite Borel subgroups. A double word \(\beta=i_1\cdots i_m\) has letters in \(\pm I\) and Demazure product \(w_0\). Weighted flags are points of \(G/U_+\); strict relative position must be distinguished from relative position allowing a torus factor. The quotient \(\mathring R_\beta\) is asserted smooth, affine, factorial and irreducible, of complex dimension \[D=d(\beta)=m-\ell(w_0).\] The rightmost positive distinguished subexpression runs backwards from \(u_m=w_0\). Its solid positions form \(J_\beta\), with \(|J_\beta|=D\). The Deodhar torus has character variables \(x_e\), determined by their orders on the boundary divisors. A solid index is mutable when the corresponding almost-positive subexpression has initial value \(\mathrm{id}\). Frozen boundary divisors lie outside the open braid variety, and the frozen variables are units there.
For beta=ii beta-prime, the leading mutable vertex meets the sink/incoming-neighbor criterion used in Theorem4.10.

In the ramified case of Proposition 2.5, the prime congruences must satisfy \(p_1+\beta p_2=p_3\), with \(\beta=2r\gamma^{n\ell}\), where \(r\) and \(\gamma\) are units at the conductor primes. The proof reduces local compatibility to \[t_1x^2+\beta t_2y^2=t_3z^2\pmod m\] and asserts that choosing \(t_1=t_3\) removes the dyadic obstruction. All three prescribed prime residues must remain units; zero or nonunit coordinates are not admissible substitutes.

In Proposition 3.1, let \(N_j\) count pairs modulo \(\mathfrak p^j\) for which \(x\), \(y\), and \(x+\beta y\) are units, and put \(Q=\operatorname{Nm}(\mathfrak p)\). The displayed local singular-series factor is \[\lim_{j\to\infty}\frac{Q}{(Q-1)^3}N_j,\] with \(N_j\) an unnormalized pair count and no additional \(j\)-dependent residue-volume factor.

With the full torus weight algebra \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z_p[[T(\mathbb Z_p)]]\), the complexes are defined by \(M_w^\bullet=\operatorname{RHom}_{T(\mathbb Z_p)}(1,\operatorname{R\Gamma}_w(K^p)\widehat\otimes_{\mathbb Z_p}\Lambda)\). Theorems 1.4.8 and 5.5.2 assert a perfect, untwisted \(\Lambda\)-bilinear pairing \[M_w^\bullet\otimes_\Lambda M_{w',\mathrm{cusp}}^\bullet\longrightarrow\Lambda[-d],\qquad w'=w_{0,M}ww_0,\] with adjoint action \(t\mapsto w_0(t^{-1})\), although no involution is specified on the second \(\Lambda\)-action in the definitions.

Section 4.4.1 defines the ordinary-chart window used in Lemma 4.4.2 by \[S_{\mathbb F_p,(w-1,w+1)}^{\rm tor}=\bigcap_i\bigl(Z_{i,<w_i+1}\cap Z_{i,>w_i+1}\bigr).\] This intersection is asserted to provide the compactification needed for that chart and the subsequent argument, using the same index \(w_i+1\) in each of the two conditions.

Let \(\kappa\in X^*(T)^{M,+}\), with Weyl representatives \(w\in{}^MW\), and define \[C(\kappa)=\{w\in{}^MW:w^{-1}w_{0,M}(\kappa+\rho)\in X^*(T)^-_{\mathbb Q}\},\] using the source's antidominant chamber. Proposition 4.3.9 normalizes the local Hecke correspondence by the character \(\nu_w=-w^{-1}w_{0,M}(\kappa+\rho)-\rho\). The global correspondence uses any \(w\in C(\kappa)\).

Remark 4.3.12 asserts that its restriction to the \(w'\)-stratum is \(p^{n_{w'}}t_{w'}\), with the printed exponent \[n_{w'}=\langle(w')^{-1}(w_{0,M}(\kappa+\rho)+\rho),t\rangle-\langle w^{-1}(w_{0,M}(\kappa+\rho)+\rho),t\rangle.\] For \(t\in T^{++}(\mathbb Q_p)\), it further asserts \(n_{w'}>0\) whenever \(w'\notin C(\kappa)\). In this exponent the extra \(\rho\) lies inside both Weyl actions; this is the original normalization/positivity assertion being examined.

Lemma 2.10.1(4) permits an arbitrary complex \(F\) in the displayed derived category, assumes coherent cohomology and proper \(Z\), and concludes finite cohomology of \[\operatorname{R\Gamma}_Z(Y,F)=\operatorname{R\Gamma}(Z,i^!F).\] No lower-boundedness hypothesis on \(F\) is imposed.

Section 3.4 defines \(U_K=K\cap U_P(\mathbb Q_p)(1)\) and \(M_K=K\cap M(\mathbb Q_p)\). After proving \(K=M_K\ltimes U_K\) for \(p>2\), it uses the exact sequence \[1\longrightarrow U_K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow M_K\longrightarrow1\] and the identification in Proposition 3.4.9(5) without retaining the restriction \(p>2\). In particular it identifies the Levi quotient with the intersection \(K\cap M\), rather than with the Levi-projection image.

Section 4.1 allows \(n\ge0\) and defines the indicated strata by requiring the graded subgroups \(\operatorname{Gr}_i\), of order \(p^n\), to be multiplicative. It asserts these strata lie in the ordinary locus, including the stated depth-zero boundary.

Proposition 4.1.13(2) asserts that \(\bigcap_i(Z_{i,>j_i}^c\cap Z_{i,<j_i}^c)\) is empty unless each increment \(j_i-j_{i-1}\) is zero or one. The assertion is written for the whole scheme, although the divisors removed are vertical.

Theorem C asserts that for every arithmetic lattice in the fixed group, the elements moving a point of the associated symmetric space \(X\) by at most \(\varepsilon_X d\) generate a virtually nilpotent subgroup, where \(d\) is the trace-field degree. The constant depends only on \(X\), and the stated class includes reducible arithmetic lattices; no irreducibility assumption is imposed in Theorem C.

In the rank-one part of Lemma 4.2, let \(\Lambda\) be a uniform lattice in \(H\). The three pairs \((G,H)\) considered are \((\mathrm{SO}(n,1),\mathrm{SO}(m,1))\) with \(0<m<n\), \((\mathrm{SU}(n,1),\mathrm{SO}(m,1))\) with \(0<m\le n\), and \((\mathrm{SU}(n,1),\mathrm{SU}(m,1))\) with \(0<m<n\). In the symmetric-space metric used in the paper, the proof assigns critical exponents \(m,m,2m\), respectively. Writing \(D=\dim\partial X\), it uses \[\lambda_0(\Lambda\backslash X)=\begin{cases}D^2/4,&0\le\delta(\Lambda)\le D/2,\\\delta(\Lambda)(D-\delta(\Lambda)),&D/2<\delta(\Lambda)\le D,\end{cases}\] to infer a uniform positive spectral gap. The dimension \(D\), rather than an independently specified volume entropy, appears in the printed formula.

Theorems E and 4.1 assert a related orbital-integral estimate for every semisimple Lie group \(G\) with finite center and every uniform lattice \(\Gamma<G\): there are \(C,\eta>0\), depending only on \(G\), such that for all \(R_1,R_2\ge0\) and all noncentral \(\gamma\in\Gamma\), \[\int_{G_\gamma\backslash G}\mathbf1_{B(R_1)}(g^{-1}\gamma g)\,dg<C e^{-\eta R_2}\int_{G_\gamma\backslash G}\mathbf1_{B(R_1+R_2)}(g^{-1}\gamma g)\,dg.\] Here \(B(R)=\{g:d_X(K,gK)\le R\}\). Unlike Lemma 4.2 itself, these theorem statements do not exclude compact factors of \(G\).

In the arithmetic-lattice setting of Proposition 2.2, let \(\mathbf G\) be the enveloping \(k\)-group, \(n=\dim\mathbf G\), and \(\gamma\in\Gamma\) an allowed semisimple element. Choose a maximal torus \(\mathbf T\) containing \(\gamma\), let \(\Phi=\Phi(\mathbf G,\mathbf T)\), and let \(k(\Phi(\gamma))\) be the field generated over \(k\) by all values \(\alpha(\gamma)\), \(\alpha\in\Phi\). The proof asserts \([k(\Phi(\gamma)):k]\le n\); this is a bound on the common field of all adjoint root values, not just on each individual value.

It chooses one representative \(\sigma_i:k\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) for each real place or complex-conjugate pair and an extension \(\tau_i\) to \(k(\Phi(\gamma))\). With \(h(\gamma)\) the height defined in (2.2), it also claims \[[k:\mathbb Q]h(\gamma)\le\sum_i\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\log^+|\tau_i(\alpha(\gamma))|\le n[k:\mathbb Q]h(\gamma).\] The middle expression is the unweighted representative sum printed in the proof.

Let \(G\) be the semisimple Lie group of §5, with the left \(G\)-invariant, right \(K\)-invariant semimetric \(d\) induced by its symmetric space. For \(\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\{1\}\), define \(S_\gamma^R=\{g\in G:d(g^{-1}\gamma g,1)<R\}\). Proposition 5.1 asserts that there exist \(\varepsilon,m>0\), depending only on \(G\), such that for every uniform irreducible arithmetic lattice \(\Gamma<G\) with trace field \(k\), every \(g\in G\) belongs to at most \([k:\mathbb Q]^m\) sets \(S_\gamma^{\varepsilon[k:\mathbb Q]}\). The asserted bound has no multiplicative constant and includes trace-field degree one.

For an irreducible arithmetic lattice \(\Gamma<G\), write \(M=\Gamma ackslash X\), let \(k\) be its trace field, and put \(S_\gamma^R=\{g\in G:d(g^{-1}\gamma g,1)<R\}\) for \(\gamma
e1\). Corollary 5.6 asserts, for every \(0<R\le\varepsilon[k:\mathbb Q]\), that \[\sum_{[\gamma]
e[1]}\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_\gamma ackslash S_\gamma^R)\ \ge\ \operatorname{vol}(M_{\le R})\ \ge\  rac{1}{[k:\mathbb Q]^m}\sum_{[\gamma]
e[1]}\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_\gamma ackslash S_\gamma^R),\] where the sums range over nontrivial conjugacy classes and \(\varepsilon,m\) are the constants of Proposition 5.1. Unlike that proposition, the corollary does not assume that \(\Gamma\) is uniform.

For an \(X\)-manifold \(M\), put \(\varepsilon_x=\min\{1,\operatorname{inj}_M(x)\}\). Lemma 6.3 chooses centers \(S\) whose balls \(B(p,\varepsilon_p/6)\) cover \(M\), with \(d(p,q)>\max\{\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_q\}/36\) for distinct centers. In the final degree estimate of Proposition 6.1, the proof counts only \(q\in S\cap B(p,\varepsilon_p/6)\) and treats that count as controlling every vertex adjacent to \(p\) in the nerve of this variable-radius cover. Adjacency itself means that the two corresponding balls intersect.

The packing input defines \(C_X(r)=\sup_{0<t<1/2}\operatorname{vol}_X(B_X(x_0,rt))/\operatorname{vol}_X(B_X(x_0,t))\). Lemma 6.2 asserts that for \(0<\eta<\delta<1/2\), every \(\eta\)-separated subset \(P\subset B_M(x,\delta)\) satisfies \(|P|<C_X(\delta/\eta)\). In addition, the cardinality argument defines \(F_p(x)=\mathbf1_{B(p,\varepsilon_p/4)}(x)/\operatorname{vol}_M(B(p,\varepsilon_p/2))\) and then asserts \(\int_MF_p=1\). These are the printed counting, packing, and normalization assertions used for the bounded-incidence conclusion.

For the lacunary Mikado potentials \(\Psi_{j,k}\) of Definition 3.1, let \(S_{j,k}=\operatorname{supp}\Psi_{j,k}\). The source defines \(\Omega_{j,k}\) as the fixed \(\delta_0\)-neighborhood of \(S_{j,k}\), and \(\widetilde\Omega_{j,k}\) as its fixed \(2\delta_0\)-neighborhood, then sets \(\Omega_k=\bigcap_{m\le k}\bigcup_{j=1}^6\Omega_{j,m}\) and likewise \(\widetilde\Omega_k\). Lemma 3.3 asserts \(|\widetilde\Omega_k|\le2^{-k}|\mathbb T^3|\), and the corresponding local cube estimate (3.6). Its proof uses \(\mathbf1_{\widetilde\Omega_k}\le\prod_{m=0}^k\varphi(M_mx)\), although the base cutoff \(\varphi\) is specified to equal one only on the original pipe supports and to vanish outside their \(\delta_0\)-neighborhood.

Definition 3.4 requires \(\chi_k=1\) on \(\Omega_{k-1}\), zero outside \(\widetilde\Omega_{k-1}\), and \(\|\nabla^m\chi_k\|_\infty\lesssim M_{k-1}^m\). In the lower-amplitude argument for Proposition 3.7, the proof additionally treats \(\chi_k\) as one on the entire new pipe \(\Omega_{j,k}\), and treats the point \(x=x_j\) as giving both the rescaled profile and oscillatory factor value one. These are assertions about the stated cutoffs and rescaled profiles, not extra conditions imposed in their definitions.

The potentials \(\psi_k^0\) are convolutions of \(\sum_j a_{j,k}\Psi_{j,k}^0\) with a mollifier at radius \(\ell_k=N_{k+1}^{-1/3}N_k^{-2/3}\). Remark 3.12 asserts \(\chi_{k+1}=1\) on \(\operatorname{supp}\mathcal D\psi_k^0\), where \(\mathcal Df=-\nabla f-(\nabla f)^{\mathsf T}+2\operatorname{div}(f)I\), and uses this to identify both principal parts' initial traces with \(\sum_k\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}\psi_k^0\). The fixed neighborhoods, cutoff plateaus, and post-convolution support containment are the construction claims under examination.

Fix the construction parameters of Section 2.4, with \(0<\alpha<1/8\), the permitted \(\gamma\), and \(0<\kappa<1/2-1/(2\gamma)-2\alpha\). Let \(Y\) consist of continuous symmetric-matrix fields \(a:(0,1]\to C^{1,\kappa}(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb S^{3\times3})\) with \[\|a\|_Y=\sup_{0<r\le1}\left(r^{1-\alpha}\|a(r)\|_\infty+r^{3/2-\alpha}\|\nabla a(r)\|_{C^\kappa}\right)<\infty.\] For either constructed principal field \(v^{(i)}\), \(i\in\{1,2\}\), let \(S^{(i)}(t,s)a\) solve \(\partial_tu-\Delta u+2\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(v^{(i)}\odot u)=0\) with \(u(s)=\mathbb P\operatorname{div}a(s)\).

Proposition 4.2 asserts, for all \(a\in Y\) and \(0<s\le t\le1\), \[\|S^{(i)}(t,s)a\|_\infty+(t-s)^{1/2}\|\nabla S^{(i)}(t,s)a\|_{C^\kappa}\lesssim s^{-1+\alpha-\epsilon}t^{-1/2+\epsilon}\|a\|_Y.\] Here \(\epsilon>0\) is chosen as small as needed, the scale parameter \(A\) is then taken sufficiently large, and the implicit constant is independent of \(A\). The printed estimate has no extra \(t^{-\kappa/2}\) loss.

In the homogeneous Hölder–Zygmund scale \(\mathcal C^s=\dot B^s_{\infty,\infty}\), (2.7) states \[\|e^{t\Delta}\nabla^mf\|_{\mathcal C^{s_1}}\lesssim t^{-(m+s_1-s_2)/2}\|f\|_{\mathcal C^{s_2}}\] for \(m\ge0\), \(s_1,s_2\in\mathbb R\), \(m+s_1-s_2\ge0\), and \(f\in\mathcal C^{s_2}\), also allowing the Leray projection \(\mathbb P\) on the left. The following paragraph claims that \(\mathcal C^0\) can be replaced by \(L^\infty\), except for \(\|e^{t\Delta}\mathbb Pf\|_\infty\lesssim\|f\|_\infty\). Its exclusions do not remove the zero-smoothing-gap case \(m=1,s_1=0,s_2=1\).

Appendix C.3 also asserts, for the Fourier multiplier \(m(\xi)=e^{-t|\xi|^2}\pi(\xi/N)\) of \(P_Ne^{t\Delta}\), the pointwise kernel estimate \[|\mathcal F^{-1}_{\mathbb R^3}m(x)|\lesssim\min\left\{1,\left(\frac{1+N^2t}{|x|}\right)^{10}\right\}\exp(-N^2t/O(1)).\] At \(t=0\), its right side stays bounded independently of the frequency scale \(N\). This is the printed scaling assertion being checked.

In Proposition 3.13 define \[III=\sum_k\int_{t_1}^{t_2}N_k^{1+\beta_1}e^{-N_{k+1}^2r}r^{-1/2}\,dr.\] Under the stated scale assumptions, including \(1+\beta_1<b\), the proof bounds this positive quantity by a constant times \(t_1^{1/2-(1+\beta_1)/(2b)}\). The assertion is used as \(t_1\) tends to zero with the other permitted parameters fixed.

After applying Grönwall in Proposition B.1, the proof bounds the squared energy supremum plus its nonnegative gradient term by \[\|w^0\|_2^2+8\exp(\|v\|_{L^2_tL^\infty_x}^2).\] The assertion is made for the homogeneous linear problem (B.1) with arbitrary admissible initial data \(w^0\), without a size normalization on those data.
Elliptic tangent weights annihilate printed caustic-preservation functionals and caustic-preserving graphs obey a quadratic bound.

Fix the caustic cutoff \(\omega_{\max}=1/q_0\) and the finite cutoff \(q_1\) used in Lemma 6.8. The paired enumeration (6.11) attaches \(f_{2j}=c_{p_j,q_j}\) and \(f_{2j+1}=s_{p_j,q_j}\) to selected caustics \(p_j/q_j<1/q_0\), while the Fourier slot \(n\) has nominal frequency \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). The small-harmonic block has row and column slots \(6,\ldots,2q_1+1\), hence size \(2q_1-4\). Its entries before scaling are the preservation coefficients \(A_{p_j,q_j,\ell}\) for column frequency \(\ell\), as in (6.30).

The diagonal scalings (6.26) give the row slot \(n\) the eccentricity factor \(e^{q_1-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) and the column of frequency \(\ell\) the factor \(e^{\ell-q_1}\), in addition to the finite nonzero caustic/parity factors specified there. Thus the combined eccentricity factor is \(e^{\ell-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\), even when the selected denominator differs from the nominal frequency. Equations (6.31) and (6.36) identify this block with the rescaled finite matrices of (4.1), (4.33), and assert its convergence as \(e\to0\) to the invertible matrix \(\widehat A\) formed from (4.4), (4.36). This asserted finite-block limit is the claim examined.

For a rational caustic \(p/q\) of an ellipse, let \(\theta=\theta_{p/q}\) be its action angle and \(\phi(\theta)\) the elliptic-coordinate angle. Define the two unmixed preservation coefficient families by \[A^+_{p,q,j}=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(j\phi(\theta))\cos(q\theta)\,d\theta,\quad A^-_{p,q,j}=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\sin(j\phi(\theta))\sin(q\theta)\,d\theta.\] The assertions after (1.2) and before (3.3) identify \(A^-_{p,q,j}=A^+_{p,q,j}\), not merely their leading asymptotics or their mixed sine–cosine integrals.

Writing \(
u\) for the elliptic nome, put \(w_0=0\), \(w_n=
u^n/[n(1+
u^{2n})]\) for \(n
e0\), and \(E=\exp_*(jw)\), where the exponential uses convolution on \(\ell^1(\mathbb Z)\). The common coefficient is then asserted in (3.15) to be \(E_{(q-j)/2}+E_{-(q+j)/2}\) when \(q,j\) have the same parity, and zero otherwise. Theorem 4.10 assumes that \(R\) is complete local of characteristic two, dimension \(d\), with perfect residue field, and that \(P\in\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{fl}}(R)\) is concentrated in degrees \([0,d+2]\). It asserts \[\beta(P)\ge 2^d\frac{h_1^\infty(P)}{h^\infty(P)},\] and, if \(\chi^\infty(P)=0\), the further bound \(\beta(P)\ge2^{d-1}\). Here \(\beta(P)=\sum_i\dim_kH_i(P\otimes_R k)\), and the superscript-\(\infty\) quantities are the Frobenius-normalized homology lengths and Euler characteristic used in the paper. The category \(\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{fl}}(R)\) includes exact complexes, so membership alone does not impose nonzero homology or positivity of the denominator.

For the map to the Cox ring, equation (3.4) gives \[\phi_C(h)=\phi(h)\prod_k t_k^{-r_k\operatorname{ord}_{E_k}(h)},\] and defines \(\operatorname{ord}_{E_k}(h)\) to be the coefficient of \(E_k\) in the zero divisor \(D_h\). The assertion concerns that divisor-coefficient convention, including weight-zero invariants, rather than a separately renormalized valuation.

In the Cox-ring construction of §3, choose \(\operatorname{Ab}(G)^\vee\)-homogeneous generators \(f_1,\ldots,f_\ell\in\mathbb C[V]^{[G,G]}\) whose associated elements generate \(\operatorname{Cox}(X)\). Let \(N_W=\mathbb Z^\ell\oplus\overline\Theta^\vee\), and let \(\sigma_W\) be the cone generated by \((\operatorname{id}\oplus\psi_C^*)(\sigma_A)\) over all GIT chambers \(C\). With \(M_W=N_W^\vee\), put \(S_W=M_W\cap\sigma_W^\vee\). Choose homogeneous generators \(h_j\) of \(\mathbb C[W]\) and fix monomial presentations \(\varphi(h_j)=f_1^{a_{1j}}\cdots f_\ell^{a_{\ell j}}\). If \(\theta_j\) is the weight of \(h_j\), let \(S'_W\) be generated by \((a_{1j},\ldots,a_{\ell j},\theta_j)\). Lemma 3.3 asserts that \[\overline Y_W=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[S_W]\longrightarrow Y_W=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[S'_W]\] is the normalization map, with the indicated closed immersions of \(\overline W\) and \(W\). The construction does not require the chosen \(f_i\) to be minimal or require every such generator to occur among the chosen monomial presentations.

Lemma 4.3 allows a face \(F\) with \(\operatorname{relint}(F)\cap\overline C\ne\varnothing\) and \(\psi_C(F)\) not full-dimensional. Its proof moves the exceptional ray to a general ray in \(\sigma_k\) and asserts that the resulting toric morphism is regular and still induces the same quotient isomorphism. The permitted faces include those meeting only the chamber boundary.

Let \(V=g-A_\tau\), let \(P_+D_VP_+\) be the boundary operator of Section 7.2, and let the unweighted holomorphic extension be defined by \(E(e^{ims})=z^m\). For a vector \(v\) in the strictly negative spectral subspace of that boundary operator, the proof of (7.2) asserts \[q_{A,g}(Ev)=\langle P_+D_VP_+v,v\rangle<0.\] Thus it claims that the image of the entire negative boundary subspace is a strictly negative trial space for the bulk form.

Remark 2.2 takes \(R=1\), \(m=-1\), and \(B(r)=(r-1/2)^2+\delta\). With \(a(r)=r^{-1}\int_0^rB(\rho)\rho\,d\rho\), it assigns the potential at \(r=1\) the value \[1-\frac4{(1+12\delta)^2}\] and asserts negativity for \(0<\delta<1/12\). The claim concerns this explicit field and the paper's stated potential convention.

Section 3.2 asserts smooth dependence of sphere diffeomorphisms as \(\mathcal X(S)\times\mathcal Y_j\to\mathcal X(S)\), where the sphere-data norm controls the lapse \(\Omega\) in \(H^6\) and \(\mathcal Y_j\) controls the diffeomorphism parameter in \(H^7\). The transversal gauge parameter uses \[\|f\|_{\mathcal Y_f}=\|f|_S\|_{H^8}+\|f_u|_S\|_{H^6}+\|f_{uu}|_S\|_{H^4}+\|f_{uuu}|_S\|_{H^2}.\] The smoothness assertion is used for the full composed matching map in a neighborhood of Minkowski data.

Lemma 6.2 asserts that its localized perturbation formula realizes the prescribed momentum charges. With \(r=1+2c\) and \(h=\Omega\operatorname{tr}\underline\chi\), equation (6.4) assigns the degree-one mode \(h^{(1m)}=16\pi\dot P_0^m/(r^2\sqrt{4\pi})\) when the other target charges vanish and \(\eta=0\), and claims that the resulting momentum is \(\dot P^m(W)=\dot P_0^m\).

For every \(G\)-invariant section of a normalized \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}_n(F)\), Theorem 9.6 asserts a bounded chain once \(\deg_{\mathbb C}G\) is sufficiently large in terms of \(n\). Definition 9.4(c) requires each irreducible constituent to have the form \[W\simeq X_1\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}X_l,\] where \(X_i\) is an irreducible \(\mathbb F_pS_i\)-module for a quasisimple factor of \(G/O_p(G)\). The tensor product and irreducibility are asserted over \(\mathbb F_p\), not over an unspecified splitting field.
Theorem1.2 allows n=1 and forces H=1 in char0 and Gamma/H of class<=n-1 while covering A by K^{O_n(1)} cosets.

Let \(\Gamma=V\rtimes G\), where \(V\) is abelian and \(G\) is a finite group generated by \(d\) elements with \(\deg_{\mathbb C}(G)\ge K^{21}\). Let \(A\subseteq V\) be a symmetric, \(G\)-invariant generating set satisfying \(|A^3|\le K|A|\). Lemma 1.8, restated as Lemma 7.11, asserts \(A^{7d}\supseteq[V,G]\). The powers are exact product sets, and the hypotheses do not require \(1\in A\).

In the trigonalizable-section setup of §8, let \(U=O_p(\Sigma)\), let \(T\) and \(\pi:\Sigma\to T\) be the indicated complement and projection, and let \(V\) be a \(\Sigma\)-invariant section of \(U\) satisfying \([V,U]=C_V(T)=1\). If \(A\subseteq\Sigma\) is symmetric, \(|A^3|\le K|A|\), and \(\langle A^\pi\rangle=T\), Proposition 8.5 asserts that either there is \(\chi\in\Phi^*(\Sigma)\) with \(1<|\chi(A)|\le2n^2K^{O(1)}\), or \(A^{O(1)}\) covers \(\langle(A^2\cap V)^T\rangle\). The bounded exponents are uniform in the setting of the proposition. Its assumptions do not include \(1\in A\), and the first alternative requires cardinality strictly greater than one, not merely a root image different from the identity singleton.

Proposition 3.1 requires \(Z_1\cup Z_3\subset P_J^1\) and \(Z_2\cup Z_4\subset P_J^2\). The proof orients \(H_1\) with \(Z_1\subset H_1^+\), \(H_2\) with \(Z_2\subset H_2^+\), and defines \[P_J^1=H_0^-\cap H_1^+\cap H_2^+,\qquad P_J^2=H_0^-\cap H_1^-\cap H_2^-.\] These are the claimed containments under the printed half-space orientations.

The concluding cap construction invokes the triple \(\{j_{l-1},j_l,j_t\}\) for every \(l\in[t]\), then takes the union of odd-indexed caps of size \(2n/t\) to obtain at least \(n\) vertices. The indexing range includes the first and last endpoints, so the asserted count relies on those triples and their associated colors/caps being available.

Proposition 2.3 assumes four disjoint sets \(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\) in spatial general position and that every segment \(x_1x_3\) lies above \(x_2x_4\). It concludes \[\operatorname{conv}(X_1\cup X_3)\cap\operatorname{conv}(X_2\cup X_4)=\varnothing.\] The definition of above permits a projected intersection at a common endpoint, and no projected-general-position assumption is imposed.

Throughout, \(X\) is smooth and projective over \(\mathbb C\), \(A\) is ample and globally generated, and \(L_m=\mathcal O_X(K_X+mA)\). Theorem 1.2 states \(N_p\) for \(m\ge n+1+p\); Theorem 1.4 states Koszulness for \(m\ge n+2\). Section 2 explicitly permits \(N_p\) for globally generated line bundles without requiring an embedding. Consequently \(X=\mathbb P^n,A=\mathcal O(1),m=n+1\), where \(L_m=\mathcal O\), is not a counterexample to the stated \(N_0\) convention.

A basepoint-free subspace of dimension \(n+1\) gives a finite flat map \(\alpha:X\to\mathbb P^n\). The enlarged diagonal is \(\Gamma_X=X\times_{\mathbb P^n}X\); it contains \(\Delta_X\), and its extra components meet the ordinary diagonal over the branch locus. The star arrangement \(\Delta^1\) uses edges \((1,j)\); the chain arrangement \(\Delta^2\) uses edges \((j-1,j)\). These are different ideals and serve different criteria.
Canonical second-factor G action makes restriction to direct sum of graph components an isomorphism on invariants, hence transports arbitrary diagonal sections into regular sections of Gamma.

Let \(M\) be a smooth oriented closed simply connected six-manifold with \(H_2(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\), primitive \(x\in H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\), and \(d=\langle x^3,[M]\rangle>0\); write \(x^2=dy\). Put \(H=H^3(M;\mathbb Z)\), \(\Delta_{d,k}=\{(du,ku):u\in H\}\), and let \(\mathcal K(M)\) be the kernel of the variation map \(v_{x,p}:\mathcal I(M)\to(H\oplus H)/\Delta_{d,k}\).

In the nonspin case write \(d=2\delta\), \(p_1(TM)=(d+48l)y\), and \(k=\delta+12l\), with \(l\in\mathbb Z\). Theorem 6.1(2) asserts \(\mathcal K(M)\cong\mathbb Z/2^a\times\mathbb Z/3^b\times\mathbb Z/7^c\), where \(b=1\) if \(3\mid d\) and \(b=0\) otherwise; \(c=1\) if \(7\mid d\) and \(7\mid l\), and \(c=0\) otherwise. The exponent \(a\) is zero for odd \(\delta\), one for \(\delta\equiv2\pmod4\), two for \(\delta\equiv4\pmod8\), and, when \(\delta\equiv0\pmod8\), two for odd \(l\) and three for even \(l\).

The calculation in §10.4 claims that this classification is obtained from the characteristic-number relation lattice (10.5), using \(\lambda=\sigma_1+3\sigma_2+\sigma_3\) and \(\mu=6\sigma_1+10\sigma_2+3\sigma_3\), with the geometric generator \(N_{-1}\) mapping to \((\mu/4,\lambda)=(-1,-2)\). The disputed assertion is the compatibility of the stated classification with that original lattice and generator image for all manifolds in the stated class.

Let \(M\) be a smooth oriented closed simply connected six-manifold with \(H_2(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\), primitive \(x\in H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\), and \(d=\langle x^3,[M]\rangle>0\); write \(x^2=dy\). Put \(H=H^3(M;\mathbb Z)\), \(\Delta_{d,k}=\{(du,ku):u\in H\}\), and let \(\mathcal K(M)\) be the kernel of the variation map \(v_{x,p}:\mathcal I(M)\to(H\oplus H)/\Delta_{d,k}\).

For spin \(M\), write \(p_1(TM)=4ky\), \(k=d+6l\). Theorem 2.16 presents the special Torelli group \(\mathcal J(M)\) using \(f_c,u,z,a_i,b_i\), \(1\le i\le b_3(M)/2\), with all commutators trivial except \([a_i,b_i]=f_c\), and with orders \[\operatorname{ord}(f_c)=2^p7^{1-c},\qquad\operatorname{ord}(u)=2^q3^{1-b},\qquad\operatorname{ord}(z)=2^r.\] Here \(b=1\) exactly when \(3\mid d\), and \(c=1\) exactly when \(7\mid(d-l)\). The exponent \(p\) equals two if \(d\equiv0\pmod8\) and \(l\equiv0\pmod4\); it equals one if \(d\equiv4\pmod8\) and \(l\) is even, or if \(d\equiv0\pmod8\) and \(l\equiv2\pmod4\); otherwise it is zero. The exponent \(q\) is two if \(l\) is even or if \(d\equiv2\pmod4\) and \(l\) is odd, and one otherwise; \(r=0\) for odd \(d\), and \(r=1\) for even \(d\).

For nonspin \(M\), the same theorem presents \(\mathcal J(M)\) using \(z,a_i,b_i\), with all commutators trivial except \([a_i,b_i]=z^6\), and asserts \(\operatorname{ord}(z)=2^{3-a}3^{1-b}7^{1-c}\), where \(a,b,c\) are the nonspin parameters of Theorem 6.1(2). Explicitly, \(b=1\) exactly when \(3\mid d\), \(c=1\) exactly when both \(d,l\) are divisible by seven, and, for \(\delta=d/2\), \(a=0,1,2\) when \(\delta\) is respectively odd, \(2\pmod4\), or \(4\pmod8\); for \(\delta\equiv0\pmod8\), \(a=2\) for odd \(l\) and \(a=3\) for even \(l\). These are claimed individual orders and a complete presentation, not only divisibility bounds.

In Section 7.3, with zero-section class \(e=[S_b^4]\), complementary class \(f=[Y]\), and intersection matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\chi&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the argument simultaneously requires the relative class \(\bar\alpha\) to satisfy \(j^*\bar\alpha=x^2\) and \(D\bar\alpha=e\).

In the proof of Proposition 8.1, the relative preimage of \(\alpha=x^2-d\bar\nu^*y\) is assigned dual \(S_{\alpha_1}+S_{\alpha_2}\), the sum of the two zero-section classes, for the displayed intersection form and normal-map evaluations.

For the family \(N_m=S(\xi_m)\), where \(\xi_m\) is the bundle over \(\mathbb{CP}^2\) with \(e(\xi_m)=x^2\) and \(p_1(\xi_m)=(3+4m)x^2\), equation (5.4) asserts \(s_1(N_m)=4m(m+3)\). The invariant uses the normal Pontryagin-class convention and the disk-bundle connected-sum construction specified in Section 5.

Let \(M\) be a smooth oriented closed simply connected six-manifold with \(H_2(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\), primitive \(x\in H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\), and \(d=\langle x^3,[M]\rangle>0\); write \(x^2=dy\). Put \(H=H^3(M;\mathbb Z)\), \(\Delta_{d,k}=\{(du,ku):u\in H\}\), and let \(\mathcal K(M)\) be the kernel of the variation map \(v_{x,p}:\mathcal I(M)\to(H\oplus H)/\Delta_{d,k}\).

Theorem 4.6 gives the extension \[0\longrightarrow(H\oplus H)/\Delta_{d,k}\longrightarrow\operatorname{MCG}(M)/\mathcal K(M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sp}(b_3(M),\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow1.\] It asserts that this extension splits when \(b_3(M)=2\), and also when \(b_3(M)\ge4\), \(M\) is nonspin, and \(d/2\) is odd; it then states that it does not split in all other cases. The standing manifold class permits \(b_3(M)=0\), which is therefore included in the printed residual nonsplitting clause.
The table for \(E^2_{2,0}\) in Section 11.2 asserts \[H_2(\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\qquad\text{for every }g\ge3.\]

Let \(\mathrm{BB}_n\) be the number of oriented fullerenes with \(2n\) carbon atoms, and let \(\mathrm{BB}(q)=\sum_n\mathrm{BB}_nq^n\). With the Eisenstein normalization \[E_{k,\chi,\psi}(q)=c_0+\sum_{n\ge1}\left(\sum_{d\mid n}\chi(n/d)\psi(d)d^{k-1}\right)q^n,\] Theorem 3.26 asserts that this counting series is exactly the displayed linear combination of Eisenstein series on publisher PDF31–32, at every coefficient. In particular, the printed combination includes \(-2672137\,E_4(q^3)/(2^1\!\cdot1\cdot3^9\cdot5)\), \(E_2(q^9)/64\), and \(2E_2(q^{12})/27\). The first denominator is printed with only the first digit of 11 superscripted. The assertion is an exact enumeration, so its coefficients must vanish for \(n<10\) and be nonnegative integers for permissible fullerene sizes; it is not merely a leading asymptotic or a formula restricted to the congruence class in Example 3.27.

Proposition 3.9 considers an even integral lattice \(\Lambda\) of even rank and a vector-valued modular or quasimodular form \(f:\mathbb H\to\mathbb C[\Lambda^*/\Lambda]\) for its Weil representation. It asserts that, whenever the discriminant group \(\Lambda^*/\Lambda\) is killed by an integer \(N\), every component \([e_\gamma]f\), \(\gamma\in\Lambda^*/\Lambda\), is modular or quasimodular for \(\Gamma(N)\). The hypothesis controls the exponent of the discriminant group; it does not separately impose level \(N\) for the discriminant quadratic form.

Proposition 3.18 further assumes that \(h\) is quasimodular for \(\Gamma(N)\), is a series in \(q^{1/d}\), and satisfies \(d\mid N\), and concludes that \(h(q^d)\) is quasimodular for \(\Gamma_H(Nd)\), where \(H\subseteq(\mathbb Z/Nd\mathbb Z)^\times\) consists of units congruent to one modulo \(N\). Theorem 3.20 applies this to every bistratum \((G,\kappa)\), claiming level \(\Gamma(L(\kappa),|G|)\) and weight \(\operatorname{len}(\kappa)-2\) for \(f_{G,\kappa}(q^{|G|})\), with the stated quasimodular exception when \(\operatorname{len}(\kappa)=4\). The reported second issue is whether the divisor hypothesis required by that invoked dilation statement is supplied for this application.

Definition 2.13 stratifies the flat-cone-sphere moduli space \(\mathcal M=P\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{CH}^9\) by conjugacy classes of point stabilizers. Proposition 2.14 asserts that these bistrata are exactly the intersections of the automorphism-group strata and curvature strata. The criterion after Definition 2.15 says that a list \(\{(n_i,\kappa_i)\}\) of quotient ramification orders and curvatures determines a nonempty bistratum if and only if its nontrivial ramification orders form a good orbifold \(\mathbb P^1/G\) from Proposition 2.12, each \(0<\kappa_i<6\) satisfies \(n_i(6-\kappa_i)\le6\), and \(\sum_i\kappa_i=12\). The issue is the claimed sufficiency of this recorded data for the inertia stratum, including the action on the collision factors.

Proposition 2.19 claims that, for an undecorated curvature profile \(\mu\), the positive-vector quotient \(\Gamma_\mu\backslash\Lambda_\mu^+\), for a Hermitian Eisenstein sublattice of signature \((1,\operatorname{len}(\mu)-3)\), is in bijection with convex sphere triangulations whose profile is a collision of \(\mu\). For a decorated profile \((G,\kappa)\), it similarly claims a bijection \(\Gamma_{G,\kappa}\backslash\Lambda_\kappa^+\) with orbitriangulations of covering group \(G\) and profile a collision of \(\kappa\), where \(\Gamma_{G,\kappa}\) has finite index in \(\Gamma_{\kappa^u}\). These are asserted bijections for the completed collision strata, so whether the quotient retains the necessary marked collision branches is part of the claim.

Example 2.22 describes the dilation parameter \(r\) in \(E(q^r)\) as the minimum triangle count, although the series convention in Definition 2.21 assigns \(q^n\) to \(2n\) triangles. The assertion under examination is this explanatory normalization of \(r\), not a new count of the table entries.

For \(d=\operatorname{len}(\kappa)-3\), Remark 3.14 gives a positive-volume formula for the constant coefficient of the weighted series, using \[c_0=\frac{d!\operatorname{Vol}(P\Gamma_\kappa\backslash\mathbb{CH}^d)}{6(4\pi)^d}\] without a factor \((-1)^d\). The formula is the one obtained from the zero-vector term in the stated derivative convention \(D=(2\pi i)^{-1}\partial_\tau\).

In Example 3.30 the individual \(T_2\) contribution is stated as \(1/(2^{11}3^{10}5)\), but the immediately following sum inserts the denominator \(2^{12}3^{10}5\) for that contribution. The assertion being checked is the equality of that intermediate sum with the stated mass total, rather than the final weight-nine coefficients.

Let \((\Lambda,\star)\) be an Eisenstein lattice of signature \((1,s)\), with Hermitian form valued in \((1+\zeta_6)\mathbb Z[\zeta_6]\), and let \(v\cdot w=\tfrac23\operatorname{Re}(v\star w)\) be the underlying even lattice of signature \((2,2s)\). No truncation or regularization is specified in this definition; the finding concerns that literal convergence assertion, rather than a separately regularized theta lift.
