Assume the Section 6 setup and \(s_{\mathbb Z}(\psi)=\infty\). Proposition 6.5 asserts at most \(\operatorname{rr}(A)\) \(H\)-orbits of biinfinite geodesics through \(H\) for which every finite subset has noncyclic stabilizer, and asserts that each such line is preserved by a hyperbolic element. The scope allows strongly inert subgroups of Magnus subgroups, including the free-base case explicitly permitted in Remark 6.2.

Theorem 5.7 assumes a hyperbolic vertex cover, an acylindrical action on the Bass–Serre tree, and prefix-closed relative quasigeodesic normal forms, and concludes that the induced normal form is uniformly quasigeodesic. It does not assume compactness of the total graph of spaces, although Theorem 3.4 invoked in its proof has that additional hypothesis.

Section 4 defines a \(\mathbb Z\)-cover by connectedness and a deck group isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z\). Proposition 4.6 then asserts a finite \(\mathbb Z\)-domain for every such cover \(Y\to X\) of a finite CW-complex, meaning a finite domain whose deck translates cover \(Y\). The definition does not require the cover to be regular.

The complexity is \[c(X)=(|\lambda|/\deg(\lambda)-|X_\lambda^{(0)}|,-\chi(X)).\] The proof of Proposition 4.12 calls \((0,0)\) the terminal value for its finite-cyclic endpoint. The assertion concerns this explicit ordered pair and the stated definition of complexity.

Let \(K\) be the one-dimensional function field with base curve \(B\) used in the paper, let \(C\subset(\mathbb P^1)^2\) be a curve over \(K\), and let \(\Phi=(f_1,f_2)\) be a split polarized endomorphism of degree at least two with at least one isotrivial coordinate. If both coordinates are isotrivial, Theorem 4.10 additionally assumes that \(C\) is not \(\Phi\)-isotrivial. For the corresponding family \(\mathcal C\to B_0\), the locus \(\mathcal C^{\Phi,\star}\) removes subvarieties that are irreducible components of \(\Phi\)-special subvarieties dominating the base. Here the special curves in Definition 1.7 are preperiodic curves and, in the exceptional-map case, images of torsion cosets in the associated algebraic groups.

Theorem 4.10 asserts that \(\mathcal C^{\Phi,\star}\) is Zariski open and that there are constants \(c_1=c_1(\Phi,C)>0\) and \(c_2=c_2(\Phi,C)\) such that \[\widehat h_\Phi(P)\ge c_1h_{\mathcal N}(\pi(P))-c_2\qquad\text{for every }P\in\mathcal C^{\Phi,\star}(\overline{\mathbb Q}),\] where \(\mathcal N\) is the ample line bundle on the base and \(\pi\) is the base projection. The universal quantifier is over this specified star locus, rather than a further open subset obtained by removing every horizontal section of geometric canonical height zero.

In Lemma 5.2 the proof asserts \[\pi_i^*\pi_{i*}\pi_{\mathcal C*}P=\deg(\pi_i)\pi_{\mathcal C*}P\] on the stated measure, with the justification that \(\pi_i\) is finite. The claimed operator order is pullback after pushforward; the local inference is stated without separately proving the required fiber symmetry of this particular limiting measure.

Let \(f_1,f_2\in\mathbb C(z)\) be rational maps of degrees at least two, not necessarily equal, with their measures of maximal entropy \(\mu_{f_1},\mu_{f_2}\). Let \(C\subset(\mathbb P^1)^2\) be an irreducible complex algebraic curve whose projections \(\pi_i:C\to\mathbb P^1\) are dominant. Theorem 3.1 asserts that \[\deg(\pi_2)\pi_1^*\mu_{f_1}=\deg(\pi_1)\pi_2^*\mu_{f_2}\] if and only if the supports of the two pullback measures intersect and there are positive integers \(\ell,k\) such that \(\deg(f_1)^\ell=\deg(f_2)^k\) and \(C\) is weakly \((f_1^\ell,f_2^k)\)-special. This equivalence includes exceptional maps; there is no restriction to ordinary maps that could exclude the algebraic-group cases. Weak specialness is the preperiodic-or-coset alternative of Definition 1.7 when both projections are dominant.

In the isotrivial case of the proof of Theorem 1.3, Section 6 infers that the curve \((M_1,M_2)(\Delta)\) is nonconstant whenever at least one of the conjugating Möbius transformations \(M_i\) varies with the base parameter. This is an assertion about the image curve, rather than merely about the individual conjugacies.

For the normalized symbol \(s(\xi)=A+\cos(\omega\xi)\), write \(H(k;A)=D^*S(A)D\), where \(\gamma_n=\Gamma(1/2+i(\omega n+k))\), \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma_n)\), and \(S(A)\) has diagonal \(A\) and adjacent off-diagonals \(1/2\). For \(A>-1\) and an integer \(N>(1+A)^{-1}\), Lemma 8.4 sets \(f_n=\gamma_n^{-1}\) on \(1\le n\le N\) and zero elsewhere, then \([F_j]_n=f_{n-(j-1)(N+2)}\). It asserts that any \(M\) such shifted vectors span an \(M\)-dimensional positive subspace for \(H(k;A)\).

In Paragraph 25, for \(n=\dim X\), an \(H^{ci}\)-curve is \[L=H_1\cap\cdots\cap H_{n-1}\cap H_n^*
 \subset X\times\mathbb P^1,\qquad
 H_i\in p_1^*|H|,\quad H_n^*\in|p_1^*H+p_2^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2)|.\] It must be smooth, and a length-two subscheme \(T\subset L\) is marked. The linear system \(H=mA\), \(A\) very ample and \(m\geq2\), is explicitly allowed. Claim 25.2 purports to lift an arbitrary reduced base curve in the marked length-two Hilbert scheme with arbitrary prescribed values in this family at finitely many base points.
Arbitrary reduced base curve in marked length-two Hilbert scheme admits rational Hci lift defined at prescribed basepoints through arbitrary prescribed smooth Hci fibers.

In Theorem 44 the ambient variety is smooth projective of dimension at least three over a perfect field. Its bounded locally closed set \(W\) of nodal handles is not required to parametrize connected curves. A comb with \(r\) teeth is balanced when every irreducible handle component has at least \(r/(2c)\) teeth, where \(c\) is the number of components. Definition 42 further requires freeness and the vanishing of \(H^1\) after a divisor of degree at most \(d\) on every handle subcurve.
For anyboundedlocallyclosednodalW, somepositiveinteger r gives connected combfibers and surjectivityonfieldpoints.

Claim 38.3 asserts that if the curves \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are free and their union \(C_1+C_2\) is locally unobstructed, then that union is free. The statement imposes no upper bound on the number of intersection points of the two components.

Let \(k\) be a perfect field and \(\{p_i:X_i\to Y_i\}_{i\in I}\) a finite collection of nonconstant morphisms of finite-type \(k\)-schemes. Lemma 60 asserts the existence of closed points \(x_i\in X_i\), with \(y_i=p_i(x_i)\), for which all residue fields \(k(x_i)\) and \(k(y_i)\) are isomorphic. Its quantitative clauses further assert an infinite set \(D\subset\mathbb N\) such that, for every \(d\in D\), there are infinitely many such points of degree \([k(x_i):k]=d\) when \(k\) is infinite, and at least \(|k|^d/2\) such closed points when \(k\) is finite. The issue concerns these degree and closed-point counting quantifiers in (60.1)–(60.2), rather than merely the existence of a compatible residue-field choice.

For a compact object \(U\) in the first localized category of Proposition 5.2 over the stated flexible characteristic-zero field, the radical of its coefficient annihilator \(\sqrt{J(U)}\) is asserted to be finitely generated. The proposition imposes no finite-height restriction on \(m\), so its quantifier includes \(m=\infty\).

At height \(m=\infty\), the coefficient-change functor preceding Proposition 7.1 is induced by \(\mathbb F_p[x]\to\mathbb F_p\), sending the polynomial generators to zero. The opening of the proof asserts that this is an equivalence on the indicated bounded numerical-motive categories; later arguments use its composite with the weight functor as conservative.

In the proof of Proposition 8.5, \(Q\) is the family of smooth projective varieties whose function fields strictly dominate the chosen field in the \(K(p,m)\)-order. The proof asserts that multiplication by \(p\) kills the identity of the bare complementary Čech projector \(\widetilde{\mathcal X}_Q\). This is stated before tensoring with the additional motives present in the subsequent maps.

In Theorem 3.26 write \(k=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\) and let \(\pi\) project to \(M\). The proof defines \[G=\operatorname{RHom}\!\left(R\pi_*k_{\{-A<F(x,-)\le-4s_1\}},k_M[\dim M+d]\right),\] where \(d\) is already fixed by the Morse–Bott relation \(H_{*+d}(F\le-4s_1,F\le-\infty)\simeq H_*(M)\). It then applies Lemma 3.27 to assert \(G\simeq k_M\); that lemma requires constant cohomology sheaves and \(R\Gamma(M;G)\simeq R\Gamma(M;k_M)\).

Let \((b,M_i,f_i,q_{ij})\) be a well-ordered twisted generating function linear at infinity with finite ordered indexing set \(I=\{1,\ldots,p\}\), where \(f_i\) has auxiliary dimension \(n_i\) and \(q_{ij}\in\mathcal Q_{n_j-n_i}\) satisfy the cocycle and stabilization identities. Lemma 3.7 claims that any change of total order can be achieved, after negligible shrinking, while preserving the generated Legendrian immersion and the equivalence class of the underlying \(\mathcal Q\)-twisted map.

For the adjacent swap \(i+1<'i\), its proof sets \(m=2(n_{i+1}-n_i)\), leaves \(n'_j=n_j\) for \(j<i\) and \(j=i+1\), and sets \(n'_j=n_j+m\) for \(j=i\) and \(j>i+1\). The final equivalence construction uses the cover \(M_k\times[0,2/3)\), \(M_k\times(1/3,1]\) of \(M\times[0,1]\), interleaves the old and primed indices as displayed on PDF27, and prescribes \(q_{k,k'}=0\) for every \(k\ne i\), together with the listed consecutive transition forms. The assertion under examination is that this specific cylinder is valid with the required dimensions and establishes the claimed equivalence; it is not a claim that no corrected reordering construction could exist.

The doubled-cover construction in Lemma 2.23 keeps the original transition forms inside each copy and sets \(q_{i' j''}=q\oplus q_{ij}\) for fixed \(q\in\mathcal Q_1\), ordering every first-copy index before every second-copy index. It asserts that these transitions form the strict \(\mathcal Q\)-cocycle required by the definitions. Strict equality of quadratic forms is required, not equality merely up to isometry or coordinate permutation.

A directed open cover \((U_i)_{i\in I}\) in Definition A.2 has a partially ordered index set such that each \(I_x=\{i:x\in U_i\}\) is finite and totally ordered. Definition A.3 permits a refinement \((V_j)_{j\in J}\) with \(V_j\subseteq U_{\sigma(j)}\), requiring \(\sigma:J_x\to I_x\) to be nondecreasing for each \(x\), not globally on all of \(J\). Lemma A.10 asserts that refining an MV-map gives an equivalent MV-map.

The printed proof defines \(K=I\sqcup J\), retains the orders within \(I\) and \(J\), and adds \(i<j\) for \(i\in I,j\in J\) when \(i<\sigma(j)\), and \(j<i\) when \(\sigma(j)\le i\). It claims that this is an order making \(U_i\times[0,2/3)\) and \(V_j\times(1/3,1]\) a directed cover of \(X\times[0,1]\), with the indicated refinement to the original cover. The issue is whether that global order construction follows from the pointwise refinement hypothesis.

Let \(M\) be a manifold without boundary, and let \(f^t:M\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(t\in[0,1]\), be a smooth family generating Legendrian immersions \((\varphi\times z)^t:L\to J^1M\). In Definition 2.1, generation requires the fiber derivative to vanish transversely and an identification of \(L\) with its critical set; no condition at infinity is imposed. For every compactly supported contact isotopy \(\theta^t\) with \(\theta^0=\operatorname{id}\), Theorem 3.6 asserts that for some finite \(m\) there exist compactly supported functions \(\eta^t:M\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{2m}\to\mathbb R\), with \(\eta^0=0\), such that \[g^t(x,u,x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_m,y_m)=f^t(x,u)+\sum_{j=1}^m x_jy_j+\eta^t(x,u,x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_m,y_m)\] generates \(\theta^t\circ(\varphi\times z)^t\). The theorem does not assume that \(L\) is compact or that critical preimages over the support of the contact isotopy are proper.

Let \(\Lambda_Z\) be a reduced symmetric clean cycle with Gauss degree \(2n\). The source defines \(\Lambda_{Z,S}^{[r]}\) as the ordered fiber product with diagonal and antidiagonal removed, then defines \[\Lambda_{Z,S}^\alpha=\sigma_{\alpha*}\Lambda_{Z,S}^{[r]},\qquad\operatorname{Alt}_S^r\Lambda_Z=\Lambda_{Z,S}^{(1^r)}\] without a stabilizer factor. It nevertheless assigns degree \(2^r\binom nr\), and degree \(2^{n-1}\) to each parity piece when \(r=n\) and the monodromy is even.

Let \(S\) be a smooth irreducible variety over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, \(A\) an abelian variety of dimension \(g\), and \(\mathcal X\subset A\times S\) a closed smooth proper family with connected fibers of dimension \(d\). Assume that the geometric generic fiber has ample normal bundle, \(d<(g-1)/2\), and satisfies Assumption 1.1 on its Euler characteristic. The main monodromy theorem asserts equivalence between: (i) the generic fiber is nondivisible, not constant up to translation, not a symmetric power of a curve, and not a product; and (ii) \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^n R^df_*\operatorname{pr}_A^*L_{\chi_i}\) has big monodromy for most torsion character tuples. Big monodromy means that the algebraic monodromy group contains the specified product of \(\mathrm{SL}\), \(\mathrm{SO}\), or \(\mathrm{Sp}\) groups as a normal subgroup, according to symmetry and parity. The hypotheses do not require \(d>0\).

Theorem A, repeated as Theorem 6.1, separately asserts that, for \(g\ge3\) and a smooth nondivisible \(X\subset A\) with ample normal bundle, the Tannaka group \(G^*_{X,\omega}\) is not simple if and only if \(X\) is the image of an isomorphism \(X_1\times X_2\to X\) induced by addition, with \(X_1,X_2\subset A\) smooth and positive dimensional. Again no positive-dimensionality assumption is imposed on \(X\) itself. The finding concerns these formulations at dimension zero, where the conditional Euler-characteristic exclusions of Assumption 1.1 do not add such a restriction.

Over the arbitrary characteristic-zero fields permitted in Section 3, characters are defined on the arithmetic étale fundamental group \(\pi_1(A,0)\). Lemma 3.12 asserts that twisting by \(L_\chi\) is a tensor equivalence and preserves the Tannaka group, without requiring a trivialization or normalization of the character local system at the identity.

The pairing \(V_\chi\otimes V_\chi\to a^*L_\chi\) takes values in a line local system, but the introductory upper bound places the full monodromy group in the corresponding scalar-valued orthogonal or symplectic group. The text also asserts finite algebraic monodromy for a family constant up to translation, without limiting that assertion to characters with finite image.

Theorem 7.6 permits \(e,r\ge1\). For smooth nondivisible \(X\) and the stated \(Z\), with both Gauss maps finite, it asserts that \(Z\) is a curve if \[\operatorname{Alt}^r\Lambda_Z=\Lambda_{[e](X)},\qquad r\dim Z<\dim A.\] The parameter range includes \(r=1\); no lower bound \(r\ge2\) is imposed.

In the construction used for Theorem 1.3, let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) be the bounded annular domain with outer boundary \(\Gamma_1\), inner boundary \(\Gamma_2=\partial\Omega^{\prime}\), and bounded hole \(\Omega^{\prime}\). The constructed nonconstant eigenfunction \(u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)\) satisfies \[\Delta u+\mu u=0\quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad \nabla u=0\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega,\qquad u|_{\Gamma_j}=c_j\quad(j=1,2),\] with \(\mu>0\); the constants on the two boundary components need not agree.

Define the velocity and pressure on the whole plane by \[v= egin{cases}(u_{x_2},-u_{x_1})&	ext{in }\Omega,\0&	ext{outside }\Omega,\end{cases}\qquad p= egin{cases}0&	ext{in the unbounded complementary component},\-	frac12(|
abla u|^2+\mu u^2-\mu c_1^2)&	ext{in }\Omega,\-	frac\mu2(c_2^2-c_1^2)&	ext{in }\Omega^{\prime}.\end{cases}\] For every \(w\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)\), put \[I_D(w)=\int_D\left(\sum_{i,j=1}^2v_iv_j\partial_iw_j+p\,\operatorname{div}wight)dx.\] The first display on source page 34 asserts \[I_{\mathbb R^2}(w)=I_\Omega(w)=-\int_\Omega ig((v\cdot
abla)v+
abla p ig)\cdot w\,dx=0.\] The quantifier is over all such compactly supported smooth vector fields, without imposing \(\operatorname{div}w=0\); these intermediate equalities are the claimed passage to the global weak Euler equation.

Theorem 6.1 concerns a smooth bounded planar domain admitting infinitely many orthogonal Neumann eigenfunctions that are locally constant on its boundary, and asserts that the domain is a disk or an annulus. At the curvature step of its proof, let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be the distinct parallel-curve constants, with \(C_1=0\), and let \(k(s)\ne0\) be the curvature on a small interval on which \(1+C_\ell k(s)\ne0\) for every \(\ell\). The stationary-phase relation (6.10) has the form \[\sum_{\ell=1}^m\widetilde\delta_\ell\left|\frac{k(s)}{1+C_\ell k(s)}\right|^{-1/2}=o(1).\]

The proof takes a nonvanishing real or imaginary part of these coefficients and normalizes it to give real unit vectors \(A_r\), then passes to a subsequence with \(A_r\to A\), \(\|A\|_2=1\). It asserts that the same normalized coefficients rewrite (6.10) as \[A_r\cdot V(s)=o(1),\qquad V(s)=\left(\frac{k(s)}{1+C_1k(s)},\ldots,\frac{k(s)}{1+C_mk(s)}\right),\] hence \(A\cdot V(s)=0\) throughout the interval. This is the claimed linear rewriting used to infer that \(k\) is constant; the components of \(V\) here are the printed fractions themselves.

Fix \(0<\tau<1/100\). A GCD graph \(G=(\mu,V,W,E,P,f,g)\) has finite vertex sets in \(\mathbb N\), edges \(E\subseteq V\times W\), a measure \(\mu\) with finite singleton masses, and the divisibility data of Definition 1. Zero singleton masses are allowed. Put \(\delta(G)=\mu(E)/(\mu(V)\mu(W))\) when the denominator is positive, using the product measure on edges, and define \[q(G)=\delta(G)^{2+\tau}\mu(V)\mu(W)\prod_{p\in P}p^{|f(p)-g(p)|}\left(1-\frac{\mathbf1_{f(p)=g(p)\ge1}}p\right)^{-2}\left(1-p^{-1-\tau/4}\right)^{-3}.\] Lemma 10.1 asserts that every such graph with \(\delta(G)>0\) has either \[\mu(\Gamma_G(v))\ge\frac{1+\tau}{2+\tau}\delta(G)\mu(W)\quad(v\in V),\qquad\mu(\Gamma_G(w))\ge\frac{1+\tau}{2+\tau}\delta(G)\mu(V)\quad(w\in W),\] or a GCD subgraph with the same \((P,f,g)\) and strictly larger quality. The degree alternative quantifies over every vertex, including vertices of zero measure.

Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathrm{GL}(V)\) with finite first moment, \(W\) a \(\Gamma_\mu\)-invariant subspace, and \(\overline
u\) a stationary ergodic probability measure on \(\mathbb P(V/W)\). Let \(V_{\overline
u}\) be the linear span of its support and assume \(\lambda_1(V_{\overline
u})\le\lambda_1(W)\), as in Theorem 1.5. A qualifying subspace \(W'\) satisfies \(\lambda_1(W'\cap W)<\lambda_1(V_{\overline
u})\) and \(\mathbb P(W'/(W'\cap W))=\mathbb P(V_{\overline
u})\). Remark 4.4(1) keeps these hypotheses, takes \(W'\) invariant under \(H_\mu\), and asserts that, when \(\lambda_1(W)>\alpha(\overline
u)\), the measure \(\overline
u\) has a unique \(\mu\)-stationary lift on the whole complement \(\mathbb P(V)\setminus\mathbb P(W)\). The disputed uniqueness is global on this complement, rather than uniqueness among lifts supported in one fixed slower-expanding subspace.

Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on a topological group \(G\), and let \(\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)\), \(\rho':G\to\mathrm{GL}(V')\) be strongly irreducible representations of \(G\). Suppose that \(\rho_*\mu\) and \(\rho'_*\mu\) have finite first moments and equal top Lyapunov exponents. Lemma 3.6 asserts that, for \(\mu^{\mathbb N}\)-almost every sequence \(b=(b_i)\), there is an increasing subsequence \((n_k)\) such that \[\inf_k\frac{\|\rho(b_1\cdots b_{n_k})\|}{\|\rho'(b_1\cdots b_{n_k})\|}>0.\] The irreducibility assumption is on the representations of the ambient group \(G\); the printed statement does not require the action generated by \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\) to be strongly irreducible.

With \(\Gamma_\mu\) the closed semigroup generated by \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\), \(H_\mu^\circ\) the identity component of its Zariski closure, and \(b_i\) independent with law \(\mu\), the first paragraph of page 7 asserts that for every \(g\in\Gamma_\mu\cap H_\mu^\circ\) and every neighborhood \(O\) of \(g\), \[\Pr\!\left(\limsup_{n\to\infty}\{b_n\cdots b_1\in O\}\right)>0.\] This is the recurrence assertion used to justify the induced-measure support identity.

In the setting of Section 3.4(i), let \(\pi\) be the idempotent obtained from the cone of the support semigroup and \(O\) the Zariski-open set used there. The argument asserts that the unnormalized sandwich set \(\pi(O\cap\Gamma_\mu)\pi\) is a compact subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}(\operatorname{Im}\pi)\). This is a claim of compactness for the linear operators themselves, beyond the compact closure of the projective image supplied by Proposition 3.7.

On \(\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2\), take an amplitude \(\alpha\) in the stated sufficiently large even-integer range. During the first half of each unit time period, the velocity is the negative vertical shear \((0,-2\alpha|x-1/2|)\); during the second half it is the negative horizontal shear \((-2\alpha|y-1/2|,0)\), using periodic torus coordinates. Let \(\phi_t\) be the resulting flow starting at time zero, and define \(T=\phi_1^{-1}\) as on source page 7.

Define the positive shear maps, modulo \(\mathbb Z^2\), by \[T_1(x,y)=V_+(x,y)=(x,y+\alpha|x-1/2|),\qquad T_2(x,y)=H_+(x,y)=(x+\alpha|y-1/2|,y).\] The identification on source page 22 asserts \[\phi_1^{-1}=T=T_2\circ T_1=H_+\circ V_+.\] This equality identifies the explicitly ordered positive shears with the inverse time-one map of the explicitly ordered negative-shear velocity.

For a bounded mean-zero function \(f\) on the torus, dyadic mixing at scale \(h=2^{-N}\) means that every dyadic square of side \(h\) has average bounded in absolute value by \(\kappa'\|f\|_\infty\), for a fixed \(\kappa'<1\). Remark 2.3 asserts that this implies the ball-average estimate (39), \[\left|\frac{1}{m(B_\epsilon(z))}\int_{B_\epsilon(z)}f\,dm\right|\le\kappa\|f\|_\infty,\] for every center \(z\) and every \(0<\epsilon\le Ch\), with fixed \(\kappa<1\) and \(C>0\). The direction and universal quantifier of the radius condition are the assertion being checked.

The proof of Theorem 2 applies the \(C^1\) correlation estimate of Lemma 2.7 to \(g\circ\phi_s\), where \(g\in C^1\) and the flow map \(\phi_s\) is controlled by a Lipschitz bound. The regularity assertion needed by that application is that these compositions belong to \(C^1\), with a uniform \(C^1\) bound on the time interval used in the proof.

The common coupling uses \(e_{N,j}(x,y)=N^{-1}e_j(N^{-1/2}x,N^{-3/2}y)\) and the same Gaussian coordinates for \(\xi_N\) and \(\xi\). The planar bridge runs for time \(N\rho s\), with covariance \(\operatorname{diag}(\nu,1)\), and its occupation coordinates are \(m_{N,j}=\beta\int_0^{N\rho s}e_{N,j}(B_N(r))\,dr\). The proof asserts that these converge to \(\beta\int_0^s e_j(b_{\rm sp}(t+r),t+r)\,dr\), yielding the target noise coefficient \(\beta\) for every \(\rho>0\). This parameter identification is the assertion being checked.

In §2, the paper uses unnormalized symmetrization \(\operatorname{Sym}g=\sum_{\sigma\in S_k}g\circ\sigma\) and defines \(I_k(\operatorname{Sym}(g_1\otimes\cdots\otimes g_k))=\pi_k(I_1(g_1)\cdots I_1(g_k))\). For a random-function chaos component \(\pi_kG(x)=I_k(g_x)\), with \(\overline g(x_1,\ldots,x_k,x)=g_x(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), (37) then defines its classical Skorokhod integral as \(I_{k+1}(\operatorname{Sym}\overline g)\). The text asserts that the resulting chaos integral agrees with the Gaussian-adjoint integral of Definition 8.

Lemma 25 assumes only \(\int_R\mathbb E[G(x)^2],d\mu(x)<\infty\) and existence of the classical integral, and claims Skorokhod integrability and equality of the two integrals. Its proof identifies the full classical domain with \(\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)\int_R\mathbb E[(\pi_kG)^2],d\mu<\infty\), and asserts the norm identity \[\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbb E\left|\int\pi_k(G)\xi\right|^2=\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)\int_R\mathbb E[(\pi_kG)^2],d\mu.\] This formulation also needs to be distinguished from the finite-absolute-mass random-function interpretation in Definition 10.

For the heat equation with delta initial data, Example 28 identifies the chaos kernel in (46) with the expected product of occupation densities of a probability Brownian bridge from zero to the endpoint \((x,t)\). In the proof of Proposition 29, (49) further asserts, for every measurable \(v\), \[\int_{\mathbb R^2}K_{x,t}(|v|)(y)\,dy=\|v\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2\times[0,t])},\qquad K_{x,t}(v)(y)=\int_0^t p(x-y,t-r)v(y,r)\,dr.\] These assertions concern the endpoint heat-kernel normalization as well as the stochastic-integral conventions.

For independent occupation-coordinate replicas \(m^{(j)}\) and the finite-coordinate randomized-shift partition function \(Z_n\), Proposition 39(c) states the \(k\)-th moment formula with exponent \(\sum_{j\ne\ell}\sum_{i=1}^n m_i^{(j)}m_i^{(\ell)}\), summed over ordered pairs without a factor \(1/2\).

Example 47 uses a circular Gaussian field with covariance \(2\log|e^{i\omega}-e^{i\omega'}|^{-1}\) and the exponential normalization \(\exp(\gamma\zeta-\gamma^2\mathbb E\zeta^2/2)\), while stating the subcritical range \(\gamma<2\).

Let \(Q\) be the probability bridge law from \((x_0,s_0)\) to \((x_{k+1},s_{k+1})\), and let \(M\) be the random measure from (85), with \(\mathbb E_PM=Q\). Lemma 87 states that its finite-time integral of \(\varphi\) equals \(\int_{\mathbb R^k}\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\prod_{i=0}^k z(x_i,s_i;x_{i+1},s_{i+1})\,dx_1\cdots dx_k\), without division by the endpoint transition density.

Proposition 84 considers independent standard planar Brownian motions \(B,B'\) on \([0,1]\), with common drift \((0,N)\) and arbitrary starting points. It asserts a universal finite \(c\) such that, for all \(N,r\ge1\) and \(0\le\gamma\le\pi/(8r)\), \[\mathbb E[e^{\gamma N\alpha(B,B')}\mathbf1_{A_r\times A_r}]\le e^{c\gamma^2},\qquad A_r=\{\sup_{0\le t\le1}|B_2(t)-Nt|\le r/2\}.\] Thus the stated bound has prefactor one uniformly down to \(\gamma=0\).

Proposition 85 takes the same drifted motions, or independent bridges from \((0,0)\) to \((0,N)\), and \(0<\kappa<1/2\). For all \(\gamma>0\), \(r>1\), and \(N\ge cr((\gamma r)^3+1)\), it asserts \[\mathbb E[e^{\gamma N\alpha(B,B')}\mathbf1_{H\times H}]\le2e^{b\gamma^2},\qquad H=\{\|B\|_\kappa\le r/2\},\] with the uncentered Hölder norm of (107). The proof of Theorem 6 uses this event to obtain, for every \(p<1\), path sets of probability greater than \(p\) and uniformly bounded truncated exponential moments. The finding concerns the printed cutoff and uniform-bound argument supplying that convergence hypothesis.

The supporting local-time formulas include the following additional claims. Lemma 76 states that \(\widehat B(s)=LB(s/t)\), \(0\le s\le t\), has occupation measure \(\widehat X=tX\circ L^{-1}\) and intersection local time \(\alpha(\widehat X,\widehat X')=t\alpha(X,X')/|\det L|\). Proposition 74(2), for the occupation measure of a space-time Brownian bridge over duration \(t\), bounds its \(k\)-th mutual-intersection moment by \(c(tk/(2e))^{k/2}/\sqrt k\). Lemma 78 states a bridge exponential bound \(\mathbb E e^{\gamma\alpha}\le e^{10\gamma}\) for \(\gamma t\le1\), and a shared-drift motion bound \(\mathbb E\alpha^2\le ct/(1+N^2t)\), with unrestricted duration \(t\). Proposition 77 defines \(\varphi(\nu,y)\) as a first moment in (102) but identifies its \(\nu=0\) value with the second moment in (103). These are the original normalization and scaling assertions, without the repairs developed in the proof record.

Let \(E\) be a bounded metric space with the binary hierarchy of §3.1: generation \(i\) consists of pairwise disjoint cells \(E_{i,j}\), each cell has two children, a unique parent and sibling, the cells give \(E=\bigcap_i\bigcup_jE_{i,j}\), and every nested sequence of nonempty cells has nonempty intersection. Flatness requires a finite bound \(A(x)\) on the number of cells contained in \(B(x,r)\) whose parents are not contained in that ball. Theorem 3.4 assumes flatness and, for every \(x\in E\), \[\Delta(E_i(x),E_i'(x))\longrightarrow0,\qquad L(x)^{-1}\le\frac{\operatorname{diam}E_i(x)}{\operatorname{diam}E_i'(x)}\le L(x)<\infty\quad(i\ge1),\] and concludes \(\dim_C E\ge1\). No shrinking-diameter or closed-cell hypothesis is included in the printed hierarchy definition.

Theorem 3.6 gives the analogous conclusion for a bounded union \(\widetilde E=\bigcup_nE^n\), with nested cells \(E_{i,j}^n\subseteq E_{i,j}^{n+1}\), uniformly bounded pointwise flatness constants, \(\lim_{i\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\Delta(E_i^n(x),(E_i^n)'(x))=0\), and two-sided bounds on the limiting sibling-diameter ratios. Theorem 3.7 instead assumes \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\lim_{i\to\infty}\Delta(E_i^n(x),(E_i^n)'(x))=0\) and sibling comparability with constants depending on \((x,n)\), and also concludes \(\dim_C\widetilde E\ge1\). These family formulations retain the same unrestricted notion of hierarchy; the finding concerns this abstract domain, rather than asserting a counterexample to a specific carpet or Brownian graph.

Let \(W\) be the Brownian path and \(X=\Gamma(W)\cap([0,T_6]\times[0,1])\) the compact graph portion used in Section 6. The measure \(\mu_X\) in (6.1), obtained by integrating level local times and equivalently restricting the pushforward of \(dt\) to this graph portion, is claimed to be doubling for the application of Theorem 3.2: almost surely there should be a finite constant \(C_X\) such that \(\mu_X(B(z,2r))\le C_X\mu_X(B(z,r))\) for the centers and radii required by that criterion.

Let \(X=\Gamma(W)\cap([0,T_6]\times[0,1])\) be the Brownian-graph piece and \(E_{n,j}\) its height-crossing tiles from §6. Define the bad tiles by \(\operatorname{diam}\pi_x(E_{n,j})\ge2^{-n}/(n\log2)\), let \(\widehat E_n\) be their union, and set \(A'=\limsup_n\widehat E_n\). With \(a_n=2^{-n}\) and \(\delta_n=a_n/(2(n+1)\log2)\), let \(S'_n\) consist of times \(t\le T_6\) for which the forward Brownian exit time from the vertical interval \(W_t\pm a_n\) exceeds \(\delta_n\).

Assertion (1) in the proof of Proposition 6.2 states that every bad tile satisfies \(\pi_x(E_{n,j})\cap S'_n\ne\varnothing\). The proof also treats a clipped tile's time projection as one interval or at most two intervals, and concludes the covering bound \[\#\mathcal D_n\le C\,\#\{i:S'_n\cap[i2^{-(n+1)},(i+1)2^{-(n+1)}]\ne\varnothing\},\] where \(\mathcal D_n\) is the set of generation-\(n\) dyadic squares intersecting \(\widehat E_n\). These auxiliary assertions are used to deduce \(\dim_HA'\le1/2\) and \(\mu(A')=0\). The finding concerns the auxiliary comparison and covering estimate, without claiming that those final small-set conclusions have themselves been disproved.

In the proof of Lemma 6.7, for each Brownian tile \(E_{n,j}\) the paper independently chooses a compact \(F_{n,j}\subset E_{n,j}\) with \(\operatorname{diam}F_{n,j}\ge\operatorname{diam}E_{n,j}-128^{-n}\). It forms the unions \(F_n\) over the good tiles and \(K=\bigcup_i\bigcap_{n\ge i}F_n\), as well as the displayed finite-stage sets \(K^N\), and intersects them with the selected vertical hierarchy. It then infers nonempty compatible hierarchical cores and near-full vertical projections, including \(\operatorname{diam}\pi_y(K\cap F_{n,j})\ge2^{-n}-16^{-n}\). The printed formula for \(K^N\) has an inconsistent tail index; even the intended finite union of tails requires the asserted compatibility to be justified.

In §6.4, for a lower-semicontinuous admissible density \(\rho\), the construction chooses a tile of minimum \(\mu\)-average within each height band and selected parent, and copies that chosen average to every tile at the same height. Writing the resulting functions as \(\rho_n\), the proof claims \[\int_X\rho\,d\mu\ge\int_X\rho_1\,d\mu\ge\int_X\rho_2\,d\mu\ge\cdots,\] and uses \(\rho_\infty=\liminf_n\rho_n\) to construct a vertically constant admissible density with no larger integral. No equal-child-mass condition or other mass-ratio identity is established for the Brownian tiles. These are the two proof inferences under examination; the deterministic selection and mass-tree models in the proof record are not asserted to be Brownian realizations.

For the carpet class with \(2\le\ell<m\), \(k\) retained columns in each row, and vertical sets selecting one child in every row, page 29 asserts a flatness constant \(A\le2\) for their cylinder hierarchies. In the flatness condition of page 16, this bounds the number of cylinders lying inside a ball whose parents do not lie inside that ball, counting across all generations. This premise is used to deduce (4.12) and then Lemma 4.6.

In the self-affine carpet construction, take \(2\le\ell<m\), with \(k\) retained columns in each of the \(\ell\) rows and equal symbolic mass \(1/(k\ell)\) on each child. The asserted dimension is \(q=1+\log_m k\). To prove doubling of the resulting measure \(\mu\), the argument on page 29 introduces a grid of approximate squares \(Q\) and asserts that \(\operatorname{int}(Q)\cap K=\varnothing\) implies \(\mu(Q)=0\), while every square with nonempty interior intersection has the same positive mass \(c_n\) at that generation. This assertion is made for the closed grid cells, including cells on whose boundaries carpet mass may lie.

For a vertical set \(E\) and a quasisymmetric image \(f(E)\), let \(I_n\) be a nested image-cylinder sequence and \(J_{i,1},\ldots,J_{i,\ell}\) the children of \(I_{i-1}\). The cylinder probability in Lemma 4.5 is used in the printed identity \[\frac{\nu(I_n)}{(\operatorname{diam}I_n)^\alpha}=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{(\operatorname{diam}I_{i-1})^\alpha}{\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}(\operatorname{diam}J_{i,j})^\alpha}\qquad(0<\alpha<1),\] equation (4.16), whose treatment of the initial image scale is under review. With the normalized measures on vertical sets, the following modulus argument asserts the strict bound \(\operatorname{Mod}_1(\mathbf E)>1\), although its displayed integration establishes a non-strict lower bound.

For the final graph-existence construction, the paper sets \(m=k\ell\), chooses \(k=2^r\), \(\ell=2^s\) with integers \(1\le r<s\), and claims that \(1+r/(r+s)\) is dense in \([1,2]\). For graphs \(K_i'\) of continuous functions with zero values at both endpoints and dimensions increasing to \(d\), it then uses \[\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(2^{-i}K_i'+1-2^{-(i-1)}\right)\] as the graph in its continuous-function existence conclusion. The endpoint of the domain of this displayed union is part of the local issue. These measure, scale, strictness and parameter assertions are distinct from the separately recorded flatness defect.

For a proper holomorphic map \(f:D_{p,q}\to D_{p',q'}\), where \(D_{p,q}=\{Z\in M_{p,q}(\mathbb C):I_q-Z^*Z>0\}\), \(q,q'\ge2\), and \(f\) has a local \(C^2\) extension preserving the Shilov boundary, the page-22 argument asserts that the nullspace image is contained in its affine second-order osculating space. In the curve notation used there, it requires \(\kappa(t)\in\kappa(0)+\operatorname{span}\{\kappa'(0),\kappa''(0)\}\); the preceding step places the velocity and acceleration of the quadratic curve \(y(t)\) in \(T_{y(0)}W_P\).

The downstream step on page 28 identifies \(L_P\) modulo the nullspace \(Z\) with the span of the first-order vectors \(V_u\) and second-order coefficients \(h_u^a\): \[\operatorname{span}\{V_u:u\le J_1\}+\operatorname{span}\{h_u^a:u\le J_1,\ a\le q-1\}=L_P\pmod Z.\] These are the local osculation and span claims used in Lemma 5.4, rather than a new formulation of the main factorization theorem.

Write \(H=\mathbb C^{p+q}\) and \([A,B]_q=\{V\in\operatorname{Gr}(q,H):A\subset V\subset B\}\). For an arbitrary subgrassmannian \(M=[V_M,W_M]_q\), the proof of Lemma 2.1 identifies the parameter space \(Z_M^r=\{(A,B)\in D_r(X):A\subset V_M,\ W_M\subset B\}\), where \(\dim A=q-r\) and \(\dim B=p+r\), with \(\operatorname{Gr}(q-r,V_M)\times\operatorname{Gr}(r-s,H/W_M)\). The symbol \(s\) is only subsequently specified for the special rank-\(s\) boundary-component case. In tube type \(p=q\), Lemma 2.2's proof identifies \(Z_P^r\) for a Shilov point \(P\) with \(\operatorname{Gr}(q-r,V_P)\times\operatorname{Gr}(q-r,\mathbb C^{2q}/V_P)\), and places \((A,A^*/V_P)\) in this product. These are the printed dimension-factor identifications at issue.

For a fixed rank-\((q-1)\) characteristic subgrassmannian \(X_\sigma\), page 7 assigns to each \(x\in X_\sigma\) a characteristic direction \(v_x\), unique up to scale, with \(T_xX_\sigma=N_{v_x}\), and asserts that \(v_x\) and \(v_y\) are parallel in fixed Harish-Chandra coordinates whenever \(x,y\in X_\sigma\cap\Omega\). This is stronger than constancy of the tangent space of the fixed interval subgrassmannian in graph coordinates.

For adapted frames \((Z,\widetilde Z,X,Y)\), Definition 4.1(i) declares the transformations \(Z'=W_0Z\), \(\widetilde Z'=BZ+\widetilde W\widetilde Z\), \(Y'=V_0Y+C\widetilde Z\), \(X'=X\) to be frame changes under its conditions \(V_0^*W_0=I\), \(\widetilde W^*\widetilde W=I\), and \(V_0B^*+C\widetilde W^*=0\). The prescribed Hermitian Gram matrix has null \(Z\) and \(Y\) blocks paired by the identity and negative orthonormal \(\widetilde Z\) vectors. The assertion is that the displayed transformation preserves that full Gram matrix. The proof of Lemma 4.2 also treats \(\operatorname{span}\{Z_\alpha+c_\alpha Y_\alpha\}\) as a null space for arbitrary real \(c_\alpha\), under the same normalization.

In the second-fundamental-form argument for a proper map with only the stated \(C^2\) boundary extension, page 24 chooses strictly increasing positive pivot indices \(v_1<\cdots<v_{q'-r}=J_1\), with \(v_0=0\), to eliminate rows. Equation (5.14) on page 25 writes \(Z_\alpha(x(t))=t\sum_U C_\alpha^UV_U+t^2\sum_U D_\alpha^UV_U+O(t^3)\) modulo the fixed \(Z_0\) space and subsequently identifies the varying coefficients \(C_\alpha^U(t)\) with constants \(C_\alpha^U\). Finally, after defining \(V_W=\widetilde Z_W-X_W\) and \(\widehat V_W=\widetilde Z_W+X_W\), page 26 substitutes \(X_W=(V_W-\widehat V_W)/2\) and uses it in (5.18). These are the local pivot, regularity, coefficient and sign assertions, not a new assertion about the main rationality conclusion.

Let \(f:\Omega\to\Omega'\) be a proper holomorphic map between the type-I bounded symmetric domains, with compact duals \(X,X'\) and the rational rank-one characteristic-moduli map \(f_1^\sharp\) used in §3. Lemma 3.1 assumes a point \(x\in\Omega\) and finitely many rank-one characteristic subdomains \(\Omega_{\sigma_j}\) through \(x\), with \(\sigma_j\in\operatorname{Dom}(f_1^\sharp)\), such that \[\bigcap_j X'_{f_1^\sharp(\sigma_j)}=\{f(x)\}.\] It concludes that \(f\) extends rationally to \(X\).

The global continuation argument in Lemma 3.2 takes a Zariski-dense set of characteristic flags where the finite-jet system has maximal rank, and uses surjectivity of the characteristic-chain projection to claim that a chain ending at any prescribed \(y\in X\setminus\Omega\) can be perturbed entirely into this good set while retaining that endpoint and an initial point in \(\Omega\). The finding concerns this fixed-endpoint avoidance inference. The retained proof record supplies a different rational reconstruction from the singleton condition; it does not claim that the rationality conclusion itself is false.

In the tube-type case of Theorem 1.2, let \(f:D_{p,q}\to D_{p',q'}\), \(q,q'\ge2\), be proper holomorphic, with a local \(C^2\) extension near a Shilov-boundary point and local preservation of the Shilov boundary. Suppose the geometric construction has produced the unique maximal characteristic spaces \(M_P=[L_P,L_P^*]_{q'}\) of Lemma 5.4, parallel for general Shilov points \(P\). Let \(\Omega'_1\times\Omega'_2\subset\Omega'\) be the maximal-rank totally geodesic product through \(f(0)\) whose second tangent factor is parallel to \(T_{f(P)}M_P\). Corollary 5.5 asserts that \(f\) takes values in this product and, writing \(f=f_1\times f_2\), that \(f_1\) is proper and rational.

Its proof claims that failure of \(f_1(S_{q-1}(\Omega))\subset\partial\Omega'_1\), together with properness of the pair, implies \(f_2(S_{q-1}(\Omega))\subset\partial\Omega'_2\) and hence properness of \(f_2\). It then invokes Corollary 5.5 again for \(f_2\) to obtain a finer product and contradict maximality. The unresolved obligation is a global proper-factor argument under the stated local boundary regularity, including justification of that recursive use.

The separate proof of Corollary 1.3 assumes global smooth boundary regularity, \(q\ge3\), and \(q'\le2q-1\). It invokes the cited rigidity result [Ki21, Corollary 1.2] either for a proper rational factor with target rank below \(2q-1\), or for a transverse boundary-orbit map with \(q'-r<2(q-1)\), to obtain a standard embedding factor. Matching those cited rigidity hypotheses is an additional verification requirement in the retained report, not a demonstrated counterexample to the stated corollary.

In the boundary-family construction on page 21, the argument asserts that the tangent space of the saturated null-base family is parallel in ambient block coordinates along an entire target boundary component. The asserted parallelism concerns this smaller saturated-family tangent space, not merely the tangent space of the fixed characteristic subgrassmannian or ambient block distributions.

For the closed oriented three-manifolds considered in the introductory \(8\pi\) systolic inequality, equation (1.2) asserts that equality \(\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}(M,g)\min_M R_g=8\pi\) implies a Riemannian covering of \((M,g)\) by a compact round product \(S^2\times S^1\), up to scale. The assertion concerns a compact product covering, not just the geometry of the universal cover.

In the doubling proof of Theorem 1.2, the two copies of \(M\) are joined by necks \(P_i=\Sigma_i\times[-T,T]\) with \(g_i=h_i+\varphi_i^2dt^2\), and the resulting Lipschitz metric is \(g_N\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1/100\), Claims 1–2 require a smooth \(g_N'\) equal to \(g_i\) on every neck, with \(\|g_N'-g_N\|_{C^0(g_N)}\le\varepsilon^3\), scalar curvature at least \(\lambda-\varepsilon\), and \(\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}(N,g_N')\ge(1-\varepsilon)A_0\), where \(\lambda=\min_MR_g>0\) and \(A_0\) is the smallest boundary-sphere area.

Claim 3 supplies a \(T\)-independent \(c_0>0\) such that a closed minimal surface meeting \(\Sigma_i\times(t-1,t+1)\), for \(-T+2<t<T-2\), has area at least \(c_0\) inside \(\Sigma_i\times(t-2,t+2)\). Claim 4 sets \(T=16A_0/c_0\) and sums over the printed slabs \([4j,4j+4]\), \(|j|\le\lfloor T/4\rfloor\), to rule out a minimizing sphere crossing the whole neck. The smoothing proof separately bounds both \(g'-g\) and \(\widehat g-g'\) by \(\varepsilon^3\), then claims the total \(\varepsilon^3\) bound, with analogous scalar-curvature error budgets. The finding concerns the slab endpoints/count and combination of these errors; the fixed numerical neck length is a proof choice, not part of the theorem's asserted existence conclusion.

For the weak inverse mean curvature flow used in Theorem 1.1, \(|\Sigma_t|=e^tA_0\), and every spherical component is claimed to have area at least \(A_0=\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}(M)\). The proof defines \(T=\inf\{t>0:\Sigma_t\text{ has at least two spherical components}\}\), chooses times approaching this infimum, and infers \(T\ge\log2\), hence \(\chi(\Sigma_t)\le2\) for \(t<\log2\). No finite splitting time has been assumed; the empty-set case of that infimum must therefore be included in this argument.

In Remark 3.2, cut a finite cover \(\#^k(S^2\times S^1)\) along a maximal disjoint collection of stable minimal spheres nontrivial in \(\pi_2(M)\), obtaining pieces \(U_i\) with stable minimal boundary. The proof claims that the absence of interior stable minimal surfaces nontrivial in \(H_2(U_i;\mathbb Z)\) forces each \(U_i\) to be a punctured 3-sphere, saying that otherwise an area minimizer in \(H_2(U_i,\partial U_i;\mathbb Z)\) gives a contradiction. The required minimization class and its interior nontriviality are the point to make explicit; the nearby phrase about a selected \(\Sigma_i\) being homotopically trivial also conflicts with its defining nontriviality.

The discussion of \(w(M)=\sup_g\{\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}(M,g)\min_MR_g\}\) includes sphere quotients and asserts \(w(M)=+\infty\) there, so its systole convention must cover \(\pi_2(M)=0\). These are topology and boundary-case clarifications in the printed arguments, not new counterexamples to the principal systolic inequality.

Let \(P\) be a finite bounded graded lattice equipped with an interval labeling \(\lambda\) that is group-like on weak three-point chains and balanced in the sense of Definitions 2.6–2.8. Theorem 2.9 asserts that the interval group \(G_P\) obtained by identifying vertices and imposing the labeled-chain relations is a Garside group. The literal labeling assumptions identify the bottom, top and total label sets, but impose no further interval-word-language or nondegeneracy requirement excluding identity labels on nondegenerate intervals.

Let \(G=\langle S\mid R\rangle\) have a finite presentation in which every relator is \(abc^{-1}\), with \(a,b,c\in S\) and repetitions allowed. Assume that the flag completion of the Cayley graph of \(G\) with respect to \(S\) is simplicial and systolic: it is simply connected, and every cycle of length four or five in every vertex link has a diagonal. Definition 3.12 explains the simplicial condition by requiring every generator to have nonidentity image in \(G\), and the images of distinct generators to be neither equal nor inverse. Theorem 3.13 asserts that these conditions imply that \(G\times\mathbb Z\) is a Garside group. Its proof applies the partial multiplication inherited from \(G\) to \(U=S\cup\{e\}\).

Let \(G=\langle S\mid R\rangle\) have a finite positive square presentation: each relation has the form \(ab=cd\), where \(a,b,c,d\in S\) need not be distinct. Let \(\Theta\) be the link of the unique vertex of its presentation complex, retaining the edges contributed by the corners of the defining squares. A link vertex has type \(o\) or \(i\) according as it represents an outgoing or incoming generator direction. Theorem 3.15 assumes that \(\Theta\) has no embedded two-cycle of type \((o,o)\) or \((i,i)\), no embedded three-cycle of type \((o,o,i)\) or \((i,i,o)\), and no embedded four-cycle of alternating type \((o,i,o,i)\). It concludes that \(G\times\mathbb Z\) is a Garside group. These are the three printed link restrictions; an additional exclusion of link loops or mixed-type two-cycles is not imposed.

Let \(U\) carry the positive partial multiplication of Section 3, with left and right divisibility orders \(\le_L,\le_R\), and let \(E\) be its two-layer poset. Proposition 3.7 assumes that both divisibility posets are weakly boundedly graded meet-semilattices. It further assumes, for all applicable elements of \(U\), that \(a\cdot u,a\cdot v\in U\) and existence of \(w=u\vee_Lv\) imply \(a\cdot w\in U\); that \(u\cdot a,v\cdot a\in U\) and existence of \(w=u\vee_Rv\) imply \(w\cdot a\in U\); and that \(a\cdot u,a\cdot v,b\cdot u,b\cdot v\in U\) imply existence of either \(a\vee_Rb\) or \(u\vee_Lv\). Under these hypotheses it asserts that \(E\) is a lattice.

The questioned assertions occur in its bowtie proof. From a mixed bowtie \((u,0),(v,0)\prec(w,0),(\bar a,1)\), the proof treats the chosen upper endpoint \(w\) as a minimal common upper bound and concludes \(w=u\vee_Lv\). In the dual configuration \((a,0),(\bar w,1)\prec(\bar u,1),(\bar v,1)\), it similarly identifies \(w=u\vee_Rv\) and then prints the comparison \((\bar w,1)\prec(a,0)\). The issue concerns these endpoint and order-direction inferences in the proof, rather than a claimed counterexample to the proposition's lattice conclusion.

Let \((W,S)\) be a Coxeter system, \(R\) its set of reflections, and \(|w|\) the reflection length. For a finite subset \(U\subset W\), put \(R_U=R\cap U\), and define \(u\cdot v=uv\) precisely when \(uv\in U\) and \(|uv|=|u|+|v|\). Lemma 4.1 assumes that every \(u\in U\) has a length-additive factorization \(u=r_1\cdots r_n\) with \(r_j\in R_U\), and that every such length-additive product in \(U\) remains in \(U\) after deleting either its first or its last reflection. The sentence following the lemma asserts that the left and right divisibility orders induced by this partial multiplication equal the restrictions to \(U\) of the ambient prefix and suffix absolute orders on \(W\). Thus, for elements of \(U\), an ambient length-additive divisibility relation is asserted to have a corresponding complement within \(U\); no separate assumption that \(U\) is an ambient order ideal is stated.

For a cyclic-type Coxeter system with cyclically ordered simple generators \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\), let \(U_i\) be the dual Garside interval of the spherical parabolic subgroup omitting \(s_i\), with Coxeter element \(\delta_i=s_{i+1}\cdots s_ns_1\cdots s_{i-1}\), and put \(U=\bigcup_iU_i\). In Proposition 5.6(6), take the elements \(a,b,u,v,x\) occurring in condition (6) of Proposition 4.2, so that \(a\cdot x\cdot u,a\cdot x\cdot v,b\cdot x\cdot u,b\cdot x\cdot v\in U\), and write \(I_z=\operatorname{Supp}(z)\). The proof seeks to show that either \(I_a\cup I_b\) or \(I_u\cup I_v\) is a proper subset of \(S\), which supplies the required right or left join.

The disputed step assumes both support unions equal \(S\), obtains \(a\cdot u,a\cdot v,b\cdot u,b\cdot v\in U\), and infers \(I_u\subset I_a\) from \(\min(I_u)-1\in I_a\) and \(a\cdot u\in U_i\), citing Lemma 5.4. Here the predecessor and minimum use the induced linear order on the relevant omitted-vertex interval. The ordered support principle expressed in Corollary 5.5 instead starts with a product \(p\cdot q\) with irreducible supports and the predecessor of the minimum of the left-factor support in the right-factor support. The assertion under review is this application with the factors in their printed order, not the cyclic-type conclusion after a corrected argument.

Theorem 2.15 and the accompanying Bestvina paragraph form the quotient \(G/\langle\Delta\rangle\) for a Garside group \(G\) with an arbitrary Garside element \(\Delta\). This use presupposes that the cyclic subgroup \(\langle\Delta\rangle\) is normal, without assuming that \(\Delta\) is central or first replacing it by a central power.

Here \(H(x,y)=\frac{1+x}{2}\log\frac{1+x}{1+y}+\frac{1-x}{2}\log\frac{1-x}{1-y}\) is binary relative entropy and \(\Phi(s)=(1+s)\log(1+s)-s\). For every \(x\in[-1,1]\), \(y\in(-1,1)\), and \(a\ge1\), Lemma 71 states \[\tfrac12H(x,y)\le(1+y)\Phi\!\left(\frac{x-y}{1+y}\right)\le2H(x,y),\qquad \frac{H(x,y)}{4a}\le a(1+y)\Phi\!\left(\frac{x-y}{a(1+y)}\right).\] The two lower comparisons (57)–(58), as printed, do not restrict the base mean \(y\) to be nonpositive.

Let \(G\) be a graph on \(n\) vertices of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), where \(\Delta\ge3\), and let \(\nu\) be its hardcore distribution with fugacity \(0<\lambda\le1/(2\Delta)\): an independent set \(I\) has probability proportional to \(\lambda^{|I|}\). Lemma 66 asserts \[\rho_{\mathrm{LS}}\bigl(P^{\mathrm{GD}}(\nu)\bigr)\ge\frac1{4n},\] where \(P^{\mathrm{GD}}\) is the paper's single-site Glauber kernel and \(\rho_{\mathrm{LS}}\) is its discrete one-step entropy-contraction coefficient. This is the endpoint estimate used for the negatively tilted hardcore law in Theorem 62. The stated proof consists of combining Proposition 51 of [AJK+21a] and Fact 3.5 of [CLV21]; the issue is whether those cited results imply this particular discrete entropy-contraction bound, rather than a continuous-time Dirichlet modified log-Sobolev bound.

For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with adjacency matrix \(A\) and degree matrix \(D\), the argument preceding Corollary 56 sets \(J_G=(D+A)/2\) and claims, for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^{V}\), that \[\sum_{(i,j)\in E}\mathbf1_{\{x_i=x_j\}}=\langle x,J_Gx\rangle,\] and that \(J_G\) is positive definite. The corollary's proof also identifies \(J_G=I-\tfrac12L_{\mathrm{sym}}\), where \(L_{\mathrm{sym}}\) is the symmetrically normalized Laplacian, and for the negative-interaction case asserts that \(I-J_G\) is positive definite with operator norm at most one. These are the graph-matrix identities and definiteness assertions used to obtain its stated Ising bound.

After Theorem 58, the paper describes the number of steps of the sampling kernel from an \(O(\exp n)\)-warm start as scaling with \(\eta\mu\log n\), where \(\mu\) is the strong-convexity parameter and \(\eta\) the step parameter. This is the iteration-count assertion being checked in the regime \(0<\eta\mu<1\); the theorem itself gives the one-step entropy coefficient \(\mu/(\mu+1/\eta)\).
