Let \(\nu_{G,\lambda}\) be the hardcore law of a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with maximum degree \(\Delta\ge3\) and fugacity \(\lambda>0\). Fix a vertex \(v\), write \(N_v\) for its neighbors, and take a feasible pinning \(u\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V}\) such that \(u_a=0\) for every \(a\in N_v\). Lemma 64 states \[\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}\left(\frac1{1+\lambda}\right)^{|N_v|}\le\Pr_{\sigma\sim\nu_{G,\lambda}}(\sigma_v=+1\mid\sigma_i u_i\ge0\ \forall i)\le\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}.\] If additionally \(\lambda\le(1-\delta)\lambda_\Delta\), where \(\lambda_\Delta=(\Delta-1)^{\Delta-1}/(\Delta-2)^\Delta\), it replaces the lower bound by \(\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}e^{-3e^2}\). The printed hypotheses leave the neighbors free but impose no condition \(u_v=0\) on the vertex whose marginal is being bounded; consequently they include feasible pinnings that already fix \(\sigma_v\).

Let \(X\) be the compact connected metric \(n\)-manifold of Theorem 1.5, \(n\ge2\), \(\mu=\mathcal H^n\), and \(D=\operatorname{diam}X\). Its stated Ahlfors condition is \(\alpha^{-1}r^n\le\mu(B(x,r))\le\alpha r^n\) only for \(0<r<D\). Linear local contractibility means that \(B(x,r)\) contracts inside \(B(x,\Lambda r)\) for \(0<r<D/\Lambda\). For Borel \(E\), put \(E_t=\{x:d(x,E)<t\}\) and \(\mathcal M_-(E\mid U)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}(\mu(E_t\cap U)-\mu(E\cap U))/t\).

Theorem 1.5 asserts, for every open ball \(B\), \[\min\{\mu(E\cap B),\mu(B\setminus E)\}\le C\,\mathcal M_-(E\mid\lambda B)^{n/(n-1)},\] with both \(C\) and \(\lambda\) depending only on \(n,\alpha,\Lambda\), without a separate total-mass bound at the diameter scale.

Let \(X\) be the compact connected metric \(n\)-manifold of Theorem 1.5, \(n\ge2\), \(\mu=\mathcal H^n\), and \(D=\operatorname{diam}X\). Its stated Ahlfors condition is \(\alpha^{-1}r^n\le\mu(B(x,r))\le\alpha r^n\) only for \(0<r<D\). Linear local contractibility means that \(B(x,r)\) contracts inside \(B(x,\Lambda r)\) for \(0<r<D/\Lambda\). For Borel \(E\), put \(E_t=\{x:d(x,E)<t\}\) and \(\mathcal M_-(E\mid U)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}(\mu(E_t\cap U)-\mu(E\cap U))/t\).

Equation (7.1) asserts the stronger fixed-dilation version \[\min\{\mu(E\cap B),\mu(B\setminus E)\}\le C\,\mathcal M_-(E\mid6B)^{n/(n-1)}.\] The subsequent local-constancy step uses one common integer on the target metric ball, although the hypotheses do not require that ball to be connected.

Let \(X\) be a compact, linearly locally contractible metric space of topological dimension \(n\ge2\). Lemma 4.2 chooses a constant \(c>0\), depending on the data of \(X\), and considers every \(0<r\le\operatorname{diam}X\) and every closed \(S\subset X\) with \(\mathcal H^{n-1}(S)<cr^{n-1}\). Its conclusion is a factorization up to homotopy of the inclusion \(S\hookrightarrow X\) through a metric space of dimension at most \(n-2\), with the homotopy contained in the \(r\)-neighborhood of \(S\).

The challenged intermediate assertion embeds \(X\) in \(\ell^\infty\) with its supremum norm and claims a finite \((n-2)\)-dimensional simplicial complex \(K\subset\ell^\infty\) and a Lipschitz map \(f:S\to K\) satisfying \[\|x-f(x)\|\le c_1\mathcal H^{n-1}(S)^{1/(n-1)}<c_1c^{1/(n-1)}r\qquad(x\in S),\] where \(c_1\) depends only on \(n\). Equation (4.1) includes the case \(\mathcal H^{n-1}(S)=0\), in which its first bound prescribes exactly zero displacement. The report questions this finite-complex approximation in the zero-measure case, not the lemma's homotopy conclusion after that case is handled separately.

Let \(P\subset V\) be a polyhedron, \(\mathcal Q\) a decomposition of \(P\), and \(\psi\) a linear functional, nonconstant on \(P\). For a face \(F\in\mathcal Q\) on which \(\psi\) is constant, define \(C(F)_\bullet=\Delta_\psi(C_\bullet^\Omega(\mathcal Q))^F\) as the objectwise subquotient consisting of all copies of \(F\) in the full augmented complex. The augmentation contributes \(P\) in degree \(\dim P+1\).

Lemma 6.9 assumes that \(\psi|_P\) is bounded above and that \(F\) is an internal face of the maximizing-face decomposition \(\mathcal Q_\psi\). It asserts the homotopy equivalence \[C(F)_\bullet\simeq F[-\dim P+\dim P_\psi-\dim F],\] where \(X[-i]\) places \(X\) in degree \(i\).

Let \(M\) be a rank-\(k\) matroid with an action of \(\Gamma\), let \(H\) be a stressed hyperplane of size \(h\), and let \(\widetilde M\) be obtained by relaxing every translate \(\gamma H\), \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). Write \(\Gamma_H\) for the stabilizer of \(H\), and let \(\operatorname{Res}^{S_h}_{\Gamma_H}\) mean pullback along its permutation action on \(H\).

Corollary 9.8 prints the following identity of graded virtual representations: \[\operatorname{OS}(\widetilde M)=\operatorname{OS}(M)+\operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma_H}^{\Gamma}\!\left(\operatorname{Res}_{\Gamma_H}^{S_h}\bigwedge\nolimits^k V_{[h-1,1]}\right)\otimes\bigl(\mathbb Q(1-k)\oplus\mathbb Q(-k)\bigr).\] Here \(V_{[h-1,1]}\) is the indicated Specht module. The exponent \(k\) is the exponent printed in this corollary.

A rank-preserving weak map \(M\to M'\) on the same ground set means that every basis of \(M'\) is a basis of \(M\). In the flag-lifting induction of Proposition 8.19, let \(F'_1\subset F'_2\) be the target flats with ranks \(k_1<k_2\). The challenged step asserts that a source lift \(F_2\) satisfying \(\operatorname{cl}_{M'}(F_2)=F'_2\) makes \(F'_1\cap F_2\) a rank-\(k_1\) flat of \(M'|F_2\).

Section 2.4 orders objects by \(X\le Y\) when there is an arrow \(X\to Y\). It forms lower-object subcomplexes \(C^{\le X}\) and \(C^{<X}\), and their quotient \(C^X=C^{\le X}/C^{<X}\). The asserted objectwise conclusion is that a minimal such part has necessarily trivial differential.

Let \(M\) be a rank-\(k\) matroid on \(E\), and let \(F\) be a stressed flat of rank \(r\): both its restriction and contraction are uniform. Put \(\operatorname{cusp}(F)=\{S\subset E:|S|=k,\ |S\cap F|=r+1\}\). Relaxation adjoins this cusp to the bases. Set \(\Pi_{r,k,F,E}=U_{k-r,E\setminus F}\sqcup U_{r,F}\), and let \(\Lambda_{r,k,F,E}\) be its relaxation at \(F\).

Theorem 3.8 states that \(M\), \(\Lambda_{r,k,F,E}\), and all their faces decompose the single-flat relaxation \(\widetilde M\). It asserts that the decomposition is trivial if \(M=\Pi_{r,k,F,E}\), and otherwise has exactly \(M,\Lambda_{r,k,F,E},\Pi_{r,k,F,E}\) as internal faces. No nonempty-cusp condition is imposed.

For a finite group \(\Gamma\) preserving \(M\), Theorem 3.10 relaxes every flat in \(\mathcal F=\{\gamma F:\gamma\in\Gamma\}\). It asserts that if \(M=\Pi_{r,k,F,E}\), the resulting decomposition is the trivial decomposition of the single-flat \(\Lambda_{r,k,F,E}\). No orbit-singleton condition is imposed. The proof of Proposition 9.6 uses the same implication \(M=\Pi_{r,k,F,E}\Rightarrow\widetilde M=\Lambda_{r,k,F,E}\).

Sections 9.2–9.3 (pp. 48–49) define the rational spaces \[V(N)=\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb R}\{x-y:x,y\in P(N)\}\cap\mathbb Q^E,\qquad
 L(N,N')=\bigwedge^{d(N)-d(N')}(V(N)/V(N')).\] The differential is specified as the class of an outward unit normal.

On the symplectization in \(\alpha\)-coordinates, \(\omega=d(e^a\alpha)\). Compatibility means that \(\omega(\,\cdot\,,J\,\cdot\,)\) is symmetric positive definite. The class \(\mathcal J(\alpha)\) permits arbitrary compatible structures in a compact middle region and requires adjustment to \(\alpha\) only at the two ends.
The proof of Theorem 10.1 on p. 49 asserts that \(f_r(a,p)=(ra,p)\) induces a bijection \(f_r^*:\mathcal J(r\alpha)\longrightarrow\mathcal J(\alpha)\).

In Section 11, p. 59 defines \(\beta_t=((1-t)S+t)\alpha_0\) and claims that its short closed orbits are independent of \(t\in(0,1]\). Page 60 then invokes Proposition 10.4 for small positive \(t\) on the ground that this coefficient is \(C^2\)-close to \(1\).

The manuscript allows contact dimension \(2n-1\) with \(n\ge1\). Proposition 3 asserts that for every Zoll contact form \(\alpha_0\), a family converging to \(\alpha_0\) in \(C^1\) can have strictly greater systolic ratio. Proposition 1 likewise asserts the existence of domains \(C^1\)-close to the ball with \(c_{\mathrm{ball}}<\operatorname{sys}\). Neither statement excludes \(n=1\).

In the sectional-hyperbolic setting of Lemma 7.4, write \(P_x\) for the normal projection and \(d_x^E,d_x^F\) for the fake-leaf lengths. The lemma claims a constant \(\lambda_R>1\) such that, for every permitted \(\rho\in(0,\rho_1)\) and radius \(r\), every orbit segment \((x,t)\) disjoint from \(W_r\), and every \(y\in B_{t,\varepsilon_2}(x)\), one has \[d_x^F(P_x(y))\ge d_x^E(P_x(y))\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_{x_t}^F(P_{x_t}(y_t))\ge\lambda_R^t d_{x_t}^E(P_{x_t}(y_t)).\] The assertion applies to real orbit lengths, with no multiplicative prefactor.

For a real duration \(t>1\), Definition 10 calls \(x_t\) a \((\lambda,cu)\)-hyperbolic time if \[\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\left\|\psi^*_{-1,x_{t-i}}|_{F_N^{cu}}\right\|\le\lambda^{-j}\quad(1\le j\le\lfloor t\rfloor).\] Definition 11, for \(t\ge1\), requires \[\frac{\#\{\tau\in[0,s]\cap\mathbb N:x_{t-\tau}\in W\}}{s+1}\le\beta\quad(0\le s\le\lfloor t\rfloor-1)\] for a \((\beta,W)\)-recurrence Pliss time. Both sample backwards from the real endpoint.

With \(\lambda_0>1\) supplied by Lemma 4.4, Lemma 4.7 claims: for every \(\beta_0\in(0,1)\) there is \(\beta_1\in(0,\beta_0)\) such that, for every open neighborhood \(W\supset\operatorname{Sing}(X)\cap\Lambda\), there is \(N_1>0\) with the following property. For every real \(t>N_1\) and orbit segment \((x,t)\in\Lambda\times\mathbb R_+\), if \(x,x_t\notin W\) and \[\frac{\#\{s=0,\ldots,\lfloor t\rfloor:x_{t-s}\in W\}}{\lfloor t\rfloor+1}\le\beta_1,\] there exists an integer \(s\in[0,t]\) such that \(x_s\) is simultaneously hyperbolic and recurrence-Pliss for \((x,s)\).

The pressure \(P(\mathcal C,\varphi,\delta)\) is defined using a limsup over real times. Lemma 5.9 claims that it is bounded by the measure pressure of every limit point \(\mu\) of the integer-indexed empirical measures in the lemma: \[P(\mathcal C,\varphi,\delta)\le h_\mu(f_1)+\int\varphi\,d\mu.\] The collection \(\mathcal C\) is arbitrary; the stated claim imposes no closure under time truncation.

Fix the orthogonal coordinate splitting \(\mathbb R^n=E\oplus F\), \(0<\dim E<n\). Let \(y=y^1+y^2\), with \(y^1\in E\), \(y^2\in F\), and let \(u=y^F\) lie in the \((\alpha,F)\)-cone while \(v=y-u\) lies in the \((\alpha,E)\)-cone; thus \(|u_E|\le\alpha|u_F|\) and \(|v_F|\le\alpha|v_E|\).

Lemma 6.1 asserts that there is \(L_0>1\) such that, for every sufficiently small \(\alpha>0\) and every such decomposition, \[|y^2|-L_0\alpha|y^1|\le|u|\le|y^2|+L_0\alpha(|y^1|+|y^2|),\] \[|y^1|-L_0\alpha|y^2|\le|v|\le|y^1|+L_0\alpha(|y^1|+|y^2|).\] The challenged lower bounds precede the lemma's additional conditional comparisons.
For a positive constant change of speed \(g_t=f_{ct}\), \(c>0\), footnote 5 on p. 11 uses the potential \(|c\varphi|\) in the normalization of the equilibrium-state problem.

Theorem 4.1 permits \(A\ge b_2>b_1>0\) and sets \(\theta_0=(b_2-b_1)/(A-b_1)\). For every finite real sequence with \(\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\ge b_2N\) and \(a_j\le A\), it asserts \(\ell>\theta_0N\) indices \(1\le n_1<\cdots<n_\ell\le N\) satisfying \[\sum_{j=n+1}^{n_i}a_j\ge b_1(n_i-n)\quad(0\le n<n_i).\] The strict count includes the allowed boundary \(A=b_2\).

Lemma 4.6 claims that for every \(\beta_0,\kappa\in(0,1)\), there is \(\beta_1\in(0,\beta_0)\) such that every set \(W\) and orbit segment satisfying \[\frac{\#\{s=0,\ldots,\lfloor t\rfloor-1:x_{t-s}\in W\}}{\lfloor t\rfloor}\le\beta_1\] have at least \(\kappa(\lfloor t\rfloor+1)\) recurrence-Pliss candidates \(x_{t-n_i}\). No large-time cutoff is imposed in this lemma.

Lemma 2.16 claims that for every \(\alpha>0\) there are \(r_0>0\) and an upper radius \(r_*\in(0,r_0)\) such that, for every \(0<r\le r_*\) and every \(x\in B_r(\sigma)\cap\Lambda\), the supremal backward stay time \[t_x=\sup\{t>0:\text{the orbit segment from }x_{-t}\text{ to }x\text{ lies in }B_{r_0}(\sigma)\}\] satisfies \[x_{-t_x}\in\partial B_{r_0}(x)\cap C_\alpha(E^c(\sigma)).\] The printed quantifier has no assumption \(t_x<\infty\); the boundary ball in the displayed conclusion is centered at \(x\) as printed.

Let \(D\subset\mathbb C^2\) be smoothly bounded, pseudoconvex and of finite type, and let \(x_*\in\partial D\) have type \(r\). For a local Levi-tangent field \(V\), use the critically tangent path \(z(\varepsilon)=(e^{\varepsilon V}x_*,-\varepsilon^r)\), with normal coordinate \(\rho=-\varepsilon^r\) and tangent coordinate \(z_{1,V}=(g_1(0),g_2(0))\).

Theorem 4 evaluates the leading model coefficient at \(z_{1,V}\) while using the scale \(-2\rho\). In particular, its diagonal case asserts \[K_D(z,z)=(-2\rho)^{-2-2/r}\bigl(\widetilde B_{p,0}(z_{1,V})+o(1)\bigr),\qquad \widetilde B_{p,0}(z_1)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-s}s^{1+2/r}B_p(s^{1/r}z_1)\,ds.\] Here \(p\) is the subharmonic model polynomial and \(B_p\) its model Bergman kernel.
For \(D_p=\{(z_1,z_2):\operatorname{Im}z_2>p(z_1)\}\), p. 11 further identifies \(\widetilde B_{p,0}(z_1)=K_{D_p}(z_1,i[1+p(z_1)])\), placing the model evaluation at depth one.
For the bounded domain \(D\) under consideration, p. 3 asserts that its Bergman kernel satisfies \(K_D\in L^2(D\times D)\).

For \(u>0\), equation (2.4) defines \[J(u)=(-1)^n\det\begin{pmatrix}u&u_{\bar\beta}\\u_\alpha&u_{\alpha\bar\beta}\end{pmatrix}.\] For any Euclidean orthonormal frame \(\{Z_\alpha\}_{\alpha=1}^n\) of \(T^{1,0}\mathbb C^n\), equation (2.5) then prints \[J(u)=\det\begin{pmatrix}u&\overline Z_\beta u\\Z_\alpha u&Z_\alpha\overline Z_\beta u-[Z_\alpha,\overline Z_\beta]^{0,1}u\end{pmatrix},\] with no \((-1)^n\) factor and no even-dimensional restriction. The frame vectors have the same norm as the coordinate \(\partial_{z_j}\) under the stated convention.

In the proof of Lemma 5.4, pp. 16–17, the annular cover is projected orthogonally onto its closed geodesic axis \(\widehat\gamma\). Equation (14) asserts \[\ell(\widehat\gamma)\le
 \ell_{\widehat S}(\widehat\gamma')
 =
 \ell(\widehat\gamma'\cap\widehat S)
 +\sum_{\widehat D\cap\widehat\gamma'\ne\varnothing}
      \operatorname{diam}(\widehat D).\] The diameter is the ambient annular-cover diameter.

In the proof of Lemma 7.3, let \(q\) be the holomorphic quadratic differential with closed trajectories in the homotopy class of a homotopically nontrivial simple closed curve \(\gamma\). Let \(\Gamma_h=\{\gamma_y:b_1<y<b_2\}\) be its closed horizontal trajectories, normalized to have \(q\)-length one, and let \(\Gamma_N\) consist of curves in that homotopy class having at most \(N\) essential intersections with each complementary domain \(D_k\). Suppose the extremal transboundary mass distribution \(\rho_0\) for \(\Gamma_N\) is purely continuous. Define \(\rho_1=|q|^{1/2}\) on \(S\) and \(\rho_1(D_k)=(N/c)\operatorname{diam}_q(D_k)\), with \(c\) from Lemma 5.4.

The proof asserts, for every \(y\in(b_1,b_2)\), \[\int_{\gamma_y}\rho_0\,ds=\int_{\gamma_y\cap S}\rho_0\,ds\ge1.\] It also prints \(\|\rho_1\|_{L^2}=\operatorname{area}_q(S)\) and \[\|\rho_0\|_{L^2}=\operatorname{mass}(\rho_0)\ge\operatorname{mod}_2(\Gamma_h)=\operatorname{area}_q(C_q)>\operatorname{mass}(\rho_1|_S)=\|\rho_1\|_{L^2}.\]
On p. 15 the collar width is written \(d=\operatorname{arccosh}(\operatorname{coth}(\ell(\gamma))/2)\).

On pp. 21–22, absence of a pole of \(L(\pi,s)\) at \(s=1\) is said to give a unique smooth \(\xi\) such that its restrictions near zero are Kirillov functions and \[(1-P)\xi=\phi,\qquad (P\xi)(x)=\xi(px).\] The proposition imposes no global support condition on \(\xi\).

Section 8.1, p. 37, defines \(\Lambda=\mathcal O_L[[\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_{p^\infty})/\mathbb Q)]]\). No odd-prime restriction or integral character-component replacement is stated. Lemma 9.2.2 says that a finitely generated torsion module with no nonzero finite submodule has principal zeroth Fitting ideal. Lemma 9.2.3 says that \(I\subseteq A\), with \(A\) of finite index, implies \(I\subseteq\operatorname{Fitt}_\Lambda(A/I)\).

On p. 42, writing \(\lambda(a)=\lambda(f,z^j,a,p^n)\), the source sets \[\lambda^\pm(a)=\lambda(a)\pm\lambda(-a),\qquad
 \phi(a)=\lambda^+(a)/\Omega^++\lambda^-(a)/\Omega^-.\] There is neither a factor \(1/2\) nor a factor \((-1)^j\). Formula (18) on p. 43 instead uses the period with sign \((-1)^j\chi(-1)\).

For a filtered \((\varphi,N,G_K)\)-module \((M,\operatorname{Fil}^\bullet)\) over \(K\), the paper uses \(\deg M=t_N(M)-t_H(M)\), calls slope-zero semistable objects weakly admissible, and calls objects with nonnegative Harder–Narasimhan slopes acyclic. Lemma 5.3 asserts that acyclicity is equivalent to the existence of a weakly admissible filtration \(\operatorname{Fil}_1^\bullet\) with \(\operatorname{Fil}_1^iM_K\subseteq\operatorname{Fil}^iM_K\) for every \(i\). Lemma 5.4 further asserts that if the \(\varphi\)-slopes lie in \([0,r]\), \(\operatorname{Fil}^0M_K=M_K\), and \(\operatorname{Fil}^{r+1}M_K=0\), the smaller filtration can retain these two endpoint conditions.

Writing \[V_{\rm st}(M,\operatorname{Fil}^\bullet)=\ker\big((M\otimes B_{\rm st})^{N=0,\varphi=1}\longrightarrow (M_K\otimes B_{\rm dR})/\operatorname{Fil}^0\big),\] Theorem 5.8 asserts for every acyclic filtered \((\varphi,N)\)-module over \(K\) that \[D^*_{\rm st}(V_{\rm st})\simeq M^*,\qquad D^*_{\rm dR}(V_{\rm st})\simeq(M_K^*,\operatorname{Fil}^{\bullet\perp}),\] as the corresponding \((\varphi,N)\)-modules and filtered \(K\)-modules.

In the proof of Theorem 8.1(c), the filtered logarithmic de Rham cohomology group \[H^i(F^rR\Gamma_{\mathrm{dR}}(X^\times/B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+))\] is asserted to have finite length over \(R=B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\).

In the Künneth argument of Lemma 8.13, with \(Y\) the proper factor and \(T\) permitted to be smooth, separated, taut and countable at infinity, the proof asserts perfectness of \[R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigl(T,R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Z_p)\bigr).\]

In Proposition 5.23, let \((M,M^+_{\rm dR})\) be an acyclic filtered \((\varphi,N)\)-module over \(C\), with \(\varphi\)-slopes in \([0,r]\) and \[M\otimes t^rB^+_{\rm dR}\subseteq t^rM^+_{\rm dR}\subseteq M\otimes B^+_{\rm dR}.\] For \(k\ge2r\), the proposition asserts that the natural map \[M^*\otimes(B^+_{\rm dR}/t^k)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm VS}(V^r_{\rm st}(M,M^+_{\rm dR}),B^+_{\rm dR}/t^k)\] has kernel and cokernel annihilated by \(t^{2r}\).
The proof selects a weakly admissible lattice \(N^+_{\rm dR}\) satisfying \[M\otimes B^+_{\rm dR}\subseteq N^+_{\rm dR}\subseteq M^+_{\rm dR},\] claiming that this is possible by adapting Lemma 5.4.
The last bullet of §3.2.2 assumes only slopes of \(E_1\geq\lambda_1\) and slopes of \(E_2\leq\lambda_2\), yet concludes that an extension has slopes in \([\lambda_1,\lambda_2]\).

In Section 3.2.6(2), write \(\lambda_j=d_j/h_j\) and \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2=d/h\) in lowest terms. The displayed formulas are \[\mathcal O(\lambda_1)\otimes\mathcal O(\lambda_2)=\mathcal O(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^{n(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)},\qquad n(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=\frac{h_1}{h_2}h,\] and \[\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O(\lambda_1),\mathcal O(\lambda_2))=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O,\mathcal O(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)),\qquad\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O,\mathcal O(\lambda))=H^0(X,\mathcal O(\lambda)).\]

The preceding proof of Lemma 3.16 considers \(\lambda=d/h>0\) and an injection \(U_\lambda\to V^N\). After factoring it through \(V^h\), the final dimensional comparison prints \(h<d\), whereas the opening reduction on the same page states the required inequality as \(h>d\).
In the index selection in Lemma 4.13, the chosen integer must satisfy \(1\le i<k\). In the allowed pure-prime-power case \(k=p^r\), the printed choice is \(i=p^r\).

Let \(\mathbb W\) be a reasonable \(B^+_{\rm dR}\)-Module in the sense used in Section 4, and set \(W=\mathbb W(C)\). For \(d\in\mathbb N\), Lemma 4.24(i) prints the isomorphisms \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm TVS}(U_d,W)\simeq W,\qquad\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\rm TVS}(U_d,W)\simeq W.\]

Let \((M,\operatorname{Fil}^\bullet)\) satisfy Corollary 5.10: it is an acyclic filtered \((\varphi,N,G_K)\)-module over \(K\), its \(\varphi\)-slopes lie in \([0,r]\), and \(\operatorname{Fil}^0M_K=M_K\), \(\operatorname{Fil}^{r+1}M_K=0\). Example 5.11 additionally assumes \(\operatorname{Fil}^rM_K=M_K\), so that \[V^r_{\rm st}(M,\operatorname{Fil}^\bullet)=X^r_{\rm st}(M):=(M\otimes_{F^{\rm nr}}B^+_{\rm st})^{N=0,\varphi=p^r}.\]

The example prints \[\operatorname{Hom}^{\rm sm}_{G_K}(X^r_{\rm st}(M),B_{\rm st})\simeq M^*\] as \((\varphi,N,G_K)\)-modules, and \[\operatorname{Hom}_{G_K}(X^r_{\rm st}(M),t^jB^+_{\rm dR})\simeq\begin{cases}M_K,&j\le0,\\0,&j\ge1.\end{cases}\]

In Proposition 5.20, let \((M,M^+_{\rm dR})\) be an acyclic filtered \((\varphi,N)\)-module over \(C\), with \(\varphi\)-slopes in \([0,r]\) and \[t^rB^+_{\rm dR}\otimes M\subseteq t^rM^+_{\rm dR}\subseteq B^+_{\rm dR}\otimes M.\] The printed definition is \[V^r_{\rm st}(M,M^+_{\rm dR}):=\ker\big((M\otimes_{F^{\rm nr}}B_{\rm st})^{N=0,\varphi=p^r}\longrightarrow(M\otimes_{F^{\rm nr}}B^+_{\rm dR})/t^rM^+_{\rm dR}\big).\]

For this object the proposition asserts \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm VS}(V^r_{\rm st},B_{\rm dR})\simeq M^*\otimes_{F^{\rm nr}}B_{\rm dR}\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm VS}(V^r_{\rm st},B_{\rm st})\simeq M^*\otimes_{F^{\rm nr}}B_{\rm st}\). The proof of the second isomorphism chooses a weakly admissible lattice \(N^+_{\rm dR}\) containing \(M^+_{\rm dR}\).

Equation (6.17) is presented as the exact sequence associated with the bicartesian period square (6.16). Both comparison arrows use plus signs: the last map adds \(\iota_{\mathrm{HK}}(x)\) and \(\operatorname{can}(y)\), while the preceding arrow uses plus signs in both components. These maps are asserted to form a complex.

Let \(n\ge2\), \(1<p\le q\), \(0\le\mu\le2\), \(H_\mu(z)=|z|^2+\mu^2\), and \(L_*,\widetilde L\ge1\). The growth condition \((7.1)_1\) is \[L_*^{-1}H_\mu(z)^{q/2}+\widetilde L^{-1}H_\mu(z)^{p/2}\le F(x,z)\le\widetilde L H_\mu(z)^{q/2}+\widetilde L H_\mu(z)^{p/2}\] for every \(x\in\Omega,z\in\mathbb R^n\). Let \(B\subset\Omega\) be a ball, \(u_*\in W^{1,q}(B)\cap L^\infty(B)\), and let \(u\in W^{1,q}(B)\) minimize \(\mathcal F(w,B)=\int_BF(x,Dw)\,dx\) over \(u_*+W^{1,q}_0(B)\).

Lemma 8.1 asserts \[\|u\|_{L^\infty(B)}\le\max\{\|u_*\|_{L^\infty(B)},c\mu|B|^{1/n}\},\qquad c=c(n,p,q,\widetilde L).\] Its two one-sided versions replace \(u,u_*\) by their positive parts, or by the positive parts of \(-u,-u_*\), respectively. The boundary-data coefficient is exactly one.

In the proof of Lemma 4.0.7, the displayed identification on p. 35 assigns \(\mathbf K_{d+1}^{MW}\) to the first nonzero \(\mathbb A^1\)-homotopy sheaf \(\pi^{\mathbb A^1}_{d+1}(\mathbb A^{d+2}\setminus0)\), and then uses \(\mathbf K_{d+1}^M\) after restriction to \(X\).

The objects are finite geometric lattices with building sets. Lemma 3.20 assigns raw inclusion to structural arrows on all non-bottom interval elements, inverse underlying poset maps to isomorphisms, and extends the assignment by composition. The assignment is claimed to respect the structural compositions, including (3) and its source identification \(\Phi\) from Lemma 3.12.

For the spanning frame of a nested set \(S\) in a finite geometric lattice with building set, Proposition 5.23 and Lemma 5.24 prohibit every rank-one local interval. The prescribed frame is \[\operatorname{fr}(S)=\{G\in S:\operatorname{rk}[\tau_S(G),G]>1\}\cup\{t\}.\] The top element is appended without an exception to the prohibition.

In the proof of Proposition 6.3, let a chain of \(n\) degree-one morphisms in \(\mathrm{LBS}\), with irreducible built-lattice target, have composite nested set \(S\). Reading the chain from right to left orders \(S\setminus\{\widehat1\}\) as \(G_1,\ldots,G_n\). For every \(\sigma\in S_n\), the proof defines \[G_i^\sigma=G_{\sigma(i)}\vee\bigvee\bigl(\{G_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,G_{\sigma(i-1)}\}_{<G_{\sigma(i)}}\bigr),\quad1\le i\le n,\] and inserts the generators \([G_i^\sigma]\), tensored with identities in the other factors, in the reordered chain. It asserts that these are well-defined structural morphisms in the current interval factors and give a free symmetric-group action preserving composition, whose orbit set is the morphism set.

Definition 6.4 presents the projective Leray algebra using generators \(e_G,x_G\), imposes \(e_t=0\), and prescribes \(d(e_G)=x_G\) for every \(G\), including the top element \(t\). This differential is asserted to descend to the quotient.

For every built lattice \((L,\mathcal G)\), Proposition 2.23 asserts the projective presentation \[\mathrm{FY}(L,\mathcal G)\simeq\mathbb Z[x_G:G\in\mathcal G\setminus\{\widehat1\}]/I_{\rm proj}.\] Here \(I_{\rm proj}\) is generated by \[\sum_{\widehat1>G\ge H_1}x_G-\sum_{\widehat1>G\ge H_2}x_G\] for every pair of atoms \(H_1,H_2\), and by \(\prod_{G\in X}x_G\) for every nonnested \(X\subseteq\mathcal G\setminus\{\widehat1\}\). The statement does not require \(\widehat1\in\mathcal G\).

The subsequent assertion says that every Feichtner–Yuzvinsky algebra has maximal nonzero degree \(2(\operatorname{rk}L-1)\), that its component in that degree is one-dimensional, and that this component is generated by \(x_{\widehat1}^{\operatorname{rk}L-1}\).

On p. 58 the source assigns \(\overline{\mathrm{OS}}(L)[-1]\) to every built lattice, and claims this assignment forms a strong monoidal cooperad. The quantifier includes reducible products and the rank-zero monoidal unit.

For a generator indexed by \(G\), the general \(\mathrm{FY}(S)\) formula chooses \(G'=\min S_{>G}\), using a strict inequality to determine the receiving interval. The stated formula includes the top generator \(G=t\).

In Lemma 5.25, let \(S\) be a cluster whose monomial \(\Psi_S\) is normal, and let \(H_G\) be the smallest atom, in the fixed atom order, satisfying \(\tau_S(G)\vee H_G=G\). Consider consecutive comparable elements \(G_1<G_2\) of \(S\) with \(\operatorname{rk}[\tau_S(G_i),G_i]=1\), and set \(T=\tau_{S\setminus\{G_1\}}(G_2)\). The proof asserts the two equalities of sets of atoms \[\{H:T\vee H=T\vee H_{G_1}\}=\{H:\tau_S(G_1)\vee H=G_1\},\] \[\{H:T\vee H=T\vee H_{G_2}\}=\{H:\tau_S(G_2)\vee H=G_2\}.\] These are used to identify the respective minima with \(H_{G_1}\) and \(H_{G_2}\) and deduce that \(G\mapsto H_G\) is increasing.

Definition 7.1 describes a matroid rank function on a finite set \(E\) as a map \(\operatorname{rk}:\mathcal P(E)\to\mathbb N\) satisfying \(\operatorname{rk}(\varnothing)=0\), \[\operatorname{rk}(A\cup B)+\operatorname{rk}(A\cap B)\le\operatorname{rk}(A)+\operatorname{rk}(B),\qquad\operatorname{rk}(A\cup\{x\})\le\operatorname{rk}(A)+1\] for all \(A,B\subseteq E\) and \(x\in E\). No monotonicity inequality is included in that definition.

Definition 7.2 assigns to every \(X\subseteq E\) a partition \(
u(X)\), requiring: if \(X\subseteq Y\), then \(
u(X)\) refines \(
u(Y)|_X\); every block \(P_i\) of \(
u(X)\) satisfies \(
u(P_i)=\{P_i\}\); and \(\operatorname{rk}(X)=\sum_i\operatorname{rk}(P_i)\). For simple loopless matroids, the following paragraph asserts that these building decompositions are equivalent to building sets of the flat lattice: take as building elements the flats with one-block partition, and conversely partition \(X\) by the factors of its closure \(\sigma(X)\).

In the polymatroid \(\mathrm{FY}\) map on p. 68, the lower branch for \(G'\le G\) is printed as \[h_{G'}\longmapsto1\otimes h_G.\] The formula is asserted to define the stated algebra map, including the matroid special case.

Let \(L^{a,b}=L^{\otimes a}\otimes(L^*)^{\otimes b}\). Section 6.1 asserts that for every algebraic subgroup \(H\subset\operatorname{GL}(L)\), there exist integers \(a,b\ge0\) and a line \(M\subset L^{a,b}\) whose setwise stabilizer is exactly \(H\).

Let \(K\) be a number field and let \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_\sigma)\) be formal power series in \(x_1,\ldots,x_\nu\) with coefficients in \(K\). Suppose finitely many polynomials \(B_i\in K[y_1,\ldots,y_\sigma]\) and \(C_i\in K[x_1,\ldots,x_\nu]\), together with \(A(0)=q\), determine \(A\) uniquely through \(B_i\circ A=C_i\). Lemma 4.3 asserts that \(A\) converges in the open \(v\)-adic ball of radius one for all but finitely many places \(v\) of \(K\).

The proof forms a fixed \(c\times\sigma\) matrix \(\boldsymbol M\) from the first derivatives of the \(B_i\), in the coefficient equations (16)-(18), and infers \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol M=\sigma\) from uniqueness of the formal solution. The statement of Lemma 4.3 assumes that uniqueness, without adding the étale hypothesis used in the preceding Lemma 4.2.

For a non-degenerate polarized Hodge structure, Lemma 7.21 asserts that the special isometry group is the \(\mathbb Q\)-simple special Mumford–Tate group of a point in the orbit. The proof excludes \(\operatorname{SO}_2\) as a possible non-simple case, but imposes no analogous rank-four exclusion.

In the proof of Corollary 7.17, put \(A_j=\{g:gP_j\in I\}\). The source replaces the incidence condition \(gM(\mathbb C)P_j\cap I\ne\varnothing\) by the condition \(gP_j\in I\). The issue concerns this quotient-incidence identification within that proof.

Let \(X\) be a separated bow variety and let \(\overline X\) be the NS5 resolution obtained by splitting a local charge \(w=w'+w''\). Let \(X\xleftarrow{p}L\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\) be the correspondence of Section 7.1. In the case where all D5 local charges are one, identify \(X=T^*\mathrm{Fl}\) and \(\overline X=T^*\overline{\mathrm{Fl}}\), with the refinement obtained by inserting one intermediate quotient dimension. The flag convention parametrizes quotients. Write \(Z_1\subseteq Z_2\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_k\) for the respective Springer images. Equation (46) asserts \[L\simeq\overline X\times_{Z_2}Z_1,\] with the map to \(\overline X\) given by \(j\).

More generally, put \(L_0=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\mu_L^{-1}(0)]^G\) and let \(X_0,\overline X_0\) be the affine bow varieties. Corollary 7.3 asserts that the induced commutative square \((L\to\overline X,\;L_0\to\overline X_0)\) is Cartesian, with vertical maps the canonical affinization maps.

Let \(D\) be a separated bow diagram and \(\widetilde D\) a D5 resolution splitting a charge \(w=w'+w''\). Proposition 6.3 asserts that the map of representation spaces prescribed by the separated column of Table 1 preserves the moment-zero and stable loci and descends to a regular closed embedding of bow varieties. For the allowed elementary split \(w''=1\), its right resolved triangle uses \[B_{\rm mid}=\begin{pmatrix}B_+&0\\b&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad A''=\binom{I}{0},\qquad a''=\binom01,\qquad b''=b,\qquad B''_+=B_+.\] The source triangle satisfies \(B_-A-AB_++ab=0\), together with conditions (S1), (S2) and the global GIT stability and moment equations of Section 2.2. The compatibility assertion requires the displayed target data to satisfy \(B_{\rm mid}A''-A''B_++a''b''=0\), as well as the other target equations.

For a separated or co-separated D5 resolution \(w=w'+w''\), take the relative chamber \(\widetilde{\mathfrak C}/\mathfrak C=\{a'>a''\}\) and the distinguished fixed point \(\widetilde f_\sharp\). Corollary 6.14, equation (36), asserts \[\left(\prod_{s=1}^{w''}\vartheta(\hbar^s)\right)\Theta(N_j^-)\operatorname{Stab}^{X}_{\mathfrak C}(f)=j^*\varphi^*\operatorname{Stab}^{\widetilde X}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak C}}(\widetilde f_\sharp),\] using the same product bound \(w''\) in both settings; \(\varphi\) is the change of torus in (33). In particular, the statement permits the co-separated split \(w'=1,w''=2\), for which its product is \(\vartheta(\hbar)\vartheta(\hbar^2)\).
On p. 19 the paper identifies the stable-envelope kernel on \(F\times\operatorname{Attr}_{\mathfrak C}(F)\) with the Thom line of the inclusion of that whole product.

Appendix A uses the change-of-group pullback after full localization of the equivariant coefficient rings. In particular, for the allowed separated D5 split \(2=1+1\), it treats the substitution \[u'\mapsto u-\eta,\qquad u''\mapsto u,\qquad\eta\mapsto\eta\] as extending to a unital homomorphism from \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb Q[u',u'',\eta]\) to the target coefficient field.

For a Gårding–Dirichlet polynomial \(\mathfrak g\) on the symmetric matrices, Proposition 3.1(2) asserts that its radial derivative \[q(A)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\mathfrak g(A+tI)\right|_{t=0}\] is \(I\)-central. The printed assertion does not require the input to be \(I\)-central or exclude the degree-one input case.

For arbitrary \(L\in\operatorname{End}(\mathcal S(n))\), write \(\mathfrak g_L=\mathfrak g\circ L\). Proposition 3.1(3)(a) asserts the two-way implication between hyperbolicity of \(\mathfrak g_L\) in direction \(B\) and hyperbolicity of \(\mathfrak g\) in direction \(L(B)\). No surjectivity or the separately stated positive-cone condition from part (e) is imposed on \(L\) in part (a).
Proposition 3.1(3)(e), p. 11, assumes \(L(\mathcal P)\subset\overline{\Gamma(\mathfrak g)}\) and asserts that \(\mathfrak g_L\) is Gårding–Dirichlet.
In the proof of Lemma 3.5, p. 10, equation (3.3) calls \(\Lambda_\pm(A)=\frac12\operatorname{tr}A\pm\lambda_1\pm\cdots\pm\lambda_n\) the \(I\)-eigenvalues on \(\mathcal S(2n)\).

In the setting of Section 7, let \(A\) be a connected semi-local ring with infinite residue fields, let \(M\) be a finite projective \(A\)-module, and let \(\sigma\) be a simplex of \(E(M)\). Define \(\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\) to consist of summands that are intersections of kernels of subsets of \(\sigma\). A full lattice \(\phi:[p_1,\ldots,p_k]\to\operatorname{Sub}(M)\) is compatible with \(\sigma\) only if, for every \(a\in[p_1,\ldots,p_k]\), \[\sum_{j=1}^k\ \sum_{x:x_j\le a_j}\phi(x)\in\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma.\] These compatible full lattices are the nonbasepoint elements of \(D^k(M)^\sigma_{p_1,\ldots,p_k}\).

Proposition 7.24 asserts for every \(\sigma\) that boundary restriction gives a bijection \[D^2(M)^\sigma_{p,q}\longrightarrow D^1(M)^\sigma_p\wedge D^1(M)^\sigma_q,\] sending \(\phi\) to \(\phi(-,q)\) and \(\phi(p,-)\). Its proposed inverse sends two flags \(\phi_1,\phi_2\) to \(\phi(a,b)=\phi_1(a)\cap\phi_2(b)\).

In the proof of Theorem 10.2, pp. 77–78, the model in (10.2) uses \(b\) of bidegree \((2,4)\) and a cell \(\rho_3\) of bidegree \((3,5)\) attached along \((\beta Q^1_3)_\mathbb Z(\sigma)-\sigma b\). After one bar construction, (10.3) and the next displays place \(\bar b\) in \((2,5)\) and the attached \(\bar\rho_3\) cell in \((3,6)\). The subsequent spectral sequence nevertheless treats \(\bar\rho_3\) as an exterior generator.

Let \(M=\bigoplus_{x\in X}M_x\) be an \(A\)-module decomposed over a finite set \(X\), and let \(\preceq\subseteq\le\) be partial orders on \(X\). The group \(\mathrm{GL}(M,\le)\) consists of automorphisms preserving each \(\bigoplus_{y\le x}M_y\). Assuming the Nesterenko–Suslin property for \((A,k)\), Proposition 5.13 asserts that \(\mathrm{GL}(M,\preceq)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}(M,\le)\) induces an isomorphism in group homology with constant coefficients in \(k\).

In its induction step, \(t\) is maximal for \(\le\), the orders agree on \(X'=X\setminus\{t\}\), and \(t\) is unrelated to \(X'\) for \(\preceq\). Writing \(M'=\bigoplus_{x\in X'}M_x\), the proof asserts that every \(f\in\mathrm{GL}(M,\le)\) preserves \(M_t\), and that the resulting epimorphism \[\mathrm{GL}(M,\le)\longrightarrow\mathrm{GL}(M',\le|_{X'})\] has kernel the full ambient subgroup \(\mathrm{GL}(M,\operatorname{fix}M')\).
Remark 8.4, p. 52 (accepted p. 64), identifies \(K_{2r}(A)/F_rK_{2r}(A)\) with the first quotient layer’s homotopy group, and then with \(H^{E_\infty}_{r+1,2r}(\mathbf R_\mathbb Z)\).

Section 9.1.1, p. 53, defines \(\mathfrak p(A)\) with generators \(x\in A^\times\setminus\{1\}\). Equation (9.3), p. 55, then assigns a term \(x\wedge(1-x)\) in an exterior construction on \(A^\times\).

The proof of Corollary D uses injectivity of the adjoint of the Steinberg pairing for a vector space over a field, without restricting that field to be infinite. This is the assertion under review in the extension of the proof to finite fields.
The paragraph following Corollary D, p. 11, says that for a coefficient field with no nontrivial zero sum of squares, \(\operatorname{St}_k(V)\) has no finite-dimensional invariant submodules.
The normal convention is \(B=-\nabla n\), and \(da\) is the signed area form determined by the lifted Epstein normal.

On p. 45, Lemma 8.6 explicitly defines \[i_W(u)=\langle DE(u),W\rangle,\qquad W=\nabla_\xi n,\] and claims \[(\operatorname{div}W)\,E^*da=d i_W .
 \tag{*}\] Its proof identifies the exterior derivative of this metric-dual one-form with divergence times area. Equation (8.5), p. 46, then uses \[\operatorname{tr}\langle\nabla_\xi(B\cdot),DE(\cdot)\rangle E^*da
 =-d i_W-2\langle\xi,n\rangle E^*da .
 \tag{**}\]

Section 4.2, pp. 22–23, permits any map \(\varphi\) continuous on the compactification, differentiable on the open \(\mathbb H^3\), with the prescribed Epstein boundary values and nonnegative Jacobian near \(\gamma\). It then concludes from compactness of the image above a cutoff that \(\int_{\mathbb H^3}\varphi^*\operatorname{vol}_\varepsilon\) is finite and independent of the chosen extension.

The proof of Theorem 6.3, p. 38, takes \(q=\mathcal S(g_{\alpha(\tau)})\) with \(\|q\|_\infty<\delta/2\) and writes \[\widetilde\mu_{\rm print}(z)
 =-\frac{2}{\bar z^4}
       \left(\frac{q}{\rho_{\mathbb D^*}}\right)(1/\bar z).
 \tag{AW}\] It asserts that this is a Beltrami coefficient of supremum norm less than \(\delta\) and uses \([s\widetilde\mu_{\rm print}]\) to construct the short path required for the distance bound.

In the proof of Theorem 5.7, the shrinking cap \(A(r)\) is parametrized as in (C2) by \(p\in S^1\), \(s\in[r,1/r]\), \(r\in(1-\varepsilon,1]\), and \(t\in[0,1]\), through a map \((p,s,r,t)\mapsto(x,y,z)\in\mathbb H^3\). The parametrization extends \(C^{3,\alpha}\) to \(r=1\) with \(z(p,s,1,t)=0\), and (C1) and Lemma 3.16 give \(z=O(1-r)\) uniformly. In these printed coordinates the proof asserts \(I,II,\delta I,\delta II=O((1-r)^{-2})\) and \(I^{-1}=O((1-r)^2)\), and hence uniform boundedness of \(H,\delta H,\langle\delta I,II\rangle\).

Under the natural identification \(T_{[\mu]}T(1)\simeq\Omega^{-1,1}(\mathbb D^*)\), Section 6 defines \(V([\mu])\) by the displayed Schwarzian formula using the associated conformal map \(g_\mu\) and Poincaré density \(\rho_{\mathbb D^*}\). Theorem 6.1 asserts that this vector field has flowlines for all time on the full universal Teichmüller space \(T(1)\). It further asserts that the flow preserves \(T_0(1)\), is the negative Weil–Petersson gradient of the Liouville functional \(S\) there, and that every flowline in \(T_0(1)\) converges to the origin corresponding to a round circle.

Identify chains in \(\Phi([0,1])\) with ordered arcs \(C\) in \(T=\{(x,y):0\le x\le y\le1\}\), using interval inclusion as the order. Lemma A.2 asserts that \((x,y)\) is the maximum of a maximal nontrivial strictly monotone subchain exactly when: \((x,y)\in C\); for some \(n\ge1\), no two points of \(C\cap([x,x+1/n]\times[y-1/n,y])\) share a coordinate with the other coordinates differing by \(1/m\), for any \(m\ge1\); and for every \(n\ge1\), there are \(m\ge1\) and two such coordinate-aligned points in \(C\cap([x-1/n,x]\times[y,y+1/n])\) whose other coordinates differ by \(1/m\).

Lemma A.3 identifies the set of chains with at least \(n\) horizontal pieces with the union, over \(m\ge1\), of chains containing \(n\) horizontal subchains each of length at least \(1/m\) and pairwise distance at least \(1/m\); it makes the analogous identification vertically. These predicates are then used to count maximal pieces and prove the stated Borel classifications.

For an arbitrary continuous action of a Polish group on a Polish space, Theorem 7.4 asserts the equivalence: the action is generically turbulent if and only if its orbit equivalence relation is not classifiable by countable structures.

Corollaries 1.5 and 7.6 assert that no homogeneous Peano continuum has a generic chain, except the circle and possibly the sphere and real projective plane. For a strongly locally homogeneous Peano continuum other than those three spaces, Corollaries 1.7 and 7.8 assert that \(\operatorname{Homeo}(X)\) lacks the generic point property, so its universal minimal flow is nonmetrizable and has no comeager orbit; the same conclusion is asserted for each closed subgroup acting locally transitively. Corollaries 1.8 and 7.9 assert that chains on such a space are not classifiable by countable structures. The stated Peano-continuum convention permits a singleton and these corollaries do not exclude it.

Let \(C\) be a circular path of circular length \(\ell\) in a graph \((G,E)\). Definition 3.2 assigns every ordered vertex pair the weight \[\operatorname{weight}_C(x,y)=\begin{cases}1,&x=C(i),\ y=C(i+1\bmod\ell)\text{ for some }i<\ell,\\-1,&y=C(i),\ x=C(i+1\bmod\ell)\text{ for some }i<\ell,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\] and asserts that it is well-defined because \(C\) is a path. The circular-path convention permits sequence length three, including \(\langle a,b,a\rangle\). The winding number of a walk is the sum of these weights over its successive vertex pairs.

Proposition 5.7 assumes that \(X\) is a Peano continuum and \(\mathcal U,\mathcal V\) are brick partitions; it does not impose the absence of locally separating points. Its printed construction starts from seeds \(\operatorname{Star}(T_V\cap U,\mathcal W_0)\) and asserts \[\operatorname{Core}(V,\mathcal W)=\operatorname{Star}(T_V,\mathcal W).\]

In the robust-cycle construction, refine a brick partition to a lasso \(v\mathbin{\frown}c_+\), with \(\rho_U^S([\rho_V^U c_+]_2)\subseteq C\). Put \(N=\operatorname{wd}_C(\rho_V^S c_+)\ge\ell>1\); let \(M_c\) be the maximum absolute winding of an initial segment of \(c_+\) or its reverse \(c_-\), and let \(M_v\) be the corresponding maximum over initial or final segments of \(v\). Choose \(k\) with \(kN>3M_v+M_c+2\) and put \(\bar w_0=c_+\mathbin{\frown}\cdots\mathbin{\frown}c_+\), with \(k\) copies. Let the spaced path \(w_0\) on the refined brick partition \(W\) have \(\rho_W^Vw_0\) monotonically refining \(v\mathbin{\frown}\bar w_0\). Claim 6.4.1(b0) asserts, for every final segment \(t\) of \(w_0\) whose image \(\rho_W^Vt\) contains \(\bar w_0\), \[\operatorname{wd}_C(\rho_W^St)>2M_v+M_c+2.\]
Lemma 2.1, p. 8, assumes only \(g\in K[[X]]\) and \(|x|\leq R^\dagger(g)\), and then evaluates \(g(x)\).

Lemma 5.8, p. 34, quantifies over all \(s\in C_0^*(\overline{\mathbb Q})\), but concludes that there is a global relation at \(x(s)\). The definition on p. 9 requires a finite algebraic parameter. The construction of \(C_0^*\) on p. 27 does not remove poles of \(x\).

Remark 5.14, p. 39, asserts that every column \((F_\lambda,G_\lambda)^{\mathsf T}\) satisfies a rank-two system over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}(X)\) because the differential forms are a basis over the function field of \(C_0\).

Remark 3.4 defines an alcoved polytope for this discussion to be an integral polytope in \(H=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i x_i=0\}\) with facet directions in \(\{e_i-e_j:1\le i,j\le n\}\), while retaining the ambient integer lattice. It asserts that intersections of these alcoved polytopes are integral, and that for any two such polytopes \(P_0,P_1\), \[\operatorname{conv}(P_0\times\{0\}\cup P_1\times\{1\})\] has a unimodular triangulation. The later complementary-subspace formulation uses \(W\cap\mathbb Z^n\) as its lattice.

The isolated implication in the proof of Theorem 3.1 is that a closed subgroup \(J\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z_p)\) surjecting onto \(\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z/p^2)\) must equal \(\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z_p)\). The argument allows \(p=2\) and \(g>1\).

For an arbitrary algebraically closed residue field \(k\) of characteristic \(p\), Section 4.1 defines inverse \(p^n\)-multiplication on \(1+t k[[t]]\) by substituting \(t^{1/p^n}\) for \(t\) while leaving every coefficient unchanged. It uses this operation as the extension of the natural \(\mathbb Z_p\)-module structure.

Let \(K\subset L\) be a finite separable field extension and let \(G\) be the Galois group of its normal closure over \(K\). Lemma 5.5 assumes that a profinite group \(H\) has no irreducible constituent in common with \(G\). For a homomorphism \(\phi:\operatorname{Gal}_K\to H\), it asserts \[\phi(\operatorname{Gal}_L)=\phi(\operatorname{Gal}_K).\] Surjectivity of \(\phi\) is not assumed; the phrase irreducible constituent is not further defined in the statement.

Over \(\mathbb Q\), let \(\mathcal H\) be the Hodge line bundle on \(\mathcal A_g[r]\), and let the degree of a proper curve be measured by its pullback. Lemma 6.1 asserts, for every Hecke operator \(\tau\) and every proper curve \(C\subset\mathcal A_g[r]\), \[\deg\tau(C)=\deg(\tau)\deg(C).\] Its proof compares the two pullbacks of \(\mathcal H\) to the Hecke correspondence.

In the proof of Theorem 6.3, \(V\) is a divisor whose line bundle is a power of \(\mathcal H\), and \(C\) has maximal monodromy. For a primitive point \(x\in C(K)\) with \(K/\mathbb Q\) Galois and monodromy index at most \(c\), the proof claims that distinct Galois conjugates contributing the same point of \(\tau(C)\cap V\) produce distinct branches there. This gives \((\tau(C)\cdot V)\ge \deg(\tau)[K:\mathbb Q]/c\). The source writes these formulas using \(\tau(C)\) without explicitly distinguishing a reduced image from a correspondence cycle.

Lemma 6.2 requires \(K/\mathbb Q\) to be Galois and the selected point \(x\) to be primitive over \(K\). The proof produces conjugate degree-\(d\) fields \(K_i/L\) by Hilbert specialization and then sets \(K=K_1\).

For positive coprime integers \(x,y\), let \(X\) be either the numerator set or the denominator set of the orbit \(\Psi\binom xy\). The square branch of Theorem 2.6 asserts that every square integer \(n\ge8xy\) belongs to \(X\), provided it satisfies the corresponding congruence condition and that coordinate has no reciprocity obstruction in Table 1.

Writing \(\chi=(x/y)\) in the paper's quadratic-symbol convention, Table 1 gives: when \((x,y)\equiv(1,0)\pmod4\), numerators are \(1\pmod4\), denominators \(0\pmod4\), and \(\chi=-1\) forbids squares in both; when \((x,y)\equiv(3,0)\pmod4\), the congruences are \(3\pmod4\) and \(0\pmod4\), with a denominator reciprocity obstruction if \(\chi=-(-1/y)\). For \(y\equiv1\pmod4\), there is no numerator congruence restriction and denominators are \(1\pmod4\), with both coordinates obstructed if \(\chi=-1\). For \(y\equiv2\pmod4\), numerators are odd and denominators are \(2\pmod4\), with no additional reciprocity obstruction. For \(y\equiv3\pmod4\), numerators have no congruence restriction and denominators are \(3\pmod4\), with a numerator reciprocity obstruction if \(\chi=-1\).

Let \(\mathcal W\) be a finite set of nonidentity matrices in \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)_{\ge0}\), with pairwise disjoint closed images \(T_\gamma([0,1])\). Lemma 7.4 sets \(\Delta_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}=T_{\gamma_{i_1}\cdots\gamma_{i_k}}([0,1])\) and asserts constants \(A,B\in(0,1)\), uniform at every depth and over all words, such that \[|\Delta_{i_1,\ldots,i_k,j}|\ge A|\Delta_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}|,\] \[\operatorname{dist}(\Delta_{i_1,\ldots,i_k,s},\Delta_{i_1,\ldots,i_k,t})\ge B|\Delta_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}|\quad(s\ne t).\] These are used to realize the limit set as a generalized Cantor set of dimension less than one.

Section 7.2 treats every nonidentity \(T_\gamma\) as a contraction and asserts a bounded-distortion property for finite systems. Proposition 7.6 applies the cited conformal-IFS finite-approximation theorem to the systems generated by the bounded-entry subsets of \(\Psi\), after deleting redundant prefix words, to conclude that their dimensions increase to one.
The proof asserts that the full orbits \(\Psi\binom{3}{2+3k}\) never contain squares in either coordinate and that their numerators are always three modulo four.

The documented function `psi_rep` decides numerator or denominator membership in \(\Psi\binom{x}{y}\) for the admissible primitive nonnegative input vector. The denominator branch is intended to test all progression terms satisfying its row congruence conditions.
Corollary 2.17 identifies denominators of rationals in \((0,1)\) built from \(4\mathbb Z^+\) with the union of both coordinate sets of \(\Psi_2\binom{0}{1}\).

Let \(L\) be the signature-\((1,3)\) Hermitian-matrix lattice of (4.1), \(\Gamma=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathcal O_D)\), and \(\mu\in L'/L\). For \(m\in\mathbb Z+Q(\mu)\), \(m>0\), put \(L^+_{m,\mu}=\{X\in L+\mu:Q(X)=m,\ a(X)>0\}\) and \[\operatorname{tr}_{m,\mu}(f)=\sum_{X\in\Gamma\backslash L^+_{m,\mu}}\frac{f(P_X)}{|\Gamma_X|}.\] Thus this trace uses the positive vectors in the single coset \(\mu\).

For \(n\ge0\) and \(\Re s>1\), Theorem 4.2 asserts \[\Phi_L^{(1-2n)}(F_{1-2n,m,\mu}(\cdot,s),P)=C_n(s)\frac{2}{\pi\Gamma(s+1/2)\sqrt m}\operatorname{tr}_{m,\mu}(G_{2s-1}(\cdot,P)),\] where \(C_0=1\) and \(C_n(s)=(4\pi m)^n\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(s+1/2-n+j)\). For \(n\ge1\), Theorem 4.3 asserts \[\Phi_L^{(1-2n)}(F_{1-2n,m,\mu},P)=(4\pi m)^n\frac{2}{\pi\sqrt m}\operatorname{tr}_{m,\mu}(G_{2n}(\cdot,P)).\] The hypothesis does not require \(\mu=-\mu\).

In the twisted-theta setting of Section 5.2, fix a primitive positive vector \(X_0\in L^{+,0}_{m,\mu}\) and let \(P,N\) be the lattices associated with it. The first identity of Theorem 5.15 asserts \[\operatorname{tr}^0_{m,\mu}(\Theta^*_{L,\chi_D}(\tau,\cdot))=\chi_D(X_0)\operatorname{tr}^0_{m,\mu}(1)\left(\Theta^*_{P(D)}(\tau)\otimes\vartheta_{N(D)^-,\chi_D}(\tau)v^{3/2}\right)^{L(D)}\!\cdot\psi_D.\] Here the outer trace is untwisted, \(\psi_D\) is the invariant vector of Lemma 5.5, and \(\Theta^*_{P(D)}\) is the weight-\(3/2\) theta series (5.10). This identity is stated without requiring \(\chi_D(X_0)\ne0\) or \(m\in|D|\mathbb Z\).

Remark 3.7(1), page 20, writes \[
 L(\chi_\Delta,1)=
 \frac{h(\Delta)\log\varepsilon_\Delta}{\sqrt\Delta}
 \qquad(\Delta>0).\] defines \(h(\Delta)\) as the class number of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt\Delta)\), and defines \(\varepsilon_\Delta\) as the smallest totally positive unit greater than \(1\).
The source calls \(h(\Delta)\) the field class number; it does not explicitly specify the ordinary versus narrow convention.

Definition 4.2 and Lemma 4.7, page 20, assign the half-line Schrödinger operator \(Q\) the domain \(H^2_0((x_0,\infty))\) and assert self-adjointness. The preceding sentence explicitly defines \(H^k_0\) as the \(H^k\)-closure of compactly supported smooth functions.
Lemma 4.8 further asserts that this operator has infinitely many negative eigenvalues tending to zero.

Fix the subextremal background \(M>0\), \(|e|<M\), \(m>0\). In Theorem 5.1, the source \(H\) of the radial equation (2.4) is supported in \(s\le s_H\), and \(m-L^{-p}<\omega<m\) for a sufficiently large fixed \(p>2\). The horizon solution is normalized by \(u_H(\omega,s)=e^{-i\omega s}(1+o(1))\) as \(s\to-\infty\).

Part (4), equation (5.10), gives a resonant Green expansion with denominator \(1+\Gamma(m)e^{2i\pi\breve k}\) and regular coefficients frozen at \(\omega=m\). For example, \[u^{\rm reg}_{1,-}(\omega,s)=\frac{u_H(m,s)}{C_W(m,L)}\int_s^{\infty}w_{1,-}(m,s')H(m,s')\,ds'\,\big(C_{\cos,-}(m)\cos(\pi\breve k)+C_{\sin,-}(m)\sin(\pi\breve k)\big).\] The analogous remaining regular coefficients also use threshold-frequency solutions and sources. The stated bounds on the sine/cosine errors and their frequency derivatives hold for every \(s\le s_{\max}\), with constants allowed to depend on \(s_{\max},s_H\), including arbitrarily negative \(s\). The source quantity is \[\mathcal N[H]=\int_{-\infty}^{s_H}\left(\sup_{m/2<\omega<m}|H(\omega,s')|+\sup_{m/2<\omega<m}|\partial_\omega H(\omega,s')|\right)ds'.\]

In the near-threshold regime \(m-L^{-p}<\omega<m\), use the Airy basis normalized by \(W(u_{\rm Ai2},u_{\rm Bi2})=L^{-4/3}Mm^2/\pi\) and the oscillatory basis normalized by \(W(B_+,B_-)=2i\). For \(2L^2/(Mm^2)\le s\le10L^2/(Mm^2)\), Corollary 5.13 writes \[B_\pm=b_{\pm,+}(u_{\rm Ai2}-iu_{\rm Bi2})+b_{\pm,-}(u_{\rm Ai2}+iu_{\rm Bi2})\] and asserts \[\left|\frac{b_{\pm,\pm}}{L^{2/3}}-(Mm^2)^{-1/2}\pi^{1/2}e^{\mp i\pi/4}\right|\lesssim e^{-\kappa_+A},\qquad\frac{|b_{\pm,\mp}|}{L^{2/3}}\lesssim e^{-\kappa_+A}.\] These are the printed inverse connection coefficients in (5.45), with the phase convention from Corollary 5.8.

Let \(H(\omega,L,s)\) vanish for \(s\ge S_0\), with \(S_0\) large, and let \(p\) be sufficiently large. Proposition 6.6 defines the quadratic source quantity \[\mathcal D[H]=\sup_{\substack{\omega>0,\ \omega\ne m\\L\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}}(1+\omega^{10})(1+L^{10+p})\int_{-\infty}^{S_0}\bigl(|\partial_\omega(e^{i\omega s}H)|^2+|\partial_sH|^2+|H|^2\bigr)(r-r_+)^{-1}\,ds<\infty.\] Let \(u\) solve (2.4), with the outgoing conditions (2.6) for \(\omega>m\) and (2.7) for \(\omega<m\).

The proposition bounds its linear inverse-Fourier response by a right-hand side with one factor \(\mathcal D[H]\). In particular, Lemma 6.7 asserts for \(t\ge1,R>r_+\), with \(p(s)=t^*(s)-t\), \[\sup_{r\in[r_+,R]}\left|\int_m^\infty e^{-it^*\omega}e^{i\omega p(s)}u\,d\omega\right|\lesssim_R(1+L)^{-4}t^{-1}\mathcal D[H].\] Proposition 3.2 likewise bounds a first-power response by weighted squared source integrals. None of these statements normalizes the source or takes a square root of \(\mathcal D\).

Let \(\mathfrak T\subset\mathfrak T'\) be an open immersion of reduced affinoid \(p\)-adic formal schemes with \(\mathfrak T'=\operatorname{Spf}A'\), \(\mathfrak T=\operatorname{Spf}A\), and \(\mathcal O(\mathfrak T')=\mathcal O^+(\mathfrak T'_{\mathbb Q_p})\). In Step 2 of Proposition 3.39, choose an object \((\operatorname{Spf}\widehat R,X^\dagger_{\mathbb Q_p})\) in the smooth pseudo-dagger site, with \(\widehat R\) the \(p\)-adic completion of a smooth \(A\)-algebra \[R=A[X_1,\ldots,X_M]/(f_1,\ldots,f_m).\] The proof asserts that this chosen presentation gives an embedding \(\operatorname{Spec}R\subset\mathbb P^M_{A'}\), whose schematic closure and \(p\)-adic completion provide the required geometric materialization over the frame.

The proof of Proposition A.13, page 31, asserts that, for \(X=\mathbb P^1_S\), the functor \[r:\mathrm{FSch}/S\longrightarrow\mathrm{FSch}/X,
 \qquad \mathfrak T\longmapsto\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_{\mathfrak T},\] is final. Here a formal model over \(X\) has a map of its reduced special fiber to \(X\), rather than a specified lift of that map to a formal projective line.
Remark 2.7, page 5, asserts that a smooth surjective dagger morphism can be straightened with \(X_h=X_0\times_{S_0}S_h\), using \(\operatorname{Int}(X_0/K)=f_0^{-1}\operatorname{Int}(S_0/K)\).

In Step 2 of the proof of Proposition 2.22, page 9, the realization of the dagger torus \(\mathbb T^{1\dagger}\) is identified with the unit. The torus of Example 2.3 is the unreduced space, whereas the Tate object in Definition 2.14 is a cofiber.

Remark 2.27, page 10, calls the canonical dagger structure of a proper rigid variety \(S\) terminal in \(\mathrm{Ad}^{\dagger}_{/S}\). Definition 2.25 allows an arbitrary analytic map from the completed source, which need not extend to a dagger map.

Fix an integer \(n>0\) and formal parameters \(\tau,t\) with \(\tau^2=t^{-1}\). Equations (2.3)–(2.4) define \(\mathbb Z_{\tau,g}=\mathbb Z[\tau^{\pm1},\{g_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}]/\sim\) by \(g_{k+n}=g_k\), \(g_0=-1\), and \(g_kg_{-k}=\tau^2\) for \(k\ne0\). Equation (2.5) identifies this quotient with the Laurent polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[\tau^{\pm1},g_1^{\pm1},\ldots,g_{n-1}^{\pm1}]\). The quantum specialization sends \(g_i\mapsto\tau\) for \(1\le i<n\) and \(g_0\mapsto-1\).

For a non-archimedean local field \(F\) with residue cardinality \(q\), Section 2.2.4 takes an additive character \(\psi\) of conductor 0 and a Haar measure giving \(\mathcal O^\times\) volume \(q-1\). It defines \(g(\sigma,\eta)=\int_{\mathcal O^\times}\sigma(u)\eta(u)\,du\), introduces \(\sigma(u)=(u,\pi)_n^{-k}\) and \(\eta(u)=\psi(-\pi^{-1}u)\), but then sets \(g_k=g(\sigma,\psi)\). The text asserts \(g_0=-1\) and \(g_kg_{-k}=q\) for nonzero residue classes, with \(q\equiv1\pmod{2n}\) for the latter relation. Section 2.3.3 claims a specialization \(\mathbb C_{\tau,g}\to\mathbb C\) sending \(t=\tau^{-2}\mapsto q^{-1}\) and the formal \(g_i\) to these Gauss sums.

For the root datum and affine Weyl action of Section 3.4, let \(V=Y\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R\). Equations (3.65)–(3.66) define the negative fundamental alcove and its upper closure by \[A_-=\{v:-1<\langle v,a\rangle<0\ (a\in R^+)\},\qquad\overline A_-=\{v:-1<\langle v,a\rangle\le0\ (a\in R^+)\}.\] The text claims that every \(v\in V\) has a unique expression \(v=x\cdot w\) with \(x\in\overline A_-\) and \(w\in W_{\mathrm{aff}}\).

For an arbitrary datum \(\mathfrak D\) and a twist \((Q,n)\) whose modified datum \(\widetilde{\mathfrak D}\) is simply connected, the dot action uses the untwisted \(\check\rho\): \(x\bullet w=(x+\check\rho)\cdot w-\check\rho\). Equations (3.74)–(3.75) assert that \[\overline A^{\bullet}_{-,(Q,n)}=\{v:-1<\langle v+\check\rho,\widetilde a\rangle\le0\ (\widetilde a\in\widetilde R^+)\}=\{v:-n(\check a)<\langle v+\check\rho,a\rangle\le0\ (a\in R^+)\}\] is a fundamental domain for \(\widetilde W_{\mathrm{aff}}\). The lower walls are strictly excluded in these printed definitions.

Let \(\mathfrak D=(Y,\{\check a_i\},X,\{a_i\})\) and its \((Q,n)\)-modified datum \(\widetilde{\mathfrak D}\) have the hypotheses of Section 3.4.7, including simple connectedness of the modified datum. Define \[\Box_{(Q,n)}=\{\check\lambda\in Y_+:0\le\langle\check\lambda,a_i\rangle<n(\check a_i)\text{ for every }i\in I\}.\] Equations (3.82)–(3.83) assert that every \(\check\lambda\in Y_+\) can be written uniquely as \(\check\lambda=\check\lambda_0+\check\zeta\) with \(\check\lambda_0\in\Box_{(Q,n)}\) and \(\check\zeta\in\widetilde Y_+\). The explanation uses the claim that simple connectedness places the modified fundamental coweights in \(\widetilde Y_+\). Here the article defines simple connectedness by the simple coroots freely generating \(Y\).

Section 7.3.6 similarly defines \(\Box_l=\{\check\lambda\in Y:0\le\langle\check\lambda,a_i\rangle<l_i\text{ for every }i\}\) and asserts that every dominant \(\check\lambda\) has a unique decomposition \(\check\lambda_0+\check\eta\), with \(\check\lambda_0\in\Box_l\) and \(\check\eta\in Y_l\).

Section 7.3.1 allows every positive integer \(\ell\): it sets \(l=2\ell\) for even \(\ell\), and permits either \(l=\ell\) or \(l=2\ell\) for odd \(\ell\). Put \(\mathbb Z_l=\mathbb Z[u,u^{-1}]/(\Phi_l(u))\), and let \(\mathbb Z_l\to A\) be a specialization. For an adjoint root datum \(\mathfrak D\), the modified datum \(\mathfrak D_l\) uses \(l_i=l/\gcd(l,d_i)\). Section 7.3.5 asserts a unique \(A\)-algebra homomorphism \(\operatorname{Fr}:\dot U_A(\mathfrak D)\to\dot U_A(\mathfrak D_l)\) with the rule (7.14): divided powers of index \(k\) are sent to the divided powers of index \(k/l_i\), with the displayed weight idempotent, when \(l_i\mid k\), and to zero otherwise, for both \(E_i\) and \(F_i\). It then claims the fully faithful exact pullback functor (7.15).

In the metaplectic setting of Sections 5–6, let \(\widetilde J_{\check\mu}\) be the genuine spherical Whittaker basis function, supported on \(\mu_nU\pi^{\check\mu}K\), with \(\widetilde J_{\check\mu}(\pi^{\check\mu})=1\), where \(\check\mu\in Y_+\). The spherical convolution uses \(\operatorname{vol}(K)=1\). For \(\check\lambda\in\widetilde Y_+\), (6.1) asserts \[\widetilde J_{\check\mu}*_K\widetilde h_{\check\lambda}=\sum_{\check\zeta\in Y_+}q^{\langle\rho,\check\zeta\rangle}\left(\sum_{x\in m^{-1}_{\check\mu,\check\lambda}(\pi^{\check\zeta})}\varepsilon(z(x))\psi(n(x))\right)\widetilde J_{\check\zeta}.\] Here \(m\) is multiplication from \(\mu_nU\pi^{\check\mu}K\times_K K\pi^{\check\lambda}K\), and \(z(x),n(x)\) are its central and unipotent factors. Equivalently, (6.2) gives the coefficient \[b_{\check\lambda\check\mu}(\check\zeta)=q^{\langle\rho,\check\zeta\rangle}\int_U\psi(u)h_{\check\lambda}(\pi^{-\check\mu+\check\zeta}u)\,du,\qquad\operatorname{vol}(U(\mathcal O))=1.\]

For a Coxeter system \((W,S)\), put \(t=\tau^{-2}\) and define the Hecke generators by \(T_s^2=t^{-1}+(t^{-1}-1)T_s\). Section 3.3.1 prints \(T_s^{-1}=t^{-1}T_s+(t^{-1}-1)\). With \(H_s=\tau^{-1}T_s\), equation (4.2) states that \((T_s-\tau^2)(T_s+1)=0\) is equivalent to \((H_s-\tau)(H_s-\tau^{-1})=0\).

For \(J\subseteq S\) with finite \(W_J\) and longest element \(w_0^J\), define \(\varepsilon_J^+=\tau^{-\ell(w_0^J)}\sum_{w\in W_J}\tau^{\ell(w)}H_w\) and \(\varepsilon_J^-=(-\tau)^{\ell(w_0^J)}\sum_{w\in W_J}(-\tau^{-1})^{\ell(w)}H_w\). Equations (3.40)–(3.41) print \[H_w\varepsilon_J^-=\varepsilon_J^-H_w=(-\tau)^{-\ell(w)}\varepsilon_J^+,\qquad (\varepsilon_J^-)^2=(-\tau)^{\ell(w_0^J)}P_{W_J}(-t)\varepsilon_J^-.\]

These are the displayed normalizations under review.

For \(\check\mu\in Y\), \(\check\zeta\in\widetilde Y\), and a simple reflection \(s_i\), the metaplectic Demazure–Lusztig product rule (4.12) is printed as \[(Y^{\check\mu}Y^{\check\zeta})\cdot(\tau^{-1}\widetilde T_{s_i})=Y^{\check\mu}\cdot(\tau^{-1}\widetilde T_{s_i})+(\tau-\tau^{-1})\frac{Y^{\check\zeta\cdot s_i}-Y^{\check\zeta}}{1-Y^{-\check a_i}}.\] The operator itself is defined by (4.8)–(4.10).

Let \(\check\eta\in\overline A_{-,n}^{\bullet}\), and choose the minimal coset representative \(\sigma t(\check\beta)\) with \(\check\mu=\check\eta\bullet\sigma t(\check\beta)\), \(\sigma\in W\), \(\check\beta\in\widetilde Y\). In the root-of-unity quantum-group setting of Section 7.3, take a restricted weight \(\check\lambda_0\in\Box_l\) and a dominant modified-lattice weight \(\check\eta\in\widetilde Y_{l,+}\). Put \(\check\lambda_0^{\dagger}=\check\lambda_0\cdot w_0+2(\widetilde\rho^{\vee}-\check\rho)\).
