In the velocity argument for the generalized SQG equation, take \(x=(a,a)\), \(a=x_*>0\), and \(0<\alpha\le1/4\). The paper defines \[B_*=\{(y_1,y_2):y_1>a,\ \min\{y_1,2a\}<y_2<y_1+2a\},\qquad G_*=\{y_1>a,\ 0<y_2<\min\{y_1,2a\}\},\] and \(B=(0,a)\times(0,2a)\). Tildes denote reflection in the vertical axis. The argument calls the contributions of \(B_*\cap([1,\infty)\times\mathbb R)\) and its reflected tail \(O(a)\), and claims in (4.18) that \[\int_{G_*\cup B\cup\widetilde B_*}\frac{y_1-a}{|x-y|^{2+2\alpha}}\,dy-\int_{\widetilde G_*\cup B_*}\frac{y_1-a}{|x-y|^{2+2\alpha}}\,dy\ge Ca\] for any finite \(C\), for all sufficiently small positive \(a\) depending on \(C\).

For \(\alpha\in[0,1/2)\), \(\beta\in[0,1)\), and vorticity \(\theta\in X_\beta\), the paper’s weighted Lipschitz class on \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^+\), define \(u\) by the half-plane Biot–Savart law (1.2), equivalently \(u(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(x-y)^\perp|x-y|^{-2-2\alpha}\theta(y)\,dy\) after odd extension in the second coordinate. Lemma 2.2, equation (2.3), asserts \[\left\|\max\{x_2^{2\alpha-1},1\}\,\partial_{x_1}u_2\right\|_{L^\infty}\le C_\alpha\left(\|\partial_{x_1}\theta\|_{L^\infty}+\|\theta\|_{L^1\cap L^\infty}\right).\] The printed range includes \(\alpha=0\).

In the proof of Lemma 2.2 with \(0\le\alpha<1/2\) and \(0\le\beta<1\), the page-8 estimate asserts, for \(0<r<3\), \[J_{\alpha,\beta}(r):=\int_{-2}^{2}|r-y|^{-\beta}|y|^{-2\alpha}\,dy\le C_{\alpha,\beta}\max\{r^{1-2\alpha-\beta},1\}.\] No separate logarithmic case is stated when \(2\alpha+\beta=1\). The subsequent main a priori estimate uses \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and \(2\alpha\le\beta\le1-2\alpha\), which includes that endpoint.

In the first ill-posedness case, \(\beta<2\alpha\), the source sets \(b_n=2^{-2(2\alpha+\beta)n/(1-\beta)}a_n\). The last display after (3.17) asserts \[\frac{a_n\lambda_\beta'(2^{-4n-1})}{3b_n}=\frac13(2-2\beta)^{\beta/(1-\beta)}2^{2(2\alpha-\beta)n/(1-\beta)}.\]

For an interval \(I=[a,b]\), the source defines \[\rho_{j,1}(I)=
 \left[\frac{a+b}{2}-2^{-j}(b-a),\frac{a+b}{2}\right],
 \qquad
 \rho_{j,2}(I)=
 \left[\frac{a+b}{2},\frac{a+b}{2}+2^{-j}(b-a)\right].
 \tag{2}\] It defines \(\Omega\) by membership in infinitely many intervals \[\rho_{1,i_1}\rho_{2,i_2}\cdots\rho_{k,i_k}[0,1],
 \qquad i_j\in\{1,2\},
 \tag{3}\] and claims \(\lambda(\Omega)=\infty\).

In the directional maximal-function construction, put \(w=2^{-h(\mathcal P)}\) and \(L=(2\eta)^{-1}+1>1\). The proof of Theorem 1 considers the parallelogram \(P=\{(x,y):0\le x\le L,\ b+dx<y<b+dx+w\}\), whose slope \(d\) lies within \(w\) of a direction in \(\Omega\). On printed page 192 (PDF page 8), it asserts that \(P\) is contained in a parallelogram oriented in a direction in \(\Omega\) with \(1/L\) times the area of \(P\). This containment is used to conclude \(M_\Omega\chi_{K_{\sigma,2,\eta}}\gtrsim\eta^2\) on \(K_{\sigma,1}\).

Proposition 2.27 states that for every integer \(k\ge1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there are \(c=c(k)>0\), \(\eta=\eta(k,\varepsilon)>0\), and \(\delta_0>0\) such that the following holds for \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\). Let \(F\) consist of polynomials of degree at most \(\delta^{-\eta}\) and \(C^k\)-norm at most 1, and let \(\mathcal R\) be pairwise incomparable \((\delta;k)\) tangency rectangles. Choose \(F(R)\subseteq\{f\in F:f\sim R\}\), and put \(\mathcal R(f)=\{R:f\in F(R)\}\). Assume for every \(f\) and interval \(J\subseteq[0,1]\) that \[\#\{R\in\mathcal R(f):I(R)\subseteq J\}\le\delta^{-\eta}|J|^\varepsilon\#\mathcal R(f).\]

Suppose \(W\subseteq[0,1]^{k+1}\) is semialgebraic of complexity at most \(\delta^{-\eta}\), has volume at most \(\delta^\varepsilon\), and contains every tangency prism \(\widehat R\). Then there exist \(R\in\mathcal R\), \(\tau\in[\delta,\delta^c]\), and a \((\tau;k+1;c)\) tangency rectangle \(R_1\supseteq R\) such that \(\#\{f\in F(R):f\sim R_1\}\gtrsim\#F(R)\). The exponent \(c\) and the implicit positive fraction depend only on \(k\), not on \(\varepsilon\).

For coefficients satisfying \(\delta\sum_j|y_j|^2=1\), the decomposition on page 53 uses \[G_0=\{j:|y_j|\le1\},\qquad G_k=\{j:2^k\le|y_j|<2^{k+1}\},\quad k\ge1,\] and treats these sets as covering the coefficient indices. The subsequent argument sums the corresponding groups.

A \((\delta,\alpha;C)\)-set in a metric space is defined in 4.2 by the covering-number bound \(E_\delta(E\cap B_r)\le C(r/\delta)^\alpha\) for every metric ball of radius \(r\ge\delta\). Let \(k\ge1\), let \(I\) be compact, and let \(\mathcal F\subset C^\infty(I)\) be uniformly smooth and forbid \(k\)-th order tangency as in (1.11). For \(0<\beta\le\alpha\le1\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), Theorem 1.11′ asserts that some \(\eta,\delta_0>0\) give, for \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), \[\left\|\sum_{f\in F}\chi_{Y(f)}\right\|_{L^{(k+1)/k}(\mathbb R^2)}\le\delta^{-\varepsilon}\bigl(\delta^{2-\alpha}\#F\bigr)^{k/(k+1)}\] whenever \(F\subset\mathcal F\) is a \((\delta,\beta;\delta^{-\eta})\)-set in the \(C^k\) metric and each \(Y(f)\subset f^\delta\) is a \((\delta,\alpha;\delta^{-\eta})\)-set in the Euclidean metric. No discrete separation condition on \(F\) is stated. For \(0\le\alpha\le1\), \(\beta>\alpha\), equation (5.2) replaces \(\delta^{2-\alpha}\) by \(\delta^{2-\alpha-(\beta-\alpha)/k}\).

In Step 2 of the localization, choose a maximal disjoint family of balls of radius \(2t\) in the ambient \(C^k\) function space. The proof asserts a uniform bounded-overlap property for their radius-\(8t\) enlargements, invoking inequality (1.11), which is assumed only for the given family \(\mathcal F\). The selected ambient centers are not required to lie in \(\mathcal F\).

Let \(s\ge2\), \(\zeta\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^s\times\mathbb R)\), and \(T^\zeta=(\partial_t\zeta,\partial_t^2\zeta,\ldots,\partial_t^{s+1}\zeta)^T\). Assume \[\det[\partial_tT^\zeta,\partial_{w_1}T^\zeta,\ldots,\partial_{w_s}T^\zeta]_{(w,t)=(0,0)}\ne0.\] For a smooth bump \(\phi\) supported sufficiently near the origin, define \[A_{\zeta,\phi}f(x,y;w)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t,y-\zeta(w;t))\phi(w,t)\,dt,\qquad G_{\zeta,\phi}f(x,y)=\sup_w|A_{\zeta,\phi}f(x,y;w)|.\]

Proposition 7.2 asserts that there exists \(p=p(s)<\infty\) such that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\|A_{\zeta,\phi}(P_kf)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^s)}\le C2^{-((s+1)/p+\varepsilon)k}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)},\] where \(P_k\) is a Littlewood–Paley projection to frequencies of magnitude \(\asymp2^k\), and \(C\) depends on \(\varepsilon,\zeta,\phi\) but not \(k\). The asserted consequence (7.5) is \(\|G_{\zeta,\phi}(P_kf)\|_p\le C2^{-(1/p+\varepsilon)k}\|f\|_p\).

Appendix A.1 proposes the translation-invariant polynomial family \[h(x,y,w_1,\ldots,w_s;t)=y+w_1(t-x)^2+w_2(t-x)^3+w_2(t-x)^4+\cdots+w_s(t-x)^{s+1}.\] It claims that every polynomial in \(t\) of degree at most \(s+1\) has a unique representation in this form. For every output \((x,y)\) in a neighbourhood of \((0,1)\), the argument further claims that one can choose \(w\) so that the graph has order-\(s\) contact with the \(x\)-axis at the fixed origin. It then applies \(f_\rho(X,Y)=(Y+\rho)^{-1/(s+1)}\mathbf1_{[0,1]^2}\), claiming a curve integral comparable to \(\log(1/\rho)\), to establish sharpness of the \(p>s+1\) range in Theorem 1.8.

For the polynomial family \(h(u;t)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}u_jt^j\) and the projection \(\Phi\) to the last \(m-s\) coordinates, Example 1.2 identifies the fiber of the jet \((h,\partial_th,\ldots,\partial_t^sh)\) at \(t\) with \[V_{u;t}=\{u':u'_j=u_j\text{ for }0\le j\le s\}.\] The slicing proof for \(s<m-1\) uses \(C^{\bar v}=\{u:\pi\Phi(u)=\bar v\}\), with \(\pi\) projecting to the last \(m-s-1\) coordinates. It calls \(\Phi\) an immersion and identifies \(T_uC^{\bar v}\) as an \((m-s-1)\)-dimensional subspace orthogonal to the jet-fiber tangent, in the step asserting full rank of the restricted jet map.

For circles, \(h(x,y,r;t)=\sqrt{r^2-(t-x)^2}+y\) near \((0,0,1;0)\), and \(\Phi(x,y,r)=(x,y)\). Appendix A identifies the fiber of \((h,\partial_th)=(1,0)\) with \(\{(x',y',r'):y'=0,\ r'=1-x'\}\), and uses its parameterization \((t,0,1-t)\) to assert rank one for the restricted center projection.

For rotated ellipses with semi-axes \(a,b\), center \((x,y)\), and angle \(\theta\), the upper graph is \[h(t)=\frac{-(Bt+E)+\sqrt{(Bt+E)^2-4C(At^2+Dt+F)}}{2C},\] where \(A=a^2\sin^2\theta+b^2\cos^2\theta\), \(B=2(b^2-a^2)\sin\theta\cos\theta\), \(C=a^2\cos^2\theta+b^2\sin^2\theta\), \(D=-2Ax-By\), \(E=-Bx-2Cy\), and \(F=Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2-a^2b^2\). Although the chosen parameter neighborhood is around \((2,1,0,0,0)\), the text asserts nonzero determinant of the order-four jet derivative at \((1,1,0,0,0)\). It then defines a fiber there by \((h,h_t,h_{tt},h_{ttt})=(1/4,0,-\sqrt2,0)\), claims a local parameterization \((1+a_1(t),1+a_2(t),0,b(t),a_3(t))\) with \(a_i(0)=0\), \(b'(0)\asymp1\), and concludes that the center projection has rank one on that fiber.

Proposition 4.4 fixes integers \(k,N\ge1\), \(0\le\alpha\le1\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), and asserts existence of \(\eta>0\) valid for all \(\delta,\tau>0\). Let \(F\) be polynomials of degree at most \(\delta^{-\eta}\), each of \(C^k\)-norm at most 1, with \(\#F\le\delta^{-N}\). For each \(f\), let \(Y(f)\subset f^\delta\) be a \(\delta\)-thick shading contained in \(f^\delta\cap(E\times\mathbb R)\), where \(E\subseteq[0,1]\) is a \((\tau,\alpha;\delta^{-\eta})\)-set. Assume that for every \(x\in[0,1]^2\), \(\rho\in[\delta,1]\), \(T\in[1,1/\rho]\), and \((\rho;k;T)\) rectangle \(R\ni x\), \[\#\{f:x\in Y(f),\ f\sim R\}\le\delta^{-\eta}T^{-\varepsilon}\#\{f:x\in Y(f)\}.\] Then (4.29) claims the unrestricted norm bound \[\left\|\sum_{f\in F}\chi_{Y(f)}\right\|_{L^{(k+1)/k}(\mathbb R^2)}\lesssim_\varepsilon\delta^{-\varepsilon}\delta^{(k+\alpha)/(k+1)}\tau^{k(1-\alpha)/(k+1)}\#F.\] The shadings are not required to lie in the tested square.

Proposition 3.1 states that, for \(M\ge1\), a semialgebraic \(W\subseteq[-1,1]^{n+1}\) of complexity at most \(M\), \(0<u\le1\), and \(L\ge1\), one can cover \(W\) by \(W_0,\ldots,W_N\), with \(N=\operatorname{Poly}(M)\). The exceptional set is \(W_0=T_0\times[-1,1]\), with \(|T_0|\le\operatorname{Poly}(M)(L^{-1/n}+|W|/u)\). Each remaining set is \[W_i=\{(x,z):x\in T_i,\ f_i(x)<z<f_i(x)+u\},\] where \(T_i\) has complexity \(\operatorname{Poly}(M)\) and \(f_i:[-1,1]^n\to[-1,1]\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz. The bands are strictly open at both vertical boundaries.

Definition 3.3 permits \(L\ge0\) and calls a continuous semialgebraic function an \(L\)-function if every existing local partial derivative has absolute value at most \(L\). For a regular \(L\)-cell \(T\subset\mathbb R^n\) and a continuously differentiable \(L\)-function \(f:T\to\mathbb R\), Proposition 3.6 asserts \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le n!L^n|x-y|\) for all \(x,y\in T\), without a lower bound such as \(L\ge1\).

Definition 2.4 calls a tangency rectangle \(R\) \(\mu\)-rich and \(\varepsilon\)-robustly broad with error \(B\) if it has an associated subset \(F(R)\) of tangent curves with \(\#F(R)\ge\mu\) and \(\#\{f\in F(R):f\sim R'\}\le BT^{-\varepsilon}\#F(R)\) for every admissible larger \((\rho;k;T)\) rectangle \(R'\supset R\), \(\delta\le\rho\le1\), \(1\le T\le1/\rho\). Remark 2.5 asserts \(\mu\ge B^{-1}(2\delta)^{-\varepsilon}\), and Remark 2.8 concludes emptiness below the corresponding threshold with \(B=\delta^{-\eta}\), despite defining \(\mu\) only as a lower bound.

In the random-sampling step, after \(\mu\le\#F(R)<2\mu\) and \(\mu>\delta^{-2\varepsilon_1}\), each curve is kept independently with probability \(p=(\delta^{2\varepsilon_1}\mu)^{-1}\). The second claimed high-probability property gives \(\varepsilon_1\)-robust broadness with error \(O(\delta^{\eta})\). The displayed lower and upper Chernoff estimates for \(\#(F(R)\cap F')\) use respectively \(e^{-p\#F/8}\) and \(e^{-p\#F/3}\), with the global cardinality \(\#F\).

For a \((\rho;k)\) rectangle \(S=S^g(I)\), \(I=[a,a+\rho^{1/k}]\), \(\|g\|_{C^k}\le1\), and \(c=((k+1)K)^{-1}\), Definition 2.18 uses the jet-coordinate transformation \[\psi_S(x,y_0,\ldots,y_{k-1})=\bigl(\rho^{-1/k}(x-a),c\rho^{-1}(y_0-g(x)),\ldots,c\rho^{-1/k}(y_{k-1}-g^{(k-1)}(x))\bigr)\] and asserts the exact identity \(\psi_S(\widehat S)=[0,1]\times[-Kc,Kc]^k\). The subsequent algebraic rescaling places the relevant prisms in a \(\widetilde\delta^{1/k}\)-neighborhood of the transformed variety. The proof of Lemma 2.21 uses \(B(cT/2)^{\varepsilon}\#F(R)\) in the estimate intended to give \(O(B)T^{-\varepsilon}\#F(R)\).

Lemma 2.22 assumes \(0<\delta<\rho\le1\), \(\rho\ge2^k\delta\), rectangles \(S=S^g(I)\), \(R=R^h(I')\), \(I'\subset I\), and a function \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) with \(\sup_I|f-g|\le\rho/2\) and \(f\sim R\). With no stated \(C^k\) bound on \(f\), it concludes \(\widehat R\subset\widehat S\).

Theorem B.2 states that a polynomial of degree at most \(D\), with leading coefficient \(a\), satisfies \(|\{x\in\mathbb R:|P(x)|\le\lambda\}|\le4(\lambda/(2|a|))^{1/D}\) for every \(\lambda>0\). In the proof of Lemma B.3, with \(K=2\cdot8^{k^2}k\), equation (B.4) claims \[K8^{-jk}\delta\left(\frac1{8^j j!}-\frac1{8^k(j+1)!}\right)\ge\frac{K}{8^{k^2}k}\delta>\delta.\] Lemma B.4 is stated for \(k\ge1\), while its interval length is \((T\delta)^{1/(k-1)}\).

Let \(S^{\pm}=S\sqcup S^{-1}\) be a finite alphabet and \(\Sigma\) a finite deterministic directed automaton with start vertex \(s\); all words labelling directed paths from \(s\) are accepted. Definition 3.2 calls \(\Sigma\) \(\lambda\)-large, \(0\le\lambda\le1\), if some \(K>0\) has the property that every path from \(s\) of length at least \(K\) ends at a vertex with at least \(\lambda|S^{\pm}|\) outgoing edges. It does not require such long paths to exist.

A language has \(A\)-density \(d'\) if it contains at least \(c|S^{\pm}|^{d'L}\) words of each length \(L\in A\), for some \(c>0\). Section 5.1 claims that \(\lambda>|S^{\pm}|^{-d}\) implies that \(\mathcal L_\Sigma\) has density \(d'>1-d\) for every infinite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\). Consequently Lemma 5.3 claims \(\Pr(R_{d,L}\cap\mathcal L_\Sigma\ne\varnothing)\to1\) as \(L\to\infty\), where \(R_{d,L}\) consists of \(|S^{\pm}|^{dL}\) uniform random length-\(L\) words.

Let the free group \(F_S\) act on a CAT(0) cube complex \(X\), with base vertex \(x\). A visible hyperplane is one closest to \(x\) separating \(x\) from \(sx\) for a letter \(s\in S^\pm\); write \(\mathcal H\) for this set. For \(H\in\mathcal H\), \(B(H)\) is the set of letters whose translates of \(x\) lie on the opposite side of \(H\).

Lemma 4.8 fixes the action and basepoint and asserts positive functions \(\varepsilon(n)\), decreasing in \(n\), and \(\alpha(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,n)\), defined when \(0<\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon(n)\) and \(\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon_1<1\). If no more than \(n\) members of \(\mathcal H\) pairwise cross and \(\varepsilon_0|S^\pm|\le|B(H)|\le\varepsilon_1|S^\pm|\), it concludes that there is a progressing checkpoint tree at \(H\) with \(\alpha\)-large growth. Its proof proposes \(\alpha=\varepsilon_0(1-\varepsilon_1)D_n(n-1)\).

The quantitative use in Theorem 4.16 requires a growth constant depending only on ambient dimension and the specified epsilon parameter, and imports this formula with the visible-clique index. The scope at issue is that uniform dependence; the opening words of Lemma 4.8 also permit a weaker reading with functions depending on the previously fixed action, basepoint, or alphabet.

The paper permits the empty word, declares it a prefix and suffix of every word, and includes trivial directed paths in an automaton’s accepted language \(\mathcal L_\Sigma\). For an action of \(F_S\) on a CAT(0) cube complex with base vertex \(x\), Definition 3.4(1) requires \(wx\ne x\) for a path from the start which meets no checkpoint, or meets checkpoints only at its endpoint. Lemma 3.5 then asserts \(wx\ne x\) for every \(w\in\mathcal L_\Sigma\).

Definition 3.6 similarly requires \(w'x\ne x\) for every \(w'\in\operatorname{Prefix}(w)\) in a progressing pair \((w,s)\). Lemma 3.13 asserts that, if the action has no global fixed point and \(|\operatorname{Fix}_S(x)|\ge\lambda|S^{\pm}|\), there is a two-vertex \(\lambda\)-large automaton with \(wx\ne x\) for every accepted word. None of these quantified statements excludes the empty word.

In the reduced-word proof of Theorem 1.3, use length-\(m\) reduced words over \(S^{\pm}\) as a block alphabet \(\widehat S_m^{\pm}\). Given a \(\lambda\)-large automaton \(\Sigma\) over these blocks, replace a nonstart vertex \(v\) by states \((v,a)\), \(a\in S^{\pm}\), routing incoming blocks ending in \(a\) to that state and retaining only outgoing blocks not beginning with \(a^{-1}\). The text claims that the resulting \(\Sigma'\) accepts only words reduced in the original letters and has growth \(\lambda-|S^{\pm}|^{-1}\).

For \(\lambda-|S^{\pm}|^{-1}>0\), the proof then transfers the remaining density argument of Theorem 1.2, choosing \(m\) so \(\lambda-|S^{\pm}|^{-1}>|S^{\pm}|^{-md}\). That argument fixes a remainder word \(w\) of length \(r\), \(0\le r<m\), and uses density \(d'>1-d\) of both \(\mathcal L_{\Sigma'}^v w^{-1}\) and \(w\mathcal L_{\Sigma'}^v\) in lengths congruent to \(r\pmod m\), to choose relators \(R_1w^{-1}\), \(wR_2\) whose concatenation gives an accepted block word.

Let the free group \(F_S\) act on a CAT(0) cube complex \(X\), with base vertex \(x\). A visible hyperplane is one closest to \(x\) separating \(x\) from \(sx\) for a letter \(s\in S^\pm\); write \(\mathcal H\) for this set. For \(H\in\mathcal H\), \(B(H)\) is the set of letters whose translates of \(x\) lie on the opposite side of \(H\).

Let \(w\) be a word with \(x,wx\in N(H)\) on the same side of \(H\). The forward set \(A_w(H)\) consists of \(s\) with \(wsx\) on that side but outside \(N(H)\); \(P_w(H)\) consists of \(s\) with \(wsx\in N(H)\) on that side. Within \(P_w\), the visibly parallel set has \((ws)^{-1}H\in\mathcal H\), and the disjoint parallel set consists of non-visibly-parallel letters with \(wsH\) disjoint from \(H\). Lemma 4.3 asserts progression for \((ws,H)\) when \(s\in A_w(H)\), for \((ws,H)\) when \(s\in P^{|}(H)\) as printed in item (2), and for \((wst,H)\) when \(s\in P_w^{\parallel}(H)\), \(t\in B(H)\). Its stated hypothesis concerns the endpoint \(wx\), without imposing safety of every prefix orbit point.

Corollary 4.5 considers a finite deterministically labeled rooted tree with root label \(H\), each nonleaf having at least \(\lambda|S^\pm|\) children. For every leaf word \(w\), assume either \(|A_w(H)|\ge\lambda|S^\pm|\), or \(|P_w^{|}(H)|\ge\lambda|S^\pm|\), or both \(|P_w^{\parallel}(H)|\ge\lambda|S^\pm|\) and \(|B(H)|\ge\lambda|S^\pm|\). The conclusion is that the tree extends to a checkpoint tree with \(\lambda\)-large growth. No prefix-safety hypothesis is added to the existing tree.

The paper defines a leaf of a tree to be a vertex incident to exactly one undirected edge. For a checkpoint tree \(T_H\) rooted at a visible hyperplane \(H\), Definition 3.8 requires \(\lambda\)-large growth only at nonleaf vertices; trees rooted at the start label \(s\) are declared \(\lambda\)-large for all \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The realized automaton identifies roots and leaves with the same hyperplane label. Lemma 3.11 asserts that a family \(\{T_H\}_{H\in\mathcal H\cup\{s\}}\) of \(\lambda\)-large checkpoint trees realizes a progressing automaton with \(\lambda\)-large growth. A root of undirected degree one is a leaf under the stated convention.

For \(\varepsilon_0>0\), define \(D_i(j)\) for \(i\ge1\), \(0\le j<i\), by \(D_1(0)=1-3\varepsilon_0\) and \[D_i(j)=(1-\varepsilon_0)D_{i-1}(j)-\sum_{0\le k<j}(1-D_i(k))\quad(j<i-1),\] \[D_i(i-1)=1-3\varepsilon_0-\sum_{0\le k<i-1}(1-D_i(k)).\] Remark 4.9 asserts \(D_i(j)\le D_{i'}(j')\) whenever \(i'+j'<i+j\). Lemma 4.10 asserts convergence to one as \(\varepsilon_0\to0\) for \(0\le j\le i\), including the endpoint outside the defined domain.

In Theorem 4.16, with \(0<\varepsilon_1<1\), the proof puts \(z=\min\{1/5,\varepsilon(n)\}\) and defines \[\varepsilon_0=\sup\left\{x\in(0,z]:\frac{\varepsilon_1}{(2(1-2\varepsilon_0)-1)^n}\le1\right\},\qquad\lambda=1-2\varepsilon_0.\] Thus the set condition uses \(\varepsilon_0\), not its dummy variable \(x\). It then sets \[\gamma(1)=1-\frac{\varepsilon_1}{(2\lambda-1)^{n-1}},\quad\gamma(i)=\min\left\{\varepsilon_0,\alpha\!\left(\varepsilon_0,\frac{\varepsilon_1}{(2\lambda-1)^{n-i}},i\right),(2\lambda-1)\gamma(i-1)\right\}.\] These expressions are asserted positive, using \(\alpha\) whose declared domain requires its second argument to lie in \([\varepsilon_0,1)\).

Definition 5.4 asserts that formal inversion is a fixed-point-free involution on the set of all plain words of every positive length \(m\). Here inversion reverses the word and replaces each letter by its formal inverse; the definition has no odd-length restriction.

In the proof of Lemma 1.7, for the action associated to the stated group extension and an \(n\)-dimensional CAT(0) cube complex \(X\), the median realization \(X_Y\) of the indicated fixed-vertex set is asserted to have dimension exactly \(n\). The preceding paragraph only states the upper bound \(\dim X_Y\le n\).

Fix integers \(\underline r<\overline r-1\) and an open set \(O\subseteq\mathbb R^2\). For \((\eta,\zeta)\in O\), let \(K_r\), \(\underline r\le r\le\overline r\), be trace-class matrix kernels on \(\bigoplus_{j=1}^n\ell^2(\mathbb Z_{>0})\), with \(I-K_r\) invertible, and suppose the following derivatives exist in trace norm: \[\begin{aligned}K_{r+1}(u,v)&=K_r(u+1,v+1),&&\underline r\le r<\overline r,\\ \partial_\eta K_r(u,v)&=K_{r-1}(u+1,v)-K_r(u+1,v),&&\underline r<r\le\overline r,\\ \partial_\zeta K_r(u,v)&=K_{r-1}(u,v+1)-K_r(u,v+1),&&\underline r<r\le\overline r.\end{aligned}\] These identities are required for all positive integers \(u,v\). Theorem 3.1 defines the invertible \(n\times n\) matrix \(Q_r=(I-K_r)^{-1}(1,1)\) and claims for every interior index \(\underline r<r<\overline r\) that \[\partial_\zeta(\partial_\eta Q_r\,Q_r^{-1})+Q_rQ_{r-1}^{-1}-Q_{r+1}Q_r^{-1}=0.\] No derivative relation for \(K_{\underline r}\) is included.

Let \(h_0\in\mathrm{UC}\) be deterministic initial data for PNG, choose \(x_1<\cdots<x_n\), and define \(r_0(t,x)=\sup_{|y-x|\le t}h_0(y)\). For integer thresholds \(r_i>r_0(t,x_i)\), let \(K_{\mathbf r}\) be the shifted extended kernel of (2.10)–(2.11) and \(Q_{\mathbf r}=(I-K_{\mathbf r})^{-1}(1,1)\). The paper introduces \(\zeta=(t-x)/2\), \(\eta=(t+x)/2\), with \(x=x_1+\cdots+x_n\) and \(\partial_x=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}\). Theorem 2.1 asserts \[\partial_\zeta(\partial_\eta Q_{\mathbf r}Q_{\mathbf r}^{-1})+Q_{\mathbf r}Q_{\mathbf r-\mathbf1}^{-1}-Q_{\mathbf r+\mathbf1}Q_{\mathbf r}^{-1}=0,\qquad \det Q_{\mathbf r}=\frac{F(t;\mathbf x;\mathbf r+\mathbf1)}{F(t;\mathbf x;\mathbf r)}.\]

In the one-point case it also writes \(\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta=\tfrac14(\partial_t^2-\partial_x^2)\) for those half-scaled coordinates and gives \[\frac14(\partial_t^2-\partial_x^2)\log F_r=\frac{F_{r+1}F_{r-1}}{F_r^2}-1,\qquad t>0,\ r>r_0(t,x).\] The relation between these displayed coordinate and derivative conventions is the claim under review.

For the upper-semicontinuous hypograph state-space topology of Sections 4.1-4.2, consider step configurations with locally finite distinct unit jumps, without a uniform bound on their number along convergent sequences. Lemma 2.4 asserts that, for every vector of an arbitrary embedded \(2\)-cube tiling lattice, its first nonzero coordinate is even, without first specifying a Hajós coordinate order. Lemma 2.6 prescribes a simultaneous transposition of the row and column containing a pure vector \(2e_i\) with the last row and column, claiming that this produces the required last-column Hajós presentation.

The article defines a graph to be 2-connected when it is connected and has neither a cut-vertex nor a loop; its blocks are the maximal induced 2-connected subgraphs. A block is trivial if it is a single vertex or a single edge. Propositions 3.2(a) and 3.3(a) assert that the indecomposable summands of \(\operatorname{Flow}(G)\) and \(\operatorname{Cut}(G)\), respectively, are exactly the lattices of the nontrivial blocks. These graph statements do not separately exclude loops or cut-edges from \(G\).

Proposition 3.8 states that if a positive definite integral lattice \(\Lambda\) has a \(d\)-invariant isomorphic to that of \(\operatorname{Flow}(G)\) for a 2-edge-connected graph \(G\), then \(\Lambda\cong\operatorname{Flow}(G)\oplus\mathbb Z^k\) for some \(k\ge0\). It adds no loopless hypothesis.

Let \(\mathcal G\) be the recursively defined planar-graph class containing the isolated vertex and the single non-loop edge, and closed under the specified composition that replaces one distinguished edge in each of two planar graphs by a joining 4-cycle. Theorem 4.4 states, for every finite planar graph \(G\), that \(\operatorname{Flow}(G)\) is a 2-cube tiling lattice if and only if every block belongs to \(\mathcal G\); it further states that \(G\) is 2-connected with such a flow lattice if and only if \(G\in\mathcal G\).

The definition of an oriented cut identifies two descriptions: an oriented subgraph \(H\) whose class \([H]\) lies in \(\operatorname{Cut}(G)\), and the full bipartition cut \(E(A,V\setminus A)\) directed out of one subset \(A\). Proposition 3.3(b) and Lemma 3.4 identify simple cut-lattice vectors with such oriented cuts. Here a vector \(x\) is simple if every integral decomposition \(x=y+w\) satisfies \(y\cdot w\le0\).

For the alternating-link diagrams \(D,D'\) in the introduction, with \(\Lambda(D)=\operatorname{Flow}(G(D))\) for the black Tait graph, the stated relation is \(\Lambda(D')\simeq\Lambda(D)\oplus\mathbb Z^n\), together with the equivalence \(n=0\) if and only if \(D'\) is reduced. Bridge-type as well as loop-type nugatory crossings are permitted in the discussion.

Let \(Z\subset H_\alpha\) be a bi-algebraic subvariety contained in an isoperiodic leaf. Proposition 6.3 claims that \(Z\) is affine in period coordinates. After labelling the \(n\ge2\) zeros, the proof takes a constant abelian factor \(A\) of dimension \(r\ge1\), with the tautological form pulled back from a fixed nonzero form \(\omega\) on \(A\). Extend \(\omega\) to a basis of \(H^0(A,\Omega_A^1)\), identify \(\operatorname{Lie}A\) with \(\mathbb C^r\), and let \(\operatorname{pr}=(\operatorname{pr}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{pr}_1):\mathbb C^{r(n-1)}\to\mathbb C^{n-1}\). Let \(\sigma=(\sigma_2-\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n-\sigma_1):Z\to A^{n-1}\), with a lift \(\widetilde\sigma\), and put \(V=\overline{\operatorname{pr}(\widetilde\sigma(\widetilde Z))}^{\mathrm{Zar}}\), \(W=\operatorname{pr}^{-1}(V)\).

When \(V\ne\mathbb C^{n-1}\), the first Ax–Schanuel step places \(\sigma(Z)\) in a translate of a proper abelian subvariety \(B\subset A^{n-1}\). The proof then asserts that the entire \(W\), not only the lifted image, is contained in a translate of the proper linear space \(L=\operatorname{Lie}B\), and uses that containment to iterate the dimension reduction.

In Step 2 of the linearity argument, \(\mathcal Y\) and \(\mathcal Y^p\) are irreducible two-dimensional affine cones, with \(\mathcal Y^p\) a linear standard \(\mathrm{SL}_2\)-representation. Let \(W\) be the linear span of \(\mathcal Y\); it maps surjectively to \(\mathcal Y^p\). The proof shows that the connected kernel of relative-to-pure monodromy acts trivially on \(W\), and then infers that \(W\) is irreducible as an \(H'(\mathbb C)\)-module because \(\mathcal Y\) has a dense \(H'(\mathbb C)\)-orbit. It concludes that \(W\to\mathcal Y^p\) is an isomorphism.

Lemma 6.7(2) takes a half-spin representation of \(\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}_{2n}\), a highest-weight vector \(v\), and the parabolic \(P\) stabilizing \(\mathbb Cv\), but prints \(\dim\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}_{2n+1}-\dim P=\binom n2\).

For a smooth projective genus-two curve \(C\), Proposition 6.9 takes the Zariski-open set \(U\subset H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\) of forms with two distinct simple zeros and the multivalued relative period \(T(\omega)=\int_{\gamma_\omega}\omega\). It claims that the lifted graph in \(U\times\mathbb C\) is not contained in a Zariski-closed set of dimension 2. In proving that its relative-cohomology monodromy has infinite image, it invokes quasi-finiteness of the period map for this unprojectivized \(U\), which still retains scalar multiples of a form.

In particular, the induced conjugation \(i(\alpha_x(n))=s(x)^{-1}i(n)s(x)\) is asserted to satisfy Definition 5.9(b): there is an open identity neighborhood \(U\subset G\) on which \((x,n)\mapsto\alpha_x(n)\) is jointly smooth on \(U\times N\).

Consider a smooth extension \(1\to N\xrightarrow{i}E\xrightarrow{p}G\to1\) of right half-Lie groups, with \(N\) a Lie group, admitting both local smooth sections and local smooth retractions as in Definition 5.1. Definition 3.1 defines \(G^\circ_{g,d}\) by the corresponding equivariant descendant integrals, with prefactor \((-1)^{g-1+d}2^{3g-3+n+m+2d}\), and constructs \(G_d^\bullet\) by allowing disconnected domains.

Theorem 3.2 states its localization formula for every \(d\ge0\). At \(d=0\), its empty-partition term asserts \[G_0^\bullet(z,w;u)=\frac{H^\bullet(tz;u/t)\,H^\bullet(-tw;-u/t)}{t^n(-t)^m},\] where \(H^\bullet\) is the disconnected series formed from \[H_g^\circ(z)=2^{2g-2+n}\int_{\overline M_{g,n}}\Lambda(2)\Lambda(-1)\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{z_i}{1-z_i\psi_i}\] and the stated unstable conventions. This range includes stable constant maps, not just the separately prescribed unstable terms.

For the general line bundle \(\mathcal O(-k)\), \(k>0\), with equivariant endpoint weights \([\alpha,\alpha+k]\), equation (3.14) assigns an edge of degree \(d_e\) the top-Chern factor \[\prod_{\ell=1}^{kd_e-1}\frac{(\ell+kd_e)(-\alpha t)+\ell(\alpha-k)t}{d_e}.\] The subsequent spin specialization sets \(k=1\), \(\alpha=-1/2\).

Use the neutral-fermion operators \(A=\alpha^B_1\), \(B=\alpha^B_{-1}\), with \([A,B]=1/2\), and write \(s(z)=2\sinh(z/2)\), \(q_0(z)=\tfrac12\cosh(z/2)\), and \(\mathcal E_0(z)=\widehat{\mathcal E}_0(z)+\tfrac14\coth(z/2)\operatorname{Id}\).

With \(z'=(z-1)/2\) and \(k'=(k-1)/2\), Definition 4.1 sets \[\mathcal B(z,uz)=e^{uz^3/12}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\sum_{j\ge k'+1}\frac{\Gamma(z'+1)\Gamma(z+2j)}{\Gamma(z+k+1)\Gamma(z'+j+1)}(uz)^j[w^{2j-1}]S(w)^z s(w)^k\mathcal E_k(w).\] For every positive odd integer \(\mu\), Proposition 4.2 asserts \[\mathcal B(\mu,u\mu)=\frac{\mu'!}{(u\mu)^{\mu'}}e^Ae^{uF_3^B/3}\alpha^B_{-\mu}e^{-uF_3^B/3}e^{-A}.\] The lower summation cutoff is part of the stated definition.

Conjecture B states that for every spin curve \((B,\vartheta)\), genera and degree \(g,d\), and descendants \(k_1,\ldots,k_n\) satisfying \(\sum_i k_i=g-1+d(1-g(B))+n\), \[\langle\tau_{k_1}\cdots\tau_{k_n}\rangle^{B,\vartheta}_{g,d}=H_d\!\left(B,\vartheta;\frac{(-1)^{k_1}k_1!}{(2k_1)!}\overline c_{2k_1+1},\ldots,\frac{(-1)^{k_n}k_n!}{(2k_n)!}\overline c_{2k_n+1}\right).\] The left side uses stationary point-class insertions. Under the stated notation, brackets and Hurwitz numbers without a bullet refer to connected domains.

Equation (1.7) defines \(\tau(x,x^\star;u,q)\) by summing \((-8u)^{g-1}(-4q)^d\langle\exp(2\sum_k[x_k\tau_k(0)+x_k^\star\tau_k(\infty)])\rangle_{g,d}\), again with unbulleted brackets. Theorem A identifies this function with the single vacuum expectation \[\left\langle e^{\sum_i x_iB_i}e^{\alpha_1^B}(q/u)^{H^B}e^{\alpha_{-1}^B}e^{\sum_jx_j^\star B_j^\star}\right\rangle.\]

For every integer \(m\), Definition 2.5 defines \[\mathcal E_m^B(z)=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^k e^{(k+m/2)z}\widehat E^B_{k-m,k}+\delta_{m,0}\frac{q_0(z)}{s(z)},\] with \(s(z)=2\sinh(z/2)\), \(q_0(z)=\tfrac12\cosh(z/2)\). Proposition 2.8 asserts \(\mathcal E_m^B(-z)=(-1)^{m+1}\mathcal E_m^B(z)\), with the same parity for the version omitting the scalar term.

For positive even \(r\), odd partition \(\mu\), and \(b=(2g-2+|\mu|+\ell(\mu))/r\), equation (2.30) rewrites the disconnected completed-cycle Hurwitz number as \[h_{g;\mu}^{\bullet,+,r}=2^{1-g}[u^b]\left\langle\prod_{i=1}^{\ell(\mu)}e^{\alpha_1^B}e^{uF_{r+1}^B/(r+1)}\frac{\alpha_{-\mu_i}^B}{\mu_i}e^{uF_{r+1}^B/(r+1)}e^{-\alpha_1^B}\right\rangle.\] Both occurrences of the \(uF_{r+1}^B/(r+1)\) exponent are positive in this printed identity.

Let \(\widehat{\mathfrak h}\) be the central extension of the algebra generated by \(S^{\pm1},H^{\pm1}\) with \([H,S]=S\), and use the coefficient operators \(E_{m,k}=[z^k]\mathcal E_m(z)\). Let \(\widehat{\mathfrak h}^B\) be the Lie subalgebra of the neutral-fermion algebra spanned by \(E^B_{m,k}=[z^k]\mathcal E_m^B(z)\). Proposition 4.8 asserts that \(E^B_{m,k}=0\) when \(m+k\) is even, and that \[p:\widehat{\mathfrak h}\to\widehat{\mathfrak h}^B,\qquad E_{m,k}\mapsto E^B_{m,k},\] is a surjective Lie algebra morphism on the full algebra. It also asserts a right-inverse Lie algebra morphism \(\iota(E^B_{m,k})=E_{m,k}\) for odd \(m+k\).

Use the neutral-fermion operators \(A=\alpha^B_1\), \(B=\alpha^B_{-1}\), with \([A,B]=1/2\), and write \(s(z)=2\sinh(z/2)\), \(q_0(z)=\tfrac12\cosh(z/2)\), and \(\mathcal E_0(z)=\widehat{\mathcal E}_0(z)+\tfrac14\coth(z/2)\operatorname{Id}\).

For every \(d\ge1\), Corollary 5.5 uses \[\langle\tau_k\rangle^{\bullet,\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-1)}_{\varnothing,g,d}=\frac{2^dk!}{(d!)^2}(-2)^{-k}[z^{2k+1}]U_d(z)\] for disconnected stationary invariants without degree-zero components. It sets \((U_1,V_1)=(sq_0,q_0)\) and, equivalently to the ordered products in (5.14), gives the recurrence \[\binom{U_d}{V_d}=\begin{pmatrix}s^2+d&(d-1)s\\s&d-1\end{pmatrix}\binom{U_{d-1}}{V_{d-1}}+(d-1)q_0\binom{s}{1}\qquad(d\ge2).\] The proof identifies these functions with \(U_d=\langle A^d\widehat{\mathcal E}_0(z)B^d\rangle\) and \(V_d=\langle A^d\mathcal E_1(z)B^{d-1}\rangle\).

For every \(\xi\in\mathbb C\), Section 5.2 defines on the space \(\Gamma\) of supersymmetric functions \[q_\xi(\phi,\psi)=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathrm{SP}}\xi^{|\lambda|}2^{-p(\lambda)}\dim(V^\lambda)\,\phi(\lambda)\psi(\lambda),\] summing over all strict partitions. It asserts that this sum is finite when \(\phi,\psi\) have bounded degree, hence convergent for every \(\xi\), and that it is positive definite for \(\xi>0\).

Assuming Conjecture D and using the stated identification of \(\Gamma\) with \(\mathbb C\{\mathrm{OP}\}\), equation (5.12) further asserts \(q_\xi(\widetilde c_\mu,\widetilde c_
u)=q_\xi(c_\mu,c_
u)\) for all odd partitions \(\mu,
u\). Together with the unitriangular transition between the two completed-cycle bases, the proof uses this to conclude that the bases coincide. The formula uses the partition values \(\phi(\lambda)\), without specifying a different finite-support coordinate interpretation.

Work over the manuscript's field \(\mathbb K\) of characteristic zero. Let \(L=L_1\cup L_2\subset S^3\) be a framed oriented link, and let \(B^4(L_2)\) be obtained by attaching 2-handles along \(L_2\). Color each component of \(L_1\) by \(c\) and each component of \(L_2\) by the total Kirby color \(\omega=\omega_0\oplus\omega_1\). Theorem C asserts an isomorphism of bigraded vector spaces between \(\operatorname{Kh}(L_1\cup L_2^\omega)\), the corresponding cabled \(N=2\) Khovanov–Rozansky homology, and the \(N=2\) skein lasagna module of \((B^4(L_2),L_1)\), without restricting the latter to a specified integral relative homology class.

For \(L_2=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\), Theorem 6.8 instead fixes \(i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in\{0,1\}^r\), colors \(K_j\) by \(\omega_{i_j}\), and asserts \[\operatorname{Kh}(L_1\cup L_2^{\omega_i})\cong\mathcal S_0^2(B^4(L_2);L_1,i,\mathbb K),\] interpreting \(i\) as a class in \(H_2(B^4(L_2),L_1;\mathbb Z)\).

Definition 2.18 calls a small category \(I\) filtered if every pair of objects admits maps to a common object and every pair of parallel arrows \(f,g:i\to j\) is equalized by some arrow \(h:j\to k\). It lists these two conditions without separately requiring \(I\) to be nonempty.

For a functor \(F:I\to J\) between indexing categories, Lemma 2.20 asserts finality under only these conditions: every \(j\in J\) has a morphism \(j\to F(i)\) for some \(i\in I\); and for any parallel \(f_1,f_2:j\to F(i)\), there is \(g:i\to i'\) in \(I\) with \(F(g)f_1=F(g)f_2\). It does not assume that \(I\) is filtered. Finality means that \(\operatorname{colim}_{i\in I}\alpha(F(i))\to\operatorname{colim}_{j\in J}\alpha(j)\) is an isomorphism for every diagram for which both colimits exist.

For an arbitrary graded linear category \(\mathcal C\), Remark 2.24 identifies the full subcategory of compact objects of \(\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal C)\) with \(\mathcal C\) itself. No idempotent-completeness assumption on \(\mathcal C\) is included in this background assertion. Convention 4.1 later works in an idempotent-complete setting for the Kirby construction.

In the polynomial representation of the dotted Temperley–Lieb category over a characteristic-zero field \(\mathbb K\), let \(d_i\) range over cap diagrams whose dots are adjacent to the upper unbounded region. Form \(\delta_i^*\) by choosing the left-endpoint variable of each undotted cap and no variable from each dotted cap. Order the monomials first by total degree and then lexicographically with \(x_1>x_2>\cdots\). Equation (19) asserts \(d_i(\delta_j^*)=1\) for \(i=j\) and \(d_i(\delta_j^*)=0\) for \(i>j\), as the triangularity step proving faithfulness.

With \(U_n:P_n\to P_{n+2}\), \(D_{n+2}:P_{n+2}\to P_n\), and \(z_n\in\operatorname{End}(P_n)\), Lemma 3.20 prints \(U_{n-2}D_n=-z_n^2=D_nU_{n-2}\). The proof of Corollary 3.23 writes its two parity inverse systems as \(\varprojlim_n\mathbb K[z_n]/(z_n^n)\), identifies their limit with \(\mathbb K[z]\otimes\mathbb K[z]\), and claims an isomorphism to \(\mathbb K[s,z]/(s^2-1)\) via \(f\otimes g\mapsto(1+s)f/2+(1-s)g/2\). The limits are taken in graded vector spaces.

Over a characteristic-zero field \(\mathbb K\), let \(\omega=\omega_0\oplus\omega_1\) be the total Kirby object. Section 5.4 states \[\omega\otimes\omega\cong\bigoplus_{n\ge0}q^{-2n}\omega.\] Separately, the proof of Proposition 5.27 defines \(Y_n=q^{-i-j-2n}\omega'_{i+j}\), while the proposition’s displayed decomposition uses \(q^{-2n}\omega'_{i+j}\); the projections are required to have degree zero under Definition 2.6. The admissible sums are the locally finite families of Definition 5.21, not unrestricted formal sums.

Let \(L=L_1\cup K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\) be a framed oriented link, and fix \(i\in\{0,1\}^r\). In the proof of the bigraded isomorphism of Theorem 6.8, equation (41) prints \[\operatorname{Kh}(L_1\cup L_2^{\omega_i})\cong\operatorname{colim}_{n\in\mathbb N^r}\operatorname{Kh}\!\left(L_1\cup K_1^{(i_1+2n_1)}\cup\cdots\cup K_r^{(i_r+n_r)}\right),\] with dotted-annulus transition maps, no displayed quantum grading shifts, and the last cable multiplicity \(i_r+n_r\). It identifies this colimit with the quotient of the direct sum in (42), whose terms carry the shifts \(q^{-|i|-2|n|}\) and the respective cable multiplicities \(i_j+2n_j\).

Over a characteristic-zero field \(\mathbb K\), Section 7.7 considers the two-term complexes \[C_l=\left(q^{-l+2}P_{l-2}\xrightarrow{U_l}q^{-l}P_l\right),\qquad l\ge0,\] with the right-hand term in homological degree zero and \(P_l=0\) for \(l<0\). The displayed arrow is labeled \(U_l\), under the earlier convention \(U_m:P_m\to P_{m+2}\). The assertion is that every morphism \(C_l\to C_{l'}\) is null-homotopic whenever \(l\le l'\), including equality.

Assume \(m>0\), \(p>1\), and \(m(p-1)>1\), and put \(\alpha=(p-1)^{-1}\). Let \(u\) be a bounded nonnegative solution of the constant-convection equation \[u_t=\partial_r\bigl(|(u^m)_r|^{p-2}(u^m)_r\bigr)+\gamma |(u^m)_r|^{p-2}(u^m)_r+h(u),\] with constant \(\gamma\ge0\). Lemma 3.1 assumes only \(h\in C^1(\mathbb R_+)\), \(h(0)=0\), and \[\kappa_h:=\inf\{\bar u\ge0:h(u)\le0\text{ for every }u\ge\bar u\}<\infty.\] Define \(v=mu^{m-\alpha}/(m-\alpha)\), \(M=\max\{\|u_0\|_\infty,\kappa_h\}\), and \(H=\sup_{[0,M]}|h'|\).

Lemma 3.1, especially (3.2) on article PDF pages 10–11, asserts that a constant \(C\) depending only on \(\gamma,m,p\) satisfies, for every \(r\ge0\) and \(t>0\), \[|v_r(r,t)|\le\begin{cases}CM^{(m-\alpha)/p}(t^{-1}+H)^{1/p},&p\ge2,\\CM^{(m-\alpha)/2}(t^{-1}+H)^{1/2},&1<p<2.\end{cases}\] In particular, this lemma's stated reaction class includes \(h\equiv0\); it does not impose compact support on every bounded solution of the auxiliary convection equation.

Assume \(m>0\), \(p\ge2\), and \(m(p-1)>1\). Let \(h\in C^1(\mathbb R_+)\) satisfy \(h(0)=0\), \(h'(1)<0\), and, for some \(a_0\in[0,1)\), \(h\le0\) on \([0,a_0]\), \(h>0\) on \((a_0,1)\), and \(h<0\) on \((1,\infty)\). When \(a_0>0\), assume also \(\int_0^1h(u)u^{m-1}\,du>0\), as required in Section 2.2. Put \(\alpha=(p-1)^{-1}\).

For \(0\le\gamma<\gamma_*\), where \(\gamma_*>0\) is the small-convection range of Lemma 4.5, let \(c(\gamma)>0\) and \(U(\xi;\gamma)\) be the speed and normalized decreasing finite wavefront of \[u_t=\partial_r\bigl(|(u^m)_r|^{p-2}(u^m)_r\bigr)+\gamma |(u^m)_r|^{p-2}(u^m)_r+h(u),\] with \(U(-\infty;\gamma)=1\) and \(U(\xi;\gamma)=0\) for \(\xi\ge0\). Write \(V=mU^{m-\alpha}/(m-\alpha)\), \(Q=m/(m-\alpha)\), and \(\mathcal P(q;\gamma)=V'(V^{-1}(q;\gamma);\gamma)\) for \(0<q<Q\).

Lemma 4.15 (article PDF pages 30–32) asserts \(c\in C^2([0,\gamma_*))\), existence of \(\partial_\gamma\mathcal P\), continuity of \(\gamma\mapsto\partial_\gamma\mathcal P(\cdot;\gamma)\) with values in \(C([0,Q])\), and the universal bound \(-m<c'(\gamma)<0\). With the positive integrating factor \(\Psi\) used in its proof, it prints \[c'(\gamma)=-(m-\alpha)\frac{\int_0^Q\Psi(q;\gamma)\,dq}{\int_0^Qq^{-1}\Psi(q;\gamma)\,dq}.\] Here \(\Psi'=-a\Psi\), where, writing \(W=-\mathcal P\) and \(s(q)=((m-\alpha)q/m)^{1/(m-\alpha)}\), \[a(q)=-\frac1{(m-\alpha)q}+\frac{\gamma(p-2)}{(p-1)W(q)}+\frac{h(s(q))}{(p-1)s(q)W(q)^p}.\]

Equation (4.14) further claims the two equal expressions \[\partial_\gamma|\mathcal P(q;\gamma)|^{p-1}=\frac1{\Psi(q;\gamma)}\int_0^q\Psi(r;\gamma)\frac{c'(\gamma)}{(m-\alpha)r}\,dr=-\frac1{\Psi(q;\gamma)}\int_q^Q\Psi(r;\gamma)\frac{c'(\gamma)}{(m-\alpha)r}\,dr.\] These are the numerator and source terms printed in the article, without the additional term proposed in the report's revision.

Assume \(N\ge1\), \(m>0\), \(p>1\), \(m(p-1)>1\), and set \(q_F=m(p-1)+p/N\). Let \(\widehat h\in C^1(\mathbb R_+)\) satisfy the monostable version of (1.2): \(\widehat h(0)=0\), \(\widehat h(u)>0\) for \(0<u<1\), and \(\widehat h(u)<0\) for \(u>1\), together with the standing nondegeneracy \(\widehat h'(1)<0\). Suppose \(\widehat h(u)=ku^{q_F}\) on \([0,b]\) for some \(k>0\) and \(b\in(0,1)\). For \(\delta\in(0,1)\), \(\sigma>p/(p-1)\), and \(\beta>0\), let \(\widehat u\) solve \[\widehat u_t=\Delta_p(\widehat u^m)+\widehat h(\widehat u),\qquad \widehat u(x,0)=\underline u(x):=\delta(1-|x|^\sigma)_+^\beta.\] Lemma 5.2 (article PDF page 34) asserts \(\widehat u(0,t)\to1\) as \(t\to\infty\) when \(\sigma\) and \(\beta\) are sufficiently large.

The specific proof step examined here asserts that the same fixed-support initial bump is a static subsolution: \[-\Delta_p(\underline u^m)-\widehat h(\underline u)\le0\quad\text{on }\mathbb R^N.\] After requiring \(\beta>p/[m(p-1)]\), the proof claims that choosing \(\beta\) large enough to make its displayed coefficients satisfy \(C_2\ge C_3\) establishes this inequality. It then uses comparison to deduce that \(\widehat u(x,t)\) is nondecreasing in time.

Assume \(m>0\), \(p\ge2\), and \(m(p-1)>1\). Let \(h\in C^1(\mathbb R_+)\) satisfy \(h(0)=0\), \(h'(1)<0\), and, for some \(a_0\in[0,1)\), \(h\le0\) on \([0,a_0]\), \(h>0\) on \((a_0,1)\), and \(h<0\) on \((1,\infty)\). When \(a_0>0\), assume also \(\int_0^1h(u)u^{m-1}\,du>0\), as required in Section 2.2. Put \(\alpha=(p-1)^{-1}\).

Let \(N\ge1\) and let \(u\) be a nonnegative spreading solution of \(u_t=\Delta_p(u^m)+h(u)\) on \(\mathbb R^N\), with bounded compactly supported initial data. Spreading means \(u(\cdot,t)\to1\) uniformly on every compact set. Write \(c_*=c(0)\) for the finite-wave speed and \(c_\sharp=-c'(0)/c_*>0\). Corollary 2.5(iii) (article PDF pages 8–9) asserts that, for every \(c>c_\sharp\), \[u(x,t)\longrightarrow1\quad\text{uniformly for }|x|\le c_*t-(N-1)c\log t.\] The stated dimension range includes \(N=1\), and the initial data in this corollary need not be radial.

Assume \(m>0\), \(p\ge2\), and \(m(p-1)>1\). Let \(h\in C^1(\mathbb R_+)\) satisfy \(h(0)=0\), \(h'(1)<0\), and, for some \(a_0\in[0,1)\), \(h\le0\) on \([0,a_0]\), \(h>0\) on \((a_0,1)\), and \(h<0\) on \((1,\infty)\). When \(a_0>0\), assume also \(\int_0^1h(u)u^{m-1}\,du>0\), as required in Section 2.2. Put \(\alpha=(p-1)^{-1}\).

For \(0\le\gamma<\gamma_*\), where \(\gamma_*>0\) is the small-convection range of Lemma 4.5, let \(c(\gamma)>0\) and \(U(\xi;\gamma)\) be the speed and normalized decreasing finite wavefront of \[u_t=\partial_r\bigl(|(u^m)_r|^{p-2}(u^m)_r\bigr)+\gamma |(u^m)_r|^{p-2}(u^m)_r+h(u),\] with \(U(-\infty;\gamma)=1\) and \(U(\xi;\gamma)=0\) for \(\xi\ge0\). Write \(V=mU^{m-\alpha}/(m-\alpha)\), \(Q=m/(m-\alpha)\), and \(\mathcal P(q;\gamma)=V'(V^{-1}(q;\gamma);\gamma)\) for \(0<q<Q\).

Define the positive coefficient \(C_{p,\gamma}\) by the maximal-wave trajectory asymptotic (4.11), \[\phi(U)=|(U^m)'|^{p-1}=C_{p,\gamma}(1-U)^{p-1}(1+o(1))\quad(U\uparrow1).\] Lemma 4.10(b) (article PDF page 28) asserts that, for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), there are \(M>0\) and \(\xi_*<0\) such that \[1>U(\xi;\gamma)\ge1-M\exp\bigl(-(C_{p,\gamma}^{\alpha}-\varepsilon)|\xi|\bigr)\qquad(\xi\le\xi_*).\] Lemma 4.14(b) (PDF page 30) asserts \[\mathcal P(q;\gamma)=-C_{p,\gamma}^{\alpha}(Q-q)(1+o(1))\qquad(q\uparrow Q).\] The coefficient in both claims is the one printed, without an additional factor \(1/m\).

Assume \(m>0\), \(p\ge2\), and \(m(p-1)>1\). Let \(h\in C^1(\mathbb R_+)\) satisfy \(h(0)=0\), \(h'(1)<0\), and, for some \(a_0\in[0,1)\), \(h\le0\) on \([0,a_0]\), \(h>0\) on \((a_0,1)\), and \(h<0\) on \((1,\infty)\). When \(a_0>0\), assume also \(\int_0^1h(u)u^{m-1}\,du>0\), as required in Section 2.2. Put \(\alpha=(p-1)^{-1}\).

Let \(u\) be a radial nonnegative spreading solution of \(u_t=\Delta_p(u^m)+h(u)\) in \(\mathbb R^N\), with bounded compactly supported initial data, and let \(\eta(t)\) be its support radius. Put \(c_*=c(0)\), \(c_\sharp=-c'(0)/c_*>0\), \(a=(N-1)c_\sharp\), and \(b=m(p-1)-1\). Let \(\gamma(c)\) be the inverse of the finite-wave speed function and let \(U(\xi;\gamma)\) be its normalized profile. The proof of Theorem 6.3 (article PDF page 39) chooses \[f(t)=1-\frac{\log(t-t_0)}{(t-t_0)^2},\quad g'=f^bc_*+(1-f^b)\frac at-\frac{\lambda\log(t-t_0)}{(t-t_0)^2}+\frac\lambda{(t-t_0)^2},\] and defines \[w(r,t)=f(t)U\bigl(r-g(t)+C;\gamma(c_*-a/t)\bigr).\] For suitable constants it claims \(Lw\le0\), with \(Lw=w_t-\Delta_p(w^m)-h(w)\), in the comparison region \(r\ge c_*t-M\log t\). Its displayed residual assigns the coefficient \(f^b(c_*-a/t)-g'+a/t\) to \(fU'\), although the printed phase has no logarithmic term.

The same section prints \(c_*-M\log t\le\eta(t)\) in Lemma 6.2 and \(c_*-a\log t-C\le\eta(t)\le c_*-a\log t+C\) in Theorem 6.3 for all sufficiently large \(t\). These displayed leading terms are \(c_*\), as printed on PDF pages 38–39. The comparison estimates also assert \(U^{(m-1)(p-1)}|U'|^{p-2}\to0\) as \(U\to1\) and \(U\to0\) for the stated range \(p\ge2\).

Two auxiliary assertions recorded with this finding are the following. For the maximal phase-plane trajectories at fixed convection, Lemma 4.6 (PDF page 25) states that if \(0\le c<d\) and \(T_c\) is nonempty, then \(\phi_d(U)<\phi_c(U)\) on \((0,U^{(c)}]\), and that the trajectories depend continuously on the speed. Lemma 4.12 (PDF page 29) takes \(0\le\gamma<\gamma_*\), \(0<c<c(\gamma)\), and \(\eta\in(\beta_c,1)\), where \(\beta_c\) is the height of the extremal trajectory from \((0,0)\), or zero if none exists. It asserts a decreasing profile \(U^{c,\eta}\) on \([0,b_0]\), for some \(b_0,\nu>0\), satisfying the traveling-wave equation and the printed data \[U^{c,\eta}(0)=\eta,\quad ((U^{c,\eta})^m)'(0)=0,\quad U^{c,\eta}(b_0)=0,\quad ((U^{c,\eta})^m)'(0)=-\nu.\] Both derivative conditions are placed at zero in (4.13).

Work in the spherically symmetric Einstein–Maxwell charged massless scalar field system, with complex scalar \(\phi\), fixed coupling \(\mathfrak e\ne0\), and gauge \(A_v=0\). The charge-to-mass ratio \(\mathfrak q\) is distinct from the coupling \(\mathfrak e\).

Theorem 2C fixes finite \(k\in\mathbb N\), \(\mathfrak q\in\mathbb R\), and \(\mathfrak r>0\). For sufficiently large \(M_f\) and \(R_f\ge\tfrac12M_f(1+\mathfrak r)\mathfrak q^2\), it constructs characteristic gluing from a Minkowski sphere to a Reissner–Nordström sphere of modified mass \(M_f\), charge \(Q_f=\mathfrak q M_f\), and radius \(R_f\), retaining \(r_u<0\).

In Gluing 3 of its proof, the charge \(Q_f\) is held constant and a collection of \(k+1\) real-valued pulses as in (4.1) is used on \(v\in[0,1]\). The terminal conditions are \(r(1)=R_f\), \(r_u(1)=-M_f\), \(Q(1)=Q_f\), and \(\varpi(1)=M_f\). For the preceding intermediate mass \(0<M'<M_f\), the proof imposes \(\varpi(0)=M'\), treats this mass condition as a sphere of pulse amplitudes with \(|\alpha|^2\asymp M_f^{-2}\), and invokes the Borsuk–Ulam argument to obtain the required vanishing of the \(k\) complex transverse scalar derivatives at the other gluing endpoint.

Work in the spherically symmetric Einstein–Maxwell charged massless scalar field system, with complex scalar \(\phi\), fixed coupling \(\mathfrak e\ne0\), and gauge \(A_v=0\). The charge-to-mass ratio \(\mathfrak q\) is distinct from the coupling \(\mathfrak e\).

Let \(k\in\mathbb N\), \(v_1<v_2\), and let \(D_1\in\mathcal D_k\) be lapse-normalized sphere data. Proposition 2.4 asserts that for every \(\phi\in C^k([v_1,v_2])\) whose derivatives \(\partial_v^i\phi(v_1)\) agree with \(D_1\) for \(0\le i\le k\), there exist unique \(r,A_u\in C^{k+1}([v_1,v_2])\) and \(Q\in C^k([v_1,v_2])\) satisfying the full tangential constraints and matching sphere data, with \(\Omega^2\equiv1\) on the whole prescribed interval.

The construction first solves \(r_{vv}=-r|\phi_v|^2\) using \(r(v_1)=\varrho(D_1)\) and \(r_v(v_1)=\varrho_v^1(D_1)\), then integrates \(Q_v=\mathfrak e r^2\operatorname{Im}(\phi\overline{\phi_v})\) and \((A_u)_v=-Q/(2r^2)\). No additional seed condition requiring this Raychaudhuri solution to stay positive throughout \([v_1,v_2]\) is stated. Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(\ell\) a prime invertible on \(S\), \(E\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), and \(A\subset E^\times\) an étale subsheaf of finite abelian groups whose order is invertible on \(S\). Let \(G\to S\) be a reductive group scheme and \(\mu:BG\to B^4A(1)\) a pointed morphism. Section 6 constructs, by étale descent from splitting covers, the twisted representation stack \(\operatorname{Rep}_{H,F_\mu}\) associated to this pair.

Remark 6.3.7 (article PDF page 63), under the standing assumptions of Section 6.0.1 on PDF page 59, asserts that every object of the global tensor category \(\operatorname{Rep}_{H,F_\mu}(S)\) has a dual and that the natural map \[E\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{Rep}_{H,F_\mu}(S)}(\mathbf1)\] is an isomorphism. The second assertion is the one examined here. No connectedness hypothesis on \(S\) is included in that standing setup or remark.

Let \(k\) be a finite field of characteristic \(p\), and let \(S\) be a smooth, separated, geometrically connected scheme of finite type over \(k\). For a closed point \(s\in|S|\), write \(n_s=[k(s):k]\), let \(F_s\) denote geometric Frobenius, and let \(a_s:\operatorname{Spec}k(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) be the structural map.

For every prime \(\ell\ne p\), let \(V_\ell\) be a continuous finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-representation of \(\pi_1(S)\). Assume the family is \(\mathbb Q\)-rational and compatible, and pointwise pure of one weight \(w\in\mathbb Z\): the Frobenius characteristic polynomial at each \(s\) lies in \(\mathbb Q[T]\), is independent of \(\ell\), and every complex conjugate of every root has absolute value \(|k(s)|^{w/2}\). Write \(G_\ell\) and \(\overline G_\ell\) for arithmetic and geometric algebraic monodromy, respectively, and choose a maximal torus \(\overline T_\ell\subset\overline G_\ell\).

Proposition 5 (article PDF page 4) asserts that, after a finite extension of the constant field \(k\) independent of \(\ell\), the invariant space \(V_\ell^{\overline T_\ell}\) has a semisimple \(\pi_1(k)\)-module structure \(\Psi(V_\ell)\), independent of the chosen torus up to isomorphism, and in particular that \[a_s^*\Psi(V_\ell)\ \text{is a submodule of}\ (s^*V_\ell)^{\mathrm{ss}}\qquad\text{for every closed point }s.\] This last assertion concerns an actual submodule after the single constant-field extension; it is not formulated only after passing separately to open subgroups in the paper's almost category.

Let \(k\) be a finite field of characteristic \(p\), let \(\ell\ne p\), and fix a nontrivial additive character \(\psi:\mathbb F_p\to\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^\times\). For a constructible \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathcal F\) on \(\mathbb A^1_k\), write \[\mathcal F_\psi(\mathcal F)=R^1p_{2!}(p_1^*\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(tx)})\] for the naive degree-one Fourier transform, where \(p_1,p_2\) are the coordinate projections. The sheaf is called elementary when \[H_c^0(\mathbb A^1_{\overline k},\mathcal F)=0,\qquad H_c^2(\mathbb A^1_{\overline k},\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(at)})=0\quad\text{for every }a\in\overline k.\]

Theorem 22 (Appendix A, article PDF page 23) assumes only these elementary conditions and finite monodromy on some nonempty open \(j_1:U_1\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k\), equivalently triviality of \(j_1^*\mathcal F\) after a connected étale cover of \(U_1\). It concludes that there are a nonempty open \(j_2:U_2\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k\) and an abelian scheme \(\pi:A\to U_2\) for which \(j_2^*\mathcal F_\psi(\mathcal F)\) is a local system and a direct factor of \(R^1\pi_*\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell,A}\). The stated hypotheses do not require \(\mathcal F\) to be a middle extension.

Let \(k\) be a finite field of characteristic \(p\), and let \(S\) be a smooth, separated, geometrically connected scheme of finite type over \(k\). For a closed point \(s\in|S|\), write \(n_s=[k(s):k]\), let \(F_s\) denote geometric Frobenius, and let \(a_s:\operatorname{Spec}k(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) be the structural map.

The setup of Section 4 does not require \(\dim S>0\). Its density is defined from \[F_\Sigma(t)=\sum_{s\in\Sigma}|k(s)|^{-t},\qquad x_\Sigma(t)=F_\Sigma(t)/F_{|S|}(t),\qquad t>\dim S,\] by \(\delta_S^u(\Sigma)=\limsup_{t\downarrow\dim S}x_\Sigma(t)\), and by the ordinary limit \(\delta_S(\Sigma)\) when it exists. Let \(\rho:\pi_1(S)\to\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be continuous, \(G\) its algebraic Zariski closure, \(\Phi\) any closed conjugacy-invariant subset of the compact image, and \(\Sigma_\Phi=\{s:\rho(F_s)\in\Phi\}\). For \(\Sigma\subseteq|S|\), let \(\Phi_\Sigma\) be the union of the conjugacy classes of \(\rho(F_s)\) for \(s\in\Sigma\).

Lemma 9 (article PDF page 9) asserts: (1) \(\delta_S(\Sigma_\Phi)=0\), equivalently \(\delta_S^u(\Sigma_\Phi)=0\), if and only if \(\Phi\) has empty interior in \(\rho(\pi_1(S))\); (2) if \(\delta_S^u(\Sigma)>1-1/|\pi_0(G)|\), then \(\Phi_\Sigma\) is Zariski dense in \(G\); and (3) if \(\delta_S^u(\Sigma)=1\), then \(\Phi_\Sigma\) is dense in \(\rho(\pi_1(S))\). Part (1) is stated for every such closed subset, with no analyticity hypothesis.

Let \(k\) be a finite field of characteristic \(p\), and let \(S\) be a smooth, separated, geometrically connected scheme of finite type over \(k\). For a closed point \(s\in|S|\), write \(n_s=[k(s):k]\), let \(F_s\) denote geometric Frobenius, and let \(a_s:\operatorname{Spec}k(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) be the structural map.

In the ghost-functor setting of Section 6.4 (article PDF page 14), let \(\overline G^{\circ}\) be the connected geometric monodromy group and let \(\overline T,\overline T'\) be maximal tori. For a representation \(V\) occurring in this construction, an element \(g\in\overline G^{\circ}(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) with \(\overline T'=g\overline T g^{-1}\) induces \[g\cdot:V^{\overline T}\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\longrightarrow V^{\overline T'}\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.\] The second functoriality bullet asserts that such \(g\) is unique up to right multiplication by \(\overline T(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\), and consequently that this map of invariant spaces is uniquely determined, independently of the choice of conjugating element. This is the asserted canonical map, beyond the preceding statement of independence up to natural isomorphism.

Let \(p\) be a prime, \((V,q)\) a nondegenerate quadratic space over \(\mathbb Q_p\), and \(t\) a semisimple isometry with monic symmetric characteristic polynomial \[F=F_0F_1,\qquad F_0=(X-1)^{n_+}(X+1)^{n_-},\qquad F_1=\prod_{f\in I_1}f^{n_f}.\] Fix determinant squareclasses \(D_+,D_-\) with \(D_+D_-=\det(q)F_1(1)F_1(-1)\), and an equivariant residue class \(\delta\in W_\Gamma(\mathbb F_p)\). Let \(I\) be the irreducible symmetric factors of \(F\), including the linear factors that occur. Notation 6.3 defines \(\mathcal C^p_\delta\subseteq(\mathbb Z/2)^I\) from admissible local decompositions with these fixed data and residue \(\delta\): its coordinates are \(a^p(f)=w_2(q_f^p)+w_2(Q_f)\), including the \(\pm1\) parts and the fixed reference forms of Sections 5–6.

Use the prime sets \(\Pi_{f,g}\) of Notations 7.1–7.2. In particular, for \(f\in I_1\), the printed definition requires a prime in \(\Pi_{f,X-1}\) to ramify in \(f\), to have \(X-1\mid f\bmod p\), and, when \(n_+=2\), to satisfy \(D_+\ne-1\); the analogous definition for \(X+1\) uses \(n_-,D_-\). Set \[C_0(I)=\{c:I\to\mathbb Z/2:c(f)=c(g)\text{ whenever }\Pi_{f,g}\ne\varnothing\}.\] The relation \(\sim_p\) is generated by simultaneously toggling the \(f,g\) coordinates when \(p\in\Pi_{f,g}\).

Proposition 8.1 (article PDF page 21) asserts that \(\mathcal C^p_\delta\) is a \(\sim_p\)-equivalence class. Lemma 8.3 (PDF page 22) asserts that for every \(a^p,b^p\in\mathcal C^p_\delta\) and \(c\in C_0(I)\), \[\epsilon_{a^p}(c):=\sum_{f\in I}c(f)a^p(f)=\sum_{f\in I}c(f)b^p(f)=:\epsilon_{b^p}(c)\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/2.\] Thus the subsequently defined \(\epsilon^p\) is claimed to be independent of the chosen admissible local decomposition. In the lattice application, \(\delta=0\) and the signature map additionally satisfies (C0), \(F(0)=1\), \(\deg F=r+s\), \(r\equiv s\pmod8\), and (C1), that \(|F(1)|\), \(|F(-1)|\), and \((-1)^{\deg F/2}F(1)F(-1)\) are squares.

Let \(F\in\mathbb Z[X]\) be the monic symmetric polynomial of even degree \(2n\) in Proposition 2.6, with \(F=(X-1)^{n_+}(X+1)^{n_-}F_1\), \(F_1(\pm1)\ne0\), and \(\deg F_1=2n_1\). In the case \(p=2\), its existence hypotheses are: if \(v_2(F_1(1))\) is odd then \(n_+\ge1\); if \(v_2(F_1(-1))\) is odd then \(n_-\ge1\); and, if \(n_+=n_-=0\), the squareclass of \((-1)^{n_1}F_1(1)F_1(-1)\) belongs to \(\{1,-3\}\) in \(\mathbb Q_2^\times/\mathbb Q_2^{\times2}\).

Let \(E\), its involution, its fixed algebra \(E_0\), and multiplication by \(\alpha\) be the étale-algebra construction in that proof, with characteristic polynomial \(F_1\); write \(b_\lambda\) for its trace form. Let \(V^\pm\) have dimensions \(n_\pm\), and let \(\epsilon\) act as \(\pm1\) on these summands. Claim 2 (article PDF page 9) asserts that for every \(u_+,u_-\in\mathbb Z_2^\times\) with \(u_+u_-=(-1)^n\), there exist \(\lambda\in E_0^\times\) and nondegenerate forms \(q^\pm\) on \(V^\pm\) such that \[\partial[E\oplus V^+\oplus V^-,b_\lambda\oplus q^+\oplus q^-,\alpha\oplus\epsilon]=0,\] the total space contains an even unimodular \(\mathbb Z_2\)-lattice, and \[\det(q^+)=u_+F_1(1)\text{ if }n_+\ne0,\qquad \det(q^-)=u_-F_1(-1)\text{ if }n_-\ne0.\] Determinants are squareclasses. These arbitrary unit prescriptions are stated even when only one of the linear eigenspaces occurs.

In the converse argument on PDF page 11, the text also asserts that \(n_+\ne0\) or \(n_-\ne0\) forces \(v_2(F_1(1))+v_2(F_1(-1))\) to be odd. This is the additional numerical assertion recorded with the finding.

Let \(\operatorname{Sym}(\mathbb R[X])\) denote the paper's symmetric polynomials, let \(\operatorname{rad}(f)\) be its monic symmetric divisor of highest degree, and let \(n_f(F)\) denote the multiplicity of an irreducible factor \(f\) in \(F\). Proposition 3.7 (article PDF page 13) considers a componentwise bounded map \(\tau:\mathbb R[X]\to\mathbb N\times\mathbb N\) attaining its maximum \((r,s)\), subject to the following printed conditions.

Condition (a) requires a unique monic symmetric polynomial \(F\) of degree \(r+s\) such that \(\tau(F)=(r,s)\) and every irreducible \(f\) with \(\tau(f)\ne(0,0)\) divides \(F\). Condition (b) is \(\tau(fg)=\tau(f)+\tau(g)\) for relatively prime symmetric \(f,g\). Condition (c) is \(\tau(f)=\tau(\operatorname{rad}(f))\) for all \(f\), and \(\tau(f)=(0,0)\) for constants. Condition (d) requires, for each irreducible symmetric \(f\), \[\tau(f)\in\deg(f)\mathbb N\times\deg(f)\mathbb N,\qquad \operatorname{sum}\tau(f)=\deg(f)n_f(F),\qquad \tau(f^k)=\tau(f)\quad(k\ge1).\] Condition (e) requires, for \(f=(X-a)(X-a^{-1})\) with real \(a\ne0,\pm1\), \[\tau(f)=(n_{X-a}(F),n_{X-a}(F)),\qquad \tau(f^k)=\tau(f)\quad(k\ge1).\]

The proposition asserts that these conditions are sufficient for a nondegenerate real quadratic form of signature \((r,s)\) to have a semisimple isometry \(t\) with signature map \(\operatorname{sign}_t=\tau\), and conversely that every such isometry has a bounded signature map satisfying (a)–(e). In particular, the uniqueness assertion occurs inside (a), and the displayed list supplies the hyperbolic condition (e) only for real reciprocal linear pairs.

In Theorem 19.1, let \(S\) be an unramified Salem polynomial of degree \(10\), and let \(\tau\) be a Salem signature map with Salem factor \(S\), trivial obstruction, and maximum \((3,19)\). The proof chooses a cyclotomic factor \(\Phi_m\) with \(\Pi_{S,\Phi_m}\ne\varnothing\) and constructs a product \(C\) of cyclotomic polynomials asserted to have degree \(12\), so that \(SC\) defines a signature map of maximum \((3,19)\) agreeing with \(\tau\) on the Salem factor. In Case 1 (article PDF page 42), the printed choice for \(m=5\) or \(8\) is \[C(X)=\Phi_m(X)^2(X-1)^2.\]

In the separate construction for Proposition 27.2 (article PDF pages 56–57), let \(C=\Phi_m\), \(m\ge3\), \(2\le d:=\deg C\le20\), with \(C(-1)=1\), and consider the branch \(C(1)=1\), \(d\equiv4\pmod8\). The proof takes an even unimodular \(L_1\) of signature \((2,d-2)\) carrying an isometry with polynomial \(C\), then prints an even unimodular complementary lattice \(L_2\) of signature \((1,22-d)\). It asserts that \(L_1\oplus L_2\cong\Lambda_{3,19}\), with the isometry equal to the identity on \(L_2\). These are the two dimension prescriptions examined here.

Let \(S\) be a Salem polynomial of degree \(d\), with \(4\le d\le18\), and let \(\alpha>1\) be its Salem root. Let \(\delta\in\mathbb C^\times\) satisfy \(|\delta|=1\). Theorem 21.3 (article PDF page 46) assumes either \(d\equiv0,4,6\pmod8\), or \(d\equiv2\pmod8\) and \(|S(1)|\), \(S(-1)\) are not both squares. It concludes that \((\alpha,\delta)\) is realizable: there exist a complex K3 surface \(X\) and an automorphism \(T\) with dynamical degree \(\lambda(T)=\alpha\) and action \(\omega(T)=\delta\) on the holomorphic two-form. As printed, the theorem assumes only \(|\delta|=1\), without imposing \(S(\delta)=0\).

Let \(S\) be a Salem polynomial of degree \(20\), let \(\alpha>1\) be its Salem root, and let \(\delta\) be a root of \(S\) with \(|\delta|=1\). Set \(F(X)=S(X)(X^2-1)\). Let \(\tau_\delta\) be the signature map with this fixed characteristic polynomial and maximum \((3,19)\) whose restriction to the Salem factor is \(\tau_{S,\delta}\): the \(\delta,\overline\delta\) plane is positive definite, the real reciprocal pair has signature \((1,1)\), and all other Salem planes are negative definite. The \(+1\) and \(-1\) eigenspaces are each one-dimensional and negative definite.

Theorem 24.1(a) (article PDF pages 51–52) asserts that, whenever \(S(1)\) and \(S(-1)\) are odd, square-free, and relatively prime, the even unimodular lattice \(\Lambda_{3,19}\) has a realizable isometry with signature map exactly \(\tau_\delta\). Realizability here includes the paper's type (P) requirement on the cyclotomic part. The claim therefore fixes the polynomial \(S(X)(X^2-1)\); it is stronger than existence of an automorphism realizing the Salem number with an unrestricted cyclotomic complement.

Let \(\widehat G\) be a simple adjoint reductive group over an algebraically closed field \(L\), and assume that the characteristic \(\ell\) of \(L\) does not divide the order of the Weyl group \(\Omega_{\widehat G}\). Fix a pinning \((\widehat T,\widehat B,(X_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Delta})\), and put \(\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(\widehat G)\), \(E=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}X_\alpha\), and \(H=\sum_{\beta\in\Phi^+}\beta^\vee\otimes1\). Appendix B.4 asserts that \(H\) is regular semisimple, that \((H,E)\) is part of a unique principal \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\)-triple \((F,H,E)\), and that the map \[\mathfrak g^E\longrightarrow\mathfrak g/\!/\widehat G,\qquad X\longmapsto(F+X)\bmod\widehat G\] is an isomorphism of varieties, where \(\mathfrak g^E\) is the centralizer of \(E\) in \(\mathfrak g\).

In the setting of Corollary 4.20(1)(b), let \(L\) be an algebraically closed coefficient field of characteristic \(\ell\ne p\), let \(I_F\) be the full inertia group, and let \(T_{\phi^\ell}\) be the torus in the chosen Borel pair of \(C_{\widehat G}(\phi^\ell)\). The action through \(\operatorname{Ad}\varphi\) preserves this pair. The proof asserts \[H^1(I_F,T_{\phi^\ell}(L))=1\] because \(T_{\phi^\ell}(L)\) is uniquely \(\ell\)-divisible and the inertia action factors through a cyclic \(\ell\)-group. It uses this assertion to obtain surjectivity on invariants from the normalizer of the Borel pair and the identity \(\pi_0(C_{\widehat G_L}(\varphi(I_F)))=\pi_0(\phi^\ell)^{\varphi(I_F)}\).

The related argument in Lemma 4.28 takes an arbitrary finite-index subgroup \(I\subset I_F\) and a diagonalizable kernel \(D\). It treats \(I\) as procyclic with topological generator \(t\), and consequently identifies \[H^1(I,D(\overline{\mathbf F}_\ell))\simeq D(\overline{\mathbf F}_\ell)_I=(D/(\operatorname{id}-t)D)(\overline{\mathbf F}_\ell)=\operatorname{Hom}(X^*(D)^I,\overline{\mathbf F}_\ell^{\times}).\]
