e\varnothing\) also has \(C(\overline{\mathbf F}_\ell)
e\varnothing\).

In its finite-image construction, the action of \(W_F/I\) preserves a Borel pair \((B_{\widehat H},T_{\widehat H})\) and factors through a finite group \(W\); write \({}^LH=\widehat H\rtimes W\). Starting with a cocycle \(\varphi\) valued in \(N_{\widehat H}(T_{\widehat H})(\overline{\mathbf Q})\), choose \(r\) such that \(g^r\in U=(T_{\widehat H}(\overline{\mathbf Q})^{{}^L\varphi(s)})^\circ\), where \(g={}^L\varphi(\operatorname{Fr})\) and \(s\) is the chosen tame-inertia element. The proof chooses \(t\in U\) with \(t^r=g^r\), keeps \({}^L(\varphi^t)(s)={}^L\varphi(s)\), and sets \({}^L(\varphi^t)(\operatorname{Fr})=t g\). It asserts that this cocycle \(\varphi^t\) has finite image.

Let \(R\) be the base ring and \(\Gamma\) a finite group whose order is invertible in \(R\). Let \(H'\to H\) be a \(\Gamma\)-equivariant central isogeny of reductive group schemes over \(R\), with finite multiplicative-type kernel \(Z\). In proving Lemma A.11(i), the paper asserts that \[1\longrightarrow Z^\Gamma\longrightarrow H'^\Gamma\longrightarrow H^\Gamma\longrightarrow H^1(\Gamma,Z)\longrightarrow H^1(\Gamma,H')\] is exact as a sequence of sheaves on the big étale site of \(\operatorname{Spec}R\). No smoothness assumption on \(Z\) is imposed. This is used in the proof that finiteness of \(\pi_0(H'^\Gamma)\) implies finiteness of \(\pi_0(H^\Gamma)\).

Section 1.5 defines the \({}^LG\)-banal primes as the primes outside a finite exceptional set \(S\), depending only on \({}^LG\), for which the geometric-reducedness conclusion of Theorem 5.7 holds. In the discussion of the GIT quotient \(Z^1(W_F^0/P_F^e,\widehat G)/\!/\widehat G\) surrounding Theorem 1.9, the paper requires a positive integer \(M\) divisible by all \({}^LG\)-banal primes in order to work over \(\overline{\mathbf Z}[1/(Mp)]\). It further states that when \({}^LG\) is the Langlands dual group of an unramified group, \(M\) may be taken to be the product of the \({}^LG\)-banal primes.

Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K\) be complex symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices, and let \(\Phi_K(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K)=M_K(Z_K)\cdots M_1(Z_1)e_{2n}\), where the elementary symplectic factors are upper triangular for odd indices and lower triangular for even indices. Write \(F_y^K=\Phi_K^{-1}(y)\) and \[W_K=\{(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K):Z_{2i-1}e_n\ne0\text{ for some }1\le i\le\lceil(K-1)/2\rceil\}.\] The generic stratum consists of the targets for which the first \(n\) coordinates are not all zero when \(K\) is even, and the last \(n\) coordinates are not all zero when \(K\) is odd.

Definition 3.19 defines \(V_K\), for \(K\ge3\), by adjoining the principal complete fiber-preserving fields from levels \(L=3,\ldots,K\). Section 3.6.2 separately defines \(V_2\) as the pushforwards of the coordinate fields on \(\mathbf C^{n(n-1)}\) by the meromorphic parametrizations \(\psi_j\) of generic two-factor fibers. Definition 3.35 sets \(Q_K=\Gamma(V_K)\), the collection generated by these fields and their flow conjugates. Theorem 3.36 asserts that for every \(K\ge2\) there is a finite set \(A_K\subset Q_K\) of globally holomorphic, \(\mathbf C\)-complete, fiber-preserving vector fields on \((\mathbf C^{n(n+1)/2})^K\) spanning \(T(F_y^K\cap W_K)\) for every generic target \(y\), with \(A_K\subset A_{K+1}\) under the stated extension convention.

Let \(M\) be a Stein manifold, \(X\subset M\) an open subset, and \(A\) a finite set of \(\mathbf C\)-complete holomorphic vector fields on \(M\) spanning \(TX\). Let \(C_A(X)\) be the saturation of \(X\) under compositions of their flows, and let \(\Gamma(A)\) consist of their pullbacks by such flow compositions. Lemma 3.30 asserts that some finite \(A\subset B\subset\Gamma(A)\) spans \(T C_A(X)\).

The proof specifically constructs \(B\) from \(A\) and finitely many sets \(B_k\) of single-flow pullbacks \((\alpha_{t_V^k}^{V})^*W\), for \(V,W\in A\), where the times are chosen using the descending analytic subsets \(N_k\). It asserts that this finite collection already spans the tangent bundle throughout \(C_A(X)\).

Let \(M\) be a Stein manifold, \(f:M\to\mathbf C\) holomorphic, and \(N=\{x:f(x)=0\}\). Let \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) be complete holomorphic vector fields with flows \(\alpha_t^1,\ldots,\alpha_t^k\). If a fixed finite sequence \(i_1,\ldots,i_n\) satisfies \((V_{i_n}\cdots V_{i_1}f)(x)\ne0\) for every \(x\in N\), Lemma 3.34 asserts \[\{\alpha_{t_n}^{i_n}\circ\cdots\circ\alpha_{t_1}^{i_1}(x):t_1,\ldots,t_n\in\mathbf C\}\not\subset N\qquad(x\in N).\] Thus the conclusion specifies this particular order of the flows.

Definition 2.7 and Theorem 2.8 assert the parametric Oka property for every stratified elliptic submersion \(\pi:E\to B\) of reduced complex spaces. The data are a reduced Stein space \(X\), a closed complex subvariety \(X'\subset X\), compact Hausdorff parameter spaces \(P_0\subset P\), an \(X\)-holomorphic map \(f:P\times X\to B\), and a continuous lift \(F_0:P\times X\to E\). The lift is holomorphic on \(X\) for parameters in \(P_0\), and holomorphic on \(K\cup X'\) for every parameter. No holomorphic-convexity hypothesis on \(K\) is included in the printed definition.

The asserted homotopy of lifts \(F_t\), \(0\le t\le1\), satisfies \(\pi\circ F_t=f\), remains equal to \(F_0\) on \((P_0\times X)\cup(P\times X')\), is holomorphic on \(K\) and uniformly close to \(F_0\) on \(P\times K\), and ends at an \(X\)-holomorphic lift \(F_1\).

In the elementary-factorization step, let \(b,d\in\mathbf C^{n-1}\) and \(c\in\mathbf C\) be the holomorphic blocks of the remaining symplectic matrix \[M=\begin{pmatrix}I_{n-1}&0&0&b\\-d^T&1&b^T&c\\0&0&I_{n-1}&d\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-b\\-b^T&-c-d^Tb\end{pmatrix}.\] The displayed elimination identity is \[M\begin{pmatrix}I_n&-B\\0&I_n\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{n-1}&0&0&0\\-d^T&1&0&0\\0&0&I_{n-1}&d\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] It is this printed upper-factor sign that is under examination.

Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K\) be complex symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices, and let \(\Phi_K(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K)=M_K(Z_K)\cdots M_1(Z_1)e_{2n}\), where the elementary symplectic factors are upper triangular for odd indices and lower triangular for even indices. Write \(F_y^K=\Phi_K^{-1}(y)\) and \[W_K=\{(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K):Z_{2i-1}e_n\ne0\text{ for some }1\le i\le\lceil(K-1)/2\rceil\}.\] The generic stratum consists of the targets for which the first \(n\) coordinates are not all zero when \(K\) is even, and the last \(n\) coordinates are not all zero when \(K\) is odd.

Lemma 3.16 states that a fiber \(F_y^K\) contains a singularity if and only if \(\pi_1(y)=e_n\), where \(\pi_1\) is projection onto the last \(n\) coordinates. Remark 3.37 repeats this as the condition \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n,0,\ldots,0,1)\), without a parity restriction on \(K\).

Let \(C\) be the smooth projective complex curve, \(c_0\in C\), \(J=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\), and \(Y(\mathbf l)=\prod_i C^{(l_i)}\). Put \(\mu^{(k_i)}(D_i)=\mathcal O_C(D_i-l_i c_0)^{\otimes k_i}\), and let \(\widetilde Y_n(\mathbf l,\mathbf k)\) be the pullback of \([n]:J\to J\) along \((D_i)_i\mapsto\bigotimes_i\mu^{(k_i)}(D_i)\), as in diagram (21).

Proposition 6.5 asserts that the integral cohomology groups of \(\widetilde Y_n(\mathbf l,\mathbf k)\) are torsion-free. It is used after the coprime-degree assumption \((d,n)=1\) for the Higgs-moduli problem; the proposition itself does not state a further restriction on these covers beyond diagram (21).

In Step 2, set \(U(l_i+1)=C^{(l_i+1)}\setminus C^{(l_i)}\), where the closed inclusion adds \(c_0\), and let \(\widetilde U(\mathbf l+1)\) be the inverse image of \(\prod_iU(l_i+1)\). The proof invokes Lemma 6.7 to infer torsion-freeness for the complementary boundary \(\widetilde Y_n(\mathbf l+1,\mathbf k)\setminus\widetilde U(\mathbf l+1)\). That lemma assumes a smooth closed subvariety of a smooth projective variety, with affine complement and torsion-free cohomology of the ambient variety.

Let \(k\) be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, \(S\) a locally finite-type \(k\)-scheme, and \(X\to S\) a flat family of integral planar curves of arithmetic genus \(g\), with a finite flat map to \(C\times S\), where \(C\) is smooth projective of genus \(g_C\). Let \(J=\overline{\operatorname{Pic}}^0(X/S)\), \(\widehat P=[J/\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)]\), and \(\pi:J\to\widehat P\) be the \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\)-torsor. Lemma 4.6 states that for every \(q\ge0\), the higher direct image of the structure sheaf under this torsor is free of rank \(\binom gq\), and in degree zero is \(\mathcal O_{\widehat P}\). Here the printed \(g\) is the arithmetic genus of the family \(X\), as defined at the start of Section 4.1.

Let \(\mathcal F\) be a locally constant sheaf of spectra on \(T^m=(S^1)^m\), with fiber \(E\) whose homotopy groups are finitely generated. Fix a prime \(p\), and assume that \(\mathcal F\) becomes trivial after pullback along the map denoted \([p^
u]:T^m	o T^m\) in Lemma 6.18. The lemma asserts \[\pi_*(E)[p]
e0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\pi_*\Gamma(T^m,\mathcal F)[p]
e0.\] Here \([p]\) denotes the subgroup annihilated by \(p\); the hypothesis is triviality after the specified finite \(p\)-power cover.

Let a finite group \(G\) act continuously on a topological space \(X\). Definitions A.3–A.4 take generalized orbits \(P=U\times H\backslash G\), with \(U\subset X^H\) open and structure map \((x,Hg)\mapsto xg\). Put \(X^{s(H)}=\bigcup_{g\in G}X^{gHg^{-1}}\). A morphism \(P_1\to P_2\), for \(H_1\) included in \(H_2\) up to conjugacy, is a \(G\)-equivariant continuous map over \(X\) defined only on \(P_1\times_X X^{s(H_2)}\).

Definition A.6 asserts that coverings in this category are families of these morphisms which are open immersions and whose images cover the target, with the empty family covering the empty generalized orbit. It asserts that this defines a Grothendieck topology. The subsequent Remark A.7 also states that its space-valued sheaves satisfy \(F(\varnothing)\simeq\varnothing\) by the empty-cover condition.

Let \(G\) be finite and let \(\mathcal X\) be a topological stack with a \(G\)-action, defined as a functor \(BG\to\mathrm{TopSt}\). For \(H\subset G\), Definition A.29(b) defines \(\mathcal X^H=\mathcal X\times_{X_{\mathrm{mod}}}X_{\mathrm{mod}}^H\), using fixed points of the coarse moduli space. Definition A.31 then asserts that, for every open \(\mathcal U\subset\mathcal X^H\), the formula \[(x,Hg)\longmapsto xg\] defines a generalized \(G\)-orbit map \(\mathcal U\times H\backslash G\to\mathcal X\). The fixed-point condition used here is the coarse-space pullback condition.

In the coprime rank-degree Higgs-moduli setting \((n,d)=1\), write \(\Gamma=J[n]\) and let \(\widehat M\) be the paper's \(\operatorname{PGL}_n\)-Higgs moduli stack. Theorem 6.11 claims torsion-freeness of \(KU^*(\widehat M^{\mathrm{an}},\widetilde\alpha)\) for an arbitrary Brauer class \(\alpha\in\operatorname{Br}(\widehat M)\).

For \(\gamma\in\Gamma\) of order \(r\), set \(c=\langle\gamma\rangle\). Over the fixed locus \(M^c=M^\gamma\), the equivariant gerbe supplies line bundles \(L_{\gamma'}\), \(\gamma'\in c\), and the character torsor \(C_c^\alpha=\operatorname{Spec}_{M^\gamma}(\bigoplus_{\gamma'\in c}L_{\gamma'})\). The geometric cover \(\widetilde M_\gamma\to M^\gamma\) is the free \(\mu_r\)-quotient cover of Proposition 6.15, obtained from rank-\(n/r\) Higgs bundles on the étale cyclic cover of the curve associated with \(\gamma\). Corollary 6.16 identifies \(C_c^\alpha\) with \(\widetilde M_\gamma\) over \(M^\gamma\), and Corollary 6.17 uses this identification in the lower-rank torsion argument. The stated Brauer-class range has not been restricted to the particular universal-family obstruction gerbe.

Let \(f:F\to G\) and \(g:G\to F\) be morphisms of complexes of constructible \(\mathbf Q\)-sheaves on a variety \(B\). Assume \(F=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbf Z}T_i[-i]\), with \(T_i\) semisimple perverse, that the support of each \(T_i\) intersects a fixed open subvariety \(B^\heartsuit\), and that \((g\circ f)|_{B^\heartsuit}\simeq\operatorname{id}\). Lemma 3.3 asserts that the induced endomorphism of \(\Gamma(B,F)\) is unipotent, and in particular that \(\Gamma(B,F)\) is a retract of \(\Gamma(B,G)\). The support hypothesis is stated for each whole \(T_i\).

Let \(W\) be a Noetherian scheme with an action of a finite group \(G\), let \(\alpha\) be a \(G\)-equivariant Brauer class, and let \(j:U\hookrightarrow W\) be a \(G\)-invariant open subscheme. Lemma 3.5 asserts that every \(F\in D^b_{\mathrm{coh}}([U/G],\alpha)\) extends to \(D^b_{\mathrm{coh}}([W/G],\alpha)\).

In the untwisted construction, after extending two consecutive differentials of a bounded coherent complex to \(\widetilde F^{b-2}\xrightarrow{\overline d^{b-2}}\overline F^{b-1}\xrightarrow{\overline d^{b-1}}\overline F^b\), the proof defines \[\overline F^{b-2}=\widetilde F^{b-2}/\ker(\overline d^{b-1}\circ\overline d^{b-2}).\] It asserts that this quotient still extends the original \(F^{b-2}\) on \(U\) and makes the composition of the two differentials zero.

Let \(G\) be finite, \(H\subset G\), and \(\mathrm{Space}^G=\operatorname{Fun}(\mathrm{Orb}_G^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Space})\). Claim A.22 asserts that the internal mapping-space functor \(\operatorname{Map}(H\backslash G,-)\) preserves arbitrary colimits: for every diagram \((F_i)_{i\in I}\), \[\operatorname*{colim}_{i\in I}\operatorname{Map}(H\backslash G,F_i)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}\!\left(H\backslash G,\operatorname*{colim}_{i\in I}F_i\right)\] is an equivalence. This is the assertion for space-valued equivariant presheaves, with no restriction to filtered colimits.

Let \(C\) be the smooth projective complex curve, \(c_0\in C\), \(J=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\), and \(Y(\mathbf l)=\prod_i C^{(l_i)}\). Put \(\mu^{(k_i)}(D_i)=\mathcal O_C(D_i-l_i c_0)^{\otimes k_i}\), and let \(\widetilde Y_n(\mathbf l,\mathbf k)\) be the pullback of \([n]:J\to J\) along \((D_i)_i\mapsto\bigotimes_i\mu^{(k_i)}(D_i)\), as in diagram (21).

For a single symmetric-power factor \(Y(l)=C^{(l)}\), the proof of Lemma 6.8 sets \(m=\gcd(k,n)\) and asserts that \(\widetilde Y_n(l,k)\) is a disjoint union of \(m\) copies of \(\widetilde Y_{n/m}(l,1)\). The claimed component count is \(m\), independently of the genus of \(C\).

Fix polynomial degree \(r\ge0\), form degree \(0\le k\le n\), and a mesh cell \(f\) of dimension \(k+1\le d\le n\). For each discrete VEM datum \(\underline\omega_f\in V_r^{k,f}\), Section 4.1.4 defines \(P_r^{k,f}\underline\omega_f\in\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^k(f)\) as the unique solution of \[(-1)^{k+1}\int_f P_r^{k,f}\underline\omega_f\wedge(d\mu+
u)=\int_f\star^{-1}\widetilde D_{\omega,f}\wedge\mu-\int_{\partial f}P_r^{k,\partial f}\underline\omega_{\partial f}\wedge\operatorname{tr}\mu+(-1)^{k+1}\int_f\star^{-1}\omega_f\wedge
u\] for every \((\mu,
u)\in\mathcal K_{r+1}^{d-k-1}(f)	imes\mathcal K_{r+1}^{d-k}(f)\). Here \(\mathcal K\) are the paper's Koszul polynomial spaces, \(\widetilde D_{\omega,f}=\star d_r^{k,f}\underline\omega_f\) if \(d=k+1\), and \(\widetilde D_{\omega,f}=D_{\omega,f}\) if \(d\ge k+2\); the boundary potential is obtained by the same construction on the facets.

Theorem 31 then asserts polynomial consistency: \(P_r^{k,f}I_r^{k,f}\omega=\omega\) for \(\omega\in\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^k(f)\). Both the uniqueness in (4.9) and this claimed reproduction use the stated trimmed trial space and complementary-form test space.

Section 3.2 assumes that \(\Omega\subset\mathbf R^n\) has trivial topology and asserts that its harmonic-form spaces are therefore trivial. For form degree \(k\ge0\) and polynomial degree \(r\ge0\), it formulates the mixed discrete Hodge–Laplace problem on \(X_r^{k-1,h}\times X_r^{k,h}\), without imposing orthogonality to harmonic forms in this case.

With the paper's discrete inner products and differential \(d_r\), the bilinear form is \[A_h((\sigma,u),(\tau,v))=(\sigma,\tau)_{k-1,h}-(u,d_r\tau)_{k,h}+(d_r\sigma,v)_{k,h}+(d_ru,d_rv)_{k+1,h}.\] Assuming the stated mesh regularity, (3.21) asserts a mesh-independent inf-sup estimate \[\|\!\|(\upsilon,w)\|\!\|_h\lesssim\sup_{(\tau,v)\ne0}\frac{A_h((\upsilon,w),(\tau,v))}{\|\!\|(\tau,v)\|\!\|_h}\] for every \((\upsilon,w)\) in that product space. The norm is the product of the discrete graph norms \((\|\omega\|_{\ell,h}^2+\|d_r\omega\|_{\ell+1,h}^2)^{1/2}\). The stated degree range includes \(k=0\).

For form degree \(\ell\ge0\), polynomial degree \(r\ge0\), a form \(\omega\in\Lambda^{\ell+1}(\Omega)\) smooth enough for the interpolators, and \(\underline\mu_h\in X_r^{\ell,h}\), define \[\widetilde E_{r,h}^{\ell}(\omega;\underline\mu_h)=(I_r^{\ell,h}\delta\omega,\underline\mu_h)_{\ell,h}-(I_r^{\ell+1,h}\omega,d_r^{\ell,h}\underline\mu_h)_{\ell+1,h}.\] Under additional piecewise regularity of \(\omega\), (3.24) asserts \[|\widetilde E_{r,h}^{\ell}(\omega;\underline\mu_h)|\lesssim h^{r+1}\|\!\|\underline\mu_h\|\!\|_{\ell,h}\qquad\text{for every }\underline\mu_h\in X_r^{\ell,h},\] with the discrete graph norm and a constant independent of mesh size. The statement does not impose a boundary-trace condition on \(\omega\).

For a two-dimensional mesh face \(F\) in the three-dimensional vector-proxy discussion, let \(x_F\) be its chosen Koszul center and let \(r\ge0\). Equation (2.11) identifies \(\mathcal K_r^1(F)\), the Koszul complement in the polynomial one-form decomposition, with \[\mathcal R_r^c(F):=(x-x_F)\mathcal P_{r+1}(F),\] while identifying \(d\mathcal P_{r+1}\Lambda^0(F)\) with \(\operatorname{rot}_F\mathcal P_{r+1}(F)\). The degree on the radial scalar-polynomial factor is printed as \(r+1\).

In oriented \(\mathbf R^3\), identify the two-form \(\omega=a\,dx_2\wedge dx_3-b\,dx_1\wedge dx_3+c\,dx_1\wedge dx_2\) with the vector proxy \(w=(a,b,c)\). Equation (A.6) defines first-slot contraction by \((\omega\mathbin{\lrcorner}v)(u)=\omega(v,u)\). The following vector-proxy list asserts that the one-form \(\omega\mathbin{\lrcorner}v\) corresponds to \(v\times w\).

For a \(d\)-cell \(f\), form degree \(0\le k<d\), polynomial degree \(r\ge0\), and local DDR datum \(\underline\omega_f\), page 47 gives the following characterization of the discrete exterior derivative: \[\int_f d_r^{k,f}\underline\omega_f\wedge\mu=-\int_f d(\star^{-1}\omega_f)\wedge\mu+\int_{\partial f}\bigl(P_r^{k,\partial f}\underline\omega_{\partial f}-\operatorname{tr}_{\partial f}(\star^{-1}\omega_f)\bigr)\wedge\operatorname{tr}_{\partial f}\mu\] for every \(\mu\in\mathcal P_r\Lambda^{d-k-1}(f)\). It is asserted to follow by integrating the defining equation (3.4) by parts; the volume-derivative term is printed with a minus sign.

Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbf N^m\)-graded Hopf algebra over \(\mathbf K\), with ribbon Drinfeld double as in the construction. Set \(G=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbf N^m}^0(H)\), the degree-preserving Hopf automorphisms fixing a left cointegral \(\Lambda_l\). Over \(\mathbf F=\mathbf K[t_1^{\pm1/2},\ldots,t_m^{\pm1/2}]\), put \(H'=H\otimes\mathbf F\), and let \(\theta(x)=t_1^{|x|_1}\cdots t_m^{|x|_m}x\) on homogeneous elements. Section 3.4 asserts that \(D(H')|_{G'}\) is \(G'\)-ribbon for \(G'=\{\alpha\otimes\theta^j:\alpha\in G,\ j\in\mathbf Z\}\), using the square root \(r_{H'}(\alpha\otimes\theta^j)^{1/2}=\prod_i t_i^{j|\Lambda_l|_i/2}\).

Accordingly, page 3 asserts that the normalized degree-twisted invariant \(P_H^{\rho\otimes\theta}(K)\) is defined for every knot \(K\subset S^3\) and every homomorphism \(\rho:\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)\to\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbf N^m}^0(H)\), and Theorem 1 gives \(\deg P_H^{\rho\otimes\theta}(K)\le2g(K)d(H)\), where \(d(H)\) is the maximal total grading degree. This full automorphism range is the claim being checked; Section 2.4 separately requires the acting subgroup to fix a Kauffman–Radford pair \((b,\beta)\), with \(b^2=a\), \(\beta^2=\alpha\), and \(S^2=\operatorname{ad}_{\beta^{-1}}\circ\operatorname{ad}_b\).

For the \(p\)-dimensional module \(V_\alpha\) used to define the ADO invariant, let \(v_0,\ldots,v_{p-1}\) be its basis, \(v_0^*,\ldots,v_{p-1}^*\) the ordinary dual basis, and \(q=\zeta_p\) the root of unity of Section 5. The right evaluation and coevaluation on page 29 are prescribed by \[\operatorname{ev}_R(v_i\otimes v_j^*)=\delta_{ij}q^{\alpha(1-p)-2i},\qquad\operatorname{coev}_R(1)=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}q^{-\alpha(1-p)-2i}v_i^*\otimes v_i.\] These maps are used as the right cap and cup in the tangle construction, alongside ordinary vector-space left evaluation and coevaluation.

Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra with ribbon double, and let \(G\subset\operatorname{Aut}(H)\) be such that \(D(H)|_G\) is \(G\)-ribbon. For a framed oriented \(G\)-tangle \((T,\rho)\), take a diagram \(D\) with \(N\) crossings and \(k\) right caps or cups. At crossing \(j\), let \(\alpha_j,\beta_j\) be the bottom-edge labels if it is positive and the top-edge labels if it is negative; let \(\gamma_i\) and \(\epsilon_i\) specify the pivotal factor at the \(i\)-th right extremum.

The precise tensor formula on page 12 uses \[R_D=\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^{N}R_{\alpha_j,\beta_j}\right)\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^{k}g_{\gamma_i}^{\epsilon_i}\right)\] for all crossings, and applies the partial-longitude automorphisms, the permutation into component order and iterated multiplication to obtain \(Z_{D(H)}^\rho(T)\). Thus this tensor formula uses \(R_{\alpha_j,\beta_j}\) without a crossing-sign exponent, whereas the preceding local rule assigns the inverse R-matrix at a negative crossing.

For the knot invariant of Section 5.6, the variable convention is \(t=\zeta_p^{2\alpha}\), and \[\operatorname{ADO}_p(K,t)=\zeta_p^{-w(D)\alpha^2/2+w(D)\alpha(p-1)}\operatorname{ADO}'_p(K),\qquad P_{H_p}^{\theta}(K)=t^{w(D)(p-1)/2}\epsilon\bigl(Z_{D(H_p)}^\theta(K_o)\bigr).\] Here \(K_o\) is the opened knot, \(D\) its diagram and \(w(D)\) its writhe. Proposition 5.4 asserts \(\operatorname{ADO}_p(K,t)=P_{H_p}^\theta(K)\).

In its proof the ADO term is instead written \(\operatorname{ADO}_p(K,\zeta_p^\alpha)\), and the final step states \[\epsilon\bigl(Z_{D(H_p)}^\theta(K)\bigr)\big|_{t=\zeta_p^{2\alpha}}v_0=Z_\alpha v_0.\] Immediately before this, writing \(Z_{D(H_p)}^\theta(K)=\sum\lambda_{ijl}\mathsf k^i\kappa^jF^lE^l\), the proof obtains \(Z_\alpha v_0=\zeta_p^{w(D)\alpha^2}\sum\lambda_{ij0}\zeta_p^{\alpha(i-j)/2}v_0\). These printed variable and writhe factors are the intermediate identities under examination.

Let \(B\subseteq X\times Y\) be bipartite, with \(|X|=|Y|=n\) and density \(\rho=|B|/n^2\ge d\). Assume \(n^{-1}\ll\alpha\ll d\), the paper's absolute cut regularity \[\bigl||B[S,T]|-\rho|S||T|\bigr|\le\alpha n^2\qquad(S\subseteq X,\ T\subseteq Y),\] and the super-regular degree bounds \(\deg_B(v)\in(1\pm\alpha)\rho n\) for every vertex. Let \(Z\) be the auxiliary bipartite graph with maximum degree less than \(n^{0.4}\).

Lemma 2.7 (printed page 1789, article PDF page 21) asserts the existence of a distribution on perfect matchings \(M\) that avoids alternating \(MZMZ\) cycles and has approximately uniform edge marginals. The particular asserted guarantee examined here is that, for every fixed \(X'\subseteq X\) and \(Y'\subseteq Y\), with high probability as \(n\to\infty\), \[\left||M[X',Y']|-\frac{|B[X',Y']|}{\rho n}\right|\le n^{0.8}.\] The subsets are fixed before the random matching is chosen; the statement includes \(Y'=Y\).

Let \(G\) be a Polish group and \(H\le G\) a Polishable subgroup, meaning that \(H\) admits a Polish group topology with the same Borel sets as its ambient subspace Borel structure. Write \(E_H^G\) for the coset equivalence relation. Potential membership in a Borel class means membership after a finer Polish topology preserving the Borel sets. Here \(D(\Pi^0_2)(G)\) consists of differences of two \(G_\delta\) subsets of \(G\), equivalently intersections of a \(G_\delta\) and an \(F_\sigma\) set.

Theorem 3.3(2) in the bound original publisher version (printed page 2201, article PDF page 5) asserts \[E_H^G\text{ is potentially }\Sigma^0_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H\in D(\Pi^0_2)(G).\] The associated assertion of Lemma 6.5 (printed page 2208, PDF page 12) gives potential \(\Sigma^0_2\) complexity for the coset relation of a Polishable \(\Sigma^0_3\) subgroup. These are the original-version claims, before the separately documented corrigendum.

For a Hopf–Berger sphere with parameter \(\tau>0\), Theorem B states that a complete submanifold \(\Sigma\subset S_{\mathbf H,\tau}^{4n+3}\), \(n\ge1\), of dimension \(d\ge2\), is totally geodesic if and only if it is congruent to one of the well-positioned examples in Table 1 or the additional examples in Table 2. Theorem C makes the analogous exhaustive assertion for complete \(\Sigma\subset S_{\mathbf O,\tau}^{15}\) of dimension \(d\ge2\), using Tables 1 and 3. The statements do not exclude the round parameter \(\tau=1\); the surrounding text explicitly describes the classification as applying to every \(\tau>0\).

Table 1 lists, in the quaternionic case, \(S_{\mathbf H,\tau}^{4k+3}\) for \(1\le k\le n-1\), \(S_{\mathbf C,\tau}^{2k+1}\) for \(1\le k\le n\), round \(S_1^k\) for \(2\le k\le n\), and round \(S_{1/\tau}^k\) for \(2\le k\le3\). In the octonionic case it lists \(S_{\mathbf H,\tau}^7\), \(S_{\mathbf C,\tau}^3\), and round \(S_{1/\tau}^k\) for \(2\le k\le7\). The extra families in Tables 2–3 are all restricted to \(\tau<1/2\). Here the subscript of a round sphere denotes its sectional curvature.

In the \(D^*\) case \(G=\operatorname{SO}^*(2n)\), decompose the dual nilpotent-orbit data into bad- and good-parity parts \(\check O_b,\check O_g\), with ranks \(n_b,n_g\), as in Section 6.3. Proposition 8.6 asserts that the sum of coherent-continuation multiplicities \[\sum_{\bar\wp\in\overline{A}(\check O)}[\tau_b\otimes\tau_{\bar\wp}:\operatorname{Coh}_\Lambda(K'(G))]\] is zero for a non-\(G\)-relevant orbit and otherwise equals \(\#\operatorname{PBP}_{D^*}(\check O_b)\,\#\widetilde{\operatorname{PBP}}_{G_g}(\check O_g)\), using the paper's painted-bipartition sets.

For the mixed-parity calculation \(n_g>0\), page 59 sets \[C_b=\operatorname{Res}^{W_{n_b}}_{W'_{n_b}}\operatorname{Ind}^{W_{n_b}}_{H_{n_b/2}}\eta,\qquad C_g=\bigoplus_{2t+a=n_g}\operatorname{Ind}^{W'_{n_g}}_{H_t\times S_a}(\eta\otimes\operatorname{sgn}),\] where \(W_j\) is the signed-permutation group, \(W'_j\) its even-sign subgroup, \(H_t=W_t\ltimes\{\pm1\}^t\), and \(\eta(g,(a_i))=\prod_i a_i\). It uses this \(C_b\) in the multiplicity factorization through \(W'_{n_b,n_g}=W'_n\cap(W_{n_b}\times W_{n_g})\), and identifies the resulting factors with the painted-bipartition counts. The bad-parity term in Proposition 8.1 is instead printed as induction directly to \(W'_{n_b}\).

For a \([D]\)- or \([D^*]\)-space, let \(V\) be a complex vector space of dimension \(2n\) with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form, and a conjugate-linear map \(j\) preserving that form up to complex conjugation, with \(j^2=1\) in type \(D\) and \(j^2=-1\) in type \(D^*\). The orientation \(\omega\in\bigwedge^{2n}V\) is required to satisfy \(\langle\omega,\omega\rangle=1\) for the determinant-induced bilinear form. Type \(D^*\) additionally imposes \(\omega=(\sqrt{-1}u_1\wedge j(u_1))\wedge\cdots\wedge(\sqrt{-1}u_n\wedge j(u_n))\) for suitable vectors.

The maximal isotropic member \(V_n\) of the flag (6.7) is called \(\omega\)-compatible when there is a basis \(u_1,\ldots,u_{2n}\), with \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\in V_n\), such that \(\langle u_i,u_j\rangle=\delta_{i+j,2n+1}\) and \(\omega=u_1\wedge\cdots\wedge u_{2n}\). Remarks 6.2(a,b) assert that exactly one of the two \(G_{\mathbf C}\)-orbits of maximal isotropic subspaces is compatible and that such a compatible flag exists, uniquely up to \(G_{\mathbf C}\)-conjugacy. These assertions are not restricted to even \(n\).

Section 8.3 identifies \(\operatorname{Irr}(W_t)\) with bipartitions \((\tau_L,\tau_R)\) of total size \(t\). For \(\tau_L=\tau_R\), it defines the type-I irreducible of \(W'_t\) by the displayed formula \[(\tau_L,\tau_R)_I:=\operatorname{Ind}^{W'_t}_{S_t}\tau_L.\] Thus the inducing representation is labelled by a partition of size \(t/2\), while the indicated subgroup is \(S_t\).

The mixed-parity proof of Proposition 8.6 also recalls \[\widetilde\tau_b=\operatorname{Ind}^{W_{n_b}}_{W'_{n_b}}\tau_b=(O'_b,O'_b)\in\operatorname{Irr}(W_{n_b}).\] This is the printed bipartition label under the same convention that the two partition sizes must sum to the Weyl-group rank; it is not the half-row construction in equations (8.6)–(8.8).

Let \(\Gamma\) be a Schottky subgroup with the disk presentation used in the paper, let \(\mathcal W_{\ge2}\) denote its reduced words of length at least two, and let \(\sigma\) be a finite-dimensional unitary representation. For every finite \(\mathcal B\subset\mathcal W_{\ge2}\), let \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal B,s,\sigma}\) be the holomorphic Bergman transfer-operator family defined in (3.2). Lemma 25 (article PDF page 17) asserts that \(\det(I-\mathcal L_{\mathcal B,s,\sigma})=0\) exactly when \(1\) is an eigenvalue, and that at each zero \(s_0\), \[\operatorname{ord}_{s=s_0}\det(I-\mathcal L_{\mathcal B,s,\sigma})=\dim\ker(I-\mathcal L_{\mathcal B,s_0,\sigma}).\] The equality of zero order and geometric kernel dimension is the assertion examined here. The lemma does not impose the later condition \(s_0>1/2\) or the main theorem's lower bound on the limit-set dimension.

For a Fuchsian Schottky group \(\Gamma\), let \(\mathcal W^\circ\) be its nonempty reduced words, \(I_w\) the associated cylinder interval, \(\widetilde w\) the mirror word, and \(w'\) the word with its last letter removed. Page 11 calls a finite set \(\mathcal P\subset\mathcal W^\circ\) a partition if every sufficiently long word has a unique suffix in \(\mathcal P\). Lemma 13 asserts \(\sum_{w\in\mathcal P}|I_w|^{\delta_\Gamma}\asymp_\Gamma1\), and its proof treats these cylinder intervals as pairwise disjoint and covering the limit set.

Equation (2.9) defines \[\mathcal B(\tau)=\{w\in\mathcal W_{\ge2}:|I_{\widetilde w}|\le\tau<|I_{(\widetilde w)'}|\}.\] With \(L_\Gamma\) as defined in (2.6), Lemma 14 asserts that \(\widetilde{\mathcal B(\tau)}\) is a partition for every \(0<\tau<L_\Gamma\). One-letter stopping words are excluded by the displayed definition.
The proof of Lemma 10 assumes a norm \(\|\cdot\|_m\) on all of \(M_2(\mathbf R)\) satisfying \(\|AB\|_m=\|A\|_m\|B\|_m\), and uses it to prove \(\|\gamma_w\|\asymp_\Gamma|I_w|^{-1/2}\).

For distinct reduced words written \(w_1=AB_1C\), \(w_2=AB_2C\), with different initial and final letters in the middle blocks, equation (4.10) defines the counting sum with summand \(|I_A|^{\delta_\Gamma}|I_{B_2\widetilde B_2}|^{\delta_\Gamma/2}|I_C|^{\delta_\Gamma}\). Lemma 35 asserts that this sum is comparable to \(\tau^{\delta_\Gamma}\#P_n^*(\tau,a,c)\).

The auxiliary counting bound is stated for every \(\varepsilon>0\). In its summation, (4.21) uses \[\sum_{a,c\ge0,\ a+c\le N}2^{(\delta_\Gamma-\varepsilon)(a+c)}=\sum_{m=0}^N(m+1)2^{(\delta_\Gamma-\varepsilon)m}\ll_\Gamma N2^{(\delta_\Gamma-\varepsilon)N}.\] The proof of Proposition 3 also chooses \(C_\Gamma=\max\{\tau_\Gamma,L_\Gamma\}^{-1/2}\) and takes \(n>C_\Gamma\) to obtain the small-scale restrictions used with \(\tau=n^{-\alpha}\), \(\alpha>2\).

Let \(1\le r\le\infty\), let \(S_r\) be the standard symmetric generators of \(F_r\), and identify \(\partial F_r\) with infinite reduced words. Let \(m\) be a stationary Markov measure with positive initial distribution \(\pi\), row-stochastic transition matrix \(P\), and \(P(a,a^{-1})=0\), so that its support is contained in the reduced words. No positivity of every allowed transition is required. Write \(\mathbf P_m\) for the induced boundary probability, and let \(\overline f\) be conditional expectation onto the invariant Borel sets of the boundary action.

For \(f\in L^1(\partial F_r,\mathbf P_m)\), Theorem 1.2 claims that on one conull set of \(x\), for every sequence of finite left-Cayley subtrees \(\tau_n\) containing the identity and not \(x(0)^{-1}\), \[\frac{\sum_{w\in\tau_n}f(wx)m(w\mathbin{\frown}x(0))}{m(\tau_n\mathbin{\frown}x(0))}\longrightarrow\overline f(x)\] whenever \(m_u(\tau_n)\to\infty\), using the uniform Markov weight in this growth condition. Corollary 5.5(a) states the analogous assertion for \(f\in L^p\), \(1\le p<\infty\), with the growth condition instead written \(m(\tau)\to\infty\) over finite-height subtrees. In both displays the denominator uses the appended-letter weight \(m(\tau\mathbin{\frown}x(0))=\sum_{w\in\tau}m(w\mathbin{\frown}x(0))\).

Let \(T\) be a countable-to-one null-preserving Borel transformation of a standard probability space \((X,\mu)\), with the surjectivity and null-preserving orbit-relation convention of Assumption 2.5. Let \(\rho_x(y)\) be the Radon–Nikodym cocycle, and define the complete backward tree as the set \(\triangleright_T^N x=\bigcup_{i=0}^N T^{-i}(x)\). Lemma 3.8 asserts, for every \(N\in\mathbf N\) and \(f\in L^1(X,\mu)\), \[\int_X f\,d\mu=\int_X\frac1{N+1}\sum_{y\in\triangleright_T^N x}f(y)\rho_x(y)\,d\mu(x).\] No aperiodicity assumption is imposed in this lemma.

Under the additional assumption that \(T\) preserves \(\mu\), Lemma 3.10 states that \(\rho_x(T^{-n}x)=1\) for each \(n\), and concludes that \(\rho_x(\triangleright_T^N x)=N+1\) for every \(N\), almost everywhere. The union in the definition is an ordinary set union, so these claims use distinct points rather than counting a periodic point once at every level.

For an aperiodic countable-to-one measure-preserving transformation \(T\), let \(\Gamma\) be a complete system of Borel partial right inverses. A finite-height inverse-word tree \(\tau\) is \(c\)-fat if \(\rho_x(\tau\cdot x)/(h(\tau)+1)\ge c>0\) almost everywhere. In proving Corollary 4.15, the paper claims that the normalized averaging operators \(\widehat\tau_n\) of a sequence of \(c\)-fat trees have \(L^p\) operator norm bounded by \(c\), for \(1\le p<\infty\), uniformly in \(n\).

Section 5.E.i describes the uniform nonbacktracking transition matrix on \(S_r\), with \(\pi(a)=1/(2r)\), \(P(a,a^{-1})=0\) and \(P(a,b)=1/(2r-1)\) otherwise, and asserts irreducibility in the stated finite-rank range, which includes \(r=1\). Section 6 then explains weak mixing of a boundary action by saying that its product with every ergodic probability-preserving action is again weakly mixing.

Fix \(0<\alpha<1\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and \(\Omega_*=(-1,1)\times\mathbf R\). Let \(C_p^{k,\alpha}\) consist of functions even in both variables and \(2\pi\)-periodic in \(x\), and let \(X_k=\{u\in C_p^{k,\alpha}:u_t\in C^{k,\alpha}\}\), \(X_k^D=\{u\in X_k:u|_{t=\pm1}=0\}\), \(X_k^{DN}=\{u\in X_k^D:u_t|_{t=\pm1}=0\}\). Let \(\mu(\lambda)\) be the first positive Neumann eigenvalue of \(-U''+\lambda\tan(\lambda t)U'\) on \((0,1)\), and normalize its eigenfunction by \(U_\lambda(1)=1\).

Equations (6.9)–(6.11) define \[h_u(x)=\frac{u_t(1,x)}{U_\lambda''(1)},\qquad M_1u(t,x)=u(t,x)-tU_\lambda'(|t|)h_u(x).\] The paper asserts that \(M:u\mapsto(M_1u,h_u)\) is a well-defined linear map \(X_2^D\to X_2^{DN}\times C_p^{2,\alpha}(\mathbf R)\). The same expression \(-tU_\lambda'(|t|)h(x)\) is used for the first variation of \(U_\lambda(|t|/(1+h(x)))\) in (6.16).

Fix \(0<\alpha<1\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and \(\Omega_*=(-1,1)\times\mathbf R\). Let \(C_p^{k,\alpha}\) consist of functions even in both variables and \(2\pi\)-periodic in \(x\), and let \(X_k=\{u\in C_p^{k,\alpha}:u_t\in C^{k,\alpha}\}\), \(X_k^D=\{u\in X_k:u|_{t=\pm1}=0\}\), \(X_k^{DN}=\{u\in X_k^D:u_t|_{t=\pm1}=0\}\). Let \(\mu(\lambda)\) be the first positive Neumann eigenvalue of \(-U''+\lambda\tan(\lambda t)U'\) on \((0,1)\), and normalize its eigenfunction by \(U_\lambda(1)=1\).

Set \(b(t)=\lambda\tan(\lambda t)\), \(a(t)=\lambda^2/\cos^2(\lambda t)\), \(A=\partial_{tt}-b\partial_t+a\partial_{xx}\), and \(L_\lambda^0=A+\mu(\lambda)\). In the proof of Proposition 6.2 take \(f\in Y=C_p^{1,\alpha}(\Omega_*)+X_0^D\) and the Dirichlet solution \(u\in C_p^{2,\alpha}\cap X_0^D\) of \(Au=f\). For \(v=u_t\), equation (6.19) asserts the distributional identity \[L_\lambda^0v=\mu(\lambda)v+f_t-b'(t)v_t+a'(t)v_{xx}.\] This is used to obtain \(u_t\in C^{2,\alpha}\) and hence membership of \(u\) in \(X_2^D\).

For \(0<\lambda<1\), let \(\mu(\lambda)>0\) be the first positive Neumann eigenvalue on \([0,1]\), with eigenfunction \(U=U_\lambda\) normalized by \(U(1)=1\): \[-U''+\lambda\tan(\lambda t)U'=\mu U,\qquad U'(0)=U'(1)=0.\] Set \[\rho(\tau)=-\left(\cos\tau+\frac{1+\tau\tan\tau}{\cos\tau}\right).\] Equation (6.28) (article PDF page 28) asserts \[\mu'(\lambda)\int_0^1U(t)^2\cos(\lambda t)\,dt=\frac\lambda2\int_0^1\rho(\lambda t)U(t)^2\,dt.\] The proof on PDF page 29 consequently asserts \(\mu'(\lambda)\le-2\lambda\) and uses this estimate for the spectral crossing in Lemma 6.3. The displayed identity contains only the integral term.

For \(N\ge1\) and \(m\ge1\), let \(U_m\) be the \(m\)-th nonconstant radial Neumann eigenfunction on the unit ball \(B_1\subset\mathbf R^N\), normalized by \(U_m(1)=1\). Remark 1.3(i) asserts that \(U_m\) has \(m-1\) nondegenerate zeros in \((0,1)\), and that the bifurcating solution \(w_s\) in Theorem 1.2 has precisely \(m\) nodal domains in \(\Omega_{h_s}\) for sufficiently small \(s\). The claim uses the \(C^1\) expansion about \(U_m(|t|)\). Remark 1.4 explicitly includes \(N=1\), where \(U_m(|t|)=(-1)^m\cos(m\pi|t|)\).

In the cylindrical setting, \(\Omega_*=B_1\times\mathbf R\), functions are radial in \(t\in B_1\subset\mathbf R^N\) and even and periodic in \(x\). Write \(D_t=t\cdot\nabla_t\), let \(u_m(t,x)=U_m(|t|)\), and take \(u\in X_2^{DN}\) and \(h\in C_p^{2,\alpha}(\mathbf R)\) with \(h>-1\). The operator is defined by \(F_\lambda(u,h)=L_\lambda^{1+h}(u+u_m)\).

In the split \(F_\lambda=F_\lambda^1+F_\lambda^2\) used to prove Lemma 3.3, equation (3.6) gives \[F_\lambda^2(u,h)=\lambda u_{xx}+(1+h)^2(1-|t|^2)\Delta_t(u+u_m)+\lambda\left(\frac{h''}{h}-\frac{(h')^2}{h^2}\right)D_t(u+u_m).\] This is claimed to map \(X_2^{DN}\times\{h>-1\}\) into \(X_0^D\); its last coefficient is printed with denominators \(h\) and \(h^2\).

Fix \(0<\alpha<1\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and \(\Omega_*=(-1,1)\times\mathbf R\). Let \(C_p^{k,\alpha}\) consist of functions even in both variables and \(2\pi\)-periodic in \(x\), and let \(X_k=\{u\in C_p^{k,\alpha}:u_t\in C^{k,\alpha}\}\), \(X_k^D=\{u\in X_k:u|_{t=\pm1}=0\}\), \(X_k^{DN}=\{u\in X_k^D:u_t|_{t=\pm1}=0\}\). Let \(\mu(\lambda)\) be the first positive Neumann eigenvalue of \(-U''+\lambda\tan(\lambda t)U'\) on \((0,1)\), and normalize its eigenfunction by \(U_\lambda(1)=1\).

For \(u_\lambda(t,x)=U_\lambda(|t|)\) and \(h\in U_{S^2}=\{h\in C_p^{2,\alpha}(\mathbf R):h>2/\pi-1\}\), (6.7) defines \(F_\lambda(u,h)=L_\lambda^h(u+u_\lambda)\). Page 25 asserts the split \(F_\lambda=F_\lambda^1+F_\lambda^2\), where \[F_\lambda^1=(1+h)^2u_{tt}-\lambda(1+h)\tan\!\left(\frac{\lambda t}{1+h}\right)u_t+\frac{\lambda^2}{\cos^2(\lambda t/(1+h))}\left(\frac{(h')^2t^2}{(1+h)^2}u_{tt}+\frac{2h't}{1+h}u_{tx}\right)\] and \[F_\lambda^2=\mu(\lambda)u+\frac{\lambda^2}{\cos^2(\lambda t/(1+h))}\left(u_{xx}+\frac{h''t}{1+h}u_t\right).\] These displayed terms sum to \(L_\lambda^hu\), with the source function \(u_\lambda\) absent, and are asserted to take values in \(C_p^{1,\alpha}\) and \(X_0^D\), respectively.

Let \(0<\lambda_*<1\) be the crossing parameter in Proposition 6.4, and let \(\mu(\lambda_*)\) be the first positive Neumann eigenvalue of \(-\cos(\lambda_*t)^{-1}(\cos(\lambda_*t)u')'\) on \((0,1)\). Let \(\sigma_{2,0}(\lambda_*)\) be the second eigenvalue of the same operator minus \(\mu(\lambda_*)\), now with mixed conditions \(u'(0)=u(1)=0\). Writing \(H(0,1)=\{u\in H^1(0,1):u(1)=0\}\), the proof asserts \[\sigma_{2,0}(\lambda_*)=\inf_{\substack{0\ne u\in H(0,1)\\\int_0^1u(t)\cos(\lambda_*t)\,dt=0}}\frac{\int_0^1|u'|^2\cos(\lambda_*t)\,dt}{\int_0^1u^2\cos(\lambda_*t)\,dt}-\mu(\lambda_*).\] The orthogonality constraint in this printed second-eigenvalue characterization is to the constant function.

For \(0<\lambda<1\) and an integer Fourier mode \(\ell\ge0\), let \(\sigma_\ell(\lambda)\) and \(V_\lambda\) be the first eigenpair of \[-V''+\lambda\tan(\lambda t)V'+\frac{(\ell\lambda)^2}{\cos^2(\lambda t)}V-\mu(\lambda)V=\sigma_\ell(\lambda)V,\qquad V'(0)=V(1)=0,\] with \(V_\lambda(0)=1\). Put \(w_\lambda(t,x)=V_\lambda(|t|)\cos(\ell x)\) and \(L_\lambda^0=\mu(\lambda)+\partial_{tt}-\lambda\tan(\lambda t)\partial_t+\lambda^2\cos(\lambda t)^{-2}\partial_{xx}\). Page 31 states \[L_\lambda^0w_\lambda=\sigma_\ell(\lambda)w_\lambda.\] It differentiates this identity at the parameter \(\lambda_*\) with \(\sigma_\ell(\lambda_*)=0\), \(\sigma'_\ell(\lambda_*)>0\), to establish transversality.

In the setting of Lemma 3.4, let \(X\) be sufficiently large and \(\exp(C\sqrt{\log X\log\log X})\le H\le X^{1/2}\). The retained configuration \(\mathcal J\subset[X/(10K),2X/K]\times\mathbb R\) has \(H/K\)-separated first coordinates and cardinality \(\gg X/H\), where \(H^{\varepsilon^2}\le K\le H^\varepsilon\), \(PP'=K\), and \(P,P'\gg_{\rho,\eta}H^{\varepsilon^2}\). Fix disjoint prime sets \(\mathcal P_1,\mathcal P_2\subset[P,2P]\), each of size \(\gg P/\log P\). The configuration has \(\gg (X/H)(P/\log P)^2\) ordered quadruples \(((x_1,\alpha_1),(x_2,\alpha_2),p,q)\), with \(p\in\mathcal P_1\), \(q\in\mathcal P_2\), satisfying \(|x_1/p-x_2/q|\ll H/(PK)\) and \(\|p\alpha_1-q\alpha_2\|_{p'}\ll PK/H\) for \(\gg P'/\log P'\) auxiliary primes \(p'\in[P',2P']\); here \(\|\cdot\|_Q\) is distance to zero modulo \(Q\).

A split path modulo \(Q\) of length \(k\) is a pre-path as in Definition 2.3, with distinct primes \(p_i\in\mathcal P_1\), \(q_i\in\mathcal P_2\) not dividing \(Q\), phase errors \(O(PK/H)\), and ordered vertices \((x_i,\alpha_i)\in\mathcal J\) satisfying \(x_iq_i/p_i=x_{i+1}+O(H/K)\). Definition 3.8 calls a subset \(\mathcal J'\) \((c,Q)\)-regular if \(|\mathcal J'|\ge c|\mathcal J|\) and every vertex is connected to at least \(c(P/\log P)^2\) other vertices by a split path of length one. Lemma 3.9 supplies such subsets for \(\gg P'/\log P'\) auxiliary primes.

Let \(k_0=\lfloor\log(X/(HB\log X))/(2\log(2P))\rfloor\), with \(B\asymp1\) sufficiently large. For each \(\delta>0\), with \(\varepsilon\) sufficiently small relative to \(\delta\), \(C\) sufficiently large relative to \(\delta,\varepsilon\), and then \(X\) sufficiently large, Lemma 5.4 asserts the existence of \(\tau\asymp1\), a fixed \((x_0,\alpha_0)\in\mathcal J\), and \(\mathcal J_0\subset\mathcal J\) with \(|\mathcal J_0|\gg X/H^{1+\delta}\). For every \((y,\beta)\in\mathcal J_0\), there is a product \(Q_y\) of \(\gg\tau^{k_0}P'/\log P'\) distinct primes in \([P',2P']\) and two split paths modulo \(Q_y\), each of length \(k_0+2\), from the prescribed initial vertex \((x_0,\alpha_0)\) to \((y,\beta)\), sharing no prime.

Fix \(Q\in\mathbf N\) and pairwise distinct primes \(p_1,\ldots,p_k,q_1,\ldots,q_k\) not dividing \(Q\). A pre-path of length \(k\) consists of phases \(\alpha_i^{(1)},\alpha_{i+1}^{(0)}\in\mathbf R/Q\mathbf Z\) with \[\|q_i\alpha_{i+1}^{(1)}-\alpha_{i+1}^{(0)}\|_Q<\varepsilon_i,\qquad\|p_i\alpha_i^{(1)}-\alpha_{i+1}^{(0)}\|_Q<\varepsilon'_i,\] where \(\|\cdot\|_Q\) is distance to zero modulo \(Q\) and all allocated errors are positive. Lemma 2.2 recursively chooses higher rows of a pyramid so that the two newly lifted errors are bounded by \(\varepsilon_i/q_i\) and \(\varepsilon_i'/p_i\).

Lemma 2.4 assumes \(\varepsilon_i=\varepsilon_i'=\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and makes a bound for every associated pyramid. In its induction step, (2.1) asserts the stronger relation between the actual residuals \[\|q_k\alpha_1^{(k+1)}-\alpha_1^{(k)}\|_Q\le\frac{\|p_1\alpha_1^{(k)}-\alpha_2^{(k-1)}\|_Q}{p_1}.\] The right-hand side here is the realized previous discrepancy, rather than the allocated error bound used in the construction.

Let \(m,n\) be nonzero integers with \(|m|<|n|\) and \(m\mid n\), and let \[\operatorname{BS}(m,n)=\langle a,t\mid ta^mt^{-1}=a^n\rangle.\] Its standard \(a\)-lines and \(t\)-lines are left cosets of \(\langle a\rangle\) and \(\langle t\rangle\). Let \(\Lambda\) be their bipartite intersection graph, with an edge exactly when two lines intersect, and identify its \(a\)-type vertices with vertices of the oriented Bass–Serre tree \(T\). For vertices \(u_i,u_j\), put \(\Lambda_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_\Lambda(u_i)\cap\operatorname{lk}_\Lambda(u_j)\).

Lemma 3.9 (article PDF page 21) assumes that \(u_1,u_2\) are strictly comparable \(a\)-type vertices in the partial order defined by positive \(t\)-edges. It asserts that their images \(\bar u_1,\bar u_2\) are adjacent in \(T\) if and only if \(\Lambda_{12}\ne\varnothing\) and there do not exist \(u_3,u_4\in\Lambda^{(0)}\) satisfying \[\Lambda_{12}\subseteq\Lambda_{34},\qquad \Lambda_{34}=\Lambda_{3i}\quad\text{for some }i\in\{1,2\}.\] The stated witness domain neither excludes \(u_1,u_2\) nor requires the four vertices to be distinct.

On the Airy spectral curve \(S=\mathbf P^1\), \(x=z^2/2\), \(y=z\), with bidifferential \(B=dz_1dz_2/(z_1-z_2)^2\), write \(x_i=z_i^2/2\) and \(D_i=D_{-x_i}\). For a one-form, \(D_i(f\,dz_i)=-\partial_{z_i}(f/z_i)\,dz_i\); on a bidifferential it acts in the indicated variable.

Equation (7.20) asserts, for \(k\ge0\), the meromorphic differential identity \[(D_1+D_2)^{k+1}\frac{dz_1dz_2}{(z_1-z_2)^{2(k+1)}}=\frac{(2k+1)!!\,dx_1dx_2}{(x_1x_2)^{2k+2}}=\frac{(D_1D_2)^{k+1}(dx_1dx_2)}{(2k+1)!!}.\] The two right-hand expressions use \(x_i,dx_i\) exactly as printed.

On the Airy spectral curve \(S=\mathbf P^1\), \(x=z^2/2\), \(y=z\), with bidifferential \(B=dz_1dz_2/(z_1-z_2)^2\), write \(x_i=z_i^2/2\) and \(D_i=D_{-x_i}\). For a one-form, \(D_i(f\,dz_i)=-\partial_{z_i}(f/z_i)\,dz_i\); on a bidifferential it acts in the indicated variable.

For the two-point genus-\(g\) differential, the second line of (7.19) states \[\omega_{2,0}^{(g)}=\sum_{\substack{i,k\ge0\\i+k=g}}\frac{(D_1^3+D_1^3)^i(D_1+D_2)^{2k}}{24^i i!4^k}\frac{dz_1dz_2}{(z_1-z_2)^{2(k+1)}}.\] After the diagonal-pole cancellation for \(g>0\), equation (7.21) writes \[\omega_{2,0}^{(g)}=\sum_{\substack{i,k\ge0\\i+k=g}}\frac{(D_1^3+D_1^3)^i(D_1+D_2)^{k-1}(D_1D_2)^{k+1}}{24^i i!4^k(2k+1)!!}\,dz_1dz_2.\] Both displayed operator factors repeat \(D_1^3\) in the second summand; the generating exponential in the preceding line contains \(w_1^3+w_2^3\).

Let \(F\) be a finite extension of \(\mathbf Q_p\), with \(p\ne2\), and let \(G=\operatorname{SO}(Q)(F)\) for a maximally isotropic nondegenerate quadratic form \(Q\) of dimension \(d\ne2\). Thus \(G\) is split special orthogonal. Proposition B.1 asserts that \(G\) has a level-zero cuspidal representation whose standard local transfer to \(\operatorname{GL}_N(F)\) is cuspidal, where \(N=d-1\) for odd \(d\) and \(N=d\) for even \(d\). In particular, its original range includes split \(\operatorname{SO}_{2n}\), \(n\ge2\).

Let \(F/\mathbf Q_p\) be finite with \(p\) odd, let \(G\) be quasi-split special orthogonal, unitary or symplectic over \(F\), excluding split \(\operatorname{SO}_2\), and let \(\ell\ne p\) be a prime. Section 9 chooses a totally real globalization \((k,w,\mathbf G)\) as in Theorem 2.1 and its specified refinements: \(k_w=F\), \(\mathbf G(F)\simeq G\), \(\mathbf G(k_v)\) compact at every real place and quasi-split at every finite place. In the unitary case \(l/k\) is the associated quadratic extension; otherwise \(l=k\).

Lemma 9.1 asserts that there is a finite place \(u\ne w\), with \(u\nmid\ell\), and a unitary irreducible cuspidal complex representation \(\rho\) of \(\mathbf G(k_u)\) which is compactly induced from a compact-mod-center open subgroup and whose standard transfer to \(\operatorname{GL}_N(l_u)\) is cuspidal. Its symplectic proof chooses \(k_u\simeq\mathbf Q_2\) and invokes Theorem C.1. The coefficient-prime range still includes \(\ell=2\).

Theorem 3.17 further assumes \(|\Lambda_j|\le C2^{cj}\), \(d_{j,n}\ge2^{dj}\), \(\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1\le Cs^{1/2-p}\), and \(\|P_{\Lambda_j}^\perp x^\dagger\|_2\le C2^{-aj}\), with \(a,c,p,C>0\) and \(0\le d\le b\). Theorem 4.6 makes the analogous assertion for the Radon or fan beam transform of \(u^\dagger\in L^2(B_1)\), using the specified compactly supported wavelet basis, independent uniform angles, and noise bounded by \(\beta\). Its program (16) minimizes \(\|\Phi u\|_1\) on the wavelets of scales at most \(j_0\), with residual radius \(\beta+C_3 2^{-j_0/2}r\), where \(r\ge\|P_{\Lambda_{j_0}}^\perp\Phi u^\dagger\|_2\). Let \(\chi,\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R)\) be compactly supported scaling and mother wavelet functions chosen so that \(\{\chi_n\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\cup\{\psi_{j,n}\}_{j\in\mathbb N,n\in\mathbb Z}\) is an orthonormal basis of \(L^2(\mathbb R)\). Here \(\mathbb N\) denotes the positive integers, \(\chi_n=\tau_n\chi\), \(\psi_{j,n}=D^1_{j-1}\tau_n\psi\), \(D^1_jf=2^{j/2}f(2^j\cdot)\), and \(\tau_nf=f(\cdot-n)\).

The two-dimensional construction sets \(\chi_{n_1,n_2}=\chi_{n_1}\otimes\chi_{n_2}\), \(\psi^{(1)}_{0,n_1,n_2}=\psi_{0,n_1}\otimes\chi_{n_2}\), \(\psi^{(2)}_{0,n_1,n_2}=\chi_{n_1}\otimes\psi_{0,n_2}\), and \(\psi^{(3)}_{0,n_1,n_2}=\psi_{0,n_1}\otimes\psi_{0,n_2}\). It then defines \(\psi^{(\epsilon)}_{j,n_1,n_2}=D^2_j\psi^{(\epsilon)}_{0,n_1,n_2}\), where \(D^2_jf=2^jf(2^j\cdot)\), and asserts that the scaling functions together with these wavelets, \(j\ge1\), \(\epsilon\in\{1,2,3\}\), form an orthonormal basis of \(L^2(\mathbb R^2)\).

For every compact set \(K\subset\mathbb R^2\), define \(\mathcal R_\theta u(s)=\int_{e_\theta^\perp}u(y+se_\theta)\,dy\), where \(e_\theta=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), initially on a dense class in \(L^2(K)\). Let \(\mathcal Ru(\theta,s)=\mathcal R_\theta u(s)\). Lemma 4.2 asserts that \(\mathcal R_\theta:L^2(K)\to L^2(\mathbb R)\) and \(\mathcal R:L^2(K)\to L^2([0,2\pi)\times\mathbb R)\) extend continuously, and that their operator norms are bounded, uniformly in \(\theta\), by a constant depending only on the area \(|K|\).

Let \(0<d<\rho\), \(u\in L^2(B_d)\), and \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\). Definition 4.3 sets \(\mathcal D_\theta u(\alpha)=\int_{\mathbb R}u(\rho e_\theta+te_{\theta+\alpha})\,dt\), for \(-\pi/2<\alpha<\pi/2\). For the compactly supported, \(L^2\)-normalized wavelet atoms \(\phi_{j,n}\), whose intersection with any line has length at most \(C2^{-j}\), the coherence proof asserts \[\|\mathcal D_\theta\phi_{j,n}\|_2^2\le\frac{C2^{-j}}{\rho-d}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_{\mathbb R}|\phi_{j,n}(\rho e_\theta+te_{\theta+\alpha})|^2t\,dt\,d\alpha=\frac{C2^{-j}}{\rho-d}.\] This is the stated change-of-variables step leading to the uniform estimate \(\|F_\theta\phi_{j,n}\|_2\le B2^{-j/2}\) for the fan beam transform.

For an invertible \(G\in\mathcal L(\ell^2(\Lambda))\), weights \(\omega_i\ge1\), \(0<\delta<1\), and \(\lambda>0\), the generalized restricted isometry property means \((1-\delta)\|Gx\|_2^2\le\|Ax\|^2\le(1+\delta)\|Gx\|_2^2\) for every \(x\) with weighted support size \(\sum_{i:x_i\ne0}\omega_i^2\le\lambda\). Theorem 5.6 assumes \(0<\rho'<1/2\), \(s\ge\|\omega\|_\infty^2/4\), and \[\lambda\ge\frac{5}{(\rho')^2}\frac{1+\delta}{1-\delta}\|G^{-1}\|^2\|G\|^2s,\] to deduce the robust null-space property with parameters \(\rho=\rho'/(1-\rho')\) and \(\kappa=\|G^{-1}\|/((1-\rho')\sqrt{1-\delta})\).

In the proof of Theorem 3.5, the chosen sparsity level is instead displayed as \(\lambda=C_0\|G^{-1}\|^2\|G\|s\). After establishing generalized RIP for \(QA\) with \(\delta=1/2\), the proof invokes Theorem 5.6 with \(\rho'=1/3\) to conclude the robust null-space property. Here \(G=(P_\Lambda\Phi F^*F\Phi^*\iota_\Lambda)^{1/2}\) is assumed invertible in the Section 2.2 measurement setting; no normalization \(\|G\|\le1\) is among the stated hypotheses.

For a group \(G\) and integers \(i\le m\), the introduction defines \(C_{i,m}(G)\) as the minimum number of simplices of dimension at most \(i\) in an \(m\)-dimensional simplicial complex \(\overline L\) with \(\pi_1(\overline L)=G\) and \((m-1)\)-connected universal cover; the value is \(\infty\) if no such complex exists. It then asserts \(C_{1,1}(G)\asymp\operatorname{rank}(G)\).

Section 8 describes \(C_{i,m}(G)\) instead as the minimum number of \(G\)-orbits of cells of dimension at most \(i\) among free cocompact actions on \((m-1)\)-connected, \(m\)-dimensional simplicial complexes. It states that every hyperbolic group has type \(F_\infty\), and hence that \(C_{i,m}(G)\) is well-defined and finite for every \(i\le m\).

The paper defines a free simplicial action \(G\curvearrowright X\) to mean that every simplex stabilizer is trivial, equivalently that the action on the geometric realization is free. It asserts that one barycentric subdivision \(\dot X\) has a simplicial quotient \(\dot X/G\), and thereafter includes existence of a simplicial quotient in its convention for a free simplicial action.

Theorem B states that for every locally finite one-ended hyperbolic graph \(X\), there is \(m\), with \(m=\dim\partial X+1\) sufficient, such that every free cocompact action satisfies \(\operatorname{Vol}(X/G)\asymp_X C_{2,m}(G)\). The deduction of Theorem C takes \(X=\operatorname{Cay}(G,S)\) for an arbitrary one-ended hyperbolic group \(G\), with no torsion-free assumption, and asserts that every finite-index subgroup \(H\le G\) acts freely and cocompactly on this Cayley graph. It therefore concludes \([G:H]\asymp_G C_{2,m}(H)\).

Let \(\varphi\in\operatorname{Out}(F_d)\) be an atoroidal outer automorphism of the free group \(F_d\). Corollary 1.1 asserts \(F_d\rtimes\langle\varphi^m\rangle\cong F_d\rtimes\langle\varphi^n\rangle\) if and only if \(|m|=|n|\). Its proof sets \(G=F_d\rtimes\langle\varphi\rangle\) and states that, for every integer \(k\), the group \(F_d\rtimes\langle\varphi^k\rangle\) is a subgroup of \(G\) of index \(|k|\), without excluding \(k=0\).

Proposition 7.1 assumes that \(Y\) is a hyperbolic simplicial complex with a proper cocompact group action, that \(m=\dim\partial Y+1\), and that \(Y\) is \(m\)-dimensional and \((m-1)\)-connected. It asserts a constant \(\xi=\xi(Y)\) such that, for every group \(G\) acting properly and cocompactly on \(Y\), every \(m\)-dimensional, \((m-1)\)-connected simplicial complex \(L\) with a proper cocompact \(G\)-action, and every continuous \(G\)-equivariant quasi-isometry \(\Phi:L\to Y\), one has \(N_\xi(\Phi(L))=Y\).

In the lower-bound proof of Theorem B, \(X\) is a locally finite one-ended hyperbolic graph with a free cocompact \(G\)-action and \(m=\dim\partial X+1\). The chosen target \(Y\) is a contractible Rips complex of \(X\), and \(L\) realizes \(C_{2,m}(G)\). The proof extends the map on \(K=L^{(2)}\) to a continuous equivariant quasi-isometry \(\Phi:L\to Y\), invokes Proposition 7.1 for this \(Y\), and concludes \(X\subset Y\subset N_{\delta_1}(\Phi(K^{(1)}))\), with \(\delta_1\) depending only on \(X\).

Let \(\phi\) be a transitive Anosov flow on a closed oriented three-manifold, with oriented stable and unstable foliations, and let \(\mathcal P=(R_1,\ldots,R_p)\) be a Markov partition. Write \(\Sigma_{\mathcal P}\) for its symbolic space, \(\sigma\) for the shift, and \(\Theta_{\mathcal P}\) for the map from invariant signed symbolic measures to invariant flow measures. The reduction \(N_R\) replaces the word segment between consecutive visits to \(R\), containing the present time, by its periodic repetition. Set \(N_k=N_{R_k}\circ\cdots\circ N_{R_1}\) and \(N=N_p\). The notation \(N_k^*\) denotes the induced map on measures.

Let \(\phi\) be a transitive Anosov flow on a closed oriented three-manifold. For a periodic orbit \(\gamma\) of period \(T_\gamma\), \(\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma\) is the pushforward of Lebesgue measure on \([0,T_\gamma]\), so its mass is \(T_\gamma\). Lemma 14 asserts that every invariant signed measure \(\mu\), and every finite union \(\Delta\) of periodic orbits, admit algebraic multi-orbits \(\Gamma_n\) with rational coefficients such that \(\operatorname{Leb}_{\Gamma_n}\to\mu\) weakly, \(\operatorname{supp}\Gamma_n\cap\Delta=\varnothing\), and \([\operatorname{Leb}_{\Gamma_n}]_\phi=[\mu]_\phi\) for every \(n\). If \(\Delta=\varnothing\) and \(\mu\) is a probability measure, the lemma additionally claims that every \(\operatorname{Leb}_{\Gamma_n}\) can be a probability measure.

Lemma 31 applies this density statement to a positive Birkhoff section \(S\), whose boundary is a positive algebraic multi-orbit. If every orbit arc of length \(T\) meets \(S\), its proof establishes \(\operatorname{link}_\phi(\operatorname{Leb}_{\partial S},\operatorname{Leb}_\Gamma)\ge T^{-1}\operatorname{Leb}_\Gamma(M)\) for positive integral multi-orbits \(\Gamma\) disjoint from \(\partial S\). Invoking Lemma 14 and continuity, it concludes \(\operatorname{link}_\phi(\operatorname{Leb}_{\partial S},\mu)\ge1/T\) for every null-homologous invariant probability measure \(\mu\), and hence that \(\operatorname{Leb}_{\partial S}\) is Reeb-like.

For a positive continuous function \(f:M\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), the paper defines a reparametrized flow \(\psi^f\) by \(f\,\partial_t\psi_t^f=\partial_t\phi_t\). For compact surfaces \(S_i\) transverse to \(\phi\), let \(T^1_{i,j}(x)\) be the original short return time from \(S_i\) to \(S_j\), on its domain \(U_{i,j}\). The atlas construction seeks \(f\in[1,2]\) for which the new short return times are \(C^{1+H}\) in the transverse atlas.

For any continuous \(g:U_{i,j}\to[1,2]\), the construction preceding the proof of Proposition 48 prescribes the constant value \(f(\phi_t(x))=T^1_{i,j}(x)g(x)\) on each intervening orbit segment, with \(t\) between \(0\) and \(T^1_{i,j}(x)\). It asserts that this makes the new short return time \(T^f_{i,j}(x)\) equal to \(g(x)\), and hence as regular as \(g\).

In the thermodynamic formalism for a transitive Anosov flow \(\phi\), let \(\mu_p\) be the invariant Gibbs probability measure of a Holder potential \(p\). Let \(\gamma\) be a periodic orbit, \(U\) a neighborhood of \(\gamma\), and \(D>C>0\). Lemma 38 assumes \(p\le D\) everywhere, \(p=D\) on \(\gamma\), and \(p\le C\) outside \(U\), and asserts \(\mu_p(M\setminus U)\le h_{\mathrm{top}}(\phi)/(D-C)\).

The proof uses \(D=\int_M p\,d\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma\) and compares \(\int p\,d\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma+h_{\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma}(\phi)\) with the maximizing pressure of \(\mu_p\). The paper's convention is that \(\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma\) has total mass equal to the orbit period \(T_\gamma\); the lemma imposes no condition \(T_\gamma=1\).

In Section 5, let \(\phi\) be a transitive Anosov flow on a closed oriented three-manifold with oriented stable and unstable foliations. Fix a primitive cyclic Markov word \(r\) and a rectangle \(R\), and decompose \(r=s_1\cdots s_n\), \(n\ge2\), so that each \(s_i\) visits \(R\) once. Set \(\Gamma=\gamma_r-\sum_i\gamma_{s_i}\). The proof of Lemma 87 constructs curves \(a_i,b_i\subset R\), an adapted two-chain \(C\) with \(\partial C=\sum_i(a_i+b_i)\), and flow strips \(e_i\) with \(\partial e_i=a_i+b_i+\gamma_{s_i}-\operatorname{segment}_i(r)\), where the segments concatenate to \(\gamma_r\).

It defines \(S=\sum_i e_i-C\) and claims \(\partial S=\Gamma\). For a null-homologous algebraic multi-orbit \(\Gamma'\) disjoint from \(\Gamma\), with the strips \(e_i\) chosen disjoint from \(\Gamma'\), it also uses \(\operatorname{link}^{ff}_\phi(\operatorname{Leb}_\Gamma,\operatorname{Leb}_{\Gamma'})=S\cdot\Gamma'=C\cdot\Gamma'\). These are the oriented-chain identities used to obtain the positive local-kernel formula in Lemma 87.

For a transitive Anosov flow \(\phi\) on a closed oriented three-manifold, let \(\mathcal M_s(\phi)\) denote invariant signed measures and \(\mathcal M_p^0(\phi)\) the invariant probability measures whose homology class is zero. Definition 20 calls \(\mu\in\mathcal M_s(\phi)\) Reeb-like if \([\mu]_\phi=0\) and \[\min_{
u\in\mathcal M_p^0(\phi)}\operatorname{link}_\phi(\mu,
u)>0.\] The definition does not assume \(\mathcal M_p^0(\phi)
e\varnothing\) or supply an empty-set convention. Theorem H explicitly includes the case in which there is no null-homologous invariant probability measure.

Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, and consider the continuous representatives of maps in \(V^1L^{n,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega,\mathbb R^n)\), meaning weakly differentiable maps whose gradients belong locally to the Lorentz space \(L^{n,1}\). The introduction states that these maps have the Lusin \(N\) property. It then asserts that, for any prescribed \(\alpha\in(0,n]\), a map in this class can send a set \(E\) with \(\mathcal H^\alpha(E)=0\) to a set with \(\mathcal H^n(u(E))>0\), as an inference from possible image Hausdorff dimension \(n\). The discussion includes \(n=1\), where the stated class coincides with \(V^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

Let \(n\ge1\) and let \(A\) be a Young function with \(0<A(t)<\infty\) for \(t>0\). The standing endpoint assumptions are \(\lim_{t\to\infty}t/A(t)=0\) and \(\lim_{t\to0^+}t/A(t)=\infty\) when \(n=1\); when \(n\ge2\), they are \(\int_1^\infty(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt<\infty\) and \(\int_0^1(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt=\infty\). Put \(B=A\) for \(n=1\); for \(n\ge2\), \(B\) is the Young conjugate of \(t\mapsto t^{n'}\int_t^\infty\widetilde A(s)s^{-1-n'}ds\), where \(n'=n/(n-1)\) and \(\widetilde A\) is the Young conjugate of \(A\).

Let \(\varphi\) be a continuous increasing gauge, vanishing only at zero, such that \(\varphi(s)/s^n\) is nonincreasing. The construction defines \(J(s)=sB^{-1}(\varphi(s)/s^n)\), \(J(0)=0\), and \(\psi(r)=\varphi(J^{-1}(r))\).

The Hausdorff measure \(\mathcal H^\varphi\) is defined using sums of \(\varphi(\operatorname{diam}E_i)\), with no additional normalization. Under the standing gauge condition, the statement preceding (2.6) asserts literal inequality \(\mathcal H^\varphi\ne\mathcal L^n\) if and only if \(\lim_{r\to0^+}\varphi(r)/r^n=\infty\). Remark 3.2 asserts the exact equality \(\psi(r)=r^n\) when \(\varphi(r)=r^n\), for every admissible \(A\). Equation (3.24) likewise asserts \(\psi(r)=r^{\alpha p/(p+\alpha-n)}\) for \(A(t)=t^p\), \(p>n\), and \(\varphi(r)=r^\alpha\), \(0<\alpha\le n\).

Let \(n,m\ge1\), \(p>n\), \(0<\alpha\le n\), and \(u\in V^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^m)\), so \(u\) is weakly differentiable and \(\nabla u\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)\). Example 3.6 asserts, for every \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[\mathcal H_\infty^{\alpha p/(\alpha+p-n)}(u(E))\le 2c_n p^{\alpha/(\alpha+p-n)}\left(\frac{p-1}{n'-p'}\right)^{\alpha(p-1)/(\alpha+p-n)}\|\nabla u\|_p^{\alpha p/(\alpha+p-n)}\bigl(\mathcal H_\infty^\alpha(E)\bigr)^{(p-n)/(\alpha+p-n)}.\] Here \(c_n\) is the dimensional covering constant, \(p'=p/(p-1)\), and \(n'\) is the conjugate exponent of \(n\). The displayed constant is asserted without an exception for the admitted dimension \(n=1\).

Let \(n\ge1\) and let \(A\) be a Young function with \(0<A(t)<\infty\) for \(t>0\). The standing endpoint assumptions are \(\lim_{t\to\infty}t/A(t)=0\) and \(\lim_{t\to0^+}t/A(t)=\infty\) when \(n=1\); when \(n\ge2\), they are \(\int_1^\infty(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt<\infty\) and \(\int_0^1(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt=\infty\). Put \(B=A\) for \(n=1\); for \(n\ge2\), \(B\) is the Young conjugate of \(t\mapsto t^{n'}\int_t^\infty\widetilde A(s)s^{-1-n'}ds\), where \(n'=n/(n-1)\) and \(\widetilde A\) is the Young conjugate of \(A\).

Let \(\varphi\) be a continuous increasing gauge, vanishing only at zero, such that \(\varphi(s)/s^n\) is nonincreasing. The construction defines \(J(s)=sB^{-1}(\varphi(s)/s^n)\), \(J(0)=0\), and \(\psi(r)=\varphi(J^{-1}(r))\).

Lemma 4.3 asserts that \(\psi\) is an increasing continuous gauge and \(\psi(r)/r^n\) is nonincreasing. Its proof identifies this last condition with monotonicity of \(\varphi(s)/J(s)^n\) and uses the displayed identity \[\frac{\varphi(s)}{J(s)^n}=\frac{\varphi(s)/s^n}{B^{-1}(\varphi(s)/s^n)}\qquad(s>0),\] followed by the monotonicity of \(v/B^{-1}(v)\). This is equation (4.20) as printed.

Let \(n\ge1\) and let \(A\) be a Young function with \(0<A(t)<\infty\) for \(t>0\). The standing endpoint assumptions are \(\lim_{t\to\infty}t/A(t)=0\) and \(\lim_{t\to0^+}t/A(t)=\infty\) when \(n=1\); when \(n\ge2\), they are \(\int_1^\infty(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt<\infty\) and \(\int_0^1(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt=\infty\). Put \(B=A\) for \(n=1\); for \(n\ge2\), \(B\) is the Young conjugate of \(t\mapsto t^{n'}\int_t^\infty\widetilde A(s)s^{-1-n'}ds\), where \(n'=n/(n-1)\) and \(\widetilde A\) is the Young conjugate of \(A\).

Let \(\varphi\) be a continuous increasing gauge, vanishing only at zero, such that \(\varphi(s)/s^n\) is nonincreasing. The construction defines \(J(s)=sB^{-1}(\varphi(s)/s^n)\), \(J(0)=0\), and \(\psi(r)=\varphi(J^{-1}(r))\).

In the critical case of Example 3.9, suppose \(A(t)\asymp t^n(\log t)^q\) near infinity, with \(q>n-1\), and \(\varphi(s)\asymp(\log(1/s))^\beta\) near zero, with \(\beta<0\). The \(\alpha=0\) branch of (3.28) asserts \[J^{-1}(r)\asymp\exp\!\left(-r^{-n/(q-n+1-\beta)}\right)\qquad(r\to0^+),\] where \(\asymp\) means comparison by positive multiplicative constants, as specified in the introduction. The preceding display for \(J(s)\), containing powers of \(\log(1/s)\), labels its regime as near infinity. The resulting gauge claimed in (3.26) is \(\psi(r)\asymp r^{n\beta/(\beta+n-1-q)}\) near zero.

Let \(n\ge1\) and let \(A\) be a Young function with \(0<A(t)<\infty\) for \(t>0\). The standing endpoint assumptions are \(\lim_{t\to\infty}t/A(t)=0\) and \(\lim_{t\to0^+}t/A(t)=\infty\) when \(n=1\); when \(n\ge2\), they are \(\int_1^\infty(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt<\infty\) and \(\int_0^1(t/A(t))^{1/(n-1)}dt=\infty\). Put \(B=A\) for \(n=1\); for \(n\ge2\), \(B\) is the Young conjugate of \(t\mapsto t^{n'}\int_t^\infty\widetilde A(s)s^{-1-n'}ds\), where \(n'=n/(n-1)\) and \(\widetilde A\) is the Young conjugate of \(A\).

Let \(m\ge n\), \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, and \(u\in V^{1,A}(\Omega,\mathbb R^m)\). Set \(\Phi_B(v)=v[B^{-1}(1/v)]^n\) for \(v>0\) and \(\Phi_B(0)=0\). Theorem 3.7 asserts, for every \(E\subset\Omega\), \[\mathcal H_\infty^n(u(E))\le2\kappa^{n+1}\|\nabla u\|_{L^A(\Omega)}^n\,\Phi_B\!\left(\frac{n^{n/2}\mathcal L^n(E)}\kappa\right),\] where \(\kappa\) is the Orlicz-Morrey constant from (2.28).

For sets with compact closure in \(\Omega\), the proof labels the image quantity in (5.28) as \(\mathcal L^n(u(E))\) and writes \[\mathcal L^n(u(E))\le\bigl(\kappa\|\nabla u\|_{L^A(\Omega)}B^{-1}(r)\bigr)^n\left(n^{n/2}\mathcal L^n(E)+\frac\kappa r\right)\qquad(r>0).\] In the zero-volume case \(\mathcal L^n(E)=0\), it sends \(r\to0^+\) to obtain the zero-image conclusion. These image labels and this limiting direction are used with the full hypothesis \(m\ge n\), not only \(m=n\).

u}\) near zero. Put \(\sigma=n

u)\), fix \(\mu>1+\sigma\), and let \(\phi(r)\asymp r^\sigma(\log(1/r))^\mu\) near zero. Theorem 6.2 asserts a map \(u\in V^{1,A}(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n)\) and a compact set \(E\) such that \(0<\mathcal H^\varphi(E)<\infty\) and \(\mathcal H^\phi(u(E))=\infty\).

Its proof prescribes, for every integer \(j\ge1\), a family \(\mathcal A_j\) of distinct dyadic cubes in \([0,1]^n\), all of side \(2^{-2^j}\), with \(\#\mathcal A_j=\lfloor2^{j\nu}\rfloor\). Every level-\(j+1\) cube lies in a level-\(j\) cube. For \(M=\bigcap_j\bigcup_{Q\in\mathcal A_j}Q\), the construction asserts \(0<\mathcal H^\varphi(M)<\infty\), a uniform bound \(\mathcal H^\varphi(Q\cap M)\le c2^{-j}\) for every \(Q\in\mathcal A_j\), and a uniform upper bound on the number of children of each cube. These are the construction data in (6.12)–(6.15) used in the subsequent finite-energy argument.

Let \(M\) be Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^N\) or a smooth orientable compact Riemannian \(N\)-manifold without boundary. Let \(\Omega=\Omega^-\subset M\) have compatibly oriented Lipschitz boundary \(\Gamma\), with \(\Omega\) bounded in the Euclidean case, and put \(\Omega^+=M\setminus\operatorname{Int}\Omega\). The operators are \(D=d+\delta\) and \(-\Delta_\ell=d_{\ell-1}\delta_\ell+\delta_{\ell+1}d_\ell\), with tangential and normal traces \(t,n\). Assumption A allows \(\kappa\in\mathbb R\), \(\lambda\ge0\) in Euclidean space, and requires \(\kappa>0\), \(\lambda>0\) when \(M\) is compact.

Writing \(S^\lambda_\ell\) for the atomic single-layer potential, (3.15a) defines \((h,v)_{-1/2,\lambda,t}=\langle h,t_\ell S^\lambda_\ell\overline v\rangle_\Gamma\) on \(H^{-1/2}_\parallel\Lambda^\ell(\Gamma)\), and asserts that this is an inner product. Theorem 3.6 asserts \[\|h\|_{H^{-1/2}_\parallel\Lambda^\ell(\Gamma)}^2\lesssim(h,h)_{-1/2,\lambda,t}\] for every density in that trace space, under Assumption A. The parallel normal-potential form is also asserted to be an inner product and coercive on its normal trace space.

Lemma 3.5 identifies the single-layer boundary quadratic form with the whole-manifold energy \(\lambda\|S^\lambda_\ell h\|_{L^2(M)}^2+\|d_\ell S^\lambda_\ell h\|_{L^2(M)}^2+\|\delta_\ell S^\lambda_\ell h\|_{L^2(M)}^2\). The coercivity proof invokes equivalence of this energy norm with the inhomogeneous \(H^1(M)\) norm. These assertions include the scalar degree \(\ell=0\), dimension \(N=2\), and parameter \(\lambda=0\), without a charge or domain-size restriction.

Let \(M\) be Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^N\) or a smooth orientable compact Riemannian \(N\)-manifold without boundary. Let \(\Omega=\Omega^-\subset M\) have compatibly oriented Lipschitz boundary \(\Gamma\), with \(\Omega\) bounded in the Euclidean case, and put \(\Omega^+=M\setminus\operatorname{Int}\Omega\). The operators are \(D=d+\delta\) and \(-\Delta_\ell=d_{\ell-1}\delta_\ell+\delta_{\ell+1}d_\ell\), with tangential and normal traces \(t,n\). Assumption A allows \(\kappa\in\mathbb R\), \(\lambda\ge0\) in Euclidean space, and requires \(\kappa>0\), \(\lambda>0\) when \(M\) is compact.

At \(\kappa=0\), consider \(DU=0\) in \(H\Lambda(D,\Omega)=H\Lambda(d,\Omega)\cap H\Lambda(\delta,\Omega)\), with either prescribed tangential trace \(tU=g\in H^{-1/2}_\perp\Lambda(d,\Gamma)\), or normal trace \(nU=h\in H^{-1/2}_\parallel\Lambda(\delta,\Gamma)\). The harmonic kernels are \(\ker D_t=\{V:dV=\delta V=0,\ tV=0\}\) and \(\ker D_n=\{V:dV=\delta V=0,\ nV=0\}\).

Equations (2.5a,b) assert that the tangential problem is well-posed on \((\ker D_t)^\perp\) provided \(\langle g,nV\rangle_\Gamma=0\) for every \(V\in\ker D_n\), and that the normal problem is well-posed on \((\ker D_n)^\perp\) provided \(\langle h,tV\rangle_\Gamma=0\) for every \(V\in\ker D_t\). In the augmented normal variational formulation (2.9b), the right-hand side is printed as \(\langle h,nV\rangle_\Gamma\).

Let \(M\) be Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^N\) or a smooth orientable compact Riemannian \(N\)-manifold without boundary. Let \(\Omega=\Omega^-\subset M\) have compatibly oriented Lipschitz boundary \(\Gamma\), with \(\Omega\) bounded in the Euclidean case, and put \(\Omega^+=M\setminus\operatorname{Int}\Omega\). The operators are \(D=d+\delta\) and \(-\Delta_\ell=d_{\ell-1}\delta_\ell+\delta_{\ell+1}d_\ell\), with tangential and normal traces \(t,n\). Assumption A allows \(\kappa\in\mathbb R\), \(\lambda\ge0\) in Euclidean space, and requires \(\kappa>0\), \(\lambda>0\) when \(M\) is compact.

For the mixed unknown \(U=(U_{\ell-1},U_\ell)^\top\), define \[M=\begin{pmatrix}-I&\delta_\ell\\d_{\ell-1}&\delta_{\ell+1}d_\ell+\lambda I\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}-d_{\ell-2}\delta_{\ell-1}-\lambda I&\delta_\ell\\d_{\ell-1}&I\end{pmatrix}.\] The compound traces are \(T_M^tU=(t_{\ell-1}U_{\ell-1},t_\ell U_\ell)^\top\) and \(T_M^nU=(n_\ell U_\ell,n_{\ell+1}d_\ell U_\ell)^\top\); jumps are exterior minus interior. Fix a pants decomposition of a marked surface \(S\) of genus \(g\) with \(n\) punctures, and let the associated Dehn twists generate \(\mathbf Z^{3g-3+n}\). Section 2.1 identifies \[T(S)/\mathbf Z^{3g-3+n}\simeq(\mathbf R_{>0})^{3g-3+n}\times(S^1)^{3g-3+n}.\] It asserts that, for any fixed simple closed curve \(\gamma\), the marked geodesic length \(\ell_\gamma\) defines a function on this quotient and extends to the corresponding chart \(\mathbf C^{3g-3+n}\).

Corollaries 1.2 and 1.5 state, respectively, the all-genus isomorphism and injection \[\bigoplus_{g\ge2}W_0H_c^{2g}(\mathcal M_g;\mathbf Q)\simeq\mathfrak{grt}_1,\qquad \mathfrak{grt}_1\hookrightarrow\bigoplus_{g\ge2}H_{4g-6}(\operatorname{HMod}_g;\mathbf Q).\] Here \(\mathcal M_g\) is the moduli space of genus-\(g\) curves, \(W_0\) denotes weight-zero compactly supported cohomology, and \(\operatorname{HMod}_g\) is the genus-\(g\) handlebody mapping class group. The printed targets are direct sums, while \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\) in the cited comparison is the standard completed Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra.

Let \(\beta_0>1\) be the real root of \(\beta_0^3-\beta_0-1=0\). Corollary 1.6 states \[\liminf_{g\to\infty}\beta_0^{-g}\dim H_{4g-6}(\operatorname{HMod}_g;\mathbf Q)\ge1.\] It presents this critical-base estimate as a consequence of the genus-graded injection and the free Lie subalgebra generated by elements \(\sigma_3,\sigma_5,\sigma_7,\ldots\), with \(\sigma_{2j+1}\) in degree \(2j+1\).

For a genus-\(g\) handlebody with \(n\) marked boundary points and \(m\) parametrized boundary disks, let \(\operatorname{HMod}_{g,n}^m\) be the corresponding handlebody mapping class group. The introductory boundary-twist assertion is the short exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mathbf Z\longrightarrow\operatorname{HMod}_{g,n}^{m+1}\longrightarrow\operatorname{HMod}_{g,n+1}^{m}\longrightarrow1,\] stated without a complexity restriction on the nonnegative integers \(g,n,m\). The map caps one parametrized boundary component by a marked point, and the claimed kernel is the infinite cyclic group generated by its boundary twist.

Theorem 4.14, second sentence (article PDF page 19; printed page 2641). Let \(T\) be a finite graph with each vertex labelled full or empty. Its countable blow-up \(T_\infty\) replaces a full vertex by a countably infinite clique and an empty vertex by a countably infinite independent set; two distinct blobs are joined completely exactly when the corresponding vertices of \(T\) are adjacent.

A random total ordering of \(T_\infty\) is consistent if every isomorphism between finite induced subgraphs preserves their induced order distributions. Call \(T\) non-uniform if \(T_\infty\) admits a consistent random ordering other than the uniform one. The sentence under review asserts that, for every such non-uniform \(T\), the underlying finite graph \(T\) is complete or empty. This sentence does not explicitly require \(T\) to be reduced; the preceding sentence does impose that requirement. A reduced template has neither adjacent full twins nor nonadjacent empty twins.

Theorem 4.1 (article PDF page 14). Let \((X,p)\) be a perverse space with \(p\leq t\), where the top perversity is \(t(S)=\operatorname{codim}S-2\) on singular strata. Let \(X=U_0\cup U_1\) be an open cover such that \(U_0\), \(U_1\), and \(U_0\cap U_1\) are path-connected in the ordinary topology, with the induced filtrations and perversities, and choose a common regular basepoint \(x_0\). Write \(\pi_1^p(U,x_0)=\pi_1(\mathcal G_pU,x_0)\).

If \(j_i:\pi_1^p(U_0\cap U_1,x_0)\to\pi_1^p(U_i,x_0)\) are the inclusion maps, the paper asserts that the induced homomorphism \[\Phi:\pi_1^p(U_0,x_0)*\pi_1^p(U_1,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1^p(X,x_0)\] is surjective and that \(\ker\Phi\) is the normal subgroup generated by all \(j_0(\omega)j_1(\omega)^{-1}\), for \(\omega\in\pi_1^p(U_0\cap U_1,x_0)\). The printed assumptions require ordinary path connectivity, without a separate connectivity requirement for allowable paths.

Theorem 4.6 (article PDF page 17). Let \(\nu:X\to Y\) be a coarsening of CS sets: \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same underlying topological space, every stratum of \(Y\) is a union of strata of \(X\), and \(\nu\) is the identity on that space. Let \(p\) be a codimensional perversity, used on both stratifications, with \(p\leq t\). Suppose no singular stratum of \(X\) is contained in a regular stratum of \(Y\); these are the excluded exceptional strata.

The theorem asserts that \(\nu\) induces isomorphisms \[\pi_0^p(X)\cong\pi_0^p(Y),\qquad \pi_1^p(X,x_0)\cong\pi_1^p(Y,x_0)\] for every regular basepoint \(x_0\). The quantified class is all codimensional perversities bounded above by \(t\); the statement does not restrict that class to Goresky–MacPherson perversities.

Proposition 2.10 (article PDF page 10). Let \(L\) be a compact filtered space, let \(\mathring cL\) be its open cone with apex \(v\) and the conic filtration, and let \(p\) be a perversity on the cone, also denoting its restriction to \(L\) by \(p\). Put \(Dp=t-p\). For every local coefficient system \(E\) on \(\mathcal G_pL\), the proposition asserts \[H_j(\mathcal G_p\mathring cL,\mathcal G_pL;E)=0\qquad\text{for every }j\leq Dp(v)+1.\] In this quantification, \(E\) is specified only on the smaller member of the pair; extension to \(\mathcal G_p\mathring cL\) is not a printed hypothesis.

Proof of Proposition 2.3 (article PDF page 8). For a perverse space \((X,p)\), a singular simplex is \(p\)-full when it and all its faces are \(p\)-allowable. Given any horn \(\Lambda_k^{\ell}\subset\Delta^{\ell}\), with \(0\leq k\leq\ell\), and a compatible map \(|\Psi|:\Lambda_k^{\ell}\to X\) consisting of \(p\)-full faces, the proof defines \(\rho_k:\Delta^{\ell}\to\Lambda_k^{\ell}\) by radial projection from the barycentre of the missing face \(\partial_k\Delta^{\ell}\).

The construction asserts that this projection is a map on the whole simplex, is affine, and makes \(\tau=|\Psi|\circ\rho_k\) a \(p\)-full horn filler. The assertion being examined is this specific projection and its asserted regularity, which the proof uses to verify allowability on every face.

First step of the proof of Theorem 6.4 (article PDF pages 25–26). Let \((X,p)\) be a perverse CS set and \(k\geq2\), and assume \(\pi_j^p(L)=0\) for every link \(L\) of \(X\) and every \(j\leq k-1\). In a conical chart \(\varphi:U\times\mathring cL\to V\), let \(\mathcal C\) be the cubes in \(U\subset\mathbb R^m\) with rational endpoints and let \(\mathring c_tL=L\times[0,t)/(L\times\{0\})\).

The proof asserts that the family \[\{\varphi(C\times\mathring c_tL):C\in\mathcal C,\ t\in\mathbb Q,\ 0<t<1\}\ \cup\ \{\varphi(C\times L\times(a,b)):C\in\mathcal C,\ a,b\in\mathbb Q,\ 0\leq a<b\leq1\}\] is a countable open basis of the entire chart \(V\), closed under finite intersections. It then uses the assertion that unions of these sets give every open subset of \(V\) in the local-to-global argument.

Proposition 3.13 and its proof (article PDF pages 29–31, equations (26)–(29)). Work over a field \(\Bbbk\) of characteristic zero. For an elementary pointed annular web of index \(k\), let \(K^{d_0}\) be the reduced Koszul complex of (26): it has total differential \(d_{HH}+d_0\), with factors \(x_i\otimes1-1\otimes x_i+1\otimes1\) for \(2\leq i\leq k\); the marked output variable is set to zero. The proposition asserts a natural isomorphism \(H^{d_0}\cong S_0\) of functors to \(\Bbbk\)-modules.
