Proposition 4.21 (article PDF page 42; coefficient convention and Definition 4.8 on page 35). Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative unital ring and \(t\in\Bbbk^\times\). For a planar singular knot \(S\), use its initial admissible Heegaard diagram with Ozsváth–Szabó twisting \(P^{OS}\), and put \(R=\Bbbk[U_0,\ldots,U_{k+s}]\). The linear complex \(\mathcal L_S\) is the tensor product over singular crossings of the two-term factors whose differentials are \(tU_a+tU_b-U_c-U_d\), with \(a,b\) outgoing and \(c,d\) incoming.

The proposition asserts that \(H_*(CFK^-(S,P^{OS})\otimes_R\mathcal L_S)\), modulo its \(\Bbbk\)-torsion, is a free \(\Bbbk[U_0]\)-module concentrated in homological degree zero with basis the Kauffman states of \(S\). For the reduced complex \(\widehat{CFK}=CFK^-/(U_0)\), it asserts the same conclusion over \(\Bbbk\). The report examines torsion with a nonzero annihilator, rather than exploiting the omitted nonzero qualifier in the printed definition. No restriction excluding the specialization \(t=1\) appears in the stated coefficient range.

Theorem A.2 (article PDF pages 55–56). Let \((M,F_M)\) and \((N,F_N)\) be filtered \(\Bbbk\)-modules with decreasing filtrations, and let \(\{f_r:E_r\to E'_r\}_{r\geq0}\) be a morphism of spectral sequences converging to them in the sense that the limiting pages identify with their associated graded modules. Suppose \(f_n\) is an isomorphism for some page \(n\).

The theorem asserts that \(f_\infty\) induces an isomorphism of the completed filtered modules \[(\widehat M,\widehat F_M)\cong(\widehat N,\widehat F_N),\qquad \widehat M=\varprojlim_s M/F_M^s,\quad \widehat N=\varprojlim_s N/F_N^s.\] The theorem as stated does not require a filtered map \(M\to N\), or a map of filtered complexes, inducing the spectral-sequence morphism.

Proof of Proposition A.7 (article PDF pages 57–58). Let \(K\) be a field, \(L=K[q,q^{-1}]\), \(k\geq1\), and let \(p(q)\in K[q]\) be coprime to \(q-1\). The preceding general exact-couple discussion on page 57 also declares the spectral-sequence differential on \(B^{(n)}\) to be \(g^{(n)}\circ f^{(n)}\), although its stated maps have types \(f^{(n)}:A^{(n)}\to A^{(n)}\), \(g^{(n)}:A^{(n)}\to B^{(n)}\), and \(h^{(n)}:B^{(n)}\to A^{(n)}\). Proof of Proposition 5.12 (article PDF page 52). Let \(\Bbbk=\mathbb Z[t^{1/2},t^{-1/2}]\), let \(\beta\) be a braid diagram of a knot with \(n\) crossings, and set \(q=t^{-n/2}\). Proof of Lemma 4.22 (article PDF pages 29–30). Let \(M\) be a finite-rank free module over a PID \(R\), and consider the flag/splitting models \(D^{a,b}(M)=L^{a,b}(M)/\mathring L^{a,b}(M)\) and the compatible join \(T^{a,b}(M)\). The latter is the subcomplex of the join of \(a\) copies of \(T(M)\) and \(b\) copies of \(ST(M)\) whose component submodules have a common basis. The lemma asserts \(D^{a,b}(M)\simeq\Sigma^{a+b+1}T^{a,b}(M)\).

For \(0\leq j\leq a+b\), the proof defines \(F_j\subset\mathring L^{a,b}(M)\) by requiring the first \(j\) factors to lie in \(T(M)\) or \(ST(M)\): a flag factor has nonzero first term and last term different from \(M\); a splitting factor has nonzero first and last terms, with zero interior terms permitted. For \(1\leq j\leq a+b\), \(N_j\) imposes only the last-term condition on factor \(j\), and \(S_j\) imposes only the first-term condition, within \(F_{j-1}\).

The proof asserts \(F_{a+b}\cong T^{a,b}(M)\), \(S_j\cap N_j\cong F_j\), \(S_j\cup N_j\cong F_{j-1}\), and contractibility of both \(S_j\) and \(N_j\). These assertions about the defined filtration, its endpoint, and its covering pieces are the steps examined in the finding.

Proposition 4.9 (article PDF pages 26–27). In the category of functors from \(\mathrm{VB}(R)\), the groupoid of finite-rank free \(R\)-modules and isomorphisms, to abelian groups, use the monoidal product \((V\otimes_{\mathrm{VB}}W)(P)=\bigoplus_{A\oplus B=P}V(A)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}W(B)\). Let \(A\) be a monoid, \(M\) a right \(A\)-module and \(N\) a left \(A\)-module. Let \(B(M,A,N)\) be the normalized-chain total complex of the ordinary two-sided bar construction with \(j\)-simplices \(M\otimes_{\mathrm{VB}}A^{\otimes_{\mathrm{VB}}j}\otimes_{\mathrm{VB}}N\).

Assume either that \(M(R^n)\) is free abelian for every \(n\), or that \(N(R^n)\) is free abelian for every \(n\). The proposition asserts \[H_i(B(M,A,N))\cong\operatorname{Tor}^A_i(M,N),\] where the right side is the absolute left-derived functor of \(-\otimes_A N\). The stated hypothesis contains no separate flatness requirement on the underlying abelian groups of \(A\).

If \(\beta\geq-2\), every \(A(R^n)\) is \((\alpha n+\beta)\)-connected, and every simplicial space \(BA_\bullet(R^n)\) is proper, it asserts that \(BA(R^n)\) is \((\alpha n+\beta+1)\)-connected for all \(n\). The model convention on page 29 retains \(D^{a,b}(0)=S^0\), while Lemma 4.22 asserts \(D^{a,b}(M)\simeq\Sigma^{a+b+1}T^{a,b}(M)\). Proposition 5.8 asserts that, for a PID \(R\) with \(T_n^2(R)\) \((2n-4)\)-connected, \(D_n^{k,0}(R)\) is \((2n+k-3)\)-connected for every \(k\geq2\), again without excluding \(n=0\).

Energy identity in Section 2.1 (article PDF page 5). Let \(\Psi:\Sigma\to S^3\) be a smooth immersion of a closed surface of genus at least one into the unit three-sphere. Collar models in Section 3.2 (article PDF page 10). The torus paragraph asserts that a flat normalized torus is isometric to \((2\pi\ell)^{-1/2}(S^1\times[0,\ell])\), for some \(\ell>0\), with the untwisted identification \((\theta,0)\sim(\theta,\ell)\). No angular shift in the gluing is included.

Causal type of the limiting line (article PDF page 11, Theorem 4.1; pages 26–27 and 31, Propositions 5.13, 5.15 and 5.19). Opening definition in Section 2 (article PDF page 5). Let \(K_0\) be a field of characteristic zero and \(C/K_0\) a smooth geometrically integral curve of genus at least two with \(C(K_0)=\varnothing\). A \(K_0\)-field means an extension field \(K\supseteq K_0\), viewed in the ring language with constants for every element of \(K_0\). The printed definition declares \[K\text{ avoids }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C(K_0)=\varnothing.\] The condition on the right uses the base field, even though the object being classified is the extension \(K\).

Theorem 1.6 (article PDF page 2; Remark 2.16 on page 10). Let \(K_0\) be an arbitrary characteristic-zero field and \(C/K_0\) a smooth geometrically integral projective or affine curve of genus at least two with no \(K_0\)-rational point. Let \(T_{C,K_0}\) be the theory of extension fields \(K/K_0\) such that \(C(K)=\varnothing\), in the language \(L(K_0)\) containing a constant symbol for every element of \(K_0\).

The theorem asserts that \(T_{C,K_0}\) has a computably axiomatized model companion \(C\mathrm{XF}_{K_0}\). The asserted computability is stated for this full language and arbitrary base field; the theorem does not impose countability, a computable presentation of \(K_0\), or a relative oracle for its diagram.

Fact 2.10 (article PDF page 7; conventions on pages 4–5). Work in an algebraically closed field \(M\) of characteristic zero. A variety is a reduced separated scheme of finite type, not necessarily integral or equidimensional. Its projective degree \(\operatorname{pdeg}(X)\) is defined by intersection with a generic projective linear subspace of codimension \(\dim X\).

For fixed integers \(n,m\), the fact asserts the existence of a single parameter-free definable family \(\{V_a\}_{a\in Y}\) containing every projective variety \(X\subseteq\mathbb P^n\) with \(\operatorname{pdeg}(X)\leq m\). It further asserts that, for every subfield \(K\subseteq M\), each such \(X\) defined over \(K\) occurs as \(V_a\) for some \(a\in Y(K)\). The bounded degree in this assertion is the paper's top-dimensional degree, with no purity hypothesis.

Proof of Lemma 4.13 (article PDF page 17). In the characteristic-zero curve-exclusion setting, let \(K\models C\mathrm{XF}_\forall\), let \(L/K\) be a proper finite extension, and let \(V\) be a geometrically integral affine variety over \(L\). Put \(W=\operatorname{Res}_{L/K}V\). Choose a primitive element presentation \(L=K[X]/(P(X))\) with \(P\) irreducible, let \(F\) be its splitting field over \(K\), and set \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(F/K)\).

The proof asserts the base-change decomposition \[W_F\cong\prod_{g\in G}(V_F)^g,\] where each factor is the indicated conjugate. The product is indexed by every element of \(G\); the lemma does not assume that \(L/K\) itself is Galois. This is the decomposition used in the argument excluding a dominant rational map \(W\dashrightarrow C\).

Corollary 4.15(1) (article PDF page 18). Fix the characteristic-zero base field \(K_0\) and excluded smooth geometrically integral curve \(C/K_0\) of genus at least two. Let \(C\mathrm{XF}'\) be the theory obtained from \(C\mathrm{XF}\) by deleting axiom \((\mathrm I_C)\), the axiom concerning proper finite extensions, while retaining curve avoidance. For every \(K\models C\mathrm{XF}'\) and every proper elementary extension \(L\succ K\) in the language with constants for \(K_0\), the corollary asserts \[C(L)\ne\varnothing.\] The printed extension hypothesis is elementary, not algebraic.

Proof of Theorem 4.24 (article PDF page 20). In the same characteristic-zero setting, \(C\mathrm{XF}\) is the model companion of the theory of fields extending \(K_0\) and avoiding the smooth geometrically integral curve \(C/K_0\), of genus at least two. If \(K\models C\mathrm{XF}\) and \(t\) is transcendental over \(K\), the proof asserts \[K(t)\models C\mathrm{XF},\] citing the absence of \(K\)-definable dominant rational maps \(\mathbb A^1\dashrightarrow C\). This is the intermediate claim that the rational function field already satisfies the full companion, including its finite-extension axiom.

Recalled definition before Corollary 4.29 (article PDF page 21). The text says that a theory \(T\) has the second tree property, \(\mathrm{TP}_2\), if there are a formula \(\varphi(x;y)\), a model \(M\models T\), parameters \(b_{i,j}\) for \(i,j\in\omega\), and tuples \(a_\eta\) for every function \(\eta:\omega\to\omega\), such that \[M\models\varphi(a_\eta;b_{i,j})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\eta(i)=j\qquad(\eta\in\omega^\omega,\ i,j\in\omega).\] This displayed realization condition is the entire recalled criterion; the statement supplies no fixed integer \(k\) requiring each row \(\{\varphi(x;b_{i,j}):j\in\omega\}\) to be \(k\)-inconsistent.

Stalk-inclusion step in the proof of Proposition 3.3 (article PDF pages 8–9). In the reduction to a smooth curve \(X\) over a number field \(F\), let \(x\in X(F)\), and choose a quasi-finite map \(f:X\to\mathbb P^1_F\) sending \(x\) to \(0\), finite étale over \(U=\mathbb P^1_F\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\). Fix any nonzero \(F\)-rational tangent \(v\) at \(0\). A compatible tangential basepoint \(x_w\) above \(0_v\) may be chosen only over \(\overline F\) when \(f\) ramifies at \(x\). Set \(H=\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X_{\overline F}\setminus f^{-1}\{0,1,\infty\},x_w)\), viewed as an open subgroup of \(\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(U_{\overline F},0_v)\).

For any \(\mathbb Q_p\)-local system \(\mathcal L\) on \(X\), put \(\mathcal L'=f_*(\mathcal L|_{f^{-1}U})\). The proof asserts a canonical inclusion \(\mathcal L_x\hookrightarrow\mathcal L'_{0_v}\) in its Galois-equivariant argument, with image stable under \(H\), such that the \(H\)-action on that image factors through \(\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X_{\overline F},x)\) and agrees with the geometric monodromy of \(\mathcal L\). The asserted compatibility must hold for the prescribed \(v\), without assuming an \(F\)-rational lift \(x_w\).

For a K3 surface \(X\) over a number field \(F\), the corollary considers the full representation \(V=H^2_{\text{ét}}(X_{\overline F},\overline{\mathbb Q}_p)\). Abelian-variety paragraph in the proof of Corollary 9.7 (article PDF page 19). Let \(A/F\) be an arbitrary abelian variety of dimension \(g\) over a number field. The proof takes \(S=\mathcal A_{g,\Gamma(3)}\), the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties with full level-three structure. Remark 2.3 after Lemma 2.2 (article PDF page 5). Let \(\Gamma\) be the topological group under consideration and \(\Gamma_1\subseteq\Gamma\) an open subgroup of finite index. Over the coefficient field \(E\), the remark asserts that the natural quotient \[\Gamma_E^{\mathrm{pro\text{-}alg}}/\Gamma_{1,E}^{\mathrm{pro\text{-}alg}}\] is the constant finite group scheme associated with \(\Gamma/\Gamma_1\). The hypothesis on \(\Gamma_1\) is finite index and openness; normality is not assumed. The word group is part of the asserted quotient structure.

Example 2.4 (article PDF pages 5–6). Let \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z\) with the discrete topology and take its proalgebraic completion over \(\mathbb Q_p\). The example asserts an isomorphism over \(\mathbb Q_p\) \[\Gamma_{\mathbb Q_p}^{\mathrm{pro\text{-}alg}}\cong\mathbb G_a\times H_0\times T_0,\] where \(H_0\) is the profinite étale group scheme corresponding to the \(G_{\mathbb Q_p}\)-module \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1)\), and \(T_0\) is the protorus with character module \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p^{\times}/\mu_\infty\) carrying its natural Galois action. Here \(\mu_\infty\) is the group of roots of unity. The asserted product is a descent statement over \(\mathbb Q_p\), so it includes a Galois-compatible splitting of the multiplicative part and the specified cyclotomic action on the profinite factor.

Example 2.6 (article PDF page 7). Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero containing only finitely many roots of unity, let \(X=\mathbb G_{m,K}\), and take the stated basepoint so that \(G_K\) acts on the coordinate ring of the proalgebraic completion of \(\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X_{\overline K},x)\cong\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1)\). For a regular function \(f\) in that coordinate ring, the example asserts \[\dim_{\mathbb Q_p}\operatorname{Span}(G_K\cdot f)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ factors through the indicated quotient }\mathbb G_{a,\mathbb Q_p}\times\widehat{\mathbb Z}.\] No number-field or finite-generation assumption is added to the stated condition on \(K\).

High-tensor-power assertion in the proof of Lemma 5.1 (article PDF page 12). For a finite Galois group \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)\), the proof chooses finitely many faithful finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_p\)-representations \(W_1,\ldots,W_N\), of dimension at most \(|G|\), representing the possibilities arising from tangential basepoints. It asserts that for all sufficiently large integers \(d\), and every \(i\), \(W_i^{\otimes d}\) contains the regular representation \(\mathbb Q_p[G]\) as a direct summand, solely because \(W_i\) is faithful. The construction does not require each \(W_i\) to contain a trivial summand.

Proposition 7.1 (article PDF page 14; arbitrary-field setup on pages 6–7). Let \(X\) be any geometrically connected scheme of finite type over a field \(K\), equipped with a rational or tangential basepoint \(x\), and let \(\mathcal L\) be a \(\mathbb Q_p\)-local system on \(X\). Write the superscript \(G_K\text{-fin}\) for regular functions whose Galois translates span a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_p\)-space. The proposition asserts that \[H^1_{\text{ét}}(X_{\overline K},\mathcal L)\] is a \(G_K\)-subquotient of \[\mathbb Q_p[\pi_1^{\mathrm{pro\text{-}alg}}(X_{\overline K},x)]^{G_K\text{-fin}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_p}\mathcal L_x.\] The statement does not exclude characteristic \(p\), and its proof asserts finite dimensionality of the continuous one-cocycle space in this full scope.

Lemma 10.1(ii) (article PDF page 20). Let \(F\) be a field of characteristic zero, and let \(f:D\to C\) be a finite surjective, possibly ramified morphism of smooth curves over \(F\). Given \(x\in D(F)\) and a nonzero tangent vector \(v\in T_xD\), the lemma asserts the existence of a tangent vector \(w\in T_{f(x)}C\) such that pullback induces \[\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(D\setminus f^{-1}(f(x)),x_v)\longrightarrow\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(C\setminus\{f(x)\},f(x)_w)\] as an isomorphism onto an open subgroup. Only the fibre over \(f(x)\) is removed; the morphism is not assumed to be étale away from that fibre.

In the Fourier calculation for Proposition 7.2, PDF page 36, take a homogeneous polynomial \(P_m=\sum_{j=0}^m\ell_jx_1^{m-j}x_2^j\), \(m\ge1\), with real coefficients. In the elliptic coordinates of (7.9), let \(\widehat V_\varepsilon=V_{\varepsilon,P_m,E_\varepsilon(L)}\circ F_\varepsilon\), and define \[a_{j,\varepsilon}(\xi)=\frac{(\varepsilon r_1)^{-m}}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\widehat V_\varepsilon(\xi,\eta)\cos(j\eta)\,d\eta,\qquad j\ge0.\] The boundary relation is used to obtain \(a_{j,\varepsilon}(0)=\ell_0c_j\), where \(c_j=\pi^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}(\cos\eta)^m\cos(j\eta)\,d\eta\).

The last paragraph of that page identifies these \(a_{j,\varepsilon}(0)\) as the Fourier coefficients of \(\ell_0(\cos\eta)^m\) relative to the orthonormal basis \[\left\{\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}},\frac{\cos(j\eta)}{\sqrt\pi},\frac{\sin(j\eta)}{\sqrt\pi}:j\ge1\right\}\quad\text{of }L^2(0,2\pi).\] The issue is this identification with coefficients in the normalized basis, given the explicit \(1/\pi\) integral normalization.

Theorem 2.4, PDF pages 10–11, assumes an odd number of half-flux poles in the bounded simply connected domain \(\Omega\), and a simple limiting eigenvalue \(\lambda_{0,n_0}\). Earlier, (2.15) fixes a real normalized eigenfunction \(v_0\) of the gauged crack problem. Its leading profile is the real function \(\Psi_0(r\cos t,r\sin t)=\beta r^{m/2}f(t)\sin(\tfrac m2(t-\alpha_0))\), with \(m\) odd and \(\beta\ne0\), and (2.30) fixes the corresponding real finite-energy minimizer \(\widetilde V\).

The theorem then allows a normalized complex eigenfunction \(u_0\) of the limiting magnetic problem and selects the moving eigenfunction \(u_\varepsilon\) by \[\|u_\varepsilon\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=1,\qquad\int_\Omega e^{-i(\Theta_\varepsilon-\Theta_0)}u_\varepsilon\overline{u_0}\,dx\in(0,\infty).\] It asserts the vector limit \[\varepsilon^{-m/2}u_\varepsilon(\varepsilon\,\cdot)\longrightarrow e^{i\Theta_1}(\Psi_0-\widetilde V)\] in the magnetic Sobolev space \(H^{1,1}(D_R,\mathbb C)\) for every \(R>0\). The displayed hypotheses align \(u_\varepsilon\) relative to \(u_0\), but do not require \(u_0=e^{i\Theta_0}v_0\) for the previously fixed real \(v_0\). The finding concerns that phase dependence of (2.33).

The converse construction in Theorem 2.4, PDF pages 8–9, starts with a holomorphic principal orbibundle \(P\to\mathcal Y\), where \(\mathcal Y\) is a compact complex orbifold and the fiber is a one-dimensional compact complex torus \(G=\mathfrak g/\Lambda\). It assumes that \(P\) is definite: its integral Chern class has rank one modulo torsion, and its image in complex cohomology is represented, up to sign, by a Kähler form. After a finite orbifold cover \(q:\mathcal Y'\to\mathcal Y\), the proof represents \(q^*P\) as \((\mathcal L\setminus0_{\mathcal L})/\langle\lambda\rangle\), where \(\mathcal L\) is ample and \(0<|\lambda|<1\).

For a Hermitian metric \(h\) on \(\mathcal L\) with positive Chern curvature, the first asserted conclusion is that \(f(s)=\|s\|_h^2\) gives a Vaisman metric \(\Omega=f^{-1}i\partial\bar\partial f\) with Lee form \(\theta=-d\log f\). For the finite deck group \(F\), acting compatibly with the fiber group, the second assertion is that \[\theta_F=\frac1{|F|}\sum_{g\in F}g^*\theta,\qquad \Omega_F=\frac1{|F|}\sum_{g\in F}g^*\Omega=-dJ\theta_F+\theta_F\wedge J\theta_F.\] This arithmetic average is then claimed to be a Vaisman metric descending to \(P\). The finding examines both the positivity of the displayed norm-square construction and this equality used for descent.

Corollary 6.6, PDF page 22, considers a small deformation \(\mathcal X\to\Delta\) of a compact Vaisman manifold \(X_0=X\) with \(c^{\mathrm{BC}}_1(X)<0\), together with the induced family of quotient orbifolds \(\mathcal Z\to\Delta\). In the stated proof, a two-form \(\omega\) on \(\mathcal Z\) restricts to a Kähler form \(\omega_t\) on every fiber \(Z_t\), and the central fiber satisfies \([\omega_0]=-c_1(Z_0)\).

The disputed implication is that these hypotheses and continuity force \([\omega_t]=-c_1(Z_t)\) for every sufficiently small \(t\), which is then used to establish negative type for the deformed manifolds. The premises stated for \(\omega\) do not require it to be closed on the total space or to have a constant cohomology class under Gauss–Manin transport. The finding concerns this cohomological inference within the deformation argument.

Example 7.1(1), PDF page 23, includes the following classification assertion: every compact properly elliptic Vaisman surface \(X\) is an elliptic orbibundle over a curve of genus \(g>1\); it then concludes \(c^{\mathrm{BC}}_1(X)<0\). Here properly elliptic means a compact complex surface of Kodaira dimension one.

The stated genus condition is imposed on the curve underlying the base orbifold of the surface itself. The sentence does not first pass to a finite cover and does not replace the genus condition by positivity of the orbifold canonical degree. The finding examines this genus restriction when the elliptic fibration has nontrivial orbifold isotropy on its base.

Example 7.4, PDF page 24, fixes positive integer weights \(w=(w_0,\ldots,w_n)\) with \(\gcd(w_0,\ldots,w_n)=1\), and a weighted homogeneous polynomial \(f\) of degree \(d\), viewed as a section of \(\mathcal O(d)\) on \(\mathbb{CP}(w)\). Assume that its punctured affine hypersurface \(\widehat X_f=Z(f)\setminus\{0\}\) is smooth, and let \(Y_f=\widehat X_f/\mathbb C^*(w)\) carry the inherited orbifold structure.

The asserted bundle identification is \[\widehat X_f\cong\bigl(\mathcal O(-d)|_{Y_f}\bigr)\setminus0_{\mathcal O(-d)|_{Y_f}}.\] It is used to make the quotient \(X_f=\widehat X_f/\langle\lambda\rangle\), \(0<|\lambda|<1\), a definite elliptic orbibundle, and hence Vaisman. The subsequent Calabi–Yau specialization imposes \(d=\sum_iw_i\), but the punctured-cone identification is asserted before that specialization. The finding concerns the degree of the line orbibundle in this identification.

The introductory definition and Definition 2.1, PDF pages 1–2 and 4–5, call a Hermitian metric \(g\) with fundamental form \(\Omega\) Vaisman when there is a closed real one-form \(\theta\) satisfying \(d\Omega=\theta\wedge\Omega\) and \(\nabla^g\theta=0\). The complex manifold is compact and has complex dimension greater than one. The printed definition does not require \(\theta\ne0\); normalization \(\|\theta\|=1\) is introduced separately.

With this definition, Theorem B(1), PDF page 2, asserts that if \(c_1(X)=0\), \(c^{\mathrm{BC}}_1(X)=0\), and \(\tau\in H^1(X,\mathbb R)\) is the Lee class of a Vaisman metric, there exists a unique Chern–Ricci-flat Vaisman metric of Lee class \(\tau\) and prescribed total volume. Theorem C asserts that every compact Vaisman manifold with \(c^{\mathrm{BC}}_1(X)\le0\) has compact \(\operatorname{Aut}_0(X)\) of complex dimension one and is quasi-regular. The finding concerns whether those conclusions hold on the zero-Lee part of the stated domain.

Theorem 2.2, PDF page 7, makes the following quotient assertion. Let \(X\) be a complex manifold and let a complex Lie group \(H\) act holomorphically, properly and locally freely on \(X\). Then the quotient complex space \(Y=X/H\) has a natural complex orbifold structure \(\mathcal Y\) for which the projection \(X\to\mathcal Y\) is a holomorphic principal \(H\)-orbibundle, with \(X\) as its underlying smooth complex manifold.

The orbifold charts used in the paper, defined on PDF page 5, have chart groups that are finite groups of biholomorphisms of the local open sets, hence act effectively. The theorem's action hypotheses do not additionally require a faithful slice action or exclude a nontrivial finite subgroup of \(H\) acting trivially on \(X\). The finding concerns the asserted principal \(H\)-bundle structure over the quotient under precisely these hypotheses.

On PDF page 7, let \(\mathcal Y\) be a complex orbifold with underlying complex space \(Y\), and let \(\operatorname{cl}:B\mathcal Y\to Y\) be its classifying-space map. A point with finite local isotropy group \(\Gamma\) has fiber of type \(K(\Gamma,1)\). The paper defines orbifold cohomology by \(H^\bullet_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,R)=H^\bullet(B\mathcal Y,R)\).

The asserted conclusion is that, for every coefficient field \(R\), the pullback \[\operatorname{cl}^*:H^\bullet(Y,R)\longrightarrow H^\bullet_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,R)\] is an isomorphism in every degree. No restriction on the characteristic of \(R\), or on its relation to the orders of the isotropy groups, is included in that statement.

In the forward direction of Theorem 2.4, PDF page 8, let \(P\to\mathcal Y\) be a principal orbibundle over a compact complex orbifold with fiber a one-dimensional compact complex torus \(G=\mathfrak g/\Lambda\). Assume that its total space carries a Vaisman metric \((\Omega,\theta)\), and identify its Lee vector field \(B=g^{-1}\theta\) and anti-Lee vector \(JB\) with elements of the fiber Lie algebra. The connection constructed in the proof gives \(c(P)=[-\omega\otimes JB]\), where \(\omega\) is the induced transverse Kähler form.

The next paragraph asserts that \(-JB\) itself corresponds to an integral element of \(\Lambda\), and consequently is a positive multiple of a uniquely determined primitive lattice element. No period normalization of \(B\), or normalization of the Vaisman metric, is imposed in this step. The finding concerns the membership \(-JB\in\Lambda\), rather than only its direction in the real span of a lattice element.

The image-criterion argument on PDF page 9 fixes \(G=\mathbb C/\Lambda\), a lattice basis \((1,b)\) with \(\operatorname{Im}b>0\), and the quotient homomorphism \(\psi:\mathbb C^*\to G=\mathbb C^*/\langle e^{2\pi ib}\rangle\). It asserts that a holomorphic principal \(G\)-orbibundle \(P'\) on \(\mathcal Y\) belongs to the image of \(\psi_*:\operatorname{Pic}^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y)\to H^1_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,\mathcal O_{\mathcal Y}(G))\) exactly when its integral Chern class lies in the copy of \(H^2_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,\mathbb Z)\) corresponding to that first lattice generator.

For the inverse implication, take a line orbibundle \(\mathcal L\) with \(c^{\mathbb Z}(P')=c_1(\mathcal L)\), and form the difference principal bundle \(P_0=P'-\psi_*(\mathcal L)\), whose integral Chern class is zero. The disputed construction claims that this general \(P_0\) can be written \(\widetilde{\mathcal Y}\times_\rho G\) with \(\rho:\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y)\to\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{hol,gp}}(G)\), and that \(\rho\) lifts to a homomorphism \(\widehat\rho:\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y)\to\mathbb C^*\), yielding \(P_0=\psi_*(\widetilde{\mathcal Y}\times_{\widehat\rho}\mathbb C)\). The specified monodromy target is the group of holomorphic group automorphisms, which fix the identity of \(G\).

The opening of the proof of Theorem 3.1, PDF page 10, considers a compact complex manifold \(X=(M,J_0)\) and a small integrable deformation \(J_t\) on the same smooth manifold. Let \(T^{1,0}_0,T^{0,1}_0\) be the original complex tangent subbundles, and let \(\pi_t^{1,0}:TM\otimes\mathbb C\to T_t^{1,0}\) be projection for the deformed structure.

The printed formula defines \[\phi_t=-\pi_t^{1,0}|_{T^{0,1}_0}\] and asserts that \(\phi_t\) is a section of the fixed bundle \(A^{0,1}_{J_0}\otimes T^{1,0}_0\), satisfies the stated Maurer–Cartan equation, and encodes the graph identity \(T_t^{0,1}=(\operatorname{id}+\phi_t)T_0^{0,1}\). The finding concerns the claimed old-\((1,0)\) codomain of this unmodified deformed projection.

In Theorem 3.1, PDF pages 10–11, let \(X\) be a compact complex manifold and \(H\subset\operatorname{Aut}_0(X)\) a compact complex subgroup. The theorem does not require \(H\) to be connected. Its proof considers the natural holomorphic representation of \(H\) on each \(H^q(X,TX)\), and chooses an \(H\)-invariant Hermitian metric to identify cohomology with harmonic \((0,q)\)-forms valued in \(T^{1,0}X\).

The intermediate assertion is that this representation is trivial for the full group \(H\), for every degree \(q\). Equivalently, with \(\mathcal A^q=C^\infty(A_X^{0,q}\otimes T_X^{1,0})\) and the associated Dolbeault Laplacian \(\Box\), equation (7) states \(\ker\Box\subset(\mathcal A^\bullet)^H\). Claim 1 then uses this to conclude that the Kuranishi germ lies in \((\mathcal A^1)^H\). The finding concerns the full-group invariance assertion when \(H\) has more than one connected component.

The proof of Theorem 6.2, PDF pages 20–21, assumes a compact Vaisman manifold \(X\) with \(c^{\mathrm{BC}}_1(X)<0\). It chooses a positive transverse Kähler form \(\eta=h(J\cdot,\cdot)\) representing \(-c^{\mathrm{BC}}_1(X)\), then asserts that the transverse Yau theorem supplies a transverse Kähler metric \(\omega_0\) with Ricci form \(\rho_0=\eta\). The paper's Ricci convention, stated on PDF page 2, is \(\rho=-i\partial\bar\partial\log\det\Omega\), representing \(2\pi c^{\mathrm{BC}}_1(X)\). The first issue is the sign and normalization of that prescribed target.

A second local assertion occurs after (25). For the normalized metric \(\Omega=-dJ	heta+	heta\wedge J	heta\), write a holomorphic vector field as \(\xi=\xi_0+fB^{1,0}\), where \(	heta^{1,0}(\xi_0)=0\). From the displayed identity \(
abla^{\mathrm{Ch}}	heta^{1,0}=	heta^{0,1}\otimes	heta^{1,0}-	frac12g(\cdot,\pi^{1,0})\), the proof claims \[	heta^{1,0}(
abla^{\mathrm{Ch}}\xi_0)=-(
abla^{\mathrm{Ch}}	heta^{1,0})(\xi_0)=-	frac12g(\xi_0,\cdot).\] The finding also examines this contraction sign under the stated orthogonality condition.

Let \(k=\mathbb F_q\), with \(q=p^a\), and \(K_0=\operatorname{Frac}W(k)\). Definition 2.42(3) calls a finite-dimensional Frobenius module \((D,\varphi_D)\) pure of weight \(i\) when every eigenvalue of the \(K_0\)-linear operator \(\varphi_D^a\) is an algebraic integer of complex absolute value \(q^{i/2}\) under every embedding. Let \(\mathcal H_k\) be the full Chow heart, the idempotent-complete additive category generated by \(M(X)\{r\}=M(X)(r)[2r]\) for smooth proper \(X/k\) and every integer \(r\). Proposition 4.44(2) asserts that \(R^i\Gamma_{\mathrm{rig}}(M)\) is pure of weight \(i\) in this sense for every \(M\in\mathcal H_k\) and every degree \(i\). The assertion therefore includes all positive and negative Tate twists, with the arithmetic Frobenius normalization \(K_0(r)=(K_0,p^{-r}\varphi)\).

In the stable, compactly generated symmetric monoidal setting of Section 2, consider the functor \(T=-\otimes t\) and its category \(\mathcal C^{T}_{\mathrm{lax}}\) of arbitrary lax fixed points \(X\to X\otimes t\), without the ind-nilpotence restriction. Remark 2.40 asserts a canonical equivalence \[\mathcal C^{T}_{\mathrm{lax}}\simeq\operatorname{coMod}_{\widehat H(t)},\qquad \widehat H(t)=\pi\rho\mathbf1\simeq\prod_{n\ge0}t^{\otimes n},\] where \(\pi\) is the forgetful functor and \(\rho\) its right adjoint. The surrounding Section 2.5 defines ordinary internal comodules by coactions \(X\to\widehat H(t)\otimes X\) with the category's ordinary tensor product. Thus the claim identifies the actual forgetful comonad with tensoring by this product object, and treats that object as the corresponding internal cofree coalgebra. It is distinct from the direct-sum coalgebra used for ind-nilpotent operators.

For \(K=\mathbb C((T))\), Remark 4.62 describes the Hodge realization into the Ind-derived category of rational polarizable mixed Hodge structures and asserts that this mixed abelian category is semisimple. In the same paragraph, for a filtered rational Hodge structure \((F^\bullet V_{\mathbb C},V_{\mathbb Q})\), it sets \(V_{\mathbb C}^{p,q}=F^pV_{\mathbb C}\cap\overline{F^qV_{\mathbb C}}\) and declares purity of weight \(n\) to mean \(V_{\mathbb C}^{p,q}=0\) whenever \(p+q\ne n\). The vanishing is asserted for all integer filtration indices, and the semisimplicity assertion concerns the mixed category, rather than just pure polarizable structures of a fixed weight.

Let \(T\) be a symmetric interval exchange on \([0,1)\) with an odd number \(d\) of exchanged intervals, and put \(f=\mathbf1_{(0,1/2)}-\mathbf1_{(1/2,1)}\) and \(S_hf(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}f(T^jx)\). Case A uses symmetric Rauzy return times \(n_k\) with a fixed positive terminal path, the center-projection identity of Lemma 6.1, and normalized lengths satisfying \(|\lambda_\beta^{n_k}/|I^{n_k}|-1/d|<1/(100d^3)\) for every label \(\beta\). Let \(1/2\in T^{\ell_k}(I_\alpha^{n_k})\), with \(0\le\ell_k<h_\alpha^{n_k}\), let \(\bar\alpha\) be the symmetric label, and define \(h_k=h_\alpha^{n_k}+h_{\bar\alpha}^{n_k}\), \(q_k=\min_\beta h_\beta^{n_k}\).

For every \(0\le i<q_k\) and \(x\in T^{-i}T^{\ell_k}(c_\alpha^{n_k}-2\lambda_\alpha^{n_k}/5,c_\alpha^{n_k}+2\lambda_\alpha^{n_k}/5)\), Claim A4 asserts \[S_{h_k}f(x)-S_{h_k}f(1/2)=f(T^ix).\] The argument subsequently asserts \(S_{h_k}f(1/2)=0\) and \(S_{h_k}f=-1\) on the tower with base \(T^{\ell_k}(c_\alpha^{n_k}+\lambda_\alpha^{n_k}/5,c_\alpha^{n_k}+2\lambda_\alpha^{n_k}/5)\). The construction explicitly permits the central label \(\alpha=\bar\alpha\), for which its defined time is \(2h_\alpha^{n_k}\). The issue concerns this local branch calculation; it does not assert failure of the almost-everywhere ergodicity theorem.

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be an ergodic probability-preserving system, \(G\) a locally compact abelian group with Haar measure \(\nu_G\), and \(\varphi:X\to G\) any measurable cocycle. The definition calls \(a\in G\) essential when, for every positive-measure \(A\in\mathcal B\) and every \(\epsilon>0\), there is \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \[\mu\{x\in A:T^nx\in A,\ \|S_n\varphi(x)-a\|_G<\epsilon\}>0.\] With this nonnegative/positive-time convention, Theorem 4.1 asserts that \(\operatorname{Ess}(T_\varphi)\) is either empty or a closed subgroup of \(G\), and that the skew product \(T_\varphi\) is ergodic for \(\mu\times\nu_G\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Ess}(T_\varphi)=G\). No recurrence or zero-mean assumption is imposed in this theorem.

For a symmetric interval exchange \(T=(\pi,\lambda)\) on a length simplex \(\Lambda_{\mathcal A}\), let \(T_n\) be its Rauzy-induced map, \(\lambda^n/|\lambda^n|\) the normalized induced length vector, \(c_\alpha^n\) the interval centers, and \(p_n\) the first backward projection onto the induced interval \(I^n\). Lemma 6.1 states that for almost every \(T\), and for every measurable \(A\subset\Lambda_{\mathcal A}\) of positive Lebesgue measure, there exist a finite positive Rauzy path \(\gamma\) and increasing times \(n_k\) such that each \(T_{n_k}\) is symmetric, \(\lambda^{n_k}/|\lambda^{n_k}|\in A\), its final \(|\gamma|\) induction steps are \(\gamma\), and \[\{p_{n_k}(c_\alpha):\alpha\in\mathcal A\}\cup\{p_{n_k}(1/2)\}=\{c_\alpha^{n_k}:\alpha\in\mathcal A\}\cup\{|I^{n_k}|/2\}.\] The disputed quantifier order gives one full-measure set of interval exchanges satisfying this for every such \(A\), including measurable sets chosen after \(T\).

Fix a smooth obstacle boundary \(\Gamma\), its interior \(\mathcal I\) and exterior \(\mathcal E\), and a smooth interior depth \(h_i\) bounded below by a positive constant as in Assumption 1. Let \(\Lambda\) be its weighted Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. For \(m\ge3\), the nonlinear shallow-water system has unknowns \(u=(\zeta,v)\), \(h=H_0+\zeta\), and boundary potential \(\psi_i\), with equations \(\partial_t\zeta+\nabla\cdot(hv)=0\), \(\partial_tv+\nabla(g\zeta+|v|^2/2)=0\), and boundary conditions \(N\cdot(hv)=\Lambda\psi_i\), \(\partial_t\psi_i+g\zeta+|v|^2/2=0\).

Theorem 5 takes \(u^{\mathrm{in}}\in H^m(\mathcal E)\), \(\psi_i^{\mathrm{in}}\in H^{m+1/2}(\Gamma)\), all compatibility conditions (134)–(135) through order \(m-1\), and the bounds \[\|u^{\mathrm{in}}\|_{H^m}+|\mathfrak d_{\mathrm{tan}}\psi_i^{\mathrm{in}}|_{H^{m-1/2}}\le M_0,\qquad gh^{\mathrm{in}}-|v^{\mathrm{in}}|^2\ge2c_0.\] Besides existence and uniqueness, it asserts \(\|u\|_{\mathbb W_T^m}+|\mathfrak d_{\mathrm{tan}}\psi_i|_{\mathbb W_{b,T}^{m+1/2}}\le C(c_0^{-1},M_0)\), with the other structural data fixed. Here \(\mathbb W_{b,T}^{m+1/2}=\bigcap_{j=0}^m C^j([0,T];H^{m-j+1/2}(\Gamma))\), so the asserted uniform estimate includes an \(H^{m+1/2}\) bound on the initial tangential derivative. That quantitative estimate, rather than the membership of \(\psi_i\) in the stated space, is the conclusion under review.

For the linear system (103)–(105), write \(u=(u^I,u^{II})\) and impose \(N\cdot u^{II}=\Lambda\psi_i+g_1\) and \(\partial_t\psi_i+u^I=g_2\) on \(\Gamma\). Proposition 16 assumes smooth uniformly positive symmetric \(S\), positive smooth interior depth, integers \(m,s\ge1\), data in \(H^m\), \(H^{m+1/2}\), \(\mathbb W_T^{m-1}\) and \(\mathbb W_{b,T}^{m-1/2}\) as specified in (111), and compatibility through order \(m-1\). For convergent approximations of \(\psi_i^{\mathrm{in}},f,g_1,g_2\) of regularity higher by \(s\), it constructs an initial correction \(w^{\mathrm{in}(n)}\to0\) in \(H^m\) intended to enforce compatibility through order \(m+s-1\).

The disputed displayed construction defines \(w_j=u_j-\widetilde u_j\) and \(\phi_{i,j}=\widetilde\psi_{i,j}-\psi_{i,j}\), uses \(\phi_{i,j+1}=-(w_j)^I|_\Gamma\), and prescribes \[N\cdot w_j^{II}=\Lambda\phi_{i,j}-\bigl(N\cdot\widetilde u_j^{II}-\Lambda\widetilde\psi_{i,j}\bigr).\] It also asserts that the parenthesized residual tends to zero, although the actual compatibility equation (110) is \(N\cdot u_j^{II}-\Lambda\psi_{i,j}=(\partial_t^jg_1)|_{t=0}\). The input \(g_1\) is arbitrary in its stated regularity class; the proposition has not reduced to homogeneous boundary data.

Let a regular solution of \(\partial_tu+A_j\partial_ju+Bu=f\) on \((0,T)\times\mathcal E\) have a symmetric symmetrizer \(S\) with \(SA_j\) symmetric, \(\alpha_0I\le S\le\beta_0I\), \(S(0)\le\beta_0^{\mathrm{in}}I\), and \(\partial_tS+\partial_j(SA_j)-2SB\le\beta_1I\) as a quadratic form. Set \(\mathcal B[u]=SA_{\mathrm{nor}}u\cdot u\), \(F_\lambda(t)=\int_0^te^{-2\lambda\tau}\int_\Gamma\mathcal B[u(\tau)]\,d\Gamma\,d\tau\), and \(I_{\lambda,t}(v)=\sup_{\tau\le t}e^{-\lambda\tau}|v(\tau)|+\sqrt\lambda\|e^{-\lambda\tau}v\|_{L^2(0,t)}\). Equation (45) asserts, for \(\lambda\ge\beta_1/\alpha_0\), \[I_{\lambda,t}(\|u\|_2)^2\le C\frac{\beta_0^{\mathrm{in}}}{\alpha_0}\|u(0)\|_2^2+C\frac{\beta_0}{\alpha_0}\bigl(S^*_{\lambda,t}(\|f\|_2)\bigr)^2+\frac4{\alpha_0}F_\lambda(t),\] where \(S^*_{\lambda,t}\) is the weighted dual norm in (29).

Definition 2 permits weak dissipativity in the form \(F_\lambda(t)\le-E_{\mathrm{bdry}}(t)+S_{\mathrm{data}}(t)+\alpha_0 I_{\lambda,t}(\|u\|_2)^2/8\), with \(E_{\mathrm{bdry}}\ge0\) and \(S_{\mathrm{data}}\ge0\) nondecreasing and determined by the data, for every \(\lambda\ge\lambda_0\). Proposition 6 then asserts the corresponding estimate with \(8E_{\mathrm{bdry}}/\alpha_0\) on the left and \(8S_{\mathrm{data}}/\alpha_0\) on the right. The disputed bound uses the signed flux at the final time to control a norm that includes the supremum over all preceding times.

For the exterior and interior shallow-water fields \((\zeta,v)\), \((\zeta_w,v_i)\), physical fluid density \(\rho>0\), gravitational acceleration \(g>0\), atmospheric pressure \(P_{\mathrm{atm}}\), and interior pressure \(\underline P_i\), the Bernoulli row in introductory equation (3) states \[P_{\mathrm{atm}}+g\zeta+\tfrac12|v|^2=\underline P_i+g\zeta_w+\tfrac12|v_i|^2\quad\text{on }\Gamma.\] The physical momentum equation uses \(\rho^{-1}\nabla\underline P_i\), and the density \(\rho\) is not fixed to one. Separately, Section 5.2 identifies the reduced energy \(\frac12\int_{\mathcal E}(g\zeta^2+h|v|^2)+\frac12\int_\Gamma\psi_i\Lambda\psi_i\) exactly with \(\mathfrak E_{\mathrm{fluid}}/\rho\), where the physical energy also includes \((\rho g/2)\int_{\mathcal I}\zeta_w^2\). The issue is these pressure and additive-energy normalizations, not the time derivative of the fixed interior potential term.

In the normal-derivative reconstruction, Assumption 5 divides the normal matrix's eigenvalues into the first \(n_1\) characteristic modes and the last \(n_2\) modes, \(\lambda_{n_1+1},\ldots,\lambda_{n_1+n_2}\), which have definite nonzero sign, with \(n_1+n_2=n\). Assumption 6(i) nevertheless requires \(\|(\lambda_{n_1}^{-1},\ldots,\lambda_{n_1+n_2}^{-1})\|_{L^\infty}\le K_0\). Lemma 3's actual reconstruction divides only by \(\lambda_j\) for \(n_1+1\le j\le n_1+n_2\). The disputed first index adds a reciprocal of a characteristic eigenvalue that is not assumed nonzero, including in the stated shallow-water application.

For a positive integer winding number \(n\), let \(f_0\) be the regular radial vortex solution in (2.9)–(2.10), with \(f_0(0)=0\) and \(f_0(r)\to1\), and define \[C_n=\lim_{r\to\infty}\left(\int_0^r t f_0(t)^2(1-f_0(t)^2)\,dt-n^2\log r\right).\] The dominant inner phase is fixed by the integral equation and its origin condition; the dominant outer phase uses the logarithmic derivative of \(K_{inq}\). For small \(q>0\), set \(\rho=(q/|\log q|)^{1/3}\), \(r_0=e^{\rho/q}/\sqrt2\), \(\epsilon=\mu e^{-\pi/(2nq)}\), and \(k=\epsilon/q\), with the cutoff chosen so that \(r_0=\epsilon^{\alpha-1}\).

Proposition 4.6 prescribes \(\mu\in[e^{-C_n/n^2-\gamma},3e^{-C_n/n^2-\gamma}]\), where \(\gamma\) is Euler's constant, and asserts that for every sufficiently small positive \(q\) the dominant matching equations (4.24)–(4.25) admit parameters \((a_0,b_0,\mu)\) with the specified small amplitude bounds. In particular, it requires the exact equality \(v_0^{\mathrm{in}}(r_0;k,q)=v_0^{\mathrm{out}}(r_0;k,q)\) in that interval. The assertion is made for all allowed winding numbers and in the overlap regime (4.19)–(4.22); the report addresses the signs of \(C_n\) and of the quadratic-wavenumber term used to derive this interval.

For the complex Ginzburg–Landau equation with real dispersion parameters \(A,\beta\), the twist is \(q=(\beta-A)/(1+A\beta)\), in the regime \(|A-\beta|<1\) used for the change of variables. A rigidly rotating single-mode \(n\)-armed Archimedean spiral has regular radial amplitude and phase, one zero at the origin, and a physical asymptotic wavenumber \(K=\lim_{r\to\infty}\Theta'(r)\), with far-field amplitude \(\sqrt{1-K^2}\) and the stated dispersion relation. Theorem 1.5 asserts a unique odd function \(\kappa_*\) of \(q\) alone such that such spirals exist if and only if \(K=\kappa_*(q)\); Remark 1.6 explicitly says that their dependence on \(A,\beta\) is only through \(q\).

The same paper's exact normalization in Lemma 2.3 relates the normalized wavenumber \(k\) to the physical one by \(K=k/\sqrt{1-Aq(1-k^2)}\). The questioned claims are the universal physical selection by \(q\) alone and its oddness at fixed physical dispersion, rather than oddness of the normalized branch after the stated coordinate and amplitude changes.

In the inner construction, write \(f=f_0+g\) and \(\widehat v=v_0+w\), where \((f_0,v_0)\) is the base solution and the perturbed phase satisfies \(f\widehat v'+f\widehat v/r+2f'\widehat v+f(1-f^2-k^2)=0\), with regular origin conditions. Equation (6.6) asserts the equivalent equation \[w'+\frac wr+\frac{f_0'}{f_0}w=g(g+2f_0)-\frac{(v_0+w)(f_0g'-f_0'g)}{f_0(f_0+g)}.\] The subsequent \(s=\sqrt2r\) source (6.16) gives its derivative term a positive unit coefficient in the displayed normalization.

For the amplitude correction, define \(L_n=\partial_s^2+s^{-1}\partial_s-(1+n^2/s^2)\). Equation (6.7) is \(L_n\delta g=N_1[\delta g,\delta v]\), with \(\delta g(0)=0\) and the explicit nonlinear source (6.8). For \(s_1>0\), the paper introduces \[\mathcal K\psi(s)=K_n(s)\int_0^s tI_n(t)\psi(t)\,dt+I_n(s)\int_s^{s_1}tK_n(t)\psi(t)\,dt.\] Lemma 6.1 asserts that the regular solutions are represented as \(\delta g=I_nb+\mathcal K N_1[\delta g,\delta v]\). These claimed equivalences, including the inverse sign and phase coefficients, are used to supply the inner nonlinear family.

Fix \(n\), \(\eta>0\), and \(0<\mu_0<\mu_1\), and let \(\epsilon=\mu e^{-\pi/(2nq)}\), \(k=\epsilon/q\), with \(\mu\in[\mu_0,\mu_1]\). Theorems 4.3 and 5.3 assert constants \(q_0,e_0,M>0\) depending on these fixed data but not on \(\alpha\), for every \(0<q\le q_0\), every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) with \(q^{-1}\epsilon^{1-\alpha}<e_0\), and the allowed amplitude parameters. The outer corrections \((G,W)\) are defined for \(R\ge\epsilon^\alpha\), with \(\|h\|_2=\sup_{R\ge\epsilon^\alpha}R^2|h(R)|\), and satisfy \(\|G\|_2+\epsilon\|G'\|_2+\epsilon\|W\|_2\le M\epsilon^2\).

The refined decomposition in Theorem 5.3(iii) has \(W=W^0+W^1\), where \(W^0\) vanishes at the allowed value \(a=0\) and \(\|W^1\|_2\le M_1\epsilon^{2-\alpha}/q\), again uniformly in \(\alpha\). Thus at \(a=0\) the theorem requires both \(\|G\|_2\le M\epsilon^2\) and \(\|W\|_2\le M_1\epsilon^{2-\alpha}/q\) throughout the full printed cutoff range, including choices of \(\alpha\) that tend to zero with \(q\). No positive lower bound on \(\alpha\) is imposed.

Put \(\epsilon=kq=\mu e^{-\pi/(2nq)}\), with \(\mu\) in any fixed positive compact interval, and let \(V_0(R)=K_{inq}'(R)/K_{inq}(R)\). The dominant fields are \(v_0^{\mathrm{out}}(r)=kV_0(\epsilon r)\) and \(F_0(R)=\sqrt{1-k^2V_0(R)^2-n^2\epsilon^2/R^2}\), expressed as \(f_0^{\mathrm{out}}\) in the original radius. Proposition 4.2(iii) asserts \(\partial_rv_0^{\mathrm{out}}(r)>0\) for every \(kqr\ge2e^{-\pi/(2nq)}\).

Part (iv), and Lemma A.3 in the outer coordinate, assert reality and the lower bound \(F_0(R)\ge1/2\) on \(R\ge R_{\min}\) whenever \(2e^2e^{-\pi/(2nq)}\le R_{\min}\le\epsilon^\alpha\), for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and sufficiently small \(q\). These are the literal starting domains under review; they do not separately require a physical-radius or radicand-positivity condition.

At the matching radius \(r_0\), set \(K=K_0(\sqrt2r_0)\), \(I=I(\sqrt2r_0)\), with primes on these Bessel functions denoting derivatives of their arguments, and let \(d=KI'-K'I\ne0\). The actual nonlinear amplitude matching equations are \(Ka-Ib=\Delta\) and \(K'a-I'b=\Delta'/\sqrt2\), where \(\Delta=\Delta(r_0;a,b;k,q)\) and \(\Delta'=\partial_r\Delta(r_0;a,b;k,q)\). Equation (4.38) asserts their equivalence to a fixed-point map whose second component is \[b=C_2(a,b;k,q)=\frac{-K'\Delta+K\Delta'/\sqrt2}{d}.\] This is the component used in comparison with \(b_0\) and in the Brouwer matching map; its algebraic equivalence to the displayed two equations is the assertion being checked.

With \(\rho=(q/|\log q|)^{1/3}\) and \(r_0=e^{\rho/q}/\sqrt2\), the phase-remainder calculation on page 33 replaces a term \(Mq^3|\log r_0|^3/r_0\) by \(M\rho^3/r_0^2\). In the subsequent amplitude matching normalization, \(b=\widehat b\,\rho^2r_0^{-3/2}e^{-\sqrt2r_0}\), the bound on \(C_2-b_0\) has size \(M e^{-\sqrt2r_0}\rho^4r_0^{-3/2}\), while (4.41) asserts \(|H_2(\widehat a,\widehat b,\mu;q)|\le M\rho^4\) for the corresponding normalized correction. These are the two displayed substitutions under review, rather than a claim that the final required \(O(|\log q|^{-1})\) remainder is unattainable.

At zero twist \(q=0\), hence \(\beta=A\), the paragraph following (1.8) writes the solution as \(\mathcal A(t,x)=e^{-iAt}\widehat A(t,x)\) and says that the rotated unknown satisfies the real Ginzburg–Landau equation \(\partial_t\widehat A=\Delta\widehat A+\widehat A-|\widehat A|^2\widehat A\). The displayed statement explicitly restricts \(\widehat A(t,x)\) to be real-valued. The report treats the intended scope of this wording as needing clarification: it does not assert an all-hypothesis counterexample within that real-valued class or silently extend the claim to general complex-valued evolution.

Let \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[T]/(T^2-1)\), with the paper's involution, and let \((P,\lambda)\) be a nonsingular even hermitian form on a free \(\Lambda\)-module. Let \(V\subset P\) be a free direct summand of half the rank. Lemma 9.12 assumes that its plus specialization \(\mathcal E_+(V)\) is a lagrangian in \(\mathcal E_+(P)\), and that its minus specialization \(\mathcal E_-(V)\) has a lagrangian complement in \(\mathcal E_-(P)\). It concludes that \(V\) has a lagrangian complement over \(\Lambda\).

The questioned construction chooses any basis \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) of \(V\), completes it by \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) to a basis of \(P\), and defines \(u_i=\widehat\lambda^{-1}(x_i^*)\), where \(x_i^*(x_j)=\delta_{ij}\) and \(x_i^*(v_j)=0\). It asserts that the vectors \(x_i,u_i\) generate \(P\). Writing \(u=Ax+Bv\), the proof treats the pairing identity after plus specialization as \(BL=I\) over \(\Lambda\), and infers that \(B\) is invertible. The issue is this particular basis construction, rather than the existence conclusion of Lemma 9.12 after a replacement proof.

Let \(R\) be a ring with involution and \(P\) a projective \(R\)-module. With \(\varepsilon=1\), Lemma 3.7 asserts that the symmetrization map \(1+\mathord\top:Q_+(P)\to Q^+(P)\), from quadratic classes to hermitian forms, is injective. Corollary 3.8 therefore asserts that every \((+1)\)-hermitian form admitting a quadratic refinement has exactly one, and that any direct summand \(L\subset P\) on which its bilinear pairing vanishes is a sublagrangian for that refinement. The printed statements do not assume absence of additive \(2\)-torsion in \(R\).

For an \(\varepsilon\)-quadratic form \((P,\psi)\), Definition 3.5 calls a direct summand \(j:L\hookrightarrow P\) a sublagrangian when \(j^*\psi j=0\), and a lagrangian when moreover \(L=L^\perp\), with \(L^\perp=\ker(j^*(1+\varepsilon\mathord\top)\psi)\). Remark 3.6 asserts that, when \(P\) is stably free, the map \(j^*(1+\varepsilon\mathord\top)\psi:P\to L^*\) is automatically surjective, without separately imposing nonsingularity of the ambient form. This is the general convention at issue; the later nonsingular quasi-formations have additional hypotheses.

Let \(F\) be a closed nonorientable surface, \(\xi\) a rank-two real vector bundle with oriented total space, \(N=D(\xi)\) its disk bundle and \(Y=S(\xi)=\partial N\) its sphere bundle. Remove an open disk from \(F\) to obtain \(\dot F\), and let \((\dot N,\dot Y)\) be the disk/sphere bundles of \(\xi|_{\dot F}\). The proof of Proposition 4.2 asserts, by excision, \[H_i(\dot N,\dot Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_i(N,Y;\mathbb Z)\qquad\text{for every }i\ge0.\] The asserted degree range is all degrees, although the subsequent calculation uses only degrees one and two.

Let \(\xi\) be a rank-two bundle of even Euler number \(e\) over a closed nonorientable surface \(F\), with oriented disk-bundle total space \(N\). Construction 4.4 uses the nontrivial fiber character to define a double cover \(Y^\varphi\) of \(Y=\partial N\); the proof of Lemma 4.5 extends it to a two-fold branched cover \(p:N_2(F)\to N\) branched over the zero section. It instructs that \(N_2(F)\) be oriented so that \(p\) has degree one, and uses that claimed degree to fix the positive sign in the Euler-number relation \(e=2e'\). The local degree of each unbranched sheet and the global degree of the two-sheeted map are the notions being distinguished.

In Corollary D, a locally linear semifree involution on \(Z=\#_a\mathbb{CP}^2\#_b\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^2\) has a nonorientable fixed surface \(\widetilde F\) of genus \(a+b\), simply connected exterior, and the specified genus/Euler-number range of Theorem A. For the quotient \(X=Z/\tau\) and its branch surface \(F\), the proof obtains \(\pi_1(X_F)=\mathbb Z_2\), \(\pi_1(X)=\pi_1(X_F)/\langle\mu_F\rangle\), and \(\chi(X)=2\).

Assuming the meridian \(\mu_F\) trivial, it constructs two independent essential mod-two homology classes and infers \(b_2(X;\mathbb F_2)\ge2\), then claims \(\chi(X)\ge1+2+1=4\). This Euler-characteristic inference is used to exclude the residual possibility \(\pi_1(X)=\mathbb Z_2\) and prove simple connectedness. The report questions this inference under that residual fundamental-group hypothesis, rather than giving an involution satisfying all of Corollary D's assumptions with a false conclusion.

Let \(F\subset D^4\) be a \(\mathbb Z_2\)-surface, choose a tubular neighborhood and a nice section \(s:F\to S(\nu F)\), and use the framed immersed disks in the exterior specified in Definition 6.14. For an oriented embedded loop \(\gamma\subset s(F)\), the definition assigns \(\widehat q_{\mathrm{GM}}(\gamma)=W(D_0)\in\mathbb Z_4\), the number of right-handed half-twists in its prescribed normal-line comparison. It then asserts that these values extend linearly from an embedded-loop basis of \(H_1(s(F);\mathbb F_2)\) to a function into \(\mathbb Z_4\). Proposition 6.15 identifies the resulting function with the Guillou–Marin quadratic refinement of the mod-two intersection form. The assertion at issue is the linear extension, with one-sided classes included, rather than the geometric quadratic identification.

Proposition A.6 takes \(V=\mathbb Z^3\) and the quadratic form represented by \[\theta=\pm\begin{pmatrix}4&4&4\\0&2&2\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}=\pm2X_3,\] and asserts that the boundary-automorphism double-coset set \(\operatorname{bAut}(V,2\theta)\) is trivial. Its proof explicitly sets \(\psi=2\theta\), but then uses the discriminant group \(\mathbb Z_8\oplus\mathbb Z_2^2\) and boundary quadratic form computed for \(2X_3\) in Lemmas A.4–A.5. The literal statement therefore concerns the boundary of \(4X_3\), whereas the discriminant calculation used in the proof concerns \(2X_3\); the doubled auxiliary statement is the one under review.

For a curve class \(\beta\) on the Enriques surface \(Y\), equation (6.2) defines \(f^{\mathrm{KM}}_\beta=[\Theta(z,2\tau)^2\eta(2\tau)^8/(\Theta(z,\tau)^2\eta(\tau)^{16})]_{q^{\beta^2/2}}\). With \(p=e^z\), the paper then sets \(\widehat f_\beta=f^{\mathrm{PT}}_\beta-f^{\mathrm{KM}}_\beta\) and \(\widehat{dt}(r,\beta,n)=dt(r,\beta,n)-8[\eta(\tau)^{-12}]_{q^{\beta^2/2-r^2/2-rn}}\). Here \(f^{\mathrm{PT}}\) and \(dt\) are the stable-pair series and the reduced Donaldson–Thomas invariants defined earlier in the paper.

Lemma 6.5 asserts, for every \(\beta\) in these series, \[\widehat f_\beta=\sum_{n>0}\sum_{r>0}(-1)^{r-1}(n+r)\widehat{dt}(r,\beta,n)(p^n+p^{-n})-\sum_{n>0}n\widehat{dt}(0,\beta,n)p^n+\sum_{r>0}(-1)^{r-1}r\widehat{dt}(r,\beta,0).\] The recorded check concerns this identity with exactly the normalization in (6.2), including its application to primitive effective isotropic classes; it does not insert an additional factor into that definition.

Let \(E_8\) be the positive definite even unimodular lattice with Gram matrix \(Q_{E_8}\), let \(\alpha_0\in E_8\) satisfy \(\alpha_0^2=4\), and let \(m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). For a quasi-Jacobi form \(f(x,\tau)\) of weight \(k\) and index \(mQ_{E_8}\) for \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\ltimes(\mathbb Z^8\oplus\mathbb Z^8)\), Lemma 2.6 defines \[M_{\alpha_0,m}f=q^{2m}e^{2\pi i m(\alpha_0\cdot x)}(e^{\xi_{\alpha_0}/2}f)(x+\alpha_0\tau,2\tau).\] The operator \(\xi_{\alpha_0}\) is the elliptic anomaly operator of Definition 2.5, obtained from differentiation of the almost-holomorphic completion.

The asserted conclusion is that \(M_{\alpha_0,m}f\) is a quasi-Jacobi form of the same weight and index \(\tfrac m2Q_{E_8}\) for \(\Gamma_0(2)\ltimes(2\mathbb Z^8\oplus\mathbb Z^8)\). In the paper's weak convention, the coefficients of the almost-holomorphic completion must have no negative Fourier powers at every cusp. The check concerns preservation of this cusp condition, including for holomorphic inputs for which \(\xi_{\alpha_0}f=0\); an additional Fourier-support restriction is not among the stated hypotheses.

Let \(Q=(X\times E)/\mathbb Z_2\) be the Enriques Calabi–Yau threefold, and let \(P_v^Q(n)\) be the Joyce–Song pair invariant for fibre-supported sheaves of class \(v\), with \(n\) sufficiently large and the relative polarization specified in Section 7. Put \(A_\delta=(-1)^{\chi(\delta v(n))}\chi(\delta v(n))\mathrm{DT}(\delta v)\). Equation (7.1) expresses \(P_v^Q(n)\) as the sum over ordered positive rational decompositions \(v_i=\delta_i v\), \(\sum_i\delta_i=1\), of \((-1)^\ell\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}A_{\delta_i}/\ell!\).

For \(f_{v,n}^Q(t)=1+\sum_{0<\delta\le1}P_{\delta v}^Q(n)t^\delta+O(t^{1+})\), the proof of Theorem 7.2 claims that the same formula can be rewritten as \[f_{v,n}^Q(t)=\exp\!\left(\sum_{\delta>0}A_\delta t^\delta\right)+O(t^{1+}).\] It then uses \(f_{v,n}^Q=(f_{v,n}^{K_Y})^4\) to obtain the analogous exponential with coefficient \(1/4\) for \(K_Y\). The recorded check concerns the signs in these two formal power-series identities, rather than a disproof of the final relation \(\mathrm{VW}(v)=\mathrm{DT}(v)/4\).

For a Laurent series \(f(\zeta,q)=\sum_{v,r}c(v,r)q^v\zeta^r\) and an integer \(\ell\ge1\), equation (2.7) prints \[f|_{k,L}V_\ell=\sum_{v\ge0}\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z^n}\sum_{\substack{a\mid(v,r,\ell)\\a\ \mathrm{odd}}}a^{k-1}c(\ell v/a^2,r/a)q^v\zeta^r.\] Proposition 2.7 asserts, for every \(\ell,s\ge1\), that this gives a map from \(\Delta^{-s}\mathrm{QJac}_{k,L}(\Gamma_0(2))\) to \(\Delta^{-\ell s}\mathrm{QJac}_{k,\ell L}(\Gamma_0(2))\), where \(\Delta=\eta^{24}\).

The issue recorded here is which Fourier exponents are intended for a Laurent input with a principal part: the displayed restriction \(v\ge0\) in (2.7) is compared with the finite-coset Hecke operator and unrestricted Fourier expansion in Appendix A.3. The report classifies this as a notation clarification and does not establish a substantive failure for the geometric inputs used later in the paper.

Let \(m>2\) be an integer and let \(f(\tau)\) be a quasi-modular form of weight \(k\) for \(\Gamma_0(2)\) whose Fourier expansion has the form \(\sum_{\ell\ge0}a_\ell q^{\ell m}\). In the quasi-modular part of the proof of Lemma 2.11, set \(\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/m\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). The proof asserts the group inclusion \[\Gamma_0(2m^2)\subseteq\gamma^{-1}\Gamma_0(2)\gamma\cap\Gamma_0(2).\] It uses this inclusion to regard the completion \(F(\tau)\) and its translate \(F(\tau+1/m)\) as almost-holomorphic modular forms for the same group before comparing their holomorphic parts. The check concerns this particular inclusion; it does not assert that the lemma's final vanishing/constancy conclusion is false.

Let \(Y\) be the generic elliptic Enriques surface used in Section 4, let \(\beta\in H_2(Y,\mathbb Z)\), and let \(\overline M_{0,n}(Y,\beta)\) be the moduli space of connected genus-zero stable maps with \(n\) marked points. Remark 4.1(c) asserts, without a stated restriction \(\beta\ne0\), that \[[\overline M_{0,n}(Y,\beta)]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0\] for dimension reasons, citing pullback from the unmarked moduli space. The recorded check concerns the scope of that assertion at degree zero, where stable constant maps are included when \(n\ge3\). It retains the paper's actual genus-zero virtual-class claim rather than replacing it by a vanishing assertion limited to nonzero degree.

Use the normalization \(G_2(\tau)=-1/24+\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_1(n)q^n\) and \(F_2(\tau)=G_2(\tau)-2G_2(2\tau)\) of equation (2.1), so that \(F_2\) has constant coefficient \(1/24\). For the half-fibre class \(s\) of the elliptic Enriques surface, Section 4.4.3 prints \[F_{1,0}(\tau_0(s))=2G_2(q)-2G_2(q^2)=G_2(q)+\tfrac1{24}F_2(q).\] The recorded check is the compatibility of the final equality with this stated normalization. The report treats it as a local normalization clarification: it does not challenge the preceding expression for the series or the subsequently computed anomaly derivative.

Let \(k\ge2\) be an integer and \(p\) a prime. A nonempty set \(A\subseteq\mathbb F_p\) is of \(S_k\)-type if, for every \(a\in A\), some \(d\in\mathbb F_p^\times\) satisfies \(a+jd\in A\) for all \(-k\le j\le k\). In the proof of Lemma 2, put \(x=\lceil p^{1/(4k+4)}\rceil\) and let \(A=\bigcup_{i=1}^{4k+4}A_i\) be the recursively constructed union on PDF pages 7–8. The claim checked is that a universal constant \(K\ge32\), independent of \(k\) and \(p\), makes this particular union satisfy \(|A|\le p^{1/(2k+2)}\) for every prime \(p>k^{Kk}\).

The construction necessarily contains \([-kx,-kx+k]\subseteq B_1\) and, for \(2\le i\le4k+3\), every \(a-jx^{i-1}\) with \(a\in B_{i-1}\) and \(2kx-k\le j\le2kx\) in both \(B_i\) and \(A_i\). These are original mandatory branches, not additional assumptions. The reported obstruction is to the size bound for the constructed union, not to the existence of some other small \(S_k\)-type set or to Theorem B itself.

For a prime \(p\ge3\), let \(S_1(p)\) be the least size of a nonempty subset \(A\subseteq\mathbb F_p\) such that every \(a\in A\) is the midpoint of a nontrivial three-term progression in \(A\): there are \(b,c\in A\) with \(2a=b+c\) and \(b\ne a\). Lemma 1 asserts \(S_1(p)=N_1(p)\le2\lfloor\log_2p\rfloor\) for every such prime. In the branch \(p=4k+3\), its halving construction uses the further identity \(2(\lfloor\log_2(k+1)\rfloor+1)+2=2\lfloor\log_2p\rfloor\). The recorded check includes the small primes and the boundary at which \(p+1\) is a power of two; neither is excluded in the original lemma.

Let \(p\) be prime, \(n\ge1\), and \(M\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p)\) have row vectors \(a_i\); let \(a_i'\) denote the columns of \(M^{-1}\). Proposition 2 claims that the condition “every \(u\in\mathbb F_p^n\) has \(u_i=0\) or \(\langle a_i,u\rangle=0\) for some \(i\)” is equivalent to the following orthogonality statement: whenever complex-valued \(f,g\) satisfy \[\sum_{v:v_i=t}f(v)=0,\qquad\sum_{v:\langle a_i',v\rangle=t}g(v)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,n,\ t\in\mathbb F_p),\] one has \(\sum_v f(v)g(v)=0\).

Proposition 3 asserts the analogous equivalence over \(\mathbb F_p\), with the covering condition replaced by \(\prod_i(1-g^{e_i})\prod_i(1-g^{a_i})=0\) in \(\mathbb F_p[\mathbb F_p^n]\). Here \(g^v\) is the group-ring basis element indexed by \(v\). Both printed hypotheses sum over the sets obtained by fixing one coordinate, namely hyperplanes (singletons when \(n=1\)); the statements being checked do not instead assume zero sums along coordinate lines.

For functions on \(\mathbb F_p^n\), the paper uses the unnormalized transform \(\widehat f(u)=\sum_v f(v)\omega^{\langle u,v\rangle}\), where \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/p}\), and the normalized convolution \((f*g)(v)=p^{-n}\sum_w f(w)g(v-w)\). Section 5 prints \(\widehat{f*g}=\widehat f\widehat g\), and the proof of Proposition 2 uses \(\sum_v f(v)g(v)=\sum_u\widehat f(u)\widehat g(u)\). The recorded check concerns these identities with those exact conventions.

The same normalization check includes the finite-field displays for \(\delta_i f(v)=f(v)-f(v+e_i)\): for \(1\le b_i\le p-1\), the claimed leading term of \(\delta_1\cdots\delta_n\prod_i x_i^{b_i}\) is \((\prod_i b_i)\prod_i x_i^{b_i-1}\); the line-sum argument identifies the sum of a reduced polynomial in one coordinate with its \(x_i^{p-1}\) coefficient; and \(\prod_i\prod_{r\ne v_i}(x_i-r)\) is claimed to equal \(1\) at \(x=v\). The report classifies these normalization/sign issues as clarifications because the zero and nonzero criteria used there survive multiplication by the missing nonzero factors.

Let \(M=(a_{ij})\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p)\), and let \(0\le r_i,s_i\le p-1\) be integers with \(Q=\sum_i r_i=\sum_i s_i\). Put \(P(x,y)=(\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}x_jy_i)^Q\). The proof of Lemma 9 computes \[ [x^s]\prod_i(\sum_j a_{ij}x_j)^{r_i}=[x^sy^r]P(x,y)\,\frac{\prod_i r_i!}{Q!},\] and makes the corresponding computation with \(s\) and the transposed matrix. These intermediate identities are asserted in characteristic \(p\) without assuming \(Q<p\). The recorded issue is whether division by \(Q!\) is defined under the allowed exponents; the report does not reject the lemma's final equivalence between the two coefficient-vanishing conditions.

Let \(k\) be a prime field other than \(\mathbb F_2\), let \(\mathrm{SH}(k)\) be the category of motivic spectra, and write \(\rho=[-1]\in\pi_{-1,-1}\mathbf1_k\). Let \(C(\rho)\) be the cofiber of \(\rho:\Sigma^{-1,-1}\mathbf1_k\to\mathbf1_k\), let \(X/2\) denote the cofiber of multiplication by \(2\), and let \(s_q\) be the effective \(q\)-slice functor. In the proof of Theorem 3.1, for a cellular \(X\) with convergent slice tower, exactness is invoked to assert \[s_*(C(\rho)\otimes X/2)\simeq C(\rho)\otimes s_*(X/2).\] The right side means the ordinary \(\rho\)-cofiber of the slice object; it does not include a shift of the slice index.

The surrounding vanishing argument additionally assumes \(p^*(C(\rho)\otimes X/2)=0\) for an algebraic closure \(p:\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}k\). The report challenges the stated formal interchange from exactness, not the conservativity implication with this additional premise: its counterexample does not satisfy algebraic-closure vanishing and therefore is not a counterexample to Theorem 3.1 or Theorem A.

Consider \(iv_t-v_{xx}-F'(|v|^2)v=0\) and a branch of positive even localized solitons satisfying \(\Phi_\omega''-\omega\Phi_\omega+F'(\Phi_\omega^2)\Phi_\omega=0\). Section 8.1.1 takes arbitrary \(C^1\) functions \(\gamma,p,y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R\) and \(\omega:[0,T]\to(0,\omega_*)\), and writes \(v(t,x)=e^{i(p(t)x-\gamma(t))}(\Phi_{\omega(t)}+u(t))(x+y(t))\). In the shifted coordinate \(z=x+y(t)\), equations (8.2) and (8.9) claim that the resulting modulation term has phase-direction coefficient \(\omega-p^2-\dot\gamma\), multiplying \(\Phi_\omega+u\) in the scalar equation and \(\Xi_0+\sigma_3U\) in the vector equation.

The claimed identity is asserted before the orthogonality conditions selecting the frame are imposed. The check therefore concerns exact differentiation of this coordinate ansatz for the stated arbitrary frame parameters, not a counterexample satisfying the later trapped-orbit or orthogonality conditions.

Let \(\widetilde f_\pm\) be the two distorted spectral components of a physical-real continuous spectral profile in the scattering setting of the paper. For \(\xi>0\), set \(F_+=(\widetilde f_+(\xi),\widetilde f_+(-\xi))^\top\), \(F_-=(\widetilde f_-(\xi),\widetilde f_-(-\xi))^\top\), and \(R(\xi)=\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\s&r\end{pmatrix}\), where the actual reflection/transmission coefficients obey \(R^*R=I\). The physical reality relation is \(F_-=-R^*\overline{F_+}\).

For the cubic coefficient \(\Theta_\rho(\xi)\) obtained by summing the scattering coefficients in Section 13.1.4, equation (13.10) asserts \(\Theta_\rho(\xi)=-|\widetilde f_\rho(\xi)|^2\widetilde f_\rho(\xi)\) for both \(\rho=+\) and \(\rho=-\). This yields the same local cubic phase evolution on both spectral branches. The report checks the negative-branch algebra on smooth small profiles satisfying the exact reality relation, weighted \(L^2\) and \(H^1\) regularity, and zero trace at frequency zero; it does not assume an arbitrary unitary matrix is realizable scattering data or that every such profile is an entire nonlinear orbit.

Let \(H=\operatorname{diag}(-\partial_x^2+1,\partial_x^2-1)+\begin{pmatrix}V_1&V_2\\-V_2&-V_1\end{pmatrix}\) have the even smooth exponentially decaying potentials and absence of embedded eigenvalues and threshold resonances assumed in Sections 3–7. Write \(P_{\mathrm e}\) for its continuous spectral projection and \(\widetilde f_\lambda\) for its distorted transform. For a positive ground-state branch \(\Phi_\omega\), Section 3.2 prints the linearized potential \(V_1=-F'(\Phi_\omega^2)+F''(\Phi_\omega^2)\Phi_\omega^2\), \(V_2=-F''(\Phi_\omega^2)\Phi_\omega^2\), and Lemma 3.4 asserts the generalized-kernel relations of (1.4), in particular \(H_\omega(\Phi_\omega,-\Phi_\omega)^\top=0\). The report concerns these intermediate formulas and retains the distinction from the local decay estimate, for which it supplies a repair.

Use the paper's distorted Fourier convention with factor \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\) in both directions, \(\sigma_3\) in the forward pairing, and branch sign \(\lambda\) in the inverse. Let \(\Xi_0=(\Phi,-\Phi)^\top\), \(\Xi_1=(\partial_\omega\Phi,\partial_\omega\Phi)^\top\), \(\Xi_2=(\partial_x\Phi,\partial_x\Phi)^\top\), and \(\Xi_3=(x\Phi,-x\Phi)^\top\). The printed leading extractions are \(\dot\omega=-c_\omega^{-1}b_0\) and \(\dot p=-\|\Phi_\omega\|_2^{-2}b_2\).

The energy calculation on PDF page 56 also expands the kinetic-minus-potential Hamiltonian of \(v=e^{i(px-\gamma)}(\Phi_\omega+u)(x+y)\) using the unboosted \(\Phi_\omega+u\) expression, without displaying momentum or \(p^2\)-mass contributions. The report checks these local reality, extraction, and energy identities; it does not identify a failure of the absolute-value modulation bounds after their correction.

Section 2.2 specifies a smooth inhomogeneous partition \(\sum_{k\ge0}\varphi_k=1\), with \(\operatorname{supp}\varphi_0=[-1,1]\) and \(\varphi_k(x)=\varphi(2^{-k}|x|)\) for \(k\ge1\), where \(\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset[1/2,2]\). It defines \(\varphi_{<\ell}=\sum_{0\le k<\ell}\varphi_k\) and subsequently uses negative-index complements such as \(\varphi_{>-m\kappa}\), \(m>0\), as cutoffs excluding a neighborhood of zero. The check concerns whether these precise definitions supply the claimed smooth partition and subunit-frequency localization.

A separate dyadic step on PDF page 79 assumes \(\langle\xi\rangle\sim2^j\), \(\langle\eta\rangle\sim2^{k_1}\), \(\langle\sigma\rangle\sim2^{k_2}\), and \(|\Phi|\sim2^J\), and asserts on the nonresonant support that \(2^J\gtrsim2^{j+k_1+k_2}t^{-\kappa}\). Let \(\phi\) be the smooth even real compactly supported function of integral \(1\) used in the singular cubic distribution, and use the unitary Fourier transform, so \(\widehat\phi(0)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\). For \(t\ge1\), \(\rho\in\{\pm1\}\), and \(F\in H^1(\mathbb R)\) satisfying \(F(\xi)=0\) and \(\|F\|_\infty+t^{-\alpha}\|F\|_{H^1}\lesssim1\), Lemma 13.4 considers \[K(t,\xi)=\operatorname{p.v.}\int e^{-i\rho t(2\xi p-p^2)}\frac{\widehat\phi(p)}p F(p)\,dp.\] It asserts, for \(\kappa>0\), \[K(t,\xi)=-\frac i2F(0)\operatorname{sign}(\rho\xi)+O\!\left(\langle\sqrt t\xi\rangle^{\kappa-1}+t^{\alpha-1/2}+t^\alpha\langle\sqrt t\xi\rangle^{-3/2}\right).\] The error is a uniform estimate on this norm-bounded class, so \(F\) may depend on \(t\).

The report also checks the concluding optimization in Lemma 13.3: from the error \(O(t^{-1-\delta}+t^{-5/4+\alpha+5\delta/2})\), its proof claims the stated gain \(\tfrac13(\tfrac14-\alpha)\). The first issue concerns both the leading constant and the full uniform remainder in Lemma 13.4; the optimization issue is confined to the displayed proof step. No counterexample to the structured nonlinear trajectory or the main stability theorem is claimed.

In Proposition 3.6 take \(\alpha>1\), \(0\le\sigma<s\), \(1<q<\infty\), and \(1/(2\alpha)<b'<b<1/2\). For nonresonant integer quadruples \(n_1-n_2+n_3-n_4=0\), put \(\Phi_\alpha=|n_1|^{2\alpha}-|n_2|^{2\alpha}+|n_3|^{2\alpha}-|n_4|^{2\alpha}\) and \(c_n=\langle n_4\rangle^\sigma g_{n_1}\overline{g_{n_2}}/(\langle n_3\rangle^\sigma\langle n_1\rangle^s\langle n_2\rangle^s)\). Restrict \(n_1,n_2\) to fixed dyadic blocks, and define \(K_\tau(n_3,n_4)=\sum_{n_1,n_2}\mathbf1_{|\tau|\gtrsim\langle\Phi_\alpha\rangle}c_n\langle\tau\rangle^{-b'}\) and \(G(n_3,n_4)=\|\langle\tau\rangle^{-(b-b')}K_\tau(n_3,n_4)\|_{L^r_\tau}\), with \(r>1/(b-b')\) chosen for the stated Hölder exponents.

The first domination on PDF page 25 claims that the absolute value of \(\int\sum_n\mathbf1_{|\tau|\gtrsim\langle\Phi_\alpha\rangle}c_n\langle\tau\rangle^{-b}f(n_3,\tau)g(n_4,\tau+\Phi_\alpha)\,d\tau\) is bounded by a constant times \(\sum_{n_3,n_4}G(n_3,n_4)\|f(n_3,\cdot)\|_{L^q}\|g(n_4,\cdot)\|_{L^{q'+}}\). The check is whether this scalar sum of coefficients controls the operator with its distinct temporal translations, including the analogous energy-kernel reduction in Lemma 5.6. The final moment bound of Proposition 3.6 is not itself disproved by the report.

Let \(\mu_s\) be the law of \(u=\sum_n g_n\langle n\rangle^{-s}e^{inx}\), with independent real and imaginary parts of \(g_n\) of variance \(1/2\), and let \(d\rho_{s,\gamma}=e^{-|M_{\mathrm{Wick}}(u)|^\gamma}d\mu_s\). For the positive-sign truncated renormalized fractional NLS flow \(\Phi_t^N\), let \(f_t^N=d(\Phi_t^N)_\#\rho_{s,\gamma}/d\rho_{s,\gamma}\). Set \(\Psi_s(n)=\langle n_1\rangle^{2s}-\langle n_2\rangle^{2s}+\langle n_3\rangle^{2s}-\langle n_4\rangle^{2s}\), and define \(Q(u)=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\mathrm{NR}}i\Psi_s(n)\widehat u(n_1)\overline{\widehat u(n_2)}\widehat u(n_3)\overline{\widehat u(n_4)}\), where NR imposes momentum conservation and the nonresonant exclusions in (5.1).

Lemma 5.1 asserts \[f_t^N(u)=\exp\!\left(\int_0^t Q(P_N\Phi_{-r}^Nu)\,dr\right).\] The check concerns the sign and coefficient of this exact transported-density formula under the fixed covariance and equation convention, including its reuse as an actual Radon–Nikodym derivative in Lemma 5.10. It does not replace the input Gaussian law by a different variance.

Let \(W\) have independent complex Brownian Fourier coefficients with \(\mathbb E|B_n(t)|^2=t\), and let \(Y(t)=\langle\nabla\rangle^{-s}W(t)\). For progressively measurable \(\theta\in L^2([0,1];L^2(\mathbb T))\), set \(I(\theta)(t)=\int_0^t\langle\nabla\rangle^{-s}\theta(r)\,dr\). Fix \(N\in\mathbb N\), and let real measurable \(F\) satisfy \(\mathbb E|F(P_NY(1))|^p<\infty\) and \(\mathbb E|e^{-F(P_NY(1))}|^{p'}<\infty\) for some \(1<p<\infty\), where \(p'\) is its Hölder conjugate. Lemma 2.4 claims \[-\log\mathbb E e^{-F(P_NY(1))}=\inf_\theta\mathbb E\!\left[F(P_NY(1)+P_NI(\theta)(1))+\frac12\int_0^1\|\theta(t)\|_2^2\,dt\right].\] The issue is this exact drift-cost normalization for the stated complex covariance; the weaker upper-bound corollary is a separate assertion.

For the Gaussian series \(u_0=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}g_n\langle n\rangle^{-s}e^{inx}\), with independent standard complex \(g_n\) in the paper's variance convention, the abstract states that \(\mu_s=\operatorname{Law}(u_0)\) is supported on \(H^s(\mathbb T)\). The check concerns this almost-sure support assertion, as distinct from the subcritical Sobolev regularity stated in the body.

For \(s>1/4\), the construction of the Wick mass considers \(M_N=\sum_{|n|\le N}(|g_n|^2-1)\langle n\rangle^{-2s}\). Equation (2.9) gives a tail upper bound with the power \(N^{-1+4s}\) for \(M\ge N\), and uses that bound to infer that \((M_N)\) is Cauchy in each finite \(L^p\). The second issue is the validity of that inference from the printed, nondecaying power; it is not a claim that the Wick mass fails to exist.

Let \(X_{p,q}^{s,b}(T)\) be the restriction norm on \([0,T]\), defined by the infimum over global extensions, and let \(\chi_T=\mathbf1_{[-T,T]}\). For \(0<T\le1\), \(q\ge2\), \(1\le p\le\infty\), \(0\le b<1/q'\), and sufficiently small \(\delta>0\), equation (3.11) claims \(\|\chi_Tu\|_{X_{p,q}^{s,b}}\lesssim T^{1/q'-b-2\delta}\|u\|_{X_{p,q}^{s,1/q'-\delta}(T)}\). The check concerns the compatibility of this global symmetric cutoff with a restriction norm on only the positive interval.

Lemma 3.2 also claims \(\|u\|_{X_{p,q}^{s,b'}(T)}\lesssim T^{b-b'}\|u\|_{X_{p,q}^{s,b}(T)}\) whenever \(-1/q<b'\le b<1+1/q'\) and \(u(0)=0\). This stated additional range includes \(b=1/q'\). The recorded endpoint check keeps the explicit zero-trace condition, rather than relying only on the failure of a general critical trace theorem; the strict range used by the later Duhamel estimates is distinguished from this endpoint.

Let \(0\le s\le1/2\), \(\alpha>1\), and \(Y\sim\mu_s\). For \(n_4=n_1-n_2+n_3\), define \(Y^{(3),N}(t)=\sum_{|n_j|\le N,\ n_2\ne n_1,n_3}\Psi_s(n)\widehat Y(n_1)\overline{\widehat Y(n_2)}\widehat Y(n_3)e^{it(|n_1|^{2\alpha}-|n_2|^{2\alpha}+|n_3|^{2\alpha})}e^{in_4x}\). For the positive unrenormalized equation \(iu_t+(-\partial_x^2)^\alpha u+|u|^2u=0\) on the torus with normalized measure, the gauge statement uses \(e^{-itM(u)}u\), where \(M(u)=\int_{\mathbb T}|u|^2\,dx\), to obtain the equation with nonlinearity \((|u|^2-2M(u))u\). Separately, the consequence stated after (2.1) claims a uniform lower bound \(|\Phi_\alpha(n)|\gtrsim1\) for nonresonant integer quadruples \(n_1-n_2+n_3-n_4=0\), \(n_1\ne n_2,n_4\), throughout \(\alpha>1/2\). Write \(\mathcal V(u_0)(t)=\Phi_tu_0-S(t)u_0\) for the nonlinear correction and \(X^{(3)}[u_0]\) for the cubic Duhamel iterate in (3.24). The recorded growth/localization issues concern the inference of \(\int e^{r(u)}d\rho_{s,\gamma}<\infty\) from an upper bound on its negative logarithm, the use of an existential time event in Corollary 6.2 where a uniform-in-time complement is needed, and replacement in the proof of Lemma 5.8 of the stated good event \(\tau_N^{-1}\le M^{a-}\) by \(\tau_N^{-1}\le M^{-a-}\), where \(a=4\alpha/(2\alpha-1)>0\), \(M>1\), and \(0<\tau_N\le1\). Let \((\mathcal M,\tau)\) be the semifinite tracial von Neumann algebra with filtration used in the paper, let \(y=(y_n)_{n=0}^N\) be a finite self-adjoint martingale, and let \(x_N,z_N\) be self-adjoint elements of \(L^p(\mathcal M)\), \(2<p<\infty\). Write \(dy_0=y_0\), \(dy_k=y_k-y_{k-1}\), and, for each \(\mu>0\), define \(R_{-1}^\mu=I\) and \(R_n^\mu=R_{n-1}^\mu\mathbf1_{(-\infty,\mu)}(R_{n-1}^\mu y_nR_{n-1}^\mu)\). Assume for every \(\mu>0\) that \[\sum_{n=0}^N\sum_{k=n+1}^N\tau((R_{n-1}^\mu-R_n^\mu)dy_kR_{n-1}^\mu dy_k(R_{n-1}^\mu-R_n^\mu))\le\tau((I-R_N^\mu)x_N^2),\] and that \(\tau(Pdy_k^2P)\le\tau(Pz_N^2P)\) for every \(0\le k\le N\) and every projection \(P\in\mathcal M_k\). These are Definition 3.2 applied to \((x_N/\mu,y/\mu,z_N/\mu)\).

Theorem 3.6 concludes \[\|y_N\|_p\le\frac{12p}{\sqrt{1-(1+1/p)^{2-p}}}\bigl(\|x_N\|_p^2+\|z_N\|_p^2\bigr)^{1/2}.\] The original assumptions impose neither positivity nor zero initial value of \(y\), and do not require the corresponding upper-crossing tests for \(-y\). The recorded check concerns this full two-sided norm conclusion under the stated one-sided tests.

Let \(\gamma\in(0,2)\) and \(\kappa_1,\kappa_2>4\). Couple two whole-plane space-filling \(\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa_i}\) curves \(\eta_1,\eta_2\) arbitrarily, independently of a unit-area Liouville quantum gravity sphere field \(h\), and parameterize both by \(\mu_h\)-mass on \([0,1]\).
