The final assertion of Lemma 2.10 states that, for each fixed \(t\in[0,1]\), almost surely \(\psi(t)\) is the unique \(s\in[0,1]\) with \((t,s)\in\operatorname{supp}\pi\).

This assertion includes the two endpoints and has no endpoint normalization of \(\psi\) or independence requirement between the two curves. It is distinct from the lemma's preceding conditional assertion, which assumes that \(\eta_2\) hits \(\eta_1(t)\) only once; that conditional assertion is not what the endpoint check refutes.

Let \(n\ge1\), \(\alpha>n\), \(p=2n/(n+\alpha)\), and \(f\ge0\) belong to \(L^p(\mathbb R^n)\). Define the star-shaped set \(S_\alpha f\) by \(\rho_{S_\alpha f}(\xi)^\alpha=\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)f(x+t\xi)\,dx\,dt\). Theorem 14 gives \(\gamma_{n,\alpha}\|f\|_p^2\le n\omega_n^{1-\alpha/n}|S_\alpha f|^{\alpha/n}\le\iint f(x)f(y)|x-y|^{\alpha-n}\,dx\,dy\), with its stated sharp constant. Its first equality clause claims equality precisely for \[f(x)=a(1+|\varphi(x-x_0)|^2)^{-(n-\alpha)/2},\qquad a\ge0,\ \varphi\in\mathrm{GL}(n),\ x_0\in\mathbb R^n.\] The recorded check concerns this necessary-and-sufficient optimizer family, including nonzero admissible functions, rather than a disproof of the inequality bounds.

Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be star-shaped with measurable radial function and positive volume, let \(f\ge0\) be nonzero and measurable, and let \(f^\star,K^\star\) be their symmetric decreasing rearrangements. Lemma 8 states, when \(q>0\), the singular-kernel integral is finite, and \(f^\star\) is strictly symmetric decreasing, that equality in \[\iint\frac{f(x)f(y)}{\|x-y\|_K^q}\,dx\,dy\le\iint\frac{f^\star(x)f^\star(y)}{\|x-y\|_{K^\star}^q}\,dx\,dy\] holds if and only if \(K\) is a centered ellipsoid and \(f\) is a translate of \(f^\star\). Lemma 11 makes the analogous translate-only assertion for the reversed polynomial-kernel rearrangement with \(\|x-y\|_K^q\).

The same restriction is carried to the equality clauses for \(|S_\alpha f|\) in Lemmas 10 and 13, under their stated finite-volume and, in Lemma 10, strictly decreasing rearrangement hypotheses. The checked conclusion is the requirement \(f(x)=f^\star(x-x_0)\); these auxiliary statements do not retain a common volume-preserving linear change of coordinates in both \(f\) and \(K\). The report challenges that equality classification, not the rearrangement or volume inequalities themselves.

In Lemma 10, let \(0<\alpha<n\), use its printed exponent \(p=2\alpha/(n+\alpha)\), and take any nonnegative \(f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)\). To treat \(|S_\alpha f|=\infty\), the proof sets \(f_{(k)}=f\mathbf1_{kB^n}\), \(k\ge1\), and asserts that these compactly supported truncations have finite \(|S_\alpha f_{(k)}|\). Here \(\rho_{S_\alpha f_{(k)}}(\xi)^\alpha=\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}\int f_{(k)}(x)f_{(k)}(x+t\xi)\,dx\,dt\). The check concerns this finiteness implication on the lemma's actual printed \(L^p\) domain, without an added boundedness truncation or substitution of Theorem 1's different exponent \(2n/(n+\alpha)\).

In the positive-parameter part of the Mellin monotonicity argument, let \(\omega\) be the nonnegative decreasing weight with finite positive moments assumed in the lemma, and let nonzero \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) satisfy \(\phi(0)=0\), with \(\phi(t)\) and \(\phi(t)/t\) nondecreasing. For \(\alpha>0\), set \[\zeta(\alpha)=\left(\frac{\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}\omega(\phi(t))\,dt}{\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}\omega(t)\,dt}\right)^{1/\alpha}.\] For \(\beta>\alpha\), equation (29) identifies \(\int_0^\infty t^{\beta-1}\omega(t/\zeta(\alpha))\,dt\) with \(\zeta(\alpha)^{-\beta}\int_0^\infty t^{\beta-1}\omega(t)\,dt\). The check is this claimed change-of-variables factor and its use in the stated monotonicity direction, rather than a counterexample to the final decreasing-function lemma.

A convex body in Definition 2.1 is any nonempty compact convex \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), including sets with empty interior. Its intrinsic volumes are the coefficients in \(\operatorname{Vol}_n(K+rB^n)=\sum_{j=0}^n\kappa_{n-j}V_j(K)r^{n-j}\), equivalently the Kubota projection averages in (2.7). The paragraph after that definition asserts, for a convex body in this stated class, \[V_{n-1}(K)=\tfrac12\mathcal H^{n-1}(\partial K),\] where \(\partial K\) is its ambient boundary. The check concerns the assertion's inclusion of lower-dimensional bodies, not the intrinsic-volume definition or the later Gaussian/Wills identity.

Let \(A=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_N\}\) and let \(\varphi:A\to B\) be a surjective contraction, retaining the same index set on \(B\), even when image points coincide. Let \(X^A,X^B\) be independent centered Gaussian vectors with covariance matrices \(\Sigma^A_{ij}=\langle\theta_i,\theta_j\rangle\) and \(\Sigma^B_{ij}=\langle\varphi(\theta_i),\varphi(\theta_j)\rangle\). Put \(X(t)=\sqrt{1-t}X^A+\sqrt tX^B\), \(\Sigma(t)=(1-t)\Sigma^A+t\Sigma^B\), and \[F_\beta(t,t)=\mathbb E\left(\sum_i e^{\beta(X_i(t)-\Sigma_{ii}(t)/2)}\right)^{1/\beta}.\] The smoothing family is introduced for every \(\beta>0\), and the argument after (4.3) asserts \(dF_\beta(t,t)/dt\le0\) on \([0,1]\) from the contraction assumption. The check is the full stated \(\beta>0\) range of this intermediate claim, rather than the limiting comparison as \(\beta\to\infty\).

Lemma 4.1 assumes positive semidefinite \(n\times n\) matrices \(\Sigma^A,\Sigma^B\), independent \(X^A\sim N(0,\Sigma^A)\), \(X^B\sim N(0,\Sigma^B)\), and twice differentiable \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) whose Hessian has at most exponential growth. The latter interpretation is explicitly a corrected domain, not a claim that a spread-out counterexample satisfies the literal definition.

Let \(P^\lambda\) be the exponentially tilted simple random walk on \(\mathbb Z^d\), with \(\lambda\in[-1,1]^d\) and one-step mean \(m(\lambda)\). Lemma 2.3(i) asserts that for every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and \(M>1\) there is a uniform \(C\) such that, for reachable endpoint pairs \((x,y),(x',y')\), \(0\le s\le t\le n\), \(t-s\ge\varepsilon n\), and the printed drift conditions \(|x-y-nm(\lambda)|,|x'-y'-nm(\lambda)|\le M\sqrt n\), \[\frac{E_{0,n}^{\otimes2,\lambda,(x,x'),(y,y')}[fg]}{E_{0,n}^{\otimes2,\lambda,(x,x'),\star}[f]\,E_{0,n}^{\otimes2,\lambda,\star,(y,y')}[g]}\le C.\] The numerator uses two independent bridges; the denominator uses the two forward and two backward free walks. The functions \(f,g\) are stated to be real-valued measurable functions of the initial and terminal path strips, respectively.

The recorded check concerns both the absence of a nonnegativity hypothesis, even with positive finite denominator, and the direction of the printed drift constraint. The later positive Boltzmann-function application is distinguished from this larger literal function class.

For nearest-neighbor simple random walk on \(\mathbb Z^d\) in iid real disorder satisfying \(\mathbb E e^{a|\omega_{0,0}|}<\infty\) for every \(a\ge0\), define \(\mu_{\omega,n}^\beta(dX)=e^{\beta H_{[1,n]}-n\lambda(\beta)}P(dX)/W_n^\beta\). Strong disorder means \(W_n^\beta\to0\) almost surely. Theorem B(ii) asserts that strong disorder implies the existence of a deterministic \(c>0\) for which \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\max_{x\in\mathbb Z^d}\mu_{\omega,n}^\beta(X_{n+1}=x)\ge c\quad\text{almost surely}.\] The \((n+1)\)-st step is unweighted by the environment in this definition. The check is this positive liminf assertion, not a limsup localization statement or the paper's weak-disorder local limit theorem.

Let the iid disorder law have finite support, as permitted by assumption (2), and define \(p^*(\beta)=\sup\{p:\sup_n\mathbb E(W_n^\beta)^p<\infty\}\). Theorem 1.2(ii) asserts that if \(p^*(\beta)>1\), then \(p^*(\beta')>p^*(\beta)\) for every inverse temperature \(0\le\beta'<\beta\). The finite-support hypothesis does not exclude a deterministic environment, and the statement does not separately assume that \(p^*(\beta)\) is finite. The recorded check concerns this missing boundary restriction in the strict comparison; it does not establish failure for nonconstant finite-support disorder.

Let \(\mu_{\omega,n}^\beta\) weight the path by the environment at times \(1,\ldots,n\), with normalizing partition function \(W_n^\beta\). For a reachable endpoint \(x\), the pinned function in Section 1.3 is \(W_{0,n}^{\beta,0,x}=E[e^{\beta H_{(0,n)}-(n-1)\lambda(\beta)}\mid X_0=0,X_n=x]\), which omits the environment at the terminal time. The introductory exact identity claims \[\mu_{\omega,n}^\beta(X_n=x)=\frac{W_{0,n}^{\beta,0,x}}{W_n^\beta}P(X_n=x).\] The check concerns compatibility of these two endpoint-weight conventions in an exact equality; it does not reject the pinned local limit result or the shifted convention used in Remark 1.7.

Under the iid exponential-moment assumptions, the display labelled (u-bd.) describes an upper-bounded environment by \(\exists K>0:\mathbb P(\omega_{0,0}\le K)=0\). The recorded item checks whether this displayed probability condition expresses an almost-sure finite upper bound on \(\omega_{0,0}\). It is retained as an editorial clarification; the report does not attribute an invalid main-theorem derivation to this display alone.

In the uniformly tilted simple-random-walk local limit argument, \(\lambda\in[-1,1]^d\), Appendix A.3 puts \(Y_i=X_{2i}/2\) and asserts that its increments are \(\mathbb Z^d\)-valued with lattice span one, so that integer-lattice Fourier inversion applies. If \(\Sigma^\lambda\) is the covariance of \(Y_1\), equation (63) additionally claims that some \(r>1\), uniform in \(\lambda\), satisfies \(r^{-1}|t|\le t^\top\Sigma^\lambda t\le r|t|^2\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R^d\).

The same proof evaluates \((2\pi\sqrt n)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-t^\top\Sigma^\lambda t/2-ix\cdot t/\sqrt n}\,dt\) with exponential factor \(e^{-x^\top\Sigma^\lambda x/(2n)}\), rather than an inverse covariance. The recorded check concerns these precise lattice, quadratic-bound, and Fourier-evaluation formulas; it does not establish a failure of the final coarse local-limit orders after correction.

Over an algebraically closed field \(k\) of characteristic zero, let \(X\) be an irreducible affine variety and \(G\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(X)\) a closed commutative unipotent subgroup, with unipotence defined by membership of its elements in algebraic \(\mathbb G_a\)-actions. Theorem A asserts equivalence of: \(G\) is maximal among commutative subgroups; \(G\) is maximal among commutative unipotent subgroups; and \(G=R_X(U)\) for a commutative unipotent algebraic subgroup \(U\), where \(R_X(U)\) is the subgroup of globally regular automorphisms generated birationally by rational invariant replicas of \(U\). Neither \(G\) nor \(U\) is required to be nontrivial.

Likewise Proposition 4.1 claims \(\operatorname{Cent}_{\operatorname{Aut}(X)}(\operatorname{Repl}_X(U))=R_X(U)\) in that full scope. The recorded check concerns the admitted identity-subgroup case in this classification and centralizer statement, without silently adding a nontriviality hypothesis.

In Proposition 4.1, let a commutative unipotent algebraic group \(U\) act on irreducible affine \(X\). On a smooth affine quotient open set \(B\), the proof has a geometric quotient \(\pi^{-1}(B)\to B\) and a product trivialization \(\rho:\mathbb A^n\times B\to\pi^{-1}(B)\). Choose \(b_0\in B\), \(x_0=\rho(0,b_0)\), and a vector subgroup \(U'\) complementary to the stabilizer \(U_{x_0}\). Define \(E=\{(u',b):u'\rho(0,b)=\rho(0,b)\}\) and \(p:E\to B\). Its fibres are irreducible and \(p^{-1}(b_0)=\{(0,b_0)\}\). The proof asserts that an irreducible component \(F\subseteq E\) with \(\dim F=\dim E\) necessarily dominates \(B\) and has the general fibre dimension of \(p\). The check is this inference about a component of maximal dimension, not the eventual centralizer conclusion after a different openness argument.

Let \(k\) be uncountable, algebraically closed, and of characteristic zero, let \(X,Y\) be irreducible affine varieties, and let \(\theta:\operatorname{Aut}(X)\to\operatorname{Aut}(Y)\) be an abstract group isomorphism. Let \(H\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(X)\) be connected algebraic and \(V\) a nontrivial generalized \(H\)-root subgroup: \(V\simeq\mathbb G_a^d\) for some \(d\ge1\), and conjugation by \(H\) acts by a common nontrivial scalar character. Proposition 8.1 assumes either that \(\theta(H)\) is algebraic or that \(H\) has a dense open orbit in \(X\), and concludes that \(\theta(V)\) is an ordinary \(\theta(H)\)-root subgroup of the same dimension as \(V\). The check concerns the ordinary-root terminology, which the paper defines to have dimension one, in a conclusion allowing arbitrary \(d\); the corresponding generalized-root conclusion is distinguished from it.

Let \(X\) be irreducible affine and \(H\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(X)\) solvable algebraic with nontrivial unipotent radical and \(H=FH^\circ\) for a finite central subgroup \(F\). In Proposition 6.1(2), fix a maximal torus \(T\), nontrivial subtori \(T_i\), and the selected \(T\)-root subgroup \(U\) of weight \(\lambda\). Choose \(T\)-semi-invariants \(f_j\in k[X]^U\) of weights \(\lambda_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), as in the proof, and put \(A_i=\{a\in\mathbb Z^m:\sum_j a_j\lambda_j|_{T_i}+\lambda|_{T_i}=0\}\). The proof asserts that every nonempty \(A_i\) is a translate of a rank-\((m-1)\) subgroup and that choosing any \(a\in\mathbb Z^m\setminus\bigcup_i A_i\) yields a regular invariant \(f=\prod_jf_j^{a_j}\in k[X]^U\), hence a regular replica \(f\cdot U\) noncommuting with every \(T_i\). The check concerns these rank and regularity inferences with unrestricted integer exponents; nonnegative exponents are not an original selection condition.

Under the uncountable algebraically closed characteristic-zero hypotheses of Lemma 8.2, let \(\theta:\operatorname{Aut}(X)\to\operatorname{Aut}(Y)\) be an abstract isomorphism between automorphism groups of irreducible affine varieties, and let \(D\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(X)\) be diagonalizable with \(\theta(D)\) closed. The proof identifies the subgroup killed by a prime \(p\) in \(\theta(D)\), equivalently in \(D\), with \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\dim D}\) for every prime. No connectedness of \(D\) or exclusion of primes dividing its component group is assumed. The recorded check concerns that torsion-rank identity, not the final dimension bound \(\dim\theta(D)^\circ\le\dim D\).

Theorem 8.5 assumes that \(X\) is an affine \(G\)-spherical variety different from an algebraic torus, with \(G\) connected reductive over an uncountable algebraically closed field of characteristic zero; its root-correspondence assertions (c)–(d) apply to closed connected subgroups \(H\subseteq G\). In the toric case of Proposition 8.6, the proof instead sets \(H=DU\), where \(G\) is a torus, \(U\simeq\mathbb G_a\) is a nontrivial \(G\)-root subgroup, and \(D\subseteq G\) centralizes \(U\), and invokes 8.5(c) for this \(H\). The first checked inference is the applicability of that theorem to the constructed group.

The first case in the proof of Theorem E also invokes 8.5(c)–(d) with source \(X=T\) an algebraic torus. The second checked inference is applicability despite that explicit source exclusion. The report identifies these hypothesis mismatches and gives alternative arguments; it does not assert that the resulting spherical reconstruction or torus characterization is false.

Over the paper's algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, Theorem 10.1 states that if \(\Gamma\) is a finite-index subgroup of \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)\) and \(Z\) is an irreducible quasi-affine variety admitting an injective homomorphism \(\Gamma\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(Z)\), then \(\dim Z\ge n\). The statement gives no lower restriction excluding \(n=1\) and no positive-dimensional hypothesis on \(Z\). The recorded check concerns this boundary case; it does not reject the later application in the range \(n\ge3\).

Let \((X,T)\) be the compact metric dynamical system satisfying the paper's ASP and MCGBP assumptions, with \(T\) Lipschitz, \(0<\alpha\le1\), strictly positive weight \(\psi\), and calibrated potential \(\bar u\ge0\) vanishing on the minimizing-support set \(Z\). For a periodic orbit \(O\), write \(N=\#O\), \(D=D(O)\) for its separation capped by the ASP scale, \(r=\sum_{y\in O}d(y,Z)^\alpha\), and \(L_O=D^\alpha/r\). Set \(a_O=\sum_{y\in O}(\bar u(y)+h(y))/\sum_{y\in O}\psi_K(y)\) and \(R=((|a_O|\|\psi\|_0+\|h\|_0)/\varepsilon)^{1/\alpha}\), where \(\psi_K\) is the time average used in the calibration.

The proof of Lemma 3.8 claims that \(L_O>2(2\operatorname{Lip}T)^\alpha\|\bar u\|_\alpha/(\varepsilon N\psi_{\min})\) and \(\|h\|_0<\varepsilon\psi_{\min}D^\alpha/[2(2\operatorname{Lip}T)^\alpha]\) are sufficient for \(R<D/(2\operatorname{Lip}T)\), using the displayed radius comparison immediately before these conditions. The check concerns those quantitative intermediate bounds in the locking proof. It is not a claim that the final stronger constants or the periodic-minimizer conclusion are refuted by every example testing the displayed comparison.

Let \(M\) be smooth compact, let a Lipschitz subsystem \((X,T)\) satisfy ASP and MCGBP, and let the periodic orbit \(O\) obey the comparison hypothesis (3.18) of Proposition 3.9. For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), set \(q=\varepsilon d(\cdot,O)\). The proof uses \(\|v\|_1=\|v\|_0+[v]_1\), chooses smooth \(w\) with \(\|w\|_1\le\|q\|_1+\varepsilon_1\) and \(\|w-q\|_0<\varepsilon_1\), and infers \(\|Dw\|_0\le\varepsilon+\varepsilon_1\) and \[\|w-q+h\|_1\le\|w\|_1+\|q\|_1+\|h\|_1\le2\varepsilon+\varepsilon_1+\|h\|_1.\] The check concerns these inferences for the full norm, rather than only its Lipschitz seminorm.

The proposition promises its minimizing-measure conclusion for every \(C^1\) perturbation with \(\|Dh\|_0<5\varepsilon\) and \(\|h\|_0<D(O)\widehat\delta_1/\#O\). The proof ends instead by imposing \(\|h\|_1<5\varepsilon\). The second issue is whether that stronger full-norm condition covers all perturbations in the original derivative-and-uniform-radius quantifier. The approximation theorem itself claims uniform approximation with an almost preserved norm bound, not convergence in the norm of the difference.

In Proposition 4.1, let \(f:M\to M\) be Lipschitz on a smooth compact manifold satisfying ASP and MCGBP, let \(\psi>0\) be Lipschitz, and let continuous \(u\ge0\) vanish on a periodic orbit \(O\). The proposition constructs an arbitrarily small smooth \(w\), nonnegative and vanishing on \(O\), so that \(\mu_O\) minimizes the weighted average of \(u+w+h\) for all sufficiently small Lipschitz \(h\). The final proof sentence instead states minimization for \(u+h\). The check concerns that dropped perturbation, not the correctly stated proposition.

For \(G=w+h-a_O\psi\), the same escape-block proof uses a positive distance cost \(\theta(r)=\min_{d(x,O)\ge r}w(x)\), separation \(D(O)\), and ASP constant \(C\). On PDF page 24 it replaces the earlier cost \(\theta(D(O)/(2\operatorname{Lip}f))\) by \(\theta(D(O)/(2C))\), asserts \(G\ge-\|h\|_0+|a_O|\|\psi\|_0\), and for \(m_3=p\#O+q\), \(0\le q<\#O\), starts the periodic remainder at \(m_3-q-1\). These are the precise local threshold, sign, and index assertions recorded for checking.

Let \(X_g\) be a closed genus-\(g\) hyperbolic surface sampled from normalized Weil–Petersson measure, let \(N(X_g,L)\) count primitive unoriented closed geodesics of length at most \(L\), and let \(N_{\mathrm{nsep}}^s(X_g,L)\) count those that are simple and nonseparating. Theorem 4(1) assumes that for some fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\), \(L(g)\ge(1-\varepsilon_0)\log g\) and \(L(g)^2/g\to0\), and concludes that there exists \(\delta(g)>0\), \(\delta(g)\to0\), such that \[\mathbb P_g^{\mathrm{WP}}\!\left(1-\frac{N_{\mathrm{nsep}}^s(X_g,L(g))}{N(X_g,L(g))}<\delta(g)\right)\longrightarrow1.\] Its printed hypotheses do not require \(\varepsilon_0<1\) or \(L(g)\to\infty\), and no value is supplied for the ratio when both counts vanish. The check concerns this boundary scope and definedness, as distinct from the later growing-length theorem.

In the proof of Theorem 30, fix \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(g\to\infty\), and take \(t>2g^4\). The spectral-mean upper expression contains \(\sum_{j=1}^{2g-3}\int_{1/2}^1(t^s/s)(c(\varepsilon)/j)g^{3-4s+\varepsilon}\,ds\). The next comparison rewrites its scale as \(c(\varepsilon)g^{3-\varepsilon}(\sum_{j=1}^{2g-3}j^{-1})\int_{1/2}^1(t/g^4)^s\,ds\), up to constants independent of \(g,t\), alongside the term \(g\operatorname{Li}(\sqrt t)\). The check is the minus sign in this extracted exponent and the claimed uniform comparison, rather than the subsequent theorem bound that uses the corrected exponent.

For stable \((g,n)\), take nonnegative intersection indices \(d=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) with \(|d|\le3g-3+n\), and choose \(2\le j\le n\). In the \(A,j\) term of Mirzakhani's recursion, equation (46) reindexes \(L_{\mathrm{new}}=d_1+d_j+L_{\mathrm{old}}-1\), but prints coefficient \(a_{L-d_1-d_2+1}\) for general \(j\). This is the first local identity checked.

For a legal \((g,n+1)\) input \(d'\), the final step of (51) also claims \[\sum_{k=0}^{d'_1-1}8(2d'_j+1)a_0\,[\tau_{k+d'_j-1}\!\prod_{i\ne1,j}\tau_{d'_i}]_{g,n}\ge8d'_1(2d'_j+1)a_0\,[\tau_{d'_1+d'_j-2}\!\prod_{i\ne1,j}\tau_{d'_i}]_{g,n}.\] The convention sets intersection numbers with a negative index to zero, and the printed range allows \(d'_j=0\). The check concerns this boundary use of monotonicity, not a refutation of the later special split with \(j=2\) and positive split indices.

Assume \(L=L(g)\to\infty\) and \(L(g)^2/g\to0\) under Weil–Petersson probability on genus-\(g\) surfaces. Put \(I(L)=\int_0^L\sinh^2(x/2)\,dx/x\). Let \(Y_1(X_g,L)\) be the ordered two-curve contribution appearing in Lemma 61, whose exact integration formula is \((4V_g)^{-1}\int_0^L\int_0^L V_{g-2,4}(x,x,y,y)xy\,dx\,dy\). The proof claims \[\mathbb E_gY_1=I(L)^2(1+O(L^2/g)),\qquad\mathbb E_gN_{\mathrm{nsep}}^s=I(L)(1+O(L^2/g)).\] The second expectation has exact formula \((2V_g)^{-1}\int_0^LxV_{g-1,2}(x,x)\,dx\). The check is the leading normalization in these two asymptotic identities, not the variance order after both factors are consistently restored.

Let \((M,g)\) be complete with \(\operatorname{Ric}_g=-g\), and let the connected semisimple Lie group \(L\), without compact simple factors and with finite center, act effectively, properly, isometrically, and cocompactly as in Assumption 5.2 and the paper's effective-action convention. Use the minimal parabolic \(Q=M_0AN\), its Lie algebra \(\mathfrak q\), and the quotient map \(\Phi:\mathfrak q\to\mathfrak q/\mathfrak n\). For \(Z\in\mathfrak m\), put \(\check Z=\Phi(Z)\) and let \(\check Z^*\) be its induced Killing field on \(N\backslash M\). The proof of Proposition 7.1 concludes from \(\check Z^*=0\) that \(\check Z=0\), and then \(Z=0\), invoking injectivity of \(\Phi|_{\mathfrak m\oplus\mathfrak a}\). The checked inference assumes no established effectiveness of the induced \(Q/N\)-action. It concerns the passage from a zero field to a zero quotient-algebra element, not a counterexample to orbit symmetry.

Let \(\mathfrak n\) be the three-dimensional Heisenberg Lie algebra with basis \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) and only nonzero bracket \([e_1,e_2]=e_3\). For any positive-definite inner product \(h\), write \(h_{ij}=h(e_i,e_j)\). With the standard orthonormal background and weights \(\beta^+=\operatorname{diag}(2/3,2/3,4/3)\), Example 3.10 claims that backwards Gram–Schmidt uses \[u_2=e_2-\frac{h_{23}}{h_{33}}e_3,\qquad u_1=e_1-\frac{h_{12}}{h_{22}}e_2-\frac{h_{13}}{h_{33}}e_3,\] and gives \(v_{\beta^+}(h)^3=h(u_1,u_1)h(u_2,u_2)h_{33}^2\). The original scope includes non-diagonal \(h\), with no assumption that \(e_2\) and \(e_3\) are orthogonal. The check is this explicit calculation rather than the abstract definition of the weighted density.

Let \(\mathfrak n\) be the nilpotent Lie algebra with the correctly gauged background used to define \(v_{\beta^+}\), and let \(h_1,h_2\) be positive-definite inner products. Lemma 3.11 states that whenever \(\phi\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak n)\) is a linear isometry \((\mathfrak n,h_1)\to(\mathfrak n,h_2)\), \[v_{\beta^+}(h_2)=\det(\phi)^{-1}v_{\beta^+}(h_1).\] No orientation-preserving or positive-determinant hypothesis is imposed on \(\phi\). The recorded check concerns that unrestricted transformation law, while the determinant-one application later in the paper is kept separate.

Let \((M,g)\) be a complete Ricci-flat Riemannian manifold, and let a Lie group \(G\) act properly, isometrically, and cocompactly. Theorem 9.2 splits the universal cover as \(\widetilde M=\overline M\times\mathbb R^k\), with \(\overline M\) compact, and additionally asserts \(G^\circ\subseteq\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb R^k)\) when the original action is effective. Its proof says that the action of \(G\) itself lifts to a proper isometric action on \(\widetilde M\). The check concerns this global lift and embedding of the same group; the statement neither replaces \(G^\circ\) by a covering group nor excludes compact \(M\). The geometric splitting conclusion is not what the reported example refutes.

Let \(S\subseteq\omega^{<\omega}\) be an \(\alpha\)-forest, meaning convexity for the true-stage order \(\le_\alpha\), and let \(Z_i\subseteq[S]_\alpha\) be pairwise disjoint and uniformly \(\Sigma^0_{1+\alpha}\) within \([S]_\alpha\). In the proof of Lemma 2.11 choose uniformly computable \(\alpha\)-open subsets \(U_i\subseteq S\) with \([U_i]_\alpha=Z_i\), arranged so that \(|\sigma|_\alpha>i\) whenever \(\sigma\in U_i\). The recursive rule declares \(\sigma\in W_i\) precisely when \(\sigma\in U_i\) and no proper predecessor \(\rho<_\alpha\sigma\) belongs to any \(W_j\) with \(j\ne i\) and \(j<|\sigma|_\alpha\).

The proof claims this produces pairwise orthogonal forests, meaning every string in one is \(\le_\alpha\)-incomparable with every string in another. The represented sets \(Z_i\) are disjoint, but neither the hypotheses nor the forest definition require the finite sets \(U_i\) to be disjoint or every finite component to have an infinite path. The check concerns simultaneous ownership under this exact recursion, not the existence of some alternative orthogonalization.

Lemma 3.11 takes an oracle \(z\), \(z\)-computable ordinals \(\xi,\eta\), indices for partial \(z\)-computable \(f:\omega^{<\omega}\to\mathbb N\) and \(\beta:\omega^{<\omega}\to\eta+1\), and a default \(n^*\). It promises uniformly computable total outputs \(g,\gamma\), with \(g\) a \((z,\xi)\)-approximation and \(\gamma\) a decreasing ordinal convergence witness. Agreement with the input limit is additionally required only when the inputs satisfy clause (iv)'s totality and validity conditions; output totality is unconditional.

At nonempty \(\sigma\), with \(k=|\sigma|_\xi^z\) and immediate predecessor \(\tau\), the proof searches for the longest \(\rho\le_\xi^z\sigma\) such that \(f(\rho),\beta(\rho)\) converge within \(k\) steps and \(\beta(\rho)<\gamma(\tau)\). In the successful branch it assigns \(g(\sigma)=f(\sigma)\), \(\gamma(\sigma)=\beta(\sigma)\). The check is whether this ancestor-based bounded search certifies the current-node values it then requests, even if the initialization is read with the intended output default.

Let \(G\) be a finite three-connected graph with Betti number \(b\ge2\), containing a simple cycle \(C\) with \(g\) edges. For nonnegative edge weights \(\lambda\) totaling one and an integer \(1\le h\le\min(g,b-1)\), the proof of Lemma 2.3 deletes the \(h\) heaviest edges of \(C\) and asserts that the remaining graph is connected, indeed that deleting all edges of \(C\) would preserve connectivity. This is used to give the remaining graph Betti number \(b-h\) in the proof of \(\operatorname{sys}(G)^{-1}\ge h/g+s(b-h)^{-1}\). The recorded check is the connectivity inference throughout that stated deletion range, not a disproof of the numerical systole bound.

The graph systole optimization uses \(\lambda(e)\ge0\) and \(\sum_{e\in E(G)}\lambda(e)=1\). For \(F_{12}\), the three symmetry orbits have sizes \(8,8,2\); writing their common weights as \(\lambda,\mu,
u\), the proof imposes \(8\lambda+8\mu+2
u=1\) and gives \((\lambda,\mu,
u)=(1,2,3)/28\) as an equality witness for \(\operatorname{sys}(F_{12})=2/7\). It likewise assigns weight \(1/4\) to each of the six edges of \(K_4\) as a witness for \(\operatorname{sys}(K_4)=1/2\). The check concerns admissibility and normalization of these displayed witnesses, not the upper bounds or the constants attained by corrected weightings.

For a fixed cographic torus representation \(\rho:T^d\to\mathrm{GL}(V)\), let the edge multiplicities of its underlying graph \(G\) define weights \(\lambda_\rho\), and put \(c(\rho)=\min_{S^1\subset T^d}\operatorname{codim}_{\mathbb C}V^{S^1}/\dim_{\mathbb C}V\). The reduction on PDF page 12 first identifies this with the minimum normalized cycle weight for \(\lambda_\rho\), and then claims \[c(\rho)=\max_{\lambda\ge0,\ \lambda(G)=1}\min_{C\text{ cycle in }G}\lambda(C)=\operatorname{sys}(G).\] The check is the equality between the invariant of a fixed representation, with its fixed multiplicities, and the maximum over all normalized graph weights. The upper-bound reduction needs only the corresponding inequality.

Let \(k\) be any commutative ring or commutative ring spectrum, as permitted by Section 0.3, and let \(gV_k\) denote the category of graded \(k\)-modules with perfect weight spaces and finite weight support. Section 2.2 asserts the equivalences \(gV_k\simeq\operatorname{Coh}(B\mathbb G_m)\) and \(fV_k\simeq\operatorname{Coh}(\mathbb A^1/\mathbb G_m)\), where \(fV_k\) is the stated category of finite filtered perfect modules. Lemma 2.18 uses these identifications, together with the assertion that smoothness of \(Y\) permits replacing \(\operatorname{Perf}(Y)\) by \(\operatorname{Coh}(Y)\) in the integral-kernel description for a proper map of perfect stacks \(X\to Y\) with \(X\) smooth. The claim under examination is the validity of these coherent/perfect identifications under the unrestricted coefficient convention, rather than the formal representability theorem or the later specialization to \(k=\mathbb C\).

For a fiber product \(X\times_Y X\), write \(p_{ij}:X\times_Y X\times_Y X\to X\times_Y X\) for projection to the indicated two factors. The paragraph preceding Proposition 2.17 claims that the operation on coherent kernels given by the literal printed formula \[M\star N=(p_{13})_*(p_{12}^{*}M\otimes p_{13}^{*}N)\] defines a monoidal product. Proposition 2.17 uses this operation in its asserted monoidal equivalence for \(X=\mathbb A^1/\mathbb G_m\sqcup0/\mathbb G_m\) and \(Y=\mathbb A^1/\mathbb G_m\); Lemma 2.18 invokes the kernel formalism for proper maps of perfect stacks with smooth source. The disputed assertion concerns the displayed operation itself, including its unit law, with the second pullback exactly as printed.

Let \(k\) be a commutative coefficient ring or ring spectrum and let \(gV_k\) be the category defined in Section 0.3: its graded objects have perfect \(k\)-modules in each weight and vanish outside finitely many weights. Section 2.2 declares the polynomial algebra \(k[x]\), with \(x\) of weight \(-1\), to be an object of \(\operatorname{CAlg}(gV_k)\), and uses it to present \(fV_k\) as graded perfect \(k[x]\)-modules. The statement being checked is that this algebra belongs to that specified finite-support ambient category.

For an integer \(n\geq1\), Definition 3.20 sets \(\operatorname{Sph}_n=\operatorname{Sph}^{\otimes n}\), with the tensor product taken in the stated category of presentable stable \(k\)-linear 2-categories. It then claims that this is concretely the 2-category of functors \(\operatorname{Adj}^{\times n}\to\mathrm{St}_k\) which carry every 1-morphism of \(\operatorname{Adj}^{\times n}\) to a spherical functor. Here \(\operatorname{Adj}\) is the free adjunction and sphericality requires the associated twist functors to be equivalences. The quantified condition on every 1-morphism, and hence on identities as well as the generating adjunctions, is the assertion under examination.

Let \(f:G\to H\) be a homomorphism of complex tori and let \(Bf:BG_B\to BH_B\) be the induced map of classifying groupoids. With \(\operatorname{Loc}^{(3)}(BG)=\operatorname{Fun}(BG_B,\operatorname{Pr}^{L,\mathrm{st}}_{2,k})\), Definition 3.5 and Lemma A.4 display a pullback functor \[(Bf)^*:\operatorname{Loc}^{(3)}(BG)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Loc}^{(3)}(BH),\] described as precomposition along \(Bf\), and claim that it has both adjoints. The issue is the compatibility of this displayed source and target with precomposition; it does not challenge the existence of Kan-extension adjoints for the correctly typed restriction functor.

For a finite directed graph \(\Gamma\), Definition 2.9 takes objects to be finite sign sequences and defines \(\operatorname{Hom}(\epsilon,\delta)\) to have basis the pairs \((p,q)\) of an \(\epsilon\)-path and a \(\delta\)-path with the same initial and terminal vertices. For composable basis elements \((p,q):\epsilon\to\delta\) and \((p',q'):\delta\to\gamma\), equation (1) specifies \[(p',q')\circ(p,q)=\delta_{q',p}(p',q).\] The claim is that its linear extension defines a complex-linear category, with the stated path-pair source and target convention, and hence the graph planar algebra used in the embedding theorem.

At \(N=4\), level \(k=8\), \(q=e^{\pi i/12}\), and \([n]_q=\sin(n\pi/12)/\sin(\pi/12)\), Section 6.6 presents a cell system on \(\Gamma_{\Lambda_1}^{4,8,\mathrm{Twist}}\) and claims that its \(U\)-blocks satisfy relation (R2), namely Hermiticity. In particular the displayed block \(U^7_{15}\), in the ordered path basis indexed by \((22,23,26,29,30)\), is asserted to be real and symmetric. Its printed entries include \[(U^7_{15})_{2,4}=\frac{\sqrt{[3]_q[5]_q^2}}{[4]_q[6]_q},\qquad (U^7_{15})_{4,2}=-\frac{\sqrt{[5]_q}}{\sqrt{[2]_q^2[3]_q[4]_q^2}}.\] The statement being tested is \(U^7_{15}=(U^7_{15})^*\) for this explicit constructive witness, rather than nonexistence of the proposed module category.

For every positive even level \(k\), Section 6.8 sets \(N=4\) and \(q=e^{\pi i/(k+4)}\), and gives \(U\)-cell blocks for the unfolded orbifold charge-conjugation graph \(\Gamma_{\Lambda_1}^{4,k,\mathbb Z_4^*}\). With \([r]_q=(q^r-q^{-r})/(q-q^{-1})\), it claims that all these blocks, in their admissible length-two path bases, satisfy the Hecke relation \[(U^a_b)^2=[2]_qU^a_b.\] The finding concerns the boundary formulas on PDF page 48, including the blocks from an unsplit vertex with \(\bar a_1=(k+2)/2\) to a split vertex \(a+\epsilon_1\pm\epsilon_2\), and the split-to-split return block with \(\bar a_1=(k+4)/2\) and \(\chi_\ell\chi_{\ell'}=\delta\). Here \(a=(i,j)\), \(\bar a=(i+j,j)\), and the path, sign, and character restrictions are those in the graph's definition. The claim uses the printed normalizations of these blocks.

Let \(N\geq2\), let \(k\) be a positive integer, and set \(q=e^{\pi i/(N+k)}\). The presentation reduction used in Lemma 2.16 and Theorem 3.4 invokes recursively normalized antisymmetrizer projections \(p_{\Lambda_i}\), whose recursion divides by \(D_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}q^{-2j}\). In an oriented unitary planar algebra with the stated generators and relations (R1), (R2), (R3), (Hecke), (Over Braid), and (Anti-Sym 1), the proof uses \(p_{\Lambda_{N+1}}\), its self-adjointness and zero trace, and positivity to infer \(p_{\Lambda_{N+1}}=0\) and the additional antisymmetry relation. The disputed step is the availability of this normalized projection throughout the stated parameter range, which includes \(k=1\); no restriction to higher levels is made in Theorem 1.1.

Let \(N\geq2\), let \(k\) be a positive level, let \(q\) have order \(m=2(N+k)\), and let \(\omega\) be an \(N\)-th root of unity. Lemma 2.14 claims that \(\overline{\operatorname{Rep}(U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_N))}^{\omega}\) is Galois conjugate to a category at the unitary root \(q'=e^{2\pi i/m}\), with a possibly changed \(N\)-th root \(\omega'\). To lift a unit modulo \(m\) to a Galois automorphism of the coefficient field with \(L=\operatorname{lcm}(m,N)\), its proof asserts \[\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z/(L/m)\mathbb Z.\] This asserted cyclic-group decomposition, made without a coprimality hypothesis on its factors, is the proof step under examination; the report does not reject the lemma after a valid unit-lifting argument.

Fix the parameters \((N,q,\omega)\) and a graph \(\Gamma\) of a KW cell system. Definition 5.5 uses a unitary matrix \(V\) on each space of parallel edges to define equivalence of cell systems. For an \(N\)-edge loop with edge labels \(i_1,\ldots,i_N\), its displayed rule for the \(B\)-cell sums over the primed labels but multiplies by only the first and last edge factors: \[B_1(i_1,\ldots,i_N)=\sum_{i'_1,\ldots,i'_N}B_2(i'_1,\ldots,i'_N)V(i'_1,i_1)V(i'_N,i_N).\] Together with the displayed \(U\)-cell rule and unitarity constraints, this is claimed to describe the coordinate action of unitary edge-basis changes, preserving KW cell systems and supplying the equivalence relation in Theorem 1.1. The assertion being checked is this literal two-factor formula for arbitrary \(N\), not the all-strand change of basis pictured in its proof.

In the Hecke-algebra portion of the skein presentation, let \(Y=q^{-1}U-\mathrm{id}\), with \([2]_q=q+q^{-1}\) and the stated eigenvalues \(0\) and \([2]_q\) for \(U\). Remark 2.13 asserts that the corresponding eigenvalues of \(Y\) are \(-1\) and \(q^2\). The finding concerns this local eigenvalue formula with the printed normalization of \(Y\).

Let \(A=\mathbb C[X]\) be the coordinate algebra of an affine torus variety, and let \(v:A\setminus\{0\}\to L\) be a maximum-convention valuation with one-dimensional leaves and finitely generated saturated value semigroup \(S\) generating the ordered lattice \(L\). Section 4.1.2 assumes a grading map \(w:L\to\Lambda\) satisfying (v1)–(v5): the order descends to \(\Lambda\), \(w(S)\) has a least element, its fibers in \(S\) are finite, homogeneous elements have degree \(w(v(f))\), and any finite collection of strict comparisons within grading fibers admits a nonnegative integral linear refinement. Fix the prescribed homogeneous Khovanskii basis \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\) and the relation generators of Lemma 4.4. For a linear map \(e:L\to\mathbb Z\) nonnegative on \(S\) and satisfying the finitely many comparisons in (15), the text claims that \[A_{\leq k}=\{0\}\cup\{f\ne0:e(v(f))\leq k\},\qquad k\geq0,\] are vector subspaces forming a filtration, so that \(\bigoplus_{k\geq0}A_{\leq k}t^k\) is the Rees algebra used in Proposition 4.5.

The same construction also asserts in Lemma 4.4 that lifts \(g_j=\bar g_j+p_j\) of homogeneous graded relations can satisfy \(v(\bar g_j(f_1,\ldots,f_n))>v(p_j(f_1,\ldots,f_n))\), and (15) uses the evaluated expression on the left to choose \(e\). These are the evaluated quantities literally displayed in the source, rather than the formal homogeneous degrees of the relation polynomials. Both this comparison and the claimed additivity of \(A_{\leq k}\) are part of the construction under examination.

Let \(K\) be compact and connected and let \((Y,\mu)\) be a connected proper Hamiltonian \(K\)-manifold in the paper's sense: \(\mu\) is proper into a \(K\)-invariant set whose intersection with the positive Weyl chamber is convex. Let \(\sigma\) be its principal stratum, \(\Delta_Y=S\circ\mu(Y)\), and let \(U\subset X_Y\) be the dense symplectic piece constructed in Proposition 6.9 using the smooth piece \(U^\sigma\) of the universal toric contraction. Proposition 6.10(iii) asserts \[\Psi_Y(U)=c^{-1}(\Delta_Y\cap\sigma)\cap\Psi(U^\sigma)\] and identifies this set with the lattice-theoretic smooth locus of \(c^{-1}(\Delta_Y\cap\sigma)\cap\Psi(X^\sigma)\). No multiplicity-free or toric hypothesis on \(Y\) is imposed. The disputed conclusion is this smooth-locus description of the particular constructed open piece, which is then used in the proof of Theorem 1.1.

Let \(S\subset\mathbb Z^4\) be the semigroup generated by \[v_1=(0,1,0,0),\ v_2=(0,1,0,1),\ v_3=(1,0,0,0),\ v_4=(1,0,1,0),\ v_5=(1,0,0,1),\ v_6=(1,0,1,1),\] and let \(\pi:\mathbb C[y_1,\ldots,y_6]\to\mathbb C[(\mathbb C^*)^4]\) send \(y_i\) to the character \(\chi^{v_i}\). Example 4.17, equation (21), asserts the set-theoretic equality \[X_S=V(\ker\pi)=\{y\in\mathbb C^6:y_3y_6=y_4y_5,\ y_1y_5=y_2y_3\}.\] The claim under examination is that these two equations cut out the indicated affine toric variety, without restriction to a torus chart or an additional saturation condition.

Let \(\pi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb C\) be a morphism of varieties, let \(Z\) be the union of its critical set and the singular locus, and assume \(Z\subset\mathcal X_0\), \(U_0=\mathcal X_0\setminus Z\ne\varnothing\), and \(\mathcal X\setminus Z\) is Kähler. Lemma A.1 assumes a connected Lie group \(K\) acting Hamiltonianly on \(\mathcal X\setminus Z\), preserving the Kähler metric and the fibers of \(\pi\), with a continuous moment map extension \(\psi:\mathcal X\to\mathfrak k^*\). Its properness assumption is that \((\pi,\psi)\) is proper as a map onto its image. Under these assumptions it claims that the normalized gradient Hamiltonian flow \(\varphi_t(x)\) exists for every \(x\in U_0\) and every \(t\in\mathbb R\). This completeness conclusion precedes the lemma's additional Duistermaat–Heckman measure assumption.

Let a compact torus \(T\) act unitarily on a finite-dimensional Hermitian space \(E\), and let \(\mu:E\to\operatorname{Lie}(T)^*\) be its quadratic moment map normalized by \(\mu(0)=0\). Lemma 2.2(ii) claims that \(\mu\) is proper if and only if the cone \(\mu(E)\) is strongly convex, meaning that it contains no nonzero linear subspace. The lemma makes no exclusion of zero weights in the representation. This final equivalence is the assertion being checked, separately from the preceding criterion involving nontrivial nonnegative relations among the weights.

Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\), \(n\geq2\), be open and connected, and let \(L=-\operatorname{div}(A\nabla)\), where \(A\) is real, bounded, measurable and strongly elliptic, without a symmetry requirement. Definition 2.12(v) asserts that, for scalar data \(H\in L^{n/2,1}(\Omega)\) and vector data \(F\in L^{n,1}(\Omega)\), the Green representation \[w(x)=\int_\Omega G_L(y,x)H(y)\,dy+\int_\Omega\nabla_yG_L(y,x)\cdot F(y)\,dy\] solves \(L^*w=H-\operatorname{div}F\), belongs to \(Y_0^{1,2}(\Omega)\), and satisfies \[\|w\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\lesssim\|H\|_{L^{n/2,1}(\Omega)}+\|F\|_{L^{n,1}(\Omega)}.\] The finding tests this uniform bound with the literal boundary-dimension exponents \(n/2\) and \(n\), while the integration takes place in ambient dimension \(n+1\).

In the boundary dyadic and Whitney-region setting of Appendix A, let \(w^*(Q)\) be the enlarged Whitney regions associated with boundary cubes \(Q\in\mathcal D_\sigma\). For arbitrary sequences of functions \(u_Q\in L^q(w^*(Q))\), define \[F(u)(x)=\frac{\sum_{Q\in\mathcal D_\sigma}u_Q(x)\mathbf1_{w^*(Q)}(x)}{\sum_{Q\in\mathcal D_\sigma}\mathbf1_{w^*(Q)}(x)}.\] Let \(N_q^s\) and \(C_{q'}^s\) denote the discrete non-tangential and Carleson functionals on sequences, and \(N_q^d,C_{q'}^d\) their function versions, as defined there. Lemma A.9 states that for \(p\in[1,\infty)\), \(q\in[1,\infty]\), and their Hölder conjugates \(p',q'\), provided either \(\Omega\) is bounded or \(\partial\Omega\) is unbounded, \[\|N_q^dF(u)\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\asymp\|N_q^su\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)},\qquad \|C_{q'}^dF(H)\|_{L^{p'}(\partial\Omega)}\asymp\|C_{q'}^sH\|_{L^{p'}(\partial\Omega)}\] for every allowed sequence. There is no coordinatewise nonnegativity assumption in these two-sided assertions.

Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\), \(n\geq2\), let \(L=-\operatorname{div}(A\nabla)\) with real bounded strongly elliptic coefficients, and let \(B^*=(1+\theta)B\subset\Omega\), where \(\theta\in(0,1]\). Lemma 2.10 permits any real-valued weak solution \(u\in W^{1,2}(B^*)\) of \(Lu=0\), and asserts, for every \(q>0\), the lower comparison \[\left(\frac{1}{|B^*|}\int_{B^*}|u|^q\,dx\right)^{1/q}\lesssim\min_{x\in B/2}|u(x)|.\] The disputed statement imposes no fixed-sign or nonnegativity condition on \(u\); it is the Harnack part of the lemma, separate from its local boundedness and Hölder estimates.

Let \((X^4,g,I_1,I_2,I_3)\) be hyperkähler with a circle action preserving the three Kähler forms, generated by \(\xi\). On its free locus, choose \(\eta(\xi)=1\) and \(\ker\eta=\xi^\perp\), define \(\phi^{-1}=|\xi|_g^2\), and set \(\alpha_i=I_i(\phi^{-1}\eta)\). Equation (2.1) asserts \[g=\phi^{-1}\eta^2+\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2+\alpha_3^2.\] Proposition 2.1(a),(c) additionally asserts that \(g_E=\phi^{-2}\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) is the pullback of a flat metric on the three-dimensional quotient and that local moment coordinates satisfy \(\alpha_i=\phi^{1/2}d\mu_i\). The problem concerns the mutual consistency of these exact normalizations, rather than the later standard Gibbons–Hawking metric written directly in the \(\mu_i\) coordinates.

Let \(L_t\) be a smooth graded circle-invariant Lagrangian mean curvature flow in the Gibbons–Hawking setting, with real grading \(\theta_t\) and time-dependent induced metric. Section 3.1 uses \(\partial_t\theta_t=-\Delta_t\theta_t\), with the nonnegative geometer's Laplacian \(\Delta_t=d_t^*d\), to assert the pointwise identity \[ (\partial_t+\Delta_t)|d\theta_t|_{g_t}^{2}=-2|\nabla^{g_t}d\theta_t|_{g_t}^{2}.\] The claim being checked is this gradient-norm evolution formula for the evolving metric, including in the flat ambient special case.

Let \(\phi=m+\sum_{i=1}^k(2|x-p_i|)^{-1}\), \(m\geq0\), and let \(\gamma_0\) be a strictly convex embedded planar arc with endpoints at two centers \(p_1,p_2\), meeting no other center. Proposition 3.4 considers a smooth solution \(\partial_t\gamma_t=\phi^{-1}\kappa_tN_t\) on \([0,T]\), with those fixed endpoints and no other center encountered, and asserts that strict interior convexity persists. Its proof sets \(f=\phi^{-1}\kappa\), obtains \(f_t\geq\phi^{-1}f_{ss}-cf\) only where \(f\geq0\), and claims this yields the strict first-contact inequality for \(f^\varepsilon=f+\varepsilon t\) at an interior first zero with \(t_0>0\). The finding concerns the validity of this sign-restricted inference at that first contact, not a counterexample to convexity preservation after a corrected argument.

With the Gibbons–Hawking potential \(\phi\), let \(\gamma_0\subset\mathbb R^3\) be an embedded planar curve avoiding all centers and satisfying \(\kappa_0\geq0\). Proposition 3.5 asserts that every smooth solution \(\gamma_t\), \(t\in[0,T]\), of \(\partial_t\gamma_t=\phi^{-1}\kappa_tN_t\) which continues to avoid the centers has \(\kappa_t>0\) for all \(t\in[0,T]\). The statement has no exclusion of a stationary straight curve and includes the initial time in its strict-positivity conclusion.

Lemma B.5 asserts the variational identity \[\inf\left\{\int_{\mathbb R}|\psi'(t)|^2\,dt:\psi\in H^1_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbb R),\ \operatorname{supp}\psi\subset[0,\infty),\ \int_0^1|\psi(t)|^2\,dt=1\right\}=2.\] This is the optimization constant used to pass from the time-average bound to the pointwise estimate in Theorem 3.1.

More precisely, let \(P_h\) be self-adjoint on an \(h\)-independent dense domain in a separable Hilbert space, let \(Q_h\) be bounded and accretive, and set \(\mathsf P_h=P_h+ihQ_h\). For \(0<\varepsilon(h)\leq\varepsilon_0<1\), take \(I_\varepsilon=[1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]\) and \(\Pi_\varepsilon=\chi((P_h-1)/\varepsilon)\), where \(\chi\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))\), \(\chi\geq0\), and \(\chi(0)=1\). If \(I_\varepsilon\subset\rho(\mathsf P_h)\) and \(\|(\mathsf P_h-\tau)^{-1}\|\leq G(h)/h\) for all \(\tau\in I_\varepsilon\), equation (3.6) claims, for every \(T_h\geq1\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and \(u\), \[\|e^{iT_h\mathsf P_h/h}\Pi_\varepsilon u\|^2\leq\left((2+\delta)\frac{G(h)^2}{T_h^2}+\frac{C_QhT_h}{\delta^2\varepsilon(h)^2}\right)\|\Pi_\varepsilon u\|^2,\] where \(C_Q=C_0(1+\|Q_h\|^2)\) and \(C_0\) depends only on \(\chi\). The finding concerns both the stated variational value and this resulting abstract estimate, not the existence of some positive logarithmic PDE lower-bound constant.

For the massless damped wave equation on a smooth compact connected manifold without boundary, let \(b\in L^\infty(M;\mathbb R_+)\), let \(\Pi_0\) project onto constants, and let \(\Pi_+=I-\Pi_0\). Corollary 2.5(6) states that for every \((u_0,u_1)\in H_+^1(M)\times L^2(M)\), the wave solution remains in \(C^0(\mathbb R;H_+^1)\cap C^1(\mathbb R;L^2)\) and obeys \[(u,u_t)(t)=e^{tA_+}(u_0,u_1).\] Thus the first component is asserted to be the actual mean-free displacement, while no mean-free restriction is imposed on velocity.

The associated generator identity (2.20) also states \[A=A_+\begin{pmatrix}\Pi_+&0\\0&I\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\Pi_0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\] with analogous additive kernel-projector terms for \(\widetilde A\) and \(\mathsf P\). These are asserted as identities of generators, separately from the resolvent and semigroup formulas where zero-mode contributions have different meanings.

In the proof of Proposition 2.11, let \(V(t)=e^{it\mathsf P_{\mathrm{cut}}}V_0\) and let \(K\) be the constructed time-independent off-diagonal correction, with \(K=O(h)\) on \(L^2(M;\mathbb C^2)\). Set \(W(t)=(I-K)V(t)\). After deriving \((D_t-\mathsf P_{\mathrm{diag}})W=RV\), with \(R=O(h^{1-2\nu})\), the proof uses \(W(0)=V(0)=V_0\) for arbitrary \(V_0\) and consequently writes \[W(t)=e^{it\mathsf P_{\mathrm{diag}}}V_0+i\int_0^te^{i(t-s)\mathsf P_{\mathrm{diag}}}Re^{is\mathsf P_{\mathrm{cut}}}V_0\,ds.\] The disputed step is this unchanged initial condition after the substitution, without a hypothesis \(KV_0=0\).

Let \(b\in C^0(M;\mathbb R_+)\) satisfy \(|b(x)-b(y)|\leq\omega(d_g(x,y))\) for a nondecreasing modulus \(\omega\). Equation (A.10) first cuts off the local representative of \(b\) by \(1-\chi(b/\omega(\varepsilon))\), then convolves it with a nonnegative normalized mollifier of coordinate radius \(\varepsilon\), and assembles the results using the stated atlas and partition of unity. Here \(\chi=1\) on \([-1,1]\) and is supported in \([-2,2]\). Proposition A.5(2) claims that this particular regularization satisfies \[b_\varepsilon(x)=0\quad\text{whenever }d_g(x,\{b=0\})\leq\varepsilon,\qquad 0<\varepsilon<1.\] The atlas is the general atlas fixed in the appendix; the statement imposes no metric-normalization condition identifying coordinate mollifier radii with geodesic distances.

Let \(P\) have \(\mathbb R\subset\rho(P)\), let \(iP\) generate a contraction semigroup on a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(C\) be bounded. Under the uniform estimate \(\|Cu\|\leq C_0\|(P-\tau+i\alpha)u\|\) for \(u\) in the stated domain, \(\tau\in\mathbb R\), and \(0\leq\alpha\leq\alpha_0\), the paragraph following Lemma 6.3 asserts \[\|\psi(t)Ce^{itP}\|_{L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal L(\mathcal H))}\leq\|\psi'\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}\sup_{\tau\in\mathbb R,\,\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]}\|C(P-\tau+i\alpha)^{-1}\|.\] It quantifies over \(\psi\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)\) supported in \([0,\infty)\) with \(\psi'\in L^2\). The claim being checked places the operator norm inside the time integral, as printed, rather than taking the norm of the map \(\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal H)\).

The exterior estimates in Proposition 3.3 are established on \(\mathcal D^e=\{t\geq2:r^2\geq t^2-2t\}\). In each dyadic time slab, the proof chooses \(\tau_k\in[2^k,2^{k+1})\cap[2,T_0)\) and, for every target point in that slab with \(r<2t\), integrates the available derivative estimate along \(\tau^2-|x(\tau)|^2=t^2-r^2\) until reaching either \(\tau=\tau_k\) or \(|x(\tau)|=2\tau\). The claimed implication is that these endpoint alternatives permit the integration using only estimates valid in \(\mathcal D^e\).

The interior argument uses \(\mathcal H_s=\{t^2-r^2=s^2\}\cap\mathcal D^i\), where \(\mathcal D^i=\{t\geq1+\sqrt{1+r^2}\}\), hence \(t\leq s^2/2\) on \(\mathcal H_s\). For a zero-circle-average field \(\mathbf W\), Proposition 4.22 evaluates the scaling ray \(p_\lambda=(\lambda t/s,\lambda x/s)\) at a fixed \(s_0\) close to 2 and claims \[|Y_{tx}(s_0)|\lesssim(s/t)^{3/2}E^i(s_0,Z^{\leq2}\mathbf W)^{1/2}.\] This use of the truncated initial hyperboloid presumes that the ray's starting point and the intermediate coefficient estimates lie in the region already controlled. The finding concerns these two path-and-domain implications, without asserting a counterexample to Einstein evolution.

Lemma 4.13 considers a smooth solution of \(\widetilde\Box_g u=F\) in the displayed region \(D_s\): \(t\geq2\), \(t/2<r<2t-3\), with \(r\leq\sqrt{t^2-s^2}\) in \(\mathcal D^i\) and \(t\leq s^2/2\) otherwise. Its lateral boundary is specified as \(r=t/2\) only for \(t\leq8/3\), together with \(r=2t-3\) for \(t\leq s^2/2\). Write \(\pi=g^{-1}-m^{-1}\). Under its stated null-component smallness assumptions, including \(|\pi_{LL}|\leq\varepsilon|t-r|/(t+r)\), it claims \[t|(\partial_t-\partial_r)u(t,x)|\lesssim\sup_{\partial_BD_s}|(\partial_t-\partial_r)(ru)|+\int_2^t|\mathcal M[u,\pi](\tau)|\,d\tau+\int_2^t\tau|F(\tau,\varphi(\tau;t,x))|\,d\tau.\] Here \(\varphi\) is the characteristic of \(\partial_t+\frac{1-\pi_{LL}/4}{1+\pi_{LL}/4}\partial_r\), and \(\mathcal M\) is the angular and metric-error integrand defined in (4.73). The claim includes both that the relevant backward characteristics reach the listed boundary and that this right-hand side controls the derivative of \(u\), rather than only the derivative of \(ru\).

The application to Proposition 4.12 asserts that the full zero-mode inverse-metric perturbation satisfies this lemma's hypotheses, including the displayed bound forcing \(\pi_{LL}=0\) on \(r=t\), despite the prescribed positive mass tail. The report examines the auxiliary estimate, its boundary geometry and this applicability claim separately.

For the scalar equation \(g^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu\partial_
u W=F\) on \(\mathbb R^{1+3}	imes\mathbb S^1\), Proposition A.1 assumes a small inverse-metric perturbation \(H\) with \[|H|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+t+r)^{-3/4},\qquad |H_{LL}+2\chi(r/t)\chi(r)M/r|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+t+r)^{-1-\delta},\quad\delta>0.\] Its flux argument on \(\widetilde{\mathcal H}=\{(t-1)^2-r^2=1,\ t\geq2\}\) compares the curved flux with a positive quadratic form containing \[\left( rac{1}{2(1+r^2)}+ rac{M}{2r}ight)|\partial_tW|^2+|\widetilde
abla W|^2\] where both cutoffs equal one. The question under examination is whether the permitted smallness of \(\varepsilon\) depends on the positive mass \(M\), and what justifies this comparison as \(M\) becomes small. The report records this dependence as unresolved for the actual Einstein data class; its auxiliary-metric test is not a counterexample satisfying the Einstein constraints or wave gauge.

The exterior energy \(E^{e,\kappa}(t,W)\) is defined with a fixed-time integral over \(r\geq t-1\) and a spacetime integral over \(r\geq\tau-1\). The stated exterior slice is instead \(\Sigma_t^e=\{r\geq\sqrt{t^2-2t}\}\times\mathbb S^1\). Equation (3.5) treats the energy bound \(E^{e,\kappa}(t,Z^{\leq N}h^1)^{1/2}\leq2C_0\varepsilon t^\sigma\) as implying the weighted gradient bound with the same right-hand side over all of \(\Sigma_t^e\). The claim being checked is this passage from the smaller integration domain to the larger slice.

The notation also gives two truncations of \(\mathcal H_s=\{t^2-r^2=s^2\}\): \(t\geq r+1\) in the definitions on PDF page 16 and \(t\geq1+\sqrt{1+r^2}\) in the interior energy setup. The finding concerns consistency of these domains in the subsequent energy statements.

For \(r<t\), set \(s=\sqrt{t^2-r^2}\) and use the paper's null frame \(L=\partial_t+\partial_r\), \(\underline L=\partial_t-\partial_r\), together with the hyperboloidal derivatives \(\underline\partial_a=\partial_a+(x_a/t)\partial_t\). If \(c_{UV}^{00}\) denotes the coefficient of \(\partial_t^2\) in the expansion of \(UV\), equation (1.18) claims, for a tensor \(\pi\), \[4(t/s)^2\pi^{UV}c_{UV}^{00}=\pi_{\underline L\underline L}\frac{s^2}{(t+r)^2}+\pi_{LL}\frac{(t+r)^2}{s^2}+\pi_{L\underline L}.\] The finding tests this exact frame-conversion identity, in particular the coefficient of its mixed null component.

On \(\mathbb R^{1+3}\) with \(\Box_{tx}=-\partial_t^2+\Delta_x\), put \(s^2=t^2-r^2\) and \(\underline\partial_a=\partial_a+(x_a/t)\partial_t\). Equation (4.62) claims the differential-operator identity \[-\Box_{tx}=(s/t)^2\partial_t^2+2(x^a/t)\underline\partial_a\partial_t-\underline\partial^{a}\underline\partial_a+\left(\frac{r^2}{t^3}+\frac3t\right)\partial_t.\] The same drift sign is used in the ray-operator expansion and in the definition of \(Q\) in Proposition 4.21. The finding concerns these exact identities and the associated equation-sign bookkeeping when isolating the second time derivative and the mass-tail forcing; it does not assert a different decay rate merely from a numerical sign correction.

Along the scaling ray, the proof of Proposition 4.21 writes the equation in the form \(b(\lambda)\omega''-c(\lambda)\omega_{yy}-d(\lambda)\omega'_y=\mathcal R\), where the coefficients are independent of the circle variable and \(c=1+(H^{1,44})^\flat\) evaluated on the ray. For \[E(\lambda)=\int_{\mathbb S^1}\bigl(b|\omega'|^2+c|\omega_y|^2\bigr)\,dy,\] the displayed integration-by-parts equality retains the derivative of \(b\) but gives the energy derivative without a \(c'\|\omega_y\|_2^2\) contribution. The claim being checked is this identity for variable \(c\), not a constant-coefficient special case.

The same ray formulas use \(\chi(t/r)\) in several mass terms, although the original tail and the quantity \(a(t,x)\) used in their derivation are defined with \(\chi(r/t)\). The asserted identification of these terms is a second local formula issue within this problem, separate from the ray-domain issue.

The exterior bootstrap has an arbitrary endpoint \(T_0\) and cumulative weighted spacetime-flux bounds of polynomial size \(C\varepsilon^2t^{2\sigma}\). The text introduces \(l\in L^1([2,T_0))\) so that tangential derivative bounds carry \(t^\sigma\sqrt{l(t)}\), and uses this in uniform time integrations and in choosing a time \(\tau_k\) in each \([2^k,2^{k+1})\cap[2,T_0)\) with the stated dyadic decay. The point under examination is whether finite-interval integrability and the cumulative polynomial bound justify those estimates with constants independent of \(T_0\), including a final dyadic interval of arbitrarily short length. It is not a claim that \(l\) fails to be integrable on any fixed finite interval.

In the zero-mode source decomposition for Proposition 4.31, let \(\chi\) be a smooth cutoff equal to one on \(B_{1/2}(0)\) and supported in \(B_1(0)\). The forcing \(F\) is split into \(\chi((r+1/2)/t)F\) and \((1-\chi((r+1/2)/t))F\). The text claims that the complementary forcing is supported in \(\{t\leq r+1/2\}\), so that the specified exterior estimates apply to it. The claim is about the support for this ratio cutoff, without an additional assumption that \(F\) vanishes throughout its transition region. The introductory split also displays zero Cauchy data at \(t=0\), while the original Cauchy problem and the subsequent proof use \(t=2\).

Let \(u_0=\operatorname{curl}y_0\) be a finite Radon measure on \(\mathbb R^2\), where \(y_0\in L^{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^2)\) is distributionally divergence-free, and let \(u\) be the vorticity solution supplied by Theorem 2.1. Theorem 2.3(iii) assumes additionally that \(u_0\in L^q\) for some \(1<q<2\), and claims, for every finite \(T>0\) and every \(p\in[1,\infty]\), \[u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^p(\mathbb R^2)),\qquad \|u\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^p)}\leq c_p\|u_0\|_{L^p}.\] The asserted membership is not conditioned on \(u_0\in L^p\) for that particular \(p\). The finding concerns uniform control up to the initial time, rather than smoothness or boundedness on intervals separated from zero.

On \(\mathbb R^2\), set \(\Phi_\varepsilon=(\varepsilon I-\Delta)^{-1}\) and \(K\varphi=k*\varphi\), where \(k(x)=x^\perp/(2\pi|x|^2)\). In the proof of Appendix Lemma .1, the display after (0.19) asserts that for every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)\), \[\nabla^\perp\Phi_{\varepsilon'}\varphi\longrightarrow-K\varphi\quad\text{in }L^1(\mathbb R^2)\quad(\varepsilon'\downarrow0).\] There is no zero-integral assumption on \(\varphi\). The issue is the global \(L^1\) topology explicitly claimed before the passage to distributions.

Let \(\Gamma\) have finite index in \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) and be normalized by \(j=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). For the \(c\)-cost, Definition 1.1 allows coboundaries with values in an abelian coefficient group. Proposition 2.6 asserts that a \(c\)-coboundary vanishes if and only if its associated \(L\)-invariant function \(\beta\) is constant; Corollary 2.7 uses this to classify coboundaries. These assertions do not exclude two-torsion in the coefficient group.

For a real vector cost \(\psi\) on the coset space and \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \(v\cdot\psi\) is a \(c\)-coboundary modulo \(2\pi\), Proposition 3.2(1) asserts a simple pole of the associated continued-fraction Dirichlet series \(L_{\Psi,J}(2s,w)\) at \(s=s(w)\), with \(s(iv)=1\). For the unweighted sample of reduced fractions with denominators at most \(M\) in a nonempty open interval \(J\subset(0,1)\), Theorem 3.8 also claims \[\mathbb E[e^{iv\cdot c_\psi}\mid\Omega_{M,J}]=R(v)+O(M^{-\gamma_1}),\qquad R(v)=\frac{\sum_{u\in\Gamma\backslash\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)}e^{i(\beta(\Gamma)-\beta(u))}}{[\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z):\Gamma]},\] for some \(\gamma_1>0\). The finding tests these assertions in the allowed torsion case, including the terminal parity contribution in the evaluated series.

Let \(\mathcal H_{\sigma,\eta}\) be the real-weight transfer operator for the skewed Gauss system, with \((\sigma,\eta)\) in a sufficiently small neighborhood \(B\) of \((1,0)\). Proposition 7.4(1) claims that for every integer \(n\geq1\) and every \(\Psi\in C^1(X)\), \[\|\partial\mathcal H_{\sigma,\eta}^{n}\Psi\|_\infty\leq C_B\bigl(|\sigma|\|\Psi\|_\infty+\rho^n\|\partial\Psi\|_\infty\bigr),\] with \(C_B\) independent of \(n\), despite allowing nonzero real costs \(\eta\). Here \(\rho<1\) is the stated branch contraction rate.

For every depth-\(n\) inverse branch \(p\), Lemma 8.4(1) additionally claims the uniform comparison \[\frac{\|\partial\pi_1p\|_\infty^{\sigma}}{\lambda_{\sigma,\eta}^{n}}\asymp_B\nu_{\sigma,\eta}(p(X)),\] where \(\lambda_{\sigma,\eta}\) is the dominant eigenvalue and \(\nu_{\sigma,\eta}\) the normalized invariant measure. This displayed comparison contains no accumulated real branch-weight factor. These two unnormalized assertions, rather than every subsequent normalized spectral estimate, are the claims being checked.

Let \(\Omega_{M,J}\) be the unweighted set of reduced fractions \(a/n\in J\), where \(2\leq n\leq M\), \(1\leq a<n\), \((a,n)=1\), and \(J\subset(0,1)\) is a nonempty open interval. Equation (3.3) asserts \[|\Omega_{M,J}|=\frac{3|J|}{\pi^2\log2}M^2+O(M^\delta),\qquad\delta<2.\] The finding concerns the leading constant for this raw counting measure, in particular for \(J=(0,1)\), rather than a ratio defining a normalized moment-generating function.

Fix an arbitrary real number \(h\) and a real cost \(\psi\) on the finite coset space. Section 9 defines the additive cost \(\Upsilon=2h\log|x|+\psi(v)\) for the \(b\)-system, with the specified two-step analogue for the \(c\)-system, and sets \(\kappa(w)=\lambda_{1+hw,w\psi}\). If \(S\) is the corresponding skewed Gauss map or its prescribed square and \(\Phi_{1,0}\,dm\) is the invariant probability measure, Proposition 9.2 claims \[\kappa''(0)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\int_X\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Upsilon\circ S^k\right)^2\Phi_{1,0}\,dm.\] The proposition does not require \(\kappa'(0)=0\), or equivalently a centered cost in this normalization, although its proof uses that equality. The issue is this uncentered statement for arbitrary \(h\), not its later use in a direction chosen to satisfy the centering condition.

Fix the paper's good bounding tree \(T\), a path \(0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k\) whose endpoint is not a leaf, and a finite nonempty \(K\subset\Lambda\setminus H_T(u_k)\). For \(i\leq j<k\), in the case \([K]_{u_{j+1}}\ne[K]_{u_j}\), the proof of Lemma 6.12 sets \[A=G_{u_i}([K]_{u_j}),\qquad\mathcal Y=G_{u_{j+1}}(A),\qquad\mathcal X=G_{u_i}(\mathcal Y).\] For each relevant child normal \(v\), it asserts \(d_v(\mathcal X)\leq C\operatorname{wd}_{u_i}(A)+O(1)\), and uses \(d_v(\mathcal Y)\leq C\operatorname{wd}_{u_i}(\mathcal Y)\). Here \(d_v(B)=\sup_{x\in B}\langle x,v\rangle\) is the uncentered support coordinate, and the constants depend only on the fixed tree and update range. No choice of origin or translation normalization is imposed. These individual coordinate bounds are the disputed proof steps; the lemma's translation-invariant weighted-diameter conclusion is a distinct assertion.

Let \(c\) be a square-free positive modulus and let \(a,b_1,b_2,b_3,q_1,q_2\) be integers satisfying \((q_1q_2,c)=1\), \(c\nmid b_2\), and \(c\nmid b_3\). Write \(e_c(z)=e^{2\pi iz/c}\) and \(S(A,B;c)=\sum_{x\bmod c}^{*}e_c(Ax+B\bar x)\), with bars denoting inverses modulo \(c\). Appendix B defines \[\mathcal C=\sum_{\gamma\bmod c}^{*}e_c(a\gamma)\prod_{j=1}^{2}S(b_1-\bar q_jb_2+\bar\gamma b_2,\ b_3(\gamma-q_j);c).\] Lemma B.1 claims the uniform bound \(\mathcal C\ll_\varepsilon c^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) whenever none of the congruences \[q_1\equiv q_2,\qquad b_1\pm b_2(\bar q_1-\bar q_2)\equiv0,\qquad b_1-\bar q_1b_2\equiv0,\qquad b_1-\bar q_2b_2\equiv0\pmod c\] holds; otherwise it states a \(c^{2+\varepsilon}\) bound. The finding concerns the generic branch for composite square-free \(c\), with nondegeneracy tested modulo the entire modulus, rather than separately at every prime factor. The parameter \(a\) is unrestricted.

Let \((M^{n+1},g)\) be a Riemannian manifold with \(\operatorname{Ric}_g=\lambda g\), and suppose a Lie group acts isometrically with one-dimensional orbit space. Section 1.1 asserts that every such cohomogeneity-one Einstein manifold is either flat or has positive scalar curvature. The stated preliminary hypotheses contain no compactness restriction on \(M\). The claim being checked is this general geometric assertion, before the later restriction to the closed sphere construction.

Let \(\gamma_i:[a_i,b_i)\to\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\), \(i=1,2\), be continuous curves without self-intersection, with the same initial point and continuous extensions satisfying \(\gamma_i(b_i)=0\). In proving Lemma 3.4, after reducing to finitely many mutual intersections, the text claims that for every sufficiently small radius \(r>0\), each curve enters the disk \(D_r\) only once and remains in it thereafter. The surrounding lemma also assumes the stated eventual winding-angle separation \(\theta(\gamma_1)-\theta(\gamma_2)\geq\theta_0\). The finding concerns this claimed disk-entry consequence of the curve hypotheses; it does not reject the intersection lower bound once a valid truncation argument is supplied.

Let \(f:R\to S\) be a map of connective \(E_1\)-ring spectra such that \(S\), as a right \(R\)-module, is homologically even, and let \(M\) be an even flat left \(R\)-module. Theorems 1.10 and 8.8 assert that the canonical base-change comparison \[\pi_0S\otimes_{\pi_0R}H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{p,q}(R,M)\longrightarrow H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{p,q}(S,S\otimes_RM)\] is surjective whenever \(p\geq q-1\). The printed theorem does not assume that \(M\) is connective; the even-flat class permits negative even suspensions. The finding concerns both the stated off-diagonal range and the absence of a connectivity restriction on the input module.

For an \(E_n\)-ring spectrum \(R\), Corollary 3.38 asserts that the even module-filtration functor \[\operatorname{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^*:\operatorname{Mod}_R(\operatorname{Sp})\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_{\operatorname{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^*(R)}(\operatorname{FilSp})\] is canonically \(E_{n-1}\)-monoidal. Under the paper's explicit convention, monoidal means strongly monoidal. Thus in the commutative case, for arbitrary \(R\)-modules \(M,N\), the tensor comparison over \(A=\operatorname{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^*(R)\) is required to be an equivalence \[\operatorname{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^*(M)\otimes_A\operatorname{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^*(N)\simeq\operatorname{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^*(M\otimes_RN),\] where filtered tensor products use Day convolution. No evenness restriction on \(M,N\) appears in the asserted domain. The issue is the strong structure, separately from the preceding lax monoidal construction.

Normalize the adjoint eigenvector by \(\langle u_{\mathrm{ad}},u_{\mathrm{wt}}'angle=1\). Equations (2.13)–(2.14) simultaneously prescribe \[\lambda_{\mathrm{wt}}(
u)=-c_g

The finding checks compatibility of these sign conventions with the displayed Bloch family and simple-eigenvalue derivative.

In the small-spectral-parameter wave-train resolvent, define \(K_\lambda\) to be the integral operator in (6.5) without its leading minus sign, and define \(K_0(\lambda)\) by freezing its Floquet matrices and neutral projection at zero while retaining \(e^{\nu_{\mathrm{wt}}(\lambda)(\xi-\zeta)}\). Equation (6.5) gives \((L_{\mathrm{wt}}-\lambda)^{-1}=-K_\lambda+\bar s_e^{\mathrm{wt}}\). The subsequent decomposition extracts \(-K_0(\lambda)\), but (6.7) specifies the remaining critical term as \(-K_0(\lambda)-K_\lambda\). This residual is then treated as possessing an extra factor of \(\lambda\) in the decay argument of Lemma 7.4. The problem concerns the exact reconstruction identity and the cancellation claimed for this residual.

In the full-front decomposition, write \(r=u_{\mathrm{fr}}'\), \(w=u_{\mathrm{wt}}'\), and \(q=q(\cdot,\sigma^2)\). Formula (6.28) splits the contribution \(\alpha_-\chi_-e^{\nu_{\mathrm{wt}}(\sigma^2)\xi}q\) into a principal part with \(r\) and a residual with \((r-w)+(w-q)\). The same construction also prints \(q(\cdot,0)=u_{\mathrm{wt}}\) in Lemma 6.10 and uses \(\Lambda_1g=(0,g_1,g_2)^T\) for the variables \((u,u_\xi,v)^T\). These are the exact signs, neutral-mode normalization and forcing normalization under examination in the resolvent identities.

In Appendix A, write \(\lambda=b+i\Omega\), \(\mu=|\Omega|^{-1/2}\), \(\kappa=\operatorname{sgn}\Omega\), \(c=c_{\mathrm{lin}}>0\), and \(\widetilde b=b+\varepsilon\gamma>0\). The diagonal operators are \(L_0^{11}=\partial_X^2-i\kappa\) and \(L_0^{22}=c\partial_X-\widetilde b\mu-i\kappa/\mu+\mu B_0\), with the actual front coefficient \(B_0\leq0\). The printed inverse for the first uses \(G^p(X)=e^{-\sqrt{i\kappa}|X|}/(2\sqrt{i\kappa})\), with the positive-real-part square root; the transport inverse uses the positive left-supported kernel of (A.3). These kernels define the explicit terms \(u_0,v_0,u_1,v_1,v_2\) in (A.10)–(A.16).

Lemma A.4 claims constants \(C,\Omega_0>0\) such that for \(-3\varepsilon\gamma/4\leq b\leq\eta\), \(|\Omega|\geq\Omega_0\), and smooth forcing \(g\) in the stated \(L^p\) class, the resolvent solution satisfies \[\left\|(L_{\mathrm{fr}}-\lambda)^{-1}g-\begin{pmatrix}u_0+u_1\\v_0+v_1+v_2\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{L^p}\leq C|\Omega|^{-3/2}\|g\|_{L^p}.\] The finding tests this estimate for the explicitly printed kernels and terms, with the actual smooth front coefficients, rather than an expansion after correcting their inverse signs.

Let \(L_+\) be the constant-coefficient leading-edge linearization and let \(\sigma\in\Delta_\delta^{\mathrm{fr},2}\), the small square-root spectral sector specified in the paper. Lemma 6.7 asserts constants \(C,\delta>0\) such that every odd forcing \(g\in L^1_{0,1}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C^2)\) satisfies \[\|(L_+-\sigma^2)^{-1}g\|_{W^{2,\infty}(\mathbb R)\times W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb R)}\leq C\|g\|_{L^1_{0,1}}.\] The input assumption is the stated one-sided polynomially weighted \(L^1\) condition and oddness, without an additional \(L^\infty\) bound. The issue is the highest claimed derivative regularity, even for a fixed small positive real \(\sigma\) in the permitted sector.

For \((3-\sqrt6)/6<a<1/2\), \(0<\gamma<4\), and sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), Lemma 3.2 specifies the pulled front's spatial decay rate as \(\eta_{\mathrm{lin}}(a,\gamma,\varepsilon)<0\), while using the shifted dispersion relation \(d_{c_{\mathrm{lin}}}(\lambda,\nu-\eta_{\mathrm{lin}})\) and the leading-edge weight convention of Theorem 1.1. The finding checks the sign of this stated branch.

Separately, the heuristic following (5.1) claims that the half-line exponentially decaying branched mode has \(L^2\)-norm of order \(|\sigma|^{-1}=|\lambda|^{-1/2}\), where \(\lambda=\sigma^2\) approaches zero in the fixed sector with \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma\gtrsim|\sigma|\). The object in that statement is the norm itself, not its square.

Let \(X_\Omega=\mu^{-1}(\Omega)\subset\mathbb C^n\) be a smooth star-shaped toric domain for the moment map \(\mu_j(z)=\pi|z_j|^2\). Write its canonical Hamiltonian as \(H_{X_\Omega}=f_\Omega\circ\mu\), where \(f_\Omega\) is homogeneous of degree one and \(\Omega=\{f_\Omega\le1\}\). The angular coordinates have period one and the standard symplectic form is \(\omega=\sum_jd\mu_j\wedge d\theta_j\).

Propositions 1.9 and 5.6 assert \[\operatorname{ru}(X_\Omega)(z)=\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_j f_\Omega(\mu(z)),\qquad \operatorname{Ru}(X_\Omega)=\sum_{j=1}^n\int_\Omega\partial_j f_\Omega\,d\operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb R^n}.\] The normalization at issue is this integral formula together with Example 1.3, which defines the symplectic-flow invariant by integration against \(\omega^n\), and Example 1.5, which uses \(\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{n-1}\) on the contact boundary; Lemma 1.7 identifies the domain and boundary invariants.

Let \(Y\) be a compact manifold with flow \(\phi_t\), let \(E\to Y\) be a symplectic vector bundle with \(c_1(E)=0\), and let \(\Phi\) be a symplectic cocycle. Fix a compatible complex structure \(J\) and a representative \(\tau\) of the chosen homotopy class of determinant trivializations. The function \(\widetilde u_T(\Phi;J,\tau)(x)\) is the lifted determinant rotation along the trajectory from \(x\) to \(\phi_T(x)\).

Lemma 3.10 asserts that there is a constant \(C>0\), independent of the symplectic bundle automorphism \(\Psi\) homotopic to the identity, such that \[\left|\widetilde u_T(\Psi^*\Phi;J,\tau)(x)-\widetilde u_T(\Phi;J,\tau)(x)\right|\le C\] for every such \(\Psi\), every \(x\), and every time \(T\). In a unitary trivialization \(\Xi\) along the trajectory, equations (3.3)–(3.4) use \(\Psi^*\Phi_\Xi(t)=\Psi_\Xi(t)\Phi_\Xi(t)\Psi_\Xi(t)^{-1}\) and its lifted analogue, and the proof takes \(C=3c\), with \(c\) the rotation-quasimorphism defect constant.

Let \(A\in\operatorname{Sp}(2n)\), write \(A=UP\) for its symplectic polar decomposition with \(U\in U(n)\), and let \(S\) be a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix. Put \(\Omega=\begin{pmatrix}0&-I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}\); thus \(\Omega S\) lies in the symplectic Lie algebra. Denote the differential of the unitary polar-factor map at \(A\) by \(TU_A\).

Equation (2.2), in the proof of Lemma 2.2, asserts the complex-to-real trace conversion \[\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb C}\!\left(TU_A(\Omega SA)U^{-1}\right)=2i\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb R}\!\left(\Omega^{-1}TU_A(\Omega SA)U^{-1}\right).\] The reviewed assertion is this exact identity and its coefficient, as used to derive the subsequent trace estimate.

Let \(M\) carry a cylindrical vector field \(V\), meaning that its flow identifies \(M\) with \(\mathbb R\times Y\) for a transverse hypersurface \(Y\). Let \(g\) be a Riemannian metric with \(\mathcal L_Vg=g\), and let \(\nabla\) be its Levi-Civita connection. A tensor has slope \(a\) when \(\mathcal L_V\Psi=a\Psi\).

The second displayed identity in Lemma 4.4 asserts, for every pair of vector fields \(U,W\), \[\langle
abla_UV,Wangle+\langle U,
abla_WVangle=	frac12\langle U,Wangle.\] Corollary 4.6 further asserts that if a function \(F\) and a vector field \(U\) both have slope \(a\), then \(
abla F\), \(\operatorname{div}U\), and \(\Delta F\) all have slope \(a-1\). The reviewed parts are the factor in the first identity and the claimed slope of the divergence.

Let \(\Omega\subset[0,\infty)^n\) be a concave star-shaped moment region, with \(\partial_+\Omega=\mu(\partial X_\Omega)\). For a nonempty subset \(S\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}\), set \((0,\infty)^S=\{x\in[0,\infty)^n:x_i>0\text{ exactly when }i\in S\}\) and \(\partial_+\Omega_S=\partial_+\Omega\cap(0,\infty)^S\).

Definition 5.13 defines, for every \(v\in(0,\infty)^S\), \[[v]_\Omega=\min\{\langle x,v\rangle:x\in\partial_+\Omega_S\},\] thereby asserting that the minimum is attained on this relatively open support stratum. The bracket is then used in Lemma 5.14 to express the least Reeb period as \(c(X_\Omega)=\min\{[v]_\Omega:v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n\setminus\{0\}\}\). The finding concerns attainment in the bracket definition.

The ordinary Conley–Zehnder index \(\operatorname{CZ}\) in Theorem 2.10 is defined on homotopy classes of symplectic paths starting at the identity whose endpoints have no eigenvalue equal to one. Definition 2.11 extends the index to all classes in \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Sp}}(2n)\) by a lower semicontinuous limit, but its displayed formula permits approximating classes from the entire universal cover while applying \(\operatorname{CZ}\) to them.

For arbitrary symplectic path classes \(\widetilde\Phi\) and \(\widetilde\Psi\), Lemma 2.12(b) prints the direct-sum identity \[\operatorname{LCZ}(\widetilde\Phi\oplus\widetilde\Psi)=\operatorname{LCZ}(\widetilde\Psi)+\operatorname{CZ}(\widetilde\Phi),\] without requiring the endpoint of \(\widetilde\Phi\) to be nondegenerate. The question is whether these formulas are defined on their stated domains, including the degenerate classes needed in the index calculation (5.1)–(5.4).

In the proof of Theorem B, let \(X\) contain a sequence of expanders \((X_n)\). For each positive integer \(k\), set \(\delta_k=1/k\) and \(\varepsilon_k=100\sqrt{\delta_k\log(1/\delta_k)}\). The construction asserts that for every positive integer \(n\) one can choose a dimension \(d(n)\) and an \(n\)-dimensional subspace \(V(n)\subset\mathbb R^{d(n)}\) such that, simultaneously for every \(k=1,\ldots,n\), \[\max_{\substack{E\subset[d(n)]\\|E|/d(n)\le\delta_k}}\left\|P_{V(n)}\big|_{\ell^2(E)}\right\|<\varepsilon_k,\] where \(P_{V(n)}\) is orthogonal projection. This all-\(k\) requirement, used before complexifying the subspaces and embedding their matrix algebras into the quasi-local algebra, is the specific existence claim under review; the cited Lemma 4 only assumes \(0<\delta<1/10\).

For a uniformly locally finite metric space \(X\), define \(N_X(R)=\sup_{x\in X}|B(x,R)|\). In a contradiction argument assuming an embedding \(\prod_{n\ge1}M_n\hookrightarrow C_u^*(X)\), write \(p_n\) for the image of the unit of \(M_n\) and set \[R_n=\sup\{R>0:N_X(R)<\sqrt n/8\}-1.\] The proof of Theorem A claims that Lemma 1 applies for each positive integer \(n\), producing \(a_n\) in the unit ball of \(M_n\) with \[\inf_{b\in(p_n^\perp C_u^*(X)p_n^\perp)_1}\operatorname{dist}\bigl(a_n+b,C_u^{R_n}[X]\bigr)\ge\tfrac12.\] Here \(C_u^{R_n}[X]\) denotes operators of propagation at most \(R_n\). The reviewed point is that the displayed definition supplies an admissible positive radius for every \(n\), as required by Lemma 1, before forming the diagonal element.
