Let \(p>48\) be prime, let \(N\) be a multiple of \(p^2\), and set \(\mathbb B=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\times\mathbb Z\). Write \(f_p(x)\) for the last nonzero base-\(p\) digit of \(x\), with \(f_p(0)=1\). An \(S_{p,N}\)-Sudoku solution \(F:\mathbb B\to(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times\) has, for every integer line \(m=jn+i\), an integer affine witness \(an+b\), with \(a,b\) not both divisible by \(p\), such that \(F(n,jn+i)=f_p(an+b)\) whenever \(0\le n<N\) and \(\nu_p(an+b)\le1\). Assume every column \(m\mapsto F(n,m)\) is nonconstant.

Corollary 4.10 asserts that the Tetris transform \(F^{\mathrm T}(n,m)=F(n,pm)\) is again an \(S_{p,N}\)-Sudoku solution and still has nonconstant columns. This is asserted for every solution satisfying the preceding hypotheses, without the special normalization of (4.11). The reviewed assertion is preservation of the column condition under this transform.

Let \(p>48\) be prime and \(p^2\mid N\), and consider \(S_{p,N}\)-Sudoku solutions \(F\) with nonconstant columns on \(\mathbb B=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\times\mathbb Z\). With \(f_p\) the last nonzero \(p\)-adic digit and \(f_p(0)=1\), Remark 4.11 writes \[F(n,m)=c f_p(m-Dn-E)\quad\text{when }m\ne Dn+E,\] for \(c\in(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times\) and \(D,E\in\mathbb Z_p\), and claims a one-to-one correspondence between these solutions and the triples \((c,D,E)\).

The accompanying uniqueness argument asserts \(F(n,m+1)-F(n,m)=c\) whenever both \(m\) and \(m+1\) differ from \(Dn+E\). It also sets \(h_{n,m}=(m-Dn-E)/p^{r-1}\), for \(r\ge1\) and \(m\equiv Dn+E\pmod{p^{r-1}}\), and prints \[F(n,m+p^{r-1}h)=c\pi_p(h-h_{n,m})\quad\text{if }\pi_p(h)\ne\pi_p(h_{n,m}),\] where \(\pi_p\) is reduction modulo \(p\). These identities, and the claim that the triple determines the values on the excluded zero locus, are the assertions under review.

A related identity at the end of the proof of Theorem 4.6(i) asserts \[f_p(An+Bm+C)=f_p(B)f_p\!\left((A/B)n+m+C/B\right)\] for all board points when \(A,B,C\in\mathbb Z_p\) and \(B\) is a unit, including points where the affine argument is zero.

In the induction proving Theorem 4.9, let \(p>48\), \(p^2\mid N\), and let \(F\) be an \(S_{p,N}\)-Sudoku solution with nonconstant columns. For \(r\ge1\), suppose \(L(n,m)=A^{(r)}n+B^{(r)}m+C^{(r)}\) has integer coefficients with \(p
mid B^{(r)}\), and \(F(n,m)=f_p(L(n,m))\) whenever \(
u_p(L(n,m))\le r\). The proof chooses integers \(D,E\) such that \[L(n,m)\equiv B^{(r)}(m-Dn-E)\pmod{p^r},\] and infers, after the shear, \[F(n,m+Dn+E)=f_p(B^{(r)}m)\quad	ext{whenever }
u_p(m)\le r.\] The reviewed implication is that the stated congruence precision determines the last nonzero digit through valuation \(r\).

The same inference is used in the reverse direction of Proposition 5.2. For distinct primes \(p_1,p_2>48\), a decorated Sudoku solution has digit descriptions \(F_l(n,m)=c_lf_{p_l}(m-D_ln-E_l)\) away from their zero loci. Given \(r_l\ge0\), the proof chooses integers \(c,D,E\) with \(\pi_{p_l}(c)=c_l\), \(D\equiv D_l\pmod{p_l^{r_l}}\), and \(E\equiv E_l\pmod{p_l^{r_l}}\), then claims \(F_l(n,m)=f_{p_l}(c(m-Dn-E))\) whenever \(\nu_{p_l}(m-Dn-E)\le r_l\), yielding (5.1) after shearing.

In the reverse domino reduction of Proposition 5.2, take distinct primes \(p_1,p_2>48\), board width \(N=p_1^2p_2^2\), and a decorated \(S^{\mathcal R}\)-Sudoku solution \(F=(F_1,F_2,w)\) whose digit components have nonconstant columns. For a fixed \(r=(r_1,r_2)\in\mathbb N^2\), the proof works after the normalization \[F_l(n,m)=f_{p_l}(cm)\quad\text{when }\nu_{p_l}(m)\le r_l,\qquad l=1,2,\] where \(c\) is an integer coprime to both primes.

For every \(0\le s_l\le r_l\), put \(j=p_1^{s_1}p_2^{s_2}\). The printed calculation asserts \[F_l(n,jn)=\pi_{p_l}(cn)\quad(0\le n<N,\ p_l\nmid n).\] Comparing with the affine line witness \(a_{j,0}n+b_{j,0}\), it concludes \(a_{j,0}\equiv c\) and \(b_{j,0}\equiv0\pmod{p_l}\) for both primes. For a horizontal domino, where \(s_1<r_1\), it further asserts \(F_1(p_1n,jp_1n)=\pi_{p_1}(cn)\) for the printed range \(1\le n\le N/p_1\), \(p_1\nmid n\). The issue is these coefficient identities after removing powers of one prime, which feed the affine comparison and valuation transitions in the domino extraction.

Let \(\mathcal R=(W,R_1,R_2)\) be a domino rule, with finite alphabet \(W\) and allowed neighboring pairs \(R_l\subset W^2\). Remark 2.4 takes the space \[X=\mathbb Z^2\sqcup\{[s,s+e_l]:s\in\mathbb Z^2,\ l=1,2\}\] and declares its open sets to be exactly \[U_\Omega=\Omega\sqcup\{[s,s+e_l]:s,s+e_l\in\Omega,\ l=1,2\},\qquad\Omega\subset\mathbb Z^2.\] It asserts that this family satisfies the topology axioms.

A domino labeling \(T:\Omega\to W\), satisfying the prescribed relation on every included edge, is then extended to \(U_\Omega\) by assigning the pair \((T(s),T(s+e_l))\) to that edge. The remark claims these section sets form a sheaf under restriction and that its stalks are identified with \(W\). The reviewed assertions concern the declared topology and its claimed stalk interpretation.

The manuscript uses \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), and Definition 4.5 permits a natural board width \(N\). Theorem 4.7 assumes only that \(p>48\) is prime, \(p^2\mid N\), and \(F:\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\times\mathbb Z\to(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times\) is an \(S_{p,N}\)-Sudoku solution. It asserts that there is an integer affine form \(A^{(0)}n+B^{(0)}m+C^{(0)}\), not identically zero modulo \(p\), with \[F(n,m)=\pi_p(A^{(0)}n+B^{(0)}m+C^{(0)})\] whenever the affine argument is a unit modulo \(p\), and that its three coefficients are uniquely determined modulo \(p\).

Under the same hypotheses, Lemma 4.8 asserts the existence of a \(4\)-by-\(4\) square on the board on which the affine description holds and the form is everywhere a unit. The reviewed endpoint is the allowed width \(N=0\), for which neither statement includes a positive-width hypothesis.

Remark 4(e), PDF page 3, concerns a continuous convex function \(\Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) with \(\Phi(0)=0\) that is not linear. For every positive semidefinite operator \(\rho\) on \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) with \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\), let \(u_\rho\) be its Husimi probability density, and define \[I_\Phi(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\Phi(u_\rho(x,\omega))\,dx\,d\omega.\]

The assertion is that the only maximizers of \(I_\Phi\) are the coherent pure states \(\rho=|\varphi_{x_0,\omega_0}\rangle\langle\varphi_{x_0,\omega_0}|\), obtained from a normalized Gaussian by translation and modulation. The hypotheses impose neither finiteness of \(I_\Phi\) nor finiteness of the coherent value \(\int_0^1\Phi(t)\,dt/t\). The finding addresses uniqueness of maximizers in this full stated class, where negative-infinite values may occur.

Two computations in the generalized Wehrl-entropy proof are at issue. First, in the proof of Lemma 10, PDF page 9, write the Husimi function of a trace-one positive operator as \(u_\rho(z)=e^{-\pi|z|^2}\sum_jp_j|F_j(z)|^2\), where \(p_j\ge0\), \(\sum_jp_j=1\), and \(F_j(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n^{(j)}\pi^{n/2}z^n/\sqrt{n!}\) are normalized Fock functions. After moving a point of maximum to zero, set \(T=u_\rho(0)>0\). Formula (22) defines the harmonic cross term using \[h(z)=\frac2T\sum_{j\ge1}p_j\operatorname{Re}\left(a_0^{(j)}\sum_{n\ge1}a_n^{(j)}\frac{\pi^{n/2}z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\right).\] No phase convention making every \(a_0^{(j)}\) real is imposed.

Second, in the pure-state argument on PDF page 18, let \(\|f\|_2=1\), \(0<\tau<1\), \(u=|Vf|^2\), \(u_0(z)=e^{-\pi|z|^2}\), \(E=\{u>\tau\}\), and \(F_\tau=\{u_0>\tau\}\). Let \(E^*\) be the centered disk with area \(|E|\), and assume the branch \(e^{-|E|}<\tau/2\). After (48), the text identifies \(s=e^{-|E|}/e^{-|F_\tau|}\) with \(\tau e^{-|E|}\), and (49) asserts \[\int_{E^*\setminus F_\tau}(u_0-\tau)_+\,dA\ge\frac{(e^{-|F_\tau|}-e^{-|E|})^2}{2\tau}.\] Here \((a)_+=\max(a,0)\). The finding concerns the conjugation, ratio and positive-part notation in these displayed steps.

The deduction on PDF page 19 fixes a normalized pure state \(\rho=|f\rangle\langle f|\), \(\|f\|_2=1\), and a continuous convex nonlinear \(\Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) with \(\Phi(0)=0\). Let \(D[f]\) be the \(L^2\) distance from \(f\) to the phase-adjusted normalized coherent functions, and let \(D[\rho]\) be the trace-norm distance from \(\rho\) to the coherent rank-one projections. Theorem 13, PDF page 16, supplies a universal constant \(c>0\) in its hinge-entropy estimate with the factor \(D[f]^2\).

Using the same constant \(c\), the deduction claims that the coefficient in front of \(D[\rho]^2\) in Theorem 3, equation (4), can be taken to be \[c_\Phi=c\int_0^1\tau\bigl(1-\tau-\tau\log(1/\tau)\bigr)\,\Phi''(d\tau).\] Here \(\Phi''\) is the convex function's second-derivative measure. In particular it states \(c_*=c/4\) for \(\Phi(t)=t\log t\). The finding concerns this explicit transfer of the unchanged constant between the two distance quantities; it does not assert a sharp upper bound on all possible stability constants.

Equation (3.24), PDF page 15, asserts a uniform translation estimate: for every radius \(r>0\), every vector \(\tau\in\mathbb R^n\), and every Lebesgue-measurable set \(L\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[\bigl|B_r\cap((L+\tau)\setminus L)\bigr|\le C r^{n-1}|\tau|,\] with a finite constant \(C>0\) independent of \(r\) and \(\tau\). Here \(|\cdot|\) denotes Lebesgue measure for sets and Euclidean length for vectors, and \(B_r\) is the radius-\(r\) ball.

The displayed observation assumes only measurability of \(L\); it does not impose finite classical perimeter, a boundary-regularity condition or minimality. It is used in the last part of the proof of Lemma 3.2 to estimate a translation symmetric difference on the covering balls. The finding addresses this universally stated auxiliary estimate, with its one-sided gain \((L+\tau)\setminus L\).

The inference in Section 2.4.7, PDF page 34, has these premises. Let \(O\) be a real open subset of the admissible weight domain \(\mathcal A_N\), contained in a compact subset \(K\subset\mathcal A_N\). For every fixed \(c\in\mathbb R^2\), assume the subtracted integrand \(\alpha\mapsto E_\alpha(c)\) is holomorphic on a common complex neighborhood \(K'\) of \(K\), and assume continuous dependence on \(c\). For some \(\xi>0\), the real-parameter estimate gives a bound \(|E_\alpha(c)|e^{\xi|c|}\le C\) uniform in \(c\) and in \(\alpha\in O\).

The asserted implication is that there is a complex neighborhood \(O'\subset K'\) of \(O\) on which the same family remains uniformly bounded in \(c\), and hence \(c\mapsto E_\alpha(c)\) is absolutely integrable for complex \(\alpha\in O'\). This supplies the domination used for the subsequent Fubini and Morera argument. The finding addresses the sufficiency of these holomorphy, continuity and real-bound premises, without identifying an arbitrary test family with the actual Toda integrand.

Proposition 3.2 and equations (3.4)–(3.7), PDF pages 35 and 38, assume that every difference between two distinct numbers in \(\{0,B_1,B_2,A_1,A_2,A_3\}\) is real and nonintegral. Put \(\ell(x)=\Gamma(x)/\Gamma(1-x)\), \(H_0(z)={}_3F_2(A_1,A_2,A_3;B_1,B_2;z)\), and, for \(i=1,2\), \[H_i(z)=z^{1-B_i}{}_3F_2(1-B_i+A_1,1-B_i+A_2,1-B_i+A_3;2-B_i,1-B_i+B_{3-i};z).\] Branches are first fixed on the slit plane and then continued.

The paper asserts that the globally single-valued real solution of the third-order hypergeometric equation, with the stated normalization at zero, has diagonal part \(|H_0|^2+D_1|H_1|^2+D_2|H_2|^2\), with \[D_i=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^3\ell(A_j)\ell(B_i-A_j)}{\ell(B_1)\ell(B_2)}\,\frac{\ell(1+B_1+B_2-2B_i)}{\ell(B_i-1)}.\] More explicitly, (3.12) multiplies this expression by \(H(0)\). The finding concerns these printed relative coefficients under the nonresonance hypotheses, as used for the BPZ solution.

The absolute-integrability assertion immediately before (4.12), PDF page 50, is made in the branch \(1<\gamma<\sqrt2\) of Lemma 4.2. Use the \(\mathfrak{sl}_3\) roots \(\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=2\), \(\langle e_1,e_2\rangle=-1\), their dual fundamental weights \(\omega_i\), and \(q=\gamma+2/\gamma\), \(Q=q(\omega_1+\omega_2)\). The insertions are \((\alpha_0,-\gamma\omega_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_\infty)\), with \(\alpha_1=\kappa\omega_2\), \(\kappa<q\). For each insertion \(\eta\), the domain \(\mathcal A_4\) requires \(\langle\eta-Q,e_i\rangle<0\) for both roots and \(\min_i\langle\eta-Q,e_i\rangle<-\gamma\). With \(s=\alpha_0-\gamma\omega_1+\alpha_1+\alpha_\infty-2Q\), it also requires \(\langle s,\omega_i\rangle>-\gamma\), and this lemma further assumes \(\langle s,\omega_2\rangle>0\). Weights are taken away from the exceptional pole set (2.23).

In the step under examination, \(\gamma<\langle\alpha_0,e_1\rangle<2/\gamma\) and \(2/\gamma<\langle\alpha_0,e_2\rangle<q\), with the latter coordinates sufficiently close to \(2/\gamma\) and \(q\) for the expansion. Put \(a=\gamma\langle\alpha_0-\gamma\omega_1,e_1\rangle\), and let \(\mathbb D\) be the unit disk. The displayed bare integral is asserted to be absolutely integrable; in absolute value its kernel is \[\int_{\mathbb D\times\mathbb D}\frac{d^2x\,d^2y}{|x|^{a+1}|y|^{a+1}|x-y|^{2\gamma^2}}<\infty.\] This assertion is used to bound a remainder by \(O(|z|^2)\). The finding concerns this kernel on the interior diagonal \(x=y\), independently of any additional damping in the original random expression.

Equations (2.33)–(2.34), PDF page 18, concern subcritical Gaussian multiplicative-chaos measures \(M^{\gamma e_i}\), \(i=1,2\), with \(0<\gamma<\sqrt2\), \(q=\gamma+2/\gamma\), and \(Q=q(\omega_1+\omega_2)\). The insertion weights satisfy \(\langle\alpha_k-Q,e_i\rangle<0\). For \[I^i(\mathbb C)=\int_{\mathbb C}\prod_{k=1}^N\left(\frac{|x|_+}{|z_k-x|}\right)^{\gamma\langle\alpha_k,e_i\rangle}M^{\gamma e_i}(d^2x),\] (2.33) asserts finiteness of the \(p\)-th moment whenever \(p<\max\{2/\gamma^2,\max_k\langle Q-\alpha_k,e_i\rangle/\gamma\}\). Here \(|x|_+=\max(1,|x|)\).

The local mixed-moment assertion (2.34) states, for a disk \(B_r(z)\) and a weight \(\alpha\) with both root deficits positive, \[\mathbb E\prod_{i=1}^2\left(\int_{B_r(z)}|x-z|^{-\gamma\langle\alpha,e_i\rangle}M^{\gamma e_i}(d^2x)\right)^{p_i}<\infty\quad\text{if}\quad p_i<\max\left\{\frac2{\gamma^2},\frac{\langle Q-\alpha,e_i\rangle}{\gamma}\right\}.\] The finding concerns the use of the maximum as a sufficient threshold, including for nonnegative exponents and first moments.

Lemma 4.3, PDF page 55, takes real \(a<2\) and \(b>-2\) with \(a-b\in(0,\infty)\setminus\{1,2\}\), and defines \[r_{a,b}(x)=|x|^b\left(\mathbf1_{\{a-b<2\}}+\mathbf1_{\{a-b<1\}}\frac b2\left(\frac1x+\frac1{\bar x}\right)\right).\] It asserts the ordinary integral identity \[\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{|x-1|^b-r_{a,b}(x)}{|x|^a}\,d^2x=\pi\,\frac{\ell(-1+(a-b)/2)}{\ell(-b/2)\ell(a/2)},\qquad\ell(t)=\frac{\Gamma(t)}{\Gamma(1-t)}.\]

The finding focuses on the permitted range \(0<a-b<1\), where the first-order subtraction in \(r_{a,b}\) has the printed plus sign. The lemma does not specify a principal-value interpretation or another regularization of the integral in this range.

Remark 6.5, PDF pages 28–29, concerns the particular limiting Hamiltonian \[K_\infty(p_v,p_u,v,u)=\frac{p_v^2}{2}+4v^2+K_2(p_u,u),\qquad K_2(p_u,u)=\frac{p_u^2}{2}-\frac2{\sqrt{1/4+4u^2}}.\] For every energy \(E\in(-4,0)\), let \(I(E)\) be the area enclosed by the periodic \(K_2\)-orbit in the \((u,p_u)\)-plane, and let \(h_u\) be its inverse, with action-angle coordinate \(\varphi\) of period one.

The specified canonical substitution is \((x,y)=\sqrt{I/\pi}(\cos(2\pi\varphi),\sin(2\pi\varphi))\). The assertion is that it makes the zero-energy hypersurface of \[\widetilde K_\infty(p_v,x,v,y)=\frac{p_v^2}{2}+4v^2+h_u\bigl(\pi(x^2+y^2)\bigr)\] strictly convex. The supporting calculation claims \(h_u''(I)>0\) and positivity of the Hessian in (6.13) throughout \(-4<h_u(I)<0\). The finding concerns this exact area-action transformation in the \(c=4\) limiting system.

The normalization after (3.9), PDF page 12, starts with positive masses, \(\alpha>0\), and the reduced Hamiltonian \[H_{\rm old}=\frac{p_r^2+p_z^2}{2}+\frac{\varpi_{\rm old}^2}{2r^2}-c\left(\frac1r+\frac{4\alpha^{-1}}{\sqrt{r^2+(1+2\alpha)z^2}}\right),\qquad c=\frac{m^{5/2}}{\sqrt2}>0,\quad r>0.\] The potential is then normalized so that the coefficient \(c\) becomes one.

The printed transformation divides the angular-momentum parameter by \(c\), namely \(\varpi_{\rm new}^2=\varpi_{\rm old}^2/c\), but states that the corresponding energy value is replaced by \(h_{\rm new}=c\,h_{\rm old}\). The finding concerns this energy transformation at the same normalization step, including its use on regular negative-energy surfaces.

The terminal application of Fact 6.3, PDF pages 21–23 (printed pages 3495–3497), is conditional on the array already constructed in the NSOP\(_2\)/SOP\(_1\) contradiction argument. Let \(r(x;y)=\operatorname{tp}(a,b/M)\) contain a formula \(\rho(x;y)\) whose instances on the selected coheir Morley sequence are two-inconsistent. The constructed pairs \((b_i^1,b_i^2)_{i<\omega}\) satisfy \(b_i^1b_j^2\equiv_M b_0b_1\) whenever \(i\le j\). For each \(n\), the switching sequence \(J_n\) uses \(b_i^2\) for \(i<n\) and \(b_i^1\) for \(i\ge n\); the instances of \(r\) along this strong canonical Morley sequence are consistent.

Choose \(a_n\) realizing those instances along \(J_n\), put \(d_j=(b_j^1,b_j^2)\), and define \(\varphi(x;(y^1,y^2))=\rho(x;y^1)\), \(\psi(x;(y^1,y^2))=\rho(x;y^2)\). The assertion used to invoke Fact 6.3 is \[\varphi(a_i;d_j)\text{ for all }i<j,\qquad\psi(a_i;d_j)\text{ for all }i\ge j,\] together with the inconsistent-pair condition for \(i<j\). In particular the second quantifier includes \(\psi(a_i;d_i)\). The finding concerns this claimed index pattern for the witnesses chosen from the printed \(J_n\).

In the proof of Theorem 9.1, PDF pages 68–70 (printed pages 5090–5092), let \(\mu=\mu_{(\mathrm{ver},0)}\) be the constructed periodic Gibbs measure for packings of \(2\times2\) squares, at sufficiently large finite fugacity \(\lambda\). The event \(J\) fixes an occupied offset tile at a specified position with even horizontal coordinate, together with prescribed nearest vacant-face positions along the two horizontal rows immediately above and below it, on both sides. It satisfies \(\mu(J)\le\lambda^{-1}\). Fix \(0<\varepsilon_1<\varepsilon_0\), choose an arbitrary event \(\widetilde\Omega\supset J\) with \(\mu(\widetilde\Omega)=\lambda^{-1}\varepsilon_1^{-4}\), and set \(\widetilde\mu=\mu(\cdot\mid\widetilde\Omega)\).

Take positive integers \(k\mid K\), \(l\mid L\), let \(R=[0,K]\times[0,L]\), and let \(E\) be \(R\)-local and invariant under reflection in each central axis of \(R\), as in Lemma 6.7(4). For each block translation \(\eta\) from \((k\mathbb Z\times l\mathbb Z)\cap([0,K)\times[0,L))\), the argument following (9.3) claims that the block set \(B=X_{K\times L}\overline{E^c}\) is \(\varepsilon\)-rare under \(\eta\widetilde\mu\), with \(\varepsilon=\max\{\lambda^{-1/4},\|E^c\|_R\}\). Explicitly, it claims \((\eta\widetilde\mu)(A\subset B)\le\varepsilon^{|A|}\) for every nonempty finite \(A\subset\mathbb Z^2\). The claimed event in this conclusion is not intersected with \(J\), although the preceding chessboard estimate contains that intersection.

Remark 4.7, PDF page 33 (printed page 5055), considers an even rectangle \(\Lambda=R_{K\times L;(0,0)}\), an integer \(M\ge1\) dividing \(L\), and the range \(M\le\max(K,L)\), \(M<\sqrt\lambda/C\). It defines the global configuration event \[\widetilde E_M=\{\sigma:\sigma(x,y)=0\text{ whenever }2\mid x\text{ or }M\mid y,\ (x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2\}.\] No evenness condition on \(M\) is imposed in the remark.

Writing \(Z^1_\Lambda\) and \(Z^0_\Lambda\) for the partition functions with fully packed and free boundary conditions, respectively, the asserted matching lower-bound construction is \[Z^1_\Lambda(\widetilde E_M)=Z^0_\Lambda(\widetilde E_M)=(Z^0_{M,\mathrm{1D}})^{KL/(2M)}\ge\left(1+\frac{cM^2}{\lambda}\right)^{\operatorname{Area}(\Lambda)/M}.\] The finding concerns this equality and lower bound for the stated integer range, including \(M=1\), while retaining the global definition of \(\widetilde E_M\) and the specified exterior boundary conditions.

Lemma 3.5(e), PDF pages 23–24, considers the signed equation \(\partial_t\rho-\mathcal L\rho-\operatorname{div}(V_1\rho)-\operatorname{div}V_2=0\) on \((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d\), with \(\rho(0)=\rho_0\in L^1\), bounded continuous vector field \(V_1\), and \(V_2\in L^\infty([0,T];L^1(\mathbb R^d))^d\). The operator is a Lévy generator with the heat-kernel assumption (K). Let \(\psi\ge0\) be a subadditive \(C^2\) function tending to infinity at infinity, with bounded first and second derivatives, and finite integrals against \(|\rho_0|\) and the large-jump part of its Lévy measure \(\nu\).

The asserted estimate bounds \(\int\psi(x)|\rho(t,x)|\,dx\), uniformly for \(0\le t\le T\), using only the initial weighted integral, \(\sup_t\|\rho(t)\|_1\), \(\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_t\|V_2(t)\|_1\), the drift bound, \(T\), and the fixed operator and weight quantities appearing in the display. It includes no weighted spatial norm or tail control of \(V_2\). The report examines this estimate in the intended, derivative-order-dependent heat-kernel class; the separate literal all-orders quantifier defect in (K) is stated in Problem 3, and the Gaussian example is not claimed to satisfy that literal defective condition.

The last step of Lemma 4.2, PDF pages 31–32, uses the following scalar implication. On \([t_0,T]\), let \(A\ge0\) be integrable, let \(c_2\ge0\), and let \(J\ge0\) be decreasing and absolutely continuous with \(J(T)=0\). Suppose that \[A(s)+c_2\int_s^T A(t)\,dt\ge J(s)\qquad\text{for every }s\in[t_0,T].\] The proof asserts that Grönwall's inequality gives \(J(t_0)\le C A(t_0)\) for a finite constant \(C\).

In the application, \(A(s)=\int u(s)^+\,dm(s)^++\int u(s)^-\,dm(s)^-\), for the differences of two solutions, and \(J\) is the integrated nonnegative convexity remainder. The decomposition assumption is \(H(x,u,p)=H_1(x,p)+H_2(x,u)\), with the stated monotonicity and upper derivative bound \(0\le\partial_uH_2\le c_2\). The finding concerns the scalar inference from the displayed inequality, rather than asserting the existence of two distinct solutions of the mean-field-game system.

Assumption (K), PDF page 14, requires the heat kernels \(K\) and \(K^*\) of a Lévy generator \(\mathcal L\) and its adjoint to be smooth probability densities. Its stated quantifiers are: there exist one finite constant \(\mathcal K>0\) and an exponent \(\alpha\in(1,2]\) such that, for both \(\widetilde K=K,K^*\), every multi-index \(\beta\in\mathbb N^d\), and every \(t>0\), \[\|D^\beta\widetilde K(t,\cdot)\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d)}\le\mathcal K t^{-|\beta|/\alpha}.\]

The same constant is placed before the quantifier over all derivative orders; it is not indexed by \(\beta\), and no finite upper order is specified. The paper includes Gaussian and other Lévy kernels as examples of its operator class. The finding addresses this literal uniform-in-order requirement and consequently the scope of results that invoke (K).

Lemma 2.6, PDF page 8, uses \(C_b^{-n}=(C_b^n)^*\), with the sum norm on derivatives in \(C_b^n\), and its subspace of measure-representable functionals. For \(n\ge0\), such a functional has \[\langle\rho,\phi\rangle=\sum_{|\alpha|\le n}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\partial^\alpha\phi\,d\mu_\alpha,\] where the \(\mu_\alpha\) are finite signed measures. The asserted exact representation property is that one can choose them so that \(\|\rho\|_{C_b^{-n}}=\sum_{|\alpha|\le n}\|\mu_\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\). Already at \(d=n=1\), the underlying test norm is \(\|\phi\|_\infty+\|\phi'\|_\infty\).

Appendix A also uses chosen norm-preserving measure representations of a Cauchy sequence of functionals to infer that those representatives are themselves Cauchy. The finding distinguishes this lift inference and the displayed exact norm formula from the separate conclusion that the measure-representable subspace is closed.

Lemma 5.9, PDF page 42, takes \(0<\sigma<1\), \(0<\varepsilon<1-\sigma\), a function \(f:\mathbb R^{m+n}\to\mathbb R\), and maps \(y_1,y_2:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\). With the displayed norms finite, it asserts \[\|f(\cdot,y_1(\cdot))-f(\cdot,y_2(\cdot))\|_{C_b^\sigma}\le2\|f\|_{C_b^{\sigma+\varepsilon}}\bigl(2+\|y_1-y_2\|_{C_b^1}^{\sigma}\bigr)\|y_1-y_2\|_\infty^{\varepsilon}.\]

The proposed bound depends on the difference of the maps, but places no separate bound on the Lipschitz norm of either \(y_1\) or \(y_2\). The finding concerns this standalone composition inequality, including bounded smooth maps satisfying every regularity requirement implicit in its norms.

Lemma 3.3(b), PDF page 21, assumes (K), \(k\ge2\), \(0<\sigma<\alpha-1\), \(z_0\in C_b^{k+\sigma}\), and \(b,f\in C([0,T];C_b^{k-1})\), with \(b\) vector-valued. For the classical solution of \(\partial_tz-\mathcal Lz-b\cdot Dz=f\), it asserts the existence of a modulus \(\omega\), independent of \(f\) and \(z_0\), such that \[\|\partial_tz(t)-\partial_tz(s)\|_\infty\le\left(\|z_0\|_{C_b^{k+\sigma}}+\sup_r\|f(r)\|_{C_b^{k-1}}\right)\omega(|t-s|).\] Equation (3.27), PDF page 29, similarly asserts a forcing-independent time modulus for the nonlinear solution. No common time modulus of the forcing is included among the controlling data.

A separate endpoint step in Lemma 3.5(c), PDF page 25, estimates \(\int_0^{t-\epsilon}(t-s)^{-2/\alpha}\,ds\) by a fixed multiple of \(\epsilon^{1-2/\alpha}\), uniformly for \(0<\epsilon<t\le T\), while allowing \(\alpha=2\). This is used for the translation bound (3.12). As with Problem 1, the report's Gaussian tests of the intended estimates use the per-order reading of (K), rather than the impossible literal quantifier described in Problem 3.

Corollary 5.8, PDF page 42, considers the solution \((z,\rho)\) of the auxiliary linear forward–backward system (5.7), with its stipulated regularity and monotonicity hypotheses, zero inhomogeneous terms \(b=c=z_T=0\), and a measure-representable initial functional \(\rho_0\in C_b^{-k-1}\), \(k\ge1\), at any \(t_0\in[0,T)\). For every \(0<\gamma<\alpha\) it asserts an extension \(\widetilde\rho(t)\in C_b^{\gamma-k-1}\) satisfying \[t^{\gamma/\alpha}\|\widetilde\rho(t)\|_{C_b^{\gamma-k-1}}\le C(V)\|\rho_0\|_{C_b^{-k-1}},\qquad t_0<t<T.\] The written weight is the absolute time \(t\), including when \(t_0>0\).

The mild formulas on PDF pages 20 and 29 represent the forward equation \(\partial_tu-\mathcal Lu+H(x,u,Du)=f\), \(u(0)=u_0\), by \[u(t)=K_t*u_0+\int_0^tK_{t-s}*\bigl(H(\cdot,u(s),Du(s))-f(s)\bigr)\,ds.\] The finding concerns the sign of the integrand for this stated forward-time equation.

Finally, the proof of Lemma 2.3 on PDF page 7 takes \(\rho\in(C_b^\gamma)^*\), \(\gamma\ge0\), and a standard smooth mollifier \(\eta_\epsilon\), and asserts \(\|\phi*\eta_\epsilon-\phi\|_{C_b^\gamma}\le C\epsilon^\delta\|\phi\|_{C_b^{\gamma+\delta}}\) for every \(\delta>0\), with \(C\) independent of \(\epsilon\) and \(\phi\). No vanishing higher-moment conditions on the mollifier accompany this arbitrary exponent. This last issue concerns the stated rate, separately from convergence in the weaker dual norm.

Equations (2.4)–(2.5), PDF pages 8–9, and the compactness setup on PDF page 17 assert the following geometric implication. If \(M\subset\mathbb R^m\) is a \(C^2\) domain whose principal curvatures are bounded by a fixed \(\kappa\), then there is a two-sided tubular neighborhood of \(\partial M\), with width bounded below by \(1/(c\kappa)\), on which the signed distance \(\rho\) is \(C^2\), the nearest-point projection \(\Pi\) is single-valued and \(C^1\), and their stated derivative bounds hold.

In Proposition 4.1 the same lower width is claimed uniformly for a varying sequence \(M_k\) with the common curvature bound. The associated maps minimize \(E_{q_k}(u)=\int(|Du|^2+q_k^2\mathbf1_{\{u\in M_k\}})\), have \(\int_{B_4}|Du_k|^2\le\epsilon_k^2\), \(q_k\le\Lambda\epsilon_k\), and mean zero, with \(\epsilon_k\downarrow0\). No separate lower bound on the reach, or on the separation of distinct boundary components, is imposed. The finding concerns the uniform tubular conclusion used to restrict the rescaled target limit to a half-space.

Lemma 3.9, PDF pages 15–16, assumes that \(u\in W^{1,2}(B;\overline M)\) minimizes \(E_q(u)=\int_B(|Du|^2+q^2\mathbf1_{\{u\in M\}})\), \(q\ge0\), with its boundary trace. The target has the paper's smooth boundary, the image lies in a tubular neighborhood of \(\partial M\), and \(\Pi\circ u\) is Lipschitz. Here \(\rho\) is positive inside \(M\), \(\nu=\nabla\rho\) points into \(M\), and \(\Pi\) is nearest-point projection.

The proof claims that every scalar competitor \(w\ge0\) with \(w-\rho\circ u\in W^{1,2}_0(B)\) yields the admissible target-valued competitor \[v=\Pi\circ u+w\,\nu\circ u\in W^{1,2}(B;\overline M),\qquad v-u\in W^{1,2}_0(B;\mathbb R^m).\] There is no upper bound on \(w\) limiting it to the tubular radius or to an inward normal segment remaining in \(\overline M\). This is the admissibility step used to infer unrestricted scalar minimality of \(\rho\circ u\).

Corollary 1.10, PDF page 5, concerns minimizing constraint maps for \(E_q(u)=\int_\Omega(|Du|^2+q^2\mathbf1_{\{u\in M\}})\) on \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\). The hypotheses inherited from Theorems 1.5 and 1.9 require \(q>0\), \(\int_\Omega|Du|^2\le\Lambda\), a \(C^3\) target domain \(M\subset\mathbb R^m\) with uniformly convex complement, and \(\partial M\) of class \(C^{k+1}\), \(k\ge2\).

The asserted dimension conclusion is that there is \(n_*\in\{5,6,7\}\) such that, whenever \(n\le n_*\), the whole interior free boundary \(\Omega\cap\partial u^{-1}(M)\) is a \(C^{k,\gamma}\) hypersurface for every \(0<\gamma<1\). The proof invokes classification of one-homogeneous scalar minimizers to supply the local flatness condition at every free-boundary point. The finding concerns the non-strict dimension cutoff \(n\le n_*\) in that deduction.

Lemma 2.3, PDF page 10, fixes the target \(M\) and considers a sequence \(u_k\in W^{1,2}(\Omega;\overline M)\), bounded in the full \(W^{1,2}(\Omega)\) norm, with each \(u_k\) minimizing \(E_{q_k}(u)=\int_\Omega(|Du|^2+q_k^2\mathbf1_{\{u\in M\}})\) against admissible maps with its own trace. Assume \(q_k\ge0\) and \(q_k\to q\ge0\).

The conclusion stated is existence of an \(E_q\)-minimizer \(u\) and a subsequence such that \(u_k\to u\) strongly in \(W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\). The lemma does not require common boundary values or strong convergence of traces. The finding concerns convergence on all of \(\Omega\), including boundary layers, rather than only on compactly contained subdomains.

Corollary 5.7, PDF page 29, takes any minimizing constraint map \(u\in W^{1,2}(\Omega;\overline M)\) for \(E_q\), with \(q\ge0\), under the paper's smooth-target setting. With positive phase \(E=u^{-1}(M)\), it asserts local finiteness of the free-boundary perimeter and, in particular, \[\mathcal H^{n-1}\bigl(\Omega\cap(\partial E\setminus\partial_{\mathrm{red}}E)\bigr)=0.\]

Here \(\partial E\) is the topological free boundary and \(\partial_{\mathrm{red}}E\) is the reduced boundary of the measurable phase. The displayed range includes the zero-weight case \(q=0\). The finding concerns the measure-zero conclusion in that case, separately from the distributional identity multiplied by \(q\).

Theorem 2.9(i), PDF page 12, takes a nonnegative \(f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)\), \(1<p\le\infty\), and asserts for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator \(M\) that \(\|Mf\|_{L^\infty}\le c(n,p)\|f\|_{L^p}\). The finding concerns the printed \(L^\infty\) norm in a statement labeled the strong \((p,p)\) inequality.

A second formula occurs in footnote 5 on PDF page 16. Under Lemma 3.9's assumptions—\(u\) minimizes \(E_q\), its image lies in the target tube, and \(\Pi\circ u\) is Lipschitz—put \(H=\operatorname{Hess}\rho_u(Du,Du)\mathbf1_{u^{-1}(M)}\). The stated strong equation is \(\Delta(\rho\circ u)-H=q\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\partial_{\mathrm{red}}u^{-1}(M)}\). The footnote identifies its weak form as \[-\int_BD(\rho\circ u)\cdot D\phi+\int_BH\phi=q\int_{B\cap\partial_{\mathrm{red}}u^{-1}(M)}\phi\,d\mathcal H^{n-1},\qquad\phi\in C_c^\infty(B).\] The second issue is the Hessian-term sign in this claimed equivalence.

The local limit arguments contain several distinct assertions. In Lemma 4.3, PDF pages 18–19, \(\epsilon_k\downarrow0\), \(|a_k|=|\rho_k(0)|\), and \(\rho_k(0)/\epsilon_k\to\gamma\in\mathbb R\) are used to claim \(|a_k|\le2|\gamma|\epsilon_k\) for all large \(k\), including \(\gamma=0\). The same proof chooses \(\widetilde R_k\to\infty\) satisfying the image inclusion (4.16), and uses \(\widetilde\epsilon_k\to0\) to conclude \(\epsilon_k\widetilde\epsilon_k\widetilde R_k=o(\epsilon_k)\), without a stated product restriction on those sequences. In (5.5), PDF page 25, the maximal-function threshold is printed as \(N_0^2\) when applying the estimate to a bound at scale \(N_0^2\epsilon^2\).

In Proposition 7.1, PDF page 31, let \(u_k\to u\) strongly in \(W^{1,2}\), \(H_k=\operatorname{Hess}\rho_{u_k}(Du_k,Du_k)\to H\) strongly in \(L^1\), and let the phase indicators \(\bar\chi_k\) converge weak-star in \(L^\infty\). The written (7.3) has \(\int H_k\phi\) on the right, omitting the phase factor, and the following passage asserts \(H_k\bar\chi_k\rightharpoonup^*H\bar\chi\) in \(L^\infty\). No uniform \(L^\infty\) bound for \(H_k\) is supplied by these premises.

Corollary 7.3, PDF page 32, assumes the uniformly convex target condition (2.13), an \(E_q\)-minimizer on \(B_2\), \(q\in[0,q_0]\), energy at most \(\Lambda\), and a singular point at zero. It claims constants \(\eta_k,C_k\) depending only on \(n,m,\Lambda,q_0,\kappa,k\), so that \(\rho\circ u\le\eta_k\) implies \(\|\rho\circ u\|_{L^\infty(B_r)}\le C_kr^k\). The written derivation selects an iteration radius using an individual continuity modulus. Finally, PDF page 35 uses almost-everywhere convergence \(u_j\to u\) to pass a lower bound on \(\sup_{B_{2r}(x_j)}\rho\circ u_j\) to the limit; its compactness setup supplies a derivative-energy bound without separately controlling target translations. The finding records these local inference and constant-dependence issues.

The Gaussian specialization following (1.24), PDF page 7, uses quadratic transport cost \(c(x,y)=|x-y|^2/2\), positive regularization \(\varepsilon\), and Hessian bounds \(\alpha_U=\beta_U=a>0\), \(\alpha_V=\beta_V=b>0\). This includes normalized marginals \(N(0,a^{-1}I_d)\) and \(N(0,b^{-1}I_d)\) in every dimension \(d\ge1\). Equations (1.19) and (1.23) define \[A=\sqrt{a^2+4a/(\varepsilon^2b)}+a,\quad B=\sqrt{b^2+4b/(\varepsilon^2a)}+b,\quad r=\varepsilon(A+B)\left(1-\frac4{\varepsilon^2AB}\right),\] under \(\varepsilon\sqrt{AB}>2\).

The prose assertion is that, as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), this rate has first-order behavior \(r\sim\varepsilon(a+b)/2\). The finding concerns the coefficient in that asymptotic description of the explicitly defined rate, rather than the general existence of exponential convergence.

Theorem A.3, PDF page 33, lets \(A\) be a bounded semi-infinite Toeplitz operator on \(\ell^2(\mathbb N)\), with coefficients \(a_k=0\) for \(|k|>l\), symbol \(f(z)=\sum_{k=-l}^l a_kz^k\), and \(N\times N\) finite section \(A_{N,l}\). Write \(\Lambda(A)\) for its operator spectrum, \(\Delta_\varepsilon=\{z:|z|<\varepsilon\}\), and \(\Lambda_\varepsilon(A_{N,l})\) for the matrix \(\varepsilon\)-pseudospectrum in the Euclidean operator norm.

For every \(0<r<1\) and every \(\rho>r\), the theorem asserts existence of a constant \(C\) independent of \(N\) such that, with \(\varepsilon=C\rho^N\), \[\Omega_r\cup\Omega_{1/r}\cup\bigl(\Lambda(A)+\Delta_\varepsilon\bigr)\subset\Lambda_\varepsilon(A_{N,l}).\] The \(\Omega\)-sets are defined by the winding numbers in (A.2). The finding concerns the separate inclusion of the entire semi-infinite spectrum plus the disk at this prescribed exponential scale; it does not require a failure of the winding-number terms.

Section 2.1, PDF pages 5–6, uses an untwisted affine root system associated with a finite root system \(\Delta\). Let \(\Delta_+\) be the finite positive roots, \(Q_+\) the cone generated by the finite simple roots, \(\vartheta\) the highest root, and \(\delta\) the null root. With affine simple root \(\alpha_0=\delta-\vartheta\), the text asserts \[\widehat\Delta^{\mathrm{re}}_+=\Delta_++\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\delta.\]

Remark 3.2.1(c), PDF page 12, also asserts \(\widehat Q_+=Q_+\oplus\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\delta\), where \(\widehat Q_+\) is the nonnegative cone generated by all affine simple roots. These are statements about the positive subsets, in addition to the group decomposition \(\widehat Q=Q\oplus\mathbb Z\delta\). The finding concerns whether the two displayed descriptions contain every positive affine root and every element of the affine positive cone.

Section 4.1, PDF page 16, allows an arbitrary integer-valued group homomorphism \(s:\widehat Q\to\mathbb Z\), with \(\widehat Q\) freely generated by the affine simple roots \(\alpha_i\), and a diagram automorphism \(\tau\) permuting those roots. The asserted equivalence is \[s\circ\tau=s\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s(\alpha_i)=\mathbf1_U(i)\text{ for a union }U\text{ of }\tau\text{-orbits}.\]

No \(\{0,1\}\)-valued restriction accompanies the original choice of \(s\). The finding concerns this characterization of all invariant integer gradings, separately from the particular \(\tau\)-minimal and principal gradings subsequently selected in the paper.

Section 4.1, PDF page 18, uses an irreducible interval-exchange permutation \(\pi=(\pi_t,\pi_b)\) on \(d\) letters with \(\pi_b\pi_t^{-1}(d)=1\). Let \(\alpha_t\) be the last top letter, \(p\) a prime, \(\vec n\in\mathbb Z^d\) with \(p\nmid n_{\alpha_t}\), and \(\widehat\lambda\) a positive length vector on the other letters with sum one. For \(F_p(\widehat\lambda,s)=((s/p)\widehat\lambda,1-s/p)\), set \(s_*=(p+1)/(2p)\) and \(\lambda^*=F_p(\widehat\lambda,s_*)\). The return map \(S_{\vec n,p}\) sends \(x\) to the first positive iterate of the interval exchange for which the accumulated \(\vec n\)-observable is zero modulo \(p\).

The construction asserts that the last interval of \(S_{\vec n,p}(\lambda^*,\pi)\) has length \(1/2\), and obtains a translation surface from \(P=[0,\sqrt2/2]^2\) by the side identifications \[(x,\sqrt2/2)\sim\bigl(\sqrt2S_{\vec n,p}(x/\sqrt2)-\sqrt2,0\bigr),\qquad(0,y)\sim(\sqrt2/2,y).\] The finding concerns whether this exact parameter choice and printed map define the claimed top-to-bottom pairing, including the intended genus-at-least-two applications.

Equation (5.5), PDF page 21, uses a fixed positive exponent threshold \(c\), genus \(g\ge2\), and prime \(p\). Let \(V_c\subset\mathbb C^{p(d-1)+1}\) be the subspace corresponding to exponents less than \(c\), set \(D=\dim V_c\), and let the \(p-1\) ranges \(O_k(\mathbb C^d)\), each of dimension \(d-1\), form a direct sum. The preceding inputs give \(D\le pd-cg^*\) and \(g^*\ge p(g-1)+1\).

With \(m=\#\{1\le k\le p-1:O_k(\mathbb C^d)\not\subset V_c\}\), the printed chain is \[\frac m{p-1}\ge\frac1{p-1}\left(1-\frac D{d-1}\right)\ge\frac{c(g-1)}d>0\] for all sufficiently large \(p\). The finding concerns this numerical dimension-counting step used to obtain a positive proportion, conditional on the geometric and exponent inputs preceding it.

Section 5.3, PDF page 42 (printed page 5154), assigns to every cusp \(b\in\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Q)\), scaling matrix \(\sigma_b\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) with \(\sigma_b\infty=b\), and \(Y>0\), the subset \[\mathfrak F_b(Y)=\{z\in\mathbb H:0<\operatorname{Re}(\sigma_b^{-1}z)<1,\ \operatorname{Im}(\sigma_b^{-1}z)\ge Y\}.\] It asserts independence of the choice of scaling matrix and equivariance \(\gamma\mathfrak F_b(Y)=\mathfrak F_{\gamma b}(Y)\) for \(\gamma\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\). These are subsets of \(\mathbb H\), with the strict horizontal inequalities as printed.

Lemma 5.4 then takes any geodesic \(\mathcal C\) with distinct rational-cusp endpoints \(b_1,b_2\), and claims existence of \[\lim_{Y\to\infty}\int_{\mathcal C\setminus(\mathfrak F_{b_1}(Y)\cup\mathfrak F_{b_2}(Y))}(R_0E)(z,\tfrac12+it)\,\frac{dz}{\operatorname{Im}z},\] as the regularised integral of the raised Eisenstein series. The permitted choices include the imaginary-axis geodesic, scalings \(I\) and \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) at its two endpoints, and \(t=1\). The finding concerns whether these cutoff sets actually implement the asserted truncation and limit for every allowed choice.

Theorem 7.2, PDF pages 21–22, fixes \(C,\delta,\varepsilon>0\) with \(C/\delta\ge1\), a reverse-indexed real process \(X_N,\ldots,X_0\), and a random set \(R\subset\{0,\ldots,N\}\), for some \(0<p<1\). Each \(X_t\) and membership \(t\in R\) is determined by an underlying random element \(G_t\). Almost surely \(X_N\le(1-\varepsilon)\delta N\) and \(X_t\le X_{t+1}+C\) for every applicable step.

Conditioned on every allowed future history \(G_N,\ldots,G_{t+1}\), the theorem assumes probability at least \(1-p\) of \(X_t\le X_{t+1}-\delta\) or \(t\in R\) when \(X_{t+1}>0\); when \(X_{t+1}\le0\), it instead assumes probability at least \(1-p\) of \(X_t\le0\) or \(t\in R\). Finally, with probability at least \(1-p\), every prefix satisfies \(|R\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}|\le\delta t/(32C)\). The claimed conclusion is \(\Pr(X_0>0)\le O_{C,\delta,\varepsilon}(p)\), with the implicit constant independent of \(N\) and \(p\). The finding concerns whether the stated initial margin suffices for this conclusion.

Lemma 3.3, PDF page 12, lets \(Z=f(X_0,\ldots,X_n)\), and assumes that changing only the \(k\)-th coordinate changes \(f\) by at most \(c_k\). It asserts the concentration estimate \[\Pr(|Z-\mathbb EZ|\ge t)\le2\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sum_{k=0}^n c_k^2}\right).\]

The variables \(X_0,\ldots,X_n\) are described only as a sequence of random variables. Independence is not stated, and neither is a conditional bounded-increment hypothesis for a corresponding martingale. The finding concerns the asserted bound under this written coordinatewise condition alone.

Lemma 6.5(A2), PDF page 20, fixes \(C>0\) and a degree sequence \(d=(d_v)_{v\in V}\) on \(n=|V|\) vertices, with nonnegative integer degrees and an even total degree so that the configuration model is defined. For the random multigraph \(G^*\) obtained by uniformly pairing all half-edges, it asserts \[\sum_{v\in V}d_v^2\le Cn\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Pr(G^*\text{ is simple})\ge c(C)>0.\]

The lower bound is claimed uniformly in the number of vertices and the degree sequence. Zero degrees are allowed by the paper's convention, and the lemma does not assume a positive lower bound proportional to \(n\) on \(\sum_vd_v\). The finding concerns part (A2) with precisely this control of the second moment.

Lemma 8.2, PDF page 22, fixes \(0<\eta<1/2\), an integer \(d\ge1\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_2}\), and \(E\subset\{1,\ldots,n_1\}\) with \(|E|\ge n_1(1-\eta/3)\). The random zero-one column \(x\) has exactly \(d\) ones, uniformly distributed on \(E\), while its coordinates off \(E\) are deterministic. If \(\ker B^{\mathsf T}\) contains an \(\eta\)-balanced vector—every level set has at most \((1-\eta)n_1\) coordinates—the claim is \(\operatorname{rank}[B\mid x]\ge\operatorname{rank}B+1\) with probability \(1-O_\eta(d^{-1/2})\).

Lemma 8.4(a), PDF page 23, makes the symmetric version for \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), the same slice assumptions with \(|E|\ge n(1-\eta/3)\), and an \(\eta\)-balanced vector in \(\ker A\): appending \(x\) as both a row and a column, with new diagonal entry zero, is claimed to increase the rank by two with probability \(1-O_\eta(d^{-1/2})\). The printed ranges include \(d=|E|\); neither lemma imposes the \(d\le |E|/2\) restriction present in the anti-concentration lemma used by the proofs.

Property P6, PDF pages 6–7, concerns Kato homology \(KH_a(X,A)\), defined from the bottom row of the niveau spectral sequence for the chosen homology theory. The paper uses Borel–Moore homology with \(A=\mathbb Z\) for complex varieties, and étale Borel–Moore homology with torsion coefficients of order prime to the characteristic. Its first assertion assumes that \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth projective varieties and stably birational, and concludes \(KH_a(X,A)\cong KH_a(Y,A)\).

The subsequent, broader assertion is that every projective birational morphism \(f:Y\to X\) between quasi-projective varieties induces \[f_*:KH_a(Y,A)\xrightarrow{\sim}KH_a(X,A)\qquad\text{for every }a.\] This second assertion does not impose smoothness on either variety. The finding concerns this extension and its proof, already over \(\mathbb C\) with integral coefficients; smoothness from the first assertion is not a hypothesis of the second as written.

Proposition 4.4, PDF page 9, lets \((X,\Delta)\) be a quasi-projective divisorial log terminal pair over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero: \(X\) is normal, \(\Delta\) is an effective \(\mathbb Q\)-Weil divisor, and \(K_X+\Delta\) is \(\mathbb Q\)-Cartier. Let \(H\) be ample and let \(\Delta_1\) be any effective \(\mathbb Q\)-Weil divisor with \(\Delta_1\le\Delta\).

The claimed conclusion is the existence of a rational \(c>0\) and an effective \(\mathbb Q\)-divisor \(D\equiv_{\rm num}\Delta_1+cH\) for which \((X,\Delta-\varepsilon\Delta_1+\varepsilon D)\) is Kawamata log terminal for all sufficiently small positive rational \(\varepsilon\). There is no requirement that \(\Delta_1\) contain every coefficient-one component of \(\Delta\). The finding concerns the universal choice of \(\Delta_1\) under precisely the printed effectivity condition.

The paragraph preceding Corollary 1.7, PDF page 4, attributes to Voisin a vanishing assertion for uniruled threefolds: \[KH_2(X,A)=0.\] In the smooth projective complex setting used to connect this statement to integral Hodge theory, the coefficients include \(A=\mathbb Z\), with \(KH_2\) formed from Borel–Moore homology. Thus the assertion includes every smooth projective uniruled complex threefold with integral coefficients.

Here uniruledness is the stated geometric condition; rational connectedness is not imposed in this paragraph. Theorem 3.3, cited as supporting this step, states the result for rationally connected smooth projective varieties in dimension three. The finding concerns the broader vanishing as written, before it is used with Theorem 6.1 to obtain Corollary 1.7.

Immediately after Theorem 3.6, PDF page 8, let \(X\) be a smooth variety of dimension \(d\) over an algebraically closed field, and let \(\mathcal H_j\) denote the Zariski sheaf associated with \(U\mapsto H_j(U)\). With étale Borel–Moore homology and \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\)-coefficients, where \(n\) is invertible in the field, the displayed formula is \[CH_i(X)/n\cong H_0(X,\mathcal H_{d-i}).\]

For a smooth complex variety and integral Borel–Moore homology, the next display is \[CH_i(X)/{\rm alg}\cong H_0(X,\mathcal H_{d-i}),\] where the left side is the group of dimension-\(i\) cycles modulo algebraic equivalence. The finding concerns the literal sheaf and degree indices in these two displayed identifications, using the homological convention fixed in Section 2; it does not replace them silently with the usual cohomological Bloch formula.

Theorems 1.6 and 6.2, PDF pages 7 and 32–33, take a convex lattice polygon \(\Delta\subset\mathbb R^2\), a field \(k\) with \({\rm char}\,k=0\) or \({\rm char}\,k>{\rm diam}(\Delta)\), and the Puiseux field \(K=k\{\{t\}\}\). For a generic configuration of \(n=|\partial\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2|-1+g\) points in \({\rm Tor}_K(\Delta)\) whose valuations are \(\Delta\)-generic, the claimed correspondence expresses the enriched multiplicity of a genus-\(g\) tropical curve as a sum of transfers of quadratic weights of algebraic curves tropicalizing to it. The diameter bound is also asserted to ensure separability of all field extensions used in this construction.

The local assertion tested is Lemmas 5.5–5.6, PDF pages 24–26. After an integral affine change of lattice coordinates, write a triangle as \(\Delta'=\operatorname{Conv}\{(0,m),(p,0),(q,0)\}\), with \(m>0\), \(0\le p<q\), and \(d_p=\gcd(p,m)\). For fixed nonzero boundary coefficients \(a,b,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\) satisfying \(\varepsilon_1^{q-p}=\varepsilon_2^{d_p}=1\), choose nonzero \(\alpha,\beta\) solving \[a\alpha+\varepsilon_1=0,\qquad b\beta^{m/d_p}(-1)^{m(q-p)/d_p}+\varepsilon_2\alpha^{p/d_p}=0.\] The text claims that every curve parametrized by \(x(t)=\alpha t^m\), \(y(t)=\beta t^p(t-1)^{q-p}\) is nodal, smooth and unibranch at the toric boundary, and that the algebra of choices is finite étale. The finding concerns whether the stated diameter bound suffices for these conclusions after the allowed lattice transformation.

Definition 3.21 and Proposition 5.10, PDF pages 20 and 29–30, concern compatible deformation patterns with fixed boundary coefficients. Let \(F/k\) be the finite field extension containing those coefficients, let \(a,b,c\in F^\times\), let \(m\ge2\), and write \[G(x,y)=ay^2+by\,g(x)+c,\qquad g(x)=a_mx^m+a_{m-2}x^{m-2}+\cdots+a_0.\] The leading coefficient \(a_m\in F^\times\) is prescribed by compatibility with the two sloping edges, and the coefficient of \(x^{m-1}y\) is zero.

Among such polynomials, Proposition 5.10 asserts exactly \(m\) choices having precisely \(m-1\) singularities, all nodes, and identifies their \(F\)-algebra as \[L_{[\sigma]}=F[u]/(u^m-1)\quad(m\text{ odd}),\qquad L_{[\sigma]}=F[u]/(u^m-ac)\quad(m\text{ even}).\] The finding concerns the odd-degree identification for general prescribed \(a_m\), already in characteristic zero; no normalization tying \(a_m\) to \(a,b,c\) is included in the boundary-data hypothesis. Equation (33) is examined as the proposed parametrization of those same choices.

The text preceding Remark 3.5, PDF page 15, asserts that tropicalization preserves the genus. In the paper's notation, for an algebraic curve \(C\subset{\rm Tor}_{K}(\Delta)\) of genus \(g\), with \(K=k\{\{t\}\}\) and associated embedded tropical curve \(A_C\), the asserted conclusion is \[g(A_C)=g(C)=g.\] Remark 3.5 uses this as the direction from an arbitrary genus-\(g\) algebraic curve to a unique genus-\(g\) tropical curve of Newton polygon \(\Delta\).

No generic point-incidence condition, maximal-rank condition, or restriction to simple tropical curves is imposed in this paragraph. Those conditions occur later in the correspondence setup. The finding concerns the unrestricted equality here, with genus of the embedded tropical curve understood as in Section 3, rather than a weighted or enriched tropical object that retains contracted component genera.

Section 2.4, PDF page 12, defines \({\rm Tor}_k(\Delta)\) for a convex lattice polyhedron \(\Delta\) by taking the cones over its proper faces, forming their dual semigroups \(S_\sigma=\{u\in\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb Z):u(v)\ge0\text{ for every }v\in\sigma\}\), and gluing \(\operatorname{Spec}k[S_\sigma]\) along their face charts.

For \(\Delta_d=\operatorname{Conv}\{(0,0),(d,0),(0,d)\}\), \(d>0\), the text then claims that this construction yields \(\mathbb P^2_k\), with the standard affine charts and coordinate boundary lines, independently of \(d\). The finding concerns the construction literally stated using cones from the origin over faces of this untranslated triangle; a normal-fan construction is not part of that definition.

Theorem 1.1, PDF page 3, assumes a Hilbertian field \(k\) of characteristic zero and irreducible binary forms \(F,G\) of the same degree \(d\), with linearly disjoint splitting fields \(k_f,k_g\). The smooth plane curves \(C_f:y^d=F(x_0,x_1)\) and \(C_g:z^d=G(x_2,x_3)\) are assumed to have Jacobians that are not isogenous over \(\bar k\). Set \(K=k(\mu_d)k_fk_g\).

In the proof on PDF page 17, after normalizing the binary forms to monic polynomials, the text invokes Remark 6.2 to conclude \(L_{f,g}\subseteq K\), where \(L_{f,g}\) is the field used to define the geometric Picard group together with the \(d\)-th roots of unity. This containment is then used to pass from an element of order \(d\) in \(K^\times/K^{\times d}\) to the degree-\(d\) extension required by Theorem 4.1. Remark 6.2, PDF page 27, establishes the containment under \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\bar k}(J(C_f),J(C_g))=0\). The finding concerns this use of the stronger vanishing under the theorem's non-isogeny hypothesis; neither geometric simplicity nor absence of common isogeny factors is assumed there.

After Corollary 1.6, PDF page 5, consider the diagonal surface \(X/\mathbb Q\) given by \(x_0^d+a_1x_1^d+a_2x_2^d+a_3x_3^d=0\), with \(a_i\in\mathbb Q^\times\). Let \(L\) be the smallest field over which the geometric Picard group of the degree-\(d\) Fermat surface is fixed. Condition \((\star)\) requires that the classes of \(a_1,a_2,a_3\) in \(L^\times/L^{\times d}\) generate a group isomorphic to \((\mathbb Z/d)^3\).

Under this condition, the asserted specialization is \[\operatorname{Br}_1(X)/\operatorname{Br}(\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Z/2^a\times\mathbb Z/3^b,\] where \(a=2\) whenever \(8\mid d\), \(a=1\) when \(4\mid d\) but \(8\nmid d\), and \(a=0\) otherwise; \(b=1\) if \(3\mid d\) and \(b=0\) otherwise. Here \(\operatorname{Br}_1\) is the kernel of restriction to the geometric Brauer group, and the map from \(\operatorname{Br}(\mathbb Q)\) is injective under \((\star)\). The finding concerns the stated uniform exponent \(a=2\) for all multiples of eight, in comparison with the invariant subgroup described by Corollary 1.6 itself.

Proposition 6.3(i), PDF page 28, lets \(L\) be the minimal field of definition of \(\operatorname{Pic}(F_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})\) for the Fermat surface \(F:x_0^d+x_1^d+x_2^d+x_3^d=0\), and asserts \(L=\mathbb Q(\mu_{2d})\) when \(d\le4\) or \(\gcd(6,d)=1\). The range as written includes the quadric case \(d=2\).

In Example 1, PDF page 23, the standing field hypothesis is \(k\supseteq L\), followed by the asserted consequence \(\mathbb Q(\mu_{2d})\subseteq k\). For \(t\in k^\times\) of order \(d\) in \(k^\times/k^{\times d}\), the example considers \(X:x_0^d+x_1^d+t x_2^d+t x_3^d=0\). If also \(k=k_0(t)\) has transcendence degree one over \(k_0\), it claims that \(\operatorname{Br}(k)\to\operatorname{Br}(X)\) is an isomorphism. The finding concerns the degree-two field identification and this consequence under containment of the actual minimal Picard field; containment of \(\mathbb Q(i)\) is presented there as a consequence, not as a separate hypothesis.

On PDF page 27, set \(E=\mathbb Q(\mu_d)\). A character \(\chi=(l_0,l_1,l_2,l_3)\) belongs to \(S^\flat\) when \(1\le l_i\le d-1\) and \(\sum_i(tl_i\bmod d)=2d\) for every \(t\in(\mathbb Z/d)^\times\), with residues in \(\{1,\ldots,d-1\}\). Such a character indexes a one-dimensional summand \(V_\chi\) of the geometric Picard group after tensoring with \(E\).

For a prime \(\mathfrak p\nmid d\) of \(E\), write \(q=N\mathfrak p\) and let \(\psi:\mathbb F_q^\times\to\mu_d\) be the \(d\)-th power residue character, extended by zero at zero. The printed definition and asserted Frobenius eigenvalue are \[J_\chi(\mathfrak p)=\sum_{x_1+x_2+x_3=0}\psi(x_1)^{l_1}\psi(x_2)^{l_2}\psi(x_3)^{l_3},\qquad h_\chi(\mathfrak p)=\psi(-1)^{l_0}q^{-1}J_\chi(\mathfrak p).\] The finding concerns the homogeneous zero-sum condition in this displayed definition and its claimed nonzero eigenvalue role, separately from the implemented Gauss-sum computation.

The paragraph preceding Proposition 6.3, PDF page 28, takes an ideal \(\mathfrak m\) of the cyclotomic field \(E=\mathbb Q(\mu_d)\), with \(I(\mathfrak m)\) the group of fractional ideals coprime to \(\mathfrak m\). It defines generalized Dirichlet characters modulo \(\mathfrak m\) as characters of \[\operatorname{Cl}(\mathfrak m)=I(\mathfrak m)/P(\mathfrak m),\] while describing \(P(\mathfrak m)\) as the group of all principal ideals coprime to \(\mathfrak m\).

The finding concerns the identification of this quotient as the ray class group. The printed description imposes no condition that a generating element be congruent to one modulo \(\mathfrak m\). In particular, the issue is already present for an imaginary cyclotomic field, where no real-place sign condition is involved.

Proposition 4.1, PDF pages 12–14, considers an integral quartic \(F=H^2G_4+HG_3+F_2+F_1\), with \(F(0,0)=0\), positive-semidefinite degree-four part, primitive integral linear \(H\), and integral quadratic forms \(G_4,G_3\) not divisible by \(H\). No square \(L^2\), for a primitive integral linear form \(L\) not proportional to \(H\), may divide \(G_3\); \(F_2,F_1\) have degrees two and one and carry no additional restriction in the proposition.

After a unimodular change with \(u=H(x,y)\), write \(G(u,v)=g_2(u)v^2+g_1(u)v+g_0(u)\), with integral coefficients, \(\deg g_2=2\) and positive leading coefficient, and \(\deg g_1\le3\). The proof asserts that the division \(g_1=2g_2q+h\), \(\deg h\le1\), gives integral polynomials \(q,h\). In the branch \(D(u)=(g_1^2-4g_0g_2)/(4g_2)\to+\infty\), it then selects the allegedly integral points \(v=-q(u)\) and concludes \[\inf_{(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^2}G(u,v)=-\infty.\] The finding concerns this division-and-selection inference, not a counterexample to the proposition's final density-or-unboundedness alternative.

Lemma 3.1, PDF pages 6–7, takes \(F=\sum_{i=1}^4F_i\in\mathbb Z[x,y]\) of degree four with \(F(0,0)=0\) and positive-semidefinite \(F_4\). As in Section 3, \(\widetilde F_4\) is obtained by removing a positive-definite factor of maximal degree from \(F_4\), and \(\gcd(\widetilde F_4,F_3)\ne1\). Let \(\Xi\subset\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\) be the common real zero directions of \(\widetilde F_4\) and \(F_3\), equivalently of \(F_4\) and \(F_3\).

For \(\xi\in\Xi\), let \(2r_\xi\) be the multiplicity of the corresponding factor in \(F_4\), and set \(\Theta_\xi(B)=\{\theta:|\theta-\xi|<c_\xi B^{-1/(2r_\xi)}\}\), with sufficiently large fixed \(c_\xi>0\). The lemma claims a constant \(C_1>0\) such that, for every sufficiently large \(B\), \[F(B\cos\theta,B\sin\theta)\ge C_1B^3\qquad\text{whenever }\theta\notin\bigcup_{\xi\in\Xi}\Theta_\xi(B).\] Its stated setup does not require every real zero of \(F_4\) to be shared with \(F_3\), nor does the lemma state a separate bounded-below hypothesis.

Section 6.3, PDF pages 23–24, treats a geometrically irreducible genus-zero affine curve \(C:K(x,y)=d_2\) with infinitely many rational points, arising from \(F=(ax+b)K\) in Lemma 6.8. Choose a rational parametrization \((R_1/Q_1,R_2/Q_2)\), with coprime pairs of integral polynomials. In the nonconstant linear-fractional case, write \(R_1/Q_1=(rt+s)/(ut+v)\), with \(rv-su\ne0\), so that \(t=(s-vx)/(ux-r)\).

For \(m=\max\{\deg R_2,\deg Q_2\}\), define \[\widetilde R_2(x)=(ux-r)^mR_2\!\left(\frac{s-vx}{ux-r}\right),\qquad\widetilde Q_2(x)=(ux-r)^mQ_2\!\left(\frac{s-vx}{ux-r}\right).\] The assertion under examination is \(\deg\widetilde Q_2=0\) if and only if \(\deg R_2=\deg Q_2=0\). It is used to treat every constant-denominator case as a constant second coordinate, without a separate polynomial but nonconstant case.

In Theorem 4.4, PDF pages 14–15, let \(A\) be a \(C^*\)-algebra and \(I\subseteq A\) an arbitrary two-sided ring ideal. The paper does not assume that \(I\) is closed or self-adjoint, or that it is complex-linear when \(A\) is nonunital. Write \(I_+=I\cap A_+\), and let \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathrm D}(I)\) be the smallest Dixmier ideal containing the entire ideal \(I\). A Dixmier ideal is positively spanned and hereditary, with a strongly invariant positive cone.

For \(a,b\in A_+\), the relation \(a\lhd b\) means that there are finitely many \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in A\) and an integer \(m\ge1\) such that \(a=\sum_jx_j^*x_j\) and \(\sum_jx_jx_j^*\le mb\). The proof asserts \[\operatorname{cl}_{\mathrm D}(I)_+=\{a\in A_+:a\lhd b\text{ for some }b\in I_+\}.\] The finding concerns this identification for arbitrary \(I\), used to deduce the squeezing inclusion \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathrm D}(I)^{1+\varepsilon}\subseteq\operatorname{int}_{\mathrm D}(I)\). The positive cone is the actual intersection \(I\cap A_+\), not a newly defined set of absolute values of elements of \(I\).

Corollary 2.4, PDF page 11, concerns the random probability measure \(\mu^\beta\) on the unit circle whose Verblunsky coefficients \((\alpha_j)_{j\ge0}\) are independent and rotationally invariant, with \(|\alpha_j|^2\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,\beta(j+1)/2)\). For this prescribed distribution it asserts, almost surely, \[\dim_H\operatorname{supp}(\mu^\beta)=1-\frac2\beta\quad(\beta>2),\qquad\dim_H\operatorname{supp}(\mu^2)=0.\] The critical measure is additionally stated to be nonatomic.

Using the identification in law with normalized circle Gaussian multiplicative chaos for \(\gamma=\sqrt{2/\beta}\), the same corollary states \(\dim_H\operatorname{supp}(GMC^\gamma)=1-\gamma^2\) for \(0<\gamma<1\), and zero for \(\gamma=1\). The finding concerns these assertions with the conventional closed topological support. The paper does not define a different meaning of \(\operatorname{supp}\) here, and a full-measure carrier or the Hausdorff dimension of a measure is a different mathematical object.

In the proof of Lemma 6.3, PDF pages 65–68, \(\beta>2\) and \(X_t\in[0,1]\) is a continuous process with \(X_0=1\), driven by Brownian motion \(B\), satisfying equation (6.3): \[d(1-X_t)=\left(X_t-\frac{2(1-X_t)^2}{\beta t}+\frac{4(1-X_t)X_t}{\beta t}\right)dt+(1-X_t)\sqrt{\frac{4X_t}{\beta t}}\,dB_t.\] The additional entrance condition is \(\sup_{0<t<1}(1-X_t)/t^{1-\varepsilon_0}<\infty\) almost surely for every \(\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\).

Set \(I_t=\int_0^t4(1-X_u)/(\beta u)\,du\) and let \(V\) have the law of the absolute supremum of a standard Brownian motion on \([0,1]\). For \(a,\alpha>0\), the first display on PDF page 68 bounds the probability that \(\sup_{0<s\le t}|\int_s^t(1-\sqrt{X_u})\sqrt{4/(\beta u)}\,dB_u|>2a\) by \(\mathbb P(I_t\le\alpha)+\mathbb P(\sqrt\alpha V\ge a)\). The next step claims that the limsup as \(t\downarrow0\) is bounded by the second term alone. The finding concerns the lower-tail sign in this particular display and its use in the limit; page 67 has the corresponding upper-tail event.

Lemma 4.5, PDF page 29, considers normal projective varieties \(V',V,W',W\), projective birational morphisms \(\beta_V:V'\to V\), \(\beta_W:W'\to W\), and proper surjective morphisms with connected fibers \(f':V'\to W'\), \(f:V\to W\), satisfying \(f\circ\beta_V=\beta_W\circ f'\). These are the paper's fiber spaces; equidimensionality is not part of that definition.

Assume that \(f'\) is a locally constant fibration with simply connected fiber, that \(W\) has klt singularities, and that there is an effective divisor \(\Delta'\) such that \((V',\Delta')\) is klt and \(-\bigl(K_{V'/W'}+\Delta'\bigr)\) is nef. The conclusion asserted is that \(f\) is a locally trivial analytic fibration. The positivity hypothesis is relative to \(W'\); the statement imposes no additional equidimensionality or contraction compatibility on the given diagram.

In Lemma 4.4, PDF pages 27–29, \(h:V\to W\) is a locally constant fibration of normal projective varieties with irregularity-zero fiber. There is an effective \(\mathbb Q\)-divisor \(D\) for which \((V,D)\) is klt and \(-\bigl(K_{V/W}+D\bigr)\) is nef, and \(B\) is a nef and big divisor on \(V\). After reducing to smooth \(W\), the proof uses \(B=B_0+h^*B_W\) and the numerically flat bundles \(E_m=h_*\mathcal O_V(mB_0)\) for sufficiently divisible positive \(m\).

It then chooses a very ample divisor \(A\) on \(W\), writes \(d=\dim W\) (the source uses \(Y\) in this line), and asserts by Nakano vanishing that \[H^i\bigl(W,E_m\otimes\mathcal O_W((d+1-i)A)\bigr)=0\qquad(i>0).\] The choice of \(A\) is required only to be very ample; no condition on \(A-K_W\) is stated, and the displayed twist contains no canonical bundle. The finding concerns this vanishing inference used to establish regularity, global generation and nefness of \(B_0\), rather than a counterexample to the decomposition conclusion itself.

Lemma 2.8, PDF pages 13–14, lets \(\varphi:M\to X\) be a surjective morphism of normal analytic varieties, \(\theta\) a smooth \((1,1)\)-form with local potentials, and \((E,g)\) a torsion-free sheaf with singular Hermitian metric satisfying \(\sqrt{-1}\Theta_g\succeq\theta\otimes\operatorname{id}\). If \(X_E\) is the locally free locus, it assumes \(\operatorname{codim}\varphi^{-1}(X\setminus X_E)\ge2\) and reflexivity of \(\varphi^*(E^*)\).

In the proof, a local dual section is written \(e=\sum_{i=1}^m s_i\otimes f_i\), with \(s_i\) sections of \(E^*\) and \(f_i\) holomorphic functions on the pullback neighborhood. On the locus where the metric is defined, the claimed estimate is \[|e|^2_{\varphi^*g^*}\le\sum_{i=1}^m|f_i|^2\,\varphi^*|s_i|_{g^*}^2.\] No orthogonality or normalization of the \(s_i\) is assumed. The finding concerns the coefficient in this pointwise estimate used for local boundedness of the norm.

Remark 4.4, PDF page 22, starts with the orientable genus-one surfaces \(\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1\), each with one boundary component, and attaches a single interior tube to each. This operation removes two interior disks and joins their boundary circles by an annulus, while keeping the original boundary fixed.

The first sentence calls the resulting pair genus-one surfaces and asserts that they are isotopic relative to their boundary in \(B^4\). The finding concerns the stated genus after this specified operation. The isotopy assertion and the associated stabilization-distance-one statement are separate from that genus label.

Lemma 5.5, PDF page 15, lets \(F(X,Y)\in\mathbb Z[X,Y]\) be a homogeneous binary form of degree \(d\) with nonzero discriminant. It asserts that for every positive integer \(m\), \[\#\{(X,Y)\in\mathbb Z^2:|F(X,Y)|\le m\}\ll_d m^{2/d},\] with the implied constant depending only on \(d\).

The set as written includes solutions of \(F(X,Y)=0\) and nonprimitive pairs. No irreducibility assumption or exclusion of rational linear factors is imposed. The finding concerns this uniform finite count and its use for the quartics in equation (5.17); the later application needs certain primitive pairs with nonzero represented value, which is a narrower counting problem.

Lemma 3.5, PDF page 9, concerns a separable binary cubic \(C\in\mathbb Z[x_1,x_2]\) with \(C(1,0)\ne0\); \(\lambda\in\{1,2,3\}\) is its number of irreducible factors over \(\mathbb Q\). The counting function \(N^\circ(B)\) counts integral quadruples with \(C(x_1,x_2)=x_3^2x_4\), \(\gcd(x_1,x_2,x_4)=1\), \(x_3x_4\ne0\), and \(|x_i|\le B\). The asserted bound is \(N^\circ(B)\ll_C B(\log B)^{\max\{\lambda,2\}}\).

The proof uses the multiplicative root-counting function \(f\) in equation (3.12) and claims \(\sum_{U\le|u|<2U}f(|u|)\ll_C U\). In the allowed subfamily \(C(1,0)=1\), its definition is simply \(f(p^v)=\#\{x\bmod p^v:C(x,1)\equiv0\pmod{p^v}\}\) for every prime power. Thus the claimed mean bound is asserted even when \(C\) splits into three rational linear factors. The finding concerns this mean estimate and the logarithmic factors retained in the subsequent sums over the auxiliary parameters \(h_1,h_2\).

Lemma 3.6, PDF page 9, asserts \(N^\circ(B)\gg_C B\) for every separable integral binary cubic \(C\). Here \(N^\circ(B)\) counts \((x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in\mathbb Z^4\) with \(C(x_1,x_2)=x_3^2x_4\), \(\gcd(x_1,x_2,x_4)=1\), \(x_3x_4\ne0\), and all coordinates bounded in absolute value by \(B\).

For a positive integer \(q=x_3\) coprime to \(\Delta(C)\) and a root \(\alpha\bmod q^2\) of \(C(x,1)\), the proof forms \(\Lambda_{q,\alpha}=\mathbb Z(q^2,0)+\mathbb Z(\alpha,1)\). It invokes Minkowski to obtain a nonzero vector with \(|x_1|,|x_2|\ll_C q\), sets \(x_4=C(x_1,x_2)/q^2\), and counts such a choice toward the lower bound. The finding concerns the inference that the short nonzero vector supplies an admissible counted point, including the required \(x_4\ne0\) and coprimality conditions.

Section 8, PDF pages 31–35, fixes integers \(A,B\) with \(A^2-4B\notin\mathbb Q^2\) and studies \(E_D:y^2=x(x^2+ADx+BD^2)\) for square-free nonzero \(D\). Put \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{A^2-4B})\), \(\alpha=(-A+\sqrt{A^2-4B})/2\), and \(L=K(\sqrt\alpha)\). For primes splitting completely in \(K(\sqrt B)\), the text treats the quadratic symbol of \(\alpha\) as an Artin symbol in \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)\), taking values in \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(\sqrt B))\cong\mathbb F_2\).

Lemma 8.4 subsequently invokes Theorem 6.1 with \(K_{21}=K\) and \(\alpha_{21}=\alpha R_{21}\), where \(R_{21}=\widetilde D\delta\gamma_1\) in the stated factorization data. Theorem 6.1 explicitly requires \(K_i(\sqrt{\alpha_i})/\mathbb Q\) to be Galois. The finding concerns whether the hypotheses on \(A,B\), and the permitted factorization parameters, ensure this normality and the asserted subfield containment. These are prerequisites of the displayed Galois groups and theorem application, not additional hypotheses imposed in Section 8.

Theorem 2.4, PDF page 4, assumes a density bound \(\#\{D\in\mathcal D(N):E_D^*(\mathbb Z)\ne\varnothing\}\ll N(\log N)^{-\kappa}\) for a fixed elliptic curve \(y^2=x^3+Ax+B\) and some \(\kappa>0\). Here \(\mathcal D(N)\) consists of nonzero square-free integers of absolute value at most \(N\), and \(E_D^*\) excludes two-torsion. Its moment conclusion is stated for every positive integer \(k\le\log\log\log N\) and every prescribed loss \(\varepsilon>0\).

In the proof, PDF page 5, the rank-moment input from Theorem 2.5 is valid only when \(0<m<C'\log\log\log N\), for a fixed \(C'>0\) depending on the curve. The substitution is \(m=qk\sigma\log c\), where \(\sigma\) is a fixed upper bound for the family’s Szpiro ratios, \(c>1\) is the integral-point bound constant, and \(q=1/\varepsilon\) for \(0<\varepsilon<1\). The text uses \(m\ll\log\log\log N\) to justify the strict input range. The finding concerns this parameter choice for all permitted \(k\) and arbitrarily small fixed \(\varepsilon\), with the input multiplier \(C'\) fixed.

Theorem 2.5, PDF page 4, fixes integers \(A,B\) with \(4A^3+27B^2\ne0\), writes \(E_D:y^2=x^3+AD^2x+BD^3\), and lets \(\mathcal D(N)\) be the nonzero square-free integers with \(|D|\le N\). It asserts constants \(C,C'>0\), depending only on \(A,B\), for which \[\frac1{\#\mathcal D(N)}\sum_{D\in\mathcal D(N)}\exp\bigl(m\operatorname{rank}E_D(\mathbb Q)\bigr)\le\exp(Cm^2)\] whenever \(N>C\) and \(0<m<C'\log\log\log N\).

The parameter \(m\) is a positive real number, with no positive lower cutoff, and the bound has neither a multiplicative prefactor nor a linear term in the exponent. The finding concerns this normalization as \(m\downarrow0\) at a fixed sufficiently large \(N\), for a twist family containing a positive-rank member.

In Lemma 8.4, PDF page 35, Theorem 6.1 is applied with maximal unlinked-set size \(M=2\) and \(\lambda=1/2\), producing an error \[O\!\left(\frac N{\widetilde D}(\log N)^{-1/2+\varepsilon}\right),\qquad\varepsilon>0.\] The text chooses \(\varepsilon=5/8\) and states that this yields exponent \(-1/8\). The finding concerns this explicit numerical substitution, conditional on the validity of the preceding character-sum application.

In Section 8.2, PDF page 37, let \(A,B\in\mathbb Z\) with \(A^2-4B\notin\mathbb Q^2\), let \(D\) be a positive square-free integer, and let \((x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2\) with \(y\ne0\) satisfy \(y^2=x(x^2+ADx+BD^2)\). The proof introduces the integral change \(X=9x+3AD\), \(Y=27y\).

The displayed target equation is \[Y^2=X^3+27(3B-A^2)x+27A(2A^2-9B).\] The finding concerns whether this printed identity follows from the stated change of variables for arbitrary allowed \(D\). The lower-case \(x\) and the absence of powers of \(D\) are retained here to identify precisely the original display.

Equation (4.4), PDF page 14, is used for \(f=n^{-1}\log u\), where \(u>0\) is a smooth solution of \(-\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}u=2n^2u^{(n+2)/n}\) on \(B_{3R}(\xi_0)\), \(R\ge1\), satisfying \(u\le aR^{-n}\) there for some \(a>0\).
