In the proof of Theorem 1.2, PDF page 18, \(n\ge2\) and \(u>0\) solves \(-\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}u=2n^2u^{(n+2)/n}\) on the whole Heisenberg group, with \(u(\xi)\le C/(1+|\xi|^n)\). The norm is \(|(z,t)|=(|z|^4+t^2)^{1/4}\). Set \(f=n^{-1}\log u\), \(g=\sum_\alpha|Z_\alpha f|^2+e^{2f}-i\partial_t f\), and \(A_R=B_R\setminus B_{R/2}\), \(R>1\).

The cutoff satisfies \(\eta=1\) on \(B_{R/2}\), \(\eta=0\) off \(B_R\), and \(|\partial\eta|\le c/R\); the exponent satisfies \(s>4\). Between equations (4.9) and (4.10), the proof integrates \(-\int_{A_R}e^{2(n-1)f}\eta^{s-2}\operatorname{Re}\sum_\alpha(f_{\alpha\bar\alpha}\bar g)\) by parts and equates it to the three displayed interior terms \(J_1+J_2+J_3\), with no boundary-flux term. The finding concerns this identity over the annulus when the multiplier has trace one on its inner boundary; neither the stated cutoff nor the decay hypothesis imposes zero inner flux.

Equation (1.3), PDF page 2, describes positive solutions of \(-\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}u=2n^2u^{(n+2)/n}\), with the sub-Laplacian normalized as in Section 2, by \[U_{\lambda,\mu}(z,t)=\frac{C}{|t+i|z|^2+z\cdot\mu+\lambda|^n},\qquad\lambda\in\mathbb C,\quad\mu\in\mathbb C^n,\quad\operatorname{Im}\lambda>\frac{|\mu|^2}{4}.\] The amplitude is stated to be an explicit positive constant \(C=C(n,\lambda)\).

The finding concerns the indicated dependence: for fixed \(n,\lambda\), the parameter \(\mu\) may vary throughout the displayed admissible set, while \(C(n,\lambda)\) is declared independent of \(\mu\). The question is whether that dependence makes every displayed member solve the equation with its fixed coefficient \(2n^2\).

Equations (1.4)–(1.5), PDF page 2, state that for \(n\ge3\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), the positive entire function \[V_{\lambda,x_0}(x)=\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda^2+|x-x_0|^2}\right)^{(n-2)/2}\] solves \[-\Delta V=\frac{n(n-2)}4\,V^{(n+2)/(n-2)}\quad\text{on }\mathbb R^n,\] where \(\Delta\) is the Euclidean Laplacian. The finding concerns the compatibility of this amplitude with the displayed PDE coefficient in the background comparison.

Lemma 4.6, PDF page 42, fixes \(1/2<s_0\le s<1\), \(n\ge2\), and a weak solution \(u\in W^{s,2}(B_{2R}(x_0))\cap W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)\) of \(\mathcal Lu=\mu\) in \(B_R(x_0)\), with \(\mu\in L^\infty(B_R(x_0))\). The operator uses an odd function \(\Phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) with \(|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|\le\Lambda|a-b|\) and \((\Phi(a)-\Phi(b))(a-b)\ge\Lambda^{-1}|a-b|^2\) for all \(a,b\), where \(\Lambda\ge1\).

For every \(\sigma\in(0,2s_0-1)\), the proof of the claimed \(W^{\sigma,1}\) estimate for \(\nabla u\) starts by choosing \(\beta=\beta(s_0,\sigma)\in(0,1)\) such that \[2s_0\beta-1>\frac{\sigma+1}{2}>\sigma.\] Equation (4.21) is subsequently used to select and simplify the bootstrap exponents on pages 44–45. The finding concerns the existence of this parameter for every advertised pair \((s_0,\sigma)\); no further lower bound on \(s_0\) or smaller upper bound on \(\sigma\) is imposed in this selection.

Equations (1.2) and (1.15), PDF pages 1–2 and 5, fix \(n\ge2\), \(0<s<1\), a finite signed Radon measure \(\mu\), and the following nonlinearity. The operator uses an odd function \(\Phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) with \(|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|\le\Lambda|a-b|\) and \((\Phi(a)-\Phi(b))(a-b)\ge\Lambda^{-1}|a-b|^2\) for all \(a,b\), where \(\Lambda\ge1\). The formal operator is \[\mathcal L_{\rm pv}u(x)=(1-s)\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi\!\left(\frac{u(x)-u(y)}{|x-y|^s}\right)\frac{dy}{|x-y|^{n+s}}.\]

For \(u\in W^{s,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)\) with \(\int_{\mathbb R^n}|u(y)|(1+|y|)^{-n-2s}\,dy<\infty\), the stated weak formulation of \(\mathcal Lu=\mu\) is \[(1-s)\iint_{\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n}\Phi\!\left(\frac{u(x)-u(y)}{|x-y|^s}\right)\frac{\psi(x)-\psi(y)}{|x-y|^{n+s}}\,dx\,dy=\int_\Omega\psi\,d\mu\] for every \(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\). The energy in (1.4) also uses the prefactor \(1-s\). The finding concerns whether these displays represent the same operator normalization, already for smooth compactly supported test functions and \(\Phi(t)=t\).

Lemma 2.3, PDF page 14, takes \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(q\ge1\) with \(n>q\gamma\), any radius \(R>0\), and \(g\in W^{\gamma,q}(B_R(x_0))\). Let \(q^*=nq/(n-q\gamma)\), and let \((g)_{B_R}\) denote the average of \(g\). The claimed inequality is \[\left(\frac1{|B_R|}\int_{B_R}|g-(g)_{B_R}|^{q^*}\,dx\right)^{1/q^*}\le c(n,\gamma,q)[g]_{W^{\gamma,q}(B_R)}.\]

The seminorm on the right is the unnormalized quantity \(\bigl(\iint_{B_R\times B_R}|g(x)-g(y)|^q/|x-y|^{n+q\gamma}\,dx\,dy\bigr)^{1/q}\). No restriction to a fixed radius or radius factor appears in the statement. The finding concerns this asserted uniform dependence on \(R\).

In Lemma 4.2, PDF page 35, let \(n\ge2\), \(1/2<s<1\), and let \(u\in W^{s,2}(B_R(x_0))\cap L^1_{2s}(\mathbb R^n)\) solve \(\mathcal Lu=\mu\) weakly in \(B_R(x_0)\), with bounded \(\mu\). Here \(L^1_{2s}\) requires integrability of \(|u(y)|(1+|y|)^{-n-2s}\). The operator uses an odd function \(\Phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) with \(|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|\le\Lambda|a-b|\) and \((\Phi(a)-\Phi(b))(a-b)\ge\Lambda^{-1}|a-b|^2\) for all \(a,b\), where \(\Lambda\ge1\). Let \(v\) be the weak solution of \(\mathcal Lv=0\) in the ball with \(v=u\) almost everywhere outside it, and put \(w=u-v\), \(h=2s-1\).

Equation (4.5) asserts \[(2-2s)\int_{B_{2R}}\frac{1}{|B_{2R}|}\int_{B_{2R}}\frac{|w(x)-w(y)|}{|x-y|^{n+2s-1}}\,dx\,dy\le c\frac{(1-h)^2}{(1-s)(s-h)}R^{-s/2+2s-n}|\mu|(B_R).\] The constant is stated to depend only on \(n,\Lambda\), and the fraction equals four for the specified \(h\). The finding concerns the power of \(R\) in this intermediate comparison estimate, with one integral averaged as printed.

Lemma 3.6, PDF page 31, fixes \(0<s_0\le s<1\) and a weak solution \(w\in W^{s,2}(B_R(x_0))\cap L^1_{2s}(\mathbb R^n)\) of \(\mathcal Lw=f\) in \(B_R(x_0)\), with \(f\in L^\infty(B_{2R}(x_0))\). The operator uses an odd function \(\Phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) with \(|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|\le\Lambda|a-b|\) and \((\Phi(a)-\Phi(b))(a-b)\ge\Lambda^{-1}|a-b|^2\) for all \(a,b\), where \(\Lambda\ge1\). For \(0<|h|<R/8\) and \(0<\beta\le1\), set \(v_h=\delta_hw/|h|^\beta\), where \(\delta_hw(x)=w(x+h)-w(x)\).

The lemma claims constants \(\gamma_1\in(0,1)\) and \(c\), depending only on \(n,s_0,\Lambda\), such that \[\|v_h\|_{L^\infty(B_{R/2})}+R^{\gamma_1}[v_h]_{C^{0,\gamma_1}(B_{R/2})}\le c\widetilde E(v_h;B_R)+c\left\|\frac{\delta_hf}{|h|^\beta}\right\|_{L^\infty(B_R)}.\] Here \(\widetilde E(v;B_R)=\frac{1}{|B_R|}\int_{B_R}|v|+\operatorname{Tail}(v;B_R)\), with \(\operatorname{Tail}(v;B_R)=(1-s)R^{2s}\int_{\mathbb R^n\setminus B_R}|v(y)|/|y-x_0|^{n+2s}\,dy\). The finding concerns the asserted radius-uniform forcing term as printed, with no \(R^{2s}\) multiplying it.

Equation (1.19), PDF page 8, takes a finite signed Radon measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), \(n\ge2\), any \(\beta\in(0,n)\), any center \(x_0\), and any \(R>0\). The two potential definitions are \[I_\beta^{|\mu|}(x_0,R)=\int_0^R\frac{|\mu|(B_t(x_0))}{t^{n-\beta}}\,\frac{dt}{t},\qquad I_\beta^{|\mu|}(x_0)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\frac{d|\mu|(y)}{|x_0-y|^{n-\beta}}.\]

The assertion is \(I_\beta^{|\mu|}(x_0,R)\le c(n)I_\beta^{|\mu|}(x_0)\), with a constant independent of \(\beta\) throughout \((0,n)\). The finding concerns this full parameter range; the later gradient applications impose the narrower \(\beta=2s-1<1\).

The proof of Lemma 2.9, PDF pages 18–19, fixes \(q\in[1,\infty)\), \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(R>0\), \(0<h_0<R\), and \(g\in W^{1,q}(B_{R+6h_0})\) with \(\sup_{0<|h|<h_0}\|\delta_h^2g/|h|^{1+\gamma}\|_{L^q(B_{R+4h_0})}<M\). Set \(G=g-(g)_{B_{R+4h_0}}-(

abla^2\xi|\le c/h_0^2\).

For \(H=G\xi\), the display following (2.15) bounds \(\sup_{h

The proof of Lemma 2.10, PDF page 20, instead takes \(g\in L^1(B_{R+6h_0})\) with \[h_0^{-1}\sup_{0<|h|<h_0}\int_{B_{R+4h_0}}\frac{|\delta_hg|}{|h|^\gamma}+\sup_{0<|h|<h_0}\int_{B_{R+4h_0}}\frac{|\delta_h^2g|}{|h|^{1+\gamma}}<M.\] With the same type of cutoff, it asserts a finite bound for \(\sup_{h\ne0}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|\delta_h(g\xi)|/|h|^{1+\gamma}\). This is a first difference as printed, although the preceding product estimate and Lemma 2.8 concern second differences \(\delta_h^2g(x)=g(x+2h)-2g(x+h)+g(x)\). The finding also concerns this difference order in the intermediate display.

Theorem 3.1, PDF page 11, asserts a capacity bound for relatively compact open subsets of symplectic four-manifolds. In its Euclidean special case, let \(Z\subset\mathbb R^4\) be nonempty, open and relatively compact, with the standard symplectic form, and define \[V_d(Z)=\operatorname{vol}\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial Z)<d\},\qquad q=\liminf_{d\downarrow0}\frac{\log V_d(Z)}{\log d}.\] This is the definition of volume-decay order in equation (2.2), PDF page 7.

Writing \(c_k(Z)\) for its ECH capacities and \(e_k(Z)=c_k(Z)-2\sqrt{k\operatorname{vol}Z}\), the claimed conclusion is a finite constant \(C>0\), depending only on \(Z\), such that \[e_k(Z)>-Ck^{(2-q)/4}\quad\text{for every positive integer }k.\] The theorem does not require connectedness and does not impose a separate bound \(V_d(Z)\le C_0d^q\). The finding concerns this exact exponent conclusion under the logarithmic liminf definition, rather than under the stronger tube-volume hypothesis in Proposition 3.2.

In Proposition 6.1, PDF pages 24–26, a nonincreasing function \(f\) with \(f(0)=1\) and \(\int_0^\infty f(r)\,dr<\infty\) defines a toric domain in \(\mathbb C^2\). The construction uses real coordinates \((x,y,u,v)\), the standard symplectic form \(\omega=dx\wedge dy+du\wedge dv\), and \(G(u,v)=v+1/2\), with the convention \(X_G=\partial_u\). It chooses \(\chi(x)=x\) for \(x\le1\) and \(\chi'(x)=\sqrt{f(x-1)}\) for \(x\ge1\), and sets \(H=\chi(x)G\).

Steps 2a–2b and equations (6.1)–(6.2) identify the resulting Hamiltonian diffeomorphism as the composition \[\Psi(x,y,u,v)=\bigl(x,\ y+(v+1/2)\chi'(x),\ u+\chi(x),\ v\bigr).\] The finding concerns the assertion that this explicitly displayed map preserves \(\omega\), as required for the bounded symplectic embedding. Both displacement signs are part of the original displayed formula.

In the proof of Lemma 2.3, PDF page 9, let \(Z\subset\mathbb R^4\) be a bounded open convex domain, and take \(d>0\) small enough that the inner erosion \(Z(d)=\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial Z)\ge d\}\) is nonempty. Write \(N_d(K)\) for the volume of the Euclidean radius-\(d\) neighborhood of \(K\), and \(N_0(K)=\operatorname{vol}(K)\).

The proof describes \(Z\) as the radius-\(d\) neighborhood of \(Z(d)\) and uses the equality \[V_d(Z)=N_d(Z(d))-N_0(Z(d)),\] where \(V_d(Z)\) is the volume of the inner boundary layer of \(Z\). The finding concerns this erosion-then-dilation identity under convexity alone. Linear decay of \(V_d(Z)\), the lemma's eventual conclusion, is a separate assertion.

Remark 4.3, PDF pages 16–17, fixes \(\lambda>0\) and endpoint distance \(\ell\ge0\). It considers immersed planar curves with endpoints fixed at \(0\) and \(\ell e_1\), with free tangent directions and variable length, and critical points of \(E^\lambda[\gamma]=\int_\gamma k^2\,ds+\lambda L[\gamma]\). Such critical points satisfy \(2k''+k^3-\lambda k=0\) and the pinned conditions \(k(0)=k(L)=0\).

Using the unit-speed wavelike elastica \(\gamma_w(\cdot,m)\) defined in Theorem 2.4, and the complete elliptic integrals \(K(m),E(m)\), the remark claims that every nonstraight critical point is an isometric image of \[\gamma(s)=N\sqrt{\frac{4m-2}{\lambda}}\,\gamma_w\!\left(N^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{4m-2}}\,(s-K(m)),m\right),\qquad0\le s\le2NK(m),\] for \(m\in(1/2,1)\), \(N\in\mathbb N\), satisfying \(\left|2(2E(m)-K(m))\sqrt{4m-2}\right|=\ell\sqrt\lambda/N\). The finding concerns the claimed completeness with exactly this scale and parameter interval, at the same prescribed multiplier \(\lambda\).

Proposition 4.4, PDF page 18, lets \(U\) have a normalized 1-unconditional Schauder basis \((u_s)\), lets \(X\) be a Banach space, and takes bounded projections \(I_s\) with \(I_sI_t=0\) for \(s\ne t\). Set \(X_s=I_sX\). It assumes a constant \(B>0\) such that, for every \(N\), \(x_s\in X_s\) and \(x_0\in\bigcap_{s=1}^N\ker I_s\), \[\left\|\sum_{s=1}^Nx_s+x_0\right\|\ge B^{-1}\left\|\sum_{s=1}^N\|x_s\|u_s\right\|_U.\]

The other hypothesis supplies \(\beta,C>0\) such that, for every subspace \(Y\subseteq X\) with \(Y\cap X_s\) infinite-dimensional for all \(s\), every \(N\), and all complex \(a_s,b_s\), there exist \(x_s\in X_s\cap Y\) and \(x_0\in Y\cap\bigcap_{s=1}^N\ker I_s\) for which \[\beta\sum_{s=1}^N|b_s|\le\left\|\sum_{s=1}^Nb_sx_s\right\|,\qquad\left\|\sum_{s=1}^Na_sx_s-x_0\right\|\le C\left\|\sum_{s=1}^Na_su_s\right\|_U.\]

The conclusion asserts that both \((I_s)\) and their classes in \(\mathcal L(X)/\mathcal{SS}(X)\) are \(BC/\beta\)-equivalent to the biorthogonal sequence \((u_s^*)\), and that the closed projection span together with \(\mathbb CI\) has zero intersection with the strictly singular operators. No hypothesis states that every \(X_s\) is infinite-dimensional or that a subspace \(Y\) meeting the premise exists. The finding concerns the quotient and directness conclusions under the printed quantifiers.

Lemma 11.5(iii), PDF page 53, considers a finite rooted tree analysis \((f_t)_{t\in\mathcal T}\) of \(f=f_\varnothing\) in the norming set \(W_q[(\mathcal A_{\widetilde n_j},\theta_j)]\). Here \(1\le q<\infty\), \(p\) is conjugate to \(q\), \(\widetilde n_j\in\mathbb N\), and \(0<\theta_j\le1\). Terminal nodes are signed coordinate functionals. At a nonterminal node, \(f_t=\theta_j\widetilde n_j^{-1/p}\sum_{r\in\operatorname{succ}(t)}f_r\), where the successors form a block sequence of length at most \(\widetilde n_j\).

For every antichain \(\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal T\) and every finitely supported vector \(x\), the lemma asserts \[|f(x)|\le\left(\sum_{t\in\mathcal B}|f_t(x)|^q\right)^{1/q}.\] The only condition on \(\mathcal B\) is pairwise incomparability; it need not meet every root-to-terminal path or cover the part of the support on which \(x\) acts. The finding concerns the estimate with this unrestricted antichain hypothesis.

Equation (7), PDF page 5, begins the proof of Theorem 1.1 by requiring two functions \(\zeta,\eta\in C^\infty([0,\infty))\) with \[\zeta=0\text{ on }[0,1/2],\quad\zeta=1\text{ on }[1,\infty),\quad0\le\zeta'\le4,\quad|\zeta''|\le16,\] and \[\eta=1\text{ on }[0,1/2],\quad\eta=0\text{ on }[1,\infty),\quad-4\le\eta'\le0,\quad|\eta''|\le16.\]

All derivative bounds are global on the half-line, with smooth matching to the constant pieces at both transition endpoints. The finding concerns the existence of functions satisfying these simultaneous endpoint and numerical derivative constraints, which are then used in the metric construction.

Theorem 1.3 (Article PDF page 5, printed page 83) concerns Ramsey–Turán densities. For positive integers \(P<Q\), let \(\alpha_P(G)\) be the maximum size of a vertex subset inducing a \(K_P\)-free graph, and let \(\rho_P(Q)\) be the limiting maximum edge density, normalized by \(\binom n2\), of \(K_Q\)-free graphs with \(\alpha_P(G)=o(n)\). Conjecture A, on PDF page 3, predicts \[\rho_P^*(Q)=\frac{(t-1)(2P-r-1)+r+1}{t(2P-r-1)+r+1},\qquad Q=Pt+r+2,\quad t\in\mathbb N,\quad 0\le r<P.\]

Let \(\ell,p,q\) be positive integers, with \(q\) even and \(\ell\ge p(q-1)\), and set \(P=2^\ell\) and \(Q=2^\ell+2^p+q-1\). The theorem constructs asymptotically equisized \(q\)-partite graphs with negligible edges inside each part and cross densities \(2^{p-\ell}-o(1)\), yielding \[\rho_P(Q)\ge 2^{p-\ell}\left(1-\frac1q\right).\] It states equality in this bound when \(q(q-2)\le 2^p\le q^2\), followed by the assertion \[q>2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho_P(Q)>\rho_P^*(Q).\]

The scope at issue is the last implication: does it use only the initial hypotheses and \(q>2\), or also the intervening condition \(q(q-2)\le2^p\le q^2\)? The report tests the former reading. The latter condition must not silently be omitted from a reading in which it qualifies both conclusions; the construction and the separate equality claim are not the asserted counterexample target.

Definition 5.2 (Article PDF page 21, printed page 99) fixes positive integers \(p\le q\). A \(p\)-weighted graph \(G=(V,w)\) has symmetric weights \(w:V^2\to\{0,1,\ldots,p\}\) with \(w(x,x)=0\), and \(\delta(G)=\min_{x\in V}\sum_{y\ne x}w(x,y)\). For a family \(\mathcal F\) of weighted graphs, \(G\) is \(\mathcal F\)-free when no induced weighted subgraph \(G[U]\), \(U\subseteq V\), belongs to \(\mathcal F\).

Take \(\mathcal F=\widetilde{\mathcal G}_p(q)\), the family in that definition of positive weighted graphs on at most \(q\) vertices admitting the stated regularity-based valid vertex weightings of total weight at least \(q\). The printed threshold is \[\pi(\mathcal F)=\sup\bigl\{d\in[0,1]:\exists n_0\ \forall G=(V,w),\ |V|\ge n_0,\ \delta(G)>dp|V|\Longrightarrow G\text{ is }\mathcal F\text{-free}\bigr\}.\] The direction of this implication, the supremum, and the inclusion of \(d=1\) are part of the definition being checked; replacing any of them would change the statement.

Lemma 5.6 (Article PDF page 24, printed page 102) asserts \(\mathcal G_p(q)\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal G}_p(q)\) for all positive integers \(p\le q\). Both classes consist of positive \(p\)-weighted graphs: the weights on every pair of distinct vertices are integers in \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\). Their definitions impose different conditions on the number of vertices.

In Definition 5.4 (PDF page 23), \(G=(\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\},w)\) belongs to \(\mathcal G_p(q)\) if some enumeration and vertex weights \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) satisfy \(\sum_j a_j\ge q\) and, for each \(j\ge2\), the sorted backward edge weights \(\{w(v_i,v_j):i<j\}\) dominate componentwise the sorted multiset consisting of \(j-2\) copies of \(p(a_j-1)/a_j+1\) and one copy of \(a_j\). There is no restriction on \(a_1\) beyond its allowed range, and no bound \(m\le q\) in this definition.

Definition 5.2 (PDF page 21) requires \(m\le q\) for \(\widetilde{\mathcal G}_p(q)\). It also requires that, for every \(\eta>0\), there exist \(\delta,\gamma>0\) and vertex weights \(a_v\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\), of total weight at least \(q\), with the following validity property: for all sufficiently large \(n\), every graph \(H\) with a vertex partition \(\{W_v:v\in V(G)\}\), \(|W_v|\ge\eta n\), \(\alpha_p(H[W_v])\le\gamma|W_v|\), and every pair \((W_u,W_v)\) \(\delta\)-regular of density at least \((w(u,v)-1)/p+\eta\), contains a clique of size \(\sum_v a_v\). Here \(\alpha_p\) denotes the largest size of a \(K_p\)-free induced vertex subset. The lemma asserts literal membership of the original weighted graph in this size-bounded class, rather than membership of a smaller induced subgraph.

In the proof of Proposition 2.3 (Article PDF page 10), let \(N\ge12\) and consider the stationary \(N\)-particle Fleming–Viot system on \((0,\infty)\): each particle follows Brownian motion with drift \(-1\) until reaching zero, when it is moved to the position of a uniformly chosen other particle. Write \(\psi^N\) for its stationary law, \(\lambda_N>0\) for the finite death rate per particle, \(\tau_0=0<\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\) for the jump times, \(Y_n=X^N_{\tau_n}\) for the post-jump chain, and \(Q\) for that chain's transition kernel.

For every positive integer \(t\), the proof defines the probability measure \[\varphi^N=\frac{1}{N\lambda_Nt}\,\mathbb E_{\psi^N}\!\left[\sum_{0<\tau_n\le t}\delta_{Y_n}\right],\] using \(\mathbb E_{\psi^N}\#\{n:0<\tau_n\le t\}=N\lambda_Nt\). It then asserts the measure identity \[\lambda_Nt\,\varphi^NQ=\sum_{n\ge0}\mathbb E_{\psi^N}\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{\tau_n\le t\}}Q(Y_n,\cdot)\right]=\sum_{n\ge0}\mathbb E_{\psi^N}\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{\tau_n\le t\}}\delta_{Y_{n+1}}\right].\] The checked assertion is this finite-time normalization and indexing step used to prove stationarity; the definition uses strictly positive jump times, while the displayed sum starts at \(n=0\).

Lemma 2.14 (Article PDF page 13) assumes integers \(k_1\ge k_2\ge2\) and \(m\equiv k_1+k_2\pmod2\), and sets \(\lambda=(k_1-1,k_2-2)\). With the paper's representations \(V_{r_1,r_2;m}\) of the maximal compact group, define \[V_0=V_{k_1,k_2;m},\quad V_1=V_{k_1,4-k_2;m},\quad V_2=V_{k_2-1,3-k_1;m},\quad V_3=V_{3-k_2,3-k_1;m}.\] These are equations (2.3)–(2.6) on PDF page 11; \(V_i^\vee\) denotes the dual representation, \(K^\circ\) the identity component, and \(\mathfrak p_-\) the antiholomorphic tangent representation.

For the holomorphic (limit of) discrete-series representation \(X^1_{\lambda;m}\), the first table asserts, for every \(i,j\in\{0,1,2,3\}\), \[\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{K^\circ}\!\left(\bigwedge^j\mathfrak p_-\otimes V_i^\vee,X^1_{\lambda;m}\right)=\begin{cases}1,&(i,j)=(0,0)\text{ or }(3,3),\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] The permitted boundary \(k_2=2\) is included: no regularity assumption \(k_2>2\), and no identification of repeated labels in the table, is imposed.

Lemma 3.6 (Article PDF page 18) is stated in Section 3.1's setting of a holomorphic cuspidal Siegel modular form \(f\) of weight \((k_1,k_2)\), \(k_1\ge k_2\ge2\), with trivial central character and rational Fourier coefficients. Put \(\lambda_1=k_1-1\), \(\lambda_2=k_2-2\), and \(w=\lambda_1+\lambda_2\). The conjectural rank-four motive \(M(f)\) has weight \(w\), and \(\operatorname{Sym}^2M(f)\) has weight \(2w\). An integer is critical when the archimedean factors of the motive at that integer and of its dual at the complementary argument have no poles.

The lemma asserts that the critical integers of \(L(\operatorname{Sym}^2M(f),s)\) are exactly \[\{n\in\mathbb Z:n\text{ odd},\ \lambda_1+1\le n\le\lambda_1+\lambda_2\}\ \cup\ \{n\in\mathbb Z:n\text{ even},\ \lambda_1+\lambda_2+1\le n\le\lambda_1+2\lambda_2\}.\] Its proof gives the archimedean factor \[\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s)\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s-\lambda_2)\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s-2\lambda_2)\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s-\lambda_1)\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s+1-w)^2.\] The comparison in this finding concerns the claimed intervals versus all factors in that displayed product. The statement does not assume \(2\lambda_2\le\lambda_1\); the report's unverified arithmetic realization of a proposed example remains a separate evidence limitation.

Lemma 8.7, equation (179) (Article PDF page 52), takes an \((I,J)\) singlestep expression \(I_\bullet\) and an \((I,J)\) double coset \(p\) in the paper's singular Soergel-bimodule setting. Let \(\mathrm{BS}(I_\bullet)\) be its Bott–Samelson bimodule, choose a reduced expression \(Y_p\) for \(p\), and let \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\not<p}\) denote the morphism space modulo morphisms factoring through strictly lower double cosets. For subordinate paths \(t_\bullet\) ending at \(p\), write \(\operatorname{def}(t_\bullet)\) and \(\operatorname{poly}(t_\bullet)\) for their defect and polynomial weight; \(\mathrm{LL}(t_\bullet,y_\bullet)\) are the corresponding singular light leaves.

The printed identity is \[\sum_{\substack{(t_\bullet,y_\bullet)\subset I_\bullet\\\operatorname{term}(t_\bullet)=p}}v^{\deg\mathrm{LL}(t_\bullet,y_\bullet)}=\sum_{\substack{t_\bullet\subset I_\bullet\\\operatorname{term}(t_\bullet)=p}}\operatorname{poly}(t_\bullet)v^{\operatorname{def}(t_\bullet)}=\operatorname{gd}\!\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\not<p}(\mathrm{BS}(I_\bullet),\mathrm{BS}(Y_p))\right).\] Here \(\operatorname{gd}\) is the graded dimension over the ground field used in Theorem 4.16 (PDF page 21), not the graded rank over the coefficient ring \(R_p\). The assertion is checked with that convention, including identity expressions and the identity double coset, which the lemma does not exclude.

Section 5(7) (Article PDF page 34) claims an extension of Theorem 3.9 to every field \(K\) with \(\operatorname{char}K\ne2\). In the notation of that theorem, let \(C\) be a nonsingular compact \(k\)-section of \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(4)\), defined over \(K\), whose projection to \(\mathbb P^1\) has only simple critical points and distinct critical values. The corresponding points \(p_i\) on the limiting conic \(C_0:y^2=xz\) determine chords \(L_{i,j}\) through distinct \(p_i,p_j\). Let \(C_t\) be the degree-\(2k\) deformation of the multiple conic constructed in Proposition 3.6 (PDF pages 20–23).

The asserted arithmetic implication is that each specified chord \(L_{i,j}\) defined over \(K\) deforms to a bitangent of \(C_t\) defined over \(K\) when \(t\in K\). In particular, for \(K=\mathbb Q\), the claim would give a \(\mathbb Q\)-defined bitangent in the branch approaching that chord at every sufficiently small nonzero admissible rational parameter \(t\). Here admissible parameters have nonsingular \(C_t\), with the genericity required for ordinary bitangents. The assertion concerns rationality after specialization, not just coefficients in a formal power series over \(K\), and does not permit replacing the specified chord by an unrelated rational bitangent.

The proof of Lemma 4.7 (Article PDF pages 32–33) applies to every integer \(k\ge1\). It starts from the real rational curve parametrized by \(\theta\mapsto(\theta^k,(\theta-1)^{4k})\), and claims that one can choose arbitrarily small real polynomial perturbations \(R_1,R_2\), of degree \(k\), of \(\theta^k\) and \(1\), respectively, such that both polynomials have only simple roots and exactly \(\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) non-real roots.

These polynomials are then used in the parametrization \[\theta\longmapsto\left(\frac{R_1(\theta)}{R_2(\theta)},\frac{(\theta-1)^{4k}}{R_2(\theta)^4}\right).\] The text also asserts that the one-dimensional real part of the resulting curve has zero vertical tangents for odd \(k\) and two for even \(k\). The checked existence condition counts individual non-real roots, as printed, rather than conjugate pairs; the admissible range includes \(k=2\) and \(k=3\).

Lemma V.1 (Article PDF page 36, equations (V.1)–(V.3)) concerns smooth critical maps \(u_k\) for the paper's conformally invariant Dirichlet-plus-two-form functional into a closed smooth Riemannian manifold \(N\). In local conformal coordinates, let \(\delta_k\downarrow0\) and \(A(\eta,\delta_k)=B_\eta(0)\setminus B_{\delta_k/\eta}(0)\). Assume that the energy on each individual doubling annulus vanishes in the stated iterated limit: \[\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\lim_{k\to\infty}\sup_{\delta_k/\eta<\rho<2\rho<\eta}\int_{B_{2\rho}(x_k)\setminus B_\rho(x_k)}|du_k|_h^2\,d\mathrm{vol}_h=0.\] Coordinates are centered at \(x_k\), so this is the origin in the definition of \(A\).

Assume also that the limiting averaged radial length is finite, with \[\Lambda=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\limsup_{k\to\infty}\int_{\delta_k/\eta}^{\eta}\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\left|\partial_r u_k(r,\theta)\right|\,d\theta\,dr\ge0.\] The lemma asserts the existence of \(\eta_0>0\), \(0<\beta<2\), and \(C>0\), independent of \(k\), such that, for \(0<\eta<\eta_0\) and \(x\in A(\eta,\delta_k)\), \[|x|^2|\nabla u_k(x)|^2\le C\left[\left(\frac{|x|}{\eta}\right)^\beta+\left(\frac{\delta_k}{\eta|x|}\right)^\beta\right]\int_{A(2\eta,\delta_k)}|du_k|_h^2\,d\mathrm{vol}_h+\frac{C\Lambda^2}{\log^2(\eta^2/\delta_k)}.\] The maps must be defined on the larger annulus appearing in the right-hand side. The finite-stage bound uses the limiting \(\Lambda\) itself, including when \(\Lambda=0\), and contains no additional remainder.

Section II.1.1 (Article PDF pages 10–11) takes a harmonic map \(u:(\Sigma,h)\to N\subset\mathbb R^m\), a smooth ambient variation \(\phi:\Sigma\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(u_t=\pi_N(u+t\phi)\), where \(\pi_N\) is nearest-point projection in a tubular neighborhood. Write \(P_z\) for orthogonal projection onto \(T_zN\) and \(w=P_u\phi\). The argument asserts \(D\pi_{u+t\phi}=D\pi_{\pi_N(u+t\phi)}\), and hence \[\frac{du_t}{dt}=P_{u_t}\phi,\qquad\left.\frac{d^2u_t}{dt^2}\right|_{t=0}=(D_wP)_u\phi\tag{II.1–II.2}.\] The ambient field \(\phi\) is not required to be tangent to \(N\) along \(u\).

For the special target \(N=S^n\), the same section writes \(P_u=I-u\otimes u\) and asserts the differential identity \[dP_u=-\bigl(du\otimes u-u\otimes du\bigr)\tag{II.14}.\] These pointwise projection and differentiation identities are the checked assertions; the final Hessian formula is a separate consequence whose repair is addressed in the proof.

The proof on PDF pages 42–43 chooses a smooth radial cutoff \(\chi_t(x)=\chi(|x|/t)\) with \(\chi=1\) on \([0,1]\) and \(\chi=0\) on \([2,\infty)\). Its outer construction sets \[\breve a(x)=(1-\chi_R(x))a(x)+\chi_R(x)a_R\quad(|x|<R),\qquad a_R=\frac{1}{|B_R\setminus B_{R/2}|}\int_{B_R\setminus B_{R/2}}a,\] before inversion across the circle of radius \(R\). The asserted function space and this precise cutoff scale are both part of the claim under examination.

Let \(f_0\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)\) be nonzero, nonnegative and even, and let \(f_t\) solve \(\partial_tf_t=\Delta f_t+\operatorname{div}(xf_t)\). After normalizing its mass to one, fix \(t>0\). For \(0<p<1\), set \(q=p/(p-1)\) and \[F_t^{(p)}(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}(e^{\langle x,z\rangle}f_t(z))^{1/p}\,dz,\qquad f_t^\circ(x)=\left(\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\in\mathbb R^n}e^{\langle x,z\rangle}f_t(z)\right)^{-1}.\]

Equation (2.6) asserts, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\lim_{p\downarrow0}F_t^{(p)}(x)^q=f_t^\circ(x).\] Footnote 7 asserts finiteness of \(F_t^{(p)}(x)\) for every fixed \(t>0,x\) and all sufficiently small \(p>0\), on the stated ground that \(f_t\) has Gaussian decay. Theorem 1.2 imposes no Gaussian-tail or log-concavity hypothesis on \(f_0\).

Let \(f_t\) solve \(\partial_t f_t=\Delta f_t+\operatorname{div}(xf_t)\) for nonzero, nonnegative, even initial data, after reduction to bounded, compactly supported data. For fixed \(t>0\), the lower-bound portion of (2.11), manuscript p. 12, asserts positive constants \(c_1,\beta\) such that, for every \(x\), each of \(f_t(x),|\nabla f_t(x)|,|\Delta f_t(x)|\) is at least \(c_1(1+|x|+|x|^2)\gamma_\beta(x)\), where \(\gamma_\beta\) is the source positive Gaussian.

For \(0<p<1\) and the positive smooth density \(f_t\), put \(\alpha=1/p-1\). In the expansion of \(L_z[e^{\langle x,z\rangle/p}f_t(z)^\alpha]\) immediately after (2.11), manuscript p. 12, the source assigns the term multiplying \(\Delta\log f_t\) the power \(f_t^{1/p-2}=f_t^{\alpha-1}\). The identity is asserted for the evolved densities used in that differentiation.

The definition on article pp. 3 and 7 calls a map \(h\) log-Lipschitz when there exists \(C>0\) such that every pair in its domain with \(0<\|x-y\|<1/2\) satisfies
\[\|h(x)-h(y)\|\le C\|x-y\|\log\|x-y\|.\]
This printed definition is also used in condition (3) of Theorem 3.1.

Use the product-tube identification \(\Psi:\Omega\to[-1,1]\times\Sigma\) and metric \(\Psi^*(dt^2+\beta^2g_\Sigma)\). The sloshing modes solve \(\Delta w_k=0\) in \(\Omega\), \(\partial_\nu w_k=0\) on \(\partial_L\Omega\), and \(\partial_\nu w_k=\mu_k(\beta)w_k\) on \(\partial_V\Omega\). Fix \(K\in\mathbb N\) and \(0<\beta<\beta_0(K)\) as in Proposition 2.1, so the first \(K\) source-indexed eigenvalues are simple.

Corollary 2.2 (article p. 7) asserts
\[\exists\delta>0\ \forall u\in C^\infty(\Omega_{1/2},\mathbb R),\quad \min_{1\le k\le K}\|u-w_k\|_{C^1(\Omega_{1/2})}<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ u^{-1}(0)\text{ has a connected component isotopic to }\Sigma.\]
Its proof also asserts \(w_k\circ\Psi^{-1}(0,y)=0\) for these modes and nonvanishing gradient on the central slice.

In Step 4, article p. 8, fix \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Let \(g_\varepsilon=g\) on \(\Omega\) and \(g_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^2g\) on \(\Omega^c\), where \(g\) is the original smooth metric. For the chosen smooth positive factors \(\rho_{\varepsilon,h}\) tending to \(1\) on \(\Omega\) and \(\varepsilon\) on \(\Omega^c\), the construction sets
\[g_{\varepsilon,h}=\rho_{\varepsilon,h}^{2}g_\varepsilon\]
and asserts that this is a family of smooth metrics converging to \(g_\varepsilon\).

In the eigenvalue comparison on the compact Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\), let \(\Omega\) be the product tube with interface \(\partial_L\Omega\) and outer boundary portion \(\partial_V\Omega\). Define \[H_1=\{\psi\in H^1(M):\Delta\psi=0\text{ in }\Omega^c\},\quad H_2=\{\psi\in H^1(M):\psi|_{\Omega^c}\in H^1_{0,L}(\Omega^c),\ \psi=0\text{ in }\Omega\},\] where \(H^1_{0,L}(\Omega^c)\) is the \(H^1\)-closure of smooth functions vanishing near \(\partial_L\Omega\). Equations (4.6) and (4.8) assert \[H^1(M)=H_1\oplus H_2,\qquad\int_M\langle\nabla\psi,\nabla\psi^{\prime}\rangle_g\,dv_g=0\quad(\psi\in H_1,\ \psi^{\prime}\in H_2).\]

For \(g_\varepsilon=g\) on \(\Omega\) and \(g_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^2g\) on \(\Omega^c\), fix the index cutoff \(K\) and sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\) depending on \(K\). In a \((k+1)\)-dimensional subspace all of whose nonzero elements satisfy \[\frac{\int_M|\nabla_\varepsilon\psi|_\varepsilon^2\,dv_\varepsilon}{\int_{\partial M}\psi^2\,d\sigma_\varepsilon}\le\mu_k+1,\] equation (4.11) asserts \[\|\psi\|_{H^1(\Omega^c)}^2\le C\|\psi_1\|_{L^2(\partial_V\Omega)}^2\] with \(C\) independent of \(\varepsilon\). Here \(\psi_1=\psi\) in \(\Omega\) and solves \(\Delta\psi_1=0\) in \(\Omega^c\), \(\psi_1=\psi\) on \(\partial_L\Omega\), \(\partial_\nu\psi_1=0\) on \(\partial_V\Omega^c\), as in (4.7).

Let \(f\) be a holomorphic fibered partially hyperbolic diffeomorphism of a compact complex threefold \(M\), and let \(\mu\) be an ergodic Gibbs \(u\)-state. Write \(\widehat M=M/W^c\), let \(\widehat\mu\) be the quotient measure, and let \(d^c\) be the distance induced on center leaves by a fixed Riemannian metric. These are the standing hypotheses of Section 3.

Definition 3.1 calls \(f\) a \(\mu\)-center isometry if there exists a fiberwise measurably defined Riemannian metric \(g^c\) with one uniform constant \(C\) satisfying \(d_{g^c_{\widehat x}}(x_1,x_2)\le C d^c(x_1,x_2)\) for every center leaf and its points, and such that \(f:W^c(\widehat x)\to W^c(\widehat f\widehat x)\) is an isometry for \(\widehat\mu\)-almost every \(\widehat x\).

Definition 3.2 calls \(f\) a \(\mu\)-center contraction if there exists \(A\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\mu\) such that
\[\forall x\in A\ \forall x^\prime\in A\cap W^c(x),\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}d^c(f^nx,f^nx^\prime)=0,\]
and \(A\cap L^{cu}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)\) has full leafwise Riemannian volume in the entire center-saturated plaque \(L^{cu}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\). Proposition 3.3 (article p. 11) asserts that every ergodic Gibbs \(u\)-state satisfies one of these two alternatives.

Example 10.2, p. 25, specifies the only nonzero brackets as \[[e_1,e_2]=[e_3,e_4]=e_5\] and defines \[Fe_1=2e_1+e_3,\quad Fe_2=2e_2+e_4,\quad
 Fe_3=e_1+e_3,\quad Fe_4=e_2+e_4,\quad
 Fe_5=e_5,\quad Fe_6=e_6.\] The construction asserts that \(F\) is a Lie algebra automorphism, hence that \([FX,FY]=F[X,Y]\) for all \(X,Y\).

In Example 10.1, article p. 24, with the displayed basis of the complex Heisenberg Lie algebra and \([e_1,e_2]=e_3\), the source defines
\[\Gamma=\exp(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Z}\{e_1,\ldots,e_6\})\]
in exponential coordinates of the first kind and treats \(\Gamma\) as a lattice subgroup defining the stated group quotient.

For the line bundle \(L\) in Proposition 9.3, article p. 23, the construction specifies \(W=L^{\oplus2n}\) and then asserts
\[\deg(\det W)=n\deg L.\]

Fix \(s\in(0,1)\). The symmetric homogeneous kernel satisfies \(K(-h)=K(h)\), \(K(h)=|h|^{-n-2s}K(h/|h|)\), and \(\lambda|h|^{-n-2s}\le K(h)\le\Lambda|h|^{-n-2s}\), with \(0<\lambda\le\Lambda\). Use \(Lu(x)=2\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x-y)\,dy\).

Let \(\gamma\in(0,s)\), \(f\in L^\infty(B_1)\), \(\omega\in S^{n-1}\), \(\omega_n\ge\delta>0\), and let \(v\) be the viscosity solution in Lemma 4.12: \[L((x_n)_+^{s-1}v)=f\ \text{in }B_1\cap\{x_n>0\},\qquad\partial_\omega v=0\ \text{on }B_1\cap\{x_n=0\}.\] It asserts \(v\in C^{1,\gamma}\) on the half-ball of radius \(1/2\), with an expansion at each boundary point \(x_0\) of that half-ball, slope \(a(x_0)\cdot\omega=0\), and bounds \[|v(x)-v(x_0)-a(x_0)\cdot(x-x_0)|\le C(\|v\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)}+\|f\|_{L^\infty(B_1)})|x-x_0|^{1+\gamma},\quad |a(x_0)|\le C(\|v\|_\infty+\|f\|_\infty).\] The constants depend only on \(n,s,\lambda,\Lambda,\delta,\gamma\).

For \(\omega\ne e_n\), its proof sets \(S(x^{\prime},x_n)=(x^{\prime}+\omega^{\prime} x_n/\omega_n,x_n)\), \(w=v\circ S\), and \(\widetilde f=f\circ S\). Writing \(K(h)=|h|^{-n-2s}a(h/|h|)\), it prints \[\widetilde K(h)=\frac{|\omega_n|}{|\omega^{\prime}|}\left|\left(h^{\prime}-\frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega_n}h_n,h_n\right)\right|^{-n-2s}a\!\left(\frac{(h^{\prime}-\omega^{\prime} h_n/\omega_n,h_n)}{|(h^{\prime}-\omega^{\prime} h_n/\omega_n,h_n)|}\right).\] It asserts that the transformed equation and normal boundary condition hold on \(B_{3/4}\cap\{x_n\ge0\}\), and that this kernel has ellipticity constants controlled only by the stated parameters.

At scales \(r_k=\rho_0^k/2\), Lemma 4.14 obtains error \(C2^{-ks}\). Pages 42–43 correctly relate the resulting exponent to the radius by \[
 \rho_0^\gamma=2^{-s},
 \qquad
 2=\rho_0^{-\gamma/s},
 \qquad
 \gamma=\frac{s\log2}{\log(1/\rho_0)}.\]

The last paragraph of the proof of Theorem 1.5 on page 45 instead prints \(2=\rho_0^{-s/\gamma}\), and argues that decreasing \(\rho_0\) allows \(\gamma\) to approach \(s\). It then claims every exponent \[\alpha=\frac{s\gamma}{s+\gamma}<\frac{s}{2}.\]

For \(s\in(0,1)\), the source assumes a symmetric homogeneous kernel satisfying \[\lambda |h|^{-n-2s}\le K(h)\le\Lambda |h|^{-n-2s},
 \qquad K(-h)=K(h),\qquad

For arbitrary real \(w_1,w_2,\varphi_1,\varphi_2\), equation (5.8), article p. 54, asserts
\[\begin{aligned} &[(w_1\wedge\varphi_1)-(w_2\wedge\varphi_2)]^2+[(w_1\vee\varphi_1)-(w_2\vee\varphi_2)]^2\\&=(w_1-w_2)^2+(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)^2-2(w_1-\varphi_1)_+(w_2-\varphi_2)_-.\end{aligned}\]
Here \(a_+=\max(a,0)\), \(a_-=\max(-a,0)\), and \(\wedge,\vee\) denote minimum and maximum.

In Lemma 5.8, \(n\ge2\), \(R\ge8\), \(K\in C^2(S^{n-1})\) satisfies (1.2), \(u\) minimizes \(I_{B_R}\), and \(t\in(-1,1)\). For the source perturbation \(u_{R,t}\), equal to \(u\) outside \(B_R\), the following displayed identity uses the coefficient \(2\):

Definition 2.5 calls the finite-field obstruction absent if, over every finite residue field \(k\) of the base and every finite extension \(k'/k\), the number of \(k'\)-points of the source does not exceed that of the target. Lemma 2.6 states that a finite \(k\)-scheme \(Y\) embeds as a closed subscheme of a nonempty open \(V\subset\mathbb A_k^1\) if and only if this condition holds and \(Y\) is a closed subscheme of some smooth \(k\)-curve [CF, p. 8]. The first sentence of its proof on page 9 uses this condition to choose an embedding of the closed point of a connected \(Y\). The actual page images confirm this wording.

Theorem 1.3 assumes a bounded indecomposable set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) of finite perimeter with \[
 \mathcal H^{n-1}(B_r(x)\cap\partial^*\Omega)\leq A r^{n-1}
 \quad\text{for $\mathcal H^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in\partial^*\Omega$, $0<r<1$,}\] and a function \(u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^n)\) satisfying, distributionally, \[
 u=0\text{ a.e. outside }\Omega,\qquad
 \Delta u=c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\partial^*\Omega-\mathbf1_\Omega\,dx .\] Here \(c>0\), and \(\nu_x\) is the inward measure-theoretic normal. The conclusion is that \(\Omega\) is a ball, up to translation, with the corresponding quadratic torsion function.

The slit extension also includes a rectifiable set \(\Sigma\), an additional measure \(2c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\Sigma\), and the specified two-sided blow-up \[r^{-1}u(x+rz)\longrightarrow c\,|\nu_x\cdot z|
 \quad\text{for $\mathcal H^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in\Sigma$.}\]

The proof uses \[
 \phi_\epsilon(x)=
 \frac{u((1+\epsilon)x)-u((1-\epsilon)x)}{2\epsilon}-2u(x).\] Writing \(a=1+\epsilon\) and \(b=1-\epsilon\), the printed singular part of \(\Delta\phi_\epsilon\) is \[\frac{c}{2\epsilon}

       -b^2\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}b^{-1}\partial^*\Omega\bigr)

Let integers \(n\ge2\), \(1\le\ell\le n-1\) specify the state space of \(\ell\)-element sets \(E=\{h_1,\ldots,h_\ell\}\subset\mathbb Z_n\), and put
\[\Delta(E)=\prod_{j<r}|e^{2\pi i h_r/n}-e^{2\pi i h_j/n}|.\]
Allowed jumps move \(h\) to a vacant \(h+1\), modulo \(n\). The paper compares jump rates \(\Delta(E^\prime)/\Delta(E)\) with TASEP rates \(1\), for the same initial state or law; \(\operatorname{Traffic}(E)=\#\{h\in E:h+1\in E\}\).

A bead configuration on \(\mathbb T_n=[0,1)\times\mathbb Z_n\) has \(k\) beads on each string, neighboring strings interlace, and its occupation number is \(\ell\). The volume \(\operatorname{Vol}^{(n)}_{k,\ell}\) measures the corresponding ordered configurations. The empty case has separately defined weights \(\operatorname{Vol}^{(n)}_{0,\ell}=\binom n\ell\).

Let \(\mathbb T_n=[0,1)\times\mathbb Z_n\), and take mixed observation points \(w_i=(\alpha_i,t_i,h_i)\in\{b,o,u\}\times\mathbb T_n\), with the prescribed distinct-time convention. Here \(b,o,u\) denote a bead, an occupied point and an unoccupied point. Let \(B\) be the number of bead observations, \(k=B/n\), and \(I(w)\) the mixed configuration indicator in (5.5)–(5.6). For a nonempty bead configuration let \(\ell_o=\ell\), \(\ell_u=n-\ell\); if \(B=0\), let \(\ell_o,\ell_u\) count the distinct strings with occupied and unoccupied observations. With \(\theta\in\{0,1\}^2\), density (5.11) is \[g_N^{\lambda,\theta}(w)=\frac12(-1)^{(\theta_1+k+1)(\theta_2+n+\ell_o+1)}e^{-\lambda\ell_o}(1-(-1)^{\theta_1}e^{-\lambda})^{n-\ell_o-\ell_u}I(w).\]

For \(\beta=\lambda+\theta_1\pi i\) with \(1-e^{-\beta}\ne0\), put \[[t^{\prime}-t]_\alpha=t^{\prime}-t+\mathbf1_{\{t^{\prime}<t\}}+\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=o,t^{\prime}=t\}},\quad C^{\beta,\theta_2}(w,w^{\prime})=(-1)^{\theta_2\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=b,h^{\prime}=0\}}+\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=o\}}}\mathbf1_{\{h^{\prime}=h+\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=b\}}\}}\frac{e^{-\beta[t^{\prime}-t]_\alpha}}{1-e^{-\beta}}.\] Theorem 5.2 asserts \[(-1)^{(\theta_1+1)(\theta_2+n+1)}(1-e^{-\beta})^n\det[C^{\beta,\theta_2}(w_i,w_j)]_{i,j=1}^N=g_N^{\lambda,\theta}(w).\]

Lemma 5.4 asserts the corresponding formula with \(\zeta=e^{-\lambda}\ne1\), the same nonzero kernel denominators, and \[A^\zeta(w,w^{\prime})=(-1)^{\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=o\}}}\mathbf1_{\{h^{\prime}=h+\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=b\}}\}}\zeta^{\mathbf1_{\{t^{\prime}<t\}}+\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=o,t^{\prime}=t\}}},\quad B^{\zeta,\theta}(w,w^{\prime})=\frac{(-1)^{\theta_2\mathbf1_{\{\alpha=b,h^{\prime}=0\}}}}{1-(-1)^{\theta_1}\zeta}A^{(-1)^{\theta_1}\zeta}(w,w^{\prime}).\] Its printed prefactor is likewise \((-1)^{(\theta_1+1)(\theta_2+n+1)}(1-(-1)^{\theta_1}\zeta)^n\), with no factor \(1/2\).

The source chooses \(t=n-2\), \(\varepsilon=n-2-1/2-(n-d)/4\), and \(\delta=(n-d)/4\) in (3.12). Under the non-strict curvature bound \(\rho\le K\), it asserts that the first coefficient can be treated as nonnegative and the second as positive.

Let \((\varphi_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a continuous semigroup of holomorphic self-maps of \(\mathbb D\), with \(\varphi_0=\operatorname{id}\) and \(\varphi_{s+t}=\varphi_s\circ\varphi_t\). It induces composition operators \(C_{\varphi_t}\) on \(H^p(\mathbb D)\), \(1\le p<\infty\). The paper asks whether the span of generator eigenfunctions is norm dense for \(1\le p<\infty\), and weak-star dense in \(H^\infty\). For a non-elliptic semigroup it phrases this on the Koenigs domain \(\Omega=h(\mathbb D)\) as the completeness of \(\operatorname{span}\{e^{\lambda z}:e^{\lambda z}\in H^p(\Omega)\}\).

The introduction asserts that the analogous completeness questions consistently have negative answers for elliptic semigroups, and gives the common interior fixed point as its reason. This is an assertion about the elliptic analogue, not a claim that the non-elliptic exponential eigenfunction parametrization itself applies unchanged there.

Let \(E\) be an indecomposable degree-zero holomorphic bundle over a torus with a fixed compatible Hermitian metric \(g\). The unipotent construction uses a small parameter \(\delta\) and a frame \(w_j\) declared orthonormal for a metric \(g_\delta\). On article pp. 7–10 the proof asserts uniform equivalence with the fixed metric as \(\delta\to0\): constants \(c,C>0\), independent of sufficiently small \(\delta\), satisfy \(cg\le g_\delta\le Cg\). It uses this to transfer the \(O(\delta)\) antiholomorphic derivative estimate and keep the component transverse to the preceding filtration step bounded away from zero.

For the indecomposable bundle \(E\) over the torus in Lemma 3.3, article pp. 5–6, assume rank \(r\) and degree \(d>r+2\). Choosing a line bundle \(L\) of degree \(2\), the proof asserts \(\deg(E\otimes L^*)=d-2\) and uses this degree to invoke its global-generation criterion for \(E\otimes L^*\).

Definition 5.5, article p. 31, sets \(Z=\mathbb C[[t]]\), \(K=\mathbb C((t))\), and defines \(\operatorname{rank}(M)=\dim_K(K\otimes_ZM)\) for its modules. For the dimer algebra \(A_D\) with vertex set \(Q_0\), it also asserts \(\operatorname{rank}(M)=\operatorname{rank}_Z(M)/\#Q_0\). The modules \(M_I\) of Definition 5.7, containing one copy of \(Z\) at each circle-quiver vertex, are assigned rank \(1\). These assertions are presented as a single rank convention.

In the induction in Lemma 3.3, article p. 15, let \(r_{j+1}\gg r_j\gg1\), and let \(\{x_a\}_{a=0}^{k_{j+1}-1}\subset\partial B_{r_{j+1}/10}(0)\) be invariant under rotation by \(2\pi/k_{j+1}\). The annuli \(A_{r_j,2r_j}(x_a)\) are pairwise disjoint and avoid the origin. On \(D=\mathbb R^3\setminus\bigcup_a B_{r_j}(x_a)\), the proof asserts existence of a smooth function \(\eta:D\to[0,\infty)\) without critical points and satisfying all four conditions:

\[\begin{aligned}\eta(x)&=|x-x_0|^2&&\text{on }A_{r_j,2r_j}(x_0),\\\eta&\text{ is affine}&&\text{on }A_{r_j,2r_j}(x_a),\ 1\le a<k_{j+1},\\\eta(x)&=|x|^2&&\text{on }\mathbb R^3\setminus B_{100r_j}(0),\\\eta(x)&\ge\tfrac12|x-x_0|^2&&\text{for all }x\in D.\end{aligned}\]

Fix the \((1,k)\)-circle bundle \(\pi_{(1,k)}:S^3\times S^2\to N\) and its base metric \(h^\alpha\) from Section 6. For \(\beta\in[0,1]\), the metric \(g_\beta^\alpha\) is defined by retaining this base metric and using fiber length and connection \[f^\alpha((1-\beta)k)^2=1+\alpha^2(1-\beta)^2k^2\sin^2\psi,\qquad\eta_\beta^\alpha=(1-\beta)\eta_0^\alpha+\beta\eta_1,\quad\eta_1=Z_1^*.\] Let \(U_\beta=f^\alpha((1-\beta)k)^{-1}\partial_t\), and let \(F_2^{\alpha,\beta}=F_2^\alpha-\beta\alpha k\sin\psi\,\partial_t/f^\alpha(k)\) be the specified unit horizontal direction.

Proposition 6.7 asserts positive Ricci curvature for this smooth invariant family when \(0<\alpha<\alpha(k)\). Its concluding estimate asserts that, for every \(\beta\in[0,1]\), the determinant and trace of \(\alpha^2\operatorname{Ric}_{g_\beta^\alpha}\) restricted to \(\operatorname{span}\{U_\beta,F_2^{\alpha,\beta}\}\) are both greater than \(1/2\) when \(\alpha\le\alpha(k)\) is sufficiently small. It then infers a lower bound greater than one for the unscaled Ricci eigenvalues.

Proposition 2.1(4), article p. 8, asserts freeness of the specified circle action for all integer weights \((a,b)\) with \(\gcd(a,b)=1\) and \(a\ne0\). On the stated product end this combines the weight-\(a\) Hopf action on \(S^3\) and weight-\(b\) rotation on \(S^2\).

For the complete six-dimensional manifold constructed in Proposition 4.4, article p. 18, the assertion is
\[\forall\eta>0\ \exists(t_i),\quad t_i\to\infty,\qquad\operatorname{Vol}(B_{t_i}(p))=t_i^{3+\eta}\ \text{for all }i.\]
The printed quantifier covers every positive \(\eta\), with no small-exponent restriction.

In Step 4 of Lemma 4.2, article p. 23, the exterior steady incompressible Navier–Stokes solution is written \(u_1=u-a\), with \(a(x)=cx/|x|^n\) and \(p_a=-|a|^2/2\). For the source cutoff \(\eta\) and divergence-free extension \(\widetilde u_1\), equation (73) uses pressure \(\eta p-\eta p_a\) and includes the forcing interaction terms
\[-(\eta u\cdot\nabla)a-(\eta a\cdot\nabla)u.\]
The asserted identity concerns this subtraction-and-extension construction with the nonzero-flux field retained.

In the four-dimensional Dirichlet half-space setting, \(u,p\) satisfy \(-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0\), \(\operatorname{div}u=0\), zero velocity on the flat boundary and \(|u(x)|\le C/|x|\). Equation (51), article p. 17, defines
\[h(R)=-\int_{(\partial B_R)_+}(\partial_r u\cdot u-\tfrac12|u|^2u^r-pu^r)\,d\sigma\]
and asserts, for \(0<R_1<R_2\),
\[\int_{B_{R_2,+}\setminus B_{R_1,+}}|\nabla u|^2=h(R_2)-h(R_1).\]

For every morphism \(f:Y\to Z\) in \(\mathsf{Stk}_k\), Proposition 3.5.5(ii), article p. 40, asserts in particular
\[f_*:\mathsf{Shv}_{\mathsf{gr},\mathsf c}(Y)\longrightarrow\mathsf{Shv}_{\mathsf{gr},\mathsf c}(Z),\]
i.e. arbitrary direct image preserves the stated constructible small category.

Let \(A\) be a rigid monoidal category and \(M,N\in\operatorname{Mod}_A\). Let \(F:M\rightleftarrows N:G\) be an adjoint pair of functors between the underlying categories, with \(F\) left adjoint. Corollary A.4.7 asserts the equivalence of all four properties: \(F\) is left-lax as an \(A\)-module functor; \(G\) is right-lax as an \(A\)-module functor; \(F\) is strict; and \(G\) is strict. The corollary does not add continuity of \(G\). The preceding Lemma A.4.6 asserts lax-to-strict automaticity only for continuous lax functors.

For the finite base-field extension \(k_m/k_n\) of degree \(r\) and base-change morphism \(g:Y_m\to Y_n\), Lemma 2.7.5 asserts, for the objects \(F\) in its sheaf category,
\[g^*g_*F\simeq F^{\oplus r}.\]
This identical-copy formula appears on article p. 23 and is reused in the proof of Theorem 3.2.19, p. 35, without an additional hypothesis identifying all Galois pullbacks of \(F\) with \(F\).

Let \(Z_n\to Y_n\) be a smooth morphism in \(\operatorname{Stk}_{k_n}\), and let \(\operatorname{\check Cech}^{\bullet}(Z_n/Y_n)\) be its Čech nerve. Proposition 2.5.10 asserts that pullback, using either \(*\) or \(!\), induces equivalences \[\operatorname{Shv}^{\mathrm{gr}}(Y_n)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}\operatorname{Shv}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\operatorname{\check Cech}^{\bullet}(Z_n/Y_n)),\qquad \operatorname{Shv}^{\mathrm{gr},c}(Y_n)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}\operatorname{Shv}^{\mathrm{gr},c}(\operatorname{\check Cech}^{\bullet}(Z_n/Y_n)).\] Its stated hypothesis is smoothness; it does not require the morphism to be surjective or a covering.

Over \(\mathrm{pt}_n=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^n}\), Remark 2.4.6 defines \(\operatorname{Vect}^\omega\) to consist of chain complexes indexed by algebraic integers whose complex absolute values are \((q^n)^{w/2}\) for \(w\in\mathbb Z\). It identifies these with the possible Frobenius eigenvalues on objects of \(\operatorname{Shv}^{m}(\mathrm{pt}_n)\). It asserts a symmetric monoidal functor \(\operatorname{Shv}^{m}(\mathrm{pt}_n)\to\operatorname{Vect}^\omega\) that forgets the Frobenius action while retaining its eigenvalues, and through which the weight-grading functor factors.

The asserted variant is \[\operatorname{Shv}^\omega(Y_n)^{\mathrm{ren}}=\operatorname{Shv}^{m}(Y_n)^{\mathrm{ren}}\otimes_{\operatorname{Shv}^{m}(\mathrm{pt}_n)}\operatorname{Vect}^\omega.\] No restriction to nonnegative Tate weights or to an integral Frobenius-eigenvalue subcategory is added to the domain of this construction.

Let \((X^{n+1},g_+)\) be Poincaré–Einstein with conformal infinity \((M^n,h)\), \(n\ge2\). Fix \(0<\gamma<1\) and \(a=1-2\gamma\). Let \(y\) be the geodesic defining function for \(h\), and let \(w\) solve \(-\Delta_{g_+}w=n\) with \(w=\log y+O(y^\epsilon)\) for some \(\epsilon>0\). Put \(\rho=e^w\), \(\bar g=\rho^2g_+\), the Fefferman–Graham compactification.

For the extension potential defined in (2.20) by \[E(\rho)=-\Delta_{\bar g}(\rho^{a/2})\rho^{a/2}+\left(\gamma^2-\frac14\right)\rho^{a-2}+\frac{n-1}{4n}R_{\bar g}\rho^a,\] Lemma 2.11 and (2.28) assert \[E(\rho)=C_{n,\gamma}\rho^aR_{\bar g},\qquad C_{n,\gamma}=\frac{n^2-3-4n\gamma+\gamma^2}{4n(n-1)}.\] Proposition 2.13 then uses this coefficient as \(J_{\bar g}=C_{n,\gamma}R_{\bar g}\) in its weighted extension equation. The questioned claim is the displayed algebraic identification of that potential.

abla_{ ar g}U)+ho^aJ_{ ar g}U=0.\] Lemma 2.15 asserts that for \(r\in(0,1]\), \( eta>1\), and \(\eta\in C_0^\infty(B_r(x_+))\), there exists \(C=C(r,a, ar g)>0\) such that \[\int_{B_r(x_+)}ho^a|
abla_{ ar g}(\eta U^{ eta/2})|^2\,dv_{ ar g}\le C\int_{B_r(x_+)}ho^a(|
abla_{ ar g}\eta|^2+|J_{ ar g}|\eta^2)U^2\,dv_{ ar g}.\] The printed right-hand power is \(U^2\), and the listed constant dependencies omit both \( eta\) and the amplitude of \(U\).

For the entire permitted range \(-1<a<1\), the radial defining-function calculation in Lemma 4.1, equations (4.9)–(4.10), asserts
\[\partial_r\rho^a=\frac{a\rho^a}{r}(1+O(r))\ge0\]
along the inward ray for sufficiently small positive \(r\). Here \(\rho>0\) and \(a=1-2\gamma\) with \(0<\gamma<1\).

Let \(n\ge2\), \(m=n+1\), and let \((X^m,g_+)\) be a complete Poincaré–Einstein manifold with \(\operatorname{Ric}_{g_+}=-ng_+\), closed conformal infinity \((M^n,[h])\), and Fefferman–Graham compactification \(\bar g=\rho^2g_+=e^{2w}g_+\), where \(-\Delta_{g_+}w=n\) and \(\bar g|_M=h\). Assume the four geometric hypotheses at the beginning of Section 4, and double \((X,\bar g)\) along its totally geodesic boundary. Fix \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), put \(a=1-2\gamma\), and let \(f\in C^\infty(M)\) satisfy \(P_{2\gamma}f=0\) on \(B_1(p)\subset M\). The solution in Proposition 4.20 is the unique even \(U\in H^{1,a}\) satisfying \[-\operatorname{div}_{\bar g}(\rho^a\nabla_{\bar g}U)+\rho^aJ_{\bar g}U=0,\qquad U|_M=f,\qquad J_{\bar g}=C_{n,\gamma}R_{\bar g},\] with the frequency bound \[\frac{\int_{B_1(p_+)}\rho^a|\nabla_{\bar g}U|^2\,d\operatorname{vol}_{\bar g}}{\int_{\partial B_1(p_+)}\rho^aU^2\,d\sigma_{\bar g}}\le\Lambda.\]

Proposition 4.20 asserts that for every \(\epsilon>0\) there exist \(\delta(\epsilon,m,a,\Lambda,\bar g)>0\) and \(r_0(\epsilon,m,a,\Lambda,\bar g)>0\) with the following property. If \(x_+\in Z(U)\cap B_{1/2}(p_+)\), \(0<r<r_0\), and a homogeneous polynomial \(P\) with \((m-2)\)-symmetries satisfies \[\int_{\partial B_1(0_+)}\rho^aP^2\,d\sigma_{\bar g}=1,\qquad\int_{\partial B_1(0_+)}\rho^a(U_{x_+,r}-P)^2\,d\sigma_{\bar g}\le\epsilon,\] then there is \(\widetilde U\in C^{2m^2}(B_{2r/3}(x_+))\), equal to \(U\) on the positive half-ball, such that \(\|\widetilde U_{x_+,r}-P\|_{C^{2m^2}(B_{2/3}(0_+))}<\epsilon\).

Writing the one-sided Taylor expansion \(U=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k_0}c_\ell y^\ell+R_{k_0}\), the proof defines \(\widetilde U=U\) for \(y\ge0\), and \[\widetilde U=\sum_{\substack{0\le\ell\le k_0\\\ell\ \mathrm{odd}}}(-c_\ell)y^\ell+\sum_{\substack{0\le\ell\le k_0\\\ell\ \mathrm{even}}}c_\ell y^\ell+R_{k_0}\quad(y<0),\] and asserts the required \(C^{2m^2}\) regularity for this construction.

At the interpolation step on article pp.23–24, the available profile has \(F-1\in C^{s-2,\beta}_{-q}\). Equations (7.5)–(7.7) interpolate \(F(\cdot,\rho)-1\) at \(s-1\) nodes by a polynomial of degree \(s-2\) and assert that an intermediate point \(\Phi(u,\rho)\in[u_0,u_s]\) satisfies
\[R(u,\rho)=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{s-1}(u-u_i)}{(s-2)!}\,\partial_u^{s-2}F(\Phi(u,\rho),\rho).\]

For the pp-wave metric \(\bar g=-2\,du\,dt+F\,du^2+|dy|^2\), Theorem 3.3, article p.6, quantifies over any spacelike initial-data slice in that spacetime and asserts the energy-density formula
\[\mu=-\tfrac12F^{-1}\Delta_\Sigma F.\]
This assertion is not restricted to the slice \(t=0\); it does not impose the asymptotic-flatness assumptions of the separate main rigidity theorems.

In (6.8), article p.18, put \(f=|\nabla u|^{-1}>0\), and write the shift as a column vector \(Y\). For the positive-definite metric matrix
\[G=\begin{pmatrix}f^2+|Y|^2&Y^T\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\]
the printed inverse has the blocks
\[G^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}f^{-2}&-f^{-2}Y^T\\-f^{-2}Y&I+YY^T\end{pmatrix}.\]

Write \(D(n)\) for strict partitions of \(n\), \(O(n)\) for partitions with odd parts, and \(\ell(\lambda)\) for the number of parts. The parity convention is that \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\) when \(n-\ell(\lambda)\) is even. For a strict partition, \(z_\lambda=\prod_j\lambda_j\). The double cover used on page 33 has central element \(z\) and generators \(t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1}\) with \[
 z^2=1,\qquad t_j^2=z,\qquad (t_jt_{j+1})^3=z,\qquad
 t_jt_k=zt_kt_j\quad (|j-k|>1).\] A spin character has \(z\) acting as \(-1\). For \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\) the self-associate irreducible character \(\varphi^\lambda\) of \(\widetilde S_n\) restricts as \(\psi^\lambda_++\psi^\lambda_-\) to \(\widetilde A_n\), with distinct irreducible constituents interchanged by odd conjugation. Basic spin characters correspond to \(\lambda=(n)\).

For every nonbasic spin character \(\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}^-(\widetilde A_n)\), Theorem 7.15 asserts that there are an integer \(1\le m<n\), \(m\ne n/2\), and \(\eta\in\operatorname{Irr}^-(\widetilde A_{n-m,m})\) with \[[\chi\!\downarrow_{\widetilde A_{n-m,m}}:\eta]=1,\qquad\mathbb Q(\chi)=\mathbb Q(\eta),\] and with one of two alternatives. Either \(\mathbb Q(\chi)=\mathbb Q\), \(\chi\) extends to \(\widetilde S_n\), and \(\eta\) extends to \(\widetilde S_{n-m,m}\); or \([\mathbb Q(\chi):\mathbb Q]=2\), neither character has the respective extension, and \(\chi^{\mathcal G}=\chi^{\widetilde S_{n-m,m}}\), \(\eta^{\mathcal G}=\eta^{\widetilde S_{n-m,m}}\), with \(\mathcal G\) denoting Galois conjugation. The theorem further asserts self-normalization of the subgroup in \(\widetilde S_n\) and the inductive Feit condition when \(n\ne6\).

Write \(D(n)\) for strict partitions of \(n\), \(O(n)\) for partitions with odd parts, and \(\ell(\lambda)\) for the number of parts. The parity convention is that \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\) when \(n-\ell(\lambda)\) is even. For a strict partition, \(z_\lambda=\prod_j\lambda_j\). The double cover used on page 33 has central element \(z\) and generators \(t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1}\) with \[
 z^2=1,\qquad t_j^2=z,\qquad (t_jt_{j+1})^3=z,\qquad
 t_jt_k=zt_kt_j\quad (|j-k|>1).\] A spin character has \(z\) acting as \(-1\). For \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\) the self-associate irreducible character \(\varphi^\lambda\) of \(\widetilde S_n\) restricts as \(\psi^\lambda_++\psi^\lambda_-\) to \(\widetilde A_n\), with distinct irreducible constituents interchanged by odd conjugation. Basic spin characters correspond to \(\lambda=(n)\).

For an even partition \(\mu\in P_{\bar0}(n)\), let \(\widetilde C_\mu\) be the inverse image of its symmetric-group conjugacy class, with canonical lift \(\widetilde s^\mu\). Lemma 7.3 asserts that \(\widetilde C_\mu\) is one \(\widetilde A_n\)-class when \(\mu\notin D_{\bar0}(n)\cup O(n)\), and splits into exactly two classes represented by \(\widetilde s^\mu,z\widetilde s^\mu\) when \(\mu\in D_{\bar0}(n)\cup O(n)\).

For \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\), Theorem 7.5 prints \[\psi_\pm^\lambda(\widetilde s^\mu)=\begin{cases}2^{(\ell(\mu)-\ell(\lambda)-2)/2}[Q_\lambda,p_\mu],&\mu\in O(n),\\\pm i^{(n-\ell(\lambda))/2}\sqrt{z_\lambda}/2,&\mu=\lambda,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Here \(Q_\lambda,p_\mu\) and their pairing are the symmetric-function quantities used in the character formula. The cases are stated without excluding \(\mu=\lambda\) from the first branch when \(\lambda\) also belongs to \(O(n)\).

Section 2.1.2 works in the category \(\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z}\) of complexes of internally \(\mathbb Z\)-graded abelian groups. Write \(\mathcal D^\mathbb Z\) for its derived category. The polynomial algebra \[\Sigma=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathbb Z(n)=\mathbb Z[t]\] has \(t\) in cohomological degree zero and internal degree \(-1\), with primitive coproduct \(t\mapsto t\otimes1+1\otimes t\). The square-zero differential graded algebra on page 7 is \[
 I=\mathbb Z(-1)[-1],\qquad E=\mathbb Z\oplus I,\qquad I^2=0.\] In cohomological notation its generator \(\epsilon\) has degree \(1\) and internal degree \(1\); all differentials are zero. The source uses the right-induced projective model structure on \(E\)-modules, and a left-induced model structure on \(\Sigma\)-modules whose weak equivalences are the underlying quasi-isomorphisms. Both present the respective usual derived module categories.

Give \(\mathbb Z\) the strict \(\Sigma\)–\(E\) bimodule structure defined by the two augmentations. Definition and Lemma 2.9, through (2.7)–(2.9), assert that the derived functor of
\[\mathbb Z\otimes_E-:\operatorname{Mod}_E(\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z})^{\mathrm r}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_\Sigma(\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z})^{\mathrm l}\]
is fully faithful.

For the Fourier mode \(e^{i(\alpha z-n\theta)}\), write \(\lambda=-i\omega\), \(\gamma=\alpha W-nV/r-\omega\). Equation (1.13), article p.4, gives a reconstruction matrix whose upper-right entry is printed as \(i\alpha r\omega+in\alpha V+\alpha^3rW\). The following assertion says this matrix is invertible for real smooth profiles \(V,W\), \(r>0\), \(n,\alpha>0\), and \(\operatorname{Im}\omega>0\). This general reconstruction is used before the separate Assumption A.

For the fixed Fourier mode in Lemma 3.5 and \(1<Q<2\), the forcing estimate (3.35), article p.31, invokes
\[\|\bar\omega\cdot\nabla u\|_2\lesssim\|\bar\omega\|_p\|\nabla u\|_Q,\qquad\frac12=\frac1p+\frac1Q,\]
as a Hölder estimate contributing to the claimed \(L^Q\cap H^k\) semigroup growth bound.

Assume the vortex background satisfies Assumption A: \(\Omega=V/r\) and \(W\) are smooth on \([0,\infty)\), all odd derivatives vanish at zero, all derivatives tend to zero at infinity, and the pitch satisfies \(0<\inf q<\sup q<\infty\). For the fixed \(r_0,\beta>0\), \(b^{\prime}(r_0)=\Lambda^{\prime}(r_0)=0\), \(b_0=b(r_0)>0\), \(\Lambda^{\prime\prime}(r_0)>0\), and no other finite \(r\) has \(\Lambda(r)=\Lambda(r_0)\). Let \(k(r)\) be the potential in the transformed Rayleigh equation \(\varphi^{\prime\prime}-k\varphi=0\).

For every \(B\ge1\), Lemma 2.9 assumes \(|\omega-\omega_{\rm app}|\le Bn^{-1/2}\) and asserts that there is \(C\ge1\) such that, for sufficiently large \(n\) depending on \(B\), \[\operatorname{Re}k(r)=O(n^{3/2})\quad\text{uniformly when }Cn^{-3/4}\le|r-r_0|\le C^{-1}n^{-1/2}.\] The assertion is the two-sided size bound printed in (2.58), over the entire indicated radial interval.

Assume the vortex background satisfies Assumption A: \(\Omega=V/r\) and \(W\) are smooth on \([0,\infty)\), all odd derivatives vanish at zero, all derivatives tend to zero at infinity, and the pitch satisfies \(0<\inf q<\sup q<\infty\). For the fixed \(r_0,\beta>0\), \(b^{\prime}(r_0)=\Lambda^{\prime}(r_0)=0\), \(b_0=b(r_0)>0\), \(\Lambda^{\prime\prime}(r_0)>0\), and no other finite \(r\) has \(\Lambda(r)=\Lambda(r_0)\). Let \(k(r)\) be the potential in the transformed Rayleigh equation \(\varphi^{\prime\prime}-k\varphi=0\).

With \(p_0=p(r_0)\), write \(\widehat\omega\) for the correction to \(\omega_{\rm app}\), and \(\mu_m\) for the fixed-mode correction in (1.28). Define \[k_{\rm err}(r)=k(r)-(k_0+k_2(r-r_0)^2),\quad\xi=(r-r_0)n^{3/4},\quad K_{\rm err}(\xi)=n^{-3/2}k_{\rm err}(r).\] For fixed \(B\ge1\), on the prescribed correction scale with \(|\mu_m|+|r-r_0|\le Bn^{-1/2}\), equations (2.7) and (A.3) assert \[k_{\rm err}(r)=i n^2\widehat\omega\frac{2p_0}{\sqrt{b_0}}+n(1+n^3(r-r_0)^4)O(1),\] where the remainder constant may depend on \(B\). Equations (2.76) and (2.87) print the corresponding rescaled expansion \[K_{\rm err}(\xi)=i n^{1/2}\widehat\omega\frac{2p_0}{\sqrt{b_0}}+(1+|\xi|^4)O(n^{-1/2}),\] for \(|\widehat\omega|\le n^{-1/2}\), \(|\xi|\le n^{1/4}\).

For \(-\pi/2<\zeta<\pi/2\), define the closed operator on \(L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)\) by \[L_\zeta\Psi=\Psi^{\prime\prime}-e^{2i\zeta}x^2\Psi,\qquad D(L_\zeta)=\{f\in L^2:L_0f\in L^2\},\] with the graph norm, equivalently the \(H^2\) norm plus \(\|x^2f\|_2\). Lemma 2.5 asserts that its spectrum consists of algebraically simple eigenvalues \(-e^{i\zeta}(2m-1)\), \(m=1,2,\ldots\), with eigenspace spanned by \(G_m(e^{i\zeta}\,\cdot)\), where \(G_m\) is the corresponding Hermite function. The full-angle argument is part of the printed eigenspace assertion.

Assumption A, article p.4, requires the pitch \(q(r)=-(rV(r))^\prime/W^\prime(r)\) to satisfy
\[0<\inf q<\sup q<\infty.\]
The next paragraph lists the displayed Batchelor profiles, whose pitch is a positive constant, as an example satisfying this assumption.

For \(d\ge2\) and \(f,g\in\operatorname{Rat}_d(\mathbb C)\), Definition 3.1 calls \(f,g\) intertwined if there exists an algebraic curve \(Z\subset\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\), possibly reducible, invariant under \(f\times g\), such that both coordinate projections are surjective. A rational map is simple when it has exactly \(2d-2\) critical values.

For \(d\ge4\), Theorem 3.3 asserts a Zariski-open set \(W_d\subset\operatorname{Rat}_d(\mathbb C)\) consisting of simple maps, with the property that whenever \(f\in W_d\) and a simple \(g\in\operatorname{Rat}_d(\mathbb C)\) are intertwined, \(f\) and \(g\) are Möbius conjugate. This is used as the nonempty generic rigidity statement; the definition does not require an irreducible curve with both projections dominant on that same component.

Let \(d\ge2\), and let \(f_V,g_V\) be non-isotrivial algebraic families of degree-\(d\) rational maps over the same irreducible curve \(V\), neither a flexible Lattès family. Assume infinitely many parameters make both maps postcritically finite. After normalization and a finite ramified cover, take \(V\) smooth with marked critical points \(a_1,\ldots,a_{2d-2}\) for \(f_V\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_{2d-2}\) for \(g_V\). In the proof of Theorem 3.4, \(\mu\) is the probability measure proportional to both nonzero bifurcation measures.

For a marked critical point \(c\), write \(\xi_{c,n}(t)=f_t^n(c(t))\). The printed PCE(\(\lambda\)) definition requires a constant \(C>0\) such that \[\left|\frac{d\xi_{c,n}}{dt}(t_0)\right|\ge C\lambda^n\quad\text{for every marked }c\text{ and every }n\ge0.\] The printed PR(\(s\)) definition requires an integer \(N>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(f_{t_0}^n(c(t_0)),C_{t_0})\ge n^{-s}\quad\text{for every marked }c\text{ and every }n\ge N,\] where \(C_{t_0}\) is the full critical set. The same definitions apply to \(g_V\). Assertions (4)–(5) claim that for \(\mu\)-almost every parameter both maps have PCE(\(\lambda_2\)) for some \(1<\lambda_2<\sqrt d\) and PR(\(s\)) for some \(s>0\). The definitions quantify over passive as well as active marked critical points.

Let \(u_n\) count zero multipliers among the fixed points of \(f^n\), and let \(m_\ell\) count critical cycles of exact length \(\ell\). At the end of the proof of Lemma 3.5, article p.16, the printed counting and inversion formulas are
\[u_n=\sum_{\ell\mid n}m_\ell,\qquad m_n=\sum_{\ell\mid n}\mu(\ell)u_{n/\ell},\]
where \(\mu\) is the Möbius function.

Let \(\alpha,\beta\) be a pair of filling multicurves in the Section 6.1 construction on the closed orientable genus-\(g\) surface, realizing intersection degree \(1\le d\le3g-3\). Let \(X\) be their geometric intersection matrix and \[\Omega=\begin{pmatrix}0&X\\X^\mathsf T&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Theorem 14 asserts that \(T_\alpha\circ T_\beta\) is pseudo-Anosov with stretch factor of degree \(2d\). Its proof asserts the criterion \[\dim\Omega>\sigma(\Omega+2I)+\operatorname{null}(\Omega+2I)>\dim\Omega-2d.\]

In Case 2, \(g<d<2g\) and \(f=2g-d\) separating curves are removed from the \(k=g-1\) construction. The retained two-by-two blocks have pairwise distinct parameters \(y_i\ge12\); the resulting one-by-one blocks may have any positive integer parameters, subject to the construction's distinctness requirements. The central parameter is specialized so that the characteristic polynomial is irreducible. The theorem is stated for examples described by those rules, without an added requirement that one one-by-one block have parameter \(3\), although its signature proof subsequently imposes that value.

Let \(M\) be a square integer matrix and \(N\) its principal submatrix obtained by deleting the first row and column. Assume \(M,N\) have no common eigenvalue and \(M\) has a simple eigenvalue \(\rho\). For every positive integer \(p\) and nonzero integer \(c\), Proposition 7 asserts irreducibility in \(\mathbb Z[t,y]\) of the characteristic polynomial of \(\widetilde M=M+cy^pE_{11}\), where \(E_{11}\) has only its top-left entry nonzero and equal to one. Remark 8 asserts the same irreducibility after replacing \(t\) by \(t^n\) for every positive integer \(n\), under the same hypotheses. The simple eigenvalue \(\rho\) is not required to be nonzero.

The opening proof of Theorem 5 asserts that for every \(g\ge3\) and integer \(1\le d\le3g-3\), the preceding filling-multicurve construction has a parameter \(y\) for which the full characteristic polynomial \(\chi_{XX^\mathsf T}(t,y)\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb Z[t,y]\). It then asserts irreducibility of \(\chi_{XX^\mathsf T}(t^2,y)\), and infinitely many specializations with this polynomial irreducible of degree \(2d\). If \(\mu\) is the leading eigenvalue, the resulting full substituted characteristic polynomial is identified as the minimal polynomial of \(\sqrt\mu\).

The earlier low-degree construction includes \(2\le d<g\), with \(f=g-1-d\) and \(f+1\) diagonal block parameters set equal to one. The opening assertion is made about the full characteristic polynomial of this construction, without explicitly replacing it by the irreducible factor carrying the leading eigenvalue. The proof treats \(g=2\) separately by the cited lower-genus examples.

The global assumptions include \(n>2s\), \(0<s<1\), symmetry and ellipticity \[\lambda |x-y|^{-n-2s}\le K(x,y)=K(y,x)\le\Lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s},
 \qquad Lu(x)=2\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x,y)\,dy.\]

In the locally frozen setup, \(L\) is translation invariant and \(\widetilde L\) agrees with it only for jumps shorter than \(1/2\). The barrier satisfies \(\widetilde L\psi=0\) in the domain \(D\) from (6.1), while (6.2) retains \(L\psi=(L-\widetilde L)\psi\). For an \(L\)-harmonic \(v\), the first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 6.6, article p.32, treats \(v-c_0\psi\) as a homogeneous \(L\)-solution when invoking Proposition 6.2(iii), with the source coefficient \(c_0\) given by the average of \(v/\psi\) on \(\Omega_R\).

Let \(0<s<1\), \(n>2s\), and let \(K\) be symmetric with \(\lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\le K(x,y)\le\Lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\). Use \(Lu(x)=2\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x,y)\,dy\). Where invoked, condition (1.3) is Hölder continuity under simultaneous translation of both kernel arguments, with exponent \(0<\sigma<s\), on the stated set.

Let \(\Omega\) be a domain whose complement satisfies the measure-density condition with constant \(c_0>0\), let \(0<p\le s\), \(q>n/(s+p)\), and set \(a=1/2+p/n-1/q\). For \(\Omega_R(x_0)=\Omega\cap B_R(x_0)\), Remark 3.2 defines \[X(\Omega_1)=\{f\in(H^s_{\Omega_1}(\mathbb R^n))^*:\|f\|_{X(\Omega_1)}<\infty\},\] with \[\|f\|_{X(\Omega_1)}=\sup_{\substack{x_0\in\Omega_{1/2}\\0<R<1/2}}\ \sup_{\substack{w\in H^s_{\Omega_R(x_0)}(\mathbb R^n)\\w\ne0}} |\{w\ne0\}\cap B_R(x_0)|^a\frac{\int_{\Omega_R(x_0)}fw\,dx}{[w]_{H^s(\mathbb R^n)}}.\] It asserts that \(f\in X(\Omega_1)\) may replace \(d_\Omega^{s-p}f\in L^q(\Omega_1)\) in the main theorems, with their other hypotheses retained. The displayed norm multiplies by the support-measure power.

Let \(0<s<1\), \(n>2s\), and let \(K\) be symmetric with \(\lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\le K(x,y)\le\Lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\). Use \(Lu(x)=2\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x,y)\,dy\). Where invoked, condition (1.3) is Hölder continuity under simultaneous translation of both kernel arguments, with exponent \(0<\sigma<s\), on the stated set.

In the lower Green-function argument, take the \(C^{1,\alpha}\) domain and kernel of Theorem 1.1, and \(x,y\in\Omega\) with \(d_\Omega(x)<|x-y|\le d_\Omega(y)\). Let \(x_0\in\partial\Omega\) satisfy \(|x-x_0|=d_\Omega(x)\), and set \(R=2|x-y|\). Choose \(z\in\Omega\) with \(R\le|y-z|\le2R\), \(R<|x_0-z|\le2R\), and \(B_{\kappa R}(z)\subset\Omega\setminus B_R(x_0)\), where \(\kappa>0\) depends only on \(\Omega\). Define \[Lu=0\ \text{in }\Omega_{R/4}(x_0),\qquad u=1\ \text{on }B_{\kappa R}(z),\qquad u=0\ \text{outside }\Omega_{R/4}(x_0)\cup B_{\kappa R}(z).\]

After obtaining \(u\ge c_0R^{-s}d_\Omega^s\) on \(\Omega_{R/8}(x_0)\), the proof considers the branch \(x\notin\Omega_{R/8}(x_0)\). It selects \(B_{\eta R}(x_*)\subset\Omega_{R/8}(x_0)\) with \(R/16\le d_\Omega\le R/8\), and asserts by a Harnack chain from that ball to \(x\) that \(u(x)\ge c_1>0\), with constants depending only on the stated structural data.

Let \(0<s<1\), \(n>2s\), and let \(K\) be symmetric with \(\lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\le K(x,y)\le\Lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\). Use \(Lu(x)=2\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x,y)\,dy\). Where invoked, condition (1.3) is Hölder continuity under simultaneous translation of both kernel arguments, with exponent \(0<\sigma<s\), on the stated set.

Fix \(\sigma\in(0,s)\), \(\varepsilon\in(0,\sigma)\), \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(R>0\). Suppose (1.3) holds with \(A=B_R(x_0)\), and \(u\) is a weak solution of \(Lu=f\) on that ball, with \(f\in L^q(B_R)\), \(q>n/(2s)\), in the source's local energy and tail class. Set \(\beta=\min\{2s-n/q,1+\sigma-\varepsilon\}\). For every \(0<\rho\le R/2\), Lemma 5.5 asserts \[\frac{1}{|B_\rho|}\int_{B_\rho}|u-(u)_{\rho,x_0}|\,dx\le C(\rho/R)^\beta\left(\frac{1}{|B_R|}\int_{B_R}|u-(u)_{R,x_0}|\,dx+\operatorname{Tail}(u-(u)_{R,x_0};R,x_0)+R^{2s-n/q}\|f\|_{L^q(B_R)}\right).\] Here \((u)_{r,x_0}\) retains the source's convention of averaging \(|u|\), and \(C\) depends only on \(n,s,\lambda,\Lambda,\sigma,\varepsilon,q\). The approximant is a constant even when \(\beta>1\).

Let \(0<s<1\), \(n>2s\), and let \(K\) be symmetric with \(\lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\le K(x,y)\le\Lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s}\). Use \(Lu(x)=2\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x,y)\,dy\). Where invoked, condition (1.3) is Hölder continuity under simultaneous translation of both kernel arguments, with exponent \(0<\sigma<s\), on the stated set.

Let \(\sigma\in(0,s)\), \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), \(R>0\), assume (1.3) on \(A=B_R(x_0)\), and let \(u\) solve \(Lu=f\) there in the local energy and finite-tail class, with \(f\in L^q(B_R)\), \(q>n/(2s)\). For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,\sigma)\), Proposition 3.5 asserts \(u\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^\beta(B_R)\), \(\beta=\min\{2s-n/q,1+\sigma-\varepsilon\}\), and \[[u]_{C^\beta(B_{R/2})}\le CR^{-\beta}\left(R^{-n}\|u\|_{L^1(B_R)}+\operatorname{Tail}(u;R,x_0)+R^{2s-n/q}\|f\|_{L^q(B_R)}\right).\] The parameter range includes \(2s-n/q=1\) and therefore the displayed \(C^1\) conclusion, without a noninteger-exponent exclusion.

The example after Theorem 1.8, article p.9, lists kernels
\[K(x,y)=|x-y|^{-n-2s}\bigl(a_x((x-y)/|x-y|)+a_y((x-y)/|x-y|)\bigr)\]
with the stated even angular densities and coefficient bounds/regularity as satisfying the additional requirement that every completely frozen kernel from (1.9) is homogeneous of degree \(-n-2s\).

For the equation \(Lu=f\), Definition 2.1, article p.11, uses the weak inequality (2.2) against every nonnegative admissible test. Its printed supersolution rule replaces \(u\) alone by \(-u\), while leaving \(f\) unchanged. Thus the rule applies the subsolution inequality to \((-u,f)\), rather than reversing both entries.

The global assumptions include \(n>2s\), \(0<s<1\), symmetry and ellipticity \[\lambda |x-y|^{-n-2s}\le K(x,y)=K(y,x)\le\Lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s},
 \qquad Lu(x)=2\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x,y)\,dy.\]

With \(G\) normalized as the inverse Green kernel in Definition 9.1, equation (9.6), article p.53, asserts for \(x\in\Omega\), \(z\in\Omega^c\),
\[P(x,z)=\int_\Omega G(x,y)K(z,y)\,dy.\]
The factor in this printed Poisson-kernel formula is \(1\) under the operator normalization above.

Let \(E\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a bounded Borel set and fix \(k\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}\). In the inductive profile argument preceding (5.15), \(f\in\mathcal L_{2,u}\) is defined on \([0,1]\), is nondecreasing and piecewise linear, is \(2\)-Lipschitz, vanishes at zero and satisfies \(f(x)\ge ux\).
