The profile is declared to map \([0,1]\) to \([0,d]\) and is defined by \[f(j/\ell)=\beta_1+\cdots+\beta_j\quad(0\le j\le\ell),\] with linear interpolation between successive grid points. This profile is then used in the asserted \(d\)-Lipschitz combinatorial construction, without a factor \(1/\ell\) in the grid values.

Definition 2.2 calls \(\rho\) \((\delta,s,r)\)-robust if \(\rho(E)>r\) implies \(|E|_\delta>\delta^{-s}\). For \(0<\delta<1\) and \(\eta>0\), Lemma 3.10, article p.18, declares the projected probability measure \((\delta,t/d+\eta,\delta^{-\eta})\)-robust and uses this clause for its adaptedness assertion.

In the joint-projection-partition argument of Lemma 3.11, article p.19, the proof asserts that each dyadic cube meets \(O_d(a^d)\) atoms of the joint partition, where \(a\) is the small separation parameter of the source directions. It uses this incidence bound to control the conditional entropy with the dyadic partition conditioned on the joint partition.

For each norm on \(\mathbb R^2\), form the unit-distance graph with vertex set \(\mathbb R^2\) and an edge between points at norm-distance \(1\). Section 8, article p.29, asserts that the minimum of the chromatic numbers of these graphs over all planar norms is \(2\).

For distinct collinear points \(a,b\) of the norm unit ball, the preliminary discussion on article p.7 asserts the dichotomy
\[\max\{\|a\|,\|b\|\}<1\quad\text{or}\quad a=-b.\]

Let \(n_1\ge n_2\ge\cdots\ge n_\ell\ge1\) be integers, \(\ell\ge2\), \(n=\sum_{i=1}^\ell n_i\), and \(n_1^{\prime}=n_1+n_\ell\). The final display in the proof of Lemma 4.4 asserts, with binary logarithms, \[n_1-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}n_i\log_2 n_i\ge n_1^{\prime}-\frac12n_1^{\prime}\log_2n_1^{\prime}-\sum_{i=2}^{\ell-1}n_i\log_2n_i\ge n-\frac12n\log_2n.\] The middle sum is printed with coefficient one; the last comparison is attributed to induction on \(\ell\).

Let \(P_{n,d}\) denote the projective space of nonzero degree-\(d\) homogeneous polynomials in \(n+1\) complex variables, and let \(\Delta_{n,d}\) be the discriminant of polynomials whose projective zero equation is singular. In dimension \(n=1\), the measure \(\mu([p])\) is the probability measure assigning to each projective root its multiplicity divided by \(d\); see pp. 45–47 and Theorem 3.8, p. 69.

Theorem 5.13, p. 86 (PDF p. 44), asserts that whenever a continuous semialgebraic curve \(\gamma:[0,1]\to P_{n,d}\) satisfies \[\gamma(0)\in\Delta_{n,d},\qquad
 \gamma(t)\notin\Delta_{n,d}\quad(0<t\leq1),\] there is a positive integer \(m\) for which \(\alpha_m(s)=\gamma(s^m)\) has finite energy.

Let \(H\) be the real Wigner matrix of Theorem 1.8(ii), with increasing eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\), and let \(k\) be in the fixed compact bulk range. Define \[\rho_{\rm sc}(x)=\frac{\sqrt{(4-x^2)_+}}{2\pi},\quad F(\gamma_k)=\frac{k-1/2}{N},\quad F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x\rho_{\rm sc}(y)\,dy,\quad\delta=\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{N},\quad c_k=\frac{\sqrt2}{\pi\rho_{\rm sc}(\gamma_k)}.\]

For a nonnegative smooth \(h\) supported on \([0,1]\) with integral one, the smoothing is \(f_E(y)=\int_0^1h(s)\mathbf1_{[E+s\delta,\infty)}(y)\,ds\), with the source's remote upper cutoff. The centered trace is \(\overline{\operatorname{Tr}}f(H)=\sum_jf(\lambda_j)-N\int f\rho_{\rm sc}\). After (6.19), the proof asserts that for fixed \(\varepsilon\), sufficiently large \(N\) depending on the bulk restriction, and every \(u>1\), \[\lambda_k-\gamma_k>uc_k\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \overline{\operatorname{Tr}}f_E(H)>(1-\varepsilon)\frac{u\sqrt2}{\pi}\sqrt{\log N},\qquad E=\gamma_k+u(c_k-1)\delta.\] It applies this implication in the claimed tail range \(u\le A\sqrt{\log N}\).

The proposition assumes that \(X\) is a smooth affine Hamiltonian \(G\)-variety, that \(Z\subset\mu(X)\) is a locally closed \(G\)-stable subset, and that a character \(\bar\lambda\in\mathfrak b^*\) has \(Z_{\bar\lambda}=Z\cap(\bar\lambda+\mathfrak b^\perp)\ne\varnothing\). It then declares the following equivalent: \[\begin{aligned}
 &\mu^{-1}(Z_{\bar\lambda})\text{ is Lagrangian in }X; \qquad\text{(a)}\\
 &\mu^{-1}(\lambda)\text{ is isotropic for every }\lambda\in Z_{\bar\lambda}; \qquad\text{(b)}\\
 &\dim F\leq \tfrac12\bigl(\dim X-\dim(G\lambda)\bigr)
 \quad\text{for every irreducible fiber component }F. \qquad\text{(c)}\end{aligned}\] There is no openness hypothesis on \(Z\) in part (1).

Let \(K\subset\widehat{\mathbb C}\) be compact with positive logarithmic capacity, let \(P\) contain exactly one prescribed point in each complementary component, and let \(f\) be holomorphic on a neighborhood of \(K\). An admissible \(R_n\) is rational of degree at most \(n\), with poles contained in \(P\).

The theorem states that if \(K\) has positive logarithmic capacity and \(f\) does not extend holomorphically to \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus P\), there is \(D>1\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every admissible sequence \(R_n\), \[
 \|f-R_n\|_K>C D^{-n}\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n.\] The quantifier on \(n\), including arbitrary subsequences, is essential.

In Section 7, let \(r\) be the rational function of degree \(d\), with level lemniscate \(L_r=\{|r|=1\}\) and one prescribed pole \(p\) in each grey face \(F\). The potential \(u_{L_r,P}\) is defined using one Green function with a unit logarithmic singularity at each prescribed pole. Equation (7.1), article p.29, asserts in each grey face
\[u_{L_r,P}(z)=d^{-1}\log|r(z)|.\]
The degree in this identity is the total degree of \(r\), rather than a separately specified local pole multiplicity.

For the data of Proposition 7.6, article p.32, put \(d=\deg r\) and let \(n\) be its positive integer approximation parameter. The proposition prescribes
\[R^{(j)}(a)=f^{(j)}(a)\quad(0\le j<n)\]
at each distinct zero \(a\) of \(r\), and asserts uniqueness among rational functions of degree at most \(dn-1\) with the prescribed poles and pole orders of the constructed approximant. No simple-zero assumption on \(r\) is included.

Lemma 3.1, printed p.420 (PDF p.13), assumes a sequence of connected smooth embedded curves \(\overline M_j\), bounded centered Gaussian length \(F(\overline M_j)<\Lambda\), and
\[\int_{\overline M_j}\left|\boldsymbol\kappa+\frac{x^\perp}{2}\right|^2e^{-|x|^2/4}\,d\mathcal H^1\longrightarrow0.\]
It asserts that a subsequence converges locally in \(C^{1,\alpha}\) to a nonempty line through the origin or a circle of radius \(\sqrt2\), possibly with multiplicity.

For the solutions in Lemma 3.2, article p.9, let \(\rho_M\) denote the spatial mean and assume \(M\ge\max(1,\sqrt{\rho_M})\). If
\[\|\rho(t)-\rho_M\|_2\le2M\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T],\]
the lemma asserts a universal constant \(C\) with
\[\|\rho(t)-\rho_M\|_\infty\le CM^2\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T],\]
including the initial time \(t=0\).

The source defines \[\widehat f_N(k_1,k_2)=\frac1\pi\int_\Omega
 f(x)e^{-ik_1x_1}\cos(k_2x_2)\,dx,
 \quad
 f=\frac1\pi\sum_{k_1\in\mathbb Z,\ k_2\ge0}
 \frac{\widehat f_N(k)}{1+\delta_{k_2,0}}e^{ik_1x_1}\cos(k_2x_2).\]

For this normalization, the final identity in Section 2.2, article p.7, asserts

The same unweighted sum is used around (6.9), pp.19–20.

For a deterministic \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), remove its last row \(Y\) to obtain \(A^*\). When \(A^*\) has full row rank, let \[s_i=\sigma_i(A^*)>0,\quad u_0\in\ker A^*,\quad \|u_0\|=1,\quad
y_i=\langle u_i,Y\rangle,\quad y_0=\langle u_0,Y\rangle,\] where the \(u_i\) form an orthonormal singular basis. Put \[t=\varepsilon n^{-1/2},\qquad
 \widetilde\chi^2=1+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{y_i^2}{s_i^2}.
 \]

The stated hypothesis is \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(s_{n-1}\geq \varepsilon^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\). The claimed implication is \[\sigma_n(A)\leq \varepsilon n^{-1/2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 |y_0|\leq (1+\varepsilon^{1/4})\varepsilon n^{-1/2}\widetilde\chi .
 \] There is no upper bound on \(\varepsilon\) in this deterministic statement.

In the neck construction, let \(s\in(0,1)\), \(\eta=1-s\), and let \(L_\infty\) be the specified limiting radial operator. At the cusp endpoint, with \(m=n+1\), \[L_\infty=\frac1m\bigl(\eta^2\partial_{\eta\eta}-(n-1)\eta\partial_\eta-(n+1)\bigr)+\mathcal R,\qquad |\mathcal R f|\le C\eta^m(|f|+\eta|f^{\prime}|+\eta^2|f^{\prime\prime}|).\] Let \(\widehat u\) be the positive homogeneous solution of Lemma 4.5, normalized by its limit one at \(s=0\) and with \(\widehat u(1-\eta)=O(\eta^{n+1})\).

Lemma 4.8 asserts that there exists \(\widehat v\le0\) solving \(L_\infty\widehat v=\widehat u\) on \((0,1)\) with \[|\widehat v(1-\eta)|+\eta|\widehat v^{\prime}(1-\eta)|+\eta^2|\widehat v^{\prime\prime}(1-\eta)|=O(\eta^{n+1})\quad(\eta\downarrow0).\] At the other endpoint it asserts \[\widehat v(s)=C_0+C_2s^{(n+1)/n}+R(s),\quad C_0\ne0,\quad |R(s)|+s|R^{\prime}(s)|+s^2|R^{\prime\prime}(s)|=O(s^{(n+2)/n}).\] Its Neumann condition is the absence of an \(s^{1/n}\) term.

Write \(F(z)=z_1^3+z_2^3+z_3^3\) and \(TY_\sigma=\{F=\sigma\}\). The base map is \(\Phi(w)_j=w_j+
u(w)\overline w_j^{2}\). For a nonzero complex parameter \(\sigma\) in Lemma 2.5 and a chosen cube root \(\lambda=\sigma^{-1/3}\), Definition 2.4 defines \(\Phi_\sigma=\lambda^{-1}\Phi(\lambda\,\cdot)\) on the stated domain. The expansion in Lemma 2.5, printed p.550 (PDF p.9), instead assigns coefficient \(\lambda

u(\lambda z)\overline z_j^{2}.\]

A group is virtually locally indicable if it has a finite-index subgroup each of whose nontrivial finitely generated subgroups maps onto \(\mathbb Z\). Definition 6.1 defines \(\mathcal T_{\rm VLI}\) as the smallest group class containing every finite group, closed under directed unions, and containing the fundamental group of any graph of groups in the class whenever that fundamental group is virtually locally indicable.

The transfinite class is defined by \(\mathcal Y_0=\{\text{finite groups}\}\); \(\mathcal Y_{\alpha+1}\) consists of virtually locally indicable fundamental groups of graphs of groups whose vertex and edge groups are locally in \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\); and \(\mathcal Y_\beta=\bigcup_{\alpha<\beta}\mathcal Y_\alpha\) for limit ordinals. Here locally in \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\) means that every nontrivial finitely generated subgroup belongs to \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\). Lemma 6.2 asserts \[\mathcal Y:=\bigcup_{\alpha\ge0}\mathcal Y_\alpha=\mathcal T_{\rm VLI},\] and its proof in particular asserts closure of \(\mathcal Y\) under the unrestricted directed unions of Definition 6.1.

Let \((N,h)\) be a connected closed oriented Riemannian \(n\)-manifold, and let integral currents \(S_i\) in a complete metric space \((E,d)\) converge flatly to \(S_\infty\). Assumption 1.3 requires that \(N_i=\operatorname{spt}S_i\), with its induced intrinsic metric, be a compact oriented Riemannian manifold with piecewise smooth metric \(h_i\), possibly with boundary, and \(\operatorname{Area}(\partial N_i,h_i)\to0\). It assumes uniformly \(\lambda\)-Lipschitz maps \(\varphi_i:(N_i,d|_{N_i})\to(N,\operatorname{dist}_h)\), \(C^1\) on the smooth parts, such that \((\varphi_i)_\#S_i\) converges flatly to the unit-multiplicity fundamental current of \(N\).

There are open sets \(R_i\) in the smooth parts with \(\operatorname{Vol}(N_i\setminus R_i,h_i)\to0\), \(\operatorname{Vol}(R_i,h_i)\to\operatorname{Vol}(N,h)\), and \[\left\|\sum_{u,v=1}^n|h(d\varphi_i(e_u),d\varphi_i(e_v))-\delta_{uv}|\right\|_{L^\infty(R_i)}\to0\] for orthonormal tangent bases. These are geometric-volume and almost-isometry hypotheses; they do not state \(S_i=[\![N_i]\!]\).

For \(O_\eta\), the \(\eta\)-neighborhood of \(\operatorname{spt}S_\infty\) in \(E\), the argument asserts \(\|S_i\|(E\setminus O_\eta)\to0\) for every \(\eta>0\), using in its proof the mass-limit identification \(\lim M(S_i)=\lim M((\varphi_i)_\#S_i)=\operatorname{Vol}(N,h)\). The curve-lifting argument additionally asserts \(M(S_i\mathbin{\llcorner}(N_i\setminus R_i))\to0\) from Assumption 1.3(c)–(e). These are statements about current mass, not merely support volume.

Let \(V\) be a real vector space of dimension \(d>1\), and let \(\Gamma<\operatorname{SL}(V)\) be a nontrivial torsion-free projective Anosov subgroup. Let \(\phi^t\) be the complete contact flow on the manifold \(\mathcal M_\Gamma\) constructed in Theorem A, let \(X\) be its generating vector field, and let \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\) be its compact trapped set. The scalar operator considered in Theorem F is \(A=-X+U\), with \(U\in C_c^\infty(\mathcal M_\Gamma;\mathbb C)\) supported in a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\). Its resonances are the poles of the meromorphically continued scalar resolvent \((A-\lambda)^{-1}\), localized to a relatively compact neighborhood of \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\) as in Theorem 9.

For \(U=0\), Theorem F asserts that the topological entropy \(h_{\mathrm{top}}(\Gamma)\) belongs to this scalar resonance spectrum and is its unique resonance with largest real part. It further identifies the corresponding product of resonant and co-resonant states, up to a scalar, with the Bowen–Margulis measure. The entropy is positive in the nonabelian case; the theorem's stated group range itself also includes elementary groups.

Let \(V\) be a real vector space with \(\dim V>1\). Definition 2.14 calls a finitely generated Gromov-hyperbolic subgroup \(\Gamma<\operatorname{SL}(V)\) projective Anosov if there are \(c,c'>0\) such that, for every \(\gamma\in\Gamma\), \[\lambda_1(\gamma)-\lambda_2(\gamma)\ge c|\gamma|_\infty-c',\qquad |\gamma|_\infty=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{|\gamma^k|}{k},\] where the \(\lambda_i\) are the decreasing logarithms of the moduli of the complex eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, and \(|\cdot|\) is a word norm. The stated definition does not require non-elementarity.

For torsion-free projective Anosov \(\Gamma\), Theorem A asserts the existence of a nonempty invariant domain with a free proper \(\Gamma\)-action whose quotient \(\mathcal M_\Gamma\) carries a complete contact Axiom A flow preserving a unique basic hyperbolic set \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\). Theorem B identifies this set, by a bi-Hölder flow conjugacy, with the full refraction space \(\Gamma\backslash(\partial_\infty\Gamma^{(2)}\times\mathbb R)\), with the cocycle action specified in the paper. Thus the unique-basic-set assertion concerns the canonical set identified with the full space of ordered distinct boundary pairs.

For every nontrivial torsion-free projective Anosov \(\Gamma\), Theorem D further asserts that the dynamical zeta function \(\zeta_\Gamma(s)\) has a meromorphic continuation to \(\mathbb C\) and a simple pole at \(s=h_{\mathrm{top}}(\Gamma)\). The additional irreducibility hypothesis in that theorem applies to its zero-free strip conclusion; it is not imposed on the stated simple-pole assertion.

Let \(B=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{p,q+1}\). For a unit spacelike tangent lift, the domain conditions are \(B(x,x)=-1\), \(B(v,v)=1\), and \(B(x,v)=0\). The map on article p.45 is printed as
\[[x:v]\longmapsto[x+v:x-v],\]
and is asserted to land in the target from p.44, whose representatives must satisfy \(B(v_1,v_2)>0\).

For \(A=-X+U\), Section 5.2 and Theorem 9, article p.41, use \((A-\lambda)^{-1}\) and define the resonant projector by
\[\Pi_{\lambda_0}=\operatorname{Res}_{\lambda=\lambda_0}(A-\lambda)^{-1}.\]
The same discussion asserts that the initial \(L^2\) resolvent exists throughout \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0\) for the permitted smooth potentials \(U\), without a potential-dependent shift of that starting half-plane.

For the source local-product radii \(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1\) and \(x\in\mathcal K_\Gamma\), Lemma 4.3(3), article p.28, asserts that for every ambient point \(y\in B(x,2\varepsilon_1)\), the local intersection
\[W^s_{\varepsilon_0}(x)\cap W^{cu}_{\varepsilon_0}(y)\]
belongs to \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\). The quantifier on \(y\) is over the ambient neighborhood, without requiring \(y\in\mathcal K_\Gamma\).

In the proof of Theorem 3.23, article p.10, the five-geometries reduction passes to a subgroup of index at most \(240\) that is cyclic, \(\mathbb Z^3\), or \(\mathbb Z^2\rtimes\mathbb Z\). The proof asserts that every group arising in this reduction embeds into \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\). The cyclic alternative is not restricted to infinite cyclic groups.

Let \(F\) be a local field of characteristic zero, \(G=\operatorname{PGL}_2(F)\), and \(\psi\) a nontrivial unitary additive character. Use the self-dual additive measure \(dy\) and \(d^\times y=dy/|y|\). Let \(\pi_1,\pi_2\) be irreducible unitary generic representations, with \(\pi_1\) \(\vartheta_1\)-tempered and \(\pi_2=I(\chi_2)\) a \(\vartheta_2\)-tempered normalized principal series, where \(0\le\vartheta_1,\vartheta_2<1/2\). The inducing convention is \(f(n(x)a(y)g)=\chi_2(y)|y|^{1/2}f(g)\); the stated setup imposes no sign condition on \(\operatorname{Re}\chi_2\).

Choose smooth Whittaker vectors \(W_i\) with \(W_i(a(\cdot))\in C_c^\infty(F^\times)\), and let \(h\) be their test function defined in (1.8). For the associated transform write \[H(y,\chi)=\int_{F^\times}h(z,yz)\chi(z)\,d^\times z,\qquad h^\sharp(\pi,\chi_0)=\int_{F^\times}h^\vee(\pi,z)\chi_0(z)\,d^\times z.\] In particular the latter integral is defined for unitary \(\chi_0\), the character range of the correspondence preceding Theorem 2.

Let the target representation \(\pi\) be \(\vartheta\)-tempered with \(\vartheta_1+\vartheta<1/2\). Theorem 2(1) asserts the forward integral identity (1.12) for every contour \(\operatorname{Re}\chi=\sigma\) satisfying \(\vartheta_1<\sigma<1/2-\vartheta\). It asserts absolute convergence of the displayed integrals and holomorphy of their \(\chi\)-integrand throughout \(\vartheta_1<\operatorname{Re}\chi<1/2-\vartheta\). This stated lower edge depends on \(\vartheta_1\), with no additional \(\vartheta_2\) term.

The inverse formula of Theorem 2(2), article p.5, is asserted for every \(y\in F^\times\). Its right-hand side contains \(\chi(1-y)\) and division by \(\chi_0(1-y)|1-y|\). The printed domain includes \(y=1\) and supplies no separate limiting-value convention there.

For \(\delta>0\), Theorem 5.1, article p.25, asserts
\[\#\{y\in Y_N^*:|P_f(y)|\le(\log N)^{1/2-\delta}\}\ll\frac{N^2}{(\log N)^{1+\min(\delta,1/4)}}.\]
In deriving this bound from the real one-dimensional Maaß-period Gaussian input, the proof puts \(\alpha=1+\min(\delta,1/4)\), \(r=c^{\prime\prime}(\log N)^{-(\alpha-1)}\), and equation (5.2) asserts
\[\int_{-r}^{r}\frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dx=O((\log N)^{-2(\alpha-1)}).\]

For the bipartite graph in (6.1), let \(e(x)\subseteq Y\) be the neighbors of \(x\in X\) and \(\deg(x)=|e(x)|\). Given any probability measure \(\mu\) on \(X\), define the graph transform by distributing \(\mu(x)/\deg(x)\) along each incident edge. The source asserts that \(G(\mu)\) is a probability measure and that, for every \(B\subseteq Y\),
\[\mu(e^{-1}(B))\le G(\mu)(B),\qquad e^{-1}(B)=\{x:e(x)\subseteq B\}.\]
No assumption excludes positive \(\mu\)-mass on degree-zero vertices.

For every continuous probability density \(F\) on \(\mathbb R\), Lemma 6.2, article pp.29–30, asserts the uniform interval comparison error \(O_F(h(n)+E(n))\). The proof uses the consequence
\[\int_b^{b+E}F(x)\,dx=O_F(E)\]
uniformly in \(b\in\mathbb R\) as \(E\downarrow0\); no global boundedness hypothesis on \(F\) is stated.

Section 4 explicitly drops the dynamical assumptions of §2. Theorem 4.1 assumes that a compact set \(R_0\) is star-shaped about zero and that \[[0,\infty)R_0\cap V_1\] is a nice compact subset of \(V_1=\{F=1\}\). Here nice means that the boundary has measure zero on \(V_1\) (Definition 2.2, p. 6). Definition 4.4 requires a finite collection of compact subsets \(\Omega\subset V_1\) such that \[R_0=E\ \cup\!\bigcup_\Omega[0,1/\operatorname{ht}(\Omega)]\Omega,
 \qquad |E|\le\epsilon,\qquad
 \operatorname{ht}(\Omega)=\sup_{\omega\in\Omega}\|\omega\|_\infty .\] Proposition 4.6 asserts that such a cutting exists under the two stated hypotheses (pp. 14–15).
The application in Section 5.2, article p.19, asserts that the indicated matrix boxes meet these radial-compactness hypotheses of Theorem 4.1.

Let \(V\) be the real linear space of a Hardy–Littlewood system \((V,F)\), with \(D=\dim V\), homogeneous degree \(d=\deg F\), and a nice compact connected set \(\Omega\subset V_1(\mathbb R)=\{F=1\}\). With Euclidean volume the source defines \[\mu_\infty(\Omega)=\lim_{\epsilon\to0}\frac{\operatorname{vol}([1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]\Omega)}{2\epsilon}.\] Lemma 2.5 asserts, as \(T\to\infty\), \[\int_{T\Omega}\frac{dx}{\log^+F(x)}=\mu_\infty(\Omega)\frac{T^D}{D\log T}(1+o(1)),\] where \(T\Omega\) is the truncated cone notation used in the paper.

For the determinant system \((\operatorname{Mat}_n,\det)\) and distinct primes \(p,q\), the proof of Lemma 3.3 asserts \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\#\{A\in\operatorname{Mat}_n(\mathbb Z/q^k\mathbb Z):\det A=p\}}{q^{k(n^2-1)}}=\frac{\#\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)}{q-1}.\] In the subsequent determinant prime count, the displayed asymptotic for the sum \(\sum_{p\le T^n}p^{n-1}(1+O(p^{-1/2}))\) uses \(T^n/(n^2\log T)\). These are the original displayed normalizations being checked.

For \(V=\operatorname{Skew}_{2n}\) with the Pfaffian polynomial, Theorem 3.5 asserts for each nice compact \(\Omega\subset V_1(\mathbb R)\), as \(m\to\infty\), \[\#(V_m(\mathbb Z)\cap m^{1/n}\Omega)=(1+o_\Omega(1))\mu_\infty(\Omega)m^{2n-2}S_m,\qquad S_m=\prod_{q\ \mathrm{prime}}\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\#\{A\in\operatorname{Skew}_{2n}(\mathbb Z/q^k\mathbb Z):\operatorname{Pf}(A)=m\}}{q^{k(n^2-1)}}.\] The exponent in this displayed local-density denominator is part of the claim under review.

For every odd prime \(p\), every integer \(n\ge3\), and every integral positive definite symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix \(S\) with \(\det S=p\), Lemma 6.2 asserts, as \(p\to\infty\), \[\alpha_p(S)^{-1}=\frac{1}{2p}\bigl(\alpha_p^{\mathrm{std}}(S)\bigr)^{-1}(1+O(p^{-2})).\] Here \(\alpha_p(S)=\tfrac12\lim_{\ell\to\infty}p^{-\ell n(n-1)/2}\#\{T\in\operatorname{Mat}_n(\mathbb Z/p^\ell\mathbb Z):T^TST\equiv S\pmod{p^\ell}\}\), and \(\alpha_p^{\mathrm{std}}\) is the standard density in (10). The asserted relative error includes rank \(n=3\).

In the indefinite symmetric-matrix setting, let \(n\ge4\) be even, let \(r+s=n\) with \(r,s>0\), and fix a nice compact set \(\Omega\) in the signature orbit \(\mathcal O_{r,s}\). For an odd prime \(q\), write \[A_q=\left(\prod_{p\ne2,q}\mu_{q,p}(V_q(\mathbb Z_p))\right)\sum_{\substack{G_2,G_q\\c_2(G_2)c_q(G_q)=c_\infty(\Omega)}}\mu_{q,2}(G_2)\mu_{q,q}(G_q),\qquad P_n=\prod_{\substack{3\le j\le n\\j\ \mathrm{odd}}}\zeta(j)^{-1}.\] The sum is over the indicated local \(\operatorname{SL}_n\)-orbits, \(c_\infty(\Omega)=(-1)^{s(s-1)/2}\), and \(V_q\) is the determinant-\(q\) fiber. In Proposition 7.4 the branch \(q\equiv(-1)^{n/2}\pmod4\), \(q\equiv\pm3\pmod8\) is printed as \[A_q=\frac12P_n\zeta(n)^{-1}L(n/2,\chi_q)(1+O(q^{-1}))\left(1-\frac{2^{1-n}}{1-2^{-n/2}}\right),\qquad \chi_q=\left(\frac{(-1)^{n/2}q}{\cdot}\right).\] The paper's convention for this \(L\)-value omits the Euler factor at \(2\).

With \(\pi(T\Omega)\) denoting the prime-determinant count and \(\psi(r,s)=1\) for even \(s\), \(\psi(r,s)=0\) otherwise, the even-rank prime-sum display on page 29 asserts \[\pi(T\Omega)=\frac12\psi(r,s)\mu_\infty(\Omega)\zeta(n)^{-1}P_n(1+o_\Omega(1))\sum_{\substack{p\le T^n\\p\ \mathrm{prime}}}L(n/2,\chi_p)p^{(n-1)/2}B_n(p),\] where \(B_n(p)=1\) if \(p\not\equiv(-1)^{n/2}\pmod4\), \(B_n(p)=1+2^{1-n}/(1-2^{-n/2})\) in the matching \(\pm1\pmod8\) classes, and \(B_n(p)=1+2^{1-n}/(1+2^{-n/2})\) in the matching \(\pm3\pmod8\) classes. The leading \(1/2\) is part of this original display. For odd \(n\ge3\) in Lemma 7.5, and even \(n\ge3\) in Lemma 7.7, the final indefinite-orbit statements instead display \[\pi(T\Omega)=\psi(r,s)\prod_{\substack{3\le j\le n\\j\ \mathrm{odd}}}(1+o_\Omega(1))\int_{T\Omega}\frac{dx}{\log^+\det x}.\] In these two displays the indexed product contains no displayed \(\zeta(j)^{-1}\) factor.

For even \(n\ge4\) and a nice compact set \(\Omega\subset\mathcal O_{n,0}\) in the positive definite orbit, let \(N(p,\Omega)\) count integral symmetric matrices of determinant \(p\) in \(p^{1/n}\Omega\). The first level-count display on page 36 asserts, as the prime \(p\to\infty\), \[N(p,\Omega)=(1+o_\Omega(1))\mu_\infty(\Omega)P_n\zeta(n)^{-1}L(n/2,\chi_p)B_n(p).\] This original right-hand side has no displayed factor \(p^{(n-1)/2}\).

For the stochastic-localization covariance process of an isotropic log-concave initial probability measure, put \(t=r/(1-r)\) and \(\Gamma_r=A_t/(1-r)\), with \(0<r<1\). The final equality in (56), article p.15, is printed with
\[\frac{d}{dr}\mathbb E\Gamma_r=\frac{\mathbb E\Gamma_r}{1-r}+\frac{1}{(1-r)^3}\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E A_t^2.\]
The square on \(A_t\) is part of the asserted chain-rule identity.

Let \(\mathbf G\) be a connected reductive real algebraic group, let \(G=\mathbf G(\mathbb R)\), and let \(\Gamma\leq G\) be Zariski dense. A linear representation \((\tau,V)\) means a representation on a finite-dimensional real vector space obtained by restricting a homomorphism of real algebraic groups \(\mathbf G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)\) to real points. Fix a Cartan subspace \(\mathfrak a\), a closed Weyl chamber \(\mathfrak a^+\), and the Jordan projection \(\lambda:G\to\mathfrak a^+\). An element \(g\in G\) is loxodromic when \(\lambda(g)\in\operatorname{Int}(\mathfrak a^+)\). For a subsemigroup \(S\subseteq G\), \(\tau\) is positively \(S\)-semi-proximal when, for every loxodromic \(\gamma\in S\), \(\tau(\gamma)\) has a positive real eigenvalue of maximal modulus. Neither simplicity nor uniqueness of that eigenvalue is required (Definition 6.3, article p. 52; eigenvalue convention, p. 51).

Lemma 6.7 (article p. 52) asserts the following implication for any such linear representation \((\tau,V)\). If \(G^\prime\subseteq G\) is an open subsemigroup with \(\Gamma\cap G^\prime\neq\varnothing\), and \(\tau\) is positively \((\Gamma\cap G^\prime)\)-semi-proximal, then \(\tau\) is positively \(\Gamma\)-semi-proximal. Thus the stated conclusion concerns every loxodromic element of \(\Gamma\), although the hypothesis tests only those in \(\Gamma\cap G^\prime\). The lemma imposes no irreducibility hypothesis on \(\tau\).

Corollary 6.8(2) (article pp. 52–53) uses the same \(G\) and \(\Gamma\). Let \(\ell\geq2\) be an integer, and for each \(1\leq i\leq\ell\) let \((\tau_i,V_i)\) be an irreducible real linear representation of \(G\), with highest restricted weight \(\chi_i\in\mathfrak a^*\). Assume that \(\tau_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\tau_\ell\) is positively \(\Gamma\)-semi-proximal. Writing \(L_\Gamma\) for the limit cone of \(\Gamma\), the corollary asserts
\[\bigl(\exists X\in L_\Gamma:\ \langle\chi_1,X\rangle>\langle\chi_2,X\rangle\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bigoplus_{i\ne2}\tau_i\ \text{is positively }\Gamma\text{-semi-proximal}.\]
There is no condition in this part comparing \(\chi_1(X)\) with the other weights \(\chi_3(X),\ldots,\chi_\ell(X)\).

Fix integers \(p,q\geq1\), following the convention of Section 2.2 (article p. 14). Let \(M\subset\mathbb H^{p,q}\) be a spacelike \(p\)-graph: \(M\) is closed, is homeomorphic to a connected \(p\)-dimensional topological manifold without boundary, and any two distinct points of \(M\) are in spacelike position (Definition 3.18, article p. 28). In a splitting \(\widehat{\mathbb H}^{p,q}\simeq B^p\times S^q\) determined by a timelike \((q+1)\)-plane, an injective lift \(\widehat M\) is the graph of a map \(f:B^p\to S^q\) (Proposition 3.21, p. 28). Here \(B^p=\{y=(y_0,\ldots,y_p)\in S^p:y_0>0\}\), and both spheres carry their standard spherical metrics (Notation 2.2, article p. 15).

The hypothesis on \(f\) is pairwise strict contraction:
\[\forall u,v\in B^p,\quad u\ne v\ \Longrightarrow\ d_{S^q}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)<d_{S^p}(u,v).\]
This is the paper's meaning of strictly \(1\)-Lipschitz; it does not impose a single uniform Lipschitz constant smaller than \(1\). Let \(\bar f:\overline{B^p}=B^p\sqcup S^{p-1}\to S^q\) be the continuous extension used in the proof of Proposition 3.28 (article pp. 32–33).

The intermediate assertion in the proof of Proposition 3.28(2) (article p. 33) is that the same strict inequality holds throughout the closed hemisphere:
\[\forall u,v\in\overline{B^p},\quad u\ne v\ \Longrightarrow\ d_{S^q}\bigl(\bar f(u),\bar f(v)\bigr)<d_{S^p}(u,v).\]
In particular, this assertion includes pairs for which both points belong to \(S^{p-1}=\partial B^p\).

Fix integers \(p,q\geq1\) and a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form \(b\) of signature \((p,q+1)\) on \(\mathbb R^{p+q+1}\), as in Section 2.2 (article p. 14). Let \(2\leq j\leq\min(p,q+1)\) be an integer, and let \(C=\{x_1^+,\ldots,x_j^+,x_1^-,\ldots,x_j^-\}\) be a \(j\)-crown in \(\partial_\infty\mathbb H^{p,q}\), and let \(\mathcal O\) be an open convex hull of \(C\) in \(\mathbb H^{p,q}\). Choose a basis \((e_1^\prime,\ldots,e_{2j}^\prime)\) of \(\operatorname{span}(C)\) adapted to \(C\) and defining this convex hull: \(x_i^+=[e_i^\prime]\), \(x_i^-=[e_{j+i}^\prime]\),
\[b(e_i^\prime,e_k^\prime)=b(e_{j+i}^\prime,e_{j+k}^\prime)=0,\qquad b(e_i^\prime,e_{j+k}^\prime)=-\delta_{ik}\quad(1\leq i,k\leq j),\]
and
\[\mathcal O=\mathbb P\!\left(\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{2j}v_i e_i^\prime:\ v_i>0\ \text{for every }i\right\}\right).\]
These are the adapted-basis and convex-hull conventions of Definition 5.5 and Remark 5.6 (article p. 42).

Identify \(A_C\) with \(\mathbb R^j\) through the action on \(\operatorname{span}(C)\) given in equation (5.1) (article p. 43):
\[\exp(a_1,\ldots,a_j)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{a_1},\ldots,e^{a_j},e^{-a_1},\ldots,e^{-a_j}).\]
Let \(d_{\mathcal O}\) be the Hilbert metric with the normalization used in equation (5.3).

The intermediate assertion in the proof of Proposition 5.9 (article p. 45) applies to every \(x\in\mathcal O\) and every \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_j)\in\mathbb R^j\setminus\{0\}\). It states that the orbit path \(\gamma_{x,a}(t)=\exp(ta_1,\ldots,ta_j)\cdot x\), \(t\in\mathbb R\), is a geodesic line of speed \(\max_i|a_i|\), and that its image is contained in a projective line. Explicitly, the asserted properties are
\[d_{\mathcal O}\bigl(\gamma_{x,a}(s),\gamma_{x,a}(t)\bigr)=|s-t|\max_{1\leq i\leq j}|a_i|\quad\text{for all }s,t\in\mathbb R,\]
and
\[\exists L=L(x,a)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(C),\quad\dim L=2,\qquad\gamma_{x,a}(\mathbb R)\subseteq\mathbb P(L).\]

Let \(r\geq1\) be an integer, and let \(\mathbf G=\mathbf G_1\times\cdots\times\mathbf G_r\), where each \(\mathbf G_s\) is a connected reductive real algebraic group. Put \(G_s=\mathbf G_s(\mathbb R)\) and \(G=G_1\times\cdots\times G_r\). Let \((\tau,V)\) be an irreducible linear representation of \(G\) on a finite-dimensional real vector space, obtained from a homomorphism of real algebraic groups as specified at the start of Section 6.1 (article p. 52).

The factorization assertion in Fact 6.9 (article p. 53) is that there exist a field \(\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\) and, for every \(1\leq s\leq r\), an irreducible real linear representation \((\sigma_s,W_s)\) of \(G_s\), such that, as real representations of \(G\),
\[(\tau,V)\cong\left(\sigma_1\otimes_{\mathbb K}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb K}\sigma_r,\ W_1\otimes_{\mathbb K}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb K}W_r\right).\]
Each \(G_s\) acts on its corresponding tensor factor.

The statement specifies \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) if some nontrivial \(\sigma_s\) has an irreducible complexification, and \(\mathbb K=\mathbb C\) if every \(W_s\) has a \(G_s\)-invariant complex structure; in the latter case those structures supply the complex scalar multiplication for the tensor product. Each factor is required to be irreducible as a real representation. This factorization is stated for every irreducible \((\tau,V)\), without a hypothesis that \(\tau\) is \(G\)-proximal or \(G\)-semi-proximal.

Lemma 7 asserts that for every smoothly bounded open set \(\omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) there is \(C_\omega>0\) such that every compactly supported \(h\in H^1(\mathbb R^2)\) harmonic in \(\omega\) satisfies \[\int_\omega|\nabla h|^2\,dx\le C_\omega\int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus\omega}|\nabla h|^2\,dx.\] The stated hole assumptions do not require the complement to be connected.

For Proposition 3, let \(M\) be a compact closed Riemannian surface, \(\Omega\subset M\) open with smooth, possibly empty, boundary, and \(O_1,\ldots,O_N\in\Omega\) distinct, \(N\ge1\). Choose conformal charts \(\psi_n:B_r\to\Omega\) with \(\psi_n(0)=O_n\), pairwise disjoint images away from \(\partial\Omega\), and pullback metric \(\rho_n g_0\). Let \(\eta_k\) be a stationary process in a Hilbert space \(E\), with compact marginal support \(K\), and let \(\mathcal E\subset K^{\mathbb Z_-}\) be its past-law support. Fix \(\iota>1\) and \(d(\xi,\xi')=\sum_{k\le0}\iota^k\|\xi_k-\xi'_k\|_E\). In the infinite-dimensional clause of (\(\eta1\)), \(\eta_k=\sum_{\ell\ge1}r_\ell\eta_{k\ell}f_\ell\), where \((f_\ell)\) is an orthonormal basis, \(r_\ell>0\), \(\sum r_\ell<\infty\), and the scalar coordinate processes are independent, stationary, and bounded in absolute value by one. Each coordinate conditional law has a jointly Lipschitz density \(p_\xi^\ell\), and \[\lim_{\xi'\to\xi}\sum_{\ell\ge1}\|p_{\xi'}^\ell-p_\xi^\ell\|_{L^1}=0.\] No common Lipschitz constant in \(\ell\) is included.

The sentence on page 29 asserts that (\(\eta1\)) implies (SF) and (DLP\('\)) in both finite and infinite dimensions. In particular, (SF) requires a conditional version \(Q(\xi;\cdot)=\mathbb P(\eta_1\in\cdot\mid\eta_{\le0}=\xi)\) and one finite \(C\) such that \(\|Q(\xi;\cdot)-Q(\xi';\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{var}}\le C d(\xi,\xi')\) for every \(\xi,\xi'\in\mathcal E\).

The literal density clause of (DLP\('\)) uses increasing finite-dimensional \(F_n\subset E\) with dense union, complements \(F_n^\dagger\), and uniformly bounded projections. In the disintegration \(Q(\xi;dy)=Q_n^\dagger(\xi;dy_n^\dagger)Q_n(\xi,y_n^\dagger;dy_n)\), it requires \(Q_n(\xi,y_n^\dagger;dy_n)=\rho_n(\xi,y_n^\dagger,y_n)\,dy_n\), where \(\rho_n\) is Lipschitz on \(\mathcal E\times E\) and supported in \(\mathcal E\times K\). Thus for each fixed past the continuous density is specified on the whole ambient \(E\), with compact support in that variable.

A further transfer assertion is Proposition 4.10. Let \((e_j)\) be an orthonormal basis of a separable Hilbert space \(H\), take independent identically distributed scalar processes \(\eta^j(t)\) satisfying Proposition 4.9, and choose nonzero \(b_j\) with \(\sum_jb_j^2<\infty\). Those scalar processes have almost surely bounded trajectories, time-1 invariant laws, and unit-time block laws satisfying (SF), (DLP\('\)), and (SRZ). The proposition asserts that \(\eta(t)=\sum_jb_j\eta^j(t)e_j\) again has bounded trajectories and all these properties in \(E=L^2([0,1);H)\), with finite-fiber spaces \(F_n=\operatorname{span}\{\phi_\ell\otimes e_j:\ell+j\le n\}\).

Let \(V\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\) be coercive, let \(\gamma_1,\gamma_n>0\), and consider the chain of oscillators \[\dot q=p,\qquad\dot p=-\nabla V(q)+(-\gamma_1p_1+\zeta_1(t))e_1+(-\gamma_np_n+\zeta_n(t))e_n.\] For a fixed budget \(M>0\), the permitted measurable controls satisfy \[\sup_{t\ge0}\int_t^{t+1}(|\zeta_1(s)|^2+|\zeta_n(s)|^2)\,ds\le M.\] Write \(\Phi_t(\cdot;\zeta)\) for the solution map and \(B(r)\subset\mathbb R^{2n}\) for the closed radius-\(r\) ball.

The bounded-absorbing-set assumption (BAS) states that for every \(M>0\) there is \(\rho>0\) such that for every \(r>0\) there is \(T_r>0\), uniform over all permitted controls and all initial points of \(B(r)\), with \(\Phi_t(B(r);\zeta)\subset B(\rho)\) for \(t\ge T_r\). Proposition 5.1 also assumes (SE): there is \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) such that the unforced flow converges to \((0,c)\) uniformly on the compact set \(X\) used in that hypothesis, \(\sup_{z\in X}|\Phi_t(z;0)-(0,c)|\to0\).

Under (BAS) and (SE), Proposition 5.1 asserts the existence of a compact set \(X\subset\mathbb R^{2n}\), depending only on \(M\), which is invariant under every such control at every real time \(t\ge0\): \(\Phi_t(X;\zeta)\subset X\). It additionally asserts that for every \(r>0\) there is an integer \(T_r>0\) such that all trajectories starting in \(B(r)\) belong to \(X\) for \(t\ge T_r\). These are continuous-time assertions for the sliding-window energy class.

Let \((\varphi_l)\) be an arbitrary orthonormal basis of \(L^2(0,1)\), and let the coefficient radii in the noise construction satisfy \(\sum_l c_l^2<\infty\), with the prescribed compactly supported Lipschitz coefficient densities. Propositions 4.9 and 4.10 assert that the resulting time trajectories are almost surely bounded. No bound on \(\|\varphi_l\|_\infty\), or summability involving those norms, is imposed in the stated basis and coefficient assumptions.

Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, \(E\) a Banach space, \((\eta_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}\) a stationary \(E\)-valued noise with compact marginal support \(K\), and \(X\subset H\) compact with \(S(X\times K)\subset X\). In \(u_k=S(u_{k-1},\eta_k)\), assume \(S\) is twice continuously differentiable, bounded on bounded sets together with its first two derivatives, and satisfies all the hypotheses of Theorem 3.4: (SF), (GD), (ALC), (DLP\('\)), and (SRZ). Here (GD) is a strict norm contraction after a fixed number of zero-noise steps; (ALC) requires the noise derivative to contain a finite-dimensional determining subspace; and the noise hypotheses impose total-variation Lipschitz dependence on the past, the stated finite-fiber density disintegration, and uniform recurrence of finite noise blocks to zero.

Under these conditions, Proposition 3.7 asserts that for an \(X\)-valued initial state independent of the noise and every fixed integer \(s\ge1\), the law of \((u_k,\ldots,u_{k+s})\) converges in the dual-Lipschitz metric to the corresponding stationary block law, uniformly over initial conditions. The sentence following (4.11) asserts that a stationary weak solution \((\widehat u_k)\) therefore has the stronger property below.

Let \(\mathcal E_u\) be the support of the law of the entire past \((\widehat u_j)_{j\le0}\), and let \(Q^m_{u,k}(\xi;\cdot)\) be the conditional law of \((\widehat u_{k+1},\ldots,\widehat u_{k+m})\) given that past \(\xi\). The asserted strong-feeble mixing conclusion is, for every fixed \(m\ge1\), \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\sup_{\substack{\xi\in\mathcal E_u\\g\in C_b(H^m),\ \|g\|_\infty\le1}}\left|\int g\,dQ^m_{u,k}(\xi)-\mathbb E\,g(\widehat u_1,\ldots,\widehat u_m)\right|=0.\] The supremum in this conclusion does not impose a uniform Lipschitz bound on the continuous test functions.

Consider the null-fiber branch of the proof of Theorem B. After the finite covers used there, \(p:E^4\to M^3\) is an oriented circle bundle over a closed oriented three-manifold, \(\pi_1(M)\) is torsion-free, and the prime decomposition of \(M\) contains an orientable aspherical summand. Assume, for the proof by contradiction, that \(E\) admits a metric of positive scalar curvature, and that the inclusion of each circle fiber is trivial in \(\pi_1(E)\). Then \(\pi:=\pi_1(E)\cong\pi_1(M)\) has cohomological dimension at most three; the bundle splitting \(TE\cong p^*TM\oplus\mathbb R\) makes \(E\) spin.

Using the cited assembly result for three-manifold groups and the Main Theorem and Remark 1.7 of the cited compression paper, the final paragraph asserts that under these hypotheses a classifying map \(f:E\to B\pi=K(\pi,1)\) is homotopic to a map with image in the two-skeleton \(B\pi^{(2)}\). This is the positive-scalar-curvature-dependent compression step whose cited proof is under review; it is not asserted here as an unconditional compression result.

Let \((M^{2n+2},\omega)\) be a closed integral symplectic manifold, \(n\ge2\), and let \(Z^{2n}\subset M\) be a Donaldson divisor with \([Z]=\operatorname{PD}(k[\omega])\) for a sufficiently large positive integer \(k\). If \(L\) is the prequantum line bundle, write \(E_Z=S(L^{\otimes k}|_Z)\), the circle-bundle boundary of a tubular neighborhood of \(Z\). The introductory argument asserts that its universal cover \(\widetilde E_Z\) naturally deformation-retracts onto an \((n+1)\)-dimensional simplicial complex arising from the spine of the divisor complement.

The separate intermediate assertion in Lemma 3.1 has the following setting. Let \(W^m\) be a compact manifold with boundary \(E\), assume that \(W\) deformation-retracts to a \(k\)-dimensional simplicial complex \(K\subset W\), and assume that \(E\hookrightarrow W\) induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups. For the boundary map \(f=r\circ i:E\to K\), replaced by a simplicial approximation, let \(B_\alpha\) be the finitely many contractible open vertex stars of a subdivision of \(K\), and \(U_\alpha=f^{-1}(B_\alpha)\). For an arbitrary Riemannian metric on \(E\), the proof asserts that \[C=\max_\alpha\operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{intrinsic}}(U_\alpha)<\infty\] because the index set is finite, and uses this constant to bound the fibers of the lifted map. The assertions being checked are this finite intrinsic-diameter step and the boundary retraction, rather than the lemma's final macroscopic-dimension conclusion.

Let \(j:Z^{2m}\hookrightarrow T^{2n}\) be an iterated symplectic divisor in the construction of Example 10, and let \(E\to Z\) be its canonical circle bundle, with Euler class \(e=k j^*[\omega]\) for the positive integer \(k\) of the final divisor step. For \(m=2\), the example proposes a branch in which the homomorphism \(\pi_1(S^1)\to\pi_1(E)\) has nonzero kernel, yielding a finite cyclic extension and the asserted dimensions \(\operatorname{asdim}\pi_1(E)=\operatorname{vcd}\pi_1(E)=2n\).

Let \(M\) be a closed Riemannian manifold of dimension \(n-2\), and equip \(\widetilde M\times S_r^2\) with the product Riemannian metric, where \(S_r^2\) is the round sphere of radius \(r>0\). The projection onto \(\widetilde M\) is asserted to give \(\mathrm{UW}_{n-2}(\widetilde M\times S_r^2)\le2r\). The unqualified dimension range includes \(n=2\), when \(M\) can be a point.

Let \(n\ge3\) and let \(\phi:D_n\to\mathbb R\) be a real analytic nondegenerate phase. Use the implicit curve parametrization \(\partial_y\phi(\Psi(\omega;t;y),t;y)=\omega\). Put \(d_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)=(n+1)/2\) for odd \(n\), and \((n+2)/2\) for even \(n\). For index sets \(\alpha,\beta\subset\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\), define \(\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)=\{(\alpha',\beta'): \alpha'\subseteq\alpha,\ \beta'\subseteq\beta,\ 0<|\alpha'|=|\beta'|\}\) and \[g_{\alpha',\beta'}(t;\omega;y)=\det\left[(\partial^2_{yy}\phi)(\Psi(\omega;t;y),t;y)\right]_{\alpha',\beta'}.\]

Hypothesis II requires index sets \(\alpha,\beta\), each of cardinality \(d_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)\), and an integer \(d\in\mathbb N\) satisfying two conditions. First, for no \((\omega,y)\in B^{n-1}\times B^{n-1}\), center \(s\in(-1,1)\), and scalars \(\mu_{\alpha',\beta'}\) does the polynomial identity \[1=\sum_{(\alpha',\beta')\in\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)}\mu_{\alpha',\beta'}P_d[g_{\alpha',\beta'}(\cdot;\omega;y),s](t)\] hold for all \(t\in(-1,1)\), where \(P_d\) is the degree-\(d\) Taylor polynomial. Second, the matrix whose corresponding columns are \((\partial_t^j g_{\alpha',\beta'}(t;\omega;y))_{j\ge0}\) has one constant rank \(r\), \(0\le r\le|\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)|\), throughout \(D_n\). The row and column sets are not required to be equal.

Proposition 4.2(II), in the form (5.5), asserts that there are \(\kappa>0\) and \(C_\phi<\infty\) such that for every measurable \(D:B^{n-1}\to\operatorname{Mat}_{n-1}(\mathbb R)\) and \(b:B^{n-1}\to B^{n-1}\), there are row and column sets \(\alpha_0,\beta_0\) of cardinality \(d_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)\) for which \[\sup_{\omega\in\Omega_\phi}\left|\left\{t\in I_\phi:\left|\det\left[(\partial^2_{yy}\phi)(\Psi(\omega;t;b(\omega)),t;b(\omega))D(\omega)-I_{n-1}\right]_{\alpha_0,\beta_0}\right|<\sigma\right\}\right|\le C_\phi\sigma^\kappa\] for every \(\sigma>0\). The constant is independent of \(D\) and \(b\).

For odd \(n\ge3\), Theorems 2.8(II) and 2.9(II) further assume that \(\phi\) is a Hörmander-type phase, satisfying the source conditions (H1) and (H2). They assert strict improvements over the universal exponents defined in the paper: for every \(2<q<q(n)\), there is \(\alpha_\phi(q)<\alpha_{\mathrm{LS}}(n;q)\) with \(\mathrm{LS}_q(\phi;\alpha)\) for all \(\alpha\ge\alpha_\phi(q)\); and for every \(p(n)<p<\infty\), there is \(\beta_\phi(p)<\beta(n;p)\) with \(\mathrm N_{p\to p}(\phi;\beta)\) for all \(\beta\ge\beta_\phi(p)\). These denote, respectively, the local smoothing and Nikodym maximal estimates in Definitions 1.1 and 1.2.

Let \(n\ge3\) and let \(\phi:D_n\to\mathbb R\) be a translation-invariant phase. For index sets \(\alpha,\beta\subset\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) of cardinality \(d_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)\), the source defines \[\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)=\{(\alpha',\beta')\in\mathcal P(\alpha)\times\mathcal P(\beta):0<|\alpha'|=|\beta'|\}.\] This is the printed index family, including the full pair \((\alpha,\beta)\).

For such \(\alpha,\beta\), let \(Z_{\mathrm K}(\phi;\alpha,\beta)\) consist of the \(y\in B^{n-1}\) for which there are scalars \(\mu_{\alpha',\beta'}\), independent of \(t\), satisfying \[\det[\partial^2_{yy}\phi(0,t;y)]_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{(\alpha',\beta')\in\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)}\mu_{\alpha',\beta'}\det[\partial^2_{yy}\phi(0,t;y)]_{\alpha',\beta'}\quad\text{for every }t\in(-1,1).\] Hypothesis I in Definition 2.6 requires that there exist such row and column sets with \(\mathcal L^{n-1}(Z_{\mathrm K}(\phi;\alpha,\beta))=0\). This is the literal hypothesis used for the claimed Kakeya non-compression improvement.

For a smooth phase \(\phi(x,t;y)\) on the stated unit-ball domain, Section 1.2 uses H1, the nondegeneracy of the mixed \(x,y\) Hessian, to assert a local inverse \(x=\Psi(\omega;t;y)\) solving \(\partial_y\phi(x,t;y)=\omega\) for \((\omega,t,y)\) near \((0,0,0)\), with \(x\) in the given domain. The assertion does not impose \(\partial_y\phi(0,0;0)=0\) or recenter \(\omega\) at that gradient.

For the smooth map \(\omega(y)\) in Example 3.1, the spatial Jacobian is \(D\omega(y)-\operatorname{diag}(t,t/(1-ty_2))\). With the source-defined coefficients \(A(y),B(y),C(y)\), the displayed general formula asserts \[J\Phi=\frac{A(y)t^2+B(y)t+C(y)}{1-ty_2}\] wherever the denominator is nonzero.

For a compact semialgebraic input set, Step 3 of Section 4.1 treats the one-point-per-fiber section furnished by Corollary A.5 as compact, and applies that assertion to \(\mathcal L_{\rm dir}\) and \(\mathcal L_{\rm ctr}\). The claimed implication is that compactness of the input plus the stated semialgebraic selection result supplies a compact section.

In the multiplicity argument following (4.18), the maps \(\widetilde\Psi_{\iota,v}\), obtained using a local inverse of a polynomial parameter map with nonsingular parameter Jacobian, are asserted to remain polynomial. This is the polynomiality assertion on which the stated multiplicity step relies.

Let \(2\le k\le n\), \(1\le p\le k/(k-1)\), and let \(\Gamma\) be a family of smooth curves given by graphs \((\gamma(t),t)\), \(-1<t<1\), with \(\sup_{\gamma\in\Gamma,t}|\gamma^{(N)}(t)|\le M_N<\infty\) for every \(N\ge1\). For \(0<\delta<
u<1\), take finite families \(\mathbb T_1,\ldots,\mathbb T_k\) of the associated \(\delta\)-tubes, \(T=\{(x,t):x\in B^{n-1},\ |x-\gamma_T(t)|<\delta\}\). Assume they are \(
u\)-transversal on a measurable set \(X\): at each \(x\in X\cap T_1\cap\cdots\cap T_k\), the wedge product of the unit tangent directions at any core points \(y_\ell\in\Gamma_{T_\ell}\) with \(|x-y_\ell|<\delta\) has magnitude at least \(
u\).

Theorem 6.11 asserts that there is \(A=A_{n,k,p}\ge1\) such that for every \(\epsilon>0\) and every radius-\(r\) ball with \(\delta<r<1\), \[\left\|\prod_{\ell=1}^k\left(\sum_{T\in\mathbb T_\ell}\mathbf1_T\right)^{1/k}\right\|_{L^p(X\cap B_r)}\le C\nu^{-A}r^{k/p-(k-1)}\delta^{k-1+(n-k)/p-\epsilon}\prod_{\ell=1}^k(\#\mathbb T_\ell)^{1/k}.\] Its final quantitative sentence requires \(C\) to depend only on \(n,\epsilon,M_1\), with no dependence on the higher derivative bounds \(M_N\), \(N\ge2\). This asserted uniformity is the claim under review.

Let \(1\le R\le\lambda\), and let \(S^\lambda=S^\lambda[\phi;a]\) be a Hörmander-type oscillatory operator with fixed phase and amplitude. Write \(\Theta(R^{-1/2})\) for the finitely overlapping caps covering \(B^{n-1}\), and \(f_\theta=f\psi_\theta\) for the corresponding smooth partition of unity. Proposition 9.1 asserts that for every \(\epsilon>0\) and \(N\in\mathbb N\), there are \(M=M(N,\epsilon)\) and symbols \(a_{\theta,\gamma}\), \(\gamma\in\mathbb N_0^n\), \(|\gamma|\le M\), with \[\operatorname{supp}_y a_{\theta,\gamma}\subset2\theta,\qquad|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_y^\beta a_{\theta,\gamma}|\lesssim_{N,\epsilon,\alpha,\beta}R^{-|\beta|/2}.\] The displayed negative power is part of the original existential assertion.

Writing \(S^\lambda_{\theta,\gamma}=S^\lambda[\phi;a_{\theta,\gamma}]\), these symbols are asserted to give, for every \(2\le q\le q(n)\) and every radius-\(R\) ball, \[\|S^\lambda f\|_{L^q(B_R)}\lesssim_{N,\epsilon}R^{\frac{n-1}{4}(\frac12-\frac1q)+\epsilon}\sum_{|\gamma|\le M}\left\|\left(\sum_{\theta\in\Theta(R^{-1/2})}|S^\lambda_{\theta,\gamma}f_\theta|^2\right)^{1/2}\right\|_{L^q(B_{2R})}+R^{-N}\|f\|_2.\] Lemmas 9.2 and 9.3 repeat the same negative derivative exponent for cap-supported amplitudes, at scales \(R\) and \(\lambda\), respectively.

The adjacent wave-packet construction decomposes \(f_\theta=\sum_{\omega\in R^{1/2}\mathbb Z^{n-1}}f_{\theta,\omega}\), with each Fourier term containing the modulation \(e^{-i\langle\omega,y\rangle}\). At a ball center \(x_B\), it defines \(f_T(y)=e^{i\phi^\lambda(x_B;y)}f_{\theta,\omega}(y)\) and hence displays \(f=e^{-i\phi^\lambda(x_B;\cdot)}\sum_Tf_T\). The associated tubes and localization bound are instead written using the derivative of the recentered phase \(\phi_B(x;y)=\phi(x_B+x;y)-\phi(x_B;y)\), namely the condition \(|\partial_y\phi_B^\lambda(x;y_\theta)-\omega|<R^{1/2+\epsilon/(100n)}\). This printed modulation/localization convention is the second assertion checked in the finding.

In the proof of Lemma 9.5, let \(\mathcal Q_k\) be the dyadic cubes of side length \(2^k\) in \(\mathbb R^n\). The relation \(Q_1\sim Q_2\) is defined by disjoint cubes whose parents are not disjoint. From this definition the proof asserts \(\operatorname{dist}(Q_1,Q_2)\gtrsim2^k\). For the superlevel set \(F_\sigma=\{x:\operatorname{Re}S^\lambda f(x)>\sigma\}\), \(\sigma>0\), and the composed kernel operator \(\mathcal S^\lambda=S^\lambda S^{\lambda,*}\), it consequently uses \[\sum_{Q_1\sim Q_2}|\langle\mathcal S^\lambda\mathbf1_{F_\sigma\cap Q_1},\mathbf1_{F_\sigma\cap Q_2}\rangle|\lesssim\min\{1,2^{-k(n-1)/2}\}\,M|F_\sigma|\max_{Q\in\mathcal Q_k}|F_\sigma\cap Q|,\] where \(M=\max_{Q_1}\#\{Q_2:Q_1\sim Q_2\}\lesssim1\).

Assuming the local estimate \(H_{\infty\to s}(\phi;\alpha)\), the proof then claims that the series \[\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\min\{2^{-k((n-1)/2-s\alpha)}\sigma^{-s},\ 2^k\}|F_\sigma|\] in (9.24) admits the stated finite geometric-series bound under the lemma's advertised parameter condition \(s\alpha<(n+1)/2\). The finding checks this summation step and the dyadic separation inference, without asserting that the lemma's global conclusion is false.

Let \(X,Y\) be Polish spaces, and let \(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be lower semicontinuous and bounded below, with \((X\times Y,c)\) satisfying NNCC. Proposition 3.17 asserts that, on any fixed probability space, the space of random elements inherits NNCC for the expected cost \(\widehat T_c(T,S)=\mathbb E c(T,S)\). The proposition does not assume Assumption 3.5. Its conclusion requires variational segments whose cost to the fixed base is finite at every intermediate time.

Let \(S_0,S_1,S_2\in\mathcal S_+^n\) be real positive semidefinite matrices, including singular matrices, with their unique positive semidefinite square roots. For the Bures–Wasserstein cost \[\operatorname{BW}^2(S,T)=\operatorname{tr}S+\operatorname{tr}T-2\operatorname{tr}\bigl((S^{1/2}TS^{1/2})^{1/2}\bigr),\] Proposition 4.12 calls the following matrices unitary (orthogonal in the real setting): \[U_i=(S_2^{1/2}S_i^{1/2})(S_i^{1/2}S_2^{1/2}S_i^{1/2})^{-1/2},\qquad i=0,1.\] The exponent \(-1/2\) in this display is explicitly described as any right inverse of \((S_i^{1/2}S_2^{1/2}S_i^{1/2})^{1/2}\). This is the source's displayed formula, including its middle square root.

The proposition then sets \(M_i=S_i^{1/2}U_i^T\), \(M(s)=(1-s)M_0+sM_1\), and \(S(s)=M(s)M(s)^T\), and asserts that \((S(s),S_2)\), \(0\le s\le1\), is a variational \(c\)-segment from \((S_0,S_2)\) to \((S_1,S_2)\). The proof asserts that these factors have \(M_iM_i^T=S_i\) and are optimal alignments with \(M_2=S_2^{1/2}\). No invertibility is imposed for their existence; invertibility of \(S_2^{1/2}S_i^{1/2}\) is imposed only for the subsequent uniqueness assertion.

For unit-mass measures \(\mu,
u\), let \(\mathcal H\) denote the Hellinger distance with the normalization (4.4). Equation (4.5) asserts the Fisher–Rao distance formula \[d_{m FR}(\mu,
u)=\arccos\!\left(1- rac{\mathcal H(\mu,
u)}2ight).\] The expression uses \(\mathcal H\), without its square.

For \(F(t)=|t-1|\), \(c=d^q\ge0\), and \(r,s>0\), the perspective construction is \[c_C=\inf_{z\ge0}\{|z-r|+|z-s|+d^qz\}.\] The paragraph following Example 4.18 identifies its value using the expression \(r+s-\min(r,s)\min(0,2-d^q)\); the printed formula also applies an outer \(q\)-th power without introducing a separate root-distance notation.

In the existence proof of Theorem 4.28, consider the isometries \(x\mapsto Qx+b\), with \(Q\in O(n)\), in the relevant transport-cost sublevel set. The last sentence asserts that their translation parameter is bounded by \(|b|\le W_2(\mu,\nu)\). No centering assumption on the two probability measures is imposed in that assertion.

Let \(X,Y\) be Polish spaces and \(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) lower semicontinuous and bounded below. Assume \((X\times Y,c)\) is NNCC, and let \(\gamma\in\mathcal P(X\times X\times Y)\) be concentrated on \(\Gamma=\{(x_0,x_1,y):c(x_0,y),c(x_1,y)<\infty\}\). Lemma 3.3 asserts that there are Borel measurable maps \(\Lambda_s:\Gamma\to X\), \(s\in[0,1]\), such that for \(\gamma\)-almost every endpoint triple, \(s\mapsto(\Lambda_s(x_0,x_1,y),y)\) is a variational \(c\)-segment from \((x_0,y)\) to \((x_1,y)\).

For fixed \(s\in(0,1)\), its proof takes the multivalued relation \(\widetilde\Lambda_s\) of all admissible intermediate points satisfying the NNCC inequality, and approximates \(c\) by increasing continuous \(c_n\). With endpoint laws \(\gamma^i=(p_i,p_3)_\#\gamma\), it chooses compact sets \(Z_k^i\) of \(\gamma^i\)-mass at least \(1-1/k\), and sets \(Z_k=Z_k^1\cap Z_k^2\), so that \(|c_n-c|\le1/m\) on \(Z_k\) for \(n\ge N(m)\). Define \(\widetilde Z_k\) by requiring only \((x_0,y),(x_1,y)\in Z_k\), and define \(F_{k,n,m}\) by these endpoint requirements, the additional requirement \((x,y)\in Z_k\), and \[c_n(x,y)-c_n(x,z)\le\frac4m+(1-s)[c_n(x_0,y)-c_n(x_0,z)]+s[c_n(x_1,y)-c_n(x_1,z)]\] for every \(z\) with \((x,z)\in Z_k\).

The step after (B.15) asserts \[\operatorname{Graph}(\widetilde\Lambda_s)\cap\widetilde Z_k\subseteq F_{k,n,m}\quad(n\ge N(m))\] and, up to a \(\gamma\)-null set of endpoint triples, \[\operatorname{Graph}(\widetilde\Lambda_s)\cap\widetilde Z_k=\bigcap_{m\ge1}\bigcap_{n\ge N(m)}F_{k,n,m}.\] These are the compact-set graph inclusions used to infer measurability; their assertion of control on the intermediate pair is the particular proof step under review.

On \(\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2\) off the diagonal, let \(c(x,y)=-\log|x-y|\). Example 3.21 asserts that \(c\)-segments exist for every endpoint pair having finite cost to the chosen base and that this space satisfies LMP, with the continuity requirement (2.35).

For the KL entropy \(F(t)=t\log t-t+1\), the perspective construction (4.19) uses \[c_C((x,r),(y,s))=\inf_{z>0}\{rF(z/r)+sF(z/s)+c(x,y)z\},\qquad r,s>0.\] The source substitutes \(c(x,y)=-\log(\cos^2(\min(d(x,y),\pi)))\) and identifies the resulting cost with the signed-cosine expression \(r+s-2\sqrt{rs}\cos(\min(d(x,y),\pi))\) in (4.22).

The spherical example then uses the Euclidean-cone interpretation and an attainment assertion for any prescribed target lift: for a fixed lift of one measure, an optimal lift of the other is asserted to realize the measure cost. These pointwise identification and prescribed-lift attainment assertions are the steps under review.

For the smooth cost in the differential preliminaries, the sentence preceding Definition 2.2 asserts that the bi-twist conditions imply nondegeneracy of the mixed derivative. This is an implication from the two gradient-map injectivity conditions to the invertibility condition (2.3), not a separate assumed instance of (2.3).
In the proof of Lemma 2.5, the comparison inequality is divided by a signed parameter \(t\), and (2.10) is asserted with the same inequality direction for both positive and negative \(t\).

Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(g\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\), and put \(X=Y=H\times(0,\infty)\). Example 2.11 equips this space with the semi-geostrophic cost \[c((x,a),(y,b))=\frac{\|x-y\|^2}{2b}+g\frac ab.\] For every \(x_0,x_1,\bar y\in H\) and \(a_0,a_1,\bar b>0\), it asserts that the path based at \((\bar y,\bar b)\) with \[x(s)=(1-s)x_0+sx_1,\qquad a(s)=(1-s)a_0+sa_1+\frac{s(1-s)}{2g}\|x_0-x_1\|^2,\quad 0\le s\le1,\] is a variational \(c\)-segment in \(X\times Y\), and concludes that the space is NNCC. This includes the requirement that the displayed \(a(s)\) remain positive. The printed parameter range allows both signs of \(g\).

Remarks 2.21–2.22 assert preservation of LMP under the stated cost-submersion identities and attainments for projection maps \(P_1,P_2\), without assuming continuity of the first projection, even though LMP requires continuous paths.

They also assert that the projected square-root cost is a metric when the upstairs square-root cost is a metric, without requiring \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) to be the same quotient map. These assertions are distinct from the algebraic NNCC conclusion of Proposition 2.20.

Under the smooth cost, twist, nondegeneracy and convex-gradient-image assumptions following Theorem 2.35, the cost is assumed to extend continuously to compact closures of the open domains. The text asserts attainment of the support infimum, or nonemptiness of the \(c\)-subdifferential, for finite \(c\)-concave functions on those domains. Compactness is imposed on the closures, not on the open domains themselves.

For matrices \(S\), the displayed Frobenius norm is defined as \(\operatorname{tr}(S^\top S)\). The log-Euclidean construction is asserted to give a metric on positive definite matrices using that definition, and the matrix logarithm is described as taking positive definite matrices onto positive definite matrices. The accompanying discussion also treats the log-Euclidean metric as congruence invariant.

The Gaussian discussion asserts geodesic completeness for the space of nondegenerate Gaussian measures. The assertion concerns positive definite covariances, without adjoining degenerate covariance matrices.

Section 3.1 fixes an arbitrary finite transitive graph of degree \(d\). It uses \[\phi(t)=1-2^{-e^t},\quad
 \delta(n)=e^{-\sqrt{\log\log n}},\quad
 R(n)=e^{(\log n)^9},\quad L(n)=\sqrt{\log n},\] and \(\mathcal L=\{n\ge3:\operatorname{Gr}(n)\le e^{(\log n)^{100}}\}\). The integer \(U_t(n)\) is the largest \(b\le n^{1/3}/8\) for which \(\mathbb P_{\phi(t)}(\mathrm{Piv}[4b,n^{1/3}])\le1/\log n\), and \[\Delta_t(n)=

The target is the union of both exterior sides.

The event \(B\) does not exclude edges directly from \(0\) to \([-N,N]^c\), which belong to neither of these portions.

Let the one-particle space be \(\mathbb R^L\), \(1\le N<L\), and \(\mathcal D=\{D=D^T=D^2:\operatorname{Tr}D=N\}\). Coordinate fragments partition the sites, with sizes \(L_x<N\). Compatibility requires each fragment to have occupied and unoccupied projections of dimension \(L_x\).

The stated symmetry of the interaction tensor is \(V_{ab\,cd}=V_{cd\,ab}\). Under that stated convention, equations (21), (25) and (30) use \(J(D)-K(D)\) for the effective one-body contraction. Proposition 8 applies this formula to a fragmentation-compatible projector \(D\), without assuming the surjectivity and response-invertibility conditions (A3)–(A4).

Let the one-particle space be \(\mathbb R^L\), \(1\le N<L\), and \(\mathcal D=\{D=D^T=D^2:\operatorname{Tr}D=N\}\). Coordinate fragments partition the sites, with sizes \(L_x<N\). Compatibility requires each fragment to have occupied and unoccupied projections of dimension \(L_x\).

Let \(h=h^T\) have a gap \(\epsilon_N<0<\epsilon_{N+1}\), and put \(D_0=\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0]}(h)\). Assume \(D_0\) is compatible with the fragments. For each fragment, let \(E_x\) be its coordinate inclusion and \(\Pi_x=E_xE_x^T\). The occupied/unoccupied impurity basis is \[C_0^x=\left(D_0E_x(E_x^TD_0E_x)^{-1/2}\ \big|\ (I-D_0)E_x(E_x^T(I-D_0)E_x)^{-1/2}\right).\] Set \(\mathfrak h_x=(C_0^x)^ThC_0^x\), \(\mathfrak p_x=(C_0^x)^T\Pi_xC_0^x\), and define \(\mathfrak L_x^+\) by \[\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0]}(\mathfrak h_x+M)=\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0]}(\mathfrak h_x)-\mathfrak L_x^+(M)+o(\|M\|).\]

For small symmetric block-diagonal trace-zero \(Y\in\mathcal Y\), define the perturbed high-level density at fixed \(D_0\) by \[\widetilde F_{h+Y}^{\mathrm{HL}}(D_0)=\sum_x\Pi_x C_0^x\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0]}\!\left((C_0^x)^T(h+Y-\mu_Y\Pi_x)C_0^x\right)(C_0^x)^T\Pi_x,\] where one common \(\mu_Y\) is chosen so that the total trace is \(N\). Equations (75)–(76) assert that its four-point response is \[R[Y]=\sum_x\Pi_xC_0^x\mathfrak L_x^+\!\left((C_0^x)^T(Y-\widetilde\ell(Y)\Pi_x)C_0^x\right)(C_0^x)^T\Pi_x,\qquad\widetilde\ell(Y)=\operatorname{Tr}(GY),\] with \(G=\sum_x C_0^x\mathfrak L_x^+(\mathfrak p_x)(C_0^x)^T\).

The following Taylor display likewise places a positive sign before the sum of \(\mathfrak L_x^+\) terms, and inside those terms writes \(Y+\mu_Y\Pi_x\), while the preceding spectral projector uses \(Y-\mu_Y\Pi_x\). It identifies the first-order chemical potential with \(\widetilde\ell(Y)\) by particle conservation. These are the original response sign, chemical-potential sign, and normalization formulas under review; the definition (54) retains the preceding negative spectral-projector derivative convention.

Let the one-particle space be \(\mathbb R^L\), \(1\le N<L\), and \(\mathcal D=\{D=D^T=D^2:\operatorname{Tr}D=N\}\). Coordinate fragments partition the sites, with sizes \(L_x<N\). Compatibility requires each fragment to have occupied and unoccupied projections of dimension \(L_x\).

Let \(\mathcal Y\) be the real symmetric matrices block diagonal with respect to the fragment projections and of total trace zero, and set \(B=\operatorname{Bd}|_{T_{D_0}\mathcal D}:T_{D_0}\mathcal D\to\mathcal Y\). For the interpolation lemma, put \[Q_{\ell,L}^0=(0,\ell)\times(0,L),\qquad
 G=\ell\int_0^L |g(t)|^2\,dt,\qquad

Let \(Q=[-\ell,\ell]\times[-h,h]\) and \(Q'=[-r,r]\times[-\rho,\rho]\), where \(0<r,\rho<\min\{h,\ell\}\). Section 5.2.1 permits real parameters \(\eta,\widetilde\eta,\mu,\widetilde\mu\) and connects the shear matrices \(D_{\eta,\mu}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\mu\\0&\eta\end{pmatrix}\) and \(D_{\widetilde\eta,\widetilde\mu}\) by the piecewise gradient \(\widehat D=\nabla v\) in (5.14)–(5.15), at parameter values where its denominators are nonzero. In the central interpolation region \(\Delta_3\), the displayed gradient is \[\widehat D_3=\begin{pmatrix}1+\frac h{2\ell}(\widetilde\mu-\mu)-\frac{h^2}{2\ell x_2}(\widetilde\mu-\mu)&\frac{\mu+\widetilde\mu}2+\frac{h^2x_1}{2\ell x_2^2}(\widetilde\mu-\mu)\\\frac h{2\ell}(\widetilde\eta-\eta)-\frac{h^2}{2\ell x_2}(\widetilde\eta-\eta)&\frac{\eta+\widetilde\eta}2+\frac{h^2x_1}{2\ell x_2^2}(\widetilde\eta-\eta)\end{pmatrix}.\]

Writing \(A=(\widetilde\mu-\mu)^2+(\widetilde\eta-\eta)^2\), equation (5.21) asserts, for \(i=3,4\), \[\operatorname{dist}^2(\widehat D_i,\operatorname{SO}(2))\le|\widehat D_i-I|^2\le C\frac{h^4}{\ell^2}A\left(\frac1{x_2^2}+\frac{x_1^2}{x_2^4}\right)+C\frac{h^2}{\ell^2}A+(\eta+\widetilde\eta-2).\] Equation (5.22) then asserts \[\int_{\Delta_i}\operatorname{dist}^2(\widehat D_i(x),\operatorname{SO}(2))\,dx\le C\left(\frac{h^3}{\ell}+h\ell\right)A\left|\log\frac h{2\rho}\right|+C\frac{h^3}{\ell}A+h\ell(\eta+\widetilde\eta-2).\] These are the printed bounds, including the unsquared final term and the absence of a mean-shear contribution.

On \(\mathbb T^2\) with normalized measure, let the \(K\) translates of \(\chi\) form the partition of unity in (3.3)–(3.5), so \(c=\int\chi=1/K\). Define \(m(t)=\int\widehat\eta(x,t)\,dx\) and \(A(t)=\int_0^t m(s)\,ds\). The earlier mean-free control is \[\widetilde\eta=\widehat\eta-c^{-1}A(t)\bar y(t)\cdot\nabla\chi-c^{-1}m(t)\chi.\]

The profiles and coefficients in (5.4), (5.14) and (5.15) instead combine as \(\widehat\eta-A(t)\bar y(t)\cdot\nabla\chi-m(t)\chi\), up to the displayed time-scaling factor. The asserted final construction is meant to reproduce the earlier mean-free control and supply the curl primitive (5.18).

On \(\mathbb T^2\), let \(H^s\) denote the paper's mean-zero scalar Sobolev spaces, fix \(\nu>0\), and let \(\Upsilon(w,A)\) be the divergence-free velocity with curl \(w\) and spatial average \(A\). Fix \(m\in\mathbb N\), \(w^0\in H^{m+1}\), \(g,h\in L^2((0,1);H^{m-1})\), and \(\widetilde U\in W^{1,2}((0,1);\mathbb R^2)\). With the spatially constant drift \(y\) fixed in Section 3.3, let \(v\) solve \(\partial_tv+y(t)\cdot\nabla v=g\), \(v(0)=w^0\). Set \(g_\delta(t)=\delta^{-1}g(t/\delta)\) and \(A_\delta(t)=\delta^{-1}y(t/\delta)+\widetilde U(t/\delta)\) for \(0<t<\delta\).

Let \(w_\delta\) solve \[\partial_tw_\delta-\nu\Delta w_\delta+\Upsilon(w_\delta,A_\delta)\cdot\nabla w_\delta=h+g_\delta,\qquad w_\delta(0)=w^0.\] Lemma 4.2 asserts \(\|w_\delta(\delta)-v(1)\|_{H^m}\to0\) as \(\delta\to0\), uniformly for \(w^0,g,h\) in bounded subsets of \(H^{m+1}\) and \(L^2((0,1);H^{m-1})\), respectively, with the mean profile fixed. Its proof additionally asserts that the bound \(\|w^0\|_{H^{m+1}}+\|g\|_{L^2H^{m-1}}+\|h\|_{L^2H^{m-1}}\le M_0\) puts \(v\) in a bounded subset of \(C([0,1];H^{m+1})\cap W^{1,2}((0,1);H^m)\).

Fix the Sobolev parameter \(k\in\mathbb N\), viscosity \(\nu>0\), and the finite family of spatial control profiles constructed earlier in the paper. Let \(h\in L^2((0,1);H^{k-1})\) and \(w^0,w^1\in H^{k+1}\), where these are mean-zero vorticity spaces on \(\mathbb T^2\). Let \(y(t)\) be the fixed spatially constant return drift, and choose the velocity-average profile \(U\in W^{1,2}((0,1);\mathbb R^2)\) equal to the prescribed initial average on \([0,1/4]\) and final average on \([3/4,1]\), as in (5.3). Set \(A_\delta(t)=\delta^{-1}y(t/\delta)+U(t/\delta)\).

Theorem 5.1 asserts that there exist functions \(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_N\in L^2((0,1);\mathbb R)\), chosen once before the limit \(\delta\to0\), such that the solutions of \[\partial_tw_\delta-\nu\Delta w_\delta+\Upsilon(w_\delta,A_\delta)\cdot\nabla w_\delta=h+\delta^{-1}\widetilde\eta_{\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_N}(\cdot,t/\delta),\qquad w_\delta(0)=w^0,\] satisfy \(w_\delta(\delta)\to w^1\) in \(H^k\). Here \(\widetilde\eta\) is the prescribed finite-profile control map, not an arbitrary space-time force. The theorem also asserts choices depending on the initial and target states for which convergence is uniform as those states and \(h\) vary over bounded subsets of the stated spaces. The original target class is \(H^{k+1}\); no smoothness of all spatial orders is assumed.

Fix \(T>0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). Definition 2.4 calls \((\phi_j)_{j=1}^n\subset L^2((0,T);\mathbb R)\) observable if, for every subinterval \(J\subset(0,T)\), every \(b\in C^0(J;\mathbb R)\), and every \(a_j\in C^1(J;\mathbb R)\), \[b+\sum_{j=1}^na_j\phi_j=0\quad\text{in }L^2(J)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b(t)=a_1(t)=\cdots=a_n(t)=0\ \text{for all }t\in J.\]

Remark 2.5 asserts the following sufficient construction. Let the \(\phi_j\) be bounded measurable functions having left and right limits at every point of \((0,T)\). Let \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\) be pairwise disjoint countable dense subsets of \((0,T)\), with \(\phi_j\) discontinuous at every point of \(D_j\) and continuous outside \(D_j\). Then the family is asserted to be observable in the above sense. The printed condition is discontinuity of the chosen representatives; it does not require a nonzero jump between their two one-sided limits.

Let \(p\in(1,\infty)\), \(d_f\ge1\), and \(\beta>0\). Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a locally finite connected simple undirected graph satisfying the source's volume regularity \(\mathrm{AR}(d_f)\), condition \(\mathrm{BCL}^{\mathrm{low}}_p(d_f-\beta)\), and capacity upper bound \(\mathrm{cap}_{p,\le}(\beta)\). In Proposition 8.8(ii), for the radius range of its proof, define \(n(R)\) by \(2\cdot3^{n(R)}<R\le2\cdot3^{n(R)+1}\). Let \(\alpha>1\), work on the unit-volume torus \(\mathbb T^d\) over a fixed finite time interval \([0,t_{\mathrm{fin}}]\), and let \(\chi_N>0\) satisfy \(N^2\chi_N^{\min(1,\alpha/2)}=O(1)\). These are the printed entropy and action normalizations, retained without replacing them by the report's corrections.

abla\varphi\), for the skeleton equation \(\partial_tu=	frac12\Delta u^\alpha-

The related formulas (11.6) and (11.17) use an action coefficient \(1/2\) in the asserted decomposition of \(\mathcal J\). The appendix claims \(\mathcal A(u)=\sup_\varphi\{B_u(\varphi)-\tfrac12\|u^{\alpha/2}\nabla\varphi\|_2^2\}\), with \(B_u(\varphi)=\langle\varphi_1,u_1\rangle-\langle\varphi_0,u_0\rangle-\int_0^1\langle\partial_t\varphi,u\rangle\,dt\), while retaining the one-half flux and one-half squared-control normalization above.

Let \(\alpha>1\), and let \(\eta^N\in\mathbb D_N\) be nonnegative lattice-valued paths on \(\mathbb T_N^d\), embedded as piecewise constant functions on the unit-volume torus. Put \(\mathcal H(v)=\int(v\log v-v+1)\,dx\), and use the printed dissipation and energy functionals \[\mathcal D_{\alpha,N}(\eta)=\frac1{\alpha N^{d-2}}\sum_{x,y\in\mathbb T_N^d}(\eta(x)^{\alpha/2}-\eta(y)^{\alpha/2})^2d\,p^N(x,y),\qquad \mathcal F_{\alpha,N}(\eta)=\sup_{t\le t_{\mathrm{fin}}}\mathcal H(\eta_t)+\int_0^{t_{\mathrm{fin}}}\mathcal D_{\alpha,N}(\eta_s)\,ds,\] where \(p^N\) is the nearest-neighbor transition probability. The continuum definitions are \(\mathcal D_\alpha(u)=\frac2\alpha\int_{\mathbb T^d}|\nabla u^{\alpha/2}|^2\,dx\) and \(\mathcal F_\alpha(u)=\sup_t\mathcal H(u_t)+\int_0^{t_{\mathrm{fin}}}\mathcal D_\alpha(u_s)\,ds\).

Lemma 5.1 assumes \(\mathcal F_{\alpha,N}(\eta^N)\le z<\infty\) uniformly in \(N\), and convergence in \(\mathbb D\) to a time-continuous path \(u\in\mathbb C\). It asserts strong \(L^\alpha([0,t_{\mathrm{fin}}]\times\mathbb T^d)\) convergence, a uniform \(L^\beta\) bound for some \(\beta>\alpha\), and the sharp bound \(\mathcal F_\alpha(u)\le z\). Equivalently, (5.4) asserts \[\inf_{\substack{\eta^N\in\mathbb D_N\\\eta^N\to u\text{ in }\mathbb D}}\liminf_{N\to\infty}\mathcal F_{\alpha,N}(\eta^N)\ge\mathcal F_\alpha(u).\] The numerical coefficient in this last lower bound is the part under review.

For the equilibrium product law and entropy \(\mathcal H\), Remark 4.5 and (4.23) assert divergence of the entropy exponential moment whenever \(\gamma\ge\alpha\). The asserted range includes the endpoint \(\gamma=\alpha\) and constant reference densities \(0<\rho<1\), with positive site size \(\chi\).

For some \(\beta>\alpha>1\) and a constant \(C=C(d,\alpha)\), Lemma 5.3(5.11) asserts, for every nonnegative lattice function \(\eta^N\), \[\|\eta^N\|_\beta^\beta\le C(1+\langle1,\eta^N\rangle)(1+\mathcal D_{\alpha,N}(\eta^N)).\] The constant is independent of the total mass, and the prefactor is linear in that mass.

In the antiferroelectric phase, Proposition 4.4 uses the model functions \(M_{\rm AF}(z),N_{\rm AF}(z)\). Equation (A.45) and footnote 20 assert that the model quantities are independent of \(n\), and the source identifies \(M_{\rm AF}(z)=\mathbf M(\gamma z)_{22}\). The saddle argument consequently treats its prefactor as one fixed analytic function in the application of Lemma 4.7.

In the ferroelectric construction, set \(w=nz/2\). The definition (A.88), on the positive real side near zero, is \[D_n(z)=\frac{\Gamma(w+3/2)e^w}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,w^{w+1}}.\] The estimate (A.95) uses this function as bounded inside the origin disk, and (A.98) asserts the corresponding global estimate for the error matrix as defined. The boundedness assertion includes approaching \(z=0\) for each fixed \(n\ge1\).

For \(t>\gamma>0\), (2.15) defines \(m=\sum_{k\ge1}2\sinh(2\gamma k)\delta_{-2k}\). Equation (2.14) asserts \(\int e^{tx}m(dx)=\phi(t;\gamma)\), and Remark 2.10 proposes normalizing this base measure to a probability measure using its total mass. These are assertions about the un-tilted measure \(m\).

Fix \(\ell\in\mathbb R\) and \(\alpha,\beta,B>0\). For a finite nonnegative symmetric spectral measure \(\mu\), let \(f_\mu\) be the centered stationary Gaussian process with covariance \(r_\mu(t)=\int e^{-it\lambda}\,d\mu(\lambda)\), and define \[\theta_\mu^u(T)=-T^{-1}\log\mathbb P\!\left(\inf_{t\in[0,T]}f_\mu(t)>u\right).\] Assume \(\mu\in\mathcal L_{\beta,B}\), the paper's uniformly bounded logarithmic-moment class of order \(1+\beta\), and \(\mu\in\mathcal M_{\alpha,A}\), meaning \(\mu((-x,x))/(2x)\ge\alpha\) for every \(0<x<A\), where \(A>0\).

Lemma 1.1 asserts that there is \(C>0\), depending only on \(\ell,\alpha,\beta,B\), such that for every such \(A,\mu\), every \(\delta>0\), and every \(T\ge\max\{4,A^{-1}\}\), \[0\le\theta_\mu^{\ell+\delta}(T)-\theta_\mu^{\ell-\delta}(T)\le C\delta+\frac{\log2}{T}.\] In particular, the same \(C\) is asserted to work for arbitrarily large \(\delta\), independently of \(A\) and \(T\).

Under the logarithmic spectral moment assumption, Lemma 2.19 bounds the absolute expected supremum \(\mathbb E\sup_{[0,h]}|f_\rho|\) by a positive power of \(\sup_{[0,h]}|r_\rho(0)-r_\rho(t)|\). The proof of Lemma 2.22 then uses shortening the interval to make this absolute supremum arbitrarily small, and claims a sufficiently short interval has the corresponding small-ball probability at least \(1/2\). The supremum is unanchored and retains the base value \(f_\rho(0)\).

For the centered Gaussian process \(W\) of Lemma 2.21, assume \(\operatorname{Var}W(t)\le\varepsilon/T\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(W(t+h)-W(t))\le a^2h^2\). The lemma asserts \[\mathbb P\!\left(\sup_{[0,T]}|W|>\delta\right)\le2e^{-\delta^2T/(8\varepsilon)}\] whenever \(T>c(a^{-1}+\delta^{-1}+1)\), with a universal \(c\).

Proposition 3.1 assumes \(\mu\in\mathcal M_{\alpha,A}\cap\mathcal L_{\beta,B}\), \(\nu\in\mathcal M_{(0,\alpha^{\prime}),D}\cap\mathcal L_{\beta,B}\), \(0<D\le1\), \(0<\alpha^{\prime}\le B\), \(0<\eta<c_1\alpha^{\prime}\), \(T\ge\max(c_2/\eta,1/A)\), and \(c_3/\eta\le L\le\alpha^{\prime} D^2T/B\). The passage after (3.9) asserts that \(L\ge1/(2\alpha^{\prime})\) gives the removed-mass estimate \(((1-h^2)\nu_{L/T})(\mathbb R)\le1/T\) required by Lemma 1.3(I).

Let \(D>0\), let \(\rho\) be any finite nonnegative symmetric spectral measure supported on \([-D,D]\), and let \(n\in\mathbb N\). Lemma 4.2 sets \[I_1=[0,D/n],\qquad I_{-1}=[-D/n,0),\qquad I_{\pm j}=\pm((j-1)D/n,jD/n]\quad(2\le j\le n),\] and, for positive-bin mass \(\rho(I_j)>0\), defines \[C_j(t)=\frac1{\rho(I_j)}\int_{I_j}\cos(\lambda t)\,d\rho(\lambda),\qquad S_j(t)=\frac1{\rho(I_j)}\int_{I_j}\sin(\lambda t)\,d\rho(\lambda).\] The stated class of measures includes measures with \(\rho(\{0\})>0\); no atom-free hypothesis at the origin is imposed.

For the centered stationary Gaussian process \(f_\rho\) with spectral measure \(\rho\), the lemma asserts the equality in distribution of processes \[f_\rho(t)\overset d=\sum_{j=1}^n\sqrt{\rho(I_j\cup I_{-j})}\,[\zeta_jC_j(t)+\eta_jS_j(t)]+R_n(t),\] where all \(\zeta_j,\eta_j\) are independent standard normal variables and the Gaussian remainder \(R_n\) is independent of them. It further asserts, for every \(T>0\), \[\sup_{0\le t\le T}\operatorname{Var}R_n(t)\le\frac12\left(\frac{DT}{n}\right)^2\rho([-D,D]),\] and \(\operatorname{Var}(R_n(t)-R_n(t+h))\le D^2\rho([-D,D])h^2\) for every \(h\in\mathbb R\).

For \(0<a<b\), define \[w_{a,b}(\lambda)=\left(\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{b-a}{2}\cos(1/\lambda)\right)\mathbf1_{\{|\lambda|\le1\}}.\] Equation (5.19) asserts that the averaged spectral density at the origin has lower and upper limits \(a\) and \(b\). Remark 1 and Section 5.4 use this density to claim nonexistence of the zero-level persistence exponent, with the final argument using the stated narrower range of \(a,b\).

For the moving-average processes of Example 3 with square-summable coefficients and the stated Fourier continuity at zero, the example asserts \(\theta_X^\ell=\infty\Longleftrightarrow\sum_kU_k=0\) for every real level \(\ell\). The all-real-level assertion includes negative levels.

Remark 3’s positivity discussion includes the full class \(\mathcal M\), which permits \(\rho^{\prime}(0)=\infty\), without the finite-origin-density restriction. The report distinguishes these peripheral assertions from the more restricted main theorem statements.

For a zero-sum field \(\varphi\) and constant shift \(y\), the analytic-continuation proof of Lemma 2.1 uses \[\sum_x|\varphi_x+y|^4\ge\sum_x\bigl(|\varphi_x|^4+|y|^4\bigr),\qquad\sum_x\varphi_x=0.\] The asserted inequality includes real scalar fields, before any extension to complex parameters.

With \(\rho_j=L^{-(d-4)j}\), the domain estimate is \(\|K_j\|_{\mathcal W_j}\le C_{\rm RG}\widetilde\vartheta_j^3\widetilde g_j^3\rho_j^{\mathfrak a}\), and \[\|K_j\|_{\mathcal W_j}=\|K_j\|_{T_0(\ell_j)}+\widetilde g_j^{9/4}\rho_j^{\mathfrak b}\|K_j\|_{T^{G_j}(h_j)},\qquad\mathfrak b=\mathfrak a-\mathfrak p.\] For \(d\ge12\), \(\mathfrak p=d(1-\varepsilon)/(2(d-4))\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1/(d-3)\). Equation (6.10) asserts the pointwise bound with decay power \(\rho_j^{3/4}\) from this domain norm, uniformly in the stated dimensions.

Let \(d\ge4\), \(0\le j<N\), and assume \((A_\Phi)\): the reference mass satisfies \(\widetilde a\ge0\), \(L\) is sufficiently large, \(\kappa>0\) is sufficiently small depending only on the field dimension \(n\), and \(\widetilde g_j\) is sufficiently small depending on \(L\). The extended norm is defined using \(\|(V,K,a)\|_{\mathcal Y(\vec\lambda)}=\max\{\|V\|_{\mathcal V(\ell)}/\lambda_V,\|K\|_{\mathcal W^\kappa}/\lambda_K,|a|/\lambda_a\}\), with a zero radius omitting that derivative coordinate. In particular, for \(\lambda_K>0\) it includes \(\lambda_K\) times the Fréchet derivative tested in arbitrary unit \(K\)-directions. The small domain radius bounds the base value \(K\), not these unit directions; the asserted \(\widetilde\vartheta_+^3\) factor multiplies the derivative contribution as well as the value contribution.

In dimension \(d=4\), let \(\widehat\gamma=(n+2)/(n+8)\), \(\widehat\theta=1/2-\widehat\gamma\), and \(w_N=A_4(\log L^2)^{\widehat\gamma}B^{-1/2}N^{-\widehat\theta}L^{-2N}\). At scale \(j\) in the paper's hierarchical model, let \(B\in\mathcal B_+\) be a block and let \(\mathbb E_+\) be expectation for the centered Gaussian fluctuation \(\zeta\) with covariance \(C_+=\gamma_+P_+\). The standing mass assumption in Section 8.2 is \(a\ge-\tfrac12L^{-2j}\), and the field shift is \(\theta V(\varphi)=V(\varphi+\zeta)\).
