For every \(\mathfrak h\ge\mathfrak c_+\), it asserts an \(L\)-independent constant \(C\) such that, for all fields \(\varphi\), \[\|\operatorname{Cov}_+[\theta V_1(B),\theta V_2(B)]\|_{T_{\varphi,y}(\mathfrak h,\vec\lambda)}\le C\left(\frac{\mathfrak c_+}{\mathfrak h}\right)^4\|V_1(B)\|_{T_{0,y}(\mathfrak h,\vec\lambda)}\|V_2(B)\|_{T_{0,y}(\mathfrak h,\vec\lambda)}P_{\mathfrak h}(\varphi)^{2p}.\] Here \(\operatorname{Cov}_+\) is covariance under \(\mathbb E_+\). The degree parameter \(p\) has no stated upper bound; the lemma is not restricted to quartic polynomials.

For the regularized compact Kähler metric, the source fixes the Green function by \[\Delta_{\omega_\varepsilon}G_x^\varepsilon=\delta_x-V_\varepsilon^{-1},\qquad\sup_yG_x^\varepsilon(y)=-1.\] The proof of Proposition 3.3 uses the symmetry \(G_x^\varepsilon(y)=G_y^\varepsilon(x)\) for this polewise supremum normalization. Let \((X,\omega_X)\) be a compact three-dimensional Kähler space with log-terminal singularities. Write \(X_{\mathrm{orb}}\) for its orbifold locus and \(Z=X\setminus X_{\mathrm{orb}}\). Theorem 4.3 assumes that every point of \(X_{\mathrm{sing}}\setminus Z\) is an ordinary double point, allowing a nonisolated singular set. It asserts an explicitly constructed closed positive \((1,1)\)-current \(\omega\) with local potentials on \(X\), smooth and Kähler on \(X_{\mathrm{reg}}\), and orbifold Kähler at each point of \(X_{\mathrm{orb}}\cap X_{\mathrm{sing}}\). The latter means that on every smooth local uniformizing chart \(p:V\to U\), \(p^*(\omega|_{U_{\mathrm{reg}}})\) extends to a smooth Kähler metric on \(V\). It also asserts \(J_\pi=\pi^*\omega^3/\omega_{\widehat X}^3\in L^p(\widehat X,\omega_{\widehat X}^3)\) for some \(p>1\) on a resolution \(\pi:\widehat X\to X\).

The proposed construction chooses local embeddings \((X,x)\hookrightarrow(\mathbb C^N,0)\) with defining ideals \(I_x=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\), sets \[\varphi_x=\left(\sum_{i,j}\left|\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial z_j}\right|^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad \omega=C\omega_X+dd^c\left(\sum_i\theta_i^2\varphi_{x_i}\right),\] and takes \(C\) sufficiently large and a finite subordinate partition of unity \((\theta_i)\). The text asserts comparability of the local potentials on overlaps and, at an orbifold singular point, comparability of their \(dd^c\)-forms with those from another local embedding; it uses these assertions to claim that the glued form has the preceding orbifold smoothness property.

For the local ordinary-double-point model \(f(Z)=Z_1Z_2-Z_3^2\) with uniformization \(\iota(u,v,z)=(u^2,v^2,uv,z)\), the construction uses the pullback of \(|\nabla f|\). Its comparison model in Claim 4.4 is \[\omega_0=dd^c(|u|^4+|v|^4+|uv|^2)^{1/2},\qquad C^{-1}\omega_{\mathrm{euc}}\le\omega_0\le C\omega_{\mathrm{euc}}\quad\text{on }\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\}\text{ near }0.\] Formula (4.5) compares \(\omega_0+dd^c|z|^2\) with the pullback of \(dd^c|\nabla f|+C\omega_{\mathrm{euc}}\); the asserted conclusion is smooth extension on the uniformizing chart, in addition to this comparison away from its origin.

Let \(\pi:\widehat X\to X\) be a log resolution of a compact klt Kähler space, with discrepancies \(a_i>-1\), smooth divisor norms \(|s_i|\), and \(V_\varepsilon=[\pi^*\omega_X+\varepsilon\widehat\omega]^n\). Equation (2.3) prescribes the regularized Monge–Ampère measure \(c_\varepsilon\prod_i(|s_i|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{a_i}d\widehat V\), and the text sets \(c_\varepsilon=V_\varepsilon/V\), where \(V=\int\prod_i|s_i|^{2a_i}d\widehat V\).

Let \(\Phi(t)\phi\) solve \(i\partial_tu+\Delta u=|u|^4u\) on \(\mathbb T^3\). For \(A>\delta>0\) and \(\phi\in H^1\), Definition A.8 calls \(-T=\tau_0<\cdots<\tau_m=T\) an \((A,\delta)\)-partition if \[\|\Phi(\tau_{j-1})\phi\|_{H^1}\le A,\qquad\|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{Z([\tau_{j-1},\tau_j])}<\delta\quad(1\le j\le m).\] The \(H^1\) bound is imposed only at the existing left endpoints. Proposition A.9 asserts that every refinement remains an \((A,\delta)\)-partition with these same constants.

Assume \(\phi\) is twice continuously differentiable and satisfies Assumptions 1–3. For a gradient flow \((\mu_t)_{t\ge0}\), Proposition 3.2 defines \(V_t(s,\omega)=(0,G_{\mu_t}(s,\omega))\), solves \(\dot X_t=V_t\circ X_t\), \(X_0=\operatorname{Id}\), and asserts \(\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0\). The sign of the characteristic field in the printed representation is positive.

For a locally absolutely continuous curve \(\mu_t\) in the conditional transport space and its minimal tangent field \(v_t\) from Proposition 2.4, Lemma 2.2 chooses \(\gamma_t^h\in\Pi_o^{\rm Leb}(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)\) and asserts, for almost every \(t\), \[\left(\pi^1,\pi^2,\frac{\pi^3-\pi^2}{h}\right)_\#\gamma_t^h\longrightarrow(\pi^1,\pi^2,v_t)_\#\mu_t\quad\text{in }W_2.\] The order \((\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)\) and the displayed difference quotient are the source conventions.

Fix \(c>0\) and real \(s\), with integer subsequences where \(m=cn\) is required integral. Set \(b=\sqrt{c+1}-\sqrt c\), \(D=b^{1/3}/(2c^{1/6}(c+1)^{1/6})\), and \(a_n=b-Ds\,n^{-2/3}+O(n^{-4/3})\). The exact duality uses LUE dimension \(m=cn\) and parameter \(1/c\): \[\mathbb P\{\lambda_{\min}>a_n^2/c\}=e^{-cn^2a_n^2}\frac{Z_n(a_n,c)}{Z_n(0,c)}.\]
Proposition 2.5(2.17), after subtracting the stated radial reference, asserts that \(\log Z_n(a_n,c)-\log Z_n(0,c)-cn^2a_n^2\) has the order-one term \(\log F_{\rm TW}(c^{-2/3}s)+o(1)\).

In the strict precritical phase \(a>b\), with \(w=F(a)=1/q>1\), Theorems 2.2 and 2.7 give respectively the free-energy constant \(\mathcal F^{\rm pre}\) and moment prefactor \(\mathcal G^{\rm pre}\), linked by the exact partition-function ratio (1.8). The expression (2.32) for the prefactor uses \((w-1)^3\) in the denominator where algebraic substitution into (2.9) gives \((w^2-1)^3\). Their claimed compatibility is within the stated relative \(\exp(O(n^{-1}))\) error.

Fix \(c>0\) and \(a>\sqrt{c+1}-\sqrt c\) in the strict precritical phase, with the associated parameters \(0<q<1\), \(R,\kappa>0\) determined by (1.16)–(1.18). Let \(\lambda=\bar\beta\) be the lower branch endpoint, let \(\Phi\) be the global parametrix in (5.5) with its branch normalized at infinity, and let \(\zeta\) be the local coordinate from Definition 5.2 at \(\lambda\). Its expansion is \[\zeta(z)=N^{2/3}\gamma_{11}(z-\lambda)\left(1+\tfrac12(\gamma_{12}/\gamma_{11})(z-\lambda)+O((z-\lambda)^2)\right),\] with \(\gamma_{11},\gamma_{12}\) given by (5.11)–(5.12). The parameter \(N\) is the large matrix-size parameter used in the source construction.

Writing \(\rho=\sqrt{R\kappa}\) and \(\Pi_{11}=\tfrac18\begin{pmatrix}1/6&i\\i&-1/6\end{pmatrix}\), Definition 5.8 specifies the pole-canceling matrix, equivalently, by \[H_1(z)=I-\frac{\Phi(z)\Pi_{11}\Phi(z)^{-1}}{\zeta(z)^{3/2}}+\frac{h_{11}}{z-\lambda}+\frac{h_{12}}{(z-\lambda)^2}.\] The printed coefficients are \[h_{11}=\frac{1+i}{128\sqrt2\,\rho^{1/2}\gamma_{11}^{5/2}N}\begin{pmatrix}3\gamma_{11}-10i\rho\gamma_{12}&(19\gamma_{11}+30i\rho\gamma_{12})/3\\(19\gamma_{11}+30i\rho\gamma_{12})/3&-3\gamma_{11}+10i\rho\gamma_{12}\end{pmatrix},\] \[h_{12}=\frac{5\rho^{1/2}}{48\sqrt2\,\gamma_{11}^{3/2}N}\begin{pmatrix}-1+i&1+i\\1+i&1-i\end{pmatrix},\qquad h_{21}=\overline{h_{11}},\quad h_{22}=\overline{h_{12}}.\] The source asserts that these choices make \(H_1\) holomorphic at \(\lambda\), and the conjugate-endpoint matrix \(H_2\) holomorphic at \(\beta\).

It also defines \[R_2(z)=I+\frac{h_{21}}{z-\beta}+\frac{h_{22}}{(z-\beta)^2},\qquad R_1(z)=R_2(z)\left(I+\frac{h_{11}}{z-\lambda}+\frac{h_{12}}{(z-\lambda)^2}\right)R_2(z)^{-1},\] and asserts that \(R_1\) has its only pole at \(\lambda\), so in particular it is analytic in the disk about the opposite endpoint \(\beta\). These holomorphy assertions are used to construct the refined parametrix with \(O(N^{-2})\) boundary error in the proof of Theorem 3.11.

Let \(0<\eta<1/2\), and let \(f,f'\) be real measurable signals on \([0,1]\), extended evenly to \([-1,1]\), with \(\|f\|_\infty,\|f'\|_\infty\le1-\eta\). Thus \(f,f'\in\mathcal S_\eta\), and the Szegő integrability condition \(\int_0^1\log(1-f(x)^2)(1-x^2)^{-1/2}\,dx>-\infty\) holds, likewise for \(f'\). Under \(x=\cos\theta\), \(z=e^{2i\theta}\), form the purely imaginary reflection-symmetric circle data \(b=if\), \(b'=if'\). Let \(a,a'\) be the normalized complementary factors of Theorem 4: \(a^*,(a')^*\) are outer on the disk, have positive value at zero, and satisfy \(|a|^2+|b|^2=|a'|^2+|b'|^2=1\) on the circle.

Set \(\delta=\sqrt{3\eta/2}\), and use \(L^2(\mathbb T,d\phi/(2\pi))\) norms. In Section 4.5 the proof asserts both \[\|a-a'\|_2\le\left\|\sqrt{1-|b|^2}-\sqrt{1-|b'|^2}\right\|_2+\frac14\left\|\log(1-|b|^2)-\log(1-|b'|^2)\right\|_2\] and the resulting estimate \[\|a-a'\|_2\le\left(\delta^{-1}+\tfrac12\delta^{-2}\right)\|b-b'\|_2.\] All three norms in the first displayed assertion are unsquared. These are intermediate assertions in the claimed \(1.6\eta^{-3}\) Lipschitz bound for the phase map.

Write \(W=\{x_1=0\}\), \(S_-=\{x\in W:x_{n+1}<0\}\) and \(S_+=\{x\in W:x_{n+1}>0\}\). The manuscript permits signed varifolds \[V=V_I+\cos\beta[S]_g,\qquad V_I\ \hbox{integral in }\{x_1<0\},\] where \(g,\beta\) are \(C^1\), \(S\) is measurable, and, for compactly supported \(C^1\) vector fields tangent to \(W\), \[
 \delta_{\beta,g}V(X)
 =\int\operatorname{div}_{V,g}X\,d\mu_{V_I}
  +\int_S\operatorname{div}_{W,g}(\cos\beta X)\,d\mathcal H_g^n
 =-\int g(H^{\rm tan},X)\,d\mu_{V_I}.\] This is Definition 1.1, p. 3, and Definition 2.1, pp. 13–14. In particular, negative wall weights are expressly allowed. The model is \[P_\theta^-=\{\cos\theta\,x_1+\sin\theta\,x_{n+1}=0,\ x_1\leq0\},
 \qquad V^{(\theta)}=[P_\theta^-]+\cos\theta[S_-].\] For \(0<\theta<\pi\), \[\Theta_{V^{(\theta)}}(0,1)+(\cos\theta)^-
   =\frac{1+|\cos\theta|}{2}<1.\] Here \(a^-=\max\{-a,0\}\). This shifted signed density must not be confused with normalized total variation.

The lemma quantifies over \(\theta\) separated from \(0,\pi/2,\pi\), a \(C^1\) metric and angle, and a capillary varifold with \[0\in\operatorname{spt}V_I,\quad
 \Theta_V(0,1)+(\cos\beta(0))^-
 \leq\frac34+\frac{|\cos\theta_0|}{4},\] and arbitrarily small \(H^{\rm tan}\), metric error and \(D\beta\). It claims that small \(\operatorname{osc}_{P_\theta}(V_I,B_1)\) forces \(\mathcal D(V,V^{(\theta)})\) small and \(\beta\) close to \(\theta\), allowing addition of an integer multiple of \(\pi\).

Let \(V=V_I+\cos\beta[S]_g\) satisfy the capillary first-variation definition, with a \(C^1\) metric and angle, integral interior part and locally integrable tangential mean curvature. Equation (2.10), the definition of \(H_{\beta,g}\), and (2.12) use \(\nabla_W^g\sin\beta\) in differentiating the variable wall weight \(\cos\beta\). The second identity in Theorem 2.2 is asserted with that printed definition. No density-smallness assumption is required for this identity.

For every \(\alpha>0\), Theorem 3.16 asserts the existence of \(\delta=\delta(n,\alpha)>0\) and \(\gamma=\gamma(n,\alpha)>0\) with the following property. Let \(g\) be a \(C^1\) metric on \(B_1\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\), let \(\beta\in C^1(B_1)\), let \(S\subset\mathbb R^n=\{x_1=0\}\), and let \(V=V_I+\cos\beta[S]_g\) be a \((\beta,S)\)-capillary varifold in \((B_1,g)\), supported in \(\{x_1\le0\}\), in the paper's sense. Suppose \[\Theta_V(0,1)+(\cos\beta(0))^-\le1-\alpha,\qquad \max\{\|H^{\mathrm{tan}}_{V,g}\|_{L^\infty(B_1)},\ |g-g_{\mathrm{eucl}}|_{C^1(B_1)},\ |D\beta|_{C^0(B_1)}\}\le\delta.\] Here \(t^-=\max\{-t,0\}\), and \(\Theta_V\) is the signed density used in the source.

Let \(BS=B_\gamma\cap\partial^*S\cap\{ eta
e\pi/2\}\), let \(\sigma_{V,g}\) and \(\sigma_{V_I,g}\) be the generalized boundary measures, let \(\eta_{V_I,g}\) be the interior boundary conormal, and let \(
u_g\) be the outward \(g\)-unit normal to the wall. In addition to rectifiability of \(\operatorname{spt}\sigma_{V,g}=\operatorname{spt}\sigma_{V_I,g}\), the theorem asserts \[g(\eta_{V_I,g}(x),
u_g(x))=\cos eta(x)\quad	ext{for }\mathcal H_g^{n-1}	ext{-almost every }x\in BS.\] The claimed resulting measure formula on \(B_\gamma\) is \[d\sigma_{V,g}=\cos eta\,d\mathcal H_g^{n-1}\!estriction BS+d\mathcal H_g^{n-1}\!estriction(\operatorname{spt}\sigma_{V,g}\setminus BS).\] The original hypotheses do not restrict all angles to \((0,\pi/2)\).

Let \(g\in C^1(B_1)\), \(\beta\in C^1(B_1)\), \(S\subset\{x_1=0\}\), and let \(V=V_I+\cos\beta[S]_g\) be a capillary varifold in the paper's sense. The wall weight \(\cos\beta\) is allowed to be negative, so its mass measure \(\mu_V\) can be signed. Given \(\alpha>0\), assume the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, with sufficiently small \(\delta=\delta(n,\alpha)>0\): \[\Theta_V(0,1)+(\cos\beta(0))^-\le1-\alpha,\qquad \max\{\|H^{\mathrm{tan}}_{V,g}\|_{L^\infty(B_1)},|g-g_{\mathrm{eucl}}|_{C^1(B_1)},|D\beta|_{C^0(B_1)}\}\le\delta.\] Here \(t^-=\max\{-t,0\}\), \(\Theta_V\) is the signed density, and \(|\mu_V|\) denotes total variation.

Remark 3.3 asserts under these hypotheses that \[|\mu_V|(B_1)\le\omega_n\Theta_V(0,1)+\bigl((\cos\beta(0))^-+\delta\bigr)\mathcal H_g^n(B_1\cap\mathbb R^n)\le\omega_n(1-\alpha/2).\] The first right-hand side adds a single copy of the possible negative wall weight to the signed mass.

The proof of Theorem 3.11 uses the corresponding hypothesis \(\Theta_V(0,1)+(\inf_{B_1}\cos\beta)^-\le1-\alpha\), the same small differential errors, and \(a=(\inf_{B_1}\cos\beta)^-\). For \(\xi\in B_\gamma\cap\mathbb R^n\), after its affine metric normalization with \(R=1-c(n)\delta\), display (3.33) asserts for \(0<r\le R-\gamma\) that \[|\mu_V|(B_r(\xi))\le\omega_n\bigl(\Theta_V(\xi,r)+(1+c(n)\delta)a\bigr)r^n\le\omega_nr^n.\] This too is stated as a bound on total variation, with one shifted wall-weight term.

For a \(C^2\)-small slanted graph, fixed \(0<\theta<\pi\), and a small \(C^1\) metric perturbation, the second Taylor expansion in Section 2.1 gives coefficient \(\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-1\) on \(D_1u\) in the boundary-normal component. In the Euclidean metric the asserted expansion is \(\nu_\theta(u,g_{\rm eucl})\cdot e_1=\cos\theta+(\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-1)D_1u+O_\theta(|Du|^2)\), with the upward-normal convention.

Let \(N\ge1\), \(d\ge1\), \(\sigma>0\), \(\beta\ge0\), and \(J=J_N\otimes I_d\), where \(J_N\) is the all-ones matrix. For \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^N\), define \(\|x\|_i=(|x^i|^2+N^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}|x^j|^2)^{1/2}\). Section 4 works with bounded classical solutions, \(C^1\) in time and \(C^4\) in space, of the quadratic Nash system \[-\partial_tu^i-\operatorname{tr}((\sigma I+\beta J)D^2u^i)+\frac12|D_iu^i|^2+\sum_{j\ne i}D_ju^j\cdot D_ju^i=f^i,\qquad u^i(T,\cdot)=g^i.\] Let \(\tau\in[0,T)\), \(M>0\), and assume that the Nash drift is Euclidean one-sided Lipschitz, \[\sum_{j=1}^N(D_ju^j(t,x)-D_ju^j(t,y))\cdot(x^j-y^j)\ge-M|x-y|^2\quad(t\in(\tau,T],\ x,y\in(\mathbb R^d)^N).\]

For \(h\in\{f,g\}\), suppose there is \(\widetilde L_h>0\) such that \[|h^i(x)-h^i(y)|\le\widetilde L_h\|x-y\|_i\qquad(x,y\in(\mathbb R^d)^N,\ 1\le i\le N).\] Lemma 4.3 asserts \[|u^i(t,x)-u^i(t,y)|\le c_1\|x-y\|_i\qquad(t\in[\tau,T]),\] with \(c_1\) depending only on \(T,M,\widetilde L_f,\widetilde L_g\), independently of \(N,\sigma,\beta\). Its proof takes \(c_1=\psi(0)\), where \(\psi(t)=e^{M(T-t)}\widetilde L_g+(e^{M(T-t)}-1)\widetilde L_f/M\).

Remark 4.4 asserts the same weighted Lipschitz conclusion when the transport term \(\sum_{j\ne i}D_ju^j\cdot D_ju^i\) is replaced by \(\sum_{j=1}^Nb^j\cdot D_ju^i\). Here \(b:[0,T]\times(\mathbb R^d)^N\to(\mathbb R^d)^N\) is continuous and bounded and satisfies the Euclidean condition (4.2), \[\sum_{j=1}^N(b^j(t,x)-b^j(t,y))\cdot(x^j-y^j)\ge-M|x-y|^2\quad(t\in(\tau,T],\ x,y\in(\mathbb R^d)^N).\] The own-player quadratic Hamiltonian remains in the equation. This is the extension of the weighted estimate that is subsequently invoked componentwise for \(D_iu^i\) in the derivation of (8.4) in Proposition 8.1.

Consider the symmetric quadratic-Hamiltonian Nash system with no common noise, \(\beta=0\), and idiosyncratic viscosity \(\sigma=\sigma_N>0\), with \(f^i(x)=F(x^i,m_{x^{-i}})\) and \(g^i(x)=G(x^i,m_{x^{-i}})\), where \(m_{x^{-i}}=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}\delta_{x^j}\). Assume the regularity of Remark 3.15: \(F,D_xF\), and likewise \(G,D_xG\), are Lipschitz for \((|\cdot|,W_1)\); additionally \(D_mG,D_xD_mG\) are Lipschitz for \((|\cdot|,W_1,|\cdot|)\), with the standing regularity needed for the finite-player solutions. Condition (3.9), assumed for both \(F\) and \(G\), is \[\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(D_xF(x^i,m_{x^{-i}})-D_xF(x^i,m_{y^{-i}})\bigr)\cdot(x^i-y^i)\ge-M|x-y|^2\quad\text{for all }x,y\in(\mathbb R^d)^N.\] The spatial argument in both terms is \(x^i\), as printed.

Assume \(\sigma_N\to0\) and \(\theta=\liminf_{N\to\infty}\sigma_N\log\log N\in(0,\infty]\). Theorem 3.17 asserts that there is \(\theta^*>0\), depending on \(T,F,G\), such that if \(\theta\ge\theta^*\) and the semimonotonicity constants of \(F,G\) are sufficiently small, then a subsequence has a limit \(U_0:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\to\mathbb R\) with bounded \(D_xU_0\). Both \(U_0\) and \(D_xU_0\) are asserted to be Lipschitz in \((x,m)\) and \(1/3\)-Hölder in time, and, for \(k=0,1\), every \(R>0\), and every compact \(K\subset\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\), \[\sup_{\substack{t\in[0,T],\ |x^1|\le R\\m_{x^{-1}}\in K}}|D_1^ku^1(t,x)-D_x^kU_0(t,x^1,m_{x^{-1}})|\longrightarrow0.\]

In Section 7 let \(\sigma=1\), \(\beta=0\), and use quadratic Hamiltonians. The data satisfy the mean-field bounds (MF) and one of the semimonotonicity assumptions (DS) or (LS), in the small-constant regime giving (7.1a)–(7.1b). For every \(i,N\), the running and terminal data have regularity \(f^i\in C^{2+\alpha}\), \(g^i\in C^{4+\alpha}\); they obey the other-player symmetry assumption (S) and the uniform label-Lipschitz condition (LP), with labels in \(\Lambda=[0,1]\) and constant \(L_\Lambda\). Write \(u_N(\boldsymbol\lambda,t,x)=u^1_{\boldsymbol\lambda}(t,x)\), \(D_x=D_{x^1}\), and \(\boldsymbol\lambda=(\lambda_1,\widehat\lambda)\).

Lemma 7.1 asserts that for every \(\boldsymbol\lambda,\boldsymbol\lambda'\in\Lambda^N\), \[\|u_N(\boldsymbol\lambda,\cdot)-u_N(\boldsymbol\lambda',\cdot)\|_\infty+\|D_xu_N(\boldsymbol\lambda,\cdot)-D_xu_N(\boldsymbol\lambda',\cdot)\|_\infty\le C\left(|\lambda_1-\lambda_1'|+\frac{|\widehat\lambda-\widehat\lambda'|}{N}\right),\] where the other-player vector norm is Euclidean and \(C\) depends only on \(T,L_g,L_f,L_\Lambda\), independently of \(N\).

For \(w^i=u^i_{\boldsymbol\lambda}-u^i_{\boldsymbol\lambda'}\), its proof also asserts (7.3): for every \(\tau\in[0,T]\), \[\sup_{t\in[\tau,T]}\|D_iw^i(t)\|_\infty\le C(T-\tau)^{1/2}\left(|\lambda_i-\lambda_i'|+\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}\sup_{t\in[\tau,T]}\|D_jw^j(t)\|_\infty+\sup_{t\in[\tau,T]}\|D_iw^i(t)\|_\infty\right).\] This displayed assertion contains no terminal-gradient term even though the label-dependent terminal data are permitted.

For bounded drifts Lipschitz in \((\lambda,x,\mu)\), Lemma 7.13 gives an all-label estimate (7.25) for the conditional solution laws, without a term depending on \(|\lambda-\lambda^{\prime}|\). The estimate therefore asserts zero distance for identical initial conditional laws even when the two labels differ.

The coupling equation used there has, for zero drift in one dimension, \(\partial_t
u-\Delta_x
u-\Delta_y
u+2\partial_{xy}
u=0\), and is treated as a synchronous-noise coupling in the subsequent cost differentiation.

After (7.32), let \(a_k=\#I_k^N/N\) be the empirical label weights and \(\theta_k\) the limiting weights. The squared joint label-state Wasserstein distance caused by changing these population weights is bounded by \(2\max_i|X^i|^2\sum_k|a_k-\theta_k|\). The joint distance includes label transportation, whereas the prefactor uses only the state values.

Under the paper’s quadratic-form order for possibly nonsymmetric matrices, Remark 3.4 asserts vanishing and the associated own-state/other-state separation when the relevant zero-diagonal mixed matrix has zero quadratic form. The discussion following (9.8) identifies two-sided quadratic-form bounds with an operator-norm bound.

Below (9.9), the mean-field assumption (MF) is used to assert the full Frobenius estimate \(\sum_{i,j}\|D_{ji}g^i\|_\infty^2\le2L_g^2\), with a constant independent of \(N\), including the diagonal terms.

Let \(\sigma>0\), \(\beta\ge0\), and \(J=J_N\otimes I_d\). Theorem A.1 assumes \(f^i\in C^{\gamma+\alpha}((\mathbb R^d)^N)\), \(g^i\in C^{2+\gamma+\alpha}((\mathbb R^d)^N)\), with an integer \(\gamma>1\) and \(0<\alpha<1\); \(H^i\in C^{1+\gamma+\alpha}(\mathbb R^d\times\Omega)\) for every \(\Omega\Subset\mathbb R^d\), bounded below and satisfying (H0); and (MF), together with either (DS)–(H1) or (LS)–(H1′). For each \(T>0\), the corresponding semimonotonicity constants must lie below the stated thresholds and \(N\) above the stated threshold. In the proof, these hypotheses are used for bounded classical solutions of the backward Nash system with terminal values \(g^i\); they impose no normalization \(H^i(x,0)=0\).

For such a solution, (A.2) asserts, for every \((s,z)\), \[u^i(s,z)=\int_s^T\!\int\bigl[H^i(x^i,D_iu^i)-D_pH^i(x^i,D_iu^i)\cdot D_iu^i+f^i(x)\bigr],\rho(t,dx)\,dt+\int g^i(x)\rho(T,dx),\] where the printed forward equation is \[\partial_t\rho-\operatorname{tr}((\sigma I+\beta J)D^2\rho)+\sum_j\operatorname{div}_{x^j}(D_pH^j(x^j,D_ju^j)\rho)=0,\qquad \rho(s)=\delta_z.\] The final asserted bound is \[\sup_{t\in[\tau,T]}\|u^i(t,\cdot)\|_\infty\le(T+1)\max\{\|f^i\|_\infty+(\inf H^i)^-,\ \|g^i\|_\infty\}.\] Both the representation signs and the absence of a positive \(H^i(\cdot,0)\) contribution are part of these original displays.

For \(v\in\mathcal X_\tau=C([\tau,T];C_b^1((\mathbb R^d)^N))^N\), the local fixed-point construction sets \(w^i(t,x)=H^i(x^i,D_iv^i)+\sum_{j\ne i}D_pH^j(x^j,D_jv^j)\cdot D_jv^i\). It asserts the scalar kernel expansion \[\Phi(t,x)=\frac{\exp[-(I-\beta J/(\sigma+Nd\beta))x\cdot x/(4\sigma t)]}{\sqrt{1+Nd\beta/\sigma}\,(4\pi\sigma t)^{Nd/2}}\] for the diffusion matrix \(\sigma I+\beta J\), and the backward integral formula \[S(v)^i(t,x)=(\Phi(T-t)*g^i)(x)+\int_t^T\bigl(\Phi(T-s)*(f^i-w^i(s-t,\cdot))\bigr)(x)\,ds.\] The occurrences of \(Nd\), \(T-s\), and \(s-t\) reproduce the source formulas.

Lemma 7.3 assumes an arbitrary metric parameter space \(\Gamma\), with the stated uniform boundedness, symmetry in the particle variables and common continuity moduli (7.4). It asserts existence of one subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of \(\Gamma\times\mathcal P_p(E)\). No separability condition on \(\Gamma\) is imposed.

Let \(d\ge1\) and \(d-2\le s<d\), and set \(g(x)=|x|^{-s}/s\) for \(s\ne0\) and \(g(x)=-\log|x|\) for \(s=0\). Let \(\mu\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\) have total mass one. The field in the factors \(v(x)-v(y)\) is explicitly fixed.

Work with the Coulomb/super-Coulomb kernel \(g(x)=|x|^{-s}/s\) for \(s\ne0\), or \(g(x)=-\log|x|\) for \(s=0\), in dimension \(d\ge1\), with \(d-2\le s<d\). The background \(\mu\in L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\) has mass one, with \(\iint|g(x-y)|\,d|\mu|(x)d|\mu|(y)<\infty\) when \(s\le0\). abla(g*F_i)|^2\le C/(N^2\eta_i^s)\), including the logarithmic case \(s=0\). Both statements concern the displayed auxiliary estimates; they do not assert a new conclusion about the ultimate higher-order theorem.

The truncation path (2.44) sets \(\eta_i^k=2^k\lambda\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(x_i,\partial\Omega)\ge2^k\lambda\), and otherwise resets \(\eta_i^k\) to \(r_i\). The passage from (2.46) to (2.47) invokes the monotonicity of Lemma 2.2 along this path, treating it as coordinatewise increasing.

Theorem 1.2 claims its high-order estimate under \(v\in C^{2n-1,1}\). In (1.13), the scale factor is \(\lambda^{-(n-p)+\sum_{k=1}^p c_{n-k}}\), although the bound summation indices are only \(c_1,\ldots,c_{n-p}\). The claimed derivative-budget upper bound is \(2n\).

The concluding estimates use \(A_{v,p}=\sum_{a_i\ge0,\,\sum a_i\le2n}\lambda^{\sum a_i}\prod_{i=1}^{n-p}\|D^{1+a_i}v\|_\infty\) and identify that control with the announced derivative budget. The convention after (5.42) also assigns \(A_{v,0}=1\).

Corollary 1.3(1.14) asserts its order-\(n\) commutator bound with prefactor \(CM\ell^{-n}\), where the inherited constant is independent of the field-amplitude parameter \(M\). The left side is of degree \(n\) in \(v\).

Equation (1.26) uses \(\|\nabla v\|_\infty\) for a squared-gradient estimate, and (1.33) uses degree \(n\) in \(v\) for a squared high-order norm. The duality test for (3.19) is printed as \((-\Delta)^{d-s}\kappa\) while claiming the \(\dot H^{(d-s)/2}\) squared norm.

With smeared particles \(\rho_i=\rho_{x_i}^{(\eta_i)}\) and the terms defined in (5.17)–(5.19), the reduction (5.48) asserts \(\mathrm{Term}_3-\mathrm{Term}_2=\mathrm{Term}_4\) using the off-diagonal term. The particle diagonal removes the Dirac–Dirac self interaction; the displayed decomposition omits the smooth–atomic and smooth–smooth same-particle contributions.

Formula (5.3) claims to construct a mollifier with the prescribed vanishing moments from arbitrary smooth compactly supported unit-mass bumps \(\psi,\zeta\). The bumps are not required to have zero first moment. In the one-dimensional second-order case, the construction subtracts \(\widehat\zeta\) times the degree-two nonconstant Taylor jet of \(\widehat\psi\) from \(\widehat\psi\) and asserts vanishing first and second moments.

Let \(T:I\to I\), \(I=[-1,1]\), be an analytic full-branch interval map. Thus \(I\) is the union of finitely many closed intervals \(I_\ell\) with disjoint interiors, and each restriction to \(\operatorname{int}(I_\ell)\) is an analytic diffeomorphism onto the interior of \(I\). Let \(\phi_\ell:I\to I_\ell\) be its inverse branches. The standing assumptions require numbers \(1<r<R\) such that \(\phi_\ell\in H^\infty(D_R)\) for every branch and \(\bigcup_\ell\phi_\ell(D_R)\subseteq D_r\), where \(D_t=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<t\}\).

Set \(\sigma_\ell=\operatorname{sgn}(\phi_\ell'(0))\). Lemma 2.3 asserts that \[(\widetilde{\mathcal L}f)(z)=\sum_{\ell=1}^d\sigma_\ell\phi_\ell'(z)f(\phi_\ell(z))\] defines a bounded operator \(\widetilde{\mathcal L}:H^\infty(D_r)\to H^\infty(D_R)\), with \[\|\widetilde{\mathcal L}\|\le\sup_{z\in D_R}\sum_{\ell=1}^d|\phi_\ell'(z)|.\] The proof treats this supremum as a finite norm bound under the stated bounded-holomorphic-branch and image-inclusion hypotheses.

For a vector \(v\) and target sparsity budget \(m\), Algorithm 5.1 is asserted to produce feasible inclusion probabilities in \([0,1]^n\). Its displayed control flow performs a single preservation “if” and then assigns the residual probabilities proportional to the remaining \(|v_i|\), using the remaining budget. The formula is presented as the implementation of the thresholding described before the algorithm.

Given inclusion probabilities \(p\in[0,1]^n\) summing to the integer budget \(m\), Algorithm 5.2 is asserted to produce a pivotal sample with those marginals. In line 6 it assigns the carry index \(\ell=h\) with the stated probability and leaves the old index unchanged on the complementary branch, rather than assigning \(u+1\).

In the retained implementation of sparsification, `rsri.py` lines 42–55 use the relaxed preservation comparison \(|v_i|>\mathrm{threshold}(1-10^{-8})\), then form the next residual threshold by dividing the remaining absolute mass by \(m-|\mathrm{keep}|\). The routine is intended to produce a valid residual sampling distribution whenever the identity branch does not apply.

Let \(\phi_{\mathrm{piv}}\) be pivotal sparsification with budget \(m\) on vectors in \(\mathbb C^n\), and let \(v^\downarrow\) denote the decreasing rearrangement of their coordinate magnitudes. Corollary 5.5 quantifies arbitrary \(u,v\in\mathbb C^n\) with \(\operatorname{Re}(\overline{u_i}v_i)\ge0\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(\overline{u_i}v_i)\ge0\) for every coordinate. Reading the undefined test vector \(f\) in its display as the quantified \(u\), the asserted bound is \[\mathbb E|u^*(\phi_{\mathrm{piv}}(v)-v)|^2\le\min_{0\le k\le m}\frac1{m-k}\left(\sum_{j=k+1}^n|v^\downarrow(j)|\right)^2.\] No bound on \(\|u\|_\infty\) is imposed in the corollary, and no factor involving \(u\) appears on this right-hand side.

Lemma 5.4 also states, for pivotal sampling with marginal probabilities \(p\in[0,1]^n\) and selected set \(S\), that \(\mathbb P\{i,j\in S\}\le p(i)p(j)\) for all \(1\le i,j\le n\), including the diagonal indices in its printed quantifier.

Finally, let \(\sigma\) order the magnitudes of \(v\) decreasingly and define \(g(q)=(m-q)^{-1}(\sum_{i=q+1}^n|v(\sigma_i)|)^2\). The final display on page 17 asserts, at integers for which its denominators are nonzero, \[g(q)-g(q+1)=\left(\frac1{m-q-1}\sum_{i=q+2}^n|v(\sigma_i)|\right)\left(|v(\sigma_{q+1})|-\frac1{m-q}\sum_{i=q+1}^n|v(\sigma_i)|\right).\] These are the original local assertions accompanying the pivotal-sparsification error argument.

Let RSRI be applied to \(Ax=b\), with \(G=I-A\), \(x_0=0\), and \(x_k=G\phi_k(x_{k-1})+b\), where \(\phi_k\) is the pivotal sparsifier. Assume \(m\ge m_G=\sum_{r\ge0}\||G|^r\|_1^2<\infty\). Fix \(E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|E|\le m-m_G\), and put \(u_i=0\) on \(E\) and \(u_i=1\) off \(E\). For integers \(t\ge1\) and \(0\le s\le t-1\), set \(c_i=u^*|G|^{s+1}e_i\). The proof of Proposition 6.5 defines \[w_i=\begin{cases}c_i\,x_{t-s}(i)/|x_{t-s}(i)|,&x_{t-s}(i)\ne0,\\0,&x_{t-s}(i)=0.\end{cases}\] Thus this printed vector uses the output iterate of the sparsification step.

With \(v=x_{t-s-1}\) and \(\phi=\phi_{t-s}(v)\), equation (6.10) asserts \[\mathbb E\left|u^*|G|^{s+1}(|\phi|-|v|)\right|^2=\mathbb E|w^*(\phi-v)|^2\le\frac{\||G|^{s+1}\|_1^2}{m-|E|}\,\mathbb E\bigl(u^*|v|\bigr)^2.\] The equality is asserted using the stated \(w\), while the conditional sparsification law and the preceding conditional expectation are based on the input \(v\). Entrywise absolute values in this formula are retained.

For PageRank, Proposition 3.1 states the variance coefficient \(16/[(1-\alpha)^2t]\). The shortcut proof on page 21 asserts that this coefficient follows directly from Theorem 6.1 under \(t\ge2t_b\), using its factor \(8t/(t-t_b)^2\). This finding concerns that derivation; the report supplies a separate argument supporting the stated coefficient.

Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full column rank, let \(x=\operatorname{argmin}_z\|b-Az\|_2\), and use the normalization \(\|A\|_2=\|b\|_2=1\). Let \(u\) be the unit roundoff and \(\kappa=\operatorname{cond}(A)\), with \(\kappa u\ll1\). Theorem 6.10 retains the floating-point evaluation conventions of Section 6, including back substitution for triangular solves. Its alternative hypothesis (C′) is that the computed preconditioner \(\widehat R\) is nonsingular and triangular, \(\operatorname{cond}(A\widehat R^{-1})\) is bounded by an absolute constant, and the computed initialization satisfies \[\|A(x-\widehat x_0)\|_2\lesssim\|b-Ax\|_2+\|x\|_2u.\]

Set \(M=\widehat R^{-T}A^TA\widehat R^{-1}\). The retained inner-solver hypothesis (D) is the absolute error bound \[\|\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{IterativeSolver}(c))-M^{-1}c\|_2\lesssim\kappa u\|c\|_2.\] The refinement computes \(c_i=\widehat R^{-T}A^T(b-A\widehat x_i)\), an approximate solution \(\delta y_i\) of \(M\delta y_i=c_i\), and \(\widehat x_{i+1}=\widehat x_i+\widehat R^{-1}\delta y_i\), with the displayed operations evaluated in floating point. Hypothesis (B) is the non-pathological-output condition (6.4), \[\|\widehat x\|_2\gtrsim\|x\|_2+\kappa(\|x\|_2+\kappa\|b-Ax\|_2)u,\] applied to the output under consideration.

Under these assumptions, Theorem 6.10 asserts that the first refinement is strongly forward stable, meaning \[\|x-\widehat x_1\|_2\lesssim\kappa(\|x\|_2+\kappa\|b-Ax\|_2)u,\qquad \|A(x-\widehat x_1)\|_2\lesssim(\|x\|_2+\kappa\|b-Ax\|_2)u,\] and that the second refinement \(\widehat x_2\) is backward stable, in the paper's matrix-perturbation sense: it is an exact least-squares solution for \(A+\Delta A\) with \(\|\Delta A\|_2\lesssim u\|A\|_2\). The stated preconditioner premise bounds a condition number; it does not impose absolute upper and lower singular-value bounds on \(A\widehat R^{-1}\).

Algorithm 4 sets sketch dimension \(d=12n\), \(\beta=d/n\), and \(\alpha=(1-\beta)^2\) for its FOSSILS iteration. It also stores column norms in \(d\), overwrites that vector with the sketch dimension, and later uses \(\operatorname{diag}(d)^{-1}\) to undo column scaling.

The periodic stopping test requires both \(i=1\) and \(\operatorname{MOD}(i,5)=0\) for the outer index \(i\in\{0,1\}\). After a rank truncation, the update adds \(+\mu^2z\) outside the projection although \(z=P\delta y\) is \(n\)-dimensional and the updated residual coordinates are \(r\)-dimensional. These are the literal printed algorithmic assertions.

Under the embedding distortion assumption \(\eta\le0.9\), the proof of Theorem 8.2 asserts \(\operatorname{cond}(M)\le40\) and invokes Fact 8.1 with that bound. The assertion is intended to follow from the permitted sketch distortion and the stated factorization hypotheses.

Algorithm 6 initializes \(\gamma=\|c\|\) and \(q_1=c/\gamma\) for its inner solve. The input specification does not exclude \(c=0\), and the printed algorithm has no zero-right-hand-side branch before this division.

Let \(N\subset\mathbb R^2\) be the closed convex gradient-constraint polygon, let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) be a bounded Lipschitz domain, and let \(h_0:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz. Assume the admissible class \[\mathcal A_N(\Omega,h_0)=\{u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega):\nabla u(z)\in N\ \text{for almost every }z\in\Omega,\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=h_0\}\] is nonempty. Define the variational obstacles pointwise by \(m(z)=\inf_{u\in\mathcal A_N}u(z)\) and \(M(z)=\sup_{u\in\mathcal A_N}u(z)\).

With the support function \(h_N(v)=\sup_{p\in N}\langle p,v\rangle\), equation (3.23) asserts for every \(z\in\Omega\) that \[m(z)=\max_{w\in\partial\Omega}\{h_0(w)-h_N(w-z)\},\qquad M(z)=\min_{w\in\partial\Omega}\{h_0(w)+h_N(z-w)\}.\] The assumption on admissible functions is the local almost-everywhere gradient constraint above, and the domain has no convexity requirement. This scope includes the paper's possibly nonconvex natural polygonal domains with admissible natural boundary values.

Let \(g\) be a bounded homeomorphism on the unit disk \(\mathbb D\), belonging to \(W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}\), and solving \[g_{\bar z}(z)=-b(z)\overline{g_z(z)},\] where \(b\) is holomorphic in \(\mathbb D\), \(|b|<1\), and \(\lim_{z\to w}|b(z)|=1\) for every point \(w\) of an open arc \(I\subset\partial\mathbb D\). Assume the boundary extension of Theorem 5.13: \(g\) extends real analytically across \(I\), and its boundary values there agree with a meromorphic function \(R\). Let \(\Gamma=R(I)\), and let \(z_0\in I\) be a critical point of \(R\) for which \(w_0=R(z_0)\) is a simple cusp. Write \(\tau_\Gamma(w_0)\) for the limiting cusp tangent line direction.

Corollary 5.17(ii) asserts that both images of the exact inward straight rays \[z_\pm(t)=z_0-tz_0e^{\pm i\pi/6},\qquad 0<t<\varepsilon,\] are asymptotic, as \(t\downarrow0\), to the line through \(w_0\) orthogonal to \(\tau_\Gamma(w_0)\). In addition it asserts \(g(z_\pm(t))-g(z_0)=O(t^3)\). The directional assertion concerns these rays in the original disk coordinate.

For the slicing representation in (3.16), the text asserts the same measure identity for nonorthogonal slices. If \(\eta\) is a unit tangent to the slice base, \(\xi_0\) its unit normal, and \(\xi\) a transverse unit slicing direction, the coordinates are \(F(s,t)=x_0+s\eta+t\xi\). The printed tensor representation of \(Du\cdot\xi\) uses \(ds\otimes D_t(u\circ F)\) without the geometric factor \(|\det(\eta,\xi)|\).

Under assumption (H), which requires the plastic region \(\Omega_{\rm pl}\) to be convex, Lemma 4.12 asserts that \(A_\delta=\Omega_{\rm pl}\cap\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)>\delta\}\) is convex and uses it in Merlet’s lemma. Theorem 4.10 does not impose ambient convexity of \(\Omega\), but the proof also invokes Proposition 3.25, which does require that ambient condition.

Let \(P\subset M_{\mathbb R}\) be any full-dimensional simple lattice polytope, let \(N\) be the dual lattice, and let \(\Sigma\) be the inner normal fan with primitive ray generators. Fix a face \(E\) and its cone \(\sigma=\sigma_E\). Form the ordinary quotient fan \(\operatorname{Star}(\sigma)\) in \(N/N_\sigma\), where \(N_\sigma=N\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\sigma\), using primitive ray generators in that quotient lattice. Let \(G_{\operatorname{Star}(\sigma)}\) and \(a_\rho(g)\) be the group elements and characters assigned to this fan by the source's Cox formulas. For the original ambient facets, write \(D_\rho=\partial/\partial h_\rho\), and let \(P(h)\) be their shifted polytope, with lattice-normalized measure \(dm\).

Equations (5.32) and (5.36) define \[\operatorname{Todd}_E^\vee(D)=\operatorname{mult}(\sigma)\sum_{g\in G_{\operatorname{Star}(\sigma)}}\left(\prod_{\rho\in\sigma(1)}D_\rho\right)\prod_{\rho\in\operatorname{Star}(\sigma)(1)}\frac{a_\rho(g)D_\rho e^{-D_\rho}}{1-a_\rho(g)e^{-D_\rho}},\] \[\operatorname{Todd}_E(D)=\operatorname{mult}(\sigma)\sum_{g\in G_{\operatorname{Star}(\sigma)}}\left(\prod_{\rho\in\sigma(1)}D_\rho\right)\prod_{\rho\in\operatorname{Star}(\sigma)(1)}\frac{D_\rho}{1-a_\rho(g)e^{-D_\rho}}.\] In the star products, \(\rho\) is identified with the corresponding ambient ray in a cone containing \(\sigma\), and the derivatives remain with respect to its ambient facet variable.

For every polynomial \(f\) on \(M_{\mathbb R}\), Theorems 5.26 and 5.27 assert \[\left.\operatorname{Todd}_E^\vee(D)\int_{P(h)}f(m)\,dm\right|_{h=0}=\sum_{m\in\operatorname{Relint}(E)\cap M}f(m),\qquad \left.\operatorname{Todd}_E(D)\int_{P(h)}f(m)\,dm\right|_{h=0}=\sum_{m\in E\cap M}f(m).\] The power series act with the finite-degree truncation appropriate to the polynomial. The stated scope is simple lattice polytopes; it imposes no Delzant condition ensuring that projected ambient rays are already primitive.

For a proper face of an \(n\)-dimensional polytope with \(r\) ambient facets, the unnormalized weighted face operators (6.14)–(6.17) retain the ambient prefactor \((1+y)^{n-r}\), and are asserted to yield the weighted face sum in (6.16). The allowed parameter excludes \(y=-1\) but includes \(y=1\). The assertion concerns the unnormalized formula, separately from the normalized formula below (6.17).

The source defines \(\operatorname{Tan}(P,v)=v+C_v\). Equations (5.22), (5.25), (5.28), (6.6) and (6.13) assert local Euler–Maclaurin formulas containing an additional factor \(e^{\langle v,z\rangle}\) in front of a lattice sum already taken over that translated tangent cone. The formulas include both the ordinary and weighted versions in their stated convergence chamber.

For the Cox group \(G\) and the finite stabilizer \(G_\sigma\) of a maximal cone, the proof of Lemma 3.20 and the alternative localization proof assert \(G\cong G_\sigma\times(\mathbb C^*)^{r-n}\). The fan is simplicial as required by the simple lattice polytope setting, without an assumption that the finite-kernel torus sequence splits.

For the stochastic cycles in the bounded \(C^3\) domain, let \(V_j=\{v:v\cdot n(x_j)>0\}\), \(t_b(x,v)=\inf\{t>0:x-\varepsilon tv\notin\Omega\}\), and \(t_{j+1}=t_j+t_b(x_j,v_j)\). Equation (9.17) defines \[V_j^\eta=\{v\in V_j:v\cdot n(x_j)>\eta\}\ \cup\ \{v\in V_j:|v|<\eta^{-1}\}.\]

For small \(0<\eta<1\), the next sentence asserts that \(t_k<\mathcal T/\varepsilon\) allows at most \(\lfloor C_\Omega\mathcal T/\eta^3\rfloor+1\) indices for which \(v_j\in V_j^\eta\). The set in the definition is the union of the two conditions.

For an integer \(n<y<10n\), define \(I_1=[-\lfloor7n/8\rfloor,-\lfloor n/8\rfloor]\cap\mathbb Z\) and \(I_2=y+I_1\). In the proof of Lemma 6.5, the indices \(\ell_1,\ell_2\) under consideration may both belong to \(I_1\). The proof asserts \(n/4\le\ell_1+\ell_2+n\le11n\) and applies the phase lower bound to \(k=\ell_1+\ell_2+n-1\).
The phase hypothesis is \(\|2\theta+k\alpha\|_{\mathbb T}\ge c^{\prime}|k|^{-b}\) for all sufficiently large \(|k|\); it imposes no condition at \(k=0\) or any other fixed finite set of indices.

Use the paper's quasi-periodic Schrödinger operator with positive off-diagonal entries, \[(H_{\alpha,\theta}\phi)_j=\phi_{j+1}+\phi_{j-1}+f(\theta+j\alpha)\phi_j,\] where \(f\) is real analytic in a strip and \(\alpha\) is an allowed strongly Diophantine frequency. Let \(\theta\in\mathbb T\), \(E\in\mathbb R\), and let \(\phi\) be a formal solution of \(H_{\alpha,\theta}\phi=E\phi\). Define \(D_n(\theta,E)=\det(H_{\alpha,\theta}-E)_{[0,n-1]}\), with \(D_0=1\).

For integers \(\ell_1\le y\le\ell_2\) and \(D_{\ell_2-\ell_1+1}(\theta+\ell_1\alpha,E)\ne0\), equation (2.8) asserts \[\phi_y=-\frac{D_{\ell_2-y}(\theta+(y+1)\alpha,E)}{D_{\ell_2-\ell_1+1}(\theta+\ell_1\alpha,E)}\phi_{\ell_1-1}-\frac{D_{y-\ell_1}(\theta+\ell_1\alpha,E)}{D_{\ell_2-\ell_1+1}(\theta+\ell_1\alpha,E)}\phi_{\ell_2+1}.\] Both coefficient signs are uniformly negative in the printed identity. The assertion is for formal solutions on an invertible finite restriction and does not require polynomial growth or that \(E\) belong to the spectrum.

With the exponent \(\delta\) from Lemma 2.6, equation (6.47) defines \(\mathcal B_n=\{u_n<L_n-n^{-\delta}\}\). Lemma 6.4 supplies the nearby-zero conclusion under the stronger threshold \(u_n<L_n-C_1n^{-\delta/2}\). The subsequent proof applies that conclusion to the displayed \(\mathcal B_n\) without explicitly changing the exponent. The interval scale also changes from \(e^{-n^{\delta/2}}\) to \(e^{-n^\delta}\) in (6.63).

For the Dirichlet quadratic-form Laplacian on an open set, write \(R_\eta^D(\lambda)=\sum_{k\ge1}(\lambda-\lambda_k^D(\Omega))_+^\eta\) and \(L_{\eta,d}^{\rm sc}=\Gamma(1+\eta)/[(4\pi)^{d/2}\Gamma(1+\eta+d/2)]\). At \(\eta=0\), use the strict counting function \(\#\{k:\lambda_k^D(\Omega)<\lambda\}\).

Set \(a=d/2\). Lemma 3.3 assumes \(d\geq2\), \(\gamma>0\), an open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) of finite volume, \(c>0\), and \(0<\Lambda\leq\infty\), with \[
 R_\gamma^D(\lambda)
 \leq cL^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\gamma,d}|\Omega|\lambda^{\gamma+a}
 \quad(0\leq\lambda\leq\Lambda).\] It claims, for every \(q=\gamma'\in[0,\gamma]\), that \[
 R_q^D(\lambda)
 \leq c f_\gamma^D(q)L^{\mathrm{sc}}_{q,d}|\Omega|\lambda^{q+a},
 \qquad
 0\leq\lambda\leq\frac{q+a}{\gamma+a}\Lambda,\] where the printed coefficient is \[
 f_\gamma^D(q)=
 \frac{(\gamma+a)^{\gamma+a}}{(q+a)^{q+a}}
 \frac{\Gamma(1+q+a)\Gamma(1+\gamma)}
 {\Gamma(1+\gamma+a)\Gamma(1+q)}.\] There is no restriction \(\gamma\geq1\) or \(c\geq1\) in the statement.

Let \(I_0\) be a continuous symmetric concave profile, positive on \((0,1)\), and consider the model slab with probability measure \(T^{-1}dt\,\varphi_{I_0}(s)\,ds\). For \(0\le v_0<v_1\le1\), let \(\ell\) be the chord of \(I_0\) between the endpoints and define \[L=\int_{v_0}^{v_1}\frac{dv}{I_0(v)\sqrt{(I_0(v)/\ell(v))^2-1}},\qquad\widetilde V_T=\frac1T\int_{v_0}^{v_1}\frac{v\,dv}{I_0(v)\sqrt{(I_0(v)/\ell(v))^2-1}}.\]

For the upper one-sided branch \(1=v_1>v_0>0\), Theorem 2.27 places the active interval at \([T-L,T]\), with fully occupied slices \(v(t)=1\) before it. Lemma 2.31 nevertheless identifies \(\widetilde V_T\) with the whole volume, and Corollary 2.32 uses \(\widetilde V_T=\bar v\), \(L\le T\) as the feasibility constraint for this branch of its profile formula.

Let \(n\ge2\), \(h\in C^{2,\gamma}(\partial B,[-1/2,1/2])\), and \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R_+^*,[0,1])\), with \(\varphi=0\) on \([0,1/4]\), \(\varphi=1\) on \([1/2,3/2]\), and \(\varphi\) nondecreasing on \([0,1/2]\). Define \[\zeta^t(x)=x+t\varphi(|x|)h(x/|x|)\frac{x}{|x|}.\] Definition 4.15 declares \(\zeta^t\) a diffeomorphism from \(B\) to \(B_{th}\) for every \(|t|\le1\); Lemma 4.17 uses its inverse and inverse Jacobian under these amplitude assumptions.

Let \(U_B\) satisfy (1.4): a smooth strictly increasing profile from zero to one, with exponential decay of \(1-U_B\) and its first three derivatives. Set \(T=1+(\gamma-1)M_a^2(1-U_B^2)/2\), \(\gamma=1.4\), and \(M=M_a(U_B-c)/\sqrt T\), \(c=c_r+ic_i\). The construction has \(M_a>1\), a simple turning point \(Y_0\), a separated critical point \(U_B(Y_c)=c_r\), and the large-\(\alpha\), positive-small-\(c_i\) regime \(\mathbb H_0\).

Equations (3.1)–(3.12) define \[L_pP=P^{\prime\prime}-2(M^{\prime}/M)P^{\prime}-\alpha^2\widetilde FP-Q_pP,\quad Q_p=\frac{M^{\prime\prime}}{M}-2\left(\frac{M^{\prime}}{M}\right)^2-\frac34\left(\frac{\eta^{\prime\prime}}{\eta^{\prime}}\right)^2-\frac{\eta^{\prime\prime\prime}}{2\eta^{\prime}}.\] They set \(E=M(\eta^{\prime})^{-1/2}\), \(A=E\operatorname{Ai}(\kappa\eta)\), \(B=E\operatorname{Bi}(\kappa\eta)\), with \(\kappa^3=\alpha^2F_r^{\prime}(Y_0)\), \(F_r^{\prime}(Y_0)\eta(\eta^{\prime})^2=\widetilde F\), \(\eta(Y_0)=0\), and assert the exact homogeneous identities \(L_pA=L_pB=0\).

Let \(U_B\) satisfy (1.4): a smooth strictly increasing profile from zero to one, with exponential decay of \(1-U_B\) and its first three derivatives. Set \(T=1+(\gamma-1)M_a^2(1-U_B^2)/2\), \(\gamma=1.4\), and \(M=M_a(U_B-c)/\sqrt T\), \(c=c_r+ic_i\). The construction has \(M_a>1\), a simple turning point \(Y_0\), a separated critical point \(U_B(Y_c)=c_r\), and the large-\(\alpha\), positive-small-\(c_i\) regime \(\mathbb H_0\).

With \((\alpha,c)\in\mathbb H_0\) and the cutoffs of Lemma A.2, Lemma 6.2 asserts, for sufficiently small positive \(c_i\), \[|\operatorname{Im}\mathcal K_B[\varphi_0]|\asymp\alpha^{5/6}e^{-\alpha w_0(\mathring Y)},\qquad\mathring Y\in[Y_c,\widetilde Y].\] The cutoff distances are fixed independently of \(\alpha\); the hypotheses do not require \(M_r^{\prime\prime}(Y_c)\ne0\).

For every representative \((g,V,\gamma)\) in the full space \(\mathcal M^{k^*}\) and every \(\gamma^{\prime}\in T\operatorname{GenCone}^{k^*}(N)\), Lemma 3.31 asserts \[|\nabla^m\nabla_VT(\gamma^{\prime})|\circ\iota\le Cr^{-2-m}\|\gamma^{\prime}\|,\qquad0\le m\le k^*-5.\] The stated quantifier ranges over generalized-cone tangent directions and all admissible representatives, without restricting to an ordinary-cone representative.

Let \(Q_1,Q_2\) be arbitrary finite-dimensional real-analytic submanifolds through a cone \(\gamma\), each satisfying the transversality condition (10.4). The last paragraph of Lemma 10.39’s proof asserts that, after shrinking both neighborhoods, their union is contained in a real-analytic submanifold \(Q_3\) of dimension \(\dim Q_1+\dim Q_2\).

In the varying finite-energy spaces \(\mathcal E_j^1,\mathcal E^1\) of Section 2, let \(E_j,E\) be the energy normalizations, \(d_{1,j},d_1\) their metrics, and \(H_j\) the entropy functionals. Fix a closed subgroup \(G\subset\operatorname{Aut}_0(X)\), subsets \(\mathcal F_j\subset\mathcal E_j^1\), \(\mathcal F\subset\mathcal E^1\), and functionals \(M_j:\mathcal F_j\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(M:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Both the domains and the functionals are invariant under translation and \(G\); \(0\) belongs to every domain; and \(M_j(0)\to M(0)\) in the stated extended-real codomain.

The other four hypotheses of Theorem 2.15 are: if \(\varphi_j\in\mathcal F_j\) converges strongly to \(\varphi\in\mathcal E^1\), then \(\varphi\in\mathcal F\) and \(\liminf_jM_j(\varphi_j)\ge M(\varphi)\); each \(\mathcal F_j\) is convex under psh geodesics and \(M_j\) is convex along them; there are uniform \(\delta,C_0>0\) such that \[M_j(\varphi)\ge\delta H_j(\varphi)-C_0(d_{1,j}(\varphi,0)+1);\] and the action of \(G\) on every \(\mathcal E_j^1\) is proper. The entropy bound is the displayed extended-functional bound on the energy spaces.

Put \(\mathcal F^0=\{\varphi\in\mathcal F:E(\varphi)=0\}\), \(\mathcal F_j^0=\{\varphi\in\mathcal F_j:E_j(\varphi)=0\}\), and \(d_{j,G}(\varphi,\psi)=\inf_{g\in G}d_{1,j}(\varphi^g,\psi)\), with the analogous \(d_{1,G}\). Let \(s\ge1\) be an integer, \(\zeta>0\), and \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}\). Suppose that \(A\) satisfies the robust null-space property of order \(s\) with constants \(0<\rho<1\) and \(\gamma>0\): for every \(v\in\mathbb C^n\) and every \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|S|\le s\), \[\|v_S\|_2\le \frac{\rho}{\sqrt s}\|v_{S^c}\|_1+\gamma\|Av\|_2.\] In the recovery setting, let \(y=Ax_{\mathrm{true}}+e\), with \(\|e\|_2\le\zeta\), and let \(\sigma_s(x_{\mathrm{true}})_1\) be the best \(s\)-term approximation error in the \(\ell^1\)-norm.

Define \[Q=\{z\in\mathbb C^n:\|Az-y\|_2\le\zeta\},\qquad f(z)=\|z\|_1,\qquad \widehat f=\min_{z\in Q}f(z),\qquad \widehat X=\operatorname{argmin}_{z\in Q}f(z),\] and use the fixed feasibility penalty \[g_Q(z)=\sqrt s\,\max\{\|Az-y\|_2-\zeta,0\}.\] Proposition 5.2 asserts that there are positive constants \(\widehat c_1,\widehat c_2,\widehat c_3\), depending only on \(\rho\) and \(\gamma\), such that for every \(z\in\mathbb C^n\), including points outside \(Q\), \[d_2(z,\widehat X)\le\frac{f(z)-\widehat f+g_Q(z)+\eta}{\alpha},\qquad \alpha=\widehat c_1\sqrt s,\qquad \eta=\widehat c_2\sigma_s(x_{\mathrm{true}})_1+\widehat c_3\zeta\sqrt s.\] This is the approximate-sharpness condition with exponent \(\beta=1\); its constants are uniform in the noise radius \(\zeta\) once the robust null-space constants are fixed.

In the convex optimization setup, \(\mathcal E(x)=f(x)-\widehat f+g_Q(x)\), where \(\widehat f=\min_Qf\) and \(g_Q\ge0\) vanishes exactly on \(Q\). The interpretation of (1.3) and the assertion preceding Theorem 2.1 treat \(\mathcal E(x)\le\varepsilon\) as giving the individual \(\varepsilon\)-feasibility bound \(g_Q(x)\le\varepsilon\), even when \(x\notin Q\) and the objective gap may be negative.
