Let \(H=(V,E)\) be a finite hyperquiver with \(V=[n]\), dimensions \(d_i\), and ordered edge tuples \(v(e)=(s_0(e),\ldots,s_{\mu(e)}(e))\), where \(t(e)=s_0(e)\) is the target. Repeated vertices and multiple edges are permitted. A representation assigns \(\mathbb C^{d_i}\) to vertex \(i\) and a tensor \(T_e\in\bigotimes_{j=0}^{\mu(e)}\mathbb C^{d_{s_j(e)}}\) to edge \(e\). Tensor contractions use \(u^{\mathsf T}v\), without complex conjugation.

Genericity is specifically Definition 2.5: the edges admit a partition \(E=\bigsqcup_rE_r\) whose within-block tuples agree under permutations of the tensor slots, with the identity permutation for an edge compared to itself, and with the target-slot separation required in Definition 2.5(i)(c). The tensors within a block agree under these permutations, and the tuple of one representative tensor from each block is Zariski generic in the product of the corresponding tensor spaces. Thus tensors in the same block are permitted to be dependent copies under permutation.

The singular-vector-tuple variety consists of \(([x_1],\ldots,[x_n])\in\prod_i\mathbb P(\mathbb C^{d_i})\) for which, for every edge \(e\), there is \(\lambda_e\in\mathbb C\) satisfying \(T_e(x_{s_1(e)},\ldots,x_{s_{\mu(e)}(e)})=\lambda_ex_{t(e)}\). Zero singular values are allowed in this definition. Theorem 3.1 sets \[N=\sum_i(d_i-1)-\sum_e(d_{t(e)}-1)\] and asserts emptiness when \(N<0\). For \(N\ge0\), let \(h_{s(e)}=\sum_{j=1}^{\mu(e)}h_{s_j(e)}\), and let \(D\) be the coefficient of \(\prod_i h_i^{d_i-1}\) in \[\left(\sum_i h_i\right)^N\prod_{e\in E}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{d_{t(e)}}h_{t(e)}^{k-1}h_{s(e)}^{d_{t(e)}-k}\right).\] The assertion is that the variety is empty exactly when \(D=0\), and otherwise is smooth of pure dimension \(N\) and has Segre degree \(D\).

Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb P^D\) be a smooth irreducible complex projective variety of dimension \(d\), let \(B\) be a rank-\(r\) vector bundle, and let \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma(B)\) be a vector space of sections. Definition 5.2 calls \(B\) almost generated by \(\Lambda\) if it is globally generated by \(\Lambda\), or if there are smooth irreducible proper subvarieties \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k\), with \(Y_0=X\), and bundles \(B_i\) over \(Y_i\), with \(B_0=B\), having the following properties: \(Y_i\subseteq Y_j\) implies \(B_i\subseteq B_j|_{Y_i}\); the evaluation image \(\Lambda(x)\) lies in \((B_i)_x\) for every \(x\in Y_i\); and equality holds away from the union of the proper smaller strata \(Y_j\subsetneq Y_i\).

For a generic \(s\in\Lambda\), Theorem 5.3(a) asserts \(Z(s)=\varnothing\) when \(r>d\). Part (c) asserts, when \(r<d\), that \(Z(s)\) is empty or smooth of pure dimension \(d-r\), and that its degree is the top Chern number of the restriction of \(B\) to a section of \(X\) by \(d-r\) generic hyperplanes; a nonzero such number implies nonemptiness. The definition of almost generation does not impose \(\operatorname{rank}B_i>\dim Y_i\). That extra rank condition appears in part (b), for the multiplicity-one and stratum-avoidance conclusion in the separate case \(r=d\).

For a hyperquiver representation \(R\) with the allowed partition of related edge tensors, Proposition 4.5 asserts that the section map \[L:\bigoplus_{\text{partition blocks}}\text{(one tensor parameter space)}\longrightarrow\Gamma(B(R))\] is bijective. The target is the full space of global sections of the bundle constructed in Definition 4.1, and the source assigns one tensor parameter to each block. Repeated vertices and self-loops remain allowed; tensor contractions are bilinear.

Let \(X,P\) be compact triangulable spaces and \(f:X\times P\to X\) continuous. In Example 3.12, a homology class is regarded as fixed up to scaling when it satisfies the induced eigenvector relation with an arbitrary scalar eigenvalue. The example asserts the stated dimension \(d-1\) for its fixed-class singular variety and, in particular, asserts that connected \(P\) yields exactly one nonzero such homology class up to scalar multiplication.

Example 3.13 asserts that its multilinear message-passing updates (3.8) converge to a fixed point, with no additional contraction or spectral-stability hypothesis. In the permitted one-vertex, one-loop specialization, this includes the iteration \(x^{(k+1)}=Ax^{(k)}\) for the edge matrix \(A\) and the supplied initial vector.

Let \(g_K\) denote the gauge of a unit-volume star body in the common-kernel class \(rB\subseteq\ker K\), let \(M_P=\mathbb E_P\|X\|_2<\infty\), and put \(C=r^{-2}\). For an \(\eta\)-net point \(K_0\) in radial distance, the proof of Theorem 11 asserts that every nearby body \(K\) with \(\delta(K,K_0)\le\eta\) has the pointwise brackets \[(g_{K_0}(x)-CM_P\eta)_+\le g_K(x)\le g_{K_0}(x)+CM_P\eta.\]

Let \(P\) be a probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^d\) with \(\|x\|_2\le1\) almost surely. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a class of star bodies containing \(r_{\mathcal C}B^d\) for some \(r_{\mathcal C}>0\). Suppose a metric \(D\) gives finite covers of \(\mathcal C\) for every \(0<\varepsilon\le\widetilde\varepsilon\), and the gauges \(g_K(x)=\|x\|_K\) satisfy \[\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}|g_K(x)-g_L(x)|\le C_{\mathcal C}D(K,L).\] Put \(\mathcal F_{\mathcal C}=\{g_K:K\in\mathcal C\}\).

For a sample \(X_m=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), define \(\|g\|_{1,X_m}=m^{-1}\sum_i|g(x_i)|\), \(c_{P,m}=\sup_{K\in\mathcal C}\|g_K\|_{1,X_m}\le1/r_{\mathcal C}\), and the empirical Rademacher complexity \(\mathfrak R(\mathcal F_{\mathcal C};X_m)=\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{g\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal C}}m^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i g(x_i)\), where the \(\sigma_i\) are independent uniform signs. The proof of Theorem 14 asserts \[\mathfrak R(\mathcal F_{\mathcal C};X_m)\le\inf_{0<\varepsilon\le\widetilde\varepsilon}\left[\varepsilon+c_{P,m}\sqrt{\frac2m\log N(\mathcal F_{\mathcal C},\|\cdot\|_{1,X_m},\varepsilon)}\right],\] and bounds the displayed covering number by \(N(\mathcal C,D,\varepsilon/C_{\mathcal C})\). The multiplier in this deterministic complexity estimate is the empirical \(L^1\) radius \(c_{P,m}\). The bodies are not required to have unit volume.

Fix dimension \(d\) and \(r>0\), and write \(\kappa_{d-1}=\operatorname{vol}_{d-1}(B^{d-1})\). The source defines \(\mathcal C^d(r,1)=\{K\text{ convex}:rB^d\subseteq K,\ \operatorname{vol}_dK=1\}\), whose members lie in \(R_rB^d\), where \(R_r=(d+1)/(r^{d-1}\kappa_{d-1})\). In the proof of Corollary 5, the covering class is the larger class \(\mathcal C(r)=\{K\text{ convex}:K\subseteq R_rB^d\}\).

The displayed assertion is that, for constants \(c,\varepsilon_0>0\) depending only on \(d\), the Hausdorff covering numbers satisfy \[\log N(\mathcal C(r),d_H,\varepsilon)\le c\,\frac{d-1}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{R_r}{\varepsilon}\right)<\infty\qquad(0<\varepsilon\le R_r\varepsilon_0).\] This is the logarithmic metric-entropy bound used to construct covers of unions of well-conditioned convex bodies.

Let \(P_1,P_2\) be probability measures with \(P_1\ll P_2\), and let \(\Phi\) be a real-valued potential with finite positive normalizers \(Z_{P_i}=\int e^{-\Phi}\,dP_i\). Define the posteriors by \(d\mu_{P_i}=Z_{P_i}^{-1}e^{-\Phi}\,dP_i\). Proposition 7 asserts \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu_{P_1},\mu_{P_2})^2\le\frac{2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\Vert P_2)}{Z_{P_1}^2}.\] No upper bound on \(e^{-\Phi}\) is included in the stated general premise.

For a positive Gaussian with covariance \(\Sigma\), write \(E_\Sigma\) for its ellipsoidal shape, with \(\operatorname{vol}(E_\Sigma)=\kappa_d\sqrt{\det\Sigma}\), and \(\kappa_d=\operatorname{vol}(B^d)\). The displayed Gaussian specialization of the unit-volume optimizer in Theorem 3 is \[K_*=\kappa_d^{1/d}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/(2d)}E_\Sigma.\] In particular, this body is claimed to satisfy the required normalization \(\operatorname{vol}(K_*)=1\).

For every \(r>0\), Theorem 7 asserts existence of a minimizer over the class \(\mathcal S^d(r,1)\) of volume-one star bodies with common kernel ball \(rB\). The claimed domain is all positive \(r\); no separate nonemptiness restriction is stated. The broader existence argument likewise applies its compactness and continuity conclusion to a closed bounded admissible class without explicitly requiring that class to be nonempty.

In the paragraph preceding Theorem 3, the source asserts that a continuous probability density \(p\) on \(\mathbb R^d\) with finite second moment satisfies the theorem's radial positivity and continuity conditions. For the gauge objective, the radial quantity is \[\rho_L(u)^{d+1}=\int_0^\infty t^d p(tu)\,dt,\qquad u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}.\] In particular, the assertion requires this quantity to be strictly positive in every direction.

For the Gibbs density \(p_K=Z_K^{-1}e^{-g_K}\), the equivalences on page 4 identify minimizers of \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\Vert p_K)\) with minimizers of the cross-entropy/gauge objective \(\mathbb E_Pg_K(X)+\log Z_K\), using absolute continuity \(P\ll p_K\). The asserted identification does not additionally assume finite entropy or a finite KL value.

Let \(C=B^{-1}F\) be an admissible transport operator satisfying (H1)–(H6), and let \(Cu^\circ=\mu u^\circ\), \(\lambda^\circ=\mu^{-1}\), with the normalization \(\|Cu^\circ\|=2\) in the chosen real Hilbert metric. The method defines \[R(u,\nu)=\begin{pmatrix}(I-\nu C)u\\1-\|Cu\|^2/2\end{pmatrix}\] and treats \((u^\circ,\lambda^\circ)\) as a zero of this residual.

Equations (3.2) and (3.5) use the block map \[(h,\eta)\longmapsto\begin{pmatrix}(I-\nu C)h-\eta Cu\\-\langle Cu,h\rangle\end{pmatrix}\] as the residual Jacobian. Theorem 3.10 then claims local quadratic convergence of the written iteration to \((u^\circ,\lambda^\circ)\), including the one-step estimate (3.59).

For the real Hilbert-space update, set \(M_\lambda=I-\lambda C\), \(f=Cu\), \(g=M_\lambda u\), and \(s=1-\|f\|^2/2\). Equation (4.29) defines \[Q(w,
u)=	frac12 igl(\|M_\lambda w-
u f+g\|^2+(s-\langle f,wangle)^2 igr).\] The displayed descent direction (4.30) uses first component \[-M_\lambda^*(M_\lambda w-
u f+g)+(\langle f,wangle-s)f.\]

The same construction asserts that the exact update belongs to \(f^\perp\) and that projected descent on that space can solve the update equations to arbitrary accuracy. This assertion is made for the displayed residual, whose second block equation requires \(\langle f,w\rangle=s\).

For the transport operator \(C\), an approximate reciprocal eigenvalue pair \(\bar\mu=\bar\lambda^{-1}\) and \(\bar u\), equation (4.33) asserts \[(I-\bar\lambda C)^{-1}C\bar u=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma\frac{\bar\mu\zeta}{\bar\mu-\zeta}(\zeta I-C)^{-1}\bar u\,d\zeta.\] Here \(\Gamma\) is the boundary of a disc centered at \(\bar\mu\), chosen to enclose the nearby principal eigenvalue, with the source's clockwise convention. The formula is intended where the left-hand inverse and the contour resolvent are defined.

Let \(C=B^{-1}F\) be the transport solution/fission operator of (2.30), acting on \(U=L^2(D\times V)\), under (H1)–(H6). The spatial domain \(D\) is bounded and convex with piecewise \(C^1\) boundary; the compact velocity domain \(V\subset\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}\) has measure one and contains a set homeomorphic to \(S^{d-1}\). The nonnegative scattering and fission kernels \(\kappa,\phi\in L^2(D\times V\times V)\) have uniformly bounded integrals in either velocity variable. The bounded cross-section \(\sigma\) exceeds each of the two scattering-kernel velocity integrals by at least a constant \(\alpha>0\). The fission kernel satisfies \(\phi\ge c_f>0\) and the continuity requirement (H6).

Let \(u_1\) be the normalized principal right eigenvector and \(\mu_1\) its eigenvalue. Section 5 initializes with any \(a_0^\circ\in U\) satisfying \(\|a_0^\circ\|=1\) and \(\langle a_0^\circ,u_1\rangle\ne0\), and defines \[a_{n+1}=Ca_n^\circ,\qquad a_{n+1}^\circ=\frac{a_{n+1}}{\|a_{n+1}\|},\qquad \rho_{n+1}=\langle Ca_n^\circ,a_n^\circ\rangle.\] Theorem 5.1 asserts that for every \(1>\bar\delta>1-\Delta\), with the relative spectral gap \(\Delta\) from (3.24), there is a finite constant \(C_0\) such that \[\|u_1-a_n^\circ\|\le C_0\bar\delta^n,\qquad |\mu_1-\rho_n|\le C_0\bar\delta^n.\] The initialization in (5.1) uses this right-eigenvector overlap; the nonnegativity condition on the initial vector in the later Lemma 5.6 is a separate, stronger hypothesis.

For pointwise finite-dimensional persistence modules, set \(\operatorname{Er}_\varepsilon(M)=\operatorname{im}(M(-\varepsilon)\to M(\varepsilon))\) and \(M\le^*N\) if \(\dim M_p\le\dim N_p\) for every parameter \(p\). Definition 4.2 defines \[d_E(M,N)=\inf\{\varepsilon\ge0:\operatorname{Er}_\varepsilon(M)\le^*N,\ \operatorname{Er}_\varepsilon(N)\le^*M\}.\] As a distance in the sense of Definition 4.1, this is claimed to satisfy \(d_E(M,Q)\le d_E(M,N)+d_E(N,Q)\) for every three modules in its domain.

Let \(M,N\) be pointwise finite-dimensional persistence modules, let \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and set \(r=\operatorname{supdim}M=\sup_p\dim M_p<\infty\). Theorem 5.4 starts with morphisms \(\phi:M\to N(\varepsilon)\) and \(\psi:N\to M(\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(\psi(\varepsilon)\phi=M_{0\to2\varepsilon}\). Part (i) asserts the existence of a \(2r\varepsilon\)-refinement \(\widetilde N\) of \(N\) whose barcode contains the barcode of \(\operatorname{Pru}_\varepsilon(M)\).

If also \(\phi(\varepsilon)\psi=N_{0\to2\varepsilon}\), so that \(\phi,\psi\) form an \(\varepsilon\)-interleaving, part (ii) asserts that \(\operatorname{Pru}_\varepsilon(M)\) itself is a \(2r\varepsilon\)-refinement of \(N\). Corollary 5.5 states that it is a \(2r\varepsilon\)-refinement of both \(M\) and \(N\), and Corollary 5.6 asserts \[f_R(M,N)\le2r\,d_I(M,N),\] using the paper's refinement dissimilarity \(f_R\) and interleaving distance \(d_I\). These statements allow \(r=0\); no positive lower bound on \(r\) is included.

In the exchange construction in the proof of Theorem 5.4, indecomposable summands of \(\ker\overline{\psi(\varepsilon)}\) are replaced by isomorphic copies lying in individual summands of \(\overline N\). The definition of a partial decomposition additionally requires each replacement \(X^S\subseteq\ker\overline{\psi(\varepsilon)}\). The exchange step sets \(Y^T=\pi_i(Y)\), with \(\pi_i\) the coordinate projection, and treats the verified inclusion \(\pi_i(Y)\subseteq\overline Z_i\) as meeting the stated partial-decomposition conditions, including the kernel inclusion.

In the construction used for Theorem 5.9, let \(n\ge2\), and set \(q=(0,6n)\), \(x=(2n^2,4n)\), \(y=(2n^2+2n,2n)\), and \(z=(2n^2+4n,0)\). For \(1\le i\le2n\), define the interval \[I_i=\uparrow\{q,x,y,z\}\setminus\uparrow\{(0,2n^2+10n),(2n^2+8n+i,2n^2+8n+i),(2n^2+10n,0)\}.\] Here \(\uparrow\) denotes upward closure in coordinatewise ordered \(\mathbb R^2\). The ambient module is \(I=\bigoplus_i k_{I_i}\), with coordinate basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_{2n}\); structure maps keep a coordinate while its target remains in its interval and otherwise send it to zero.

Put \(q_i=q+(2n^2-in,2n^2-in)\), \(x_i=x+(i,i)\), \(y_i=y+(i,i)\), and \(z_i=z+(i,i)\). The submodule \(M\subseteq I\) is generated, for \(1\le i\le2n-1\), by \(e_i\) at \(q_i,x_i\), by \(e_i-\widetilde e_{i+n}\) at \(y_i\), and by \(e_i-\widetilde e_{i+n-1}\) at \(z_i\), where \(\widetilde e_j=e_j\) for \(j\le2n\) and \(\widetilde e_j=e_{2n}\) thereafter. There are also generators \(e_{2n}\) at \(q_{2n},x_{2n},y_{2n},z_{2n}\).

For \(0\le\delta<n-1\), the proof of Lemma 5.10, in its analysis of a decomposition \(M_1\oplus M_2\in\mathrm{EN}_\delta(M)\), uses the equality \[M_{x_c+(\delta,\delta)}=k^{c+n-2}\qquad(1\le c\le n),\] where \(k^j=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_j\}\). The subsequent proof defines \(f:I\to I(1)\) by \(e_i\mapsto e_{i+1}\) for \(i<2n\), \(e_{2n}\mapsto e_{2n}\), on the corresponding source/target interval overlap, with zero outside, and restricts it to \(M\). With \(T=M_{0\to1}\), it asserts that at every index \(p\), \[\operatorname{im}(T-f)_p\subseteq\operatorname{span}\{-e_1+e_2,\ldots,-e_{2n-1}+e_{2n}\},\qquad e_{2n}\notin\operatorname{im}(T-f)_p.\] These are the two intermediate assertions being examined.

Let \(d\ge2\), let \(\eta\) be a Poisson process of fixed intensity \(\alpha>\alpha_c(d)\) in \(\mathbb R^d\), and join points at distance less than one. Let \(\eta_*\) be its unique unbounded component and \(\eta_*(U_m)\) the selected well-connected component in \(U_m=3^mU_0\), where \(U_0\) is a fixed convex or \(C^{1,1}\) domain. The graph Laplacian is \(\mathcal Lu(x)=\sum_{y\sim x}(u(y)-u(x))\). Under the intended Dirichlet convention used in the report, the graph equation holds at vertices more than distance two from the boundary and the solution vanishes in the width-two boundary shell.

Theorem 1.1 asserts the existence of a deterministic positive matrix \(\bar a\), constants \(C,s>0\), and one random scale \(\mathcal X\) with \(\mathbb P(\mathcal X\ge Ct)\le2e^{-t^s}\) for all \(t>0\), such that simultaneously for every \(m\in\mathbb N\) with \(R=3^m>\mathcal X\) and every \(\bar u\in H^2(U_m)\cap H_0^1(U_m)\), the solution of \[-\mathcal Lu(x)=-\nabla\cdot\bar a\nabla\bar u(x)\] satisfies \[\|u-\bar u\|_{\underline L^2(\eta_*(U_m))}\le C(d,\alpha,U_0)\|\bar u\|_{\underline L^2(U_m)}R^{-1}L_m,\qquad L_m=\begin{cases}1,&d\ge3,\\\sqrt m,&d=2.\end{cases}\] The norms are the normalized norms used in the source. The forcing is evaluated at graph vertices; this assertion imposes neither a frequency restriction nor averaging of that forcing.

Use the unit-radius Poisson graph at fixed \(\alpha>\alpha_c(d)\), its selected connected component \(\eta_*(U_m)\), and \(U_m=3^mU_0\). Write \(N_m=|\eta_*(U_m)|\), \(I_m(f)=N_m^{-1}\sum_{x\in\eta_*(U_m)}f(x)^2\), and normalize continuum functions by \(|U_m|^{-1}\int_{U_m}f^2=1\). For \(\psi_{0,k}(y)=\phi_{0,k}(3^my)\), the proof of Lemma A.2 calls the variables \(Z_y=\psi_{0,k}(y)^2\), indexed by \(y\in3^{-m}\eta_*(U_m)\), independent and identically distributed, and asserts the variance-only bound \[\mathbb P(|I_m(\phi_{0,k})-1|\ge t)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{N_mt^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\quad(t>0),\] where \(\sigma^2\) is their stated variance.

In (2.12)–(2.13), the same empirical-normalization argument is used under a variational maximum over continuous continuum-normalized competitors, initially restricted by (2.8) to \(\|f\|_\infty\le4\|\phi_{0,1}\|_\infty\) and \(|U_m|^{-1}\int|\nabla f|^2\le4\cdot3^{-2m}\lambda_{0,1}\). The claimed concentration scale is \(3^{-m}\sqrt{\lambda_{0,k}}\) for \(d\ge3\), with tail \(2\exp[-C(d,U_0)(3^m/\sqrt{\lambda_{0,k}})^{d-2}]\); in \(d=2\) the scale is \(3^{-m}\sqrt{m\lambda_{0,k}}\), with tail \(2e^{-C(U_0)m}\).

For the reverse comparison, (2.20) defines \[\mathcal A_T=\{f\in C(U_m)\cap L^2(U_m):\|f\|_{\underline L^2}=1,\ \|f\|_\infty\le4T\lambda_{0,1}^{d/4}\}.\] The proof asserts a bound for the maximum Rayleigh quotient over \(\mathcal A_T\), with failure probability \(2\exp[-C(d,U_0)(3^m/\sqrt{\lambda_{0,1}})^{d-2}/T^2]\) for \(d\ge3\), or \(2e^{-C(U_0)m/T^2}\) for \(d=2\), and then maximizes over \(T\) because the asserted numerical bound is independent of \(T\). The sampling model throughout is the selected graph component; no independent-sampling replacement is part of the original hypotheses.

Let \(\alpha>\alpha_c(d)\), \(U_m=3^mU_0\), and let \(\lambda_{0,k}\) be the ordered continuum Dirichlet eigenvalues of \(-\nabla\cdot\bar a\nabla\) on \(U_0\), with associated rescaled eigenfunctions \(\phi_{0,k}\) on \(U_m\). The discrete eigenvectors \(\phi_{m,k}\) belong to the selected Poisson graph with the intended zero boundary-shell condition. Theorem 1.2 uses one random scale \(\mathcal X\) with stretched-exponential tail, and covers every \(m,k\) such that \(R=3^m>\mathcal X\) and \(R^{-1}\sqrt{\lambda_{0,k}}L_m<C_1\), where \(L_m=1\) for \(d\ge3\) and \(L_m=\sqrt m\) for \(d=2\).

The prescribed normalizations are \(|U_m|^{-1}\int\phi_{0,k}^2=1\) and empirical average \(\operatorname{Avg}_{\eta_*(U_m)}(\phi_{0,k}\phi_{m,k})=1\). The gap is \[\gamma(\lambda_{0,k})=\min_{j:\lambda_{0,j}\ne\lambda_{0,k}}|\lambda_{0,j}-\lambda_{0,k}|.\] The theorem asserts the individual-eigenvector comparison (1.11), and the proof expresses its claimed normalized discrete \(L^2\) rate as \[\|\phi_{m,k}-\phi_{0,k}\|_{\underline L^2}\le\frac{C}{\gamma(\lambda_{0,k})}R^{-1}\lambda_{0,k}^{3/2}L_m.\] No simplicity assumption on \(\lambda_{0,k}\) is imposed; (2.35) nevertheless calls its maximizing continuum eigenfunction unique.

For the ground-state argument, put \(v=\phi_{0,1}+\sum_i\partial_i\phi_{0,1}\varphi_{e_i}\) and \(w_{m,1}=\phi_{m,1}-v\), where \(\varphi_{e_i}\) are the first-order correctors. The original displayed residual identity (2.25) is \[(\mathcal L-\lambda_{m,1})w_{m,1}=-\mathcal Lv+\nabla\cdot\bar a\nabla\phi_{0,1}+(R^{-2}\lambda_{0,1}-\lambda_{m,1})\phi_{0,1}+\lambda_{m,1}\sum_i\partial_i\phi_{0,1}\varphi_{e_i}.\] This residual is tested against \(w_{m,1}\); the printed argument contains no projection away from the resonant eigenspace.

In the supercritical Poisson graph setting \(\alpha>\alpha_c(d)\), let \(R=3^m\), \(U_m=RU_0\), and use the eigenfunctions and normalization of Theorem 1.2. Let \(\mathcal X\) be that theorem's global random scale. Theorem 1.3 assumes \(R>\mathcal X\) and the spectral condition \(R^{-1}\sqrt{\lambda_{0,k}}L_m<C_1\), where \(L_m=1\) in \(d\ge3\) and \(L_m=\sqrt m\) in \(d=2\). Put \(v_{m,k}=\phi_{0,k}+\sum_i\partial_i\phi_{0,k}\varphi_{e_i}\).

With the intended boundary-distance reading used in the report, it asserts that one deterministic \(C(d,\alpha)\) gives, for every \(x=R\zeta\in\eta_*(U_m)\), \(\zeta\in U_0\), \[|\phi_{m,k}(x)-\phi_{0,k}(x)|\le\frac{C}{\operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\partial U_0)}(1+\sqrt m\,\mathbf1_{d=2})(1+\lambda_{0,k})^{d/4+3/2}R^{-1}.\] The same right side is asserted to bound \[|\phi_{m,k}(y)-\phi_{m,k}(z)-(v_{m,k}(y)-v_{m,k}(z))|\] for every adjacent pair \(y\sim z\) in \(\eta_*(B_{\mathcal X}(x))\). The quantification is over all these vertices and edges, with the single stated global-scale restriction.

The local regularity step (2.27) instead invokes the radius \(R_x=\tfrac12R\operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\partial U_0)\) and requires \(R_x\ge\mathcal X(x)\), the random regularity scale at that center. The subsequent (2.31) and pointwise argument use powers of this local scale. These local conditions/factors are the ones compared with the uniform theorem statement in this finding.

The printed negative-Sobolev-norm definition uses the expression \[\sup_{g\ne0}\frac{\langle f,g\rangle_{H^1}}{\|g\|_{H^1}},\] where the test functions have zero boundary values. It is presented as the negative norm used in the subsequent Dirichlet estimates; the numerator is the displayed \(H^1\) inner product.

Let \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{al\times al}\) be the symmetric orthogonal matrices of the adjacent transpositions in an isotypic representation of \(S_n\), and let \(B_i=\rho_\lambda(\tau_i)\in\mathbb R^{l\times l}\) be the canonical Young orthogonal matrices. For \(X\in\mathbb R^{al\times l}\), Theorem 2 defines \(\operatorname{vec}(X)\) by concatenating columns and uses \[K_i=A_i\otimes I_l-I_{al}\otimes B_i\] as the linear system encoding \(A_iX=XB_i\). The resulting nullspace, reshaped with that same column convention, is asserted to supply the intertwiners used in Corollary 4 and Algorithms 2–3.

The application discussion describes a general hook partition \(\lambda=(m+1,1^{n-m-1})\) as having only quadratic dimension growth in \(n\), without restricting \(m\) to a fixed quadratic-size family.

For the two tensor-product families in Figure 3, of dimensions \(D_1=(n-1)^2\) and \(D_2=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)/4\), the discussion gives worst-case operation counts \(O(n^7)\) and \(O(n^{13})\). Those counts are presented alongside Corollary 3, whose proved constituent/multiplicity bound is \(O(n^2D^3)\) in the stated real-arithmetic model.

In the proposed validation sketch, suppose \(Q_{\rm fp}\) is invertible and \[Q_{\rm fp}Q_{\rm fp}^{\mathsf T}=I+E,\qquad Q_{\rm fp}^{-1}=Q_{\rm fp}^{\mathsf T}+\widetilde E.\] The printed similarity expansion uses \[Q_{\rm fp}A Q_{\rm fp}^{-1}=Q_{\rm fp}A Q_{\rm fp}^{\mathsf T}+A\widetilde E.\] The sketch is used with Algorithm 1, where the columns of \(Q_{\rm fp}\) are approximate joint eigenvectors and the computed transformed matrix is \(Q_{\rm fp}^{\mathsf T}A Q_{\rm fp}\).

For a discrete or continuous dynamical system \(X\) on a topological space \(M\), Definition 2.2 requires one universal Turing machine \(T_U\) such that, for every initial configuration \(c\) of \(T_U\), there exist a computable point \(p_c\in M\) and a computable open set \(U_c\subset M\) satisfying \[T_U\text{ halts on }c\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{the positive trajectory of }X\text{ through }p_c\text{ meets }U_c.\] Both the point and the open target may depend on \(c\). The surrounding convention requires coordinates of the point to be exactly computable in finite time from \(c\), and describes computability of the open set as approximation to arbitrary precision, without a fixed geometric presentation.

Remark 4.4 asserts that Seifert flows \(l\partial_{\phi_1}+k\partial_{\phi_2}\), with \(l,k>0\), and rigid disk rotations cannot be Turing complete in this sense. Its argument grants an oracle deciding whether two computable sets intersect, associates a computable invariant circle to a rational ratio \(l/k\) or an invariant torus to an irrational ratio, and identifies positive-orbit reachability of \(U\) with nonemptiness of the intersection of \(U\) with that invariant set. It treats the halting/reachability problem of a Turing-complete system as undecidable even under the stipulated oracle.

In the proof of Proposition 4.3, the classified flow is orbitally conjugate to \(R_{l,k}=l\partial_{\phi_1}+k\partial_{\phi_2}\), where \(l,k>0\). On the standard section \(\{\phi_1=0\}\), the return angle is \(2\pi k/l\). The proof asserts that this angle is zero modulo \(2\pi\) because the return map of the constructed transverse disk is the identity near its boundary, without identifying that disk with the stated standard section.

Open problem 4 asks whether there exist a compact Riemannian three-manifold, with the manifold and metric freely chosen, and a Turing-complete steady Navier–Stokes flow on it. In this question the viscous operator is the Hodge Laplacian, as specified in Remark 6.1.
In the steady Euler/Beltrami discussion, the printed Bernoulli function is \(B=p+\|X\|/2\), used with the stated identity relating \(\iota_Xd(X^\flat)\) to \(-dB\).

In the planar encoding, the one-dimensional interval \(I_{(q,t)}\) is translated in the printed formula by the vector \((2j,2j)\), while the initial point is printed as \(p_{c_i}=(i+\phi(c_i),0)\) for the strip \([2i,2i+1]\times[0,\infty)\). These are the original coordinate assignments to be checked against the subsequent construction.

Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a bounded polyhedral Lipschitz domain and \(\mathcal T\) a conforming simplicial mesh, with no restriction \(n\ge2\). Define \[c_{\mathcal T}=\max_{T\in\Delta_n(\mathcal T)}\frac{\operatorname{diam}(T)}{\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb B_T)},\] where \(\mathbb B_T\) is the largest inscribed ball. Proposition 8.1 claims that the constructed operators \(W^k\) and the squared sum of bubble norms satisfy uniform \(L^2\) stability with a constant depending only on the fixed dimension and \(c_{\mathcal T}\). In particular, \(\|W^0u\|_{L^2}\le C(n,c_{\mathcal T})\|u\|_{L^2}\) on its stated domain, which includes continuous piecewise polynomial zero-forms.

Let \(\mathcal T\) be the simplicial mesh, let \(f\in\Delta_{m-1}(\mathcal T)\) with \(1\le m\le n-1\), and let \(f^*\) be its \((n-m)\)-dimensional link manifold. On the simplicial cochain spaces \(C^k(f^*)\), write \(\delta_k\) for the coboundary and \(\partial_{k+1}\) for its adjoint in the standard cochain inner product. The augmented complex (2.7) retains the terminal map \[\delta_{n-m}c=\sum_{e\in\Delta_{n-m}(f^*)}o(e,T_e)c_e,\qquad T_e=\langle e,f\rangle,\] with the orientation signs of (2.9). The source says this map is always defined, while describing the last arrow as possibly redundant when \(f\) meets the boundary.

Lemma 2.1 asserts that for every \(0\le k<n-m\) and every \(c\in C^k(f^*)\) with \(\partial_kc=0\), there exists \(\widetilde c\in C^{k+1}(f^*)\) such that \[\partial_{k+1}\widetilde c=c,\qquad\delta_{k+1}\widetilde c=0,\] and that these conditions determine \(\widetilde c\) uniquely. The statement is also used with values in a finite-dimensional vector space. In (3.8), when \(n-m=1\), the source explicitly defines the gauge operator \(\delta_1\) by the same terminal functional (2.9), including the boundary-link setting under discussion.

The displayed exterior derivative of a \(k\)-form on PDF page 6 uses \[\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}\partial_{v_j}u_x(v_1,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_{k+1})\] without an alternating sign. The link discussion on PDF page 10 designates \(m=n-1\) as the zero-dimensional case, although it uses \(f\in\Delta_{m-1}\) and \(\dim f^*=n-m\).

The proof of Lemma 4.4 prints the range \(0\le j<m-n\). Equation (5.4) gives target form degree \(k\) for \(Q^k_{e,f}\), whose preceding definition uses \(\Pi_{j+1}\). These are local formula and index assertions in the construction.

Let \(\alpha_i\in(0,1]\) be the permitted regularities. Let \(\mathcal{PB}\) be the vector space with basis planar rooted trees with edge labels \(0,1,\ldots,n\): each nonzero-labeled edge ends at a leaf, and at each vertex there is at most one such outgoing edge and it is rightmost. Give an undecorated (label-zero) edge degree \(1\) and an edge decorated by \(i\) degree \(\alpha_i-1\), and add these edge degrees to define \(|\tau|\). Set \[A=\{0\}\cup_i\alpha_i\mathbb N\cup_i(\alpha_i\mathbb N-1).\] The construction imposes no additional reciprocal-integer or nonresonance restriction.

Lemma 3.5 asserts that \((A,\mathcal{PB},G)\) is a regularity structure. In particular, the edge-sum degree must grade the entire declared tree space by \(A\): every permitted basis tree \(\tau\) must satisfy \(|\tau|\in A\), and \(\mathcal{PB}=\bigoplus_{\beta\in A}\mathcal{PB}_\beta\).

Let \(\alpha_i\in(0,1]\) be the permitted regularities. Let \(\mathcal{PB}\) be the vector space with basis planar rooted trees with edge labels \(0,1,\ldots,n\): each nonzero-labeled edge ends at a leaf, and at each vertex there is at most one such outgoing edge and it is rightmost. Give an undecorated (label-zero) edge degree \(1\) and an edge decorated by \(i\) degree \(\alpha_i-1\), and add these edge degrees to define \(|\tau|\). Set \[A=\{0\}\cup_i\alpha_i\mathbb N\cup_i(\alpha_i\mathbb N-1).\] The construction imposes no additional reciprocal-integer or nonresonance restriction.

Definition 2.8 requires the degree-zero homogeneous space of a regularity structure to be isomorphic to \(\mathbb R\). Lemma 3.5 applies that definition to the full declared tree space, and therefore asserts \(\mathcal{PB}_0\simeq\mathbb R\), with the one-vertex unit tree spanning the zero sector, for the permitted regularities. No quotient identifying distinct basis trees is imposed.

For \(S_1\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\), let \(K=\{X:s(X)\ge0\text{ for every }s\in S_1\}\). For \(S_2\subseteq\mathcal M\), let \(\mathcal K\) be the probability measures supported on \(K\), having all marginal moments finite and satisfying every moment constraint in \(S_2\). The moment-polynomial algebra is \(\mathcal M=\mathbb R[\mathrm m_\alpha:\alpha\ne0]\), with \(\mathrm m_0=1\).

For \(f\in\mathcal M[x]\), Proposition 2.4 asserts equivalence between \(f(\mu,X)\ge0\) for every \((\mu,X)\in\mathcal K\times K\), where the point \(X\) is chosen independently of the measure, and \(f[\pi,F]\ge0\) almost everywhere for every admissible random-variable representation on a probability space. In particular, the reverse implication quantifies over all points of \(K\), not merely almost every point under \(\mu\).

For \(S_1\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\), let \(K=\{X:s(X)\ge0\text{ for every }s\in S_1\}\). The moment-polynomial algebra is \(\mathcal M=\mathbb R[\mathrm m_\alpha:\alpha\ne0]\), with \(\mathrm m_0=1\).

For a moment polynomial \(f\) nonnegative on \(\mathcal K\times K\), it asserts the stated moment-cone membership of \(f+\varepsilon\), for every \(\varepsilon>0\), using the cone generated by square-free products of the constraints. Its proof in particular asserts that the ordinary preordering generated by \(S_1\) is archimedean from boundedness of \(K(S_1)\) alone.

For \(S_1\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\), let \(K=\{X:s(X)\ge0\text{ for every }s\in S_1\}\). The moment-polynomial algebra is \(\mathcal M=\mathbb R[\mathrm m_\alpha:\alpha\ne0]\), with \(\mathrm m_0=1\).

In Theorem 6.9, \(S_1\) may be arbitrary, \(S_2\) is finite, and \(f\in\mathcal M[x]\) is nonnegative on \(\mathcal K\times K\). When \(\mathcal K=\varnothing\), Case (b) introduces \(z=x_{n+1}\) and \[S_1^\prime=z(\{1\}\cup S_1),\qquad S_2^\prime=\mathrm m_{1,0,\ldots,0}^{\,2}S_2.\] The printed moment index denotes the first original coordinate. The proof asserts that \(zf\) is nonnegative on the new feasible measure-point product and can therefore be treated by Case (a).

For arbitrary \(S\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\), let \(\zeta\) fix the free variables \(x\), fix \(\mathrm m_0=1\), and send every nonconstant moment symbol \(\mathrm m_\alpha\) to zero. The proof of Corollary 6.14 asserts \[\zeta(\operatorname{QM}(S,\varnothing))\subseteq\operatorname{QM}(S),\] where the source moment cone includes the generators \(\mathrm m(g^2s)\) for \(s\in\{1\}\cup S\), and the target is the ordinary quadratic module in \(\mathbb R[x]\).

Let \((x_1,\ldots,x_6)=(A_1,A_2,A_3,B_1,B_2,B_3)\) be jointly defined \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variables, with no zero-mean assumption. Let \(E_3\) be the six-dimensional \(\mathbb F_2\)-space of even subsets of an eight-letter alphabet modulo complementation, with symmetric difference as addition and symplectic pairing \(\langle I,J\rangle=|I\cap J|\pmod2\). Definition 6.2 calls a subspace merotropic unless it is isotropic of dimension greater than one. Proposition 6.3 asserts that every such merotropic subspace belongs to one of the eight representatives in Table 8, up to the natural \(S_8\) action and orthogonal complementation.

Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(T>0\), \(m\ge1\), and \(\alpha>0\). Section 2 sets \(d(m)=2(m+1)+\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) and \(\mathcal H_m=H^{d(m)}([0,T]\times\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^{n\times n})\times H^{d(m)}([0,T]\times\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n)\), with the time/space Sobolev convention defined there. The coefficient class \(\mathcal H_m^{+,\alpha}\) means \((a-\alpha I,b)\in\mathcal H_m\), with \(a-\alpha I\) symmetric positive semidefinite pointwise. The generator is \(L_t\varphi=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\partial_{ij}\varphi+\sum_i b_i\partial_i\varphi\).

Under Assumption (A), \(p_0\in H^{2m+1}(\mathbb R^n)\) is a nonnegative probability density, and \(p(t,\cdot)\) is the marginal density of \(dX_t=b(t,X_t)dt+\sqrt{a(t,X_t)}dW_t\). At equally spaced times \(t_\ell=T(\ell-1)/(M-1)\), take \(N\) independent samples with density \(p(t_\ell,\cdot)\), using the stipulated product law across times. For \(R>0\), define \[\widehat p(t,x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^M c_\ell(t)\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N\rho_R(x-X_{\ell,j}),\qquad\mathcal F\rho_R=\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le R\}},\] where \(c_\ell(t)=e_\ell^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}(K_{m+1}(t,t_j))_{j=1}^M\), \(G_{ij}=K_{m+1}(t_i,t_j)\), and \(K_{m+1}\) is the time Sobolev reproducing kernel.

For \(u\in H^{1,2}\), the error functional is \[L(u)=\int_0^T\left(\|\partial_t p-\partial_tu\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^n)}^2+\|p-u\|_{H^2(\mathbb R^n)}^2\right)dt.\] Theorem 5.3 asserts that a constant \(C=C(n,m,T)\) gives, for \(M,N\in\mathbb N\), \(M\ge2T\) with the sampling grid defined above, and confidence \(0<\delta<1\), probability at least \(1-\delta\) of \[L(\widehat p)\le C\left(\|p\|_{H^{m+1,2}}^2+\|p\|_{H^{1,2(m+1)}}^2\right)\left(M^{-2m}+R^{-4m}+\frac{R^n\log(4M/\delta)}N\right).\] The constant is independent of \(M,N,R\).

Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(T>0\), \(m\ge1\), and \(\alpha>0\). Section 2 sets \(d(m)=2(m+1)+\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) and \(\mathcal H_m=H^{d(m)}([0,T]\times\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^{n\times n})\times H^{d(m)}([0,T]\times\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n)\), with the time/space Sobolev convention defined there. The coefficient class \(\mathcal H_m^{+,\alpha}\) means \((a-\alpha I,b)\in\mathcal H_m\), with \(a-\alpha I\) symmetric positive semidefinite pointwise. The generator is \(L_t\varphi=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\partial_{ij}\varphi+\sum_i b_i\partial_i\varphi\).

In the setting of Theorem 8.7 with zero forcing, take initial datum \(\bar p\in H^{2m+1}(\mathbb R^n)\) and let \(p\) be the unique weak solution of \(\partial_tp=L_t^*p\), \(p(0,\cdot)=\bar p\). Theorem 8.11 asserts the mixed Bochner regularity \[p\in H^{m+1}(0,T;H^{2(m+1)}(\mathbb R^n)).\] This is a claim about time derivatives up to order \(m+1\) taking values in the spatial Sobolev space \(H^{2(m+1)}\), rather than only separate time and space estimates. The initial datum need not be a probability density for Theorem 8.7; when it is nonnegative of unit mass, its solution is also a density.

In the proof of Theorem 5.8, let \(p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}\) be the Fokker–Planck density for the fitted coefficients with prescribed initial law \(p_0\), and let \(\widehat p\) be the empirical cardinal interpolant, for which \(\widehat p(0)=\widehat g_1\). For \(\rho=p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}-\widehat p\), the proof asserts the zero initial condition \(\rho(0)=0\) and applies an energy estimate without an initial discrepancy term. The construction does not identify the empirical first density \(\widehat g_1\) with \(p_0\).

Fix an integer base \(b>1\), an integer \(m\ge0\), \(K=b^m\), and \(0<p<\infty\). A perturbed lattice \(\omega\subset[0,1)\) has exactly one point in each interval \([j/K,(j+1)/K)\). A translation \(T_v\omega=\omega+v\) is valid when it remains in \([0,1)\). For a \(K\)-point multiset \(Y\), put \[F_Y(t)=K^{-1}\sum_{y\in Y}\mathbf1_{[0,t)}(y)-t,\qquad D_p(Y)=\int_0^1|F_Y(t)|^p\,dt.\] Thus \(D_p\) is the \(p\)-th-power discrepancy, without taking its \(p\)-th root.

The proof of Theorem 5 claims, for valid translates with \(v\in[0,1)\), \[D_p(T_v\omega)\le D_p(\omega^{\prime\prime})\le K^{-p}\frac{2^p}{p+1},\] where \(\omega^{\prime\prime}\) is the displayed limiting arrangement of pairs at \(0,2/K,4/K,\ldots\). The transfer theorem uses the smaller translation set \(W_m^{\infty,b}=\bigcup_{k\ge0}([0,b^{-m})\cap b^{-k-1}\mathbb Z)\), with validity still required, and \(h_m^\infty\) is the supremum of \(K^pD_p(T_v\omega)\) over those lattice/translation pairs. The resulting assertion is \(h_m^\infty\le2^p/(p+1)\).

For the \(K\)-grid \(\{0,1/K,\ldots,(K-1)/K\}^d\), Corollary 2 uses the upper bound \[\sup_{a\in[0,1]^d}\left|\#\bigl([0,a)\cap\omega\bigr)-K^d\prod_{i=1}^d a_i\right|\le K^{d-1}.\] The proof asserts the same bound after taking its supremum over the permitted grid translates. This is the unnormalized anchored-box discrepancy.

The transfer theorem allows real-valued \(f\) and \(\mathcal D\), subject to the admissibility inequality \[\mathcal D\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^r\nu_i\right)\le f(r)\sum_{i=1}^r\mathcal D(\nu_i)\] and the stated additional signed control where differences are used. For the base-\(b^d\) digits \(\epsilon_j\) of \(N\), equation (2) replaces the finite block costs \(h_j^n\) by their larger infinite-domain suprema \(h_j^\infty\) in an ordered upper-bound chain with multiplier \(f(\sum_j\epsilon_j)\). No condition that this multiplier is nonnegative is imposed in Definitions 2–3.

Let \(n\) be even and \(x=(\mathbf1_{n/2},-\mathbf1_{n/2})\) encode two equal communities. Fix \(0\le p_{\rm out}<p_{\rm in}\le1\) in the stated sparse-signal regime \(p_{\rm in}\gtrsim n^{-1}\log n\). In the semi-random variant of Corollary 2.7, the symmetric adjacency matrix has Bernoulli entries \(A_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Ber}(p_{ij})\), with \(p_{ij}\ge p_{\rm in}\) for same-community pairs and \(p_{ij}\le p_{\rm out}\) for different-community pairs. These are the raw entries printed in that corollary.

For an integer factor rank \(p\ge4\), consider \[\min_{S_i\in S^{p-1}}-\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}\langle S_i,S_j\rangle.\] Corollary 2.7 imports the condition of Corollary 2.5, \[\frac{2C_0^{\prime}\sqrt{n(p_{\rm in}+p_{\rm out})\log n}}{n(p_{\rm in}-p_{\rm out})}\le\frac{p-3}{p+1},\] and asserts a benign landscape with high probability: every local minimizer \(S\) is global and satisfies \(SS^{\mathsf T}=xx^{\mathsf T}\). The earlier model (2.8) subtracts \((p_{\rm in}+p_{\rm out})/2\) from Bernoulli observations, whereas the input displayed in Corollary 2.7 has no such subtraction.

Work over \(\mathbb T=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) with maximum as tropical addition and ordinary addition as tropical multiplication. Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\) have actual supports contained in finite a priori sets \(A_i\subset\mathbb Z^n\), and put \(Q=\sum_i\operatorname{conv}(A_i)\). For a nonempty finite column set \(E^{\prime}\subset\mathbb Z^n\), the truncated Macaulay matrix \(M^{\mathcal A}_{E^{\prime}}\) has a row \((i,\alpha)\) exactly when \(\alpha+A_i\subseteq E^{\prime}\); its entries are the actual coefficients of \(X^\alpha f_i\), with \(-\infty\) for absent monomials. A finite vector \(y\in\mathbb R^{E^{\prime}}\) belongs to its tropical kernel when the maximum of coefficient-plus-coordinate is attained at least twice in every row; if there are no rows, every vector is in the kernel.

Algorithm 6.13 claims to return a nonzero telescoper \(L\in K(t)\langle S_t\rangle\) and rational difference certificates when \(L(f)=\sum_j\Delta_{x_j}g_j\) is possible, and to return false otherwise.

After shift-equivalence reduction and partial fractions, consider a remainder component \(a_{i,j,\ell}/\sigma_t^\ell(d_i)^j\), where \(d_i\) is an irreducible denominator representative. Let \(G_{t,d_i}\) be its isotropy subgroup under the time and spatial shifts, and \(G_{d_i}\) the spatial isotropy subgroup. This is the original last-shift sign used by the decision algorithm.

Let \(\epsilon(u)=(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T})/2\). The elasticity tensor \(\mathsf C\) is bounded, symmetric on symmetric matrices, and satisfies \(C_{\min}|\tau|^2\le(\mathsf C\tau):\tau\le C_{\max}|\tau|^2\), with \(0<C_{\min}\le C_{\max}<\infty\). In static elasticity, \(B_D(u,v)=\int_D(\mathsf C\epsilon(u)):\epsilon(v)\), and \(H_B(D)\) consists of \(H^1\) fields satisfying the physical Dirichlet condition and \(B_D(u,v)=0\) for tests vanishing also on the artificial boundary.

For the nested patches and real \(C^1\) cutoff \(\eta\) of Lemma 6.1, which vanishes on the artificial outer boundary, set \(\Theta_\eta(u)=u(\nabla\eta)^{\mathsf T}+(\nabla\eta)u^{\mathsf T}\). Equations (6.33) and (6.36) assert respectively \[B_{D^*}(\eta u,\eta v)=\int_{D^*}\mathsf C\Theta_\eta(u):\Theta_\eta(v),\] and, for a partition-of-unity cutoff \(\chi_i\), \[\int_{\omega_i^*}\mathsf C\Theta_{\chi_i}(\phi_i):\Theta_{\chi_i}(v)=\lambda_iB_{\omega_i^*}(\phi_i,v)\qquad(v\in H_B(\omega_i^*)).\]

For elastic waves with \(\omega>0\), bounded density \(\rho\), and positive-definite symmetric bounded boundary coefficient \(A\), the local form is \[B_D(u,v)=\int_D\bigl(\mathsf C\epsilon(u):\overline{\epsilon(v)}-\omega^2\rho\,u\cdot\bar v\bigr)-i\omega\int_{\partial D\cap\Gamma}Au\cdot\bar v,\] and \(B_D^+\) is its elastic-energy term. Generalized harmonic fields annihilate tests vanishing on the artificial boundary. Equations (6.107) and (6.110) assert \[B_{D^*}^+(\eta u,\eta v)=\int_{D^*}\bigl(\mathsf C\Theta_\eta(u):\overline{\Theta_\eta(v)}+\omega^2\rho\eta^2u\cdot\bar v\bigr),\] \[\int_{\omega_i^*}\bigl(\mathsf C\Theta_{\chi_i}(\phi_i):\overline{\Theta_{\chi_i}(v)}+2\omega^2\rho\chi_i^2\phi_i\cdot\bar v\bigr)=\lambda_iB_{\omega_i^*}^+(\phi_i,v).\] In all four printed identities, the quadratic term uses \(\Theta\) with coefficient one.

Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real space with \(\|x\|^2=\langle Bx,x\rangle\), \(B\succ0\). Let \(f\) be convex and differentiable on all of \(E\), with \(L_f\)-Lipschitz gradient and a nonempty minimizer set. The algorithms allow \(L\ge L_f\) and use \(\tau=1/L\).

IGMM permits arbitrary-quality feasible simplex solutions of its auxiliary quadratic program, using genuine oracle records for its global lower model. With \(r_u>1\ge r_d>0\), Algorithm 3.1 asserts progress through backtracking and the fallback triggered by \(a_{k+1}<\tau\). After a failed trial, its printed line 21 sets \(a_{k+1}=a_k/r_u\), with the previous iteration's value \(a_k\) fixed throughout the inner loop. This update is claimed to produce the iterates needed for the subsequent rate bound.

Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real space with \(\|x\|^2=\langle Bx,x\rangle\), \(B\succ0\). Let \(f\) be convex and differentiable on all of \(E\), with \(L_f\)-Lipschitz gradient and a nonempty minimizer set. The algorithms allow \(L\ge L_f\) and use \(\tau=1/L\).

For a feasible simplex vector \(\lambda\), equation (4.30) gives the minimized normalized estimate function \[\omega_\lambda^*=\langle S,\lambda\rangle-\frac{A+\tau}{2}\langle\lambda,Q\lambda\rangle.\] The Newton validity test in Algorithm 4.2 instead uses \(\langle S,\lambda\rangle-A\langle\lambda,Q\lambda\rangle/2\), and claims that accepting this test preserves the normalized estimate-sequence certificate of Proposition 4.2. The auxiliary QP solution is required to be feasible and nonworsening relative to its prescribed starting point.

For a fixed real design matrix \(A\), label vector \(y\), and real argument \(x\), equations (7.2)–(7.3) define \[f(x)=I(Ax)-\langle y,Ax\rangle,\qquad I(z)=\sum_i\log(1+e^{-z_i}),\qquad \mathcal L(z)_i=(1+e^{-z_i})^{-1},\] and assert \(\nabla f(x)=A^{\mathsf T}(\mathcal L(Ax)-y)\). No condition \(A^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=0\) is imposed on the design.

The proof of Lemma 2.17 treats the totally positive Jacobian of the weighted generalized power-sum map as having positive simple eigenvalues, and infers that \[v^{\mathsf T}Av>0\quad\text{for every }v\ne0.\] The allowed Jacobians include the Jacobian of \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto(x_1+x_2,x_1^2+x_2^2)\) at distinct positive coordinates, with positive unit weights and increasing positive exponents. No symmetry assumption on the Jacobian is supplied.

Let \(p\in\mathbb R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_k]\), let \(M=100\deg(p)\sum_\beta|p_\beta|\), and set \(g(y)=2y^2-y\). Define \[q(Y,Z)=p(Y)\prod_{i=1}^k(1-Y_i)^6+M\sum_{i=1}^k(Z_i-g(Y_i)).\] Let \(L\) be the continuous piecewise-linear function joining \(L((n-1)/n)=(n-1)(n-2)/n^2\), for \(n\ge1\), with \(L(1)=1\), and let \(\mathcal R=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:y\ge L(x)\}\).

For \(k\) disjoint groups of nonnegative simplex variables, write \(e_{j,(i)}\) for the elementary symmetric function of degree \(j\) in group \(i\). The printed homogenization map is \[\tau(f)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^ke_{1,(i)}^{3\deg f}\right)f\!\left(\frac{e_{2,(1)}}{e_{1,(1)}^2},\ldots,\frac{e_{2,(k)}}{e_{1,(k)}^2},\frac{e_{3,(1)}}{e_{1,(1)}^3},\ldots,\frac{e_{3,(k)}}{e_{1,(k)}^3}\right).\] It is a multihomogeneous product-symmetric polynomial because the stated exponent clears the denominators.

The proof of Theorem 6.6 asserts equivalence of (a) \(q(x_1,\ldots,x_k,y_1,\ldots,y_k)<0\) for some \((x_i,y_i)\in\mathcal R\), and (b) \(\tau(q)<0\) somewhere on \(\Delta^k\), where each \(\Delta\) is the probability simplex with \(e_1=1\). The geometric realization used in the proof has coordinates \((2e_2,6e_3)\), whereas the displayed map above contains the unscaled elementary symmetric functions.

Let \(n\ge d\ge2\), let \(2\le\alpha_1<\cdots<\alpha_{d-1}\) be integers, put \(\beta_i=2\alpha_i\), and write \(p_j(x)=\sum_{r=1}^n x_r^j\). For \(c\in\mathbb R^{d-2}\), assume the equality fiber \(\{p_{\beta_i}=c_i:1\le i\le d-2\}\) and its intersection with \(p_2=1\) are both smooth. Lemma 2.28 classifies critical points of \(p_{\beta_{d-1}}\) on the constrained fiber \[\{x\in\mathbb R^n:p_2(x)\le1,\ p_{\beta_i}(x)=c_i\ (1\le i\le d-2)\}.\]

In the ordered nonnegative-coordinate convention, a multiplicity vector \((m_0,m_1,\ldots,m_\ell)\) counts zeros and increasing distinct positive coordinates; \(\ell\) is its length. Type (1) has \(m_{2i-1}=1\), and type (2) has \(m_0=0\) and \(m_{2i}=1\), for every index in range. The lemma asserts that every critical point is either (a) length \(d-2\), of type (1) or (2), or (b) length \(d-1\), of type (1), with \(p_2=1\). It also calls the local extrema strict: for odd \(d\), case (a)/type (1) gives maxima and the other listed cases minima, with the roles reversed for even \(d\). The stated critical-point classification includes zero coordinates and inactive ball constraints \(p_2<1\).

Let \(n\ge d\ge2\), let \(2\le\alpha_1<\cdots<\alpha_{d-1}\) be integers, set \(\beta_i=2\alpha_i\), and let \(W_n\) denote the ordered nonnegative chamber. For \(1\le k\le d\) and \(c\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{k-1}\), Lemma 2.29 asserts connectedness of \[\widetilde V_k^\beta(c)\cap W_n=\{x\in W_n:p_2(x)\le1,\ p_{\beta_i}(x)=c_i\ (1\le i<k)\}.\] Equivalently, coordinatewise squaring gives the claimed connectedness of \[M=\{z\in W_n:\sum_jz_j\le1,\ p_{\alpha_i}(z)=c_i\ (1\le i<k)\}.\]

The proof supposes \(M=A\cup B\), where \(A,B\) are disjoint nonempty closed sets. It uses connectedness of each nonempty slice \(M\cap\{\sum_jz_j=s\}\) to place that slice entirely in one part. Its final contradiction is drawn after positing an unattained intermediate sum between slices in \(A\) and \(B\). The original conclusion being examined is connectedness of the entire fiber, without a genericity or smoothness qualification in Lemma 2.29.

With \[g(x,y,z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n_C+n}\sum_{c_1=0}^j\sum_{c_2=0}^{j-c_1}\mu_{j,c_1,c_2}x^{n_C+n-j}z^{c_1}y^{c_2},\] formula (A.16) is asserted to evaluate the derivative/specialization from (A.14). After differentiating \(\widehat k\) times in \(y\) and setting \(y=0\), its summand selects \(\mu_{j,c_1,\widehat r}\). The prescribed row and column counts \(\widehat r\) and \(\widehat k\) need not coincide.

For real matrices \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_B}\), and \(C\in\mathbb R^{n_C\times d}\), with requested counts \(k\le\operatorname{rank}B\) and \(r\le\operatorname{rank}C\), Algorithm 1 claims a valid successive row/column selection. Its lines 3 and 10 normalize every remaining projected candidate before the zero-projection exclusions in lines 5 and 12. The input rank conditions do not require every candidate column or row to have nonzero projection.

For a \(d\times d\) matrix \(M\), the printed identity in Lemma A.2 places the factorial as \[\frac1{k!}\sum_{\substack{S\subset[d]\\|S|=d-k}}\det(xI_{d-k}-M_{S,S})=\partial_x^k\det(xI_d-M).\] The assertion includes the nontrivial integer case \(k=2\) for a real diagonal \(3\times3\) matrix.

In Theorem 1.3 and Lemma 5.2, \(U\) is an orthonormal basis matrix for the selected column space of \(B\). The parameter \(\alpha\) is defined using \[\frac{U^{\mathsf T}AA^{\mathsf T}U}{\|U^{\mathsf T}AA^{\mathsf T}U\|_2}.\] The stated domain does not separately exclude \(U^{\mathsf T}AA^{\mathsf T}U=0\), even when the target matrix \(A\) itself is nonzero; the subsequent condition is asserted with this normalized parameter.

Let \(d\ge2\) and \(p(x)=\prod_{i=1}^d(x-\lambda_i)\), with \(0\le\lambda_i\le1\), and put \(\beta=d^{-1}\sum_i\lambda_i\in[0,1]\). Lemma 6.1 asserts, for every positive integer \(k>\beta d/(1+\beta)\), \[\operatorname{maxroot}\bigl((\partial_x\,x\,\partial_x)^kp\bigr)\le\left((1-\beta)\left(1-\frac kd\right)+2\sqrt{\left(1-\frac kd\right)\frac kd\,\beta}\right)^2.\] The stated integer range has no upper restriction \(k<d\), and the statement gives no separate largest-root convention for the constant or zero polynomials reached by iteration.

On a partition into Lipschitz elements \(K\), let \(W_h=\prod_KW_h(K)\), with \(W_h(K)\subset H\Lambda(K)\cap H^*\Lambda(K)\) and both traces in \(L^2\Lambda(\partial K)\). Use the local \(C^1\) source maps and the symmetric linearized-source setting of the multisymplectic formulation. Let both approximate trace spaces equal the broken facet space \(M=\prod_{K,e\subset\partial K}M(e)\), with matching tangential spaces on the two sides of an interior facet, and let \(P\) be its \(L^2\)-orthogonal projection.

The penalty \(\alpha=\prod_{K,e}\alpha_e\) is a bounded symmetric facetwise operator; the source does not require it to preserve \(M\) or commute with \(P\). With LDG-H flux \(\Phi=(\widehat z^{\rm nor}-z^{\rm nor})+\alpha(\widehat z^{\rm tan}-z^{\rm tan})\), equation (49) gives \[\widehat z^{\rm nor}=P\bigl[z^{\rm nor}-\alpha(\widehat z^{\rm tan}-z^{\rm tan})\bigr].\] Theorem 4.21 asserts strong multisymplecticity whenever \(W_h^{\rm nor}\subseteq M\) or \(W_h^{\rm tan}\subseteq M\): the multisymplectic boundary pairing of any two first variations vanishes on every union of mesh elements, with internal traces cancelling. In the normal-containment branch, the proof identifies the projected-penalty formulation with the previously treated LDG-H method.

In the proof of Proposition 4.6, for a simplex \(K\) and facet \(e\), the printed trace identity assigns the same space \(\mathcal P_r\Lambda^{n-1}(e)\) to both the full space \(\mathcal P_{r+1}\Lambda^{n-1}(K)\) and the trimmed space \(\mathcal P_{r+1}^{-}\Lambda^{n-1}(K)\). The assertion includes \(r=0\) and \(n=2\).

The exterior-boundary branch of the piecewise formula following (43) states \[\check z_h^{\rm nor}=-\alpha\check z_h^{\rm tan}\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega.\] It is asserted for the XG correction defined by (42b), using Definition 3.2, under which the tangential jump on the exterior boundary equals the original trace \(z_h^{\rm tan}\).

Let \(\mathcal M\) be a compatible transport family whose image cone \(\operatorname{cone}(\mathcal M)_\#\rho\) is polyhedral. Write \(\mu_\lambda=(T^\lambda)_\#\rho\) and let the positive-definite Gram matrix \(Q\) give \(W_2^2(\mu_\lambda,\mu_\eta)=\|\lambda-\eta\|_Q^2\). Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R_+^{|\mathcal M|}\) be convex, and assume \(F\) is geodesically \(m\)-strongly convex and \(M\)-smooth on the corresponding constrained family \(K_\#\rho\), with minimizer \(\mu_*\).

Algorithm 1 starts with \(\eta^{(0)}=\lambda^{(0)}\in K\) and updates \[\lambda^{(t+1)}=\operatorname{proj}_{K,Q}\!\left(\eta^{(t)}-M^{-1}Q^{-1}\nabla_\lambda F(\mu_{\eta^{(t)}})\right).\] If \(m>0\), put \(\kappa=M/m\) and \[\eta^{(t+1)}=\lambda^{(t+1)}+\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}(\lambda^{(t+1)}-\lambda^{(t)}).\] Theorem 4.2 asserts \[F(\mu_{\lambda^{(t)}})-F(\mu_*)\le(1-\kappa^{-1/2})^t\left(F(\mu_{\lambda^{(0)}})-F(\mu_*)+\frac m2W_2^2(\mu_{\lambda^{(0)}},\mu_*)\right),\] and \(W_2^2(\mu_{\lambda^{(t)}},\mu_*)\lesssim\kappa e^{-t/\sqrt\kappa}W_2^2(\mu_{\lambda^{(0)}},\mu_*)\).

For \(m=0\), the algorithm uses \(\gamma_0=1\), \(\gamma_{t+1}=(1+\sqrt{1+4\gamma_t^2})/2\), and extrapolation coefficient \((\gamma_t-1)/\gamma_{t+1}\); the asserted objective rate is \(\lesssim Mt^{-2}W_2^2(\mu_{\lambda^{(0)}},\mu_*)\). The smoothness and convexity assumptions are stated only on \(K_\#\rho\), while the gradients are evaluated at the extrapolated \(\eta^{(t)}\); no hypothesis in the theorem ensures those extrapolated points stay in \(K\).

For a uniform partition \(\mathcal I\) into intervals \(I=[a,a+\delta]\), Appendix C.3 uses the scaled coordinate functions \(\psi_{I,i}(x)=\psi((x_i-a)/\delta)e_i\). Its scalar generators are \(\psi^{\rm lin}(x)=x\), \(\psi^{\rm quad,\pm}=\pm q\), and \(\psi^{\rm cub,\pm}=\pm c\), where \[q(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\le0,\\x^2,&0\le x\le1,\\2x-1,&x\ge1,\end{cases}\qquad c(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\le0,\\x^2(3-2x),&0\le x\le1,\\1,&x\ge1.\end{cases}\]

For the positive linear offset \(\alpha\) of the construction, maps have the form \(T(x)=\alpha x+\sum_{T_j\in\mathcal M}\lambda_jT_j(x)+v\), with \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) and all coefficients \(\lambda_j\ge0\). Equation (24) imposes only \[\lambda_i^{\rm lin}+\frac2\delta\sum_{I\in\mathcal I}(\lambda_{I,i}^{\rm quad,+}-\lambda_{I,i}^{\rm quad,-})\ge0\quad(i\in[d]),\qquad\frac{6\lambda_{I,i}^{\rm cub,-}}\delta\le\frac\alpha2\quad(I\in\mathcal I,\ i\in[d]).\] The stated consequence is that every feasible map has coordinate slopes at least \(\alpha/2\), hence is increasing and a gradient of a strongly convex function, as required for the compatible transport family in Theorem 5.7. The quadratic constraint is the total signed sum over all intervals.

Let \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), choose a truncation radius \(R>0\), and partition \([-R,R]\) into \(J\) intervals \([a_j,a_j+\delta]\) of width \(\delta=2R/J\). The piecewise-linear dictionary in Theorem 5.6 uses ramps \(\psi_j(x)=\min\{1,\max\{0,(x-a_j)/\delta\}\}\). After centering, put \(s_j(x)=\psi_j(x)-\mathbb E\psi_j(Z)\), \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_J)\), and \(Q=\mathbb E[s(Z)s(Z)^{\mathsf T}]\). The multivariate family is the coordinatewise direct sum of this univariate family.

Assumption (\(\Xi\)) requires one finite \(\Xi>0\) satisfying \[s(x)^{\mathsf T}Q^{-1}s(x)\le\Xi J\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R.\] Lemma 5.15 asserts \(\Xi\lesssim J^2\) for the piecewise-linear families of Theorem 5.6, including their varying truncation and mesh choices as approximation accuracy increases. The proof claims a Gram lower bound of order \(\delta^2\), then identifies the resulting \(\delta^{-2}\) bound with order \(J^2\), without retaining a Gaussian-tail or truncation-dependent factor. This uniform parameter is used in Corollary 5.18.

Section 7 equips the coefficient-and-translation parameter space with the metric \(Q\oplus I\). With \[b_T=\int\left\langle\nabla\log(\mu_P/\pi)\circ T^{\lambda,v},T\right\rangle\,d\rho,\] Theorems 7.1 and 7.2 print the coefficient velocity \(\dot\lambda_T=-b_T\) for the asserted mixture gradient flow, and the intervening particle formula uses the same coordinate velocity. No identity-Gram assumption is made.

Let \(\pi\propto e^{-V}\) be a strongly log-concave probability measure on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\mathcal C\) be any geodesically convex subset of \(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\). Lemma 5.1 asserts that the variational problem \[\min_{\mu\in\mathcal C}\operatorname{KL}(\mu\|\pi)\] has a unique minimizer. The lemma itself assumes strong log-concavity; it does not require the additional upper Hessian bound of the later well-conditioned setting, closure of \(\mathcal C\), or separate attainment of the infimum.

In the projected stochastic-gradient proof, let \(x_\star\) minimize an \(m\)-strongly convex, \(M\)-smooth objective over the constraint set \(K\), using the \(Q\)-metric. The smoothness step bounds the full gradient norm by \[\|\nabla f(x)\|_{Q^{-1}}\le M\|x-x_\star\|_Q,\] without an assumption that \(x_\star\) is an unconstrained stationary point.

For Gaussian KL divergence with trial covariance \(A\) and target covariance \(\Sigma\), the displayed formula in Appendix D.2 uses the log-determinant contribution \(+\log\det(\Sigma^{-1})-\log\det A\). It is asserted for positive-definite covariances, including identical trial and target covariances.

Appendix D.3 specifies the conditional data model \[Y_i\mid X_i\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\exp(\theta^{\mathsf T}X_i)),\] with no restriction excluding positive values of \(\theta^{\mathsf T}X_i\). This is the printed Bernoulli-parameter formula for the logistic experiment.

Section 6.1 defines negative differential entropy by \(H(\mu)=\int\rho\log\rho\) and proposes, for particles \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the surrogate \[\widetilde H_+(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\frac1{2n}\sum_i\log(\epsilon+\|x_i-x_{N(i)}\|^2),\] where \(N(i)\) is the nearest neighbor other than \(i\). On a region where nearest neighbors are unique, the printed positive outgoing-neighbor field is used as its particle entropy gradient. The supplied plotting snapshot uses the negative-sign surrogate and negative outgoing field, again omitting incoming-neighbor terms when differentiating that same particle functional.

Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) be nonsingular positive semidefinite, and let \(\mu\) have finite, nonsingular uncentered second-moment matrix \(\Sigma_\mu=\int xx^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(x)\). Define \[\mathcal L_{A,\mu}[v](x)=2Av(x)+2\left(\int yv(y)^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(y)\right)x,\qquad \mathcal I_\mu=\left\{v\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d):\int xv(x)^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(x)\text{ is symmetric}\right\}.\]

Proposition 10.1 takes arbitrary \(w\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\), starts with the horizontal condition \(v\in\mathcal I_\mu\), and asserts a unique inverse solution \(v\in L^2\) to \(\mathcal L_{A,\mu}v=w\). Its formula is \[v(x)=\tfrac12A^{-1}w(x)-\tfrac12(x^{\mathsf T}\otimes I)(I\otimes A^2+\Sigma_\mu\otimes A)^{-1}\int(y\otimes I)w(y)\,d\mu(y).\] The derivation writes \(v=\tfrac12A^{-1}w-A^{-1}Bx\), with \(B=\int v(y)y^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(y)\), and claims a unique symmetric solution of \[AB+B\Sigma_\mu=\tfrac12\int w(y)y^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(y).\] The proposition is stated for general \(A\); only its last invariance assertion specializes to \(A=\Sigma_\mu\).

Let \(\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) have nonsingular uncentered second moment \(\Sigma_\mu=\int xx^{\mathsf T}d\mu\). On \[\mathcal I_\mu=\{v\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d):\int xv(x)^{\mathsf T}d\mu\text{ is symmetric}\},\] consider \(\mathcal L_{\Sigma_\mu,\mu}v(x)=2\Sigma_\mu v(x)+2(\int yv(y)^{\mathsf T}d\mu(y))x\). If \(\Lambda_\mu=\{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d\}\) is the spectrum of \(\Sigma_\mu\), put \(\Gamma_\mu=\{\lambda_i+\lambda_j:1\le i,j\le d\}\). Proposition 10.2 asserts the exact equality \[\operatorname{spec}(\mathcal L_{\Sigma_\mu,\mu}|_{\mathcal I_\mu})=2(\Lambda_\mu\cup\Gamma_\mu).\]

For \(\lambda/2=\lambda_i\in\Lambda_\mu\setminus\Gamma_\mu\), its proposed eigenfields take values in the \(\lambda_i\)-eigenspace of \(\Sigma_\mu\) and satisfy \(\int v(x)x^{\mathsf T}d\mu=0\). The theorem nevertheless includes every element of \(2\Lambda_\mu\) in the spectral set, without requiring a nonzero field of this form or excluding atomic measures.
The metric derivative in Lemma 5.1 is defined by a two-sided limit with denominator \(h\), namely the quotient of \(\operatorname{IGW}(\rho_{t+h},\rho_t)\) by \(h\), rather than by \(|h|\).

The reparametrization definition before Lemma 5.3 permits any nondecreasing map \(h:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) relating the two curves, without requiring that it preserve endpoints or traverse the whole interval. Part (2) of that lemma asserts equality of curve lengths under this stated reparametrization.

In the two-grid estimate, equation (26) uses the weights \(1-\ell_\eta(s)\) and \(\ell_\tau(s)\) for the interpolation on the \(\eta\)-grid, where \(\eta\) and \(\tau\) are distinct mesh sizes and \(\ell_\eta,\ell_\tau\) are their respective local linear interpolation parameters. The expansion on the next page repeats this mixed pair as the coefficients of the interpolated quantity.

Let \(\mu_0\in\operatorname{Dom}(F)\subset\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\), with nonsingular second-moment matrix \(\Sigma_{\mu_0}=\int xx^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu_0(x)\). Assumption 1 requires \(F\) to be rotation invariant, bounded below by \(F_*>-\infty\), weakly lower semicontinuous, regular in the subdifferential sense cited there, and to have \(\operatorname{Dom}(F)\subset\mathcal P_2^{\mathrm{ac}}(\mathbb R^d)\). For some \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), it must also satisfy, along every generalized IGW geodesic \(
u_s=((1-s)y+sz)_\#\pi\) of Definition 3.2, \[F(
u_s)\le(1-s)F(\mu_1)+sF(\mu_2)-\lambda s(1-s)\int(\langle y,y^{\prime}angle-\langle z,z^{\prime}angle)^2\,d\pi(x,y,z)\,d\pi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime},z^{\prime}).\] Here \(\pi\) glues optimal IGW couplings from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu_1,\mu_2\), after the PSD, nonsingular cross-covariance alignments required in that definition. Assumption 2 requires a first variation with \(\partial F(\mu)=\{
abla\delta F(\mu)\}\) for every \(\mu\in\operatorname{Dom}(F)\).

Write \(c=\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{\mu_0})\) and \(E=F(\mu_0)-F_*\). For step size \(\tau=\delta/n\), scheme (13) minimizes \(F(\rho)+\operatorname{IGW}(\rho,\rho_i)^2/(2\tau)\) and then rotates a minimizer into alignment with \(\rho_i\). Theorem 4.1 states that, whenever \[0<\delta<\frac{(1-1/\sqrt2)c}{2^{5/4}E},\] its piecewise-constant interpolations converge uniformly in IGW at rate \(O(\sqrt\tau)\) to a \(W_2\)-continuous curve, with \(W_2\) convergence along a subsequence. The local discrete estimates used in that argument are stated separately in Proposition 4.1 under \[0<\delta\le\frac{\bar\delta^2}{2E},\qquad\bar\delta=\frac{(1-1/\sqrt2)c}{2^{1/4}}.\] They include existence of the iterates and \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{\rho_i})\ge c/2\). The first displayed interval is the original theorem’s interval; the second is the proposition’s original interval.

Equip \(\operatorname{Gr}(k,n)\), \(1\le k<n\), in the symmetric-involution model with the Frobenius metric. Write \(l=n-k\) and \(m=kl\). The range in (a) includes \((k,n,r)=(3,4,1)\), and the range in (b) includes \((2,6,4)\). In the latter case, the product of four two-spheres and the target Grassmannian both have dimension eight. No additional codimension or complementary-dimension condition is included in the displayed ranges.

Equip \(\operatorname{Gr}(k,n)\), \(1\le k<n\), in the symmetric-involution model with the Frobenius metric. Write \(l=n-k\) and \(m=kl\). The source identifies scalar curvature with both \(\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Ric}\) and \(\sum_{a<b}\kappa(e_a,e_b)\), and defines a subspace scalar curvature using the same unordered-pair sum. The final normalization step of Theorem 5.22 concerns an orbit \(O\subset\mathbb R^n\) of an almost-faithful, possibly nonorthogonal representation of a compact Lie group \(G\), its uniform measure \(\mu_O\), and a finite cloud \(X\) with empirical measure \(\mu_X\). Let \(\sigma_{\min}^2\) be the least nonzero eigenvalue of \(\Sigma[\mu_O]\), \(P_O\) the orthogonal projection onto \(\operatorname{span}O\), and \(P_X\) the projection onto eigenvectors of \(\Sigma[\mu_X]\) above the PCA threshold \(\epsilon\). Its sampling and PCA assumptions in particular give, with \(W=W_2(\mu_X,\mu_O)\), \[W\left(2\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{Z\sim\mu_O}\|Z\|}+W\right)<\epsilon\le\tfrac12\sigma_{\min}^2.\] The additional LiePCA radius and spectral-cutoff hypotheses of Theorem 5.22 concern the subsequent reconstruction; the assertions inspected here compare the normalized input cloud and orbit.

Define \(M_X=(\Sigma[\mu_X]^+)^{1/2}\), \(M_O=(\Sigma[\mu_O]^+)^{1/2}\), \(\widetilde X=M_XP_XX\), and \(\widetilde O=M_OP_OO\), with \(+\) denoting the Moore–Penrose inverse. In the full-span case these are inverse square roots. Writing \(d_H(A\mid B)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}\|a-b\|\), the proof asserts \[d_H(\widetilde X\mid\widetilde O)\le\|M_X-M_O\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,\|P_X-P_O\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,d_H(X\mid O)\le\frac{d_H(X\mid O)}{\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\min}}.\] The first inequality is the product-of-differences step immediately preceding (64).

For the pushforward empirical and uniform measures, the final proof step similarly asserts \[W_2\big((M_XP_X)_\#\mu_X,(M_OP_O)_\#\mu_O\big)\le\|M_X-M_O\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,\|P_X-P_O\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,W_2(\mu_X,\mu_O).\] The same product bound is then used to obtain the coefficient \(1/(\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\min})\) in the concluding Wasserstein estimate. These are assertions about the theorem’s orbit and sample data, with the two distinct normalization maps.

For input polynomials \(p,q\in\mathbb C[x]\) with nonzero initial leading coefficients, problem (16) minimizes their coefficient perturbation norm subject to \(\deg\gcd(p+\delta p,q+\delta q)\ge d\), using the ordinary polynomial GCD defined by divisibility in \(\mathbb C[x]\). Let \(X\) be a finite complete CAT(0) cubical complex, \(\bar x\in X\), and \(C\) a cell incident to \(\bar x\). Let \(A\) be a nonempty finite subset of a geodesic metric space \((X,d)\), let \(p\ge1\), and write \(d_A^p(x)=(d(x,a)^p)_{a\in A}\). For a Euclidean space \(Y\), \(b\in\mathbb R^A\), a nonzero \(c\in Y\), and a linear map \(G:Y\to\mathbb R^A\), consider \[\inf\{\langle c,y\rangle:x\in X,\ y\in Y,\ Gy-d_A^p(x)\ge b\}.\] Assumption 3.1 requires strict primal feasibility: some \((\widehat x,\widehat y)\) satisfies \(G\widehat y-d_A^p(\widehat x)>b\) componentwise; and dual feasibility: some \(\widehat w\in\mathbb R_+^A\) satisfies \(G^*\widehat w=c\).

Theorem 4.3 assumes that \(X\) is reflexive and has a conical bicombing \(\sigma\): each \(t\mapsto\sigma(x,y,t)\) is a constant-speed geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\), and \[d(\sigma(x,y,t),\sigma(x^{\prime},y^{\prime},t))\le(1-t)d(x,x^{\prime})+t\,d(y,y^{\prime}),\quad0\le t\le1.\] Reflexivity means that every decreasing sequence of nonempty bounded closed convex sets has nonempty intersection. The source defines a convex set to contain every geodesic segment joining any two of its points. Under these assumptions, the theorem asserts that the displayed optimization problem has an optimal solution.

The particular proof claim concerns its finite optimal value \(\nu\), the halfspaces \(H_k=\{y:\langle c,y\rangle\le\nu+1/k\}\), and \[F_k=\{x\in X:\text{some }y\in H_k\text{ satisfies }d_A^p(x)\le Gy-b\},\qquad k=1,2,\ldots.\] The proof claims that each \(F_k\) is convex in the preceding all-geodesics sense after verifying closure along the selected bicombing geodesic, and then invokes reflexivity for \((F_k)\).

In the unit-cube trace/lifting proof on regular quasi-uniform meshes, for every pair of bottom-side mesh faces \(f,g\) with centroids \(x_f,x_g\), Section 3.2 sets the horizontal path height to \(r=|x_f-x_g|\). For a boundary-face pair \(f_l,f_m\), Section 6 defines the local scalar array by \(\Delta_{ij}=\overline\phi_i^{\,f_l}-\overline\phi_j^{\,f_m}\) and takes the contribution to be \(K\Delta^{\mathsf T}\Delta\), with \(K>0\) the pair weight. Let \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^N\) be a polynomial map of degree at most \(d\), and put \(N^\prime=\min\{N,n^d\}\). Let \(S=G/\sqrt m\), where the entries of \(G\) are independent, mean zero, variance one, and have \(\psi_2\)-norm at most \(\alpha\). Corollary 3.13(26) asserts that, for an absolute constant \(c\), \[m\ge c\alpha^2\varepsilon^{-2}\bigl[n\log(ndN^\prime)+\log(1/\delta)\bigr]\] suffices for the stated uniform \((1\pm\varepsilon)\) norm preservation on \(p(\mathbb R^n)\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\), for the permitted positive integer dimensions/degrees and \(\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)\).

Let \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^N\) have polynomial coordinates of degree at most \(d\), and define \(\pi(z)=z/\|z\|\) for \(z\ne0\). Let \(L=u+P\) be an affine subspace of codimension \(m\), and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) be an orthonormal basis of \(P^\perp\). In proving Lemma 2.15(c), the source defines \[S=\{(x,w):\|p(x)\|^2w=1,\ \pi(p(x))\in L\}\] and asserts that this is exactly the solution set of \[\langle p(x),e_i\rangle^2=\langle u,e_i\rangle^2\|p(x)\|^2\quad(1\le i\le m),\qquad\|p(x)\|^2w=1.\] This equality is used to obtain the claimed \(((4d+1)^{n+1},n)\) regularity of the normalized polynomial image.

For Lemma 2.16(c), let \(V=\{y\in\mathbb R^N:f_j(y)=0\ \forall j\}\) have dimension at most \(n\), with \(\deg f_j\le d\) and \(d\ge2\). The proof analogously identifies \[\{(y,w):y\in V,\ \|y\|^2w=1,\ \pi(y)\in L\}\] with the polynomial system \[\langle y,e_i\rangle^2=\langle u,e_i\rangle^2\|y\|^2\ (1\le i\le m),\quad f_j(y)=0\ (\forall j),\quad\|y\|^2w=1,\] and uses this equality for the claimed \(((2d+1)^{N+1},n)\) regularity of \(\pi(V)\). The asserted equalities concern the whole solution sets, including the nonzero constraint supplied by \(w\).

Under Definition 3.15, a rational map may be restricted to any open dense domain on which its displayed coordinate ratios are defined. For such a map from a domain in \(\mathbb R^n\) into \(\mathbb R^N\), with coordinate numerator/denominator degrees at most \(d\), Lemma 2.17 asserts image regularity with \[K=(2Nd+1)^{n+1}.\] In particular, the codimension-zero part bounds the number of path components of the image by \(K\), with no separate complexity bound on extra domain deletions.

Let \[U=\{y\in\mathbb R^N:p_k(y)=0\ \forall k,\ q_\ell(y)\le0\ \forall\ell,\ r_j(y)<0\ \forall j\}\] be a semialgebraic set of dimension at most \(n\). This is a bound on the number of connected components of generic affine slices, together with the stated dimension bound.
The statement permits \(b=0\); the proof of Lemma 2.16 explicitly invokes this case for varieties. The same minimum, including the branch \((cb^2)^N\), is used at that boundary value.

Let \(V\subset\mathbb R^N\) be \((K,n)\) regular: almost every affine slice of codimension at most \(n\) has at most \(K\) path-connected components, and almost every slice of higher codimension is empty. Assume \([V]_N\le t\), meaning that a rigid motion of the cube \([-t,t]^N\) covers \(V\). For the Euclidean \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood \(T(V,\varepsilon)\), Corollary 2.19 states \[\operatorname{Vol}(T(V,\varepsilon))\le\mathcal N(V,\varepsilon)(2\varepsilon)^N\operatorname{Vol}(B^N)\le\operatorname{Vol}(B^N)2^N\varepsilon^{N-n}K(ctN^{3/2}n)^n,\] with an absolute constant \(c\). The covering-number estimate invoked in its proof, Theorem 2.6, has the explicit range \(0<\varepsilon\le\operatorname{diam}V\), on which it asserts \[\log\mathcal N(V,\varepsilon)\le n\log\!\left(\frac{2tnN^{3/2}}{\varepsilon}\right)+\log(2K).\]

Corollary 3.13(26) asserts the row bound \[m\ge c\alpha^2\varepsilon^{-2}\bigl[n\log(ndN^\prime)+\log(1/\delta)\bigr],\qquad N^\prime=\min\{N,n^d\},\] for every permitted positive integer \(n,d\), including \(n=d=1\), and every \(\delta\in(0,1)\). Let \(E,F\) be \(k\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(P^E,P^F\) be their orthogonal projections. Lemma 3.3 states that, if \(\|P^E-P^F\|_2\le\varepsilon\), then for every basis matrix \(Q^E\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) of \(E\) there is a basis matrix \(Q^F\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) of \(F\) satisfying \[\|Q^E-Q^F\|_2\le\sqrt2\,\varepsilon.\] Here the norms are operator \(2\)-norms. In the Gaussian-noise multi-reference-alignment model \(Y_i=g_i\cdot x+\varepsilon_i\), the group is compact, its action is orthogonal, \(g_i\) are Haar-distributed and the independent noise is \(N(0,\sigma^2I)\). Corollary 4.3 asserts that, under those stated prior/identifiability conditions, consistent recovery necessarily requires \(n/\sigma^4\to\infty\) as the noise level grows, regardless of the algorithm. No additional first-moment nonidentifiability premise is imposed in this conclusion.

For the ambiguity group \(H\) and transformation group \(\Gamma\), define \[\Gamma(x,y)=\{\theta:\theta x\in H(\theta y)\},\qquad x\sim y\Longleftrightarrow\Gamma(x,y)=\Gamma.\] The fiber-lemma proof treats nonequivalent pairs under this relation as having collision-fiber codimension at least \(K\), and asserts that a parallel pair has empty collision fiber unless it is equivalent. The general action framework requires every fixed group element to act by a semialgebraic automorphism. The proof then asserts that the joint collision incidence in \((\theta,x,y)\) is semialgebraic, without separately requiring the action map \(\Gamma\times V\to V\) to be jointly semialgebraic.

For the product of orthogonal ambiguity groups acting by left multiplication on the irreducible-block coefficient matrices, the sentence after (3.4) asserts that the orbits are connected exactly when every irreducible dimension \(N_i\) exceeds one. The condition is stated without restricting the multiplicity \(R_i\) or the rank of the \(N_i\times R_i\) coefficient block.
