Fix \(\alpha>3\). Equations (3.1)–(3.4), driven by the same \(W\), define \[\begin{aligned}\partial_tv&=\Delta v+v^{-\alpha}+\sigma(v)\dot W,&v(0,x)&=\max\{u_0(x),1\},\\ \partial_tv_-&=\Delta v_-+v_-^{-\alpha}+\sigma(-v_-)\dot W,&v_-(0,x)&=\max\{-u_0(x),1\}.\end{aligned}\] The noise term in the second equation has the plus sign printed in (3.3).

For \(z=v\) or \(v_-\), define \(\tau^{\inf}_\varepsilon(z)=\inf\{t>0:\inf_{x\in D}z(t,x)<\varepsilon\}\), \(\tau^\infty_n(z)=\inf\{t>0:\sup_{x\in D}z(t,x)>n\}\), \(\tau^{\inf}_0(z)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\tau^{\inf}_\varepsilon(z)\), and \(\tau^\infty_\infty(z)=\sup_n\tau^\infty_n(z)\). Proposition 3.1 asserts, with probability one, \[-v_-(t,x)\le u(t,x)\le v(t,x)\] simultaneously for every \(x\in D\) and all \[0\le t\le\tau^{\inf}_0(v)\wedge\tau^{\inf}_0(v_-)\wedge\tau^\infty_\infty(v)\wedge\tau^\infty_\infty(v_-).\]

Let \(Z^\varphi\) be the periodic stochastic heat convolution of an adapted field \(\varphi\) on \(D=[-\pi,\pi]\). For \(p>6\), Theorem 1.2 asserts a constant \(C_p\), independent of every \(T>0\), such that whenever the right side is finite, \[\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T,x\in D}|Z^\varphi(t,x)|^p\le C_pT^{p/4-3/2}\mathbb E\int_0^T\int_D|\varphi(s,y)|^p\,dy\,ds.\] The estimate is stated for all positive time horizons, not only bounded or small times.

Let \(H_0=A+UBU^*\), with deterministic real diagonal matrices \(A,B\) and Haar unitary \(U\). The limiting input laws \(\mu_\alpha,\mu_\beta\) are compactly supported and absolutely continuous, with mean zero and densities satisfying \(f_\iota(x)\asymp(E_\iota^+-x)^{t_\iota^+}\) near their right endpoints, where \(-1<t_\iota^+<1\), for \(\iota=\alpha,\beta\). Assumption 2.3 requires their empirical laws to approximate them in Lévy distance by \(N^{-1+\varepsilon}\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large \(N\); no upper outlier farther than any fixed \(\delta>0\) above \(E_\iota^+\); uniformly bounded lower spectral edges; and \(\operatorname{Tr}A=\operatorname{Tr}B=0\).

In the comparison argument, \(H_t=H_0+\sqrt t\,W\), where \(W\) is an independent GUE matrix and \(0\le t\le N^{-1/3+\chi}\) for a sufficiently small fixed \(\chi>0\). Put \(\mu_t=\mu_\alpha\boxplus\mu_\beta\boxplus\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}^{(t)}\), let \(E_{+,t}\) be its regular right edge, and evaluate the subordination points there: \(\omega_\iota=\omega_{\iota,t}(E_{+,t})>E_\iota^+\). They are uniformly separated from the input supports as in Lemma 3.3. Write \[m=m_{\mu_t}(E_{+,t})=\int\frac{d\mu_\iota(x)}{x-\omega_\iota},\quad (u_\iota)_j=\int\frac{x^{j-1}}{(x-\omega_\iota)^2}\,d\mu_\iota(x),\quad(w_\iota)_j=\int\frac{x^{j-1}}{(x-\omega_\iota)^3}\,d\mu_\iota(x),\] for \(j=1,2,3\), and \(v_\iota=((\omega_\iota+m^{-1})^2,-2(\omega_\iota+m^{-1}),1)^{\mathsf T}\).

The separate input-coefficient assertions (5.40) are that, for a fixed \(c>0\) uniformly in this regime, \[L_\alpha=v_\alpha^{\mathsf T}w_\alpha-mv_\alpha^{\mathsf T}u_\alpha\le-c,\qquad L_\beta=v_\beta^{\mathsf T}w_\beta-mv_\beta^{\mathsf T}u_\beta\le-c.\] For each input, (5.41) identifies this coefficient with \[L_\iota=\frac{m_\iota^{\prime\prime}(\omega_\iota)}{2m^2}-\frac{m_\iota^{\prime}(\omega_\iota)}m=\frac{s_\iota}{m^2}-\frac{q_\iota}m,\quad q_\iota=\int\frac{d\mu_\iota(x)}{(x-\omega_\iota)^2},\quad s_\iota=\int\frac{d\mu_\iota(x)}{(x-\omega_\iota)^3}.\] The proof uses that displayed identity to infer the two negative signs separately.

Fix a nonempty Young diagram \(\lambda^0\), let \(\lambda^N\) be its \(n\times n\) dilation, and set \(N=n^2|\lambda^0|\) and \(\eta=|\lambda^0|^{-1/2}\). Let \(a_0<b_1<a_1<\cdots<b_m<a_m\) be the Russian interlacing coordinates of \(\lambda^0\). A uniform Poissonized tableau \(T_N:\lambda^N\to[0,1]\) has normalized Lebesgue law on the order polytope, with entries increasing along rows and columns. Its bead configuration is \(M_{\lambda^N}=\{(x,T_N(x,y)):(x,y)\in\lambda^N\}\). Fix \(x_0\in[\eta a_0,\eta a_m]\), \(t_0\in[0,1]\), and impose the source arithmetic condition \(x_0\sqrt{|\lambda^0|}\in\mathbb Z\). Define the locally scaled process by \[\widetilde M_{\lambda^N}^{(x_0,t_0)}=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb R:(x_0\sqrt N+x,t_0+t/\sqrt N)\in M_{\lambda^N}\}.\]

The liquid region \(\mathcal L\) consists of those \((x,t)\) in the closed parameter rectangle for which \[U\prod_{i=1}^m(x-\eta b_i+U)=(1-t)\prod_{i=0}^m(x-\eta a_i+U)\] has two nonreal solutions. Theorem 16 asserts that, for every \((x_0,t_0)\notin\mathcal L\), the scaled process converges in probability to the empty point process as \(n\to\infty\), in the standard point-process topology of Section 2.2. This includes the frozen boundary and the time endpoints. Propositions 37 and 40 respectively state the same empty limit for \(0\le t_0\le t_-(x_0)\) and \(t_+(x_0)\le t_0\le1\), including \((0,0)\) and \((\eta b_i,1)\).

On \(\mathcal L\), let \(U_c\) be the critical root with positive imaginary part and set \(\alpha(x,t)=\operatorname{Im}U_c/(1-t)\); set \(\alpha=0\) outside \(\mathcal L\). In proving Theorem 5, the source asserts that the diagonal scaled kernel \(\widetilde K_{\lambda^N}^{(x,s)}((0,0),(0,0))\) converges to \(\alpha(x,s)/\pi\) for every \((x,s)\in[\eta a_0,\eta a_m]\times[0,1]\), uniformly on compact subsets of that closed rectangle. It uses this to interchange the limit and the integral over \([0,t]\), obtaining \[H^\infty(x,t)=\frac1\pi\int_0^t\alpha(x,s)\,ds\qquad\text{for all }(x,t)\in[\eta a_0,\eta a_m]\times[0,1].\]

Proposition 11 allows \[r>0,\qquad -1<p<r,\qquad |p|<q\le\min(p+2,2r-p),\] and equation (20) sets \[a_0=-1,\quad b_1=(p+q-2)/2,\quad a_1=p,\quad b_2=(p-q+2r)/2,\quad a_2=r.\] It treats these coordinates as strictly interlacing. For \(r=1\), the stated continuity characterization requires \(p=0\) or \(q=2-\sqrt{2-p^2}\), including the admitted equality boundary of the displayed q-range.

In the proof of Proposition 5.1, the random finite measures \(\chi_\alpha\) have uniformly bounded random mass and converge in the Appendix A topology: for every fixed bounded random continuous function \(f(x,\omega)\), \[\mathbb E\int f(x,\omega)\,d\chi_{\alpha,\omega}(x)\longrightarrow\mathbb E\int f(x,\omega)\,d\chi_\omega(x).\]

For the bounded continuous truncated energy kernel \(K_\kappa(x,y)=\kappa\wedge\widehat\delta_e(x,y)^{-h}\), the proof infers for every \(\kappa\ge0\) that \[\mathbb E\iint K_\kappa\,d\chi_\alpha\,d\chi_\alpha\longrightarrow\mathbb E\iint K_\kappa\,d\chi\,d\chi.\] Both factors in each self-product are the random measure from the same outcome.

Its only first-noise coefficient is the spatially constant \(\phi=\phi_1^{(1)}=a+ib\), where \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(b
e0\); every other first-noise mode vanishes and \(W_2=0\). Thus \(W_1(t)=i\phi B_t\), with \(B\) a real Brownian motion, and \(\mu=|\phi|^2/2\). The equations are \[ egin{aligned}i\,dX+\Delta X\,dt&=\operatorname{Re}(Y)X\,dt-i\mu X\,dt+iX\,dW_1,\\alpha^{-1}i\,dY+|

For every fixed \(0<T<\infty\), Theorem 1.7 states \[\mathbb P\{X(t)\text{ does not blow up on }[0,T]\}\longrightarrow1\qquad\text{as }\phi\to\infty.\] The displayed limit is written in terms of the complex coefficient \(\phi\), without a specified ray or a separate requirement that \(|\operatorname{Im}\phi|\) diverge.

The proof’s transform uses \[\widehat\mu=\tfrac12(|\phi|^2-\phi^2)=b^2-iab,\qquad h(t)=e^{2\operatorname{Re}(W_1(t)-\widehat\mu t)}=e^{-2bB_t-2b^2t}.\] Step 3, (8.44)–(8.45), claims for the fixed positive deterministic \(C_3=C_3(T,\|X_0\|_{H^1},\|Y_0\|_2)\), independent of \(\phi\), that \[\mathbb P\!\left\{\|h\|_{L^4(0,\infty)}^4\ge C_3^{-4}\right\}\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{as }\phi\to\infty.\] This auxiliary probability limit, with the same displayed amplitude notation, is the specific step examined by the report.

With \(L(t)=\mathbb E e^{tX}\), Esscher tilt \(Q_h\), and standard Gaussian density \(\varphi\), the source prints \(Q_h\varphi(x)=\varphi(x+h)\), uses \(L(t)\) as the denominator of \(L(t+h)\) in the proof of Proposition 3.2, and prints the tilted-variance numerator without the factor \(L(h)\) multiplying \(L^{\prime\prime}(h)\). These are asserted as probability-tilt identities under the paper's mean-zero, variance-one and Laplace-transform assumptions.

The periodic Laplace-factor display on page 3 uses the negative Gaussian exponent, whereas the characteristic-function comparisons on page 13 use the positive Gaussian exponent. Example 9.5 states \(L(t)=1-c\Psi(t)\) for its positive \(c\) and normalized periodic factor.

In the \(c_0=0\) weighted-convolution calculation, the printed second density factor and its Gaussian factor are evaluated at \(y/c_1\), although the second summand has weight \(c_2\). These are the literal sign and normalization identities being checked, not new hypotheses on the Gaussian diagnostic.

Corollary 1.2 permits arbitrary exterior boundary loop configurations \(\xi_k\) for the stated near-\((n,x)=(1,1)\) parameter regime. Let \(f_k\) be uniform among the interior faces \(F_k\) of \(D_k=\Lambda_k(0)\), independently of the loop configuration. Let \(L(f)\) be the length of the longest loop bordering \(f\), with value infinity for a bordering bi-infinite path, and let \(V(f)\) use the outermost surrounding loop in the entire configuration.

The first display after (4.10) asserts, with an absolute isoperimetric constant \(c>0\), \[\mathbb P[V(f_k)>s]\le6c\,\mathbb E[L(f_k)\mathbf1_{\{L(f_k)>\sqrt{s/c}\}}].\] The right side averages over interior faces although the preceding loop sum includes global outermost loops and all their bordering faces.

For a fixed uncolored loop configuration, Lemma 4.5 claims a bijection from the full bit cube \(\{0,1\}^{V}\) onto its coherent triples. The construction includes face coordinates that the preceding definition makes deterministic functions of edge and selected-loop coordinates, while the stated projection to coherent triples discards those face coordinates.

Let \(\xi\) be the paper’s stationary, summably \(\psi\)-mixing random environment on \(\mathbb R\), with almost surely locally Hölder continuous paths and \(0<\mathrm{ei}=\operatorname{ess\,inf}\xi(0)<\operatorname{ess\,sup}\xi(0)=\mathrm{es}<\infty\). The offspring law \((p_k)_{k\ge1}\) has no zero offspring, mean normalized to \(\sum_k kp_k=2\), and finite second moment \(\sum_k k^2p_k<\infty\). These are Assumptions 1–2 and the normalization (3.4).

Assumption 3 requires the branching front speed \(v_0\) to exceed the critical speed \(v_c\). Fix a compact interval \(V\subset(v_c,\infty)\) containing \(v_0\) in its interior, and a compact negative tilt interval \(\Delta\subset(-\infty,0)\) containing the associated tilts for \(V\) in its interior. For Brownian motion started at \(x\), set \[U_\xi(t;x,y)=E_x\!\left[e^{\int_0^t\xi(X_s)\,ds};X_t\ge y\right].\] Proposition 5.1(a) states that, for every \(A,\delta>0\), there are a deterministic \(C_1>1\) and an almost surely finite \(T_1\) such that, uniformly for \(t\ge T_1\), \(0\le h\le t^{1-\delta}\), \(x,y\in[-At,At]\), \(x<y\), and both \((y-x)/t,(y-x)/(t+h)\in V\), \[U_\xi(t+h;x,y)\le C_1e^{C_1h}U_\xi(t;x,y).\]

In its proof, put \(\zeta=\xi-\mathrm{es}\), \(v=(y-x)/t\), \(v^{\prime}=(y-x)/(t+h)\), and \[Y_v^\approx(x,y)=E_x\!\left[e^{\int_0^{H_y}\zeta(X_s)\,ds};H_y\in[(y-x)/v-K,(y-x)/v]\right],\qquad H_y=\inf\{s\ge0:X_s=y\},\] with the fixed window \(K\) of Lemma 5.5. Equation (5.23) is a two-sided comparison of \(Y_v^\approx\) with \(U_\zeta\). The next display, (5.24), asserts under the temporal perturbation conditions above that \[\frac{U_\xi(t+h;x,y)}{U_\xi(t;x,y)}\le C_{12}^2\frac{Y_{v^{\prime}}^\approx(x,y)}{Y_v^\approx(x,y)}.\] This is the ratio as printed, with its fixed prefactor.

Proposition 5.1(b) states that for every positive function \(\delta(t)\to0\) and every \(A>0\), there are \(C_2>1\) and an almost surely finite \(T_2\) such that, for \(t\ge T_2\), \(0\le h\le t\delta(t)\), \(x,y\in[-At,At]\), \(x<y\), and \((y-x)/t,(y+h-x)/t\in V\), \[U_\xi(t;x,y+h)\le C_2e^{-h/C_2}U_\xi(t;x,y).\] In deriving this upper-ratio decay, (5.30)–(5.31) bound the first action difference in absolute value by \(C_{16}h\) and the remaining difference by \(O(h^2/t)\), then declare the proof complete. These are the two original perturbation-proof steps examined in the report.

In equation (6.17), the change-of-measure density is stopped at the Brownian hitting time \(H_y\). On the stopped-path event \(A=\{H_y\in[t-K,t],\ T_{y,t}\ge t-K\}\), the next equality nevertheless uses \(p_y^{\zeta,\eta}(t-H_y)\), the endpoint probability for a tilted continuation, with \(\eta<0\) and bounded nonpositive \(\zeta\). The original process after \(H_y\) is Brownian under this stopped density.

Let \(\xi\) be the paper’s stationary, summably \(\psi\)-mixing random environment on \(\mathbb R\), with almost surely locally Hölder continuous paths and \(0<\mathrm{ei}=\operatorname{ess\,inf}\xi(0)<\operatorname{ess\,sup}\xi(0)=\mathrm{es}<\infty\). The offspring law \((p_k)_{k\ge1}\) has no zero offspring, mean normalized to \(\sum_k kp_k=2\), and finite second moment \(\sum_k k^2p_k<\infty\). These are Assumptions 1–2 and the normalization (3.4).

For \(y\in\mathbb R\), let \(w^y\) solve \[\partial_tw^y=\tfrac12\partial_x^2w^y+\xi(x)F(w^y),\qquad w^y(0,x)=\mathbf1_{[y,\infty)}(x),\qquad F(w)=(1-w)-\sum_{k\ge1}p_k(1-w)^k.\] Fix \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), and define \(\tau_y^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:w^y(t,0)\ge\varepsilon\}\). Corollary 3.6 asserts that there is an almost surely finite \(T=T(\xi)\), with \(\varepsilon\) fixed, such that for every sufficiently large \(y\) and every \(t\) satisfying \(w^y(t,0)=\varepsilon\), \[w^y(t+s,0)\ge1-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }s\in[T,T+1].\] One \(T\) must work for all such levels and observation times; the condition does not restrict \(t\) to \(\tau_y^\varepsilon\).

The proof writes \(t=\tau_y^\varepsilon+s_0\) and uses the locally uniform limit \(w_\varepsilon^\infty(s,x)=\lim_{y\to\infty}w^y(\tau_y^\varepsilon+s,x)\). It chooses \[s_1=\inf\{s>s_0:w_\varepsilon^\infty(s^{\prime},0)\ge1-\varepsilon/2\text{ for every }s^{\prime}>s\}\] and sets \(T=s_1-s_0\), invoking uniform convergence on \([s_1,s_1+1]\). The asserted uniform quantifiers in the corollary are the object of this finding.
With \(w(t,x)=\mathbb P(M(t)\ge x)\), equation (1.5) uses \(w(t,m+r)-w(t,m-r)\) as a quantity at least \(1-\varepsilon\), for \(\varepsilon<1\).

Remark 2.3 states convergence of \((M(nt)-v_0nt)/\sqrt{\sigma^2n}\) to standard Brownian motion but then assigns that same standardized marginal an \(N(0,\sigma^2)\) limit. These are the printed survival-sign and variance conventions.

Let \(\mathfrak h\) be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space with conjugation \(\Theta\), and write \(\langle\!\langle f,g\rangle\!\rangle_\Theta=\langle\Theta f,g\rangle\). Let \((X_s)\) be a norm-compatible Grassmann Brownian martingale in the filtered noncommutative probability space of Definitions 2.15 and 2.18, with differentiable covariance \(G_s\) satisfying \(G_s^\Theta=-G_s\). In particular, it is a centered Gaussian anticommuting process with independent increments and \[\omega(X_r(f)X_s(g))=\langle\!\langle f,G_{r\wedge s}g\rangle\!\rangle_\Theta.\] Let \(0\le t\le T\), \(X_{t,s}=X_s-X_t\), and let \(V_T\in\bigwedge^{\mathrm{even}}\mathfrak h\) be any even Grassmann polynomial.

The derivative convention in Definition 3.1 is the left anticommuting derivative: for an orthonormal basis \((v_i)\), \(\partial_{v_i}v_jF+v_j\partial_{v_i}F=\delta_{ij}F\), \((DU)(v)=\sum_i\langle\!\langle v,v_i\rangle\!\rangle_\Theta\partial_{v_i}U\), and \[D_C^2=\sum_{i,j}\langle\!\langle v_i,Cv_j\rangle\!\rangle_\Theta\partial_{v_i}\partial_{v_j}.\] The row action in (3.17) is \((\dot G_sDU)(v)=\sum_i\langle\!\langle v,\dot G_sv_i\rangle\!\rangle_\Theta\partial_{v_i}U\). These are the conventions used in the claimed positive \(\tfrac12D^2_{\dot G_s}\) Itô term and in the following dynamics.

Theorem 3.12 assumes that an adapted Grassmann process \(\Psi_s\) solves, for \(s\in[t,T]\), \[d\Psi_s=-\dot G_s\,\omega_s(DV_T(\Psi_T))\,ds+dX_s,\qquad\Psi_t=0.\] It then asserts for every \(P\in\bigwedge\mathfrak h\) and every \(s\in[t,T]\) the Gibbs identity \[\omega_t(P(\Psi_s))=\frac{\omega_t\!\left(P(X_{t,s})e^{V_T(X_{t,T})}\right)}{\omega_t\!\left(e^{V_T(X_{t,T})}\right)}.\] The theorem assumes existence of the solution on the whole interval; its statement does not separately impose a nonzero partition function. The covariance, left derivatives, and row action in these displays are the original ones.

For the source covariance family \(G_s^\varepsilon\), take a cutoff \(\varepsilon\in2^{-\mathbb N_\infty}\), a truncation order \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(C>0\), and \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\kappa\ge0\) satisfying \[\begin{gathered}\alpha-3\beta\ge0,\\5\beta-\alpha-2\gamma-\kappa>0,\qquad d+4\beta-2\alpha-2\gamma-\kappa>0,\\3\beta+2-\alpha-2\gamma-\kappa>0,\qquad d+2\beta+2-2\alpha-2\gamma-\kappa>0.\end{gathered}\] Let \(c_\ell=(1-\ell/n)\bar c/2\), with \(\bar c\) from the source propagator estimate. The coefficient \(F_s^{\varepsilon[\ell](k)}\) has Grassmann degree \(k\) and perturbative grading \(\ell\). The spaces \(\mathcal L_t^{(k)}(s;c_\ell)\) are the antisymmetric, translation- and reflection-invariant weighted kernel spaces of Definition 4.2, with the derivative and spatial-decay weights prescribed there.

The truncated flow is (4.11), with \(\ell\) restricted to the retained orders: \[\partial_sF_s^{\varepsilon[\ell+1](k)}+\mathbb D_{\dot G_s^\varepsilon}^2(F_s^{\varepsilon[\ell](k+2)})+\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=0}^{\ell}\sum_{k^{\prime}=0}^{k-1}\mathbb C_{\dot G_s^\varepsilon}\!\left(F_s^{\varepsilon[\ell^{\prime}](k-k^{\prime})},F_s^{\varepsilon[\ell-\ell^{\prime}](k^{\prime}+1)}\right)=0,\] where \(\mathbb D^2\) and \(\mathbb C\) are the lifted Laplacian and contraction operators of Definition 4.8. At order zero, \(F_0^{\varepsilon[0](k)}=K^{(k)}\mathbf1_{k\in\{1,3\}}\), with \[\sup_{k\ge0}\sup_{0\le t\le s}C^{-k}2^{-(\alpha-\beta k)s}\|K^{(k)}\|_{\mathcal L_t^{(k)}(s;c_0)}<\infty.\] For \(\ell\ge1\), the boundary data are \(F_\infty^{\varepsilon[\ell](k)}=0\) for \(k\ne1\), \(\operatorname{Ren}F_\infty^{\varepsilon[\ell](1)}=0\), and \(\operatorname{Loc}F_0^{\varepsilon[\ell](1)}=0\), using Definition 4.5. Local linear data \(K^{(1)}\) as well as cubic data are permitted.

Theorem 4.13 asserts a unique global solution in these spaces, and its proof claims finiteness of the graded norm \[\|F\|_{C,\alpha,\beta,\kappa}=\sup_{\ell,k}\sup_{0\le t\le s}C^{-k}2^{-(\alpha-\beta k-\kappa\ell)s}\|F_s^{[\ell](k)}\|_{\mathcal L_t^{(k)}(s;c_\ell)}.\] In particular, writing \(A_\ell=\|F^{\varepsilon[\le\ell]}\|_{C,\alpha,\beta,\kappa}\), (4.23) and (4.24) assert, for \(0\le r\le t\), \[\begin{aligned}\|(\operatorname{Loc}F_t^{\varepsilon[\ell+1](1)})_0\|_{\mathcal L_r^{(1,(0))}(t;c_{\ell+1})}&\lesssim C^2 2^{(\alpha-\beta-\kappa(\ell+1))t}(A_\ell+A_\ell^2),\\\|F_t^{\varepsilon[\ell+1](1)}\|_{\mathcal L_r^{(1)}(t;c_{\ell+1})}&\lesssim C^2 2^{(\alpha-\beta-\kappa(\ell+1))t}(A_\ell+A_\ell^2).\end{aligned}\] The constants may depend on the fixed grading and parameters. These estimates are asserted for the theorem’s general boundary data; the exclusively cubic initial datum appears separately in Corollary 4.15.

Definition 2.16 gives a Wick recursion for a product of \(n+1\) Grassmann variables but sums its contractions over \(j=1,\ldots,n\). It is asserted to produce the Wick observables used in Proposition 2.17's martingale statement. In particular, for a product of two variables the printed contraction range includes only the first-variable self-contraction.

For \(A=\varepsilon^{-1}\ge1\), the regularizer specified before Definition 3.16 is a smooth nondecreasing function \(\min_\varepsilon\) satisfying \[\min_\varepsilon(a)=a\quad(0\le a\le A),\qquad \min_\varepsilon(a)=A\quad(a\ge A+1).\] The source requires both exact identity and plateau intervals with those endpoints.

Theorem 1.3 permits \(\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\) with \(\|\chi\|_{L^1}=1\), without assuming \(\chi\ge0\) or \(\int\chi\ne0\). For the stated covariance range \(0<2\gamma<d\), Remark 1.4 uses the free smeared two-point comparison with a lower scale \((\varepsilon\vee r)^{-2\gamma}\) in deriving the lower-order interacting-field comparison. The test-function class is the same as in the theorem.

For \(d\ge2\), IID absolutely continuous passage weights supported in \([a,b]\), \(0<a<b<\infty\), with positive uniform density lower bound, Proposition 4.1 allows globally positive summable smooth weights \(q_e\) and sets \(\tau_e=q_e/\|q\|_2\). The proof of Lemma 4.3 defines \(t_e^+=g_{\tau_e}^+(t_e)\) on every edge and asserts that \(t_e^+=t_e\) outside \([-n^2,n^2]^d\), citing localization of the geodesic. No zeroing of the exterior \(\tau_e\) is included in the displayed definition.

For \(d\ge2\), set \(p=2d/(d-1)\) and \(S_{j_0}(\beta)=\sum_{j=1}^{j_0}2^{j(p-\beta)}\). The first case of the display after (5.2) asserts \[S_{j_0}(\beta)\le C\,2^{j_0(p-\beta)}\quad\text{for }1<\beta\le p,\] even though the next case separately assigns the critical value \(\beta=p\) a \(Cj_0\) bound. The stated \(j_0=\lfloor\frac{d-1}{d+1}\log_2n-d\log_2\log n\rfloor\) grows with \(n\).

Let \((\omega_{t,x})_{t\in\mathbb N,x\in\mathbb Z^d}\) be IID real weights with \(\mathbb E e^{b|\omega_{0,0}|}<\infty\) for every \(b\ge0\), and let \(X\) be nearest-neighbor simple random walk. For \(\beta\ge0\), put \(\lambda(\beta)=\log\mathbb E e^{\beta\omega_{0,0}}\), \(\eta_{t,x}=e^{\beta\omega_{t,x}-\lambda(\beta)}\), \(W_n=E^{\mathrm{SRW}}\prod_{t=1}^n\eta_{t,X_t}\), and \(W_t^{s,x}=W_{t-s}\circ\theta_{s,x}\). The polymer measure has density \(W_n^{-1}\prod_{t=1}^n\eta_{t,X_t}\) relative to the walk. Weak disorder means \(\mathbb P(W_\infty>0)=1\). Define \(p^*=\sup\{p\ge1:\sup_n\mathbb E W_n^p<\infty\}\), \(a(p)=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log\mathbb E W_n^p\), and \(q^*=\inf\{p\ge1:a(p)>0\}\), as in (4), (14) and (15).

For \(d\ge3\), weak disorder, and any nonzero real-valued \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)\), set \(\mathcal X_n^f=n^{-d/2}\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^d}f(x/\sqrt n)(W_n^{0,x}-1)\). Theorem 1.4(i), equation (19), asserts that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P\!\left(|\mathcal X_n^f|\le n^{-d/2+(d+2)/(2q^*)-\varepsilon}\right)=0.\] The paragraph after Theorem 1.4 expressly removes the main theorem's upper-bounded-environment assumption and restriction \(\beta>\beta_{\mathrm{cr}}^{L^2}\). The stated model therefore still allows \(\beta=0\) and does not impose nonconstancy of \(\eta_{t,x}\).

These finite-critical-value assertions and the auxiliary lower bound above are the original claims examined here.

On the periodic two-dimensional Ising torus, encode spins by \(s_x\in\{-1,1\}\) and use the unordered-disagreement Hamiltonian. Let \(A_x=s_x(s_{x+e_1}+s_{x+e_2})\), \(B_x=s_x(s_{x-e_1}+s_{x-e_2})\), so a flip changes the Hamiltonian by \(A_x+B_x\). Fix integers \(11\le K\le L\) and the periodic lattice \(\Lambda=(\mathbb Z/K\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)\). For \(q\ge3\), let \(\tau_x\sigma\) increase the spin at \(x\) by one modulo \(q\), and put \(R_\beta(\sigma;x)=\exp[-\beta(\max_{c\in S}H(\sigma^{x,c})-H(\sigma))]\), where \(\sigma^{x,c}\) replaces the spin at \(x\) by \(c\). The cyclic dynamics has rate \(r_\beta(\sigma,\tau_x\sigma)=R_\beta(\sigma;x)\) and zero rate for other transitions. Its edge height is \(\max_{c\in S}H(\sigma^{x,c})\); the communication height \(\Phi(\sigma,\zeta)\) is the minimum, over directed paths from \(\sigma\) to \(\zeta\), of the largest edge height on the path. The barrier used in Sections 8–9 is \(\Gamma=2K+4\).

Fix nonempty disjoint \(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q\subset\mathcal S\), and use Notation 7.1: \(\mathbf a\in\mathcal P\), \(\mathbf b\in\mathcal Q\), and \(\mathbf c\in\mathcal S\setminus(\mathcal P\cup\mathcal Q)\). In the auxiliary graph of Definition 6.20, \(r(\eta,\eta')=1\) on edges with both endpoints different from \(\mathbf a\); an edge from a saddle vertex to \(\mathbf a\) has rate equal to the number of its MH neighbors in \(\mathcal N(\mathbf a)\). Other rates, including \(r(\mathbf a,\mathbf a)\), are zero.

On this projection domain, (6.15) is asserted for \(\eta_1,\eta_2\ne\mathbf a\), and (6.16) for \(\eta_1\ne\mathbf a\): \[\frac1q e^{-\Gamma\beta}r(\Pi\eta_1,\Pi\eta_2)=(1+o(1))\mu_\beta(\eta_1)r_\beta(\eta_1,\eta_2),\] \[\frac1q e^{-\Gamma\beta}r(\Pi\eta_1,\mathbf a)=(1+o(1))\sum_{\xi\in\mathcal N(\mathbf a)}\mu_\beta(\eta_1)r_\beta(\eta_1,\xi).\] Here \(o(1)\to0\) as \(\beta\to\infty\) on the fixed lattice. The stated exclusions concern the single configuration \(\mathbf a\), rather than its whole collapsed neighborhood \(\mathcal N(\mathbf a)\). The proposition also asserts the transposed version when \(K=L\).

In the auxiliary finite chain, the invariant law is uniform on \(\overline V\), and the trace is explicitly taken on \(Z=\mathcal Z_\ell^{a,b}\). For its disjoint target sets \(A=\overline A_\ell^{a,b}\), \(B=\overline B_\ell^{a,b}\) contained in \(Z\), equation (D.8) uses \[|\overline V|\operatorname{cap}_{\overline V}(A,B)=(|A|+|B|)\operatorname{cap}_{Z}(A,B).\] The trace domain can contain interior states outside \(A\cup B\).

Proposition 8.5 allows an arbitrary directed path \((\omega_n)_{n=0}^N\), but (D.1) and the threshold-crossing proof restrict the relevant indices by the lattice volume \(KL\). The path hypotheses permit repeated local cycles.

In Lemma 7.16, the proof uses a nonzero test-function difference to require \(\min\{H(\eta),H(\xi)\}\ge\Gamma\). Appendix C then equates the whole-space gateway energy sum exactly with its restriction to \(\mathcal E\cup\mathcal B\), dropping crossing edges to the complement. These are exact index, minimum-energy and truncation assertions, rather than statements only up to an asymptotically small error.

Fix an integer \(d\geq3\), birth rate \(\lambda>0\), and splitting rate \(v>0\). A herd shape \(A\) is any finite nonempty subset of the infinite \(d\)-regular tree. It need not be connected (Definition 2.1, p. 756). A state \(\xi\in\mathcal S\) is a finite multiset of such shapes. For an edge \(e\), write \(A_{e,1},A_{e,2}\) for the portions on the two sides of \(e\). An edge is active precisely when both portions are nonempty.

In this herd process, particles die at rate one, each occupied-to-unoccupied neighbor arrow within a herd produces a birth at rate \(\lambda\), and each active edge of each herd copy splits at rate \(v\). Different herds evolve independently. Write \(X(\xi)\) for the total particle count and \(S_v(t)\xi=\mathbb E_{\lambda,v}[X_t\mid\Xi_0=\xi]\), and put \(F_v(t)=S_v(t)\delta_{\{o\}}\).

For every \(\xi\in\mathcal S\) and \(t\geq0\), (20) defines \[
 g_v(\xi,t)=\sum_A\xi(A)\sum_{e\text{ active in }A}
 \bigl[S_v(t)(\delta_{A_{e,1}}+\delta_{A_{e,2}})
                  -S_v(t)\delta_A\bigr].\] Equation (27) replaces the first \(v\) in each bracket by \(v+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon>0\), and calls the result \(g_{v,\varepsilon}\). Definition 3.2 defines \(G(\xi)\) as a set of successor configurations and, for the shape \(A\) split to obtain \(\xi'\), sets \(m(\xi,\xi')=\xi(A)\). Equations (28) and (29) assert, respectively, that the preceding edge sums equal \[\sum_{\xi'\in G(\xi)}m(\xi,\xi')
       [S_v(t)\xi'-S_v(t)\xi],\qquad
 \sum_{\xi'\in G(\xi)}m(\xi,\xi')
       [S_{v+\varepsilon}(t)\xi'-S_v(t)\xi].\]

Fix an integer \(d\geq3\), birth rate \(\lambda>0\), and splitting rate \(v>0\). A herd shape \(A\) is any finite nonempty subset of the infinite \(d\)-regular tree. It need not be connected (Definition 2.1, p. 756). A state \(\xi\in\mathcal S\) is a finite multiset of such shapes. For an edge \(e\), write \(A_{e,1},A_{e,2}\) for the portions on the two sides of \(e\). An edge is active precisely when both portions are nonempty.

In this herd process, particles die at rate one, each occupied-to-unoccupied neighbor arrow within a herd produces a birth at rate \(\lambda\), and each active edge of each herd copy splits at rate \(v\). Different herds evolve independently. Write \(X(\xi)\) for the total particle count and \(S_v(t)\xi=\mathbb E_{\lambda,v}[X_t\mid\Xi_0=\xi]\), and put \(F_v(t)=S_v(t)\delta_{\{o\}}\).

For \(t\ge1\), Lemma 3.8 compares a herd consisting of two adjacent particles with two singleton herds and asserts a gap of at least \(\gamma F_v(t)\), for a positive \(\gamma\) depending continuously on \(\lambda,v\). Its proof uses the intermediate assertion \[\min_{t-1\le s\le t}F_v(s)\ge \frac{F_v(t)}{\min_{0\le r\le1}F_v(r)}.\] Proposition 3.6 subsequently applies the same lemma at remaining time \(t-s\) throughout an integral over \(1\le s\le t\).

Fix an integer \(d\geq3\), birth rate \(\lambda>0\), and splitting rate \(v>0\). A herd shape \(A\) is any finite nonempty subset of the infinite \(d\)-regular tree. It need not be connected (Definition 2.1, p. 756). A state \(\xi\in\mathcal S\) is a finite multiset of such shapes. For an edge \(e\), write \(A_{e,1},A_{e,2}\) for the portions on the two sides of \(e\). An edge is active precisely when both portions are nonempty.

In this herd process, particles die at rate one, each occupied-to-unoccupied neighbor arrow within a herd produces a birth at rate \(\lambda\), and each active edge of each herd copy splits at rate \(v\). Different herds evolve independently. Write \(X(\xi)\) for the total particle count and \(S_v(t)\xi=\mathbb E_{\lambda,v}[X_t\mid\Xi_0=\xi]\), and put \(F_v(t)=S_v(t)\delta_{\{o\}}\).

Under the subcritical assumptions \(\lambda<\bar\lambda(v)\) and \(0<\varphi<1\), fix \(p\ge1\) and \(x>1\), and define \(t_x=(p+1)\log x/|\log\varphi|\). In the proof of Corollary 3.15, \(N_t\) counts births up to time \(t\). The asserted union bound covers the event \(\{N_{t_x}>x\}\) using only birth increments \(N_{k+1}-N_k\) for \(k=0,\ldots,\lfloor t_x\rfloor-1\), also when \(t_x\) is not an integer.

Theorem 1.4, p. 4, equation (1.8), asserts uniqueness among \(x<1-\kappa/8\), for every \(a>0\) and \(4<\kappa<8\), of the solution to \[
 \sin u=a\sin(ru),\qquad
 u=\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{(\kappa-4)^2+8\kappa x},\qquad
 r=\frac{8-\kappa}{\kappa}.\] The definition of \(\operatorname{Root}(a)\) and the first paragraph of Section 5, p. 36, use this uniqueness.

On p. 20, Section 3.3, the paper sets \[\mathbf a^2=\frac{2}{\sin(\pi\gamma^2/4)}\] and defines its two-dimensional Brownian motion by \[
 \operatorname{Var}(L_t)=\operatorname{Var}(R_t)=t,\qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(L_t,R_t)
 =-\cos(\pi\gamma^2/4)\mathbf a^2t .\] Here \(\gamma=4/\sqrt\kappa\) and \(4<\kappa<8\). The excursion measures immediately following (3.7) are based on this motion.

Let \(\sqrt2<\gamma<2\), \(Q=\gamma/2+2/\gamma\), and \(Q<\alpha<4/\gamma\). In Lemma 4.9 and the proof of Proposition 4.4, the parameter is defined and its range asserted as \[p=\frac{\gamma\alpha}{2}-1\in\left(\frac{\gamma^2}{4}-1,0\right).\] The proof uses this parameter in Lemma 4.7, whose hypothesis is \(\gamma^2/4-1<p<0\), and in Lemma 4.5, whose hypothesis is \(-1<p<0\).

Fix the symmetric \(q\)-state broadcast model, in particular \(q\in\{3,4\}\) in the application to Theorem 1.12, with channel \(K_\lambda=\lambda I+(1-\lambda)J\), where every entry of \(J\) is \(1/q\) and \(-1/(q-1)\le\lambda<1\). Let \(T\sim\operatorname{GW}(\mu_d)\), with root offspring \(\gamma\sim\mu_d\), mean \(d>1\), and child subtrees \(T_j\). Assume \(K(\theta)=\sup_{d>1}\mathbb E e^{\theta X_d/d}<\infty\) for every \(\theta\ge0\), and that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exist positive \(C_1,C_2,d_0\) such that \(\mathbb P(X_d/d\in[C_1,C_2])\ge1-\varepsilon\) for all \(d\ge d_0\), as in Assumptions 1.10–1.11. The global near-critical restriction (16) is \(d^5|\lambda|^9>1+c_0\) and \(1-c_0\le d\lambda^2\le1\), for the fixed universal \(c_0>0\).

For observations \(\sigma(n)\) at depth \(n\), let \[x_n(T)=\sum_{i=1}^q\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\left(\mathbb P(\sigma_\rho=i\mid\sigma(n),T)-\frac1q\right)^2\right],\qquad x_n=\mathbb E_Tx_n(T).\] Lemma 5.2 asserts that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(d^\prime(\varepsilon)>0\) such that, for \(d>d^\prime(\varepsilon)\), uniformly in the depth and channel parameters in this regime, \[\mathbb E_T\left|\widehat x_n-x_n\right|<\varepsilon,\qquad \widehat x_n=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^{\gamma}x_n(T_j).\] This is the original deterministic centering by \(x_n\); the assumptions do not say \(X_d/d\to1\).

For \(s\ge0\), put \[Q_s(x)=\left[1+e^{-16s/3}\sum_{1\le i<j\le3}e^{\sqrt{16s/3}(x_i+x_j)}\right]^{-1},\qquad g_4(s)+\tfrac14=\mathbb E Q_s(G),\quad G\sim N(0,I_3).\] Let \(P_s(x)=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^3}Q_s(\epsilon_1x_1,\epsilon_2x_2,\epsilon_3x_3)\). Lemma B.2 supplies the explicit cell bound \(\phi(i,n)\ge\int_{i/n}^{(i+1)/n}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx\) for \(i\ge0\), without a Gaussian normalization factor.

For integer \(n>0\), the cell terms in (140) are \[S_n(i,j,k;s)=P_s(i/n,j/n,k/n)\phi(i,n)\phi(j,n)\phi(k,n),\] and \[T_n(i,j,k;s)=Q_s(i/n,j/n,k/n)\prod_{a\in\{i,j,k\}}\phi(\min\{|a|,|a+1|\},n).\] Writing \(A_n(s)\) for the sum of \(S_n\) over \(0\le i,j,k\le n-1\) and \(T_n\) over \(\{-5n,\ldots,5n-1\}^3\setminus\{-n,\ldots,n-1\}^3\), the printed bound is \(g_4(s)\le-1/4+2\cdot10^{-6}+A_n(s)\). In contrast, both Gaussian integrals in (138) include the factor \((2\pi)^{-3/2}\).

The subsequent certification claim uses \(n=200\) on the first two grids of (137) and \(n=100\) on the remaining four. The six claimed bounds, with each grid specified by first point, step, and last point, are \[\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{first}&\text{step}&\text{last}&\text{upper bound for }g_4(s)\\0.0615&0.0003&0.069&s-0.0003\\0.0695&0.0005&0.08&s-0.0005\\0.0805&0.0005&0.095&s-0.0005\\0.096&0.001&0.2&s-0.001\\0.21&0.01&0.5&s-0.01\\0.75&\text{single point}&0.75&0.5\end{array}\] Each upper inequality is strict. The assertion under review is that the printed unnormalized sum certifies these bounds; the report does not claim that (140), considered merely as a loose upper bound, is itself false.

In the broadcast model with \(q\) spin states and root offspring number \(\gamma\), the message convention on the event \(\{\gamma=0\}\) is \(Y_{i1}=1/q\). With this convention, Proposition 2.3(b) asserts unconditional independence of the child messages, and Lemma 3.4, equation (23), asserts the unconditional first-moment identity \[\mathbb E(Y_{11}-1/q)=\lambda x_n.\] These assertions are stated for the paper's offspring models, including those allowing \(\mathbb P(\gamma=0)>0\). Remark 3.3 additionally asserts \(x_n(T)>0\) without excluding trees whose level \(n\) is empty.

In Lemma 3.8, under Assumption 1.10 for the offspring distribution and the admissible broadcast-channel parameters, the proof obtains \(x_{n+1}\ge c\lambda^4x_n^2\). For \(|\lambda|\ge\kappa>0\), it then infers the linear lower bound \(x_{n+1}\ge c\kappa^4x_n\). Here \(x_n\ge0\) is the paper's averaged magnetization quantity; the finding concerns this implication between the two displayed bounds.

Let \(\gamma\) denote the offspring number, with mean \(d\), and let \(q,\lambda,x_n\) have the broadcast-model meanings used in the expansion. Equation (105) gives the bracket multiplying \(\{\mathbb E\binom{\gamma}{2}\}^2\lambda^6x_n^3\) as \[B=\frac{4q^2(q+1)}{(q-1)^2d(d-1)}-\frac{24q^2(q-2)}{(q-1)^2d(d\lambda-1)}.\] The overview formula (15) represents the same cubic coefficient but prints the bracket \(B/4\). The claim under examination is the consistency of these two expressions wherever their denominators are defined.

Let \(\{\mu_d\}_{d>1}\) be offspring laws with mean \(d\) satisfying Assumption 1.10: for every \(\theta\ge0\), \(\sup_{d>1}\mathbb E_{\mu_d}e^{\theta X_d/d}<\infty\). For the symmetric \(q\)-state broadcast channel, the admissible parameter interval is \([-1/(q-1),1)\). Define \(\lambda^-(q,d)\) as the infimum of admissible negative \(\lambda\) for which nonreconstruction holds almost surely for \(T\sim\operatorname{GW}(\mu_d)\).

Theorem 1.13 sets \[d^*=\inf\left\{d>1:\frac{15+36(\sqrt d-1)}{7d(d-1)}\le\frac{\mathbb E_{\mu_d}[X(X-1)(X-2)]}{(\mathbb E_{\mu_d}[X(X-1)])^2}\right\},\] with the infimum of the empty set equal to infinity. If \(d^*>1\), it asserts for every \(1<d<d^*\) that \(\lambda^-(4,d)>-d^{-1/2}\), describing this as failure of sharpness of the Kesten–Stigum bound in the antiferromagnetic regime. The following paragraph interprets the theorem as existence of reconstruction below that bound with positive probability. The finding concerns this existence interpretation on the stated range of \(d\), with the original admissible channel interval retained; it does not challenge the numerical threshold inequality by itself.

In the proof of Proposition 5.3, let \(V_1,\ldots,V_D\in\mathbb R^q\) be independent bounded increments satisfying its moment approximation assumptions (119), and let \(Z_j\sim N(\mathbb EV_j,\operatorname{Cov}(V_j))\) be independent Gaussian replacements, independent of the \(V_j\). Let \(\phi:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R\) be bounded and three times differentiable, with bounded derivatives through order three. Appendix A prints \[S_k=\sum_{j\le k-1}V_j+\sum_{j\le k}Z_j,\qquad T_k=\sum_{j\le k-1}V_j+\sum_{j\le k+1}Z_j,\] and asserts that \((T_k,V_k,Z_k)\) are independent.

For \(U=V_k\) and for \(U=Z_k\), the displayed Taylor estimates assert \[\left|\mathbb E\phi(T_k+U)-\mathbb E\langle\nabla\phi(T_k),U\rangle-\tfrac12\mathbb E\langle\nabla^2\phi(T_k)U,U\rangle\right|\le C_{q,\phi}\mathbb E\|U\|_\infty^3.\] These are the printed sums and estimates, including their lack of the constant Taylor term. In the preceding Gaussian comparison, with \(Z\sim N(0,I_q)\), the calculation also replaces \((\mathbb E\|(\Sigma^{1/2}-\Sigma_V^{1/2})Z\|_2^2)^{1/2}\) by \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}-\Sigma_V^{1/2}\|_F^2\), where \(\|\cdot\|_F\) is the Frobenius norm.

Consider the symmetric sparse stochastic block model \(G\sim G(n,q,a/n,b/n)\), with fixed model parameters as \(n\to\infty\). Write \(\sigma_u\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\) for the hidden community of vertex \(u\), and put \(d=(a+(q-1)b)/q\) and \(\lambda=(a-b)/(a+(q-1)b)\). Under Theorem 1.5, \(q\in\{3,4\}\), \(d\ge d_0\) for a universal sufficiently large constant \(d_0\), and \(d\lambda^2\le1\).

Corollary 1.6 asserts that for any fixed vertices \(u,v\) and every color \(i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), \[\mathbb P(\sigma_u=i\mid G,\sigma_v=1)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathbb P}\frac1q.\] The stated quantifier over \(u,v\) does not require the vertices to be distinct; that endpoint of the quantifier is the assertion under review.

Fix \(0<q<1\) and real \(t>0\). Partitions are finite and padded with zeros; for \(\rho\subseteq\lambda\), the exponential Schur specialization is \(s_{\lambda/\rho}(\gamma)=\gamma^{|\lambda/\rho|}f^{\lambda/\rho}/|\lambda/\rho|!\), where \(\gamma=t(1-q)\) and \(f^{\lambda/\rho}\) counts standard tableaux.

A partition is finite, padded with zeros as needed. For a skew partition \(\lambda/\rho\), \(\rho\subseteq\lambda\), write \(s_{\lambda/\rho}(\gamma)\) for its exponential Schur specialization. Definition 2.4 and (2.11), pages 16–17, give \[
 P_t(\lambda/\rho)=K_t q^{|\rho|}s_{\lambda/\rho}(\gamma)^2,\quad
 \gamma=t(1-q),\quad K_t=e^{-t^2(1-q)}(q;q)_\infty.\] Here \(s_{\lambda/\rho}(\gamma)=\gamma^{|\lambda/\rho|}f^{\lambda/\rho}/|\lambda/\rho|!\), with \(f\) the number of standard tableaux. All these weights are positive. Equation (4.35), page 48, defines \[
 \mathcal T_t(a)=-t^{-2}\log\sup_{\rho\subseteq\lambda,\ \lambda_1\le at}P_t(\lambda/\rho)
 \quad(a\ge0),\qquad \mathcal T_t(a)=+\infty\quad(a<0).\] Keeping \(K_t\) explicitly avoids any change of probability normalization.

Proposition 4.13 claims that, for all \(a,a^{\prime}\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large \(t\) satisfy \[\mathcal T_t\left(\frac{a+a^{\prime}}{2}+\frac1t\right)\le\frac{\mathcal T_t(a)+\mathcal T_t(a^{\prime})}2+\varepsilon.\] For arbitrary admissible \(\lambda/\mu,\nu/\rho\) with \(\lambda_1\le at\) and \(\nu_1\le a^{\prime} t\), its proof chooses whichever coordinatewise ceiling or floor averaged skew shape has the larger unweighted Schur square. It asserts for that choice \[\Delta=|\text{chosen averaged inner partition}|-\frac{|\mu|+|\rho|}{2}\le1.\] The same proof prints the contribution \(+t^{-2}\log q^\Delta\) in the resulting logarithmic upper bound.

Let \(J_n\) be the Bessel function of the first kind of integer order \(n\). For every fixed \(u>2\), Lemma 3.4, equation (3.14), asserts, as real \(t\to\infty\), \[2\pi t\sqrt{u^2-4}\,J_{\lfloor ut\rfloor}(2t)^2 e^{t\Phi_+(u)}\longrightarrow1,\qquad \Phi_+(u)=2u\operatorname{arccosh}(u/2)-2\sqrt{u^2-4}.\]

Let \(\mathbb N^{\prime}=\{1/2,3/2,\ldots\}\) and \(\mathbb Z^{\prime}=\mathbb Z+1/2\), so \(a+\ell\) is an integer. For \(r>0\), \(2+r<\gamma_1<\gamma_2\le\infty\), \(v\ge0\), and \(t\ge1\), Lemma 3.7 asserts a finite exponential upper bound for \[\sum_{a\in\mathbb N^{\prime}}\ \sum_{\substack{\ell\in\mathbb Z^{\prime}\\a+\ell\in[\gamma_1t,\gamma_2t]}}J_{a+\ell}(2t)^2e^{v\ell}.\] In particular, the displayed estimate includes the endpoint \(v=0\) in its asserted domain.

Let \(S\) be a discontinuous subordinator with Laplace exponent \[\phi(\lambda)=b\lambda+\int_0^\infty(1-e^{-\lambda s})\mu(s)\,ds,\qquad b\ge0,\] where \(\mu\not\equiv0\) is a Lévy density and \(\int_0^\infty(1\wedge s)\mu(s)\,ds<\infty\). Assume a finite constant \(c>0\) satisfies \(\mu(s)\le c\mu(2s)\) for \(0<s<8\) and \(\mu(s)\le c\mu(s+1)\) for \(s>1\). Let \(X_t=W_{S_t}\) in \(\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge1\), with independent Brownian motion \(W\), and generator \(\mathcal L_\phi=-\phi(-\Delta)\). No positive-drift or infinite-activity hypothesis is imposed.

Theorem 1.6 asserts that the scale invariant boundary Harnack principle holds for \(\mathcal L_\phi\) in an open set \(D\subset\mathbb R^d\) if and only if the Green comparison (1.6) holds: there exist \(\delta>0\) and \(C\ge1\) such that, with \(D_r(z)=D\cap B(z,r)\), \[G_{D_{4r}(z)}(x_1,y)\le C\frac{\mathbb E_{x_1}\tau_{D_{2r}(z)}}{\mathbb E_{x_2}\tau_{D_{2r}(z)}}G_{D_{4r}(z)}(x_2,y)\] for every \(z\in\partial D\), \(0<r<\delta\), \(x_1,x_2\in D_r(z)\), and \(y\in D_{4r}(z)\setminus D_{3r}(z)\).

Here Definition 1.1 requires \(G_U\) to be an occupation density: \[\mathbb E_x\int_0^{\tau_U}f(X_s)\,ds=\int_U G_U(x,y)f(y)\,dy\] for every bounded nonnegative Borel \(f\) and \(x\in U\), with the stated excessivity properties. The deduction invokes Corollary 1.5 and its assumption (A1), requiring absolute continuity of all positive resolvents, on the preceding assertion that every subordinate Brownian motion has a continuous transition density. The finding concerns this density framework on the full stated class.

For a Lévy process in \(\mathbb R^d\) with covariance matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\) and Lévy measure \(\nu\), fix \(r>0\) and the constant \(c_2>0\) in (4.5), and put \[B_i=\int_{|z|\le2r}z_i^2\,\nu(dz).\] The chain after (4.5) in Lemma 4.1 asserts the identity \[\max_{1\le i\le d}\left(\frac12a_{ii}+c_2B_i\right)=\frac12\max_{1\le i\le d}a_{ii}+c_2\max_{1\le i\le d}B_i.\] No common maximizing-coordinate hypothesis is imposed on the two families.

The model is dyadic branching Brownian motion with unit Brownian variance, drift \(-\mu\), killing at zero, and rate \(r(x)=(1+W(x))/2\). Assumptions (A1)–(A2), page 1383, require a nonnegative \(C^1\) function \(W\) supported in \([0,1]\). For the process also killed at \(L\), let \(v_L\) be the positive Dirichlet principal eigenfunction of \[\tfrac12 v_L''+\tfrac12 Wv_L=\lambda_1(L)v_L,\qquad v_L(1)=1.\] Write \[\lambda_\infty=\lim_{L\to\infty}\lambda_1(L),\quad
 \beta=\sqrt{2\lambda_\infty},\quad
 \mu=\sqrt{1+2\lambda_\infty},\quad
 \alpha=\frac{\mu+\beta}{\mu-\beta},\quad
 w_L=\lambda_\infty-\lambda_1(L).\] The pushed assumption \(H_p\) is \(\lambda_\infty>0\). The main theorems assume \(H_{fp}\), namely \(\lambda_\infty>1/16\), equivalently \(\mu<3\beta\) or \(\alpha>2\). The cutoff in (19) and the weights in (20), page 1393, are \[
 L=L_N=\frac{\log N}{\mu-\beta},\qquad
 H_L(x):=h(0,x)=\frac{e^{\mu x}v_L(x)}
                    {\widetilde c\|v_L\|_2^2},\qquad
 h(s,x)=e^{w_Ls}H_L(x),\] where \(\widetilde c^{-1}=\int_0^\infty e^{-\mu x}v_\infty(x)\,dx\). Here \(v_\infty(x)=e^{-\beta(x-1)}\) for \(x\geq1\), and \(I:=\|v_\infty\|_2^2\in(0,\infty)\).

Under (A1)–(A2) and the fully pushed condition \(H_{fp}\), let \(u(s,x)=\mathbb P_x(Z_s^L>0)\). Lemma 15 asserts positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), depending on \(\lambda_\infty\) but independent of the interval \(0<T_1<T_2\), and an integer \(\widetilde N(T_1,T_2)\), such that for every \(N\ge\widetilde N\), \(x\in[0,L]\), and \(t\in[T_1,T_2]\), \[u(tN,x)\ge\frac{C_1H_L(x)}{1+tN}.\] Its proof asserts corresponding bounds on the one- and two-spine expectations independent of \(x,T_1,T_2\).

The proof of Corollary 8, immediately after (94), additionally claims a bound on \[Q_x^{2,L^2}\!\left[r(\zeta_v)h(|v|,\zeta_v)\right]\] uniform in \(N\) and \(x\in[0,L]\). Here \(v\) is the unique branch point of the unaccelerated two-spine tree of depth \(L^2\); its time is uniform on \([0,L^2]\), and conditional on that time its position follows the one-spine diffusion with generator \(\tfrac12\partial_{xx}+(v_L^\prime/v_L)\partial_x\). Thus the particular expectation being bounded is \[\frac1{L^2}\int_0^{L^2}\mathbb E_x^Q[r(\zeta_s)h(s,\zeta_s)]\,ds.\]

The model is dyadic branching Brownian motion with unit Brownian variance, drift \(-\mu\), killing at zero, and rate \(r(x)=(1+W(x))/2\). Assumptions (A1)–(A2), page 1383, require a nonnegative \(C^1\) function \(W\) supported in \([0,1]\). For the process also killed at \(L\), let \(v_L\) be the positive Dirichlet principal eigenfunction of \[\tfrac12 v_L''+\tfrac12 Wv_L=\lambda_1(L)v_L,\qquad v_L(1)=1.\] Write \[\lambda_\infty=\lim_{L\to\infty}\lambda_1(L),\quad
 \beta=\sqrt{2\lambda_\infty},\quad
 \mu=\sqrt{1+2\lambda_\infty},\quad
 \alpha=\frac{\mu+\beta}{\mu-\beta},\quad
 w_L=\lambda_\infty-\lambda_1(L).\] The pushed assumption \(H_p\) is \(\lambda_\infty>0\). The main theorems assume \(H_{fp}\), namely \(\lambda_\infty>1/16\), equivalently \(\mu<3\beta\) or \(\alpha>2\). The cutoff in (19) and the weights in (20), page 1393, are \[
 L=L_N=\frac{\log N}{\mu-\beta},\qquad
 H_L(x):=h(0,x)=\frac{e^{\mu x}v_L(x)}
                    {\widetilde c\|v_L\|_2^2},\qquad

For a positive-definite covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), write \[p_\Sigma(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 x^T\Sigma^{-1}x\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.\] Let \(\Sigma,\bar\Sigma\) be the symmetric covariance matrices in Lemma 3.11, satisfying its comparison condition \(K^{-1}I\leq\Sigma\bar\Sigma^{-1}\leq KI\) for some \(K>0\).

For the operator construction in Section 5, Conditions A1 and B are in force. The individual diffusion has bounded coefficients \(b,c\), with \(b\in C^1\), \(c\in C^2\), bounded \(c'\), and \(c\) bounded away from zero. Its branching rate is \(\kappa\geq0\), and its forward operator is \[L^*u=\partial_x^2(au)-\partial_x(bu)+\kappa u,\qquad a=c^2/2.\] The initial measure \(\xi_0\) is any probability measure, including an atomic one. The injection measure \(\alpha\) is nonnegative and locally finite in time. Its cumulative mass \(I\) satisfies either the spatial domination condition \(\alpha(dx,dt)\leq C\,dx\,dI_t\) with positive temporal Hölder regularity, or temporal Hölder regularity strictly greater than \(1/2\). The removal mass \(J\) is nondecreasing, absolutely continuous, Hölder continuous with a positive exponent and zero at zero. The mass equation \[m_t=1+\kappa\int_0^t m_s\,ds+I_t-J_t\] has a strictly positive global lower bound.

The weak formulation couples \(\partial_tu-L^*u=\alpha-\beta\) with \(\beta(\mathbb R\times[0,t])=J_t\), nonnegativity, and \[\beta\{(x,t):U(x,t)>0\}=0,\qquad
U(x,t)=\int_{-\infty}^x u(y,t)\,dy.\] This orientation describes removal on the left.

Consider nearest-neighbor ASEP on \(\mathbb Z\), with right rate \(p\in(1/2,1]\), left rate \(q=1-p\), \(\gamma=p-q>0\), density \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and a tagged particle initially pinned at the origin.

The three displays below are asserted to be entropic hydrodynamic evolutions of the changed initial profiles, for \(0<t\leq1\). In each smooth region they must therefore satisfy \(\partial_t r+\gamma(1-2r)\partial_u r=0\). For the intermediate upper tail, assume \(\gamma(1-\rho)<A<\gamma\), \(0<\epsilon<\gamma-A\), and put \(a=A+\epsilon\). Equation (4.5) prints \[r(t,u)=\begin{cases}\rho,&u<m(t),\\ \rho+\dfrac{1-a/\gamma-\rho}{s(t)-m(t)}(u-m(t)),&m(t)\leq u<s(t),\\1-a/\gamma,&s(t)\leq u<\ell(t),\\1-a/\gamma+\dfrac{\rho-1+a/\gamma}{r_+(t)-\ell(t)}(u-\ell(t)),&\ell(t)\leq u<r_+(t),\\\rho,&u\geq r_+(t),\end{cases}\] with the printed boundaries \[m(t)=-\gamma\rho t,\quad s(t)=at,\quad \ell(t)=\gamma-a+(2a-\gamma)t,\quad r_+(t)=a-\gamma+2\gamma\rho+\gamma(1-2\rho)t.\]

For the positive lower tail in Section 4.4, assume \(0<A<\gamma(1-\rho)\), \(0<\epsilon<1\), and put \(a=A(1-\epsilon)\). The printed evolution is \[r(t,u)=\begin{cases}\rho,&u<(a-\gamma\rho)t,\\1-a/\gamma,&(a-\gamma\rho)t\leq u<\gamma-(\gamma-a)t,\\\rho+\dfrac{\rho-(1-a/\gamma)}{t[\gamma-a+\gamma(1-\rho)]}\bigl(u-\gamma-\gamma(1-\rho)t\bigr),&\gamma-(\gamma-a)t\leq u<\gamma+\gamma(1-\rho)t,\\\rho,&u\geq\gamma+\gamma(1-\rho)t.\end{cases}\] The first two constructions are used to assert convergence of the scaled tagged position to \(a\) under the corresponding changed initial law.

For Section 4.5, assume \(A<0\), \(0<\gamma<1\), \(\epsilon>0\), and set \(x_0=A-\gamma-\epsilon\). The evolution of the profile with an initial empty interval is printed as \[r(t,u)=\begin{cases}\rho,&u<x_0-\gamma\rho t,\\-\dfrac{\rho}{\gamma(1+\rho)t}(u-x_0-\gamma t),&x_0-\gamma\rho t\leq u<x_0+\gamma t,\\0,&x_0+\gamma t\leq u<\gamma(1-\rho)t,\\\rho,&u\geq\gamma(1-\rho)t.\end{cases}\] These are the original rarefaction branches and joins being checked, before any proposed correction.

Let \(a<b\), \(0<\rho<1\), and let \(H:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)\) be continuously differentiable, strictly convex, and strictly increasing. Define \(h_\rho(z)=z\log(z/\rho)+(1-z)\log((1-z)/(1-\rho))\). Section 6.2 fixes \(\lambda>0\), small \(\delta>0\) with \(a+\delta<b\), and \(0<\epsilon\leq H^{\prime}(a+\delta)\), and minimizes the penalized functional \[J_{\lambda,\delta,\epsilon}(v)=\int_{a+\delta}^b h_\rho(v^{\prime}(u))\,du+\int_{a+\delta}^b e^{-\lambda(H(u)-v(u))}\,du\] subject to \[\epsilon\leq v^{\prime}(u)\leq1-\epsilon,\qquad 0\leq v(a+\delta)\leq\min\{H(a+\delta),\delta\}.\] The right endpoint value is not fixed, and \(v\leq H\) is enforced here through the penalty, not as an additional hard constraint.

For a minimizer \(v=v_{\lambda,\delta,\epsilon}\), Step 2 asserts the equality \[\int_{a+\delta}^b h_\rho^{\prime}(v^{\prime}(u))\phi^{\prime}(u)\,du=-\lambda\int_{a+\delta}^b e^{-\lambda(H(u)-v(u))}\phi(u)\,du\] for test functions \(\phi\) vanishing at both endpoints. It concludes that \((h_\rho^{\prime}(v^{\prime}))^{\prime}=\lambda e^{-\lambda(H-v)}\) and, in Step 3, obtains the pointwise identity \[v^{\prime\prime}(u)=\lambda v^{\prime}(u)(1-v^{\prime}(u))e^{-\lambda(H(u)-v(u))}\qquad(a+\delta<u<b).\] These are asserted for the constrained minimizer without an inactive-derivative-constraint hypothesis, including in the third case of Proposition 6.1 where \(H(a)=0\) and \(H^{\prime}(b)\leq\rho\).

In the upper-tail proof of Section 5.1, fix \(A>\gamma(1-\rho)\) and the truncation interval \([-R,R]\). The compact measure class \(\mathcal M_R\) consists of measures satisfying \(\mu([a,b])\leq b-a\) for \(-R\leq a<b\leq R\), with the weak-measure metric (1.6). Centers are profiles \(\beta_0\) obtained by restricting continuous \(\beta:\mathbb R\to(0,1)\) to this interval. Let \[K(\beta_0)=\int_{-R}^{R}\left[\beta_0(u)\log\frac{\beta_0(u)}{\rho}+(1-\beta_0(u))\log\frac{1-\beta_0(u)}{1-\rho}\right]du.\] Let \(v_\beta(t,x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}r_\beta(t,u)\,du\), where \(r_\beta\) is the entropic evolution from \(\beta_0\), and put \(F(\beta)=v_\beta(1,A)-v_\beta(0,0)\).

Write \(L_A=\limsup_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log P_{\eta_{\mathrm{step}}}(Z_N\geq AN)\) for the step-process comparison term. With the empirical initial measure \(\pi_0^N\), Step 1 ends with the local bound \[\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log P_{0,\rho}\bigl(X_N\geq AN,\ \pi_0^N\in B_\delta(\beta_0)\bigr)\leq L_A-\mathbf1_{\{F(\beta)<\epsilon+\delta\}}\bigl(K(\beta_0)-2\delta\bigr),\] where the allowed small radius is chosen using the center-dependent local estimates (5.4)–(5.5).

Step 2 asserts that these balls over the continuous interior-density centers form an open cover of \(\mathcal M_R\), selects a finite subcover with centers \(\beta_0^1,\ldots,\beta_0^j\), and obtains a cost term \[\min_{1\leq i\leq j}\mathbf1_{\{F(\beta^i)<\epsilon+\delta\}}\bigl(K(\beta_0^i)-2\delta\bigr).\] It then asserts the further bound (5.7), \[\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log P_{0,\rho}(X_N\geq AN)\leq L_A-\inf_{\beta_0:\,F(\beta)<\epsilon+\delta}\bigl(K(\beta_0)-2\delta\bigr).\] The claim under examination is this passage from the displayed local bounds and proposed cover to the constrained global infimum.

Consider nearest-neighbor ASEP on \(\mathbb Z\), with right rate \(p\in(1/2,1]\), left rate \(q=1-p\), \(\gamma=p-q>0\), density \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and a tagged particle initially pinned at the origin.

Let \(h_\rho(z)=z\log(z/\rho)+(1-z)\log((1-z)/(1-\rho))\), and define \[G(z)=\begin{cases}0,&z<-\gamma,\\\dfrac{\gamma}{4}(1+z/\gamma)^2,&|z|\leq\gamma,\\z,&z>\gamma.\end{cases}\] For \(A\geq\gamma\), Optimization 1 minimizes \(K_1(v)=\int_{A-\gamma}^{A+\gamma}h_\rho(v^{\prime}(u))\,du\) over differentiable nonnegative \(v\) with \(v(A-\gamma)=0\), \(0\leq v^{\prime}\leq1\), and \(v(u)\leq G(u-A)\). For \(\gamma(1-\rho)<A<\gamma\), Optimization 2 has the same derivative and obstacle constraints on \([0,A+\gamma]\), with \(v(0)=0\), and cost \(K_2(v)=\int_0^{A+\gamma}h_\rho(v^{\prime}(u))\,du\).

Put \(z_\rho=A+\gamma(2\rho-1)\) and \(L_A(u)=\rho(u-\gamma(2\rho-1)+A)+G(\gamma(2\rho-1))\). Proposition 2.9 prints the unique minimizers as \[v_1(u)=\begin{cases}G(u-A),&A-\gamma\leq u\leq z_\rho,\\L_A(u),&z_\rho\leq u\leq A+\gamma,\end{cases}\] and \[v_2(u)=\begin{cases}(1-A/\gamma)x,&0\leq u\leq\gamma-A,\\G(u-A),&\gamma-A\leq u\leq z_\rho,\\L_A(u),&z_\rho\leq u\leq A+\gamma.\end{cases}\] Both terminal pieces contain the printed \(+A\) translation. The \(x\) in the first branch of \(v_2(u)\) is also the variable printed in that display.

For \(A\geq\gamma\), Theorem 2.7 asserts \[\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log P_\rho(X_N/N\geq A)\leq-I^Z(A)-K_1(v_1)=-I_\gamma(A),\] where \[I^Z(A)=A\log c-pc-q/c+1,\qquad c=\frac{A+\sqrt{A^2+4pq}}{2p},\qquad I_\gamma(A)=I^Z(A)-A\log(1-\rho)-\gamma\rho.\] In this equality, \(K_1\) is integrated only on \([A-\gamma,A+\gamma]\); the displayed expression contains no separate cost for the initial empty interval \([0,A-\gamma]\).

The related general problem in Section 6 takes \(a<b\) and a continuously differentiable, strictly convex, strictly increasing \(H:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)\). It minimizes \(\int_a^b h_\rho(v^{\prime}(u))\,du\) subject to \(v(a)=0\), \(0\leq v^{\prime}\leq1\), and \(0\leq v\leq H\). The first case of Proposition 6.1 states that, when \(H(u)\geq\rho u\) throughout \([a,b]\), the zero-cost minimizer is \(v(u)=\rho u\). The left endpoint \(a\) remains general in this assertion.

Consider nearest-neighbor ASEP on \(\mathbb Z\), with right rate \(p\in(1/2,1]\), left rate \(q=1-p\), \(\gamma=p-q>0\), density \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and a tagged particle initially pinned at the origin.

Let \(X_t\) be the tagged position, \(\eta_t\) the occupation configuration, and \(a_\pm(s)=1-\eta_s(X_s\pm1)\). The last display of Section 3.3 asserts an exponential martingale with logarithm \[\lambda X_t-\int_0^t\left[p(e^\lambda-1)a_+(s)-q(e^{-\lambda}-1)a_-(s)\right]ds.\] The printed compensator subtracts the left-jump contribution.

Consider nearest-neighbor ASEP on \(\mathbb Z\), with right rate \(p\in(1/2,1]\), left rate \(q=1-p\), \(\gamma=p-q>0\), density \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and a tagged particle initially pinned at the origin.

Equation (1.3) asserts a decomposition \(X_t=\operatorname{Poi}_t+\chi_t\), where \(\operatorname{Poi}\) is a Poisson process and \(\chi\) is stationary. The paper fixes \(X_0=0\); under the ordinary zero-start convention for the Poisson process, the representation is asserted without an additional random initial offset. The claimed ASEP domain includes \(q>0\).

Consider nearest-neighbor ASEP on \(\mathbb Z\), with right rate \(p\in(1/2,1]\), left rate \(q=1-p\), \(\gamma=p-q>0\), density \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and a tagged particle initially pinned at the origin.

For the nice density profiles in its introductory path large-deviation discussion, the paper prints \[\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log\mathbb P(B_\delta)=K(\rho_0)+I_{\rm JV}(\rho).\] Here \(B_\delta\) is the profile-neighborhood event, \(K\) the nonnegative initial entropy cost, and \(I_{\rm JV}\) the nonnegative dynamical cost. The displayed equality uses the positive sum of costs.

In Section 7.3, the zero-range state space is compactified by allowing each coordinate \(\zeta(k)\) to take the value \(\infty\). For every invariant probability measure \(\mu\) on that space, the argument applies stationarity directly to the coordinate function and asserts \[0=\mathbb E_\mu L_{\rm ZR}\zeta(k).\] The assertion is made without a stated finiteness or generator-domain restriction on that coordinate test.

The real or complex metric vector bundle has finite rank, and the connections are smooth and compatible with the bundle metric. A connection has an arbitrary probability law \(P\). For a real pair of smooth test sections \(s_1,s_2\), the covariance integral printed in Theorem 6.8 is \[\widetilde C_\nabla(s_1,s_2)=\int_0^\infty\int_{M^2}\mathbb E^m_{t,x,y}\!\left[\left\langle s_1(x),\operatorname{Hol}^\nabla_{t,0}(W)s_2(y)\right\rangle\right]dx\,dy\,dt.\] The symbol \(\mathbb E^m_{t,x,y}\) is a normalized Brownian-bridge expectation with mass/killing weight. The real and complex moment identities both use covariance factors without an additional transition-density factor \(p_t(x,y)\).

In Theorem 7.1, let \(M\) be the compact smooth two-dimensional Riemannian manifold of the paper, let \((E,h_E,\nabla)\) be a smooth real or complex metric bundle of finite rank with a compatible connection, and let \(f,m\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\), \(m\geq0\). Assume either that \(\partial M\ne\varnothing\) or that \(m\) is not identically zero. The conformal comparison changes \((g,m)\) to \((e^{2f}g,e^{-2f}m)\). For a loop \(\ell\), let \(T_\ell\) be its original duration and \(\widehat T_\ell=\int_0^{T_\ell}e^{2f(\ell_s)}\,ds\) the duration after time change; set \(C_f=\|e^{-2f}\|_\infty\).

For \(\delta>0\), the proof defines \(X_\delta\) as the product of normalized holonomy traces over the additional loops satisfying \(T_\ell\leq\delta\) and \(\widehat T_\ell>\delta/C_f\). Write \(U(W)=\operatorname{Hol}^\nabla(W)\), let \(p_t(x,x)\) be the diagonal heat kernel, and let \(\mathbb E^m_{t,x,x}\) denote the Brownian-bridge expectation with its mass weight. In the loop-soup normalization of the proof, its displayed first-moment estimate is \[0\leq-\log\mathbb E X_\delta=\int_0^\delta\!\int_M\frac{p_t(x,x)}{t}\,\mathbb E^m_{t,x,x}\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{\widehat T_W>\delta/C_f\}}(1-\operatorname{tr}U(W))\right]dx\,dt\] \[\leq\frac12\int_0^\delta\!\int_M\frac{p_t(x,x)}{t}\,\mathbb E^m_{t,x,x}\!\left[|1-\operatorname{tr}U(W)|^2\right]dx\,dt.\] The assertion under examination is this integrated cutoff inequality for the scalar normalized trace in arbitrary rank; the subsequent argument uses it to obtain an \(O(\delta)\) first-moment bound.

In the spatial white-noise specialization, \(d=\alpha=1\), \(\gamma=\delta_0\), and \(\mu(d\xi)=d\xi/(2\pi)\). With the energy normalization in (1.11), \[\mathcal M=\sup_{\substack{g\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R),\ g\ \mathrm{real}\\\int g^2=1}}\left\{\left(\int g^4\right)^{1/2}-\int|g^{\prime}|^2\right\}.\] The source asserts \(\mathcal M=\tfrac14(\tfrac32)^{1/3}\).

The general asymptotic coefficient in Theorem 1.2 is \[C_\alpha=\frac{3-\alpha}{2}\left(\frac{2\mathcal M^{1/2}}{4-\alpha}\right)^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}.\] For the hyperbolic Anderson equation \(\partial_t^2u=\Delta u+\dot W(x)u\) with \(u(0,x)=1\), \(\partial_tu(0,x)=0\), Corollary 1.4 prints the coefficient \(C_{\rm cor}=\tfrac12(3/4)^{1/4}\) in both its long-time fixed-integer-moment and fixed-time high-absolute-moment asymptotics.

Let \(p,n\) be positive integers and \(0<\alpha<2\) in the source's covariance-scaling domain, including \(d=\alpha=1\) white noise. For arbitrary \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p>0\), put \[\beta=\frac{2-\alpha}{2}>0,\qquad\theta_j=\frac{\lambda_j^{-2}}{\sum_k\lambda_k^{-2}}.\] In the proof of Lemma 5.1(1), the function \[H(x,y)=\prod_{j=1}^p\left(\frac{x_j+y_j}{x_j}\right)^{x_j}\left(\frac{x_j+y_j}{y_j}\right)^{y_j}\theta_j^{x_j+y_j}\] is maximized over strictly positive \(x_j,y_j\) satisfying \(\sum_jx_j=n\) and \(\sum_jy_j=\beta n\). The source asserts that a maximum occurs at \(x_j=\theta_jn\), \(y_j=\beta\theta_jn\), also for unequal Laplace parameters.
For \(a>0\), \(\mathcal L_T^{2a;H}\) is the variance-one Brownian bridge on \([-T,T]\) from \(H>0\) to \(H\), weighted by \(\exp(-2a\int_{-T}^T X(s)\,ds)\) and conditioned to stay positive.

Fix \(\lambda>1\). Section 6 treats large \(T\), with its high-probability convention applying for all sufficiently large \(T\), and defines \[n_0(T)=\max\{j\in\mathbb N:T^{-15}\leq T\lambda^{-(j-1)/2}\}.\] Lemma 6.8 takes an integer \(k>n_0(T)\), \(a=\lambda^{k-1}\), a positive boundary height \(H\leq2T^2\), and \(0<\delta<1/20\). Set \[\Delta_1=T\lambda^{-k/2},\qquad\Delta_2=T^\delta\lambda^{-(k-n_0(T))/5}.\]

The stated envelope is \[E_T(s)=\begin{cases}H+\Delta_2,&s\in[-T,-T+\Delta_1],\\\Delta_2,&s\in[-T+\Delta_1,T-\Delta_1],\\H+\Delta_2,&s\in[T-\Delta_1,T].\end{cases}\] The lemma asserts \[\mathbb P\bigl(X(s)\leq E_T(s)\ \text{for every }s\in[-T,T]\bigr)\geq1-\exp\!\bigl(-\Theta(\lambda^{k\delta/2})\bigr),\] and explicitly describes the constant hidden in \(\Theta\) as absolute. No numerical lower threshold for \(T\) is specified. The printed endpoint strips overlap the central interval at their joins; the finding concerns points strictly inside the central interval and retains the original width \(\Delta_1\).

For the stationary Ferrari–Spohn diffusion law \(\mu^{a,\mathrm{FS}}\) at area strength \(a>0\), Lemma 2.6(5), equation (2.3), asserts constants \(C,c>0\), independent of all \(T\ge1\), \(t>0\), and \(a>0\), such that \[\mathbb P\left(\max_{s\in[-T,T]}X_a(s)>t\right)\le CTa^{2/3}\exp(-c\sqrt a\,t^{3/2}),\qquad X_a\sim\mu^{a,\mathrm{FS}}.\] The same lemma defines the scaling relative to strength two by \[X_a(s)\stackrel{\rm law}= (a/2)^{-1/3}X((a/2)^{2/3}s),\qquad X\sim\mu^{2,\mathrm{FS}}.\]
